Cuphead is a great game that pays a homage to the 30's era of cartoons.  And it does that aspect really well, the art is on point consistently throughout the game and the amazing soundtrack only makes it better.  One of the best looking games I've seen, honestly.
However, the gameplay itself can be a bit iffy for some.  It's very unforgiving and can be seen as unfair in many situations.  Thankfully, that's the exact type of game I'm looking for, but others may not see it the same way.  A lot of attacks can come out of nowhere and land hits that you aren't expecting, which can be devastating with your low HP, and may feel unavoidable without prior knowledge.  And this definitely is an issue, the game suffers under similar issues with games like "I Wanna Be The Guy" where some progress is behind trial and error rather than "skill."  The parry mechanic will also take some getting used to and may also feel frustrating at times until you adjust.  All in all, it's a pretty difficult game - although sometimes for the wrong reasons - and it should be treated as such.  Know what you're getting into before buyig it as it can come as a shock if it's not the type of game you're really into.
Despite all of that, this is very much a game I enjoyed and only wish that there was more of it to enjoy.

Thoughts after ~8h of play:
The Long Journey Home is a good game. It features exploration, discoveries, suprises (good and bad). While the tutorial does a decent job of teaching you the basics, a LOT of thing - including game mechanics - are for you to discover (for the better or worse). I caught myself a couple of times going "what? no, right, of course, that IS common sense" - (as an example that should not give too much away: people kinda dislike it when you start digging for their stuff in their back-yard)
Please do not believe that under the lighthearted writing and the well-looking graphics that TLJH is a simple or casual game. While the "Storyline" Difficulty mode is told to reduce the difficulty by quite a bit, this game is not something you can learn, master and beat in half an hour. Expect to fail. A lot.
All that said, it still has a few rough edges, where gameplay could be a bit more polished (e.g. could please someone tell the autopilot that breakneck downward velocity is not the optimal initial appoach for landing on a high-G world?) But overall the The Long Journey Home is a good game, worth its price.

If you're familiar with Japan and UndeadZ, nothing is really changing: the pieces are floating in the water, the more you advance, the more puzzles with a big number of pieces you'll find and the forms are different. There is a new mechanism for getting some bonus: you have to catch crabs.
Also, you have a bonus level on the TV interface, which is nice.
Anyway, I've enjoyed this game less than the other three (I'm counting Anime in it as I've played at the time of the writing). I suppose it's due to the fact that it's real pictures and not drawing or with effects like in Japan. However, you wanted birds, you have all kinds of them.
If you like jigsaw puzzles, go for it.

Time for a long review for this game :D
This is a really good game, it's really difficult, I thought that I was going to beat this game in under 2 hours and then just go bug hunting or something, Not the case, I've even tried the easiest difficulty it's still pretty hard, Getting to the first "Nebula" is insanely easy, then it's just get harder then on, you encounter raiders, it's ridiciolus and I haven't found any "Good Parts in the first 3 nebula's, but that could also be because I'm creating random seeds, but one thing I've noticed that is annonying is that your lander constantly slides on any convection, and for the low grav light planets it's almost impossible to mine and you just have to keep wasting fuel until randomly the wind changes direction or just stops completely for enough time to mine the minerals.
And the Gas planets, never go to those unless you have a damn deathwish, seriously they are a pain to do collect the resources it isn't even worth it, and the majority of them all have Searing or higher, High Grav or higher (Which makes some sense) and High Convection, and then the gas you need to harvest doesn't even follow that convection, Sadly I can't seem to find a guide any where, so currently I'm trying to find any way to make it easier to get the gas.
The races are pretty neat, though I find my self on the default seeds that it generates for you the majority of them just give you a slave question from the Ilitza, and the only way I found to be allies with them is to defeat them, but their so called honor is like the worst, They retreat just like every other race when you are beating them, and the only way to beat them is by grabbing the Endurance, then your stuck in like a 5 minute battle where the only thing you get is "Friendship"
Ok now to what makes this game unique and fun.
The game has a really werid story, but knowing some people you might not have gotten it for the story, which is good because the game is kind of like KSP meets Elite Dangerous and then somehow becomes a top down game, and this is probably my 3rd favorite Side/Top-down game, but certainly deserves a straight 3rd place in my space games I have played, next to KSP and ED.
The game only has 3 Motherships, 3 landers, but certainly a lot of crew to choose, it's just I feel like they either need more ships, or you should be able to buy ships from other Races, there is upgrades, but I still haven't found any "Good" upgrades, well I shouldn't say that because your starter shield is garbage but, I just feel that it isn't really worth the Credits you have to spend to get them.
Another possible bug IDK, but if you lose the ablility to trade with a merchant, you can no longer talk to that person it could just be me not waiting long enough but I feel that a week in game is enough.
The game is really fun, but a personal note to the devs, it's too hard, I think even players that are really conservative, and friendly might have a difficult time with the game, the reason is because of your trading system, though that is my opinion, the trading system is a little wack and could really use a nice fix, maybe add a few more upgrades, and make the current ones cheaper, and fix the mining, it outputs too little, and it's a little broken how your like 3 ton Lander just slides with 5 mile per hour winds.

This is the third Pixel Puzzles game that I own and it's one of the best of the series, along with Undeadz. The rotation mechanic is great and I hope to find it in future Pixel Puzzles games.
Pros
+ Rotation of puzzle pieces! = higher difficulty
+ 25 puzzles (significantly more than Japan/ Undeadz), longer gameplay ~16h total
+ Fun tile edges e.g. bird beaks (as in Undeadz)
+ Ingame bonuses: sorting tray, shuffling pieces +/- collect crabs for your hints
+ Menu small bonus: minigame, art gallery, instructions
+ You can access easily puzzles with a lot of pieces and return later to smaller ones (unlike in Japan/Undeadz)
Cons
- birds birds birds photography, no sketches, paintings etc (unlike Undeadz)
- annoying detailed texture background for the puzzle (cliffs with water) - somtimes too similar to the puzzle pieces
- ads in main menu for other games
Great game so far, very promising with lots of new features planned! Definitely worth the price!

Outlast is full of frights and creates an eerie atmosphere that I wanted to like, but unfortunately the game is unmemorable and too linear. The game features decent graphics and fantastic sound and music effects that do not adequately conceal its shortcomings. The linearity leads Outlast to unfold like a movie or novel, in that there is a structured progression throughout and you have little choice of where to go. This is contrary to an interactive game and this limitation hindered me from enjoying this title. There is no randomness and unfortunately everyone’s play through will be the same and there is no replay value.
The gameplay is overlaid with a superficial sense of exploration as you have freedom to walk around the game’s set path and look through an occasional room. There is not much to do in these rooms though as you do not open drawers, look through boxes desks or anything to actually conduct your investigation. Everything you find is conveniently lying out in the open with glowing blue outlines. The items that you find are limited to files and the lowest grade batteries imaginable.
The encounters do little to improve this disappointment. Adversaries have set movement patterns that you must watch and wait through. Outlast is like a very limited Splinter Cell in the dark. In game conflict can only be resolved by hiding and running. That is not my style; I would like an option to fight, even if it needs to be especially difficult. These are deranged patients you are faced with and not supernatural beings that cannot be overcome. A game needs options to cater to different playstyles. Running, hiding, waiting and repeating gets old and did not keep my interest to even see this one through to completion.

It instills a sense of contentment that even its inspiration really never managed. And it is the kind of game where, there are no great screenshots you can really choose to represent the game  because every great screenshot you could take is something players should experience themselves.
The game is based heavily off Super Mario 64, but more specifically Super Mario Sunshine. The way the game it presents itself has a lots of roots in the gameplay themes Super Mario 64 started, but it feels significantly more inspired by Super Mario Sunshine in particular. The protagonist has the classic lean-in whenever they turn, along with the same leaping slide and laying sprawled out while sliding; all very reminisicent of the animations Mario had. The game has multiple gameplay and or theme concepts which are quite similar to Super Mario 64, Super Mario Sunshine and other games from the Mushroom Kingdom.
However the difficulty is not nearly as mind flaying as it could be in older Mario games, and the platforming is forgiving yet still stimulating to control. The game presenting a variety of different features which while not being overly complex or unique still give the gameplay a satisfying level of diversity. The maps are filled with meaningful collectibles used to either unlock cosmetics or new hats, presenting various platforming or soft puzzles to get to them. It is very satisfying to explore and just wander around in for the sake of it.
The world itself is the strongest point, a silly cartoon dream of a place which is just dripping with sly humor that players can just stumble into while exploring the world map. It all feels just so simply enjoyable to be a part of. The music is wonderful and builds so much onto the atmosphere, and the boss fights are creative and fun.
The game goes beyond the open world with multiple objectives and scenarios theme however. There are all kinds of different unique levels and gameplay concepts implemented into them, almost none of the main levels in the game are just platforming; there is almost always a catch to it. The creativity never really goes dry, much like the games humor.
The game does show some signs of being a small developer title, some of the animations and such having a very unpolished look to them. Rough edges like this being visible in random places throughout the game but it is never really impairing in any way, it just serves as a reminder that this was not a full production game. Which is better anyways since if it was it would not be remotely as good.
The default camera can be overly sensitive at times, zooming in when the player gets too close to certain things in the environment which can make looking around for secrets tedious rarely. The presentation of various platforming obstacles players need to unlock the ability to use is also quite odd. Players can find them at the very start of the game and it just feels very crowding to be shown so many things you cannot do, so early in the game and with no explanation. Sometimes when the protagonist climbs up something and reaches the top they will vault up and ontop of it, but if the object is too narrow the protagonist will randomly vault too far and fall off. There is one level where players are expected to platform around for long periods, but at certain points the game freezes the player and shows them something changing in the map. Then it unfreezes the player and changes their camera to face that thing, so if the player is in the middle of something this will potentially screw them over and make them mess up the platforming. Which is extremely frustrating when there is an achievement for never failing the platforming in this level. The game has no autosave or manual save features for when players are just running around the open worlds, so if you spend any amount of time collecting everything in the open world maps; then your power goes out or the game crashes or anything, you lose all your progress. The only way to save to ensure this does not happen is to return to the hub, which makes the game autosave, but also wastes time and takes you away from wherever you were in the map. Certain dialogue in the game is not voice acted, even though almost all of it is. The Snatcher has the same dialogue for two different instances where you trigger his traps. The point based competition in one of the worlds is extremely biased against one of the sides. I put casual effort into one side, and repeated the levels until I got them almost flawlessly on the other side, yet the first side still won by a significant amount. The graphic for the grappling hook is not actually visible, the hook and umbrella do not appear it's just a chain that connects to things, and the trigger for status based hats is really over sensitive with the controller. You have to quickly flick in the trigger button to activate the hat, if you leave the trigger pushed in even for a fraction of a second it will turn off the hat effect when you release it again. Yet if you hold the trigger for an actual duration of time, then release it it will not cancel the hat effect. It exclusively only cancels it for no reason if you release the trigger soon after having pushed it initially; but not if you quickly flicked the trigger.
It would also be nice if there were more uses for the basic and yarn currencies, as there are way more ways to get them then there are to spend. Which feels very unsatisfying in the late game if you accumulated a lot of them.
The single significant problem with the game is the Alpine Skyline. It is an open world platforming collectathon. There is no humor, no story, no creative design, no missions, it is just an open map with various platform intensive sections where players acquire the most important items needed from the world. None of the things that make this an amazing game are in the map, it is just padding basically. It is really boring and empty compared to the rest of the game, and only serves to highlight how far beyond other platformers this one is; because Alpine Skylines is basically a regular platformer that somehow snuck into this game.
A really wonderful platformer, certainly the best one I have played. Would wish there will be a sequel but it is hard to imagine this being topped by anything.

Bioshock I don't even know where to begin the good, the bad, the scary, the funny the impressiveness, the uninspiring.  This game has to be one of the best story’s I have ever played.  I went in not liking the game not wanting to play the game.  And even though it did take me about a month or two of casual gaming to achieve the ending because I did not want to play it.  The game play and story won me over.  This has to be one of the scariest, 80's hack and slash style movie, rolled into a first person shooter.  Now if you have read my other reviews you know I'm not a huge fan FPS's (first person shooters).  I do like to play video games so I play them and above all else I love video games with a fantastic story and this has one.  Bioshock is like the Twilight Zone meets Alfred Hitchcock and they had a baby.  Now I think it took me so long to get into the game because it starts off slow and you are leveling your character getting new ability’s, weapons, and getting the crap scared out of you by the slicers and the enviroment.  It takes you awhile to start to understand this game its set in the 1950's in an underwater city called Rapture.  If you are going to play it the biggest element to the game are the audio diaries.  They give you an inside look into the minds of the citizens of Rapture and explain how the city has evolved into its current state of commotion.  There are some essential lines in the game and one of the best is at the very begin as you ascend to the majestic city.
This honestly does set the tone for the rest of game.  Now if you are going to play this game beware there are three different endings.  Make up your mind at the begin which way to go kill, save, or do both on the little sisters those three options determine your ending.  The game is 14-20 hours long depending on your play level and style.   Now I can't stress the audio diaries enough they are essential for you to get the whole story out of this phenomenal game.  Just when you think you are like this is it this is the ending nope hold on to your hat.  I think that was a decisive turning occurrence for me to start apprenticing this game and seeing why it has a 96 meta critic score.   Now the downside the game crashed on me a few different times. (Windows 7 user)  So just save often.  The story little slow at first but it picks up.  Wallet has a cap.  Hacking certain machines not set up to well I thought. Bots not the brightest.  Now the last couple I'm nitpicking because honestly this game doesn't have a lot of flaws in my opinion other then being a first person shooter :)  Get it love and play it again and again.

LIMBO is a superlative illustration of a dystopian world. Nightmares turn into reality for a small boy who wakes up in this pitch-black cataclysm. With nothing to tell him where to go or what to do, he wanders forth into the unknown.
From the short introduction into the boy's predicament, the shadows and darkness encroach him in a perfect noir setting. The graphics are simple, but compliment the setting impeccably. The game runs perfectly on any machine, and never leaves a steady frame rate, running at 60 frames per second on higher-performance machines.
Sound effects in LIMBO are stunning. An eerie atmospheric stereo soundtrack sounds so realistic with headphones, it's almost like you are in the game. Water, footsteps and enemies sound mysterious and create a mood that both intrigues and repels, which is a rarity in video game soundtracks.
LIMBO's story is one of mystery. The solemn-looking boy has no words, but at the same time he can convey a meaningful message of despair and sorrow. His agility is quite good, even if his jump is somewhat feeble. The platforming elements of LIMBO are simple, but work wonderfully. Ladders, boats and vines are utilised in obvious but unique ways, and makes gameplay different after every stage. Enemies are not the only threat in LIMBO. Yes, there is a giant spider, but you can die just as much by this than a gap in the floor or vicious spikes protruding out of the ground in hap-hazard directions. Death is everywhere in LIMBO, and the scene painted by Playdead is definitely bone-chilling.
In my opinion, LIMBO is a wonderfully dark portrait of a universe that both frightens and invites. LIMBO is definitely melancholy, but its wonderful mechanics, story, sounds and controls combine to create a game that should be a must-have for anyone who enjoys an unknown adventure. LIMBO's world left me speechless, but at the same time I wouldn't hesitate to dive into its hellish depths again.

This game requires study. It requires the player to appreciate this work as seriously as any monologue in a theatrical production.
This game requires introspection. It requires the player to have a good understanding of themselves as well as a willingness to engage their sense of empathy.
This game isn't about what it says on the tin. Though it lacks enemies, health bars and jumping puzzles, it invites the player to take what it presents and engage with it through interpretation.
This game requires an appreciation of art as a medium with which to communicate ideas. It requires the player to accept that whatever price you pay for this game should not affect your reaction to it.
In my view, this game is a simple experience with the potential for numerous intepretations and discussions. To call this a walking simulator would do it a major disservice. I think a more apt description would be a thinking simulator.

If you are looking for a new experience or maybe you want to be left thinking and perhaps even inspired then you may wish to experience this relatively short but intriguing game.
At only an hour and 45 minute, give or take, there is not much to the game as far as hours to dollar but you may value more then hours played as in you may value your overall experience more, if so then I can recommend the game to you. Otherwise go get any other number of open world games that can provide 100's of hours of gameplay, if you are tired of those or just want something completely different then give The Beginner's Guide a try, it is the cost of a coffee and a donut so though short you could do much worse for your investment.

Wreckfest is.. an ok game. I personally have just picked up an interest for racing games and I remembered this was in my steam library, so what I'm saying is this is the closest I have to any kind of racing game.
So i downloaded the game and I've had a good amount of fun with it so far. The crash physics seem to be pretty good (not sure how they compare to real life), and the racing experiences on maps from the workshop (SHOUTOUT TO THE VERYTRACKS PACK) give a good racing experience.
I do understand that the game isn't meant for a racing game and more a demolition derby kind of game, however this is the closest thing I currently have to a racing game so that's how I personally used it. However you will get a different experience if you play the demolition derby side of the game.
Here's a list of pros and cons:
PROS:
-Fun racing experience
-Good crash physics
-well designed levels
CONS: (partly personal)
-Inactive workshop community
-Inactive dev team
-Practically no updates
-Still no campaign (after 4 years from what I've heard)
-Cars still drive normally even if crushed to a pancake (cars don't take damage easily)
-Hardly any customisation options for vehicles (apart from american 5)
-AI is too easy to beat with good upgrades
-Lots of maps are missing descriptions
-No support for mod creators by the dev team (RIP Nascar addon)
The game is ok for an early access game, however it seems like it'll never ascend that level. It's a good concept, but it's for the most part abandoned. Also, there isn't much else to do than change maps and cars. After you've gotten all the cars, there's no replay value.
In it's current state I can't recommend it. If the devs come back and work on this game more, then I'll probably change the review.

(which is currently the only episode released)
+ The quick time event (QTE) combat scenes although few and far between are done exceptionally well and are a lot of fun even if they are just inputing a few buttons while watching an epic fight go down. - There really wasn't enough action in Episode 1, there's basically a great scene at the very beginning and then there's nothing but talking for about 1-1.5hours...and then you get a great fight scene at the end.

I really enjoyed most aspects of Banished, but found the late game and replay value a little unsatisfying. The art is nice, the sound is decent, gameplay's pretty good, and the interface (while a little overwhelming at first) is well-designed, for the most part. The beginning stages of the game are really neat, presenting some interesting challenges with a variety of solutions.
My only problem with the game is that once you've built a sustainable little village, expansion isn't very interesting. The challenges and solutions are the same as they were in the beginning of the game, but the stakes are lowered, since you have a larger population and (presumably) more stored resources. There's only a very minimal progression of buildings and technology, so you spend the late game doing pretty much the same things you did in the mid- and early parts. The result is that (for me, at least) the more successful your town is, the more bored you are. Likewise, I didn't find that starting a new town was super-fun either; starting my first town was, since I didn't have any idea what problems and solutions would crop up. The second (and third, etc.) time around, though, I already knew what to do. The game isn't really flexible enough to make varying your successful strategy any fun (a counter-example might be Crusader Kings 2 -- also mechanically formulaic, but with an insane amount of replayability).
That said, I do think Banished is worth playing. It's different enough from other city builders I've played that I feel like I got my money's worth.

Ill start this review by saying that Ive played a great deal of WWII games in my time, including franchises such as Medal of Honor, Brothers in Arms, Call of Duty, Day of Defeat, and many other small companies many people probably haven't heard of. After all of this times spent on WWII gaming (as it is a historical interest of mine as well) I had lost a bit of my interest. Red Orchestra, however, reinvigorated my passions by delivering a realistic and unique shooter. Although the single player campaign is fun to play, most gamers will find the most fun in the multiplayer. The game blends class-based skills and teamwork on detailed maps that will bring you as close as you would want to be to the Eastern Front. Sometimes you will experience weapon jams, suppressing fire, fatigue, and non-lethal wounds that you cannot simply walk away from. For example, if you are hit in the leg while sprinting from cover, you will slow down or even stop, simulating something that most franchises cannot. I will end the review with some simple advice: If you are looking for another Call of Duty, don't look here. Play Red Orchestra for the realism and the unique fun that it offers.

I will say this ahead of time, as I feel it might be important. I have a very... interesting relationship with Telltale. It's interesting in the fact that I love them and hate them at the same time.  See, the last game of theirs I finished was the Game of Thrones one. And I hated it with a passion. Don't get me wrong, it was a good game. But every time a new episode released, something always happened to delete my save files. And I had to play through it all. Every. Single. Time. So you can imagine my blissful crying session when I found that Cloud Saving was a thing in Batman. No longer would I be forced to keep my save files on an external hard drive. Now, I shall talk about the game.
This is a ♥♥♥♥ing great game.
No, that was not all I have to say about it. Without offering spoilers... or at least too many, I can say that this will not be a single-villain game. From what I can tell, we may be facing one main antagonist per episode, slowly building up the stories for others as we play through. The game focuses on who you would expect a Batman game to. Alfred. No, that was a lie, although Telltale... Alfred DLC? :D The game focuses on Bruce, which is actually something different from a Batman game. It's not 100% Batman. It's about finding that spot between Bruce being a person, this billionaire who wants to do something for Gotham while at the same time trying to balance it between his nightly activities as what can only be described as a bat fetish. Or you can do what I did in my second playthrough. Make Bruce a complete and utter prick and Batman a "Ha... you looked at me. I WILL BREAK YOU!" kind of guy. You know. As you do. The new engine runs great, at least from my experience with it. I think that there is only one real issue I have with the game... Shift + Q(or E) QTE prompts. Telltale games were the only things keeping my Q key loved, the only thing that it really got used for. And now I have to schedule a time OUTSIDE of a Telltale game to spam the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it, as it was replaced with pressing Shift at the same time. There there, Q..... qqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqqq. Feel better?
Buy the game, you won't regret it.

This game is a fun single-player time-filler when your friends aren't around.  I enjoy the fact that the villagers all have their odd little names, and that they reach adulthood and begin to procreate and labor at age 10.  Although I'd enjoy the ability to have more control over assignment of jobs, the lack of role-play is replaced by that god-like feeling ala Sim City and other such games.
The vague back-story of the villagers having been banished from their former town leaves me guessing, but when you discover their propensity of spending the majority of their free time socializing in the village cemetery or complaining about the lack of firewood, you realize they are likely a bunch of oddball whiners who were always cold in body and heart.
My two biggest complaints would have to be the repetitive music and ambient sounds of wind/water, which tend to drive one insane after some time, leading the player to imagine why the villagers had been banished from the town as I described above; additionally, a difficult winter or bad crop may lead to a food shortage, leading to half the village dying from starvation, and the ensuing lack of workers makes it very difficult to recover.  You have to hope you're able to have a few seasons of fruitful harvests and hunting so you can easily survive a tough winter!
Overall, a fun game that can pass the time for a few minutes or absorb you for an hour or two.  Well-worth the purchase!

This is the fourth Pixel Puzzles game I've played, and the only one so far that I would not recommend.  I love puzzles, both physical and digital, and I finished every puzzle in this game, but there were so many built-in and unnecessary annoyances that I couldn't recommend it to anyone else.
First and most importantly, someone had the idea to make the background patterned.  I'm sure they meant well, but building a patterned puzzle on a patterned backdrop is extremely difficult, especially with the larger puzzles that have smaller pieces.  With some, seeing the edges was nearly impossible, even with changing the color of the patterned backdrop.  Without being able to make out the shape of the edges, adding pieces became a sort of "trial-and-error" of dropping every somewhat-matching piece into the spot and hoping one will fit.  There is, as far as I could see, no way to get a nice solid background to work with, only color-changes of the pattern; this can help but doesn't solve the problem.  To me, this is a game-ruining design flaw.
The hint system isn't awful but it adds another layer of annoyance.  The crabs you have to gather to "spend" on hints spawn directly under your cursor.  If you're trying to work in an area, you have to drop the piece you're working on to move the damned crab out of the way.  If by some chance the crab spawns where you have a few pieces piled up, you have to move every piece before you can grab the crab.  If you have a LOT of pieces piled up (i.e. if you're sorting them), it can take forever to get everything moved so you can get the crab moved.  Not game breaking, but very annoying.
The other problem I had with it was purely aesthetic.  Birds aren't the most interesting thing to me, but I was expecting bright birds with pretty plumage, tropical birds and pea♥♥♥♥♥, things that are pretty and make great puzzles.  Instead, you get a lot of penguins, ducks, and raptors, and very few were bright and engaging.  The end result for me personally was boredom.  By the final, largest puzzle, I was sick of brown birds, brown ducks, and hundreds of penguins.  So I opened the last puzzle to fiinish this game off, and there were more penguins (I shook my head with a sigh and sallied forth anyway).  There was some variety in the pictures, but even the variety was dull.  Now, this is a personal preference so others might not agree here, but it was my personal opinion on it.
So after 20+ hours playing the game and finishing every puzzle for the sake of my own achievement-seeking OCD, I just can't recommend it to anyone else unless the poor background and annoying hint system aren't likely to bother you.

The Long Journey Home is a space exploration game with rogue-like elements and is the first game from developers, Daedalic Studio West.
In the Long Journey Home, you take control of a crew of four people on the maiden journey of a star ship fitted with prototype technology: the faster-than-light jump drive. Your journey is supposed to be to Alpha Centauri, but the first use of the drive damages the ship and sends it careening through interdimensional space to arrive in a debris field surrounding a strange metallic sphere orbiting a planet in a very distant star system from Sol.
Exploring the sphere and then the planets of its star system, and then the surrounding star systems, you quickly discover where you are and that you're not alone; the universe is inhabited with all manner of aliens: friend, foe and otherwise. Can you elicit their help -- or at least avoid their wrath -- for long enough to escape the galaxy and begin your long journey home?
The Long Journey Home's graphics are very well produced and of high quality, but differ immensely in complexity and presentation. There are essentially four distinct graphical modes, which for want of better names I'll call on-board, interplanetary travel, local area, and lander.
The ship's on-board systems are presented in a tab-based format, with text and graphical displays. The interface is smooth and works well with mouse or controller, and in the background of many of the screens you'll sometimes see crew or your occasional passengers lounging around. These little touches are great, bringing life to the ship. There's a communications screen, too, showing video of any aliens you encounter.
Interplanetary travel has your ship represented by an arrow with a small thruster when accelerating. It shows your current solar system as a plane in three dimensions, with a grid shown over the background star field, and a simple curved line representing your current path across the plane. The grid dips based on the gravity wells of the stellar objects in the system, and it works exceptionally well as an aid to piloting your ship.
Local area mode starts when you encounter an alien craft or enter an asteroid belt or other non-planetary object. This shows a zoomed-in top-down view of your craft, with you taking direct control over the forward and side thrusters. Objects are rendered in 3D and are, for the most part, very pretty, though I find most asteroids to look rather more shiny than I'd expect.
Finally, the lander mode is shown when you choose to land on a planet. This shows a brief and very well rendered cut scene of your lander detaching from your ship, and then displays a side-on view of the lander and surface of the planet, Lunar Lander style. The graphics here, too, are exceptional, with different planets having different atmospheres, lighting, surfaces, and other objects. It's just a shame you can't zoom in to get a better view of your lander once you've touched down.
Overall the graphics are truly excellent, and the different modes work well together. There's a handful of detail and performance-related options, allowing you to customise for your PC as required. I played on a GTX1070 and experienced no slowdown with everything set to maximum.
The music is brilliant: some of the best I've heard in a computer game. From dramatic, heart-pounding scores when you're close to death, piloting your lander through the clouds of a gas giant in a last-ditch attempt to gather some fuel, or to the beautiful and emotion-charged uplifting title screen track, I love it all.
Sound effects are good, with nice landing thruster sounds and cool weapon-charging beeps. It's just a shame there are no voices or alien communication sounds.
The Long Journey Home tells a grand story of four people on an epic journey through unexplored space, on a ship that's slowly deteriorating, doing what they can to survive. The game as a whole is quite unlike anything I've seen before, with traditional Newtonian physics for space flight and landing, and rogue-like elements to ensure replayability and variation. Its various components most definitely add up to a game that is more than the sum of its parts.
People have suggested that The Long Journey Home is basically just a graphical update for Lunar Lander. I guess you could look at it that way, but that's a bit like saying that Grand Theft Auto V is just a graphical update for Road Race. Yes, the landing stages play a lot like Lunar Lander, but they make up only one part of the game.
The game begins with you selecting your crew of four out of 10 applicants. You then select your ship, from a choice of three, and lander, also from three. And you specify a random-number generator seed by typing in a short character string. This is a bit of a gimmick, but it's also more than that; you see, it allows you to replay with a seed that you particularly like, or share the seed with others to compare performance. It's a great addition to the genre; I hope we see more procedural generation games allowing manual seed input.
After the introductory piece, the remainder of the game is all about survival. You explore each system, landing on planets to harvest resources in order to proceed to the next system and, eventually, to Sol and the Earth. Interplanetary travel is quite calming, with a good degree of patience required to use gravity wells and orbit efficiently, so as to reduce your fuel burn. Landing can be frustrating, and even after watching the various videos available I feel as though I'm still missing something, as I often seem to take a lot of damage mining or collecting gas, for very little gain. Alien encounters are varied and interesting, and seem to usually offer at least two alternative results.
The odds against your crew succeeding are astronomical (heh), and I'd suggest success will take both luck and skill, especially at the highest difficulty level. The game apparently includes eight main alien races, with each seed only including four of them, leading to many of the quests being different with each game. There are other minor races, too, who appear in every game.
The game does have a few problems, though. Lander sequences seem to be based on attrition, with luck determining whether you'll successfully mine enough components to counter the damage your lander will take from mining. There also seems to be no way to use relative controls for interplanetary travel, though they work fine in lander and local area modes. The in-game information for beginners is quite limited, with a title-screen link taking players to youtube videos for tutorials, and the loading times really are pretty terrible, and far too frequent. Cash is hard to come by, and I also have to wonder why my ship has a top speed of 6 AU/h in interplanetary space, no matter how much I accelerate. Oh, and it does need to be said: the game is rather expensive.

I loved the first game and was excited to try this with some of my friends who weren't able to pick up the original.
The two of us that had played DD1 were immediately offput by the less-intuitive and unexplained changes to loot and mana, as well as the extremely clunky UI and default keybinds, especially as compared to the first game. We also had a sense that some towers were virtually useless, compared to the original in which everything had at least one good purpose.
All four of us were disheartened seeing the price of new characters (10k tokens) compared to token gain (4-5 per map in the beginning, some reading told us 25 is a high amount later on, plus 100-300 for dailies and a few thousand for monthlies).
We were surprised to fail the fifth level, having one of each starter character across the four players. Upgraded walls were dying in half a wave, and our resources were spread thin due to sprawling map design and two spread-out defense points. None of us could discern enemy paths before they were shown to us.
Inventory and gear management were beyond nightmarish. There was no sorting that we could find, so items got lost a lot. Comparisons are fine most of the time, but totems/medallions/orbs/whatever seem to compare to a random equipped one but always replace the one in the first slot. Shards took a while to figure out.
In general nothing is explained except the very obvious basic controls.
From what I've heard a lot of this is due to a recent patch, but in the current state I cannot recommend the game as a game, at least to new players. It may be fine to certain groups of friends who are wanting the challenge or who don't really care much about playing the game in a way that makes sense, I guess.
Overall I would have put DD1 as an 8/10 overall and a 10/10 for its genre. I'd put DD2 as a 6.5/10 for the genre and a 3.5/10 overall.

Axis Football 2016 is the second edition in Axis Games’ professional football sports simulation franchise.
As an Australian who considers themselves to be an armchair football fan, I tend to anticipate every quality American football game that hits PC. Unfortunately, this has been an all too rare occurrence. There are very few viable options when it comes to football games that allow you to actually play the game. Gamers do have a few other options when it comes to actual sports management games. Sadly, EA has spat in the face of PC gamers by not publishing Madden on PC since 2008. This is naturally something that I am quite bitter about even though I realize Madden is as guilty of the ‘annual roster update’ issue.
Let’s get the potential deal breaker out of the way immediately. Because Madden controls the licenses for the NFL and they would cost much more than a small indie developer could afford Axis Football lacks official licenses. What this obviously means is that the team names, uniforms, etc. are not in the game. More significantly, it means that there are no official NFL players featured within the game. However, I believe that the developers have done a very reasonable job in attempting to replicate the real deal so far as teams and players are concerned. For example, one of my favorite NFL teams is the Seattle Seahawks. The Seattle team is called the ‘Seattle Warhawks’ in the team. Furthermore, although the Warhawks players are not given the same names as the real Seahawks players their attributes are a reasonable match to what last season’s Seahawks team was.
Although the game lacks officially licensed rosters there are community mods. That means although the game may lack official licenses that there are people within the game’s community who have dedicated themselves to creating a realistic experience. By this, I mean that there is an ‘NFL Experience 2016’ mod. This has been painstakingly created by ‘thesackmaster’ and several other community members. There is also a NCAA mod. You will find these two mods and others in the official ‘Axis Football Mods’ forum. There are other mods including create your own league starter kids, broadcast graphics, and stadium graphics downloads.
The community is one of the game’s strongest points.
Being Australian gridiron is not a native sport. Therefore, I find the game to be very complex. Consequently, anything beyond position names and basic functions has been beyond me. There are many so many technicalities within each play that trying to understand everything is difficult. I have often found myself taking an automatic option or coach’s pick in football games. However, I do not believe that this function is within the game. This may be perceived as a negative but I’ve personally found it to be a major advantage. By playing the game I am naturally increasing my understanding of formations and of the technical aspects that go into each player’s role within each given play. Therefore, I believe that the game deserves recognition as an easy and enjoyable way to learn American football.
Arguably the greatest negative that I have encountered thus far is that the game is arguably too easy. In my second game, I ran the score up into the 70’s while my computer opponent put out a single touchdown. I am finding that this repeats itself and that the only scores the computer often makes are the fluke-like plays that are unstoppable. I’m finding that this may soon turn into a game where I target specific achievements to perfect the game and return for my dose of pro football action.
The reason why I am finding it too easy is because the AI does not react – at least noticeably – to the same tactics being employed again and again. In one game I used blitz for every single play. Unless the quarterback dishes off the pass quickly enough I can generally get the sack as no one is there to cover the blitz. On offense, I prefer the long throwing game. I can generally always count on one of my receivers getting open but the occurrence on 1-on-3 (offense-defense) catches is far too common. I’ve thus far found that the likelihood of throwing an interception is far less than my single receiver catching the ball.
However, I must suggest that I am finding the running game to be quite challenging. The majority of my big scores have been performed through the throwing game. I have yet to unlock the 200+ rushing yards in a single game. This may be because I’m not entirely familiar with the nuances required for the running game.
This is where the game is lacking most of all. The graphics are not at all current generation. The features are lacking in contrast to a fully fleshed out feature complete game (e.g. Madden).
If I could have one wishlist item fulfilled on the next entry in the franchise it would be a complete franchise mode. I understand that there are other games on the market (the management simulators) that allow you to do this but it would be a fantastic feature. The current franchise mode is insufficient in this regard and feels as though it has only been implemented to give players an option besides single game quick matches. Although it’s a good thing that there is something else in the game its lack of depth is a little concerning.
The developers have an understanding that the game isn’t where they want it to be. What the game currently is an opportunity for PC gamers to get their football on. They have ideas and plans to implement what they want to. However, they are open to advice, feedback and even criticism (please make it constructive). They are a very hands-on development team and want to make their game the best that it can possibly be. In complete honesty, you have to start somewhere and what they have now is an already highly playable and enjoyable football experience.
It certainly is. There are trading cards and Steam achievements. I would, however, like to see them do away with their mod forum and try and implement Steam Workshop compatibility. This would encourage mod makers to create content for the game. This would increase the activeness of the community which would work wonders for the game.
Axis Football 2016 offers PC gamers the opportunity to play entertaining football games. The developers are willing to work with their community on the continued improvement of the game’s quality. If you’re a fan of American football, then the $20 investment is well and truly worth it.

I loved this game where more than I really thought I would, and I really believe it's because the game is so filled with it's own character and playful atmosphere you can't hate it. It's a game that I can relate to Super Mario Sunshine through experience, but I feels more like this is what playing Banjo and Kazooie back in the day would have felt like from how people talk about it.
Pros:
- The levels are fairly vast and fun to explore! This is where it feels like Sunshine because you have the ability to run and bounce around the levels fluidly, and there are rewards to being adventurous evrywhere you go. Each is also nothing like the last, and brings its own charm to the table every time.
-  The main character is absolutely adorable.
- The game never feels tense or stressful. Some may argue this can be a negative/lack of challenge, but I found it allowed me to focus more on the art, jokes, characters, and game itself. It was so casual that I don't remember the last time I had this much fun just wandering around and finding all the little things the designers added in for those who looked to find.
- I've read some comments about the game being too short, and I think that's a load of crap. This game maintains the right amount of content to be short but sweet, and should give you a sense of your money's worth at the very least. 10 hours game time is more than reasonable for a $30 game if it takes you only 3 hours to make $30.
- The game has a slot machine element that allows you to earn different looking hats for each power, different colour layouts for your outfit, and music remixes of the game's soundtrack. I thought this was a brilliant way to utilise it because getting a dinosaur hat has never been more rewarding and the customization feels just right. It's not overwhelming but it's incredibly noticable and fulfilling to experiment with.
Negatives:
- The combat isn't very well designed as in they just didn't focus on it as an integral part of the game, which I can agree it isn't. The boss fights play fine but the rest of the enemies are all the same really. You either do a basic swing attack, or jump and attack which auto glides you to them and that's pretty much it.
- There's some false sense of rewards in this particularly designed for the completionist, or at least that's how it feels. You can collect yarn in hard to reach places, but it only takes one yarn of a type to create a new hat, and after that it serves no purpose at this point in time. It seems like it would have been used to craft new customizations for the hats or something but that was left out. They just serve as a number, no real point to them.

I was intrigued as soon as I saw the promo video for Medieval Kingdom Wars and truth be told a little excited.  The game is based in an era that I find brutally fascinating.  Based on the promo video’s alone it comprises a huge amount of potential.
I received this for free for review purposes and this review was written on the same day that the title was released for EA, as such this review will need to be altered, updated and edited as the game releases patches, updates and ultimately content.
First Patch Update Review : (Massive Stability Improvements)
See my First Look Review Here: (Stability and FPS Issues)
What is this Game?
==============
MKW (Medieval Kingdom Wars) is a Historically Accurate Simulated RTS with elements of management and survival thrown in.  There are currently 17 resources available and a complex tech-tree system to master.
It is based in the 15th Century at the time of the hundred year’s war and is situated in Medieval Europe.  The map is huge and geographically accurate with great detail being placed upon each of the included cities.
The game currently includes 4 factions, English, Romans, Castile and the French; at the time of writing this only the French were accessible in-game.
Graphics
=======
This game appears to be running in DX9 like Rome: Total War, a little behind the times maybe but despite this it is graphically quite pleasing, at least the environment and buildings are.  The units themselves are somewhat disappointing at this stage of development.
The maps are huge and densely populated in areas whilst farmlands obviously are not.  The camera allows pretty close inspection of the objects strewn all over each map and the general standard is high.
Gameplay
========
Unfortunately this is the biggest concern for me.  It is early access and everything else looks and sounds pretty good but I felt that the battle animations were very poor.  This might well change over time, but as it is today I was a little disappointed to be honest.  The units are halfwits at best, standing still and looking around whilst a mindless battle ensues around them.  There is little 1v1 and instead units tend to enact random swipes with their weapon in the vague direction of the enemy.
The maps and the castle structures are fantastically accurate and immersive but are sadly let down by the military units, of which there appear to be a decent variety.  The Military Units also just traipse over the map without any hindrance or due care and attention in order to navigate what otherwise looks to be a treacherous route to the Palisades.
An example; You see before you a historically accurate twisty path leading up a massive incline to the castle walls, this being a well-known defensive tactic of the Medieval era, except that in MKW it is navigated in a completely straight line without any impeachment on speed or direction.
There are some nice new and unique features implemented too.  For example there is the scavenging of corpses to obtain resources.  Also I believe that climbing up the latrine might well be an option, if not now then perhaps in the future, the premise certainly seems to be there.
The tech tree is reportedly large and complex but as I had performance issues I was unable to really gets my teeth into this aspect of the game.  With the attention to detail already shining through I would expect this to be considerable at the very least.
Performance + Physics
=================
It is EA so crashes and poor optimisation are part and parcel of that; so when I tell you that the game crashed multiple times in an hour and the FPS was all over the place 14-60 that shouldn’t surprise or worry you at this stage, much more development is planned and expected.
The game physics are in need of some more attention too, arrows lodging themselves in mid-air and deceased military personnel in various `copy and paste` states of demise, this IMHO was far better presented in Rome: Total War, but this is still EA and feedback is critical to highlight areas which need the most attention.
AI
===
The AI, according to the developers is actually quite advanced and adds new level of gameplay I have not seen before.  Unfortunately I have yet to get this far into the game and as such cannot fully vouch for it.
What you should be able to experience are things like; dynamic peasants, in the sense that if you’re not meeting their needs they will turn on you, maybe even open the doors to an army whom are besieging your castle.  They might even form gangs and cause troubles in other ways like withholding taxes or destroying property.
The military level of AI is much lower though, frequently standing still during hand to hand combat and they are simply not averse to firing on their own units either, who don’t even move away for long periods of time.
If I had to compare the capacity of the military AI to something I would say it is like Command and Conquer of old.  Build a Massive army and attack a single point of interest, then move onto the next point of interest.
PROs
=====
- Price for a little more than £10 I think is perhaps worth a chance. (My opinion only)
- Progress price increases throughout EA.  I have spoken about this a lot; this is the way it should be done.
- Attention to historical accuracy.
- The maps and environments look great and audio is pleasing (music; not so much)
- Huge playing areas + Multi Player and Co-Op is potentially a big Bonus! (Not managed to test yet)
- The campaign Storyline could also be a very good feature for this title as the art and script directors do seem to have perfectly captured the time and the mind-set for it.
- Environement, sound and design.
- Storyline and ambiance.
CONs
=====
-The camera is not great.  The angle available on the vertical axis is very shallow and does not allow a tactical viewpoint to assist with military progression.
- Equally there is no option in the menu at this time to turn off screen scrolling, so turning the camera frequently makes you shoot across the map.
-The menu is in its infancy and seems a little buggy; an example would be; turning Fog of war off does not actually turn fog of war off.
-Stability, I played for an hour and found that FPS hits and crashes were too frequent at this time; I hope to play again after the first patch.
Overall
======
As this title is just released in EA most issues can be overlooked but it is fair to say that the huge potential has not yet been fully realised.  Much more needs to be done, especially in the area of combat animations and military AI.  It is expected to remain in Early Access for around 10 months, with release in Q1 2018, so I’m not too worried just yet.
There does appear to have been enormous attention to detail applied for most areas of the game but perhaps not necessarily so much where it matters most.  I am a little concerned this might not be fully fleshed out enough to be a fun and enjoyable experience; certainly for me it is not stable enough to fully appreciate the title at this time.
The foundations are set and reasonably solid, let’s hope to see those intricate pieces of the puzzle materialise over the next year.  My fingers are crossed because this is one I want to be Brilliant!

Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

The Long Dark is a brilliant survival game (even at current stage) and one of the most candid examples of how to correctly manage a development of a early access game.
The sense of loneliness, desperation, isolation, and urgency you'll feel during a playthrough (which are ALL important in a wilderness survival experience) is palpable enough to give you an illusion that you ARE actually stranded in northern Canadian outdoors. The Long Dark manages this perfectly even during these earlier stages of the development, and has successfully handled creating a "survival game" that doesn't fall into the category of cookie-cutter so-and-so cliche'd survival toss-off. (That we see too f--king many of these days.)
The devs are dedicated in making this game better and better with each update. The level of feedback communication and dedication towards quality is comparable to those of the devs of "Prison Architect". (Which is another astounding early access experience.)
If you're interested in survival games done right, and wouldn't mind getting along with constantly evolving - thus everchanging - gaming experience, you should have a look into this game. It's really superb.

Banished - Game Review - 7/10
This game, I have put so many hours into. Partly because I'm a perfectionist and I don't like to leave a game without 100% of the achievements finished, but also because this game is a nice city-builder.
My first instinct is to call it "casual". I'm not actually sure if that's accurate or not. I mean, you aren't really playing against anything besides the elements, and basic human survival. The goal of the game is to make a settlement/village/town/city/whatever-you-want-to-call-it. You don't have to worry about being attacked by anything besides tornadoes and fires. It's just you and your people. As long as you make sure they have enough food and supplies, they're good to go.
So in terms of a city-builder, this is a really fun game. Even though you don't have to play "against" anything, and don't have any specific goal besides making a city and keeping your people alive... this game captures enough attention to keep me playing it even when there's only one achievement left to get... that takes FOREVER I might add.
The only thing about this game I can REALLY harp on is the fact that it slows down a ton as your population increases. I assume it's a problem with having to render/calculate every one of the sprites in the game. Figuring out what each and every one of them have to do, because they all have their own lives. I would imagine the more powerful your computer, the better the game would run at higher populations. Now, I have a pretty beefy machine... and my game starts to crap out around 200 population. I've searched for fixes for this kind of thing and unfortunately haven't really come across anything. I'm pretty sure it's just the way the game is made/encoded.
Now, saying that. I do highly recommend this game. I have found it very interesting to learn how to take care of my people. If you're into tackling achievements, then that's what really makes this game worth it's money is the time you have to take to figure out how to get those elusive achievements.
I'm going to give this game 7/10 for a city-builder. I haven't played many of them, but this one caught my eye. It could be better, but it's not bad at all.
~ Kyle

In general I feel like if this game catches your interest, pick it up, especially on sale, and it might just surprise you.

TLJH looks nice and plays alright for the most part, but I can't recommend it because core elements of the game are completely at odds with each other, draining away all the fun.  The most central thing to understand is you cannot save your game.  This is a roguelike entirely in the FTL mold, where you have one current game you can continue, or you can start new each time.   However, instead of FTL's fast-paced combat, you have dialog and quests with aliens, exploration, and piloting the ship and lander.  The frustrating thing is it kind of sounds cool, and really wasn't all bad.  But the game play is very methodical and slow paced, and every time you want to try something new or explore something you're basically throwing away all the time you've spent on that game because doing things you don't already understand will almost always end your run in one way or another.  This is my biggest problem with the game, as the optimal way to 'win' (get home), is to bypass as much of the content as possible to reduce the chances of bad things happening.  FTL did not have this problem because how they designed the end game and the progression of your ship rewarded you for acquiring as many resources as you could along the way.
In TLJH, every jump to a system damages you and includes an RNG roll to damage (or if already damaged, destroy) a ship system.  This random device damage is always annoying and can be crippling, such as reducing your only armament to 20% effectiveness, and there is no way to stop it.  The ability to repair damage devices, compared to how often it happens, seems absurdly rare and subject to annoying limitations.  It is entirely possible for your weapons or shields to become damaged and then irretrievably destroyed by RNG events as you move between stations that can actually repair devices.  The same applies to lander devices every time you launch it - be prepared for that nice new grav plating you bought to get damaged and lose half its effectiveness the first time you use the lander after installing it.
For anyone looking at this game and thinking about the classic Star Control 2, I would say be prepared for massive disappointment.  The similarities are all superficial, and TLJH is completely missing some of the critical design elements that made SC2 work.  Ship to ship combat in TLJH is like using the stock precursor ship for all your battles, albeit with prettier backgrounds.

The music, graphics, and combat mechanics are really great in Sunless Sea and I think that's enough for me to recommend it, but I have two major problems with the game.
First, probably through design convenience, everything is treated as an item in the game. For example, instead of having a storytelling skill that gets better that you make a storytelling check with, you literally get a "tale of terror" item which you can sell or trade to somebody else. It just bugs me that the game treats a story, which you should be able to retell just like a barrel of fuel or a crate to be traded. It's the same with memories. I obtain a memory item from my time at shore. OK - makes sense. But then I sell my memory for money and lose it???
Second, I have a more material criticism. The game is a story driven roguelike, which sounded great to me, but it's maybe too story driven. The really great story with pages and pages of writing and the fact that you die and start over once an hour work against each other. Just think, you have to click through extra dialogues to get your items and reports, but once you are on your 10th try you just really wish they would just give you the report already. Ideally, the game would have been designed to skip the story that you've already read (with the option to reset the storytelling for some ports), but at this point I think that option would be too expensive and time consuming to implement. I have clicked through the 3 sisters story like 6 times now, and I decided I better post a thumbs up review before it really starts to♥♥♥♥♥♥me off.

My complaint is not that the game is hard, because, really it is not that hard, but that playing the mechanisms that present a challenge is not fun. Landing is essentially Lunar Lander, circa 1981. Planet allocation feels like an oil mining game that came on 3.5" floppy discs, because what you can get has less to do with skill than whether the planet is an inferno, and that is basically a roll of dice you never see and cannot change. If I go to a planet, I might gain metal, but lose so much fuel that I cannot go anywhere that does not get me rocket fuel. Which I don't want to mine, even if it is there, because flying through clouds or ungodly winds is not fun, nor is mining fuel interesting, but because it will cause so much damage to my ship that I will have to land somewhere else in system to Lunar Lander a trivial amount of metal just to try to mine for more fuel. And that never counts the third resource that allows me to jump between systems.
Pluses as they are. The aliens have intersting dialogue that reminds me of Starflight or Star Control 2, but I don't feel that gives it playability, becuase even in those games, the aliens were out to screw the player. Having brutal aliens who offer less advantage than the tiring planets, and are only a flipped card more entertaining, goes about...4 hours into keeping me playing.
I want to fly a spaceship home. I want to land on planets and gains resources. I want a game to navigate those in 12 hours, instead of having a dozen losses that take four hours each. For 50 hours, I better need to wash my pants, and not because I got bored and went to bed 4 times.

The game features quick matchups against the AI or in coaching mode (where only plays are called); games can be customized according to weather conditions and quarter length. A simple franchise mode consists of twelve games against randomized opponents (that can repeat with no rhyme or reason). Mod support is strong, with easily editable rosters, uniforms, and logos. An improved user interface makes calling plays look and perform better. Updated graphics and improved (though still repetitive) commentary are also new this year. There are only eight plays for each formation (a slight improvement over last year’s six), but hot routes make for more flexible options. Mouse-based passing remains engaging, where a portion of the field is aimed at instead of a specific player. Kicking controls are improved and appropriately difficult. Axis Football 2016 lacks a play clock (time runs down a specific amount between plays) and does not have player fatigue, eliminating substitutions during a game. The simulation is much better this year, resulting in more plausible results. In short, Axis Football 2016 is a vast improvement over last year’s iteration.

[Disclaimer] I used to have a non-steam copy that i finished the game on. Hence my low steam playtime.
As a general rule, you can always find a problem with a game. There will always be that one little thing that breaks immersion, flow or isn't fun.
This game is the exception to that rule. Everything about it is perfect. Clever puzzles with an astoundingly well-designed progression in artistic theme and difficulty, also helped by the fact that there's no flow-breaking loading screens at any time. A subtle, but deeply highly interesting story is effortlessly conveyed through gameplay organically.
Puzzles were generally not hard, but they were just hard enough that you sometimes had to stop and think. It felt like it hit a sweet spot where you got just enough challenge that you were engaged, but never slowed down.
Artistically, this is the only game i've ever played where i can't even find something to nitpick. The attention to detail is astounding, and while the scope of the game is small - admittedly, it triumphs in every field it dips its toes in.
ONLY complaint is that it's not very replayable, but i don't think it's fair to punish a puzzle game for that since that's an inherent flaw of the genre.
Verdict: 10/10

Five Nights at Freddy's has a different take on most horror games. The staying still point and click method is quite an interesting choice for the game, which I approve.

It took me about two hours to complete night 1-6, I have not tried the custom night in which you set the animatronics AI level. (The custom night is definitely a plus, your goal may even be to beat 20/20/20/20 mode, even if it seems impossible.)
Over all I'd say this games worth a shot, unless you don't like games that rely on jump scares to create the "terrifying" atmosphere.
TL;DR: I hope you're ready for Freddy.

The name itself says a lot about the game. There is a definition of the word "limbo" that refers to a state of being between life and death. And as such, this game is like an adventure through the unknown world between worlds.
It's really a great game. I especially loved its style, which was simplistic yet horrifying. The minimalistic sounds were also used effectively, as the noises are well placed and really make you jump if you're not paying attention. The map and layout of the game itself is genius, as it's one, big continous map that gives you a great sense of discovery, which was cool. Levels were well thought out and interesting, there were a couple at the end that I  struggled with (of course after solving them I then realized how easy they actually were), and they were all very cleverly created. Not once did I find myself bored while playing this, and, if I had the time, I probably would have sat down and played through the whole thing all at once. It's mysterious atmosphere and somewhat ambiguous plot leaves you wondering about state of the young boy, and that grey area between life and death. With it's mild horror and clever puzzles, the game sucessfully draws the gamer in. I definitely reccomend it.

Banished - Game Review - 7/10
This game, I have put so many hours into. Partly because I'm a perfectionist and I don't like to leave a game without 100% of the achievements finished, but also because this game is a nice city-builder.
My first instinct is to call it "casual". I'm not actually sure if that's accurate or not. I mean, you aren't really playing against anything besides the elements, and basic human survival. The goal of the game is to make a settlement/village/town/city/whatever-you-want-to-call-it. You don't have to worry about being attacked by anything besides tornadoes and fires. It's just you and your people. As long as you make sure they have enough food and supplies, they're good to go.
So in terms of a city-builder, this is a really fun game. Even though you don't have to play "against" anything, and don't have any specific goal besides making a city and keeping your people alive... this game captures enough attention to keep me playing it even when there's only one achievement left to get... that takes FOREVER I might add.
The only thing about this game I can REALLY harp on is the fact that it slows down a ton as your population increases. I assume it's a problem with having to render/calculate every one of the sprites in the game. Figuring out what each and every one of them have to do, because they all have their own lives. I would imagine the more powerful your computer, the better the game would run at higher populations. Now, I have a pretty beefy machine... and my game starts to crap out around 200 population. I've searched for fixes for this kind of thing and unfortunately haven't really come across anything. I'm pretty sure it's just the way the game is made/encoded.
Now, saying that. I do highly recommend this game. I have found it very interesting to learn how to take care of my people. If you're into tackling achievements, then that's what really makes this game worth it's money is the time you have to take to figure out how to get those elusive achievements.
I'm going to give this game 7/10 for a city-builder. I haven't played many of them, but this one caught my eye. It could be better, but it's not bad at all.
~ Kyle

So, you're interested in Blood Bowl. Let's start with the basics. I think a lot of reviews tread the same (not necessarily correct) ground. So, I thought I'd make my own.
Blood Bowl is set in an alternate universe of Warhammer Fantasy, where instead of war all conflicts are solved through the titular sport Blood Bowl. In Blood Bowl you play as a coach guiding your teams through games. It plays like the unholy cross between turn based strategy and American football. It also has elements of persistence between games, you can build up you're bench, and/or, have your player get injured or skilled up.
Onto the main question, why should I play Blood Bowl? It's truely a unique experience (and I don't use that lightly.) This is for two main reasons. First, the experience of training, playing with, and occasionally rebuilding your team is wildly different between races and even individual teams. This team might have a previously useless fodder of a zombie score a touchdown, get strength on a level up, and then become a star of your team. The next team's ogre could die to a foul the second game of the season and you could save and play well to make your team the favorite for the next season.
If you've read other reviews you've probably heard some combination of three things: 1. "It's just luck." In Blood Bowl every action can fail. Usualy the closest thing to a guarantee you get is a 1/36. This can lead to similar experience to a competitive card game, trying to minimize risk and maximize reward. However due to the fact you have 11+ actions a turn, and most actions have a (very) small chance of permanently killing a player. This leads to a lot of people getting very salty, so if you have a propensity towards getting tilted, this may not be the game for you.
2. "Claw/Mighty Blow/Pilling On is broken." The review section isn't really the place for balance complaints, unless it's totally game breaking. None of these are more prevalent than block or dodge. What people have an issue with is not the balance, but the fact that they help bashy teams get more injuries. It's easy to be tilted at claw when it gets you're star Dwarf killed by a Skaven.
3. "Just get Blood Bowl Chaos Edition." This has a lot of validity. Let's look at pros and cons. Chaos Edition has more teams, and is less expensive. Because of this, I would recomend Chaos Edition if you are already familiar with Blood Bowl. However, Blood Bowl 2 has infinitly better and more useful U.I. If you want to learn the game, then you're are gonna have a lot easier time with Blood Bowl 2, than Chaos Edition, or even the physical game. In addition the team gap is shrinking, because more teams are still being released, but the price gap is getting bigger, at the same time.
So, I've played this game once or twice.  A modkit is available, giving it even more replay value than it originally had.

This game is currently quite enjoyable w/ it's lite village management ++ tower defense design.

-- Boss monsters - and the blood moons

-- Reasons to try to expand your walls

A few annoying things/complaints here and there--
-- Majority of enemies in the game are resistant 40%+ to piercing damage - making it pointless to build bow towers or ballistae irregardless of what the "helpful" hint says
-- No AOE towers - there is a static tower - that is useless by the time you get the resources to build it because of its hilariously low damage and lack of damage upgrades

-- road upgrades are tedious - should happen automatically as the waymakers collect resources

-- storm + earthquake power - despite incredibly high costs are useless as damaging spells - storm's is only effective as a utility to force rain - and earthquake has basically no purpose

-- No rock/wooden tools or armor - all require rare iron
-- Cannot convert resources - like stone to iron
-- Golems - march out single-file rather than in groups - completely useless endgame - since despite essence cost - do no magic damg
