My first captain went to zee with the ambition of being the best adventurer there ever was, zailing the unterzee in the search of all its mysteries and treasures. That dream was cut short after a long trip to the other side of the zee...He was almost back home when fear and sanity took its toll. It was near Hunter's Keep that Matthew the Elusive would meet his demise at the hand of his crew.
Years later, Matthew The Second would zail the zee in search of his father's bones, somehow ending up on a wise goose chase across the unterzee, even though his father died right next to Fallen London... I suppose that death is never final, he could be a drownie for all his son knows.
A year on the zee as passed for his son and death still hasn't come. One would think that such luck or talent would be a blessing, but poor Matthew the Second had lost so much over the year that sweet death would be nothing but a mercy at this point.
He had lost his one and only true love from Salt's Curse, having being murdered when he returned to Wolfstack Dock one evening , leaving him with nothing but her keepsake, a locket with her picture inside, she never quite knew how to smile...
All because he chose to be foolish and didn't listen to his crew when they told him to offer a blessing to Salt in the form of a rough diamond.
Now owning an empty zeeside mansion full of trinkets his father left him, he would be full of sorrow and despair in the eyes of his miserable existence.
Months later he would meet Maybe's Daughter on shoreleave at the Mangrove College. It would be love at first sight and, although it would take a time for him to gain back his composure and move on from his previous love, he would soon find everything he ever asked for and more. He was hopeful again, happy even.
Until the day he finally helped her realise her dream of meeting her mother in Irem...
Things would take a grim turn once again...
Promising to help her achieve her goal and wishing her good luck on her quest to become like her mother under the Baazar, she would see him, for the last time. She never came back.
Once again stricken by grief and the unforgiveness of his fate, he now zails the zee on his new Phorcyd-class Corvette, the Maybe Memory, in the vain hope of fulfilling his legacy in longing misery.
What would be the hopes and dreams of many, turned out to be a curse for him only.

There is just so much I could say about this game, but the best I can come up with is that this contains one of the single greatest moments in my personal gaming history. A moment that truly had me going "... what the ♥♥♥♥?". A point where everything that you'd been doing up until then, and everything ou thought you knew about who to trust, gets turned on its head, all because of three simple words. Words you don't even notice until you're forced to.
To have a game take how we've been conditioned to play games over the years, and play with it in such a seemingly minor, yet profound way makes the story presented here, one ultimatly about the illusion of choice and free will, all the more powerful. You're given a narrative that compels you to rethink all of your past actions and honestly ask yourself, did I really choose to do that or did the game choose for me? And that right there, is why this is still one of the finest games ever made, and one everyone should experience for themselves.

Outlast has a greatly designed environment of a asylum that is supported by an amazing atmospheric ambient which keeps the player engaged all the time.
Outlast's atmosphere psychologically affect the player, in my own experience, the most unsettling feature is Miles Upshur's breathing. Unlike most horror games, in Outlast the main character behavior is similar to how the player would behave in identical situations, which, in my opinion, not only forces the player to be more engaged with the character and the environment as the story progresses but also creates a disconcerting feeling in the player.
The graphics are good and the gameplay is great, also, the game mechanics are pretty simple.
Outlast is a highly recommended game for any horror game fan.

(OBVIOUSLY, I don't want to start or feed a campfire with fir wood- that's a required material for repairing my very important items! Despite my whining, I think this is turning out to be a great game. I look forward to future improvements and expansions from the creators. I look forward to playing Story Mode.
But if they remove Pilgrim sandbox mode, it's over. No joking.

New update ruined the game for me. Some might like it, but i just don't like the new system.
Pros:
1. Certain defenses attack speed, range, power have been buffed (Very late end game [but radically nerfed early game])
2. Gold and medal consumption has increased to actually make the resource valuable
3. Micro transcationed tower and hero skins
4. Art style and game hub appearance keeps on improving
5. Additional maps and heroes being added
6. Pets and pet abilities
7. New special enemies
8. The music in the harbinger throne room map is on point.
Cons:
1. Range stat was removed (Only found in rare shards and as skill gambles) As a result, defenses such as cannons barely have range beyond a barricade. It used to be that most hero's would have insane range by maxed lvl.
2. The Shard and medalion system is less efficient than before in being able to control stat allocation to a certain degree
3. Ascension isn't even an ascension system, it's a grind more because the max hero lvl won't do you any justice. Even then, ascencion skills are sometimes useless. For ex. The gun witch asc. skill for the twin broom pistols duration time doesn't increase the attck dmg so other skills completely makes this one obsolete.
4. Gold consumption has been increased drastically which is good, but the items and upgrades you spend it on just suck. Defense speed stat without the shard is worthless (Have fun grinding for this and the range shard)
5. In response to the point above, RNG has increased exponentially, and not in a positive way. (Shards and Ascencion have also increased grinding)
6.  Player choice has been decreased even further by removing the ability of the player choosing which chaos map they could play in.
7. Micro transaction for shards ( Devs are getting closer to p2w)
8. Player choice reduced by removing the players ability to allocate heroes and tower stat points from lvl1-50
9. Gameplay systems have been merged making the game alot more confusing
a) Inventory system is a mess compared to before
b) Stat boosts, substats, passives, and elemental damage systems all merged and replaced by only 2 systems: relics and medallions. It used to be that stat boosts and passives were run by the sphere system, items would run substats and elemental dmg.
10. Game balance has been broken for players in chaos 1. Defenses now act more as a supporting roles to heroes instead of before where both were equally important.
11. Special enemies makes certain defenses completeley useless. For example, instead of the shield goblins in chaos 1 receiving reduced dmg from cannons and other similar defenses, they instead receive no damage from them. As a result, freedom to play your way has decreased in favor of making the game more challenging.
12. Heroes now have less defenses than before and their roles have all become generic (For ex. Monk had a sphere which made lightning aura transform into lightning strike aura. The monk also had a boost defense aura that also healed/buffed other heroes inside it in a large range. This made the monk more of a support role but none the less important and fun to play with. Now they made him as a general attack role like all other heroes. The apprentice had the fireball tower that could transform into the flamethrower tower with the passive sphere)
13. Removal of sphere passives: Spheres were an amazing aspect to the gameplay that allowed players to buy passives with in- game money, at certain level milestones that changed the way the hero uses abilities or defenses behave. A bit of confusion existed as the devs muddied and merged substats with sphere passives by allocating them to the wrong type (Legendary items weapons would have substats that acted like passives and spheres would have passives that acted like substats) but even then, spheres was a welcoming addition to the game that seperated dd2 from dd1 in a positive way.
14. Legendary weapons have stats that increase hero's health? Really? Why?! I understand if armor had it but weapons don't need it and it doesn't make much sense. Also, it has become harder than ever before in order to get good legendary gear with the correct needed stats . (Thank the devs for increasing rng in a negative way again.)
15. Invisible walls placed in many areas of the map to stop players from flying out of them or using them as strategic long range sniping points. Freedom to move around and tower placement freedom have also been decreased as a result. Map placement now gives off the illusion of freedom placement. In reality you are restricted to placing most defenses on ground level and in the path of enemies.(With a few high altitude placement exceptions that can be considered strategically unwise)
16. Playing with other players feels like a shore. Enemies absrob alot of damage when playing with 3 other players which does 2 things: Decreases the chance of winnning and decreasesd the desire to play with others in the community.
17. Nightmare modes (NM) now renamed chaos modes, no longer allow the player to choose the map they want to play in.
18. Some defenses have been greatly nerfed or watered down (The volcano tower was a fast shooting, hell breaker, an epic defense that made the lavamancer a viable and actually good hero despite his limitations. The earth shatter tower, although weak in late game, would do great aoe dmg the more it was upgraded, etc...)
19. Upgrading defenses have lost value in terms of importance. Before, defenses when upgraded would not only increase in dmg but in attack range as well.
20. Inventory system is a mess. Too many shards that accumulate in your inventory.
21. Defense resource has become unbalanced ever since the trials upate. Defenses such as volcano that cost around 100 DU is no longer viable considering how watered down, slow, and limited range it has. (Most defenses now exist for the sole purpose of dealing damage or absorbing it.)

This is a sleek and fun first person puzzle platformer that executes a couple good orignial ideas well without bloating itself by getting overly long and tedious.
Basically, you use "rifts" to travel between parallel rooms, which can be differentiated by the monochromatic background (white or black). The rifts will be in the same place in both rooms, but nothing else necessarily will be. The puzzles are primarily based on orienting the rifts properly to over obstacles and reach switches to eventually make it to the exit. It starts off very simple and the difficulty builds in a very natural way. At the end I definitely felt challeneged, but never so much so that I wanted to stop playing. Eventually you are required to use platforms that manipulate gravity, which where the game really shines and will put your spatial reasoning to the test.
The aesthetic may not be for everyone (I personally loved it) and there's no plot to speak of, so if you're for anything besides puzzles you might want to keep looking. Otherwise this game provides a fascinating and unique take on the genre of first person puzzlers. The "perfect" number of moves also provides an extra challenge that I found engaging in most instances.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a simple game, with a very simple objective: survive the night shift for an entire week.
Sound easy? Well, you haven't played it yet.
The basic idea is that you are alone in an abandoned restaurant, a la Chuck E. Cheese, where animatronic robot animals power on at night and roam the halls. The only problem, is that if they see you, they think you're an animatronic that isn't inside it's suit. Why is that an issue? Well, because they'll  cram you into a suit, simply mashing your entire body against an array of gears, springs, metal wire, and whatever other horribly painful and deadly things are contained within one. Because, well, the animatronics they want to jam you into aren't exactly "empty suits".
Between the strange hallucinations of words appearing on screen from time to time, as well as carnival music, camera malfunctions, limited power that if it runs out you die, and animatronics trying to, essentially, kill you, it's a tense ride if you're willing to get on board.
Maybe it's not the scariest game in the world, but try sitting alone in the dark, playing this game with headphones on, and try not to get freaked. It's great fun, and the jump-scares really provide a good amount of amusement, if you want that sort of thing.
"Not my kind of game", you say.
"I don't like horror games; they're boring", you tout.
Yeah? Well, you're either a wimp, a 'fraidy cat, or both.
Bad excuse :l
"I don't have the money".
Then don't buy it. What a nice reason that would be :)
Oh, and all the whiney people on the internet posting videos and shrieking?
Just ignore that; you'll have a great time with this one :)

I am a fan of Telltale games and have been so for years. Mostly I have had little or no problems with running them. In a way that was mostly true of this. The game only lagged up a few times, so I was spared that inconvenience that others have had and mostly could go through the game. However towards the end, it ended up crashing and then making me restart the game apparently losing my progress, which is really frustrating, there is still no option to skip dialogue and I'll have to replay through all that again. I think I still recommend this title but only in the hopes that these issues will continue to be fixed and that for the vast majority of players they won't encounter the difficulties I have had, or the ones others have had. On a positive note, I thoroughly enjoyed the writing, the combat is the same old quicktime prompts that it would be far too late to complain about, it's telltale, interactive storytelling for all the positives and all the limitations. Apart from playability I don't feel like I've got less from this game than other games.
Edit: They were quick to patch it and now it runs just fine, I don't get the smoothest animation, not sure if that is the game or because I haven't switched the settings to performance, pretty sure my hardware should be up to scratch and is in the recommended so... Only real remaining issue though is that cloudstream is not working, which is new. Anyway, hope episode 2 is released without the issues I faced. Having now been able to play it through to completion, I do not know if the story is gripping me as much as other titles, and trying to reconcile it with the image I have of the DC universe as a DC fan is a bit trialling but overall I am liking the quality of the story and look forward to the next installment.

I love the idea and potential of this game, but with such limited gameplay, the experience very quickly became boring.
The races are unique and fascinating different, the dialogue is qwirky and well written, the designs of ships and worlds are gorgious. But unfortunately the gameplay itself really boils down to - fly to a planet, mine it, fly to a planet, mine it, etc.  The only difference is what you are mining, and if mining is even possible - e.g. is this planet so hot your lander will melt before you land, or is the wind so impossibly strong that your lander will be blown along the ground unable to stay still long enough to mine, or is the gravity so high you will crash into the planet on entry no matter what you do. Many, many times I left a planet and then needed to use all the resources I mined JUST to repair the damage of mining. And this is the only real game mechanic in the game - not counting moving around the map between planets, or space battles, of which I had one in 3 hours.
It may have also just been my bad luck, but due to the random generation of worlds and systems I kept ending up in situations that seemed hopeless, like jumping to four systems in a row that were flooded with radiation (period damage to ship and all crew, all throughout system), or getting stuck in systems where the only source of EM (needed to go to new systems) was in a planet I could not feasibly mine.
Part of this may just be me - I don't really enjoy games like Don't Starve which seem less about making progress, and more about seeing how long before the game kills you on wihim. I hoped this game would be different, with a lowest difficulty seeing called Story Mode, and the clear goal of getting back to Earth. I was wrong, and at the end of 3 hours, having run out of fuel again with the whole crew suffocating, while getting periodically arradiated from a nearby pulsar and orbiting a planet whose fuel source I couldn't mine because the mine was underwater - I just didn't care enough to keep going or try again, having felt that I'd already experienced all the gameplay available.
I love the potential of this game and would heartily recommend it, especially to fans of survival games, IF more content and balance were added. But as it is, there is not enough of either.

Forget about being a hero:
War is about survival, following orders. Red Orchestra 2: Heroes of Stalingrad (Rising Storm too btw) captures this very same feeling to the perfection. Forget about running on the field and firing two machine guns akimbo like Rambo. You're a soldier, russian or german, american or japanese. The fight will always seem unfair and it is: get over it. Then how can you win and enjoy you may ask? Keep your head down, take cover, watch out for your teammates, follow your commander's orders, go for the objectives: be a soldier. The slightest misstep can kill you and your teammates. And if you win the battle, always remember that you would never have made it without your team, your squad leader and your commander.
Footmen win wars, but don't get credit:
More often then you'd want, you will have the role of a lousy footman, a bolt action rifle and 2 grenades. That is it, but you must make the best out of it. And if you do well enough, you'll have the opportunity to get promoted: sniper, automatic rifle, anti-tank or even tank crewmember. Don't worry, this game is hard at first, but always try your best, take time, don't rush things.
A pearl is always difficult to acquire:
This game is hard because it is different. It requires patience and strategy. It may seem hard and it can be frustrating. But trust me, if you want to see what war really is, i think Red Orchestra 2 gives a decent vision of that.

I would have recommended this game before it became $20.00. I think the asking price is a bit much for a game that gets boring very soon after you have played about 20 hours. For a city builder, it's unique in that you have to manage a wide array of basic resources to survive. However, it's also very short for a city builder.
Edit: Yeah, I'm still playing the game. It's good even w/o anything added
Once you attain a population of about 300 or more, there simply is no reason to play the game any longer. There needs to be a 'next-level' for players, after they've built past the survival stage, where grander buildings, regional conflicts (perhaps building an army for defense), or new villager specialist professions become available.
I've been waiting for almost a year for updates in this game that would bring it to the next level, and offer a fuller building experience. I've held off writing my review in lieu of the developer's promise to improve the game. Yet, alas, it seems those promises were false.
If one has money to spend, and wants to try something different for a small amount of time, they maybe will feel ok spending the $20.00 on this game. However, If you want a more enjoyable long-lasting game, buy Sim City 4. It's also only around $20.00 and is far superior to this game.

First-up, it looks great, sounds great and has actual puzzles - no real issues there.
I'm not recommending it for a few reasons tho - they're kinda personal and MIGHT not apply to you but I'm raising em because they might!
1 - it's a puzzle game with no story/aim/objective or goal - just "solve the puzzles".  I thought I could cope with that but after a while you do kinda wonder why you're bothering?
2 - you could solve most puzzles if you could jump a slightly larger gap or run (you can't) or just climb around the side of the portals - e.g the difficulty is in the limitations of movement and not the cleverness of the puzzles - no locked rooms or impossible leaps here, just roadblocks.
3 - puzzles can solved by elimination or deduction.  These puzzles quickly add a LOT of combinations which means lots of elimination but are involved enough to make deduction pretty hard (and all the puzzles I saw were single-solution)
4 - I got motion sickness/a headache after about 5mins of play - after 2 attempts I gave-up.  It's not something I've had much before (The Ball did it - that's about it) but this does it really well!
So, it's a fine game where everything works but it lacks some stuff.  It needs some sort of a carrot to keep you playing, some reason for accepting the limitations of movement and it could feel a bit more of a puzzle to be deduced and a bit less of rat maze to be beaten by sheer effort.

Core Gameplay:
You defend your crystals, build towers, kill waves of enemies, level up, loot and get better equipment, kill even stronger waves of enemies and have fun.
Review:
While the game undertook several changes since it first appeared on steam, it stayed pretty consinstent over the time. It had some weak patches, but it also had some pretty neat changes. I got bored of the first part of the franchise, because my towers were basically godlike and I could take on everything. They changed this with the sequel. You need to kill the special enemies and bosses yourself and can't just layback (at least I haven't reached the item-power to do so yet) and it's very entertaining. I think we can all agree, that a game, in which you got nothing to do is a bad game.
The game is meant to be played with up to 3 other defenders, which can be very funny or very frustrating (like every other online game, where you have to work together), but overall I prefer to play this game alone. Some maps are way easier as a team, especially the harder difficulties in the game, but it's still somehow doable.
The only problem I have with this game is, that it takes some time to unlock the heroes themselve. When I remember correctly, you start with the 4 basic heroes and have to unlock the other 5 with wyvern coins or real money. You get wyvern coins for finishing a map and completing daily or monthly quests.
One important point is, that you don't get any advantages by investing real money. You can only unlock skins and heroes with the premium currency. Personally, I think the 4 starting heroes are all you need. The others are just for optimizing your defense.
All in one: The game is f2p, it's fun, try it yourself. You don't lose anything beside some of your time.

SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT. After playing a little over 6 hours, I think it's pretty safe to say that SUPERHOT is one of the most interesting games I've played in a while. There are a few flaws and an intimidating price tag, but it's worth your time if you get it on sale.
The visuals have gotten mixed reception, but I'm personally a fan of the art style here. It's simple without feeling lazy, like many other indie games when it comes to their graphics. Plus, I can't help but watch the red guys as they crumple to the ground after they were killed. It makes every kill feel ten times more satisfying. Overall, the art style is simple in a good way.
I'm not going to lie, this game is incredibly fun. It definitely deserves the title as one of the most innovative shooters in years, and surprised me with the amount of content post-campaign. Yes, the main story IS really short, but I'll get in depth with that in the "Replayability" section of my review. The gameplay mechanics are unique and really creative. Watching a replay of you after you die/win (depending on the mode) makes you feel really badass. I don't need to explain the gameplay much, as you can just watch a video of it and know what you're in for. I will say, however, that it was executed very well and is about as fun as it looks. Plus, when you beat the game, you unlock endless and challenge modes, which give the game much more to do after you finish the campaign. Let the videos speak for themselves with this section.
The game comes off as a "kill bad guys" sort of game, but as you progress through the main storyline, you'll start to notice the game getting increasingly suspicious, without getting into details. It gets increasingly interesting as you go on, and while some people find it kind of absurd or weird, I found it to be pretty good. I'm starting to notice an increase in games that break the fourth wall frequently and try to toy with your mind, examples being
and
as some of the better ones. SUPERHOT doesn't get to levels of those two in terms of mind♥♥♥♥ing, but saying that the plot is boring or underwhelming would be a lie. The ending is one of the most clever endings I've seen in a video game. Once I was brought back to the menu, I stared at the screen, slowly clapping because of how creative it was. To conclude, I am pleasantly surprised with the story here.
There isn't much in terms of audio. Some music, but the game is usually quiet. It relies on sound effects and the constant "SUPER. HOT. SUPER. HOT." to make your ears happy. Not much to say here, to be honest. As I said, the game is pretty quiet, and the sound effects aren't all that noteworthy. The only thing you'd remember here are the two words that you should probably know at this point.
Okay, I understand that the storyline is very short. Some people have finished this game in about an hour or two. I'm not very good at this game, and I did take my time with some parts, so I finished it in around three hours. The story is very interesting, but it didn't leave much else to question. So yes, the main story IS very short and that is a problem with the game. However, with the endless and challenge modes I talked about earlier, you'll probably spend some more time with the game. Rather than feeling like filler content, I actually wanted to play more of the game because of how much fun the mechanics are. No, this isn't like Skyrim and you're probably only going to get a few more hours of content, but at least there's more to do post-game.
Overall, SUPERHOT is very different and I am overall satisified with the experience. There are a few flaws, but the pros definitely outweigh the cons, so I can recommend this game. Just be cautious with that $25 price tag and know what you're getting into if you do decide to buy it at that price.

Oh where to begin...
Up front:  The Pros here are outnumbered by the cons.  Do not buy unless you understand two things.
1.  This is not anywhere near as good as Madden was well over a decade ago.
2.  You're not paying for a superior football simulation so much as helping a (tiny!) developer create an alternative to EA.
Pros:
-Decent number of mod options apparently available.  None used so far, just the game "out of the box."
-Franchise mode! For when you're in it for the long haul.
-Quick Play mode...for when you want a...quickie.
-Passing game control using mouse is easy/intuitive and innovative. Allows you to put the ball where you want.
-Good audible and hot route system, but no option to simply flip play direction at the line of scrimmage.
-32 teams to choose from...wonder how they arrived at that number...
Bugs/Cons/Gripes:
Complaints and negative generally fall into the three categories below:  gameplay, graphics and sound.
Gameplay:
-No sense of physical inertia in the game at all.  When there is a collision, players simply fall down at the point of contact.
-No substitutes.  The players on the field are who you have, period.
-No injuries
-No fake punts or fake field goals
-There is only a small difference between how a lineman looks and handles on defense versus a defensive back.
-No defensive audibles.
-No real options/special moves available if playing as a defensive lineman...or any defensive player for that matter.
-No instant replay or option to record matches.
-In a game with 10 minute quarters there was a grand total of ONE broken tackle.  Spins and jukes are basically useless.
-Announcer is bland, repetitive and sounds like he is referring to powder puff football.
-Quarterbacks can throw the ball 95 yards in the air.
-Scale of field to players is off.  Field feels like it is 30 yards wide, not 43 and change.
-Far too many dropped passes.
-Zero receiver animation in some cases, the ball simply bounces off a guy with arms at his sides.
-In first (only) game played, my QB had over 40yds rushing...but had no rushing stats.
-NO PLAY CLOCK.  What time is it?  Tea time you say?  I'll leave my boys at the line of scrimmage for a half hour then!
-Game clock only moves 10 seconds at a time after a play.  My team had 130 plays in a 40 minute game.
-Zero indication of when a quarter has come to an end other than looking at the clock.
-No wind or wind indications, even in the kicking game.
-Kicking and punting controls make it much easier to kick to the right than to the left.
-TINY PLAYBOOKs.  All teams have same playbook with a total of up to 8 plays for each of the half dozen formations.
-On punts, kickoffs and incomplete passes, THE BALL DOES NOT BOUNCE when it hits the ground!?!  (#VelcroBowl2016)
Graphics:
-Wideout animations are odd before the snap and freeze to the point they don't look alive till the snap occurs.
-Runner animations have a very high center of gravity and wierd arm movements.  (Special Olympics, is that you?)
-Quarterback animation upon dropping back is same goofy one from Axis '15.  Zero NFL QBs act/look like they're chilling at the disco. Once you notice, you can't un-notice.
-Crowd sprites would not be awful if they had more than two colors and weren't in the shape of the stadium seats!
-1920x1080 resolution looks like 1024x720
Sound:
-Announcer bland, repetitive and annoying.  Zero references to team, field position, player name.
-After playing one game, started a second but quit out of annoyance because of a wierd persistent ringing tone.
Closing Thoughts:
I played a quick match to generate this review and quit during the second quick match because of a game bug.  Despite the fact I won that first game 43-42 in overtime on pro difficulty, there were far too many shortcomings for it to be a satisfying gaming experience.  I love playing football in real life, watching football on TV, playing football on consoles.  I want to like playing football on the PC.  Axis Football 2016 as a competitor to EA just is not there yet.  We're not talking not in the same league, zip code, area code, state...no my friend, that would be too kind. We're talking in terms of a pseudo third-world video game in comparison virtually across the board here.  This is the kind of game that cohabitates the abstract space occupied by AK-47s and angry black people shooting other angry black people.  This game had to learn DirkaDirka on the same streets as the neighborhood suicide bomber before it came across the border into the US, got on to Steam without a photo ID and voted 3,000 times in Florida and Idaho as an undocumented democrat.  (I can't resist, it's an election year)
The feature set that is in place is decent enough, but the core gameplay itself is so unengaging and flawed that I would have to force myself through a season, and that's something I've never had to do going all the way back to the age of Tecmo.  With ALL that said, I hate EA.  I hate EA enough to shave my chest hair and eat it if they would simply stop being EA.  I hate EA enough to give this tiny developer a thumbs up despite the fact their game probably doesn't deserve it.  The effort put forth here IS somewhat praiseworthy for all the negatives.  Football is not simple to simulate as compared to say, golf, and EA has had large, well-funded teams refine their product over many years.  I want to support an alternative to EA very badly, but I also need to write a review that gives prospective buyers an idea of what they are purchasing.  Do I regret paying $20 for this game?  Kinda.  If it were just the game, oh my yes.  If it were just the game itself being judged, it is worth 5-10 bucks in my book.  But you're not just buying a game, you're buying hope for the little man and hope for a rebirth of football on the PC that isn't run by the cash-grabbing *BLEEEEEP* at EA.  All that said, odds are you're gonna want something better too, even with the lowered expectations from this review - you have been warned.
In the end, (<-that's this part of the review->) I give Axis 2016 only a 5 out of 10 but a thumbs up for heading in the right direction...that and not being EA.

Superhot is a very innovative shooter, with a new mechanic that no other game [to my knowledge] has tackled before. The twist to it, is that time only moves when you move. If you are standing completely still, time will move at an extremely slow pace. Turn your head, and time will move at half speed. Walk or jump, and time moves at full speed. You may think that this would make the game much too easy, however you are always outnumbered, and a single shot or punch kills you. That's right, no health bars, no health pack, just one life. The game itself is fantastic, runs smoothly, and has a neat art style, which makes its con all the more painful. It only has two hours of content. You could stretch it to three, but you would have to play slowly. I am almost finished with my second playthrough, and only 5 hours was put into it. My reccomendation, is to put it on your wishlist, and wait for a sale, but for now, it just can't justify its 25 dollar price tag.

Lighting and weather effects look amazing and the sound design is great as well.

This is not a completed game. And before you think "well, he's probably asking too much" I want to point out that I don't mean in a 90% kind of way, but in a 30% kind of way... The first 30% of the game is there, I can't deny that. There is a genuine satisfaction in overcoming the first obstacles and trying to form your little village. Alloting the work so that there is no shortage of food, wood etc. Building the structures in such layout so that everything works in the best possible way. There is even the added effect of season change. You eventually reach the best part of the game where you can trade with other villages for otherwise inaccessible resources. Aaand that's where the game ends.
The choice of buildings is meagre to say the least. 2 types of houses. If that's not the bare minimum then what is? 1 type? You can pretty much build all the available structures after 4-5 hours of playing.
The villagers could well have been simply dots on a map, lacking any kind of realism. They move around at random, deep inside the forest or hovering around buildings. There is no pattern to work around and no sense of recreation or resting. They follow a random program of their own, in the absence of a night/day cycle at times farmers will suddenly drop everything and return to their homes.
The units of resources make no sense. The balance if you manage to find it is extremely precarious, one small change (like a disaster that kills a small percentage of your population) can have irreversible effects leading to a close extinction simply because there are no factors that work to pull the system back together. 2 farmers die -> 100 units of food are missing -> the forester dies of starvation -> 20 logs missing -> the fisherman freezes to death ---> and the population spirals to almost half the original one.
This is just another example of the decline of the game industry. More than a decade ago, a game like Evil Genius was released offering hundreds of hours of gameplay with numerous types of units with excellent AI. Minions that didnt wonder around aimlessly but started conversations with each other or seeked various types of recreation. The game had depth, with countless unlockable objects, new rooms, new quests, a change of island. And now we get Banished.. A game stuck eternally in Beta with no hope of improving. Graphics slightly (if at all) better than Evil Genius and that's about it. The developer probably left this game forever, cashed in with fake promises and spent a week in Barbados.
I don't understand economics so I don't know what the best move for us the community is. If we buy it then we're accepting the bad quality of gaming. If we don't buy it then the city builder genre amongst many others that are not CoD related may simply die out. In any case this game is bad, unfinished.

I enjoyed The Long Journey Home right from the start, but the addition of Story Mode has really opened it up. Ships and crew are significantly more durable, money is easier to come by, aliens seem more hospitable, and it's become a true game of exploration rather than survival. It remains very challenging - you'll still need to manually land on planetary surfaces, deal with hostiles, keep your ship intact, avoid flying into black holes, and all that sort of thing - but it's not nearly as aggressive in its efforts to kill you in this mode. I'm having even more fun with it now.

Bored with playing civil servant? Fed up with Giant Developers ruining great city building series? Want a REAL challenge? Then go play Dark Souls or something.
Banished takes you away from the urban jungle and plops you in the middle of the actual jungle with a few families, homes, and some basic start-up supplies. Grow your population, Cultivate the land, Forage for food in the wilderness, Gather raw materials, all of this and a hell of a lot more is going to be required if you want to go from a small settlement of a couple families to a thriving town of a few hundred... or more with some luck and even more persistance.
Dont expect an easy ride though. Balancing Hunger, Housing, Health, Disaster and disease all at the same time will keep you occupied while your citizens look for new and exciting ways to get themselves completely wiped off the map. Its a struggle from beggining to end and takes very little time to go from a comfortable position to the very edge of disaster.
With Solid Gameplay Mechanics, Charming graphics, a wonderful UI, and fitting soundtrack Banished is a unique entry into the City-Building / Management genre and is worth a look if you're after something a little different.

I've had this game for all eternity, and just now realized that I haven't written a review for it. So here goes:
Rise to Ruins (or Retro-Pixel Castles, if you're an old-timer) is a crazy mix of town-building, sandbox survival, and tower defense. It's not a terribly easily game to pick up, but it's not anywhere near the most difficult I've ever played. It is in nearly constant flux, because the one-man development crew works on this game nonstop. New features and major game-changing elements come up once every few months, and they all add something useful to the game. That being said, the difficultly from one version to the next can fluctuate a little bit (much more in the earlier builds than now).
There's a crapton of maps to choose from, and every map has at least two good spots to start building the town camp from. There's as much variability as you could reasonably want, between the maps, the weather, and the variable monster spawns. So yeah. Make a town, gather food and water, and build up walls and towers. Or skip the tower defense and make masses of combobulators, and watch your stone and wood army of golem demolish everything in their path. Most important of all, don't die.
Good luck.

- Cute to a fault. The characters don't have much development but to be fair, neither does Mario

- Midair homing attack is worse than Sonic's. Many times it doesn't even trigger.
Other thoughts:
- I was spoiled by Super Mario Odyssey. Cappy just makes things too easy and while the Hat Kid's dive technique is helpful, it's not "stop all momentum and change directions in midair" like Cappy. I found myself trying to Cap jump my way up many walls.
- The hookshot should have just been an umbrella upgrade instead of a badge. Once it's unlocked you pretty much keep it equipped.

At first he is a mix between the Comic, Arkham Games and Nolan Batman’s but as soon as you reach the warehouse (about an hour or so into the game) you can be the Batman YOU want to be. Be a♥♥♥♥♥♥or a “nice” Guy or be with the press instead of the police.
Another new and kind of unseen feature is the “attack planning”. It only happened once in this Episode, but I’m sure it’ll happen more frequent in the next 4. The attack planning happens before you start infiltrating a party and lets you choose different ways of disposing of enemies. When you got all that covered a QTE barrage starts, which is surprisingly entertaining considering it’s a QTE. That may be because it isn’t punishing. If you make a mistake it will be a little bit longer, but it doesn’t automatically kill you (sometimes), so that is very nice. Aaaand that’s it with the Gameplay, the rest is basic Telltale stuff.
The story is nice so far as it sheds a new light on the Wayne family and its dealings in the past, and Alfred gets a little more involved into the story instead of just being the butler that fixes him up when he gets his♥♥♥♥♥handed to him.
Graphics are okay. The cell shading look is fitting, resolution is okay, could be better, but the animations are sometimes very clunky. Can be overlooked though because it’s mostly during combat.
And that’s it for the first Episode. Can’t wait for the second to find more out about the Wayne’s past!

This game is amazingly beautiful. Not only in the way it works with words, nor the landscapes of impossible corals, but in the feeling it envokes. The calm of zailing through the Bonny Reefs-- the desperation as you realise you don't have the fuel to get home-- the terror as the Tree of Ages appears in front of you, out from the dark-- the severe lonelyness as you zail slowly through endless black.
The story of this game is rich, combining unique aspects of a culture crafted around this Victorian-era, dangerous, subterranean world. Countless possibilities can be unlocked. You can explore dangerous islands using only candles. You can burn down an entire island, you can drive yourself insane by seeing too much sunlight. You even sell your soul to a monkey. I did, once, because I needed some more fuel and I didn't have the money.
Not only this, but you can play the game the way you want. Some people might want to go and shoot as many things as possible, while others would rather try and find love back in London. The one thing you must know about this game is that you WILL die. And the death is permanent. Whether it be to mutiny, zee-beasts such as angler-crabs and bound-sharks, or just repeatedly crashing your ship into various coastlines, you will die. A lot. But the game doesn't restart completely when you die. Time progresses, and you create a lineage of captains. Choices you make in one life affect later generations, but that doesn't mean you shouldn't care about dying.
Overall, this game is darkly intriguing, beautiful, and full of things to discover. It may not be for everyone, but I highly recommend this game to fans of roguelikes as well as other dark and immersive games.

I played Bioshock for first time just now. So this review can be viewed as seen from more recent perspective.
I think Bioshock is a perfect example of a fantastic story and very interesting and engaging gameplay.
I played it on hardest difficulty with resurrection disabled. It proved to be a good challenge, but not difficult enough that I wasn't having fun experimenting with all the different ways combat can be done. Bioshock is good at that: it gives you a big playground where you experiment with various ways of doing things. In that sense, the game should appeal to those who loved Dishonored for precisely that reason.
Every level has its own theme that is shown in a very convincing way. It always completely makes sense that the game's world may have had a place(level) like this. The same counts for characters: they are presented in several ways and through different channels, so to speak, but all have distinctive and very interesting personalities. There is not much communication with them, but they are so believable and insanely interesting.
In modern eyes the graphics might seem a little bit out-dated, naturally. But the game still looks extremely convincing, distinctive and very pretty.
I would recommend this game especially to FPS fans and those who like an atmospheric and immersive world accomanied by a very engaging, interesting and even mindblowing story.

Parallax is a minimalist game done right.
Placing you in a world where you can pass between two dimensions by passing through portals, this game offers quite the challenge. You use buttons to rotate certain elements of the world in order to gain access to an exit platform. It is very easy to mash buttons and win here, but the reall challenge is doing it in exactly the required number of moves [or trying to break the game and do it in less]. If you can think logically and think of moves ahead of time, this will be your type of game.
The first two chapters are moderately easy, but things get very tricky in the second half of the game. With various aspects like lasers and gravity reversal introduced, it can be a real mind bender. The music for this game isn't too energetic, which helps you get in a thinking mood.
It is worth noting that while the game looks black and white, you can change the colour scheme in the game options or the main menu to other presets, so you needn't be put off by the stark contrast you may see in screenshots. And even though there are only two colours ever used [not even shades of colours], the game never seems to lack detail in the graphics. Everything always looks clear, and doesn't look boring, which is very impressive [the same could not be said for some other minimalist ventures].
There are a total of 32 levels, some people might find that to not be enough, but I think the game had a good enough length.
Definitely buy this game if you like a challenging, but not impossible, puzzle.

Disclosure: review key provided by the developer.
I first saw Professor Why at Hall of Games in Wrocław in 2014. It was by far the best of the show and my kids spent a good deal of time there. To my surprise they managed to port the game on PC and it can now work with just any webcam.
This is not exactly a game, but a toy which is best played by kids together with their parents. This cooperativity begins early, as you and your kid will have to prepare the set of cards youself. This requires a printer, scissors, and a pair of small hands to manipulate them. We also applied some glue and cardboard. Great! Now it was ready to launch.
Immediately after running the game we noticed that our desktop is so much smaller than the large table available at the exhibition :). Also it turned out that in winter afternoons it quickly gets too dark for our webcam to recognize the card patterns efffectively. Last but not least, the game is a bit "too fair" and incorrect combinations get recognized as easy as correct ones, which can get frustrating for little chemists. These are all but minor technical issues. The only real problem is the scoring system. The very idea of substracting points for mistakes in a game for kids relying and showing experimentation is horribly wrong. It would be much better if the mistakes were officialy allowed and resulted in funny comments, reactions, even explosions :) since this is why we do chemistry on PC, not in father's garage or mother's kitchen, don't we.
So it's not a type of game which you can leave your kids with and go away... which is, actually, good again, for those of us who miss time spent with their kids. The play itself gives kids a good laugh and a big boost of chemistry knowledge (and why you should keep your working area clean and tidy :)). If you have curious kids, would like to spend time with them but they prefer the computer, you should give this game a try; it is - as far as I know - unlike any other here on Steam.
Especially if you have a large table in front of your web camera :)

I want to give as detailed and unbiased review as possible so no one is misled.
I recommend this game not just because it's the only football game on steam, but also because this game has also showed a good amount of progress from last year's version. With that in mind, I'm not saying this game is perfect. This game is most likely slightly overpriced. Not as overpriced as 2015, which I couldn't see spending 15 dollars on. That price, is probably more fit for this game, and for '15, a cool $6-10 dollars. The game needs funding though, so overpaying isn't awful because Danny puts the money back into the game.
Now, for the animations and features of the game. Jukes, Spins and Dives were added to the game which is an incredible upgrade considering in 2015 all you did was run. Which is upgraded in itself, your player no longer is holding the ball like he's asking for a defender to knock it out of his hand. He properly holds it like he has played football before. The UI also like the running animation, recieved a huge update and no longer looks as outdated. Blocking animations are improved now, engaging in a block is no longer engaging in a hug. There is a push mechanic that allows a better blocker/defender to be able to push back the opponent. A speed burst feature was added,(not sure if it was in '15) it's really unrealstic at the moment as players all speed burst at the same speed. There are real handoff and pitch animations instead of the ball glitching to the player. The playbook recieved a small upgrade, was hoping for even more of an upgrade I must point out. There are 8 plays for each formation, Not sure how many formations there are, I believe around 7-8 for each side of the ball. Franchise mode is not implemented and is the same as '15, very simple and nothing other to do besides play games. Full 4 quarter games, instead of two halfs.
The final part of the game, the gameplay. There are still some flaws, most noticeably happens in the passing game. No swat animation or catching animation means balls thrown in coverage are often times a coin flip. The lack of catching animations makes it hard for receivers to catch certain balls on the run. So you'll often have to throw them to a stop. DB's don't properly play the ball and will often times run behind the WR and sit there. DB's backpedal a set amount of time, which causes them to get burnt in coverage sometimes. No fouls in the game don't hurt, besides the lack of offsides. This means you can easily blitz around edge and get sacks. The most improved part of the game though is clearly the blocking. Danny did a great job in changing how awful blocking was in '15. Kickoffs no longer clump the players together in the center which means you can have fun in the return game. Including on punt returns. The best way to make defenders miss is to manually swerve/spin after you bait them in, opposed to using a spin or juke. No physics system in the game, so the player movement and ball carrier moves are real arcadish.
PROS
-Gameplay improvements since '15 (Money play removal, blocking AI is no longer complete garbage)
-Football game on steam
-Unique passing system
-Controller support
-Very moddable (Personal favorite is hot route mods)
-Community feedback is listened too
-10x better animations than '15
Cons
-pretty awful interactions in the passing game(Including defensive zone and man coverage AI)
-Very simple franchise mode
-Inability to make hot routes on defense (Was hoping for this feature)
-No online multiplayer
-Very small playbook
-No penalties
-Defense is pretty bland, feels like you have no control
The game isn't great, but it's worth the $20 dollars if you're a football fan on PC, or just upset with the direction of madden.

Calling this equivalent to FTL is calling any random cardgame the same as any other random card game.
The similarities Between FTL and LJH are background, but have nothing to do with game play. LJH is a game of trying to get the angle right while thrusting with your ship or lander. FTL would be a game of tactics, where you can pause the game to decide your next move.
Even though LJH is a graphicaly wonderful expansive galaxy compared to FTL, the downgrade from smart play to "point the angle of your ship correctly" is horrendous.
Once you figured out the game, it ends up being nothing more than Ignore all the fun stuff we added. They are meant to distract new players, until they figure out that the only thing that matters is the Exotic Matter and some Credits.
While with FTL, you were constantly busy thinking about the final boss fight while upgrading your ship, with LJH, you are not even thinking about traveling home ... only the next step is important. Not a goal, just a means to end a game play to avoid it being endless.
As for actual duration differences between FTL and LJH, that would be 1,5-2 hours vs. 30-40 hours. Meaning, you have to pick up the thread you left every time in a game where only the next step is truly important, over a 30-40 hour play through.
Those 30-40 hours are only game wise useful to give the game time to break the ship down, so you need to collect a few extra credits to fix it.
I feel sorry for myself. the only games I ever want to play that are 30-40hours are actual stories. Not games that are artificialy lengthend without need.

This game eats away time, but in the good way.
When I think about The Long Journey Home,
and
are the words that come to my mind first - which is odd because the universe, while created by a 'random' seed, can become very populated and buzzing with life and the decisions you get to make are nerve-wrecking more often than not.
But when I close the game, what stays is not a feeling of pressure or distress, but of appreciative calm, reminiscent of me faring the most beautiful galaxies, accompanied by an utterly fitting soundtrack.
Because most of all, this universe of TLJH is, while very hostile at times, beautiful. The endless space comes in all hues of color and sound. The creatures that populate the galaxies are multifacted and the crew you chose for your adventure quirky and loveable.
The Long Journey Home is a work of art, both visual and auditive. (The major reason I bought the Captain's Edition is that I love the soundtrack. If they have released a version including the OST of this game by the time you are reading this, consider getting that version - it is definitively worth it!)
I am more an explorer than a rogue-like player. And boy there's a lot to explore! Yet your resources are few, and often you see yourself facing decisions about unforeseeable risks. (Thus I am very glad the Story Mode came along, to at least ease my pain about not daring to explore everything a tiny bit. ;) )
There's only two things that cloud my playing experience from time to time, none of them severe though.
First, while the different alien species and the crew have quite their personalities, I feel longing for even more different interaction reactions and possibilities. You have quite the array of possible interactions when encountering a foreign vessel but most of them return the same responses which don't come in many variations either (and you get shut down quickly because everyone gets annoyed with you for wasting their time).
Second, I keep wondering about the design decisions behind the controls. ;) Using the D-Pad to navigate the menus feels a bit clunky, especially when trying to haggle for the last credit. Additionally, I am more used to pressing 'A' to confirm a move and 'B' to decline it as well as one of the primary buttons for firing whatever weapon I have. That sometimes makes me instinctively use the wrong button to do something - loweing my shielding instead of firing weapons or even deploying the lander when I wanted to leave because the hull would not take survive the heat below. (RIP Alessandra - I am so so sorry!)
Also, if you encounter any problem, as noticeable in steam and also in the game's official discord, the devs are eager to help everyone to get the best possible experience, open to criticism and trying to fix any issues as quickly as possible.

I was able to land now (Loosing 50% of my hull) and I was able to get some minerals. But my last landing I broke an arm and my lander was down to 15% of integrety. - Always allow someone to heal, at least one injury.
- Always allow someone to repair if they have the resources.
- Allow Keyboard control of the ship. Let me use the arrow keys to stir the ship, not relying on the movement of my mouse.

Banished is about balance and patience. Managing the lives of these people is almost zen, like slowly and gently tending a bed of flowers, monitoring needs and providing room for growth. At first, the game is stressful, full of overwhelming micromanagement as you struggle to survive. Advancing too fast or failing to predict what will be needed and plan for contingencies won't end your game immediately, but will put you on a path to a slow death.
The early game is the most fun, fighting for survival and being forced to be patient. The mid-game will make you feel accomplished as you can safely use new buildings and resources. One thing I was impressed with was the fact that a vital layer of statistical information I was looking for was only provided later once I could afford the town hall. Unfortunately, the end game provides no more challenge. It gets boring. I was expecting more content to be unlocked, but was disappointed. Fortunately, the Steam Workshop provides many new buildings and even ways to make the game easier.
This is one of the most powerful experiences I have ever had with a game.

Banished is a survivalist city builder loosely set to medieval times. You're tasked with keeping your few followers fed, clothed and homed, gathering resources to expand and battling the elements and the terrain. This is much harder than it sounds like, as disasters in the form of disease or fire can hit without warning, nevermind more common occurrences like starvation or hypothermia caused by your mismanagement. All in all, an enjoyable game once you figure out how to grow and diversify your settlement a bit.
The biggest issue I have with the game is how housing distribution is handled, and how little control you have over it. Your citizens will not have children unless they have homes of their own (i.e. adult children do not reproduce). This means that you will either have to constantly build more homes, or suffer devastating generation crashes every so often as widowed old people greedily demand a full household until they die, meaning you'll have fewer families and ultimately even
people above child-rearing age. A demographic disaster can be harder to recover from than anything else the game throws at you, save perhaps a wildfire scorching half your town. If you have a town hall and the ability to bring in nomad settlers, it'll be easier, but often the first pop crash happens long before you get that far.
Given that this
a survivalist game, though, overcoming such challenges is a large part of the game experience. The game does grow on you after a while, and the soothing, perpetual music urges you to continue for that

Firstly, Banished is amazing. It blends city building and survival well... a little too well. Well enough for any goal to merge into one. If the game were to have a larger array of feature then it'd be even better. So I give it a 75/100.
My ideas on how the game can be improved-
-add another entity other than yourself in the world. It's a good single player game but it gets a little lonely. Maybe add various NPCs to the game.
-NPC houses, towns, settlements etc. Places where the player has to connect a path to so that an exchange can be made. Maybe have specialastions varying from a farming town (sells crops over a period of a year for tools), mining town (sells iron and stone for food and other items) and a lumber town (sells wood and firewood for tools and food).
-NPC raiders or equal threat. A disaster event: a group of hostiles temporarily take over your town, slowly draining 50% of your food. To get rid of you must build a police station of sorts and train militia to protect your town. After they have been defeated they have a lower percentage of coming back to your town, until the threat equals 0.
-Multiplayer- build a seperate towns in seperate areas of a MASSIVE map. To trade, you either must build a trade port and assign people to be merchants and fill boats with materials, or build a road to their town and assign people to be caravans to begin trade. Caravans should have a chance of being raided so (from earlier) the police should be able to protect it.
Those are my ideas, if anyone thinks this should be in the game then why not send messeges to the creater to get this in. THE HYPE!

Sunless Sea has managed to do what many games fail to do. Learn about my true nature and ambitions.
I've smuggled contraband, left a few people to their doom, have taken many risks for profit, and helped the unfortunate only to get screwed in the end.
STORY- There are no true handouts in this game including the story. Every snippet or rumor you learn as you explore lets you decide how the world and its inhabitants have come to be. Spoiling the story for you would be a sin.
SOUNDTRACK- My god do the composers who assisted this game know how to instill tension when you enter where no man should, or the glorious music of civiliZation when nearing a port. 10/10

Sunless Sea is a pretty interesting exploration sandbox set in what I assume is basically Hell but with ships and water and what not. Seriously, souls are literally a tradeable commodity. But anyways, London fell down into this cavern called the "Neath" some time ago, and you happen to be the captain of a ship in the zee. You'll die a lot and sail a lot in the hopes that one day, one of your captains will make it.
The game's mechanics are pretty simple if not repetitive. You explore in your ship and complete missions, going back and forth between the vast zee and Fallen London peddling goods and services for money. There are three key elements to your survival: fuel, food and terror, which is essentially just sanity. You must also manage your crew, as there are penalties for letting them fall below half your ship's maximum capacity; conversely, having too many crew members can also drain your food very quickly. Combat can be avoided easily, as you are much faster than most enemies and the enemies seem to have a very small aggro range. You can complete the game by finishing one of three goals you establish at the beginning of the game or by a hidden fourth, and you can pass on your wealth to future generations with a will. Events on islands are text-based and make use of probability, so if that isn't your cup of tea, look elsewhere.
Your main goal in this game is money. There are two highly lucrative trade routes in Sunless Sea: coffee and sunlight, both of which will end entirely after you have made a certain amount of runs. This is one of two big issues I have with the game: once these trade routes are gone, it is virtually impossible to establish a consistent source of income through trade. You have to scrape by with whatever you made during those runs because you won't be getting much money that you don't have to spend on supplies or fuel just to survive. I never felt like I was succeeding in the game after reaching this point.
The second issue I take with the game is the story, which has a lot of problematic similarities to a game like Dark Souls II.  They give you just enough lore and background to make the world seem interesting and grand, but inevitably, it's disappointing and relies too much on its predecessor. In this case, Sunless Sea is the child of an interactive text adventure named Fallen London, and unfortunately, the developers seemed a bit too proud of Fallen London to let it go. Much of the story in Sunless Sea is reliant on concepts developed in Fallen London, so the game's own story is underdeveloped and very unwelcoming to newcomers. The world established is interesting but vague at best, and Sunless Sea cannot stand on its own, which is unfortunate because it is a good game.
Overall? Sunless Sea is a good game. The story is underdeveloped, and the game itself has moments where it is very poorly balanced. Still, it's quirky and fun and good for sinking (ha!) a few hours in the immersive world. I would buy it on sale if it appeals to you because I personally think it's a fun game to play with a lot of good ideas and heart and soul.

A decent game. Set with absolutely no context and the simplest, most efficient graphics that set the bar for what it means to be minimalistic, Parallax exists as a pure puzzle game. They are so tightly built that solving them feels like staring at a tangled knot, figuring out what order to pluck strings, and then doing it. There aren't many choices in these puzzles; progress is measured, rightly so, in switches pushed, and so at any given time, the fork in the road ahead rarely has more than three paths. When you do figure the puzzle out, you don't feel smart -- you feel like the level designer was smart, albeit very, very smart.

Hat in Time is as close to a 3D Mario Platformer clone I've seen yet.
While the game has collect-a-thon elements, it shines in how Hat-Kid controls.
The tricks and strategies you can learn to improve your overall movement strikes a strong resemblance in a lot of the 'king of platformers' such as Mario and Banjo. This is important because even after the credits roll there are things to learn how to control Hat-Kid more efficiently/quickly through levels. The game offers a decent challenge in terms of platforming. It welcomes newcomers, while offers an extra layer of challenge for those who want it. Supposedly NewGame+ will be a part of the free DLC coming to this game. There is also Steam-Workshop for community made levels/
The games story is charming, and the voice-acting is on point.
The replayability is there, but is up the the player. There is a 100% incentive, but is more a self-accomplishment type of reward. I found myself going back because of how enjoyable a lot of the platforming levels tend to be.
9/10, if you're looking for a satisfying platformer itch look no further.

GET THIS GAME! It feels redundant to have to type out a review when all I'm going to say is a bunch of ways to say "GET THIS GAME!", but if you want details... well:
This is a classic 3D platformer with clear influences from Mario and Banjo Kazooie. You've got bright, colourful worlds with unique and varied designs, even within the same hub; there is an interesting and fun cast of quirky chararacters that all serve well to keep things interesting; and most importantly, Solid gameplay that is fun. That last one is important, at no point did I feel like the game was lazily padding out the runtime for the sake of being called a long game. What's here is focused and beautifully crafted.
The controls are smooth and tight with the possible exception of the camera. Let's get one thing straight.
To Sacred 1 fans, this game is a total disaster and an affront to old fans like myself.
To everyone else, this is an amazing CASUAL game where you sit on the couch and you play on the controller with your buddies.
This game can't be considered a true-to-Sacred game. You will be severely disappointed if you expect awesome loot sets, lots of cities and landscapes to explore, dragons to slay, and quests to undertake. It's NOT that kind of game. Sacred 3 is not Sacred 1 or 2. Not even remotely close.
This is a pure, casual hack'n'slash with terrible humor (that I love, because I'm a pun-man), cheesiness, and just plain fun. The game does not take itself serious. Even the bad guys joke about craving fish. This is not your in-depth Witcher story RPG, nor your immersion-filled world explorer like the old Sacred was.
The only thing that this game beats Sacred 1 at is the humor. Quite literally, the small, sarcastic remarks your Seraphim would make in S1 this game is saturated with that.
It beats Sacred 2 only with its camera. S2 camera was awful, but that's another topic for another time.
That said, would I recommend this game? Yes, because I'm 25 now and I have become a filthy casual. When I was a teen, I had all the time in the world to play Sacred. And I did. And I kicked♥♥♥♥♥with my level 206 Battlemage who destroyed everyone online. Those were the days. Those were times when I could play 12 hours a day and not worry. But I'm an adult now. I need a game that gives me something quick, something not too serious.
This game is perfect for that. And now that we have a TV with the Steam Link hooked up to it, it's perfect to just wind down after a long day with the missus and kill some monsters without having to worry what kind of loot we need. There's no backpacks to fill up here, no too intensive skill or talent trees to build. Anyone can pick up this game and have fun with it.
Don't get thrown away by the name. Sacred 3 is everything a casual game should be, but it is nothing like its predecessors. Other than a few references to the old Ancaria and its people and cities, the game doesn't resemble the old ones. The story and world still takes place in Ancaria, but that's about it.
TL;dr: Hack'n'slash. Casual. Fun. Kill stuff. No deep immersion, just pure enjoyment. Only casuals will enjoy this.

The Long Dark - Alpha
Slowing fading away of hunger in an abandon car was not the way I was going to die.  The blizzard had been going for two hours, and only the sound of my stomach growling kept me from trying to wait it out.  The last shelter I had seen was half an hour ago and the chances of finding it in the pitch darkness were nil.  My shivering was becoming constant.  No, I would not die here in this car.

Opening the door and lighting my last flare, I knew I could end up a frozen slab of meat on the side of the highway, or worse; a warm slab of meat for a wolf or bear.  Who knows, maybe dying warm would be better...no, follow the road, there is always civilization at the end of a road, but which way?  To go back was certain death, but to go foward was to make progress.  To what exactly I could not say, but it was further from death, further from the dark.
Shivering and walking at a limping pace, the sight of my own breath was a constant reminder that I was freezing to death, and if I didn't stop my sprained ankle would never heal.  If only the storm would let up for a just minute I could find my way...my condition was only getting worse.  I did not bother to pick up fuel for a fire anymore, what was the point?  No, this would not be how it ends, this is not how I die.
I think of where I have been so far, what little I have learned about surviving in this barren wasteland.  How to start a fire, what wood is the best to use, and what clothes can protect me from the wind.  I thought about the last cabin that I last slept in, it had everything I needed.  A pot belly stove, bunks with thick sheets, and most importantly four walls and a roof to protect me from the wind.  There was so much food in it, the cans of soda, jerky, even a cooked fish.  The moment I walked in I knew I had been saved; most of the food was gone within the day.  There was no choice but to leave the cabin if I was going to survive, even had I known I was going to sprain my ankle I still had to leave.
The flare has now died and I keep walking in the dark knowing there is no going back.  All of a sudden I was hung up on something in the darkness.  Remembering the matches, I lite one and see at my feet is an overturned row boat on a frozen lake.  There must be a cabin.  I rush around in the darkness lighting matches frantically and see the small simple structure.  Entering the cold room I rush to the stove and start an emergency fire with my last acclerant.  The fire starts quickly giving me my first respite from the cold.  The dimly lit room is bare of items but under the bunk is a dusty forgotten MRE, I have hit the lottery.  Eating the packaged meal immediately the darkness slowly begins to subsides.  I purify the melted snow on the fire and drink my fill of water.
The crackling fire's warm glow begins to fill the room with heat, but it will be out in a few hours without more fuel.  I need to rest if I am going to get more wood.  I go to sleep in the bunk taking in all of its warmth.  Upon waking up the fire is out but the room is filled with light.  Eleven hours of daylight left and I have survived for three days.
I go outside to find the storm has ended and the morning sky is now a pale gold.  There is a cabin is out in the middle of the lake and I am going to need more food and fuel if I am going to survive any longer.  I start walking towards it picking up whatever loose firewood I can find along the way before stepping onto the lake.  Today could be my last day here, then again it might be tommorow.
But with every day I spend out here, I find it easier and easier to live on the edge of 'The Long Dark'.
20 minutes later I was mauled by a wolf and bled to death.

They say it's not about the destination, it's about the journey, and it couldn't be any more true with The Long Journey Home.  Three jumps in, and my crew vastly underestimated how vital it is be keep on top of fuel. Life support systems fail, all but one of my crew dies from suffocation, to be rescued by an emergency refueling drone summoned by a hail mary distress signal. It is now my Botanist, alone with his prized plant from Earth, left to struggle against an unforgiving, uncaring universe.
I've yet but scratched the surface of The Long Journey Home, but I'm already mesmerized. The gameplay is similar to a mix of FTL, and Sunless Sea. Old timers who remember the game Starflight from the 1990s will be thrilled, it seems to nod in homage to many similar elements.
The biggest element of frustration, aside from the roguelike elements of RNG games,  can come from the orbiting and lander mechanics, players familiar with Kerbal Space Program may find the orbiting mechanics familar, while those new to it will likely find it a source of extreme frustration from the learning curve.
The lander mechanics can be downright seemingly oppresive, you WILL crash and burn, my first landing outside of the tutorial had me careen into a mountainside and cause systems failure. As the old adage goes, sometimes all you learn from failure is that you failed, but in games like these the joys of overcoming such hardships are the driving force of the game.
Story mode seeks to quell a bit of the brutal difficulty, a response in turn to alot of complaints of difficulty, it's almost imperative you choose this option for a first time playthrough. The Devs are listening!
For those who enjoy a triumph in the face of adversity (Alot, alot of unforigiving adversity,) the story of your Long Journey Home may be one of your best gaming experiences, I'm one failed journey home, and I'm positively thrilled with my experience so far.

Limbo is 2D puzzle platformer hailed as an artistic masterpiece for its black and white style. Solid objects are always pure black and the eerie backgrounds are beautiful tones of grey. You'll start in a deadly forest and work your way through even deadlier factories and sewers. Everything in the game is deadly, falling too far, crushed into a pile of goo, impaled on spikes, bear traps, mutilated by saw blades, giant spiders, horrifying insects and even shallow water. You will feel every death, the game will show the boy's body being torn apart and the white eyes turn to black. Then you'll restart from the last checkpoint. The restarting from the checkpoint feels like it takes a second too long for a game with so many deaths.
The controls are simple, left and right to move, a jump button and an interact button. Sadly the up doubles as a jump button, which can sometimes result in deaths when using an analog stick. The other button is a use button that is good for pushing and pulling objects, which plays a big part in traversal (puzzle solving). The game makes use of physics and momentum, objects can fall, wheels will roll, crush and in later levels there is reverse gravity. Objects have buoyancy and will float, except for your character, making for water puzzles (traversal). One of the most unique elements to the game are the brain slugs that will force you to move forward with no stopping until they hit a light where you then turn around. That shows some out of the box creativity.
You'll make it through the quick game if you just keep playing. There's nothing really that requires skill since this is puzzle solving. Its more like stand here, jump there, pull this, jump on that. Everything has been done before, but this just makes it look really good. For the explorers out there, you can find 10 or so eggs in the game that unlock a challenging secret level.
Overall, its a good game that hangs its hat on its art style. I'm not sure if its worth $10 anymore, you can find it on sale.

Sunless Sea is the sibling game to the fantastic text-based browser game Fallen London. It allows you to explore more of the atmospheric Neath and really does a great job of fleshing out the world with the trademark writing Failbetter is so good at. Sail a ship around the Sunless Sea and balance light between terror and fuel, encountering strange monsters and even stranger islands along the way.
Sunless Sea IS NOT FOR EVERYBODY. If you prefer a more fast-paced or "action-y" experience, you will probably not enjoy it. The combat mechanics are "basically functional" at best, your ship is fairly slow, and the Sea (more properly known as the Zee) is huge. But the combat is not the main point.
The point is the story. Possibly the Ztory, but I'm not sure. (Zure?)
The game shines through when you dock at an island and meet a deviless for tea. When you deliver a mostly-dead but still surprisingly lively corpse to a party. When you find two warring tribes of rats and guinea pigs. When you wash up on an island populated entierly by postmen. When you sail to the West and find the machine that powers the Sun.
Bottom line: Slow paced, atmospheric, tension building, utterly fantastic game. Perhaps try Fallen London if you want to get a taste of the writing before paying.
