I'll start by saying Parallax and The Talos Principle are
first-person puzzlers of the past 12 months.  At their core, they are each archetypal puzzle games: begin at a starting point and arrive at a predetermined goal with the means provided using logic and reasoning. Like any well-constructed puzzle game, the levels start simple and gradually become more complex while introducing more concepts which build upon themselves.
However, they are also much different from one another. TTP is immersed in a story which drives and motivates the player (much like Myst or Portal) with its mystery and philosophical ideas. It has large, beautiful environments that provide enough to explore and add to the experience.  Parallax is a straightforward puzzler. There is no story, no environments or landscapes to explore, nothing -- just level after level of puzzles. But this isn't exactly a negative. The game really works in its simplicity. It somehow creates a lot of incentive in the player to move forward and to complete the game (I would say
to the extent of the recent Qbeh-1: The Atlas Cube and non-director's cut Q.U.B.E.).
The unique concept to this game are the portals to a parallel "world." The portals shouldn't be dismissed as a sort of copy of those from the Portal series. They are only alike in name and that you walk through them. The portals here lead to and from another environment that has elements connected to both environments and also has elements local to only each respective environment. The player moves to and from each environment to activate switches and traverse to other portals in order to reach the goal. The swtiches can rotate portals the opposite direction so that the player can enter once inaccessible switches or portions of the level, and the switches can even rotate portions of the level itself.
The level design is mostly very intelligent. Most have that "aha!" moment. And I really think it is because of those moments that the player is rewarded and driven. There are a small number of poorly designed levels, ones which make use of laser beams that have no purpose to the overall puzzle and only hinder the player's ability to traverse, and ones that obscure the player's ability to see where switches lead and what they activate.
It is a wonderful exercise of the mind, and it is a rewarding experience. Any fan of the genre would be sorry to miss this addition. I only hope a level editor becomes available before interest subsides.

Parallax is a fun game with cool mechanics, but I find myself a thrid of the way through the game without any challenge. It's worth picking up if you really need another puzzler.
Video Review:
(Spoiler alert in the video)
What is it?
Parallax is a black and white (or a variety of other pairs of colors that can be chosen in the settings) puzzle game. The idea is that you have portals that transport you between a blak on white world and a white on black world. These two worlds are different and what is done in one world can effect the other. You're goal is to use what you have at hand to get to the exit each time. There are booster, objects that change gravity, flippable portals and moving platforms to complicate your efforts.
Pros:
-Cool mechanics. The idea of travelling between two worlds to effect each puzzle (although not entirely novel) is a cool idea.
-Great visuals. These visuals are created by cascading portals and flipping of perspectives that can be trippy at times (in a good way).
-SImple gameplay. It's fairly obvious what you can interact with and what you can't. That helps to make the puzzles more streamline.
Cons:
-I'm a third of the way through the game and have not been challenged. The puzzles barely rquired throught to complete them. Admittedly, things like boosters and lasers havn't been introduced yet, but one would expect to see some diffuculty in the first third of a puzzle game.
-There is no penalty for death. Death came to me in the form of an endless fall, and death was a merciful companion. When you die, things do not reset. In a puzzle game that has so far been so easy, I see this as strange. There is no risk involved is you hurtle yourself to your doom.
In the end, how do I feel about Parallax? Well, (as I've said already) I got a thrid of the way though the game in twenty minutes, with no challenge. I hope that the challenge will come. As I play the game more I'll update this review. I feel that Parallax is a good idea that could have been executed a bit better. That being said, these twenty minutes have been fun. If you're looking for a puzzler, this is a decent game to check out.

If you want an action-packed game of excitement, you're in the wrong place.
If you want an exploration game with a steampunk asthetic that just oozes atmosphere, play this game.
Set in the universe of 'Fallen London', you take the role of a Zeecaptain on a mission. Who you are, and what your mission is, is entirely up to you. The narrative driven story feels like a combination of Terry Pratchet and H.P. Lovecraft.
The game itself is equal parts exploration, trading, and resource management. Run out of fuel? Scuttle the ship and start again. Run out of food? Eat the crew. "We were merciful, our knives were sharp."
The best things about this game, are the aforementioned narrative, and the soundtrack. The soundtrack is wonderful, with shanty-like tunes heard in the Fallen London port, to opressingly foreboding ambient sounds of the Frozen Norrth, and Kingeater Castle.
The only downsides to this game are the difficulty, and the learning curve. It's easy to learn what to do, but it will take time to learn what you're doing.

It's a pretty decent first-person-puzzle game. Not too dissimilar from "Portal" in the sense that you need to use circular portals in order to solve puzzles. However in "Parallax" they're fixed in place and the only way you can interact with them is rotating them by enabling switches that are placed throughout the level. Also the portals themselves aren't connected in the same dimension, there's a parallel dark world with different platforms and switches, so you have to find a path through the level using both worlds. It can be really disorienting at first when you walk through portals and expect that the level design stays the same and later on it can get really difficult to keep track of all the portals, platforms and switches. Especially when it introduces the mechanic by which you can shift gravity and walk on the walls and ceilings.
If there's one thing I'm not too fond of is that there aren't that many levels in it. 32 levels in total and it took this numbnut of a player 2.5 hours to get through all of them. The problem is that the first couple of levels of each chapter only take a few seconds or maybe up to a minute to beat, since they introduce new elements, while later ones can take between 10 and 15 minutes per level, so a few harder ones wouldn't have hurt the game. Though I guess it's not too few, "Portal" also wasn't much longer than this, so it's only a minor criticism. It's definitely worth recommending to people with good spacial awareness and a knack for puzzles that require you to think ahead two or three steps.

Parallax is a first-person puzzler with minor platforming aspects. And it's pretty great.
First off, the presentation is very appealing. The game is monochrome (though this can be changed) and rather minimalist; platforms and portals have a very crisp feel to them that looks great. Everything's very visually distinct too, rather important in a monochrome game. And the music adds to the atmosphere, playing downtempo electronic music in the "light" zone and ambient noise in the "dark" zone. It looks and sounds great.
But that would mean nothing if the gameplay itself wasn't good. But it is. The game is primarily focused around two-state objects, and puzzle solutions involve pressing the right buttons to turn the right objects the right way. Such objects include lasers, platforms, portals that take you between the game's two dimensions, and ramps that fling you into the air. There's also gravity shenanigans that happen in the later levels to make for a further level of confusion.
But surprisingly, despite how much the game works to confuse you, the puzzles are still surprisingly logical, and that's due to them being grounded in this two-state system. Figuring out the correct order of events isn't too tough with a bit of observation and a bit of experimentation, but doing so in the minimal amount of moves is the real challenge. The game's puzzles are also quite variedl; each structure is unique and most every level has a small little nuance to it not seen in previous levels to keep you thinking. I never felt bored solving the game's puzzles.
The biggest gripe I'd have is that there are a few occasions where, even solving a puzzle as optimally as possible, you're going to end up waiting around for spending some time doing nothing. It's mostly a result of the way the puzzles are designed, but there are a few instances of long transition session or having to wait on a particularly long switch. The game is also rather brief, though I'll take a brief, varied experience over a long, unnecessarily bloated one any day. Personally it took me around 5 hours to clear all the puzzles perfectly, but other people have taken twice as long or more, so it may just depend on how used you are to these kinds of puzzle games.
All in all a very enjoyable experience and definitely one I'd recommend to fans of puzzle games.

Sunless Sea is a game about exploring a vast subterranean sea. It offers permadeath and is not a roguelike. You start by gathering some supplies for a ship and then sail into the black unknown, map uncharted. The map’s cut into zones that points of interest (PoIs) can randomly spawn in, with the exception of the border PoIs being static. In every playthrough, all PoIs will be available, and thereby nearly all stories that the game has to offer. The stories are both the game’s strongest and weakest points.
Positives
Stripped entirely of story, the game would be boring: bring something here, revisit this place when, slowly (very) upgrade your ship. Standard fare. It’s the story that you come and stay for, and it kept me playing far longer than I expected to. The writing is almost always of Excellent quality. The story is fairly plausible within Fallen London’s most-anything-can-happen internal logic. I had no trouble being immersed in the atmosphere.
The graphics are pretty and the character/quality pictures are drawn well. I’ll never forget a certain moment in my first fight against a certain zee (sea) creature.
The combat is good. I feel like it could be just a little more, but it doesn’t need to be more. I personally enjoyed hunting zee beasts.
It feels like a roguelike in the regard that a minor miscalculation can ruin your voyage quickly. I remember a long procession of misery that all stemmed from my inclination to fight a bound-shark when I had low fuel, leaving me at the mercy of the gods, who happened to think sending me to a far-away DEATH ISLAND was a great means of salvation. I got so many Steam “achievements” for that one and I barely made it out alive. Was a good time!
Criticism
The islands are insular and only very rarely (do they even?) will the stories overlap between PoIs. “I need Scintillack, which you can get at this place.” does not count as two islands interacting with each other. In a way this is good because each island is manageable, but it certainly isn’t plausible and a more dynamic Sunless Sea would have been appreciated. For example, in the case of the Isle of Cats, I took a shipment from a Cat-Woman to London. I then screwed her over by selling it for double. I then returned, beat her up, and made a similar deal with a tiger who I proceeded to do the same thing to, but I never returned. That was early on and I didn’t heard a peep of it for the rest of the game.
The stories are great -- the first time. On the second playthrough, you can make different choices, but it’s still the same base story you’re playing. This diminishes replay value when the game’s drawing feature is how great the stories are. The saving grace is that I still had a few PoIs to really dig into, and the reality is the stories will less fresh when I play again in two years.
Upgrading your house and to a smaller extent, your boat, are hardly upgrades. You essentially upgrade your house to pay more to sleep in it. With boats, they get heavier and thereby slower, with the first major upgrade only offering a Forward slot for all that trouble. It comes with higher crew requirements and it’s slower, so you’re paying more than just the 3,000 echoes after the fact. Where boats should expand the gameplay or offer an alternative, you really only have access to a merchant-vessel for making (poorly defensible) big trips carrying loads of cargo, but it’s still ponderous and you can only have one ship at a time.
I broke out my mobile phone a little too often during long, boring commutes from island to island. Something should be done when the player hasn’t touched the keyboard for 15+ seconds. Only when I bought the +2,500 engine power engine did it really feel like I was blazing around -- then I upgraded the ship and it got a bit slower, buzzkill. There’s some method of getting a great engine and then going at Full Power, but I never tried it and it’d be noisy as Hell anyway.
Finally, the Supremacy mechanic could be much more fun than it really is. I made London Supreme, so where are our navy boats floating around the zee? Why did the Khan seem to give absolutely no care about it?
OVERALL

FANTASTIC first episode!
Where the Arkham games let you "Be the Batman", this one lets you be Bruce Wayne, in and out of costume, and is surprisingly deep!
The game takes place during Batman's early days, and as such features some of the classic mob elements, a still sane DA Harvey Dent, and early encounters with some of the rogues. Still, Bruce plays a large part as a main sponsor for the Dent campaign, which puts him in the eye of some powerful (good and not so good) figures in the city, and sheds a light on his legacy and the Wayne's role as Gotham's rich and finest.
As usual in Telltale games, you're usually presented with choices which change the outcome of the game, and everything you choose to say or do may or may not have some repercussion later. As the plot thickens, you start to feel the weight of your decisions. (Remember, Bruce is a most public figure, and so, his actions are noticed). However, Bruce's dual identity as the Batman bring about a few more gameplay aspects. You get to take on multiple enemies through awesome QTE sequences which really do convey Batman's snap-reflexes and skills, and you also get to show why Batman is the "world's greatest detective", examining and reconstructing crime scenes, interrogating perps, and carefully plotting your strikes.
The episode takes about 2/3 hours to complete, and the story really is engrossing, feels absolutely authentic (the dialogues, settings and characters all ring true to the comics and even some of the films), and the conclusion leaves you absolutely HYPED for the next episode.
If you're a Batman fan, love the Telltale games, or both, do yourself a favor and get this gem!

Really enjoyed this game—I knew nothing about it until a friend told me about it a couple months ago, and shrugged it off at the time. He was insistent and got me the game for my birthday, and man...am I glad he did. As Super Mario Sunshine is, was, and remains my favorite 3D platformer of all time, this game hearkens back to it, and various other late 90s-mid 2000s 3d platformers, perfectly.
The game is beautiful, the soundtrack is wonderful and charming, there's lots of cool little rewards to get (as an incentive for careful exploring), the voice acting is enjoyable to listen to (rare in this genre), and the movement (about 95% of the time) feels natural and responsive. There's enough content in here for a super slowpoke completionist like me to get 20 hours out of the game, so if you're not willing to spend $30 for that amount of playtime, steer clear. That's the only reason I'd advise caution in this release; however, the Steam Workshop is in full effect, and allowed me to experience some surprisingly amazing user-created content on top of the "official" game.
I highly recommend this game if you're into 3D platformers at all, or need a good nostalgia trip from the days of your youth (if you were born in the early-mid 90s at least). With more official content inevitably on the way, even if you're done with the game quickly you probably will still feel like you got your money's worth, due to the amount of heart and character in the game. I can't say for SURE considering I got the game for free, but still, I would have spend the money without a second thought if I knew the game was this enjoyable. And you should too! Support these awesome indie devs!

An absolutely excellent First-Person Shooter which everyone should play at some point, despite its flaws.
It's impossible to properly review this game without spoiling certain plot points, as the discovery of the world around you is one of the game's greatest strengths, so I will simply leave the story content - which is the game's forte - at that. From a gameplay perspective, it is sadly starting to show its age (for example, there are two methods of fighting - guns and Plasmids, or the game's form of magic - which require you to toggle between the two instead of having both available together), but the game was designed with those limitations in mind so it is largely non-intrusive. Aside from that, there are portions of the game which seem to drag on a little too long, and the game would have been better served by a different ending sequence, but these are all only seemingly glaring because they're compared to the rest of the game.
Very highly recommended for all those who have any interest in first person shooters, and even those who don't particularly care for the format, but enjoy a good story and will tolerate it.

I absolutely love this game man! Absolute gem! It is definately the most innovative game I've played in years! The best thing about this game is how badass it feels to complete a level and to then watch your replay.
Quite some people seem to complain about the length of the game compared to the price. And even though I agree it should be a longer game considering the price, I don't mind at all! The replayability is definately there, especially because the developers added over ten challenge modes. These challenge modes are pretty interesting and most definately add a new challenge to the game! There also is an endless mode which is just as fun aswell. The game also has a lot of easter eggs which quite fun to discover. They are pretty rewarding aswell.
I completely recommend this game, but it does have it's minor issues. The story mode is not all that interesting, and even though that wouldn't normally mind me, the fact that most of the 'cutscenes' are unskippable is very annoying. But this isn't that much of a problem, because after you finished the story mode once, you will never have any cutscenes again. And the majority of the fun I have had was after I completed the story.
As for bugs, I have played this game a lot (like a LOT) and I have not been bothered with any bugs ever. Except for one bug, which is that the killstagram doesn't work (for me). The game allows you to save your replays and it is supposed to automatically upload your replay to killstagram, which is a website. But this isn't too big of a deal, because all the replays that you saved are still stored on your computer.
In conclusion, the game is amazingly fun, maybe just a bit short, but that's only if you don't consider the great replayability. The unskippable cutscenes are annoying, but there aren't that many, so that's not a big deal.
If you ask me, it would be a dream come true if Valve bought the game and created a SUPERHOT2, which would be just as amazing as Portal2!

Now that the gushing is over:
Pros:
- Difficulty: Don't think you're going to just triapse across the wilderness and survive. It keeps you on your toes constantly, which is part of why its so damn addicting.
- Simplistic design: at times, the game is beautiful.
- Mechanics: Gameplay is smooth and straightforward (although, sometimes you get randomly screwed over, but hey, its not supposed to be a cakewalk).
- No multiplayer: FINALLY
-Developers: Actively involved in the community, you can tell they want to make the game shine.
- NO ZOMBIES
Cons:
- The RNG gods hate you at higher difficulty levels.
- How frustrating it is at times is both a pro and a con i think.
- No story mode yet :( (patiently waiting though)

If I wait until I exhaust all the possible scenarios Sunless Sea has to offer before I write my review.....there will never be a review. I love love love this game. Imagine a Victorian Steampunk world with a heavy dose of Lovecraftian goodness and a Choose Your Own Adventure style of playing, and you get SUNLESS SEA!
First the positives. There is absolutely tons of material. Readers will love this game because there are so many stories and it would be impossible to cover them all with one captain. You give your captain a history and profession, and depending on what you choose will determine your crew and your stats. You then head out into the black sea to explore and discover. You can either choose to find your father's bones, amass a lot of sea stories for a book, or retire wealthy in your seaside mansion. While you are pursuing your goals, there is also your crew members. Like in Mass Effect, they have interesting side missions and also help boost your stats. There is also the romance option. The music in this game is very original and is enjoyable to listen to as you play.
Now for the potential negatives (for me this game is almost perfect). This game is not for everyone, and I would be lying if I said that I didn't see how other people couldn't adore this game as much as I do. First of all, don't play this when you are tired. Since you have to read everything, you need to be awake and alert, or the game can come off as boring. Also, there are no cut scenes, voice overs, or AAA graphics. If any of these things turn you off, do not invest in this game. You will die A LOT. But that is okay because you are supposed to. With each captain you learn more about the harsh world you are playing in and your strategy improves. However, many will probably not like having to die a lot to achieve headway.
For me, this game is highly enjoyable. It may not be for everyone, but for those who love stories and a steam punk Victorian setting, it is a gem. If you are wondering whether this game is for you, check out the game Fallen London done by Failbetter Games. It is free and it gives one a good idea of the gameplay storywise. I look forward to many many more hours of exploration and new stories.

Sunless Sea does everything it sets out to do.  Buuut those goals aren't necessarily good ones to have.  This game is basically two in one.  When you're in port, the game is about using key items to unlock the storylines, which affect other storylines.  You pick up new officers, gain political connections, become a black market dealer,...acquire questionable dining habits.  All of that is fun and awesome and I love it.  The Fallen London universe, which I only know from SS at the moment, is beautifully imagined and I just want to learn every square inch of the Unterzee and just what the hell is the Dawn Machine, anyways?
Trouble is I don't want to have to wait hours for it.  The second part of the game involves real-time travel between the islands of the zee, fighting pirates and killing sea monsters.  The combat is terrible.  Either you exploit predictable patterns to annihilate them or you're just banged into until you or they die.  It's annoying and rarely profitable.  I only ever killed anything when a story required it, otherwise I found it a waste of time.  And that's the problem with Sunless Sea, you waste a lot of time.  They created a beautiful and fascinating world, visually as well (seriously, wtf is the Dawn Machine?) but it takes so long to get around it I started to lose my mind for real.   On one tour, through re-stocking of supplies, I was out at sea for two hours of real time, and very little of that time was spent in port uncovering stories or even just doing basic moneymaking tasks like cursory investigations and shore leave.  nearly all of my 30+ hours at Zee were spent navigating through very non-treacherous waters watching my fuel gauge slowly dip.
The term 'Roguelike' is a flag of convenience in Sunless Sea.  When you die, you take over as a new character.  You repeat the storylines, which go much faster now that you know them, and you get something of your predecessor's gains in the process.  But, as they say in Venderbight, death doesn't come easily in the Neath.  I only actually 'died' once in my game, and that was by choice because I'd locked myself out of a story and, really, I was curious about what death was like.  If you've made a will, you get more stuff.  But some of the most important gains like money, your ship, and your stats, are largely lost.  In a typical roguelike, where a runthrough lasts fifteen minutes to half an hour, this isn't so bad.  But in Sunless Sea, where a single captain could zail for a full day of real time, opening the whole map and resolving lots of stories, death is less like "take two' and more like "my little brother deleted my save and now I have to start over."  The mechanic isn't fun.
That's kind of crippling for Sunless Sea.  The game is designed 'almost' roguelike.  But instead of focusing on short individual runs and long term meta-gains, the individual runs are where long-term gains are made and the meta is more about salvaging something from the disaster.  And those gains come with such a time investment that losing them is enough to make you want to quit.
Despite these problems, I still recommend it.  Because this game is very rich in lore, atmosphere, and humor, things I really appreciate in a game.  The fun dies around the twenty hour mark because the more complicated quests require more and more 'downtime' in transit.  But up until then you'll have a lot of fun and find yourself laughing at the delightfully macabre refinement of Fallen London and the Unterzee's inhabitants.  It's a worthwhile pickup, but it'll run its course a little fast for the pricetag.

Preface: This review was written after completing the game with all Perfect ranks.
Parallax is one of these small gems you tend to overlook while browsing through the vast collection of games Steam has to offer. Nowadays every new puzzle game has to have a unique gimmick to it to make it interesting and challenging for the player. In Parallax's case, it's parallel dimensions coupled with some gravity defying platforms in the later levels. The challenge is fair and balanced and the difficulty increases steadily as you progress through the game. While some levels can look quite intimidating at first, with a bit of thought, careful planning and memorization you can beat everything fairly fast and achieve perfect level completion within very few actions.
Even if Parallax doesn't break any new grounds in the audiovisual department, its simple yet futuristic looking monochromatic art style along with electronic beats lend themselves well to the game creating a pleasant overall experience.
The game's price is perfect for its length of 4 chapters with 8 levels each and it still has a lot of replayability to offer after completion. As of March 14th 2015, the developers have already added a game mode specifically designed for speedrunners, which will exponentially increase Parallax's lifespan.
If you're a fan of first person puzzle games that are not only well designed, but offer substantial replay value, then you mostly likely already own Parallax. On the slim chance you don't, buy it. You certainly won't regret the purchase.
The Good:
- Balanced difficulty
- Very good level design
- Simple, but fitting audiovisuals
- Good replay value
The Bad:
- Might be too short for some players

This is a great puzzle game, a little like Portal but different. Here the 'Portals' are fixed, and like mirrors have a front and a back face - Only side transports you to an 'inverse' dimension and the other side acts as a blocker. Switches and wires link to mechanisms that can spin these faces around to help you reach the exit.
The individual elements of the game are pretty simple and it breaks you in gently with the first few puzzles, but things get quite a bit more complex in the end. Getting your head around what's happening in each dimension at the same time as working out how to use the mechanisms is very rewarding.
The graphics are simple and you can change the two colours involved, but you are still limited to only two colours. This is a good thing in a way, as the game runs very smoothly and does not clutter up your screen with unnecessary details. There's no story or enemies in the game, although it does have a weird inter-dimensional atmosphere and some mood music. Really this is all you need - The puzzles are very good and are allowed to stand as the main feature of the game.
I'd definitely recommend it.

I absolutely love this game man! Absolute gem! It is definately the most innovative game I've played in years! The best thing about this game is how badass it feels to complete a level and to then watch your replay.
Quite some people seem to complain about the length of the game compared to the price. And even though I agree it should be a longer game considering the price, I don't mind at all! The replayability is definately there, especially because the developers added over ten challenge modes. These challenge modes are pretty interesting and most definately add a new challenge to the game! There also is an endless mode which is just as fun aswell. The game also has a lot of easter eggs which quite fun to discover. They are pretty rewarding aswell.
I completely recommend this game, but it does have it's minor issues. The story mode is not all that interesting, and even though that wouldn't normally mind me, the fact that most of the 'cutscenes' are unskippable is very annoying. But this isn't that much of a problem, because after you finished the story mode once, you will never have any cutscenes again. And the majority of the fun I have had was after I completed the story.
As for bugs, I have played this game a lot (like a LOT) and I have not been bothered with any bugs ever. Except for one bug, which is that the killstagram doesn't work (for me). The game allows you to save your replays and it is supposed to automatically upload your replay to killstagram, which is a website. But this isn't too big of a deal, because all the replays that you saved are still stored on your computer.
In conclusion, the game is amazingly fun, maybe just a bit short, but that's only if you don't consider the great replayability. The unskippable cutscenes are annoying, but there aren't that many, so that's not a big deal.
If you ask me, it would be a dream come true if Valve bought the game and created a SUPERHOT2, which would be just as amazing as Portal2!

I have mixed feelings about this game. What I personally liked about the game was the various characters you could play as (base game- 4 and all DLC- 6), which I greatly enjoyed. It is also within these characters you can play different playstyles (some are the same as others though). It is also a good game to play with firends as it is clearly made for it given some of the mechanics. However, this game has some glaring flaws. First, this game has very little in common with previous Sacred games as other reviews will tell you. Secondly, this game is very simple. Almost every level is "watch out for falling rocks" or "turn the wheel six times." The final big point I will state is the dialogue. This tries to be funny but will fall short and become annoying. In fact, the bosses even have jokes in their intro, clearly mimicing Borderlands. It also felt like every 20 seconds Aria, your telepathic companion, pesters you about not doing the objective, even though you are currently swamped by enemies. Overall, I would recommend doing what I did. Just get this game on sale ( I got it for $4) with all the DLC and grab a copy for your buddy. It will at least be a fun few hours.

This is a great game but not those who seek a casual exprience or to have their hand held the entire way. This game is difficult and is supposed to be difficult. It is to simulate the desperation of the long journey home with a ship and crew that are not prepared for it. It is a great game that challenge you to balance risk and rewards in your decisions. How confident are you in your landing skill to get that one resources? All of this challenges make it more rewarding when you finally reach home.
Below is some of the common complain people have and my own opinion on the matter.
- Landing control is hard. To some degree, yes this is true. It will take time to learn the nuances of the control. Good news is, even with rogue difficulty, crash landing is mostly forgiving. You will just end up with a few less hull point, instead of you know, exploding. Learn from your mistakes.
- It is impossible to land on high danger planet. It is supposed to be impossible or almost impossible on planet with high danger rating, at least at first. You can, along your journey, install devices that nullify high gravity, high wind or extreme heat.
- Sometime the random seed gave me a bad start. Sadly that's the reality of a random generated universe. On the other side, you can try story mode, which tone down the difficulty in general or just reroll or find another seed from someone else.
- Stuff kept on breaking randomly. This is an abstract mechanism to simulate the randomness of space. This would be a very annoying, IF, one single part breaking down mean the end of your ship. It does not. You can have all of the devices broken down and you can still continue. It just mean that some function of your craft become less effective. This forced you to decide, do you want to continue on or find the nearest space port. This also play on the desperation of the journey. The ship wasn't design for this and yet it have to continue.
Ultimately, this game is designed in such way that you have to earn your fun through learning your mistakes and improving your decision making. If you do not like that, well then, this game isn't for you after all.

TL;DR: Buy this game, it's amazing and fun.
Long review:
I bought the game as a birthday gift to myself and am incredibly pleased. It's fun, entertaining, and has more depth than you might suspect. The art style is simple and clean. Game play is simple to learn while offering great challenge.
Resource management is efficient: Wood, Stone, Food, and Crystals are the basic four to be gathered from the map. They can each be refined into secondary, advanced resources.
Your citizens are not directly managed other than being able to pick them up and move them around. They operate by AI based on how you manage your village development. This saves a lot of click and drag that bogs down other titles. It was a great design choice. Citizens also level up based on their work, becoming more efficient and stronger over time.
Your village succeeds or fails based on your method of developing it, and defending it. Monsters will start attacking your village within a few days of starting it. The game brings in aspects of RTS games and Tower Defense as your primary combat systems. Much of your defense is managed by tower construction and building obstacles to slow the advance of attacking nasties.
The game can be played in settings from Sandbox mode to Nightmare mode, meaning from "no monsters" to "Do you feel lucky, punk?" The hardest level can pose a challenge to the most advanced village-building gamer.
The game is not complete, but updates are frequent. The developer is present on the Steam forums and hosts Twitch streams to keep players up to date with development. He's also very interactive with the player base and open to new ideas. This is the kind of developer who keeps improving the game and providing new content on a regular basis. Check in on his streams, you'll like the guy and his video-bombing cat.
I give this game a 10/10 because it's great as is, getting better all the time, and the developer is a fantastic example of how to conduct business when creating a game.

If you're not easily emotionally manipulated or otherwise do not get emotionally invested in a piece of media, LIMBO is not worth the purchase.
Outside of that highly subjective criteria, LIMBO's positive points are few and far between. It is "Another World" with a monochromatic art style, ragdoll physics, and absolutely none of the tight narrative focus that, while lacking in dialogue, drove "Another World" to the status of cult classic. It is a cinematic platformer without the cinema, relying on the "feel" over the execution.
On a technical level, LIMBO is not just competent but surprisingly well done. The platforming is precise, the hitboxes are accurate, the many different platforming mechanics the game throws at you all perfectly executed and without a single glitch or snag in sight. But on a design level it is atrocious - long stretches of simply heading right, stock puzzles and cliche mechanics that aren't even explored particularly indepth before being forgotten about. It quickly becomes a chore for anyone who's touched a small-budget platformer before.
The game does have its high points - with the secret level in particular actually exploring the mechanics indepth and being well worth playing, but those are few and far between the boring standard puzzles that make the game feel like it belongs on Newgrounds.
On the whole I can't recommend paying for this game - if you want superb platformer, play Super Meat Boy or Dustforce. If you want a well-done cinematic platformer, play Abe's Odyssey, Flashback or Another World. If you want to play a simple, fairly boring platformer whose redeeming points have to be actively sought to see, play LIMBO.

For me, this game is a real big thing. You've got to explore the universe in your own ship, with your own crew. You have to manage ressources and your social connections. You have to make decisions. So, if you are looking for a game, in what you can get in and play with action and ease, then maybe move on or at least try story mode. But if you like to learn, if you like to reflect on what's good or bad, what gives you advantages or disadvantages, then go and buy!
The dialogues with the races - or even the races itself - are very entertaining. Every race has its own history, its own characteristics and follow ups.
The graphics are, so far, nothing that can be compared to a "Mass Effect" or similar... but that's not one of the main features of the game. Nevertheless the artworks are really, really great. The graphics style is exactly what this game needs. You fly to a planet and - after some hours of play, you WILL notice, what the planet will be like. Is it poisenous? Is it hot? Is there high gravity?
And even when you pass the sun, you really got the feeling, that YOU are THERE.
I could write so much more about this game... there are so many "little" mechanics, which are fun. Consequences, story, reasonability, farming, diplomacy..... and so on....
But for now I will stop writing and start playing!
FYI: The developer (e.g. AndiDev) is very present on twitch. You'll get many information from streams with him.

The Long Dark - Alpha
Slowing fading away of hunger in an abandon car was not the way I was going to die.  The blizzard had been going for two hours, and only the sound of my stomach growling kept me from trying to wait it out.  The last shelter I had seen was half an hour ago and the chances of finding it in the pitch darkness were nil.  My shivering was becoming constant.  No, I would not die here in this car.

Opening the door and lighting my last flare, I knew I could end up a frozen slab of meat on the side of the highway, or worse; a warm slab of meat for a wolf or bear.  Who knows, maybe dying warm would be better...no, follow the road, there is always civilization at the end of a road, but which way?  To go back was certain death, but to go foward was to make progress.  To what exactly I could not say, but it was further from death, further from the dark.
Shivering and walking at a limping pace, the sight of my own breath was a constant reminder that I was freezing to death, and if I didn't stop my sprained ankle would never heal.  If only the storm would let up for a just minute I could find my way...my condition was only getting worse.  I did not bother to pick up fuel for a fire anymore, what was the point?  No, this would not be how it ends, this is not how I die.
I think of where I have been so far, what little I have learned about surviving in this barren wasteland.  How to start a fire, what wood is the best to use, and what clothes can protect me from the wind.  I thought about the last cabin that I last slept in, it had everything I needed.  A pot belly stove, bunks with thick sheets, and most importantly four walls and a roof to protect me from the wind.  There was so much food in it, the cans of soda, jerky, even a cooked fish.  The moment I walked in I knew I had been saved; most of the food was gone within the day.  There was no choice but to leave the cabin if I was going to survive, even had I known I was going to sprain my ankle I still had to leave.
The flare has now died and I keep walking in the dark knowing there is no going back.  All of a sudden I was hung up on something in the darkness.  Remembering the matches, I lite one and see at my feet is an overturned row boat on a frozen lake.  There must be a cabin.  I rush around in the darkness lighting matches frantically and see the small simple structure.  Entering the cold room I rush to the stove and start an emergency fire with my last acclerant.  The fire starts quickly giving me my first respite from the cold.  The dimly lit room is bare of items but under the bunk is a dusty forgotten MRE, I have hit the lottery.  Eating the packaged meal immediately the darkness slowly begins to subsides.  I purify the melted snow on the fire and drink my fill of water.
The crackling fire's warm glow begins to fill the room with heat, but it will be out in a few hours without more fuel.  I need to rest if I am going to get more wood.  I go to sleep in the bunk taking in all of its warmth.  Upon waking up the fire is out but the room is filled with light.  Eleven hours of daylight left and I have survived for three days.
I go outside to find the storm has ended and the morning sky is now a pale gold.  There is a cabin is out in the middle of the lake and I am going to need more food and fuel if I am going to survive any longer.  I start walking towards it picking up whatever loose firewood I can find along the way before stepping onto the lake.  Today could be my last day here, then again it might be tommorow.
But with every day I spend out here, I find it easier and easier to live on the edge of 'The Long Dark'.
20 minutes later I was mauled by a wolf and bled to death.

Six months ago, I enjoyed this game. Wolf aggression in anything but the lowest level seemed extremely exaggerated, but hey-- at least one game level setting fixed that.  Menus worked, environment was realistic enough, item and animal placement made sense.  And then... things changed.  This game is constantly under development, which means sometimes changes are made for the good, and sometimes, well, they are made for the bad.  Unfortunately, the bad changes very often stick for good, because the game developers seem to completely ignore player input on what is and isn't working.  What was a playable game six months ago has become completely unplayable now-- white on white text, difficult to organize item menus, tiny text/big pictures on items that are unrecognizeable by picture alone.  This whole game depends on being able to navigate your items quickly and effectively, and you just can't any more; what's more, for six months players have been posting and complaining about these things, and still nothing has been done to un-do the 'fix' which made these problems happen in the first place.  My advice:  pick another survival title, or wait to get this one until they quit messing with it and you know what you're buying.  I know I wouldn't have wasted the cash.

This is one of those games that has sat in my Steam library for years in the 'Another Artsy Indie Game I'll Try Someday' category.
And now I wish I had tried it sooner.
The first time your character gets decapitated by a bear trap, you will feel a tingle up your spine. When the spider catches you and spins you into its web, you will shudder with revulsion. When you finally (and brutally) tear the final leg from the spider's  body, you will marvel at how satisfying such a gruesome act could be.
And all this is after just 48 minutes of playing the game! Any game that can tap my emotions so deftly will earn a resounding recommendation from me, regarless of how good/bad/ugly those emotions happen to be. Bonus points for acheiving this feat in such a minimalist environment with no vocals/text or any other in-game guidance (other than said environment itself).
Final thought: I don't enjoy horror games. While this game has caused me to feel terror, I don't clasify it as 'horror'. This game is not violent or scary for the sake of being violent/scary, but uses the induced emotional state as a mechanic within the game (although you may not realize this at first).
Duly recommended.

If I could give this game a thumbs sideways then that's what it would get.
It's a decent roguelike with a lot of depth to it and an immense amount of lore to explore.
The difficulty level is set at just the right level to give you the "one more turn" effect.
However, all the good content, lore, and interesting quests are hidden behind a slow grind for cash. It's not the same kind of grind you would get in a dungeon delving roguelike where you gradually get stronger so that you can delve deeper. It's the kind of grind where you have to do the same trade routes repeatedly with no variation just so you can save up for a slightly bigger/faster/better ship to do it all again.
Repetition is the heart of a roguelike, learning the systems and going at them again and again, but a good one will pepper each life with something interesting and new; and this is where Sunless Sea fails to hit the spot. There's just not enough there at the start to justify getting to the end.
It's worth buying at a sub $10 price, but it won't be a game that endears itself for years to come. Buy it or don't.

This is obviously a project of pure passion by the entire team over at Gears for Breakfast; you couldn't get a game of this calibre otherwise. And the camera was about to be my ONLY complaint about the game, but then I realized that they added an option to change the camera to however you like it! So, there goes my only complaint about the game.
The team over at Gears for Breakfast are ALL about community. They LOVE mods, they encourage it, and they love showing off the best and the funniest of them. Probably one of the most active Twitter profiles for a game that I've ever seen, and a very lively and friendly development team. A Hat in Time is exactly what it advertises and more, being a 'cute as heck 3D platformer' inspired by original classics of the genre doesn't even begin to describe how awesome this game is. Shattered any expectations I had of it.
Should you get it?: Absolutely. This is my personal Game of the Year, no doubt. I'm already way excited about the updates to come to this game, and if you get the game, I hope you will be too.

review:
Dungeon Defenders II. The sequel to Dungeon Defenders I. Last game, the focus was a Tower Defence with First-Person Combat on the side. This game, it's the opposite. It's a mix of Sanctum 2, and a bland MMORPG game. Not necessarily a bad combination, at least in my opinion. You can either go in, collecting and equipping items only for boosting your damage, instead of focusing on the other aspect of the game, Tower Defence. Towers, they do not do as much as would seem viable for a game which has them as one of the two subjects. Only barricades are actually needed. You can go into a match and be able to just place a few walls here and there, on chokepoints or in corridoors, then take out the whole enemy squadron using nothing but your 'Wizardly Stick of Purple Flames and♥♥♥♥♥♥. Or, well, that's my experience. You can have geat on yourself to only help make your Towers and Defences more powerful. Health. Damage. Range. Speed. Those sorts of upgrades. Minor numbers, however, you will not be seeing a Catapult dealing 203 Octillion damage within 2.7 seconds (approx). You will mainly be using your weapons instead of your skills, too, I actually have forgotten that they even exist in my few latest missions. Unless, well, you are too weak. Then, they will become useful. Otherwise, the damage does not scale too well, my weapons are truly able to take care of all problems. Weapons aside, other parts of the game include:
+ Skill Trees.
+ Private and Public HUBs.
+ Matchmaking system (not the best at all).
+ Daily Missions.
+ "First Win" modifiers.
+ NPC merchants.
+ A bunch of maps and difficulties.
+A Terraria crossover.
- Not much endgame content.
- A really bad UI in the Inventory menu, especially trying to sell all your loot.
- Inventory being spammed by items which were useless, even 5 levels below.
The RPG element, it's... Satisfactory. Put the bar, well, not too high though. It's not yet finished and the minor flaws, are a lot in number. The gameplay, though repetitive, it is alright enough for me to carry on a little longer. I recommend playing with a friend, however, as the matchmaking system is, well, about as basic as a stick and stone. Sure, you can say how strong players must be in order to be able to join the lobby, but there's not much else to it. But, the levelling and progression aren't that great or a real "wow cool" moment. They're more of an "ok..." moment. You can't care less. Especially while you're in a mission, and reach a certain level when you unlock something new, then there's this huge black box which takes up a lot of the screen. Disturbing. Unneeded. The weapons, I have mixed feelings about. There should be a way to filter things when in your inventory, from best to worst. Or, only let us have collected some real goodies instead of the same trashy ring from level 2 or so we still get on one of these endgame missions, for whatever reason. Just, let us have the useful gear when we need it. Not some OP gear before we reach that level. Not some weapon which deals feathercuts in terms of damage.
Endgame. Endgame. What do you mean, endgame? There is not much endgame. There is repeating missions, however. But no real endgame. There's harder difficulties. Those are fine. But something which is just unfairly difficult but actually accomplishable, is not. I want to feel I have done enough Radiation damage to take out a good 20x15x30xkm blast in the planet, while I am trying to survive with all of my thoughts and mind on the task. Something which is a real kicker. You either are dying all the time, or only die because you fell off the map because of the very slippery movement. Not much inbetween. Either Zeus or a peasent. The closest experience to such a thing in Dungeon Defenders II is going to be a Nightmare mode mission, or the gear, or the pets.

This brings me onto my next point: pets. It's an RPG. There will be pets. You can either buy pet eggs using paid currency, or find them from some more difficult and later missions in the game, then hatch those eggs. There's different eggs, each bringing a different theme of creature. From dragons to cats. All pets have their own powers, damage types, rarities, really what you could expect. They're not too great when  you first get them. Their at their hatchling/junior stage, and have not been evolved or powered up in any way. This costs time, and money. The latter is not a problem at all, as you can easily grind a ton of gold within 2 hours. I have actually not needed to grind for gold at any stage in the game so far, actually. In order to evolve your pet, you must first fill up its 'Affection' bar, which is how often or how much you've been using that pet in missions. After the evolution, your pet will grow up a bit, changing the looks and stats. It's a simple system but I don't mind it at all in the game, just seems a bit bland what you could do with a pet, as they do not deal that much damage, though, they are not meant to, they are meant to act as a support for your character.
Characters. There's classes: Squire, Monk, Huntress, Apprentice (The main ones), with some others which are more difficult to unlock. Some are more poweful in certain situations than others. The Apprentice has stronger towers than the Squire, however, the trade of lower base HP for them, is the price. The Monk has some powerful towers, such as ones which automatically damage enemies unlucky enough to walk into them. And do they damage. They damage a ton. He also can play a Supportive class as he has a healing tower to help back up your noob teammates if they die too quickly or too often. The Squire is a tank and can deal damage relatively nicely. Just what you could expect. Not much more to talk about. The Huntress is a ranged bow-user. A Ranger or Archer. Good damage. Good range. Overall, the characters are all used for different situations, and they deal with them in different ways.
That's all I have for now. Potential. Not yet met.
~Wilkowaty

I have zero experience with any BB games, but I like dice games and strategy, and this title sort of reminded me of the old battle chess games.
The basics are pretty easy to get a handle on, simple strategies can be learned by playing a few games against the AI and watching how they move and make formations.
All in all, I've found it to be a so-so experience. I like the idea of permadeaths, character upgrades, and getting to tune your team a little bit to fit your playstyle. Graphics might seem a touch dated, but it doesn't really effect a title like this.
What sh-ts me off the most is I'm convinced the AI cheats.
- 4 out of 5 of my kick-offs are somehow negative (high kick etc), yet I have not seen the AI once get a high kick or anything else. It's to the point where I just assume that anytime I kick the ball it's gonna start out with some benefit to the AI.
- AI rolls a single dice, knockdown with a knockout.
- You roll 3d6, 3x critical failures (attacker self knockdown).
- You roll 2d6, 2x critical failures -> use a team reroll -> 2x more critical failures.
Seriously, what are the statistical odds of this? I have literally seen the AI roll an attacker knockdown only once, ONCE, in 4.5 hours of playing versus the AI.
I can't speak for multiplayer because I don't really enjoy multiplayer. I'd refund this if I could and get BB1 based on my personal play preferences, but since I can't, I will play it little by little - maybe finish the campaign, get my 11 dollars worth of "entertainment" and never touch it again.
Oh and one final thing, my game just soft-crashed (cursor still visible and moving, and sounds indicating keyboard presses were interfacing the game, but rest of the screen gone black - and yes, I literally updated my drivers yesterday)

Parallax is a fun and creative first-person puzzle game where you have to tackle not one, but two overlapping worlds, trying to solve each level's complex puzzle/s, in a timely fun, mind scratching, and "wait, what?" manner.
The game has a simple graphic style that's customizable if you don't like the black and white, with extremely slick and smooth, not filled with unnecessary flashiness, main menu and UI, which I really appreciate considering most games have slow responding menu and UI.
The controls are simple with normal movements and a mouse click interaction. The soundtrack is neat and fitting with how the game looks, and just overall the game has a slick smooth gameplay experience with a lot of creative puzzles that look really cool and is actually fun to play around in. I couldn't find the Vodka though.
There isn't a story or anything in the game, unless it's hidden and I couldn't find it, it's just a straight out fun puzzle game with a handful of them to finish, and I had fun solving all the puzzles, confusing at times of course, but with how the levels were designed, making me think with dimensional portals, I had a fun time solving them. For the asking price and for the creative fun content you'll play around with, it's definitely worth the purchase and playthrough.
Also, I'm hoping that the developers would think of adding a level editor and Steam workshop for community created levels, if the game sells well, and if that's the case, then buy two copies, because if it has a level editor and new levels coming in, the value of the game doubles in my eyes, so let's hope it sells well to merit a level editor.

My Quick Look:
Parallax is a first person puzzler, in the same vein as Portal.  There are portals, but they transport you to an inverse world that may or may not have the same platforming elements.  The whole of Parallax is governed by extremely simple rules yet the puzzles can get extremely complex as you iterate through the chapters, requiring you to keep another world in your head as you manipulate the inverse world to bend the other.
The game is also executed perfectly.  Each chapter introduces a new iteration of puzzle design that "shows you the ropes" and from there the puzzles get progressively harder.  Game runs smooth like butter even when downsampling from 3200x1800.
Recommended.

I played this game quite a lot before i got it on steam. Perhaps players get frustrated expecting it to be a RPG series parts 1 and 2 successor. Well it's not. It's an action couch/coop game in hack and slash tradition. Made for those who don't like to pass an entry threshold of a full time RPG to prepare themselves in terms of character/items and get ready for multiplayer/online game. It's like get your weapon (keyboard/controller) and play some missions with friends.
I did enjoy this game. Some pros and cons from where i see it:
pros:
+ combat arts customization like for pure damage or crowd control (freeze / stun)
+ weapon selection (though every class has a top pick which makes the other two not really needed from a midgame)
+ weapon spirits add variety to playstyle
+ graphics and animation
+"skirmish" type side missions
+ Good boss fights (to extent of a non full time RPG action game)
+ nice foes smashing, physics makes them fly sometimes
on the fence:
*healing potions can heal you fully up and even bring you back to action once being down. This makes it on the casual side.
*power attack becomes a ranged one "force wave type". I prefer it in a classic way: melee attack is supposed to be closed quarter, not a ranged one. This opens a possibility to disable shields/skills or even knock enemies down at distance in groups which is imballance.
*humor ingame may be a fun for some but get's tiresome and i was forced to mute Aria's voice (and all of them) for the sake of replayability
*opening a big chest is fun but collecting all those coins reminds me countess Bathory quest in Diablo 2. Instead of picking up one hefty pile of gold i need to walk all over the olace to get it. In small change.
cons:
-while baddies heroes are few classes you 'll meet them again and again. "well hello again, haven't we met before?" which makes it kinda repetitive.
-weapon upgrades description doesn't explain where bonus (critical chance, damage, attack range) applies to autoattacks only or affects the combat arts aswell. I had to make my own research, spent some time.
-online multiplayer lacks a chat (or i didn't see one atleast). Players may leave suddenly or be waiting in the lobby for idk what reason.

Fantastic "little" village survival game. The developer steadily brings out updates with brand new content, with a massive "defence" patch (2nd June 2017), allowing upgrades of defence positions, in addition to all the other upgradeable buildings.
The visuals are crisp and satisfying to look at, with everything from colors and shape of everything falling properly into place, and several varieties of every tile-set, apart from water. There is a world map where you can choose any map to visit to look at this variation; blue forests to ashen sands, and marble mountains to blackstone.
After choosing a map on the world screen, you start off the game on an uninhabited map, prompting you to place your village center where you want it to be. Taking a close look at the map for a minute or two can make things much harder or easier depending on location. Shortly afterwards you start to notice the myriads of buildings at your disposal, and work you have to do in order to survive; it might be overwhelming at first, but it really is quite simple once you get going:
- Select resources for collection.
- Build stuff you need: Collection buildings for wood/stone etc, production, defences, refining, etc etc.
- Don't die!
- Repeat.
You cannot control villagers directly, however. They will do the jobs that are given to them via the resources you select and the job list UI on the left side of the screen. This is somewhat a weak point, as the control you have is extremely low. I would like to have something of a flag system; where you can place flags at certain locations that works like additional orders to your villagers. Like flags for avoiding areas, prioritizing resource collection at a certain area so you don't have to reassign those orders all the time. or even attacking an area. The Avoid Area flag would be great, as villager AI is very bad when they fight monsters, often dying for no reason when they could run away into their houses to heal. The AI is the game's biggest weakness, but really is not a big issue.
The gameplay is affected by several factors. Weather and seasons play a huge role. If it's windy and rainy, your villagers gets slowed down significantly. It does not rain in the winter and nothing grows, and in the summer villagers drink more water and heat up frequently. It's a lot to take into consideration. Luckily, you have several spells to use! Your spell points regenerate over time and from particles floating around the map after something has died, and can be spent to cast storms, picking things up, quickly growing nature stuff, healing and more. Be careful where you cast that fireball though!
You are probably gonna fail spectacularly the first times around, unless you picked the easiest difficulties at the world screen.  Either way it's a good time, and really satisfying to build your favorite village. The game is very cheap for what you get for it, the replayability is immense, and increased by several magnitudes by the map editor and ability to share maps over the workshop. Enjoy!

The Long Journey Home is a fantastic game focused on exploration.
The controls and mechanics are a bit tricky at first, but one gets used to them quickly.
Most important: This game is intended to be understood, in a sense that the player is given very few information and must discover things on his own.
Therefore, at the beginning you know nothing about the different alien races you meet in the game. You only get to know them by talking to them, asking questions and other interactions.
All other mechanics, like the trading system and resource manageent work in a similar way: try, gain knowledge, make it better the next time.
Additionally, this game is describe as roguelike, meaning that failing and starting all over again is a essential part of the experience. Also, this game is meant to be played more than once, for in one playthrough you can never meet all aliens and never see all the quests it has to offer.
Summary:
This game is meant for explorers and the like who can handle to fail from time to time, only to make things better or differently on the next trial.

Boy, what a colorful mixed bag, that one!
Please note:
There has been a patch since I’ve made my Long Journey Home.
A lot of polarizing things have been taken care of with a new difficulty setting.
If you still want to play on the default setting, keep some of this in mind, though.
Also, a helpful guide:

This being said, let’s break it down:
Friggin beautiful.
Very Interesting alien, ship and planet design. Space looks gorgeous, so do most of the effects.

The UI has some problems:
It’s perfectly serviceable and fits the theme. It’s very basic though, inventory gets cluttered pretty quickly and the whole thing is not particularly interesting to look at.
Often suns like white dwarves or similar bright bodies will block out your minimap and screw up your orientation.
The popup while picking a place to jump also sometimes blocks view of outer sectors.

Awesome.
Very fitting and with very good context-sensitivity.
The whole soundtrack evokes the beauty and dread of the journey perfectly. As a bonus for me, it has some very Firefly-esque themes.

Elegant and intriguing in it’s simplicity: you’re lost in space, find your way home.
I really liked the idea of this and enjoyed the bits I got of characters and the aliens’ personalities and backstories.

But here’s  the thing: it’s not that much you get per playthrough.
Most major storylines and backstories of ancient species are gated pretty hard, hidden behind a wall of relentless gameplay (more on that later) and are subject to chance and guesswork.
The quest log is bare bones and there is no Codex or glossary. That may make it hard to connect the dots about what you’ve learned during each session, considering there are a dozen alien species, not counting ancient or secret aliens. And since every time you fail, you potentially get a new, random galaxy, a lot of that beautiful background info is lost or so obscure you just stop to care.
Those aliens are getting bored by your inquiries disappointingly fast and there’s a point where you just start to look if they’re willing to trade and that’s it. Because if they don’t care about me, why should I care about them?

Your crew has some nice banter, but it gets repetitive fast (yes, thanks Malcolm, please stop telling me you need medical attention passive-aggressively…), since injury complains take priority over other banter, I guess.
A lot of what your crew says feels weirdly disconnected and that disconnects you, the player, from caring about them.
By the end, I cared more about the alien plant slowly taking over the lab.
My other main concern was to coat Malcolm in as much regenerative slime as humanly possible and make sure that Ash sucked mentioned slime out of the more unlucky plants and disgusting mutated carcasses.
So I guess that counts as a connection?
The other two? I could’ve made the trip entirely without them and they contributed virtually NOTHING to the overall atmosphere or my gameplay solutions, sadly.

The crew feels often more like your remaining pool of injury capacity than your beloved team of misfits.
For all I care, my ship could’ve been run by drones: one to fly the lander, the other a quirky sentient toolkit or something.
The problem here is, with all their background and potential, there is a great amount of humanity and emotional factor implied, but the game fails to deliver, again, because it hides all that from you.

I think this would work way better if you would actually interact with them.
I’d love to CHOOSE when to talk to them and learn about them. Either by prompting them to talk to each other, or by proxy of a captain/crew/sentient coffee machine character I create at the start of the game.
In this case, intrinsic storytelling just didn’t work out.
The texts, however, are genuinely cool and funny, alien and crew alike. Shame that you won’t see much of them.

But there’s still the wonder of exploration and the stories behind the many worlds and the universe, right?
Exploration can be a very unpleasant experience.
90% of the planets seem to hate you and your whole family and have some form of super-hazard that makes landing there too big a gamble for some lines of text.
Accordingly, I did what exploration I could, but by the end, I just wanted to get the hell out of that unfriendly universe. When the game offers you candy, and candy is just its codeword for a swift kick to the balls, you very quickly refrain from taking candy from it.
The last third of the long journey for me felt more like the last minute of a back alley bareknuckle box fight I just wanted to finish, indifferent to the actual outcome, since the operating premise was nothing but me getting beat the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of me anyway.

.

This game is not a nice game.
This game kicks your dog while spitting in your face and relentlessly punching your crotch, laughing at your misery.
With no warning, the game piledrives you into the ground, just like you plant the lander into the dirt at every opportunity.

At best, the controls are an acquired taste.
While 2 of the 3 ships you can pick are a bit sloggy and control fairly well and intuitively overall, the lander is just  a randomly rotating piece of leftover scrap metal with rockets ductaped to it. You will probably straight up pancake on planets during your 10-20 first landings.
After that, you have either given up, switched to the easy mode or you’re a vengeful husk driven by grim determination to master the art of the lander.
Still, there’s fun in there somewhere. But sometimes it takes effort and either rage or zen to find it.

And let me tell you, you’ll have plenty of opportunities for that.

Handling your vessels, however, is a matter of training.
You’ll get there, and you’ll smile at your rare perfect landings, fuel efficient drifts into orbit and epic space battles (which work fine enough, by the way).
Regarding that, you just git gud and chew threw the content at some point, maybe even happy with yourself.

But here’s what’s really the problem:
Your crew gets hurt very easily and can’t heal on their own (5 injuries are lethal). Especially the lander pilot, if they’re unlucky enough to return at all, will return mangled, burned, bruised, infected with brain parasites or insane most of the time.
You get punished for everything you do. EVERYTHING and ANYTHING.
No matter what in-game action, ship parts have a chance to break, either becoming less efficient or outright destroyed. And there’s no way for you to mitigate that.
You have no idea why stuff breaks. In some cases, I literally did nothing more than entering a harmless atmosphere with the lander and parts I just repaired were damaged.
Theoretically, you can take an engineer character with you, but she repairs RANDOM parts, chosen from ship and lander. This consumes items so rare that you might as well try to win the lottery while getting struck by lightning during a shark attack.
And since the game tells you little to nothing about anything mechanics-wise, this is utterly frustrating.

And that’s where intend and gameplay seem to clash.
You feel that this game is not designed for exploration and wonder, but for survival and its inherent unfairness.
Playing this game does not feel like accepting a challenge and going on a harrowing journey, exploring a distant galaxy.
It feels more like fighting a particularly mean bully.

However!
All the good stuff, the mood, the stories and depth of texts and characters, human and alien alike, all shine through.
There are perfect moments where everything this game wants to be rings crystal clear.
And if nothing else, The Long Journey Home is a captivating game you will enjoy talking about with other people.
Maybe not for the qualities that were advertised, but still, after roughly 30 hours I can say, it was well worth playing and I really recommend trying this.

The game is difficult without being oppressively so, and allows you to pick between game types that increase or decrease the difficulty depending on how hard-core you are about your survival games. The art style is lovely, the game itself runs really well, and in dedicating themselves to a single-player experience the devs are able to really focus and fine-tune the experience. Speaking of the devs, I have a lot of respect for how they've handled development of this project and how they interact with their community. It takes a lot of guts to not cave to every fans whim, even if doing so would result in an inferior product. And the cherry on the cake, for my fellow lady gamers: Yes, you can play as a fully voiced female character! Enjoy being Commander Shepard in the Candian wilderness!

This game IS addictive, challenging, relaxing, and really a pleasure to play.
The background music is almost hypnotic - I think there must be something subliminal buried in it xD.  Hours after I've turned off the computer, I find that repeating tune stuck in my head.  God help me, I love it.
As of this writing, over 91% of the reviews are Positive, and there is good reason for that.  The game is a winner.  There are an almost infinite number of scenarios to choose from, with some childishly easy to succeed at (a good place for beginners to start), and the difficulties go all the way up to essentially unsurvivable.
The incredible number of MODs available to choose from in the Workshop also adds so much richness and variety to the game.  There is a HUGE Banished community growing and supporting the game and its MODS.  The one scenario that seems to disturb me most is the two settlers, Adam & Eve scenario - LOL, where brothers wind up marrying sisters, and then 1st cousins, etc.  Now, that's a genuine Uncle Daddy & Aunt Mama family tree.  Anybody on earth should find that hilariously funny, with no disrespect meant to Arkansans.... Bless their hearts.
I've seen a few critical reviews that reference Sim City, and such, and if that's all they see here with Banished, they came in the door with the wrong expectations.  I own multiple generations of the Sim City series dating back to Win95, as well as, Cities XL, Cities in Motion, and so on.  Banished has little in common with those, IMHO.
The Banished player gets the chance to more closely manage resources and activities, and essentially 'craft' to build more complex structures, more sophisticated clothing, etc. (Hint - warmer settlers work more efficiently in harsh winters).  This is not a high pressure, can't go AFK for a coffee or bathroom break, kind of game.  So, settle in, relax, and enjoy.  For frenzied, Constant ACTION, Run 'n Gun players, there's always a CSGO / COD server somewhere, right?!
In short, the Banished player chooses the region and number of initial settlers, as well as starting resources in the game menu.  The race is on to get sufficient shelter, food, and fuel (firewood/coal) before winter sets in.  When it gets cold, you won't see much production from the settlers.  The strategy you start with is up to you.  As for me, early in the game I prefer to focus on Gatherers and an Herbalist (the Healer) before that first winter.  I've had great starts where there were tons of firewood, food, etc., only to see everyone die off to sickness, because I forgot the Herbalist.  Another point I keep in mind is to stockpile absolutely every scrap of firewood, food, and medicine that you can lay hands on to the point of ridiculous excess, so that you can spare settlers to be teachers, preachers, and healers.  Sure, it sounds corny, but Education is important, since educated workers here simply produce more.  Be leery of nomads.  When they show up, they usually lack education, have scores of unproductive, hungry children, and invariably bring disease, so you better have a hospital.  The game never makes it clear what the disease is, but I suspect some nasty STD - LOL.  Again, no offense intended, Arkansans.
When I first started the game, I had settlers dropping like flies, and sadly, my major concern seemed to be having a large enough cemetery.  But now, regardless of difficulty, I manage to keep things balanced enough that the only deaths seem to be from old age - as it should be.  I also highly recommend one of the Mods that change the passage of time to one actual year of gameplay for each year of the settler's life.  The default seems to be several years of life for each four-season Banished year.  When everything is stable for a moment, and little direct input is required, it has a great Fast-Forward x10 that moves things along until a point where more input is required.
A satisfying moment for me is when I'm 8 or 9 game years into a scenario, and I have some of the original potatoes from the wagon in the barn.  That's when you know the food production is more than under control.  Anybody hungry for a 9 year old spud?  I'll pass!
I bought Banished during an earlier Sale, so keep your eyes open for sales.  Frankly, for me it would be worth the money at full retail, so jump at the chance to buy it either way.  More than 91% of the buyers think you'll be glad you did.  I hope this was helpful.  Cheers
