TL;DR: Do you like crashing cars? Do you like realistic racing games? BUY THIS. This is one of the best racing games I've owned in my entire life.
PROS:
- Graphics are really good
- Controls feel tight but this game is best with a wheel or controller
- Sound effects are nice
- The menus are incredibly clean, and make sense
- The different terrains actually change how your car performs, like they would IRL
- The different tracks are very nicely designed, and challenge you to channel your inner Stig
- The feedback when you hit another car is extremely satisfying
- There's a decent selection of cars
- The game is addicting due to the fact that it's incredibly satisfying to play
- The cars all handle well
- Each car handles differently from others
- The cars all feel like they have a good amount of weight to them
- The upgrades you make drastically change your cars performance
- The upgrades make sense and aren't over the top
- The game runs incredibly smoothly at 60
- The AI is about the smart-ness of a human, so it makes it a much better experience to play offline
- The online is fun and the community is very good
- Steam workshop support, hell yeah
- The modding community was pretty good, and I assume it'll be again once this game gets off the ground again
CONS:
- This game has been in Early Access for three and a half years, the devs don't seem to be updating this game much
- The customization of vehicles is extremely limited, hell, you can only visually upgrade the STARTING CAR, the rest are just paintjob customizations
- You can't create your own paintjobs (yet) you have to choose from the premade ones, or download a mod that has more
- The community has mostly died due to this game almost being "abandon-ware", but it seems the devs are starting to pick the game back up
- The game doesn't really have performance damage, I mean, you can lose health, but you don't get slower from a damaged engine, you don't lean and get forcefully turned from bent axles, and other things that would be prevalent in a real life scenario
- The car selection is decent, but it's not enough, although apparently they will be adding more cars
- Lack of game-modes, there's Banger Races, Demolition Derby...and that's it. Why not a stunt mode so we can earn points from doing jumps, drifting, going up on two wheels, stuff like that. You have 1-5 minutes to perform stunts, and at the end, your points are compared to the other players, player with the highest points wins
- You'd expect there to be a drag-racing mode in this game, but NOPE.
- The replay system is good, but I'd love if there was a record button so you could record clips directly to your PC, and maybe even a button to upload to Youtube.
- You can't upgrade the lawnmower, I know, that's a strange thing to be sad about, but it'd be kind of fun to have a race with V8 powered lawnmowers, wouldn't it?
- There is barely any music in the game, the main menu is completely silent, the menu where you look at your cars and upgrade them is silent, there's no race music, the only music I could find was at the end of the race when the leaderboard shows up, showing who won. Can we have some Disturbed? Killswitch Engage? Slipknot? Alter Bridge (Specifically Isolation, cause that song is badass)? Bulletproof Messenger (Specifically Bring Me To Life, I think that'd be a great addition)?
- More car upgrades, like Drift tires, or maybe Drag racing engines (the drag engines make it super easy to do wheelies), Jump suspension (makes it so you don't take damage from jumps, but reduces handling and cornering), stuff like that.

A Hat in Time is a very beautiful platformer that places you in the control of Hat Kid (or Hat Girl if you prefer), and the story starts merely because one of the enemy types called The Mafia want payment from Hat Kid while floating in their air space.  After some silly shenanagins you are thrusted onto the world to recover your lost Time Pieces that was sucked out ship.
I won't go too far into the story as it is very simple, but for what story is there it is told very well.  You gain a different hat power up through out each world you visit, changing up the ways you can play the game.  The game also requires you to switch hats during certain situations in order to progress.
Hat Power:
KId's Hat:  Your starting Top Hat.
Power of Hat: Points you in the direction of your objective, other than that not much else.
Sprint Hat: Increases movement speed and even when combined with the Scooter Badge your movement speed is increased even more.
Brewing Hat: Allows you to throw explosives to blow up crates.
Ice Hat: Gives you the ability to ground pound and with certain platforms, be bounced to to new areas or cuts travel time depending on the Ice Platform.
Dweller's Mask: Helps you jump on platforms that are intagnible.
Time Stop Hat: While it doesn't necessarily stop time completely, this is probably the most powerful hat in the game as it slows down time so you can catch your breath or catch an enemy off guard easier.  This hat also works on boss fights.
There are also badges you equip to increase your abilities.  Some are useful, some are not so useful, and one allows you to fire a laser from your umbrella, which is a pretty dang cool thing in my book.
There are time rifts you have to dive into later on when you find relics hidden throughout the levels.  The style of the time rifts are very reminicent of Super Mario Sunshine, and this is in no way a bad thing since I actually liked the side areas in Mario Sunshine.  There are also one unique time rift connected to each world where you go through a small bit of the past of those areas and collect pictures, which you are then rewarded of why the world you are at is the way it is.
The only two negative I can say about this game is that the Ice Hat doesn't get much use and other than the ground pound, there is no other practical use for it outside of the ice panels.  It would have been interesting if it wiped away fires nearby but it's not total let down.  The only hat that I think is impractical when you find out how to move fast anyway IS the Sprint Hat.  Even with the badge extension I found myself hardly ever using the Sprint Hat, but it's a good first hat to introduce you to the hat mechanics later on.
The only glitch I come acrossed was at the very beginning when you play Patty Cake with one of the Mafia and he hits you after you were done.  I couldn't jump and was hovering in the air for some reason going down a hill.  A restart fixed it and the bug did not happen since the start.
The pros definitely outweigh any minor con I could give it.  This game was made with so much love and understanding from people who love platformers.  Gears for Breakfast are going places.  A very simple but great story and amazing gameplay with amazing visuals that made me wanting more.  I don't know if there would be A Hat in Time 2 or not, but it's something I would love to see happen.  This game is worth every single dime and I highly recommend it!

This is by far the most intense multiplayer game I have ever played, in fact I'd go as far as to say RO2/RS is the best multiplayer game I've ever played. A single bullet will kill you, making every move you make matter, every action you do could be your last. The action is brutal, realistic and extremely immersive thanks to outstanding audio and gameplay, guns handle well and feel deadly and accurate. The cover system can be a touch buggy sometimes, but when it works it works well and adds to the experience. Out of all the multiplayer games I've ever played RO2/RS has been the most rewarding, enjoyable and thrilling.The community that is still playing this game is for the most part well mannered and objective focused making for a much more coordinated and friendly team that actually cares about objectives more than K/D ratios. One of the only problems I have had with RO2/RS is finding a server where players get a ping below 150, however sticking to servers with a 1/2 mixture of bots and people usually yields better results without taking away from the game. The bots may not be the smartest, and can get some rather cheap kills in but they help keep the game going without taking away from the immersion too much. Both factions are extremely well balanced, with each having different weapons and abilities (such as the Japanese Banzai charge) and the maps are also extremely balanced and are open enough to allow for most play styles to be successful. Overall, RO2/RS is a must play for FPS fans and an absolute masterpiece, with free updates and maps coming every few months to help keep it fresh. It's completely woth the price, and once you get used to the gameplay you'll be hooked. 10/10 would banzai again.

Banished is a spectacular game. I do admit that initially I went in thinking it to be a city builder and thats how I treated it. I bit me back very hard and I was very displeased. But then I really thought about how I was playing. I cahnged it to a more "initally i'm screwed so husband your resources and educate your folks (so they do things more efficiently)", and once I started my games with that mentality the game itself became a true challenge and a blast. This is a very well done SURVIVAL game.
The Bad....
If you get a huge batch of nomads, it can throw you into a death spiral with food or plague (once of my nomad requests brought in almost 50 people, within 5 minutes those 50 added such a strain on my food that half of my city died to starvation).
You need to play very methodically. Build here, watch and see if it stabilizes, fix if it doesnt or leave it alone if it does. Rinse and repeat.
Growing your population. Holy christ this one can hurt. You basically need to be in a constant state of building new homes (which is rough because that adds more strain on your initially reduced resources). Thats the only way to populate the village/town/city.
Sometimes ya just get bad luck. The randomly generated map sometimes just gets ya in a stupid spot.
The Great
Damn, this is a fun game. There is always something to fix, tweak or build to make your village/town/city more efficient.
Plenty to build, plenty of ways to influence how your city looks and grows (with a forrester you can essentially make "parks".
Great mods. I recommend the terrains plus and the Banished plus. They both add difficulties and streamline the overall gameplay.
Tough as nails. This game was a great challenge to husband your resources and grow in a stable and healthy manner for your folks.
Conclusion
If you like to build vast cities off the bat with no challenge, dont buy it.
If you want to build a small village, work up to a bustling town, and finally grow to a massive city. But during each step of the way you encounter a good logistical struggle for stability. Buy this game. I cant tell you how much fun this was for me. Great job Shining Rock!

Beginner's Guide is very interesting. Its hard to discuss without giving up the plot, but I should start out with a warning - this is an hour-ish long game that most likely would be tagged as "Walking Simulator." You play the role of someone investigating games designed by Coda, which are narrated over by Davey Wrenden.
There are no traditional mechanics anywhere in this game. You start in one of Coda's games, Wrenden then describes to you his interpretation. As you play through it topics are addressed such as the role of the consumer's interpretation of art, the role of the artist's life in their work, as well as frustration relevant to being a creative person.
It may be a bit expensive, but I think the game provides a worthwhile perspective if you create art on your own, or think about the role of art as it relates to the creator and consumer.

I like to state things quickly, so that's how I'll format this. Quickly stated, The Beginner's Guide is a beautiful work of digital art.
Firstly, if you don't enjoy games like this, (sometimes called "Walking Simulators", games that focus on the message sent instead of the action or mechanics) you may not enjoy this, honestly. You can watch a YouTube video and skip to the end, if you want the story quickly.
However, if you have felt any interest in story-based games in the past, then I highly suggest this experience. This shows you a real-life struggle that many people go through. This isn't about zombies or time travel, it takes you on a journey through the mind of a pained individual and sends you dozens of life lessons in such a subtle way you won't even know. You could watch a video, but there's something special about experiencing the game with only your thoughts. No one else's.
If you think that's worth it for you, and I do believe it was for me, then I fully recommend you become a part of this experience.

I will be writing this post from the point of view of a player that has never played Dungeon Defenders I.
This game is pretty much Sanctum meets Diablo and Borderlands.
It is a pretty looking FPS (first person shooter) set in a tower defense game. The game itself is mainly centered around loot. Getting weapons, armor and pets which upgrade your hero(es).
Pros:
•	Pretty looking visuals.
•	Fun loot system (rarities, traits, certain map/mission bound loot).
•	Great co-op play with friends or random other players.
Cons:
•	Lack of/bad difficulty scaling. It will be impossible to beat a difficulty higher than hard with a low level character as it does not scale with your level but instead is set to level 50.
•	Bugs. Lots and lots of bugs. For example: People joining private lobby sessions, loot being sent to bags which have autoloot disabled and many more.
•	No support for Borderless Windowed mode (alt tabbing is a pain and might get your cursor stuck).
•	“Early access” after two years of release. Feels like an excuse to not do/delay bugfixes.
•	Pricing of “DLC” and currency. While the game is free to play, I would consider paying 20 Euros for some stuff. However that would be able to get me a single character. In order to buy all “year 1” characters I would have to pay 60 Euros, the price of an AAA game title. As long as the prices stay this way I will not make a single purchase.
•	Currently unobtainable currency locks skills in certain stores.
•	Very slow free to play progression for additional heroes. Your first 10K medals costing hero can be bought in about a week due to campaign rewards. After that you will be getting like 300 medals a day for daily quests on average while heroes still cost 10K medals.
•	Goblin Siege Rollers.
While this game has issues, lots of them, I will still be giving it a thumbs up because I simply enjoy the (free to play) gameplay, and that is the most important thing about a game.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a horror game, where the horror doesn't come mainly from the scary-looking things. No, it's your mind that's making the game gradually scarier for every night you complete, as the difficulty keeps rising and you'll be more likely to receive a jumpscare with a loud scream. Yup, the game over here is a loud screamer nobody likes.
You may think now that screamers make a bad horror game, but you should definitively think again here: this is one of the most true horror games out there, as it's actually a proper game instead of just walking around. You'll need to focus on many things at the same time: forget one, and you'll be screwed. It's like those tactical games many gamers appreciate, expect the fact that it's single player.
Overall, I'd rate this one high, as it's a horror game with very good gameplay. Also, many horror games keep you awake at night or make you feel scared even after playing it, but Five Nights at Freddy's is only scary when you're playing it, which I find a good thing. However, I've heard many tougher horror gamers (I'm a little scaredy cat) getting nightmares, so you'll probably want to try it out yourself.

TL;DR: A great Run & Gun game with amazing graphics and great music, with extreme hard but fair difficulty.
A Must-Buy for every Retro-Gamer.
Cuphead "Don't Deal With The Devil".
After 3 years of waiting for it's release, the wait was worth, as it deliveres the perfect Run & Gun Gameplay I've been wanting soo much to be revived. Hopefuly, we'll have more Run & Gun games in the future that will follow Cuphead's steps.
Let's get the obvious out of the way:
Graphics: Fantastic! If you're a fan of old 1930 cartoons, you'll love the unique art style that this game proudly shows, as everything in this game is made by hand-drawing. Everything is beautiful to look at and the animation is greatly detailed. Definitly it's strongest point.
Gameplay: Simple as it can get. You dodge everything that is thrown to you and shoot down your enemies. Like old fashion, the bosses don't have any health indicator, as it should be, but clues are thrown into the mix, like becoming more aggressive, or changing their forms. There is a variety of weaponry you can choose, and end up being used at least once for a specific boss, and along side weapons, there are charms that can help you with sustaining damage or dodging projectiles or enemies.
Dificulty: Now here's a tricky one. Retro games (Specially Run & Guns) were always easy to learn, hard to master. Cuphead is one of those cases where you'll die alot, but it's never the games fault. Do not pay attention to the people who say the game is too hard or is too unfair. Nothing in the game is unfair. It can and will get hard the more you acomplish, but when you die, you learn from your mistake. You start memorizing the bosses's attack patterns, and the more you study them, the easier it gets. It's not a final exam, but memorizing the attacks always help. It's how most Run & Gun games work.
Audio: The sounds are satisfying to listen to, and the music is amazing. It really captures the old instrumental vibe that every 30's cartoon had. I can guarantee you, it won't go through your head to turn the volume down or to even turn the music off. It is that good to listen to. And never 2 musics are the same, every stage and worlds have their own unique theme.
Replayability: In the end of every level, you'll be graded depending on how good you do. You can always replay the same levels to aim for a higher grade. There is also the Expert Mode, where it changes the bosses attack patterns, by making them faster or stronger. It actually has a 200% Completion, so see if you can beat all the bosses in a higher difficulty, see if you know your Cupheaded ways.
Final Thoughts: It is an amazing game that I recomend for every Retro fan to get. The difficulty is insane, but fair and passable, altho sometimes it might be annoying, but not game-breaking. Haven't run to any game bugs, and it runs at 60 stable FPS. Great graphics, amazing music and tight and responsive controls.
Verdict: 9/10

This game is delightfully charming in almost every avenue. Its music is fantastic, its controls are tight, the artistry is a callback that's as gorgeous as it is reverential. Everything is crafted with care. The odd transformative enemies with the not-quite-solid-enough-to-support-a-body bone structure that the old cartoon characters used to have are all present. It's a fantastic treat.
Enough gushing, brass tacks:
If you like platformers, if you like side scrolling shooters, if you like 1930's motif, you'll like this game on that alone, I think $20. That said, this game is difficult as all hell. It is brutally unforgiving, but rewards good play and knowledge (which often comes at the price of dying). Co-op scales this up a lot, so if you're playing with a friend, prepare to suffer. (It is still very fun, just understand going in that it is NOT the same game as single player, but I don't think in a bad way. However, you will die). It's not all doom and gloom as far as difficulty goes, there is a 'simple' mode on each level, so you can more casually enjoy the style.
This game's individual levels are predominantly 'boss rushes', in that each level is mainly comprised of a unique boss that you have to defeat, the only traditional side scroller levels are titled aptly "run and guns" are used to gather money for various upgrades. Combat is straightforward, though nuanced given the aforementioned 'upgrades' you can buy, i.e. new weapons or accessories that alter how you fight. The parry system, which consists of being midair, then 'slapping' the particular target, does offer an interesting option for players, since parrying in a lot of situations is an optional choice that offers decent reward for some risk.
All in all. It's hard, it's delightfully fun. It's not for the faint of heart, but if you want to challenge yourself at a price that I consider a steal, I think that this might be right up your alley.

The sense of control and interaction on the part of the gamer are critical to the impact of the phenomenal story, all of which takes place in one gaming's most celebrated environments. The underwater city of Rapture is aptly named, as its visual and audio splendor is a pleasure that I often desire to re-experience. Equalling the game's aesthetic appeal is the deep and satisfying game design, which makes each playthrough feel unique. Everything that makes games great is at its best in BioShock, and I can't recommend it enough.

OK.  This is a fun game but there's alot to be to desired about it.  FIrst, the tutorials and general intro to the controls and game mechanics are ♥♥♥♥ing abysmal.  I like to explore to find stuff but honestly you leave too much to the player to figure out.  For instance, why do i sometimes take lander damage when mining?  And what does the little indicator thing that pops up while i'm mining do?
i dunno if there are upgrades for this but i really just want to land and collect resources and go rather than try to ♥♥♥♥ing hover.
Also i think the combat system could use a little work as well because it seems like systems go down in combat but you don't see anything on screen to tell you that.
Other major issues are the stupid way you go into jump, i just wind up accidentally not going into the jump because i thought the animation was over.  Just give me a button with a confirmation.
The other main problem is loading screens.  About 1/3 of my time in this game is spent looking at the darn loading screen.  If you're going to have animations after each loading thing why not show us the animation while the loading is going on in the background?
The other thing is the seemingly random attitude that your ship has when coming out of a ship-to-ship interaction or an asteroid belt.  I love coming out of a pointless "hello fellow alien" meet and greet only to be sent rocketing into the sun for no particular reason.
All this said, I really like this game.  Fun gameplay and challenging piloting.  I dunno what the other reviewers are complaining about with the lander.  Other than just wanting to land to get resources I think it's one of the main draws of the game.  A++ but it could be A+++ with a few tweaks.

The compelling element of gameplay: increasing building technology requirements (i.e. materials) to allow a larger number of buildings.
That little game mechanic drives the whole game, blocking new buildings from coming up until prerequisite buildings have been placed and required materials are available. It is implemented by requiring the city center to get upgraded, and each subsequent upgrade requires new materials that must be manufactured. Great design and I thoroughly enjoy the amount of decision-making generated by the mechanic. Each new building consumes a "building slot".
This game is sort of a combo: tower defense and city building are the main mechanic. But the game also adds a god spell-casting mechanism, which allows casting fireballs, earthquakes, holy golems, healing aura, resurrect the ghost, and a few others, all with varying essence costs, which is slowly building up over time according to how happy villagers are.
Most importantly, there is a "grab anything" spell that allows grabbing enemies, friends, resources -- just not buildings. You can use it to move enemies away if they are causing too much trouble, or saving your villagers before certain death, or collecting resources your villagers aren't collecting fast enough. Each time you use it it burns essence depending on how long you grab something. This has the side-effect of making game-pause disallow touching the board in any way (pause also won't let you use the building-selection menus, but the dev claims he will change this eventually). Not being able to change a paused board I find annoying, especially when it's only reason is to support a strange game-play mechanism. The game develops an arcade-like feel (i.e. frantically moving things around), when it's supposed to be a city-builder. It's odd.  [Most city builders involve dropping "blueprints" that workers eventually build the buidings on top of - but this is the first city builder I have seen that won't let you pause and place as many blueprints as you like - you have to unpause the game to do that.]
Another odd mechanism is that the global map (where you choose the submap the village will be placed in) can have units (enemy or ally) in "limbo", and they can be portalled out of a map or back in as you like. I scratch my head at why this was put in - but there it is.
But wait! There's more! There are also 2 other mini-games: - collect the essence and - find the friend or foe.
Collect The Essence
Collect the essence involves moving your mouse around essence that results from enemy deaths or other triggers that have it free-floating in the atmosphere. The way the essence follows bezier curves is fun to watch and it's a bit relaxing break from the rest of the game.
Find The Friend Or Foe
The other minigame "find the friend or foe" involves hovering the mouse close enough to ground units to see whether they are enemies or friends (your own villagers or nomads). If you don't have your mouse close enough, you can't see what they are. This I think was a really bad UI choice for the sake of creating a mini-game. I find it purely annoying. Your mileage may vary.
Conclusion
The game involves several mini-games, some add and some detract from the core gameplay, which is castle (or city) building. Because this is still early access, who knows? But I feel I've already gotten my money's worth purely for the mechanisms I like, and it's very easy to keep playing this until the late hours of the night. For that reason alone, it's worth a buy.

What I loved about this game is that is starts out as a seminar and analysis of not only a designer's games, but of the designer himself. I loved the short stories of the discussions and how the characters seemed to be so alive. I love how the designer has the mind of a true artist and how narrator's narration and interference with the designer's art gives you the power to envision the art as it should be experienced according to the designer, but without having to go through the hardship it entails.
The game has a brilliant twist towards the end upon which I just froze.
After that, however, I felt the narration, and game in general, broke the walls it had built up - I could feel how the narrative broke and became absurd.
In all: I absolutely loved the concept and the story, up until the very ending, which disappointed me. I'd still recommend it to anyone with a taste for storydriven games, though!

This game is terrifying, it's a point and click game but it has a crushingly terrifying atmosphere, because you could be jumpscared at any moment.
In this game, you play as a man who got himself a job at a kids pizza store named Freddy Fazbear's Pizza. You have been hired to work the night shift and you begin the game at Night 1. You cannot move in this game, you can only operate the door lights, peek up at your security cameras or shut/open your doors. You are unaware of the fact that the animatronics you are looking after (which are basically animal robots which are mascots to the store) actually move around at night, and if they find you...they will kill you.
You spend the five nights of this game constantly peeking up at the cameras making sure all of the animatronics are in place, and when they move you must keep track of them otherwise they will get into your office and horrifyingly jumpscare you.
That is basically how you survive in this game, you keep an eye on the animatronics and when they get near your office, you just shut the doors so they can't get in. Sounds pretty easy huh?
Well, these animatronics cut off your camera when they move around, which means that you have no idea where they are and they could have just ran straight next to your door without you knowing and get you. Also, if you're late catching them they will cut off the power to your doors, meaning certain death.
If that wasn't enough however, you have a power bar which means that you must be careful with the amount of power you use. (You lose power by looking at your camera, using the door lights and shutting the doors.) And once that percentage hits 0, you have only a matter of seconds to live before Freddy comes and finishes you off.
There are various ways you have to handle the animatronics in order to survive, and they all work differently but I am not going to tell you how to handle them because then the experience just won't the the same for you!
The jumpscares will make you jump, and will make you scream and it WILL happen so if you're going to buy this game, make sure you know what you're getting into!
The couple of negative things I could say about this game is that it does get tedious because once you know how to survive, that's it! That's it for the rest of the nights and you'll be safe, once you know the way around the game you will breeze through it. Another thing is that, after a certain amount of jumpscares; you do get used to them and they will not scare you so much, which does ruin the atmosphere a bit and may just frustrate you if you fail.
Overall, I'd definitely recommend giving this game a try and it will be challenge to complete all seven of the nights (yes, seven!) Just make sure you're prepared before going on this rollercoaster!

Tldr: This is a city building tower defense god game that makes time go by far more quickly than you'd like.
This game is basically some wierd fusion of city building, tower defence, and god games (you have a floating hand and you can pick stuff up). Now I can't say everyone will enjoy it. Especially since you are basically guarenteed to lose your first few games. However, the reason why you lose, often times will not be the same. I've lost due to starvation, dehydration, lack of defences, overbuilding, stupid lightning storms (this problem was actually solved in a recent update) random monsters appearing in areas I didn't check, random monsters breaking in because my own towers betrayed me by destroying the terrain, and just plain being overran by slimes and zombies. This is one of those games that will cause you to be like, okay, I lost because of this, what can I do to live longer? And this will haunt you till you finally last longer than one year in game. Even then, maybe another year.
After that.....I'm sorry, Ray (the developer), there's no real end game. Not yet anyways. Although, for you random people reading this, this game is updated literally every month or two. Opt into unstable releases and you can play a new update roughly every two to three weeks.
Also for you complete and total over-achievers, you should try to conquer the map by building fire pits all over it. And then, strip mine it and deforest the land. By this point.....not going to lie, you just spent an entire day or two in the real world questioning, just what did you even do with your life?
I swear, every update I spend like 8 hours testing out the new content. I only recently managed to shrink this time by using cheat engine. Which I completely and thoroughly recommend you do. Not because of cheating (which I haven't figured out how to do yet nor feel the need to do) but because there isn't a time warping ability yet. Simply enable the speed hack and you've shrunk the time from 8 hours to 4. Possibly even 3. Well.....I say this, but somehow I still end up playing for 8 hours even though I had it sped up by three times, two when my town got large enough.
Right, I should talk about your giant floating hand. It floats. Picks up stuff, given that you have enough influence/essence. Other abilities include launching fireballs from heaven, calling lighting storms to bring rain, and really horrifying lighting (picture having a wall with a large of amount of zombies on the other side of it, then picture said wall getting blown up by lightning. Begin to cry because you've just been overrun by zombies.) call an earthquake that is equally terrifying, call a holy golem which needs a serious buff because it's far more expensive than what it could be used for, regrow entire forests and large amounts of food (which while they may say they are different vegetables, they are really and honestly carrots with different colors), banish your enemies, recall all resources, nomads, and stray villagers to your town center, warp things in and out of limbo (your global map storage), and even disolve any and all living and once living things for more essence. Oh, did I mention your villagers tend to freak out by your hand?
Most importantly, you will fail, and that is okay. You will simply doom this world thus erasing any and all evidence of failure, and start again.

Purchased the game with high hopes as I thoroughly enjoyed the previous edition, sadly this was a disappointment as the gameplay is so drastically different from the original, and from the board game that I know and love, that this shouldn't have the name "Blood Bowl" associated with it at all. From no visibility to what block dice you rolled (for those times when maybe a both down is better than a pushback), nor any option to either follow up, nor pick where your opponent goes, this game may have potential for fun, but it really isn't Blood Bowl.
What's a crying shame is that the graphics are an improvement, Jim and Bob are vastly improved and the campaign mode felt like it had a real story to get going but being forced to play humans, with no option to change to a different team, nor pick things like re-rolls (or at least no obvious way to do so!), it will get dull really quickly.
Frankly, if you like Blood Bowl, avoid this game and get the previous edition instead.

I bought Rise to Ruins a very long time ago. played the game for an hour or two, said "meh" I won't return it because I want to support the developers...
Recently I reinstalled Rise to Ruins and am extremely happy with where the game has come! I myself am a huge strategy game fan so I was able to pick up the resource management playstyle very quickly and jumped in to game at the hardest difficulty.. now almost 8 hours into the same game I have to say I still enjoy it! Replay value is pretty solid. I will definitely consider starting another game in the future.
For the rest of this I'll write out some likes / dislikes I have with the game..
Likes:
-For an early access game. it runs extremely smooth!
-Initial start to games is very intense on high difficulties and is fun to try to get a perfect strategy going.
-Art style is very simple and pleasant.
-AI is few solid!
-Reminds me of old Warcraft 3 Castle defense games which I spent far too many hours playing!
Dislikes:
-UI is very clunky and feels unorganized.
-----the two side menus for managing citizens and choosing what to build should be streamlined.. For example, when the mouse is positioned over the menu I want to be able to use the scroll wheel to go up and down, not having to click the arrows. (I'm sure this will be fixed in the future!)
-End game loses the "oh no I can't leave my computer feel"
-----after the base is set up and you have a decent power generation you don't have to worry about monsters a whole lot as your towers do so much damage. I think I have 4 ballistas and they take out any strong monsters before they reach me.
-My villagers eat turnips.. only..
---- I would love to see some more variety in food resources and ways to gather them in the future! Ex: hunting, fishing, other crops.
I have extremely high hopes for this game and love how involved the developers are in the process! This game is simple when you look at it but there is a lot of strategy to learn behind it which makes it extremely fun in my opinion.
I hope this review helped you all! Enjoy the game if you choose to purchase it :)

Probably the best 3D platformer on PC so far.
What makes a platformer good? The answer is: controls. And Hat Kid controls are responsive and allow the player to do a lot of things, while keeping it simple. Casual players won't have any problems with getting used to them, while more advanced players have tools to pull off some insane shortcuts and stunts.
The sound design is great. Music fits the locations, voices fit the characters and the voice-acting itself is well done.
2D art, special effects and world design is on point, everything is distinct, colorful and pretty. The only thing artstyle-wise I disagree with is how character faces have been implemented (2D texture for eyes and mouth), but eh, I can get used to it.
A Hat in Time is not a very long game, though there's 2 more worlds coming as a free DLC in the future. Also, it supports modding, so the community can provide some new content for the time being.
I absolutely love this game. It's a love-letter to the classics, which captures their charm, while improving upon them in every way.

LIMBO is one of the most atmospheric games I've ever played. You're immediately drawn into this darkly beautiful, gloomy world. It's a space that is both contemplative and dangerous; the visuals are as likely to please you as they are to kill you. Your job is to get this little boy back to his sister, traversing a gloomy forest, dead city, caves, factories, and other bleak locales along the way. Puzzles are both short and challenging; many will reward you with a gruesome death if you're not quick enough. The game's minimalist approach to storytelling may leave those yearning for more (like me)  a bit unsatisfied, but the environment is its own story, backed by grain, shadows, and ambient music. This is my favorite platformer, for these reasons.

I really enjoy playing this game, and the developer is great and always makes great improvements to the game while listening to feedback.  With the most recent update (as of June third, 2017) you can now change the difficulty higher, or even make your own custom difficulty, which is really neat.  The game also includes a built-in map editor to make your own maps (steam workshop support planned for the future to introduce better map sharing).  All-in-all this is a really fun game, and well worth the price tag.

BioShock puts you in the shoes of a survivor of a mid-ocean plane crash. With no where else to go, you swim to a nearby lighthouse but... why is it there?
The game was designed for consoles so this is a PC-port. If you use a controller, you'll be in good hands. If you prefer the mouse and keyboard, then you'll probably want to fiddle with the .ini files in order to "fix" the mouse control. To do this, run the game once, and close it. Now, navigate to your documents folder and find the "AppData" folder. It is hidden so make sure you are showing hidden files in Windows. You're looking for the folder: [username]\AppData\Roaming\Bioshock
In there, you'll find a user.ini and a bioshock.ini file.
In the user.ini file find/add the following lines: (you can change the MouseAccelThreshold to 1.0 if you'd like some acceleration)
MouseSmoothingMode=0
MouseAccelThreshold=0.0
In the bioshock.ini file find/add the following lines: (they appear twice each, so make sure to set both to false)
CaptureMouse=False
ReduceMouseLag=False
DoubleBufferMouseLag=False
If the game ever crashes on you (which it will if you alt-tab or if you use the Steam overlay too many times), then these two files will be overwritten with a default file (bye bye custom controls =/ )
To circumvent this, make a copy of these two files after you set up your graphics/sound/control options. If the game crashes, relaunch it, close it, and copy your backup files over the existing user.ini and bioshock.ini files to quickly restore your settings.
Anyways, once your mouse settings are good to go the gameplay is great, and the story is engaging. If you haven't played this game yet then you're missing out. Have fun!

Short opinion: Solid graphics, wonderful music, good story - but VERY DIFFICULT to beat. If you like a sci-fi challenge, The Long Journey Home is for you.
Long Opinion:
The Long Journey Home.... thats a tough one, literaly!
A sci-fi game that puts you in charge of what was supposed to only be a test run for a new jump drive but accidently threw you across the universe. Your goal? Similar to the premise of Star Trek: Voyager, you try to get your ship and crew back home.
The problem with this is that your ship and its "shuttle" are far less advanced than an Intrepid-class starship or, for that matter, the various alien species you will come across in Long Journey Home.
Plus your ship and crew are constantly subject to fatigue, various damaging threats and a always a bit too low supply of fuel.
The goal on this is indeed making the journey.... a survival experience of a different kind, and a VERY difficult one too. Unlike many other games, Long Journey Home does not help you much figuring things out, you have to learn yourself. Which makes it almost impossible to beat the game on the first attempt.
Graphics are ok and fit the premise of the game well; music is simply awesome. There's a lot of text to read as practically nothing is vocalized.
It's hard. It's not the most advanced game. But if you like a challenge, if you like story, if you like sci-fi.... this is the game for you.
Recommended!

If first-person survival is at all your thing, you owe it to yourself to get The Long Dark. In a spin on the genre, it's you vs nature instead of you vs the supernatural. As much as I love zombies, the lack of dealing with the undead is refreshing. The game is difficult without being oppressively so, and allows you to pick between game types that increase or decrease the difficulty depending on how hard-core you are about your survival games. The art style is lovely, the game itself runs really well, and in dedicating themselves to a single-player experience the devs are able to really focus and fine-tune the experience. Speaking of the devs, I have a lot of respect for how they've handled development of this project and how they interact with their community. It takes a lot of guts to not cave to every fans whim, even if doing so would result in an inferior product. And the cherry on the cake, for my fellow lady gamers: Yes, you can play as a fully voiced female character! Enjoy being Commander Shepard in the Candian wilderness!

Plays pretty much like the original Red Orchestra. Can give you a very rewarding feeling getting something done in it provided you are patient enough to adapt to it's very hardcore-ish design. Along with Armed Assault, Insurgency, Forgotten Hope and maybe Battleground Europe one of the most realistic and unforgiving shooters I know. One or two hits from any weapon can put you down. The firearms are not fully locked to the center of the screen, which gives a more "plastic" and difficult feeling of holding and handling them. Sprinting into the open will you get you killed most of the time unless you do it with numerous teammates hoping for at least some of you to slip through. Or unless you get some smoke cover by the few squad leaders each team has and who serve as mobile spawn points. If you die you will often not know where the bullet that kiled you came from. People's silhouettes easily disappear among the grey-brownish tones of the game, you need to have your eyes peeled at all times and watch for the slightest pixel irregularities - a muzzle flash, an arm moving, a rifle barrel extending out of a window. People will go prone and hide all of their body they can behind brick and stone and within grass. If you manage to kill somebody, or even go on a killing spree behind enemy lines, you may feel some adrenaline rush, and a greater sense of achievement than your ordinary hand-holding shooter would give you. But so one may also more easily feel useless or frustrated when the own attempts to defend or attack objectives keep failing over and over, and you don't even really understand why or where you keep getting pounded from by the enemy.
Tools and tactics include gaining higher ground, coordinating the team to focus attention on one out of often two points (the maps are not "mirrored", teams don't switch sides or something, but both of them can often attack, defend and recapture locations), flanking, smoke grenades, artillery fire (still called in via radios placed around the world I think, but the attack spots are marked/tagged by the squad leaders and only the commander of the team can call them in; or so it seem, I haven't played them myself yet), recon planes to temporarily highlight the location of enemies on your map, tanks and armored transport vehicles as well as MGs and marksmen for decoy, cover or suppressing fire. And players can "spot" targets with a button. From what I've seen they, or at least their rough position, will appear on the map/radar. Your character will yell it out acoustically too. There is some cooldown to it so people won't be spamming positions all over.
Additionally, the "Territory" game mode has a "Lockdown" feature. If the attacking team is not able to gain control of the next capture point within some time they will fail the whole round, or so I understood it. This prevents rather hopeless matches to continue longer than what is good, and gives reason for the attacking team to do what they are supposed to do.
The game, or at least it's "Realistic" game setting (there are a few more to choose from, but most servers are playing "Realistic"), utilizes a system that makes your character's screen shake and blur when bullets hit the area around you. Zooming in (holding your breath) is prevented that way too, I think your movement is hindered too. This may feel a bit forced and irritating as the player himself may not actually feel this artifical "panic", stress and tension, but I think it's an interesting idea and gives some added, realistic value to suppressive fire.
Also, when charging up with around four teammates or so you do a charge attack. You run a bit faster I think, you hear your characters yell out and from what the tooltips say hostiles nearby get suppressed too, in the ways I mentioned in the previous paragraph. I haven't seen people do coordinated charge attacks, but it sure won't hurt either when there is a chance to and no other way to flush out your enemies than by running directly foward.
There is some real physics in it it seems. Guns do seem to have falloff, you can adjust the sights of the rifles to different ranges, though I've been able to do relatively fine without. When attacking tanks with anti-tank rifles or other tanks you need to be aware of the weak spots within their damage models. Passengers can get killed individually, or certain vehicle parts disabled. Crew members and gunners can be as helpful as vulnerable to small arms fire, so manning vehicles and turrets will not render anyone semi-invulnerable. Tanks have AP and HE shells to kill other vehicles or infantry with respectively. The guides say the angles at which you shoot from (or get shot at) matter too. These are details one probably has long to experiment with to fully understand, but there are guides on Steam and the internet that will probably help.
There is some XP system, but it appears underdeveloped. At least when compared to other games. You gain XP with each gun when killing with it, and apparently this will unlock alternate versions. By default you have a rifle without and with a bayonet attachment. If I am asked I'd say I prefer it to be as rudimentarily as it is, as I personally think that "metafeatures" like XP, cash, customization and crafting features are massively overrated in many games these days and that they in the worst case hurt the gameplay design as they bring in either imbalancing or silly, artificial reasons to grind (I'm looking at you, Payday 2).
I don't fully understand why there are no airplanes. Some of the maps are pretty big. There are small recon planes that launch and move automatically above the sky to fulfill the purpose I mentioned earlier. Real airplanes could be designed to work as difficult to control as in the Battlefield mod "Forgotten Hope" to prevent them from becoming "overpowered". Warfare back then included airplanes, and if they wish to be truly faithful to it they should consider bringing them in too I believe.

Initially, I was excited for this game as it sounded like a send up to Star Control II and Starflight.
It's not.
What it is, sadly, is a game with frustrating, unintuitive controls that are worse in some ways than the Lunar Lander game from the 80s that clearly inspired it.  Overuse of thrust can send you spinning, fuel is used up way too rapidly, the lander tips over easily and receives random component damage....But that's just the Lander, surely?  No.  The ship itself handles like a brick with a thruster attached.  The entire gameplay revolves around you colliding with objects to receive damage states, many of which you won't be able to repair unless you get very lucky.
And here it is.  Roguelike.  The authors claim on several steam posts that it's a 'gentler' roguelike but I disagree; if anything it's a more callous because the sheer  amount of status injuries and ship and vehicle damage states each have to  be handled and approached with different repair methods that don't all show up at the few stations you encounter.  What ends up happening is a gradual wear down of your crew as the injuries and damage mount up until you either die or throw up your hands in frustration.
Here are 3 key problems with the game in my first hour:
1.  Trying to gather fuel is an exercise in futility.  You have to hover constantly with the lander, using up fuel while trying to gather it.  Every single time I went out to get fuel I ended up with a net loss.
2.  Ship and crews have lots of damage states that are applied randomly (having a clogged pollen filter from tipping over) and often have no way to fix them, especially early on.
3.  Controls that I would call broken were it not so obvious they were intentionally made to be bad.  Understand, these controls were designed to make you hit objects in the ship, have navigation issues and flop around and hit things in the Lander.  I just can't see how it wasn't intentional to have the controls be so loose and sloppy.
My guess is  they thought this would all create challenge and something to drive you, but it's heavyhanded and frustrating with the way the ship and lander controls work and you often have to concede that the game is designed for your ship and crew to sustain needless injuries from a lander tipping over or hitting an asteroid because your ship turns like a brick.
So what's the problem with that, really?  None if you enjoy games that punish you for playing them.   I thought The Long Journey Home was going to be about discovering aliens, trading, finding secrets on our way home.  What it turned into was a triage simulator, and I'm not pretending it isn't frustrating and disappointing.
Since my previous review was removed I'm probably missing some other issues I encountered with the game, but I will continue posting my honest thoughts on this game until they stick.
And the one point that is clear is that I cannot recommend this game at all in its present state.  I'm not sure they will drastically overhaul the controls to make them worthwhile and not intentionally obtuse, but if they do I will consider altering my review.

BioShock is a rather interesting title. While it fails to introduce any unseen elements into the action-RPG genre, it does utilise those tools we well know in a rather interesting and intelligent way.
The moral choices in the game are rewarded with there-abouts the same way, but with extra benefit given for the "good" choices. In the end, they are really a some-what cosmetic choice and their real impact is on the player's conciousness, which may well have been the intention, based on seeable evidence.
The combat system and weapons choices were somewhat limited, but nonetheless functional. All enemy types are encountered early on, and it's not long before enemies because predictable and mostly boring. That said, the areas in which they are encountered constantly distract the player from noticing such things.
My main praise goes to the mood and story of the game. While the mechanics it was told using are nothing original, the setting and plot goes above and beyond what would have been great for a game of this calibur, and has thrust it into it's current fame.
My foremost critcism goes to the closing levels of the game: Particularly the mesuem escort mission. As any of my friend will tell you: I've put a LOT of time and effort (a lot more than is reasonable or appropriate :P) Into what I believe would have been a far better end phase, but the past can not be rewritten, and we are left here with an ending that utterly fails what is otherwise a try 10 contender.
Final Score: 9.2/10

I really love driving games, and this is the kind of game that just lets you jump right in and blow off some steam. Great graphics with lots of particle effects. The physics really make the game too. I never get bored of ploughing through a tyre wall and seeing all the tyres bounce around! The handling is spot on, and you really feel like you are maneuvering some real weight around the track. Each car handles very differently too.
You can customise your car visually, and upgrade pretty much anything mechanical. So if you have a favourite car but want to ramp up to the Class A races, then you have to race and save up some cash to upgrade it. The game needs a career mode, and right now there is none, but the game still holds up without it. I love to load this up and have a few races, smash some cars into each other and watch back the replays in slow motion.
It's open to modding, and I have to say my favourite mod by far is 'Real 2 Life'. This adds almost a survival element to the game by making damage a lot more realistic. One crash could lose you a wheel, and then you are fighting your car round the track to try and finish. Going over big jumps too fast can kill your engine, so 24 cars off the start line quickly turns into 6 cars, and you find yourself limping round the track with smoke pouring out your car, trying to avoid all the wrecks left behind on previous laps. There is a real satisfaction to finishing in 1st place, with 3 wheels and black smoke pouring out your car :)
This is a great game, that has so much further potential. I hope to see them implement a survival mode like I mentioned with the mod above. I feel this would add a whole new aspect to the game and something different. Maybe a race series with limited repair time between races, so you might have to sacrifice your broken exhaust to fix your wheels for example.
Anyway, this game fills the gap between the every growing amount of clean, high speed racing games. Sometimes I just want to smash up some stuff, and this game really hits the spot :)
Finally some tactical and realistic First Person Shooter! I can do nothing but recommend it!

The Long Journey Home is an inspired, fun, and often frusrating game that is... likely going to be divisive.
The game is topdown/sidescrolling, and feels familiar to many arcade titles of the past. These familiar gameplay mechanics are combined together to make some of the fundamental game dynamics, such as navigating your ship, using the lander to go planetside, or dialogue/diplomacy with alien species.
These mechanics can be tedious or frustrating to players, since they're very much the same task over and over with randomized environments and often very punishing conditions that can make the risk vs. reward choices often lean to, "I'll skip this entirely," if given the option.
That being said, the roguelike elements and challenge haven't become tedious enough to stop playing for myself, and I've looked forward to making changes to strategy and learning more about the universe to improve the likelihood of success on my next mission. The outcome of choices can be frustrating, but it's often because the universe feels indifferent and punishing when you don't know "the rules" of galaxies or other species.
The world building is familiar but enjoyable, and the game doesn't take itself too seriously. Some of the dialogue between crew members is... obnoxious, but it's also easily ignored. If anything you can find creative ways to sacrifice them for the benefit of the rest of the mission. Exploring and learning more about the locations and creatures of the varying galaxies is absolutely the motivator, by design, to keep you coming back. If it's not pulling you in - this may not be for you.
The new Story Mode just went live in a patch, which may bridge the gap for some folks that disliked certain gameplay elements or their frustration/forgiveness, which may change some folks opinions of the game in regards to tedium.
Either way, I don't feel compelled to write many reviews, but I thought this game deserved some good mentions, as I've enjoyed it.

It is truly unfortunate, when a promising game receives a lot of negative attention (and reviews) because of its difficult control scheme. I am torn over this matter since I cannot disagree with some of those critics. A PC game that is best experienced with a controller instead of mouse+keyboard, can be a tough sell for the Steam crowd. I didn’t use a controller for The Long Journey Home, yet I did manage to “train” myself enough to avoid frustration from the many failed attempts to steer either the ship or the lander. More on that further below, I shall focus a bit on the developer now.
Daedalic Studio West may not have other Steam projects to brag about, but you cannot call them debutants. Daedalic Entertainment is celebrating 10 years of activity in 2017 and they were quite prolific, with several dozen launched Steam projects (some as multiplatform titles as well) and a handful new ones always in development. You can say what you will, but these guys know what they’re doing and the “gamble” with a more realistic space exploration game that might integrate some laws of physics along with elements of astrophysics, should have payed off. It looked great on paper, of that much I’m certain. Yet something didn’t quite click right…
The Long Journey Home is a narrative-driven experience, despite some procedurally generated elements in regards to the planets themselves. Replay value can be found in the sense in which, you become accustomed to the various alien races that you meet across multiple playthroughs. It’s important to understand that you won’t be able to encounter every single species of creatures or plants, alien ruins or planet types in a single sitting and profile. Your main goal is to get back home, on Earth and everything else, from planetary exploration, diplomatic endevours, experiments upon alien technology and resource gathering, are just secondary objectives.
Players assume control of the ship and crew of the Daedalus-7 Jump Test mission, tasked by the IASA (International Aeronautic & Space Administration) with the exploration of Alpha Centauri, the closest star system to our own Solar System. As the case with most prototype equipment and forays into the unknown, Daedalus-7 is an apparent failure, with the ship & crew declared lost after they can no longer contact mission control and have in fact, overshot their intended destination by a large margin. They are now stranded, more than 37847 parsecs away from Terra. A parsec is a unit of measurement, equal to about 3.26 light-years (31 trillion kilometres or 19 trillion miles) in length. You better get used to a lot of terms and principles related to space travel, because The Long Journey Home aims for a more comprehensive vision than its genre competitors.
The game’s being powered by the Unreal Engine 4 in a skilled manner in which I encountered no frame rate dips or glitches and could run it on a 4K resolution and constant 60fps. Ideal conditions and The Long Journey Home sure provides plenty of screenshot opportunities, with its beautiful simulation of alien worlds and spaceship battles. Some assets and characters make use of the large pixel visual style, yet that is isolated enough to make room for high res textures in other parts. No complaints from me, in regards to the title’s looks.
The sounds on the other hand, would have benefitted from more variety. The soundtrack is fine, as are the sound effects, but my main gripe with the game’s audio department, is the lack of voice acting. It was not enough to mark it as a weak point, but for a title that wants you to feel attached to your crewmembers and ensure their survival and well-being, it felt a bit disappointing just to read the chat between themselves or the feedback they offered on occasion. Their quirky personalities coulds sure use the boost offered by a handful of spoken dialogue lines. At least the aliens emit some jibber-jabber to compensate for your silent team.
The gameplay in The Long Journey Home, depending on how much patience you have, may be either a blessing or a curse. It is no understatement that the control scheme and ship/lander movement mechanics took a toll upon my own self-composure, yet I could never conceive rage quitting on a review project. I got better at the handling part, so that helped as well. Just be wary that it will require a hefty amount of careful planning (along with trial & error), before you’ll achieve the perfect landing without breaking the limbs of your lander pilot or enter a planet’s orbit without overshooting or passing the atmospheric threshold (bringing your massive ship too close to a planet).
I honestly think that the control scheme itself may not be the issue and the speed of your lander/ship trajectory is in fact the main culprit. The simulation of the space travel aspect is on fast-forward, since it obviously still takes days for your vessel to move around a single star system, even if we’re in deep Sci-Fi realm and speculation already. So at least the option of moving slower, should be implemented in a subsequent update. Yeah, I know that the chaotic speed and gravity pull is affected by the various planetary conditions. I think we’re going a bit too realistic with this though. I’m all for throwing arcade elements out the window, only for as long as the fun factor remains intact. And this isn’t Space Flight Simulator 2017.
As for the actual gameplay outside of getting your ship into orbit or landing on a planet in order to explore or harvest its resources, a large part of The Long Journey Home focuses on your human crew’s interaction with various alien species. Some may be friendly, others quite hostile and most of them are plain weird while it’s up to your team to cater to their unusual needs. Be diplomatic and you will find you journey back home, far more pleasant. If you wish to be aggressive, bear in mind that you’re not in control of a warship and that your motley crew are of scientific background, not trained killers.
As of this writing, the dev team did respond in a timely manner to criticism relating to the high overall difficulty and have implemented a Story Mode, which is addressing some of the issues I mentioned above. You can still pick between the intial Adventure (“normal) and Rogue (unforgiving) Modes, but I strongly recommend you get acquainted with the gameplay mechanics in the new Story Mode. I congratulate Daedalic Entertainment on this speedy recovery in terms of crowd-pleasing.
I admit that few devs correct gameplay mistakes or unbalance in a swift manner, unless we talk of the dreaded day 1 patches. Still, it’s a nice move from a developer that clearly cares about its customers and players. I was going to comment on the game’s price tag, but really if it bothers you, just wait for an inevitable Steam Sale. I will be enjoying The Long Journey Home a lot more, now that some of my complaints are no longer valid. Hope you will like it too.
EDIT: Trading Cards have been added after almost a month from the publishing of this review.

+ Beautiful graphics.
+ Steam Achievements & Steam Trading Cards.
+ Complex simulation on the perils of space exploration.
+ Customization and procedurally generated assets ensure replay value.
+ Developer listened to criticism and quickly offered a lower difficulty option.
- “Realistic” or not, the control scheme is an issue outside of Story Mode.
- The gameplay gets repetitive fairly fast.
- Astronauts lack sufficient personality.

A solid, spooky, mournful sandbox game -- ineluctably the best of its breed and class, with the potential to redefine an entire genre of gaming -- sadly hindered by the worst EA development communications strategy I've ever seen.
The Long Dark is one of my favorite gameplay experiences of all time. Because that's what it is -- not just a game, but an experience that draws from the traditions of Canadian literature: themes of bleakness, isolation, great expanses, and the erosion these challenges can present to humanity. This isn't just a hunger/thirst/sleep meter-feeder with wolves. We don't even have the story yet, but the world itself is its own story, somewhere between tragic bildungsroman and existentialist ennui. This game is art, man.
THAT SAID.
TLD's development team are brilliant artists, but absolutely dismal business professionals. And given the understandable mistrust in the Early Access community, this unprofessionalism --combined with grand but premature ambitions -- has frequently devastated their reputation among their player base.
Hinterland is its own worst enemy. It has struggled with a troublesome history of foolish communications choices, worrying periods of silence, launch failures, nebulous goal-setting, feature rollbacks, and manipulative (or maybe just woefully novice) marketing tactics; historically, the team has also been more likely to passive-aggressively withdraw than to learn from these blunders. It pains me to say this, because I LOVE the sandbox experience even as an unfinished product. But even if the baby's cherished, this bathwater has got to be dumped.
Look me in the eyes: I. LOVE. THE. LONG. DARK. But as a consumer, I have to be clear: I recommend you do NOT full-price purchase this one until the baby's been out of the womb long enough that it's grumbling about gas prices and worrying about tuition.
The Long Dark is like a promise of a spectacular bestselling novel caught between drafts. It's been a sloppy road, but you can see the gold beneath the mess, and you want to get lost in it. You can trust it will be well worth the price of admission...but only if that final draft is ever complete.

Sunless Sea is a trade and exploration game set in an underground ocean environment chiefly inspired by the works of H.P. Lovecraft, with a dash of Neil Gaiman and perhaps a touch of Hinchcliffe-era Doctor Who? Not sure about that last one. In any case, it's dark, funny, macabre, sometimes touching and never less than atmospheric. It's also, depending on your taste, slow, frustrating, and a bit light on content. But I'll get into that later.
The good first. Sunless Sea is primarily an exercise in atmosphere and imagination, and on those terms it's very well built. The game encourages you to avoid straight combat and stay illuminated or close to land at all times, forcing you to weigh consuming more fuel with a roundabout route against trips into dark waters that will slowly drive you and your crew insane. The result is a well-defined sailing environment which is easy to comprehend but never friendly. The imagination is lovely, too: settlements built into the carcasses of leviathans, an island of alcholic monks, an economy which thrives on storytelling and rumor. You get to hunt terrifying sea monsters, learn forbidden secrets, conduct espionage between Londoners and underground Mongols...
It's great stuff, and what's best about it is that it duplicates the Lovecraftian trick of making the universe utterly indifferent to you. You're not the Chosen One, you're not the revealer of all things or the savior of worlds. You're just a captain with a boat and a dream, and fate - or whatever force governs it - could crush you like a bug without noticing.
All of this is sweet and awesome and correct and I'll be playing this game for a long while. But there are, inevitably with a game this complex, some issues.
The first hurdle is speed. You can never sail at anything faster than what feels like a snail's pace. The reason for this probably has something to do with preventing the player from discovering too much of the game world too quickly, but while it's undoubtedly a relaxing experience there's just large segments of playtime when I'm not really engaging with the game. The process of uncovering the map early in a playthrough compensates for this, but once you're no longer a beginner it really starts to grate.
The sailing speeds feel like they hit just the right spot of too uninvolving to be rewarding and yet too involving to let you, for instance, pop into the kitchen and get a snack. This is why fast-travel systems were invented, people. Still, a fast-travel system would hardly be fair in a game so heavily dependent on immersing yourself in the actual business of sailing. I might recommend something like a waypoint system, letting you predetermine a path that you can set your ship to automatically follow - but that risks cutting the player out completely rather than simply weakening engagement, so what do I know.
I'm not entirely certain I like the text interface, either. Once you're used to it it's not that hard to navigate, but a beginning player especially is going to look at their journal and see a whole bunch of icons with meanings utterly mysterious to them. Discovering gameplay as you go is all well and good but for a long time I was essentially making decisions at random, which felt more frustrating than rewarding.
The book item that explains things is all well and good, except I'm not sure it's wise to put a beginning player through the process of pausing, finding their way to their inventory, picking out the book, finding the particular passage, et cetera et cetera. For use as a reference or a reminder on certain topics, yes, but I feel like I shouldn't have to basically stop playing to find out how to play for the first time.
The game economy is lovely and intricate, though occasionally it feels like there are gaps. That basically anything can be traded in the right venue - even "experience points", news, stories and memories - is pretty friggin' sweet. As a player you aren't just a sailor scrounging for bigger numbers of things - you're a witty raconteur, a spymaster, and a scholar of terrifying secrets. The trade really is the story. That's kind of brilliant.
Making the trade system work for you, on the other hand, is kind of difficult. Of course there's an intentional element of trial and error to be had here, but I do get the distinct feeling that there isn't enough variation in demand for different commodities to allow a player to figure out more than three trade routes (and at least two of those take advantage of the fact that parts of the map don't change in subsequent playthroughs). There are a couple of conspicuous dead ends where content was cut (e.g. the Antiquarian thing, which apparently doesn't go anywhere), which makes me think the developers are still getting a handle on the dizzying complexity of the economy and environment they built. No bad thing in a fairly ambitious indie project, but you can see the seams on occasion.
I suspect the game's main flaw is that its world is just a bit too small. Reshuffling parts works with a roguelike structure, but the fact that you can quit the game and keep going where you left off means that there are going to be playthroughs which succeed for hours upon hours - perhaps indefinitely - and content and sailing will inevitably start to get repetitive and - dare I say it - grindy. A bigger world would allow for faster sailing that wasn't overpowered, as well as more room for interesting strategy in setting up trade routes.
Overall, though, this is still a remarkably fun and intriguing game - if I wrote more about the negatives than the positives, it's simply because it's so damn hard to speak for gameplay that speaks for itself, and so much easier to spot flaws than triumphs (otherwise we'd all be master artisans, wouldn't we?). Point is, I'm looking forward to discovering more of Sunless Sea and what the developers plan on doing with it.

Yet another good game doomed to fail because of a developer team that can't listen to even the most simple of feedback.
EDIT: Hey guys, remember when
Because they sure as hell don't. You can now buy shardpacks in the ingame cash shop, which most people have to bust their butts doing Chaos tiers for. So yeah. that's definitely an advantage. So not only are they developers who do not care about their game or their fans, they're also blatant liars.
Dungeon Defenders 2 was fantastic before the release of the Trials update, then everything seemed to begin snowballing downward. Not only was the initial jump from campaign mode to the new Chaos difficulty nearly impossible, but the people who managed to do not only that were punished instead of being congratulated. I'm sorry, but you don't reward players for getting to certain difficulties by randomly nerfing all the heroes and raising green mana costs on things that were just fine on their own. You do not make your new difficulty more difficult by making players weaker and making some heroes completely unviable.
Another thing that the Trials update has done to doom this game is player scaling. In what screwed up universe is it a good idea to make your players feel like a burden just by playing with other people? The more people that join, the harder the Old One's Army gets. And it's not even to a challenging difficulty, a Chaos 1 or 2 map with four players is nearly impossible to beat, and it's gotten to the point where most people swear by the playstyle of "solo or nothing" because of how much of a burden playing with other people is. You've really messed up when people don't want to play with their friends by no fault of said friends. Trendy tried to fix this by lowering the scaling, but they refused to listen when their playerbase said "We want it GONE". That description I used for player scaling? It was referring to after the nerf. So even after they believed they had done good and entirely ignored their fans cries, their multiplayer-centric game still entirely discourages multiplayer.
The loot scaling system is a damned mess to the point where most players in the chaos difficulty are just waiting around for the blacksmith or relic hunter to stock something that's even some semblance of an upgrade. Because apparently the very simple idea of "Stronger enemies and higher difficulty = better loot" is too bland and stupid for Trendy Entertainment. There are far too many stories about how players are confronted with the choice to either sacrifice all their shards because a piece of equipment is far better than what they have but has no shard slots, so they opt to just sit around and wait for the blacksmith or relic hunter to have something better. Waiting around for an upgrade despite having clearly earned it is not okay.
Trendy doesn’t seem to care about proper game care, either. Reports abound of gamebreaking bugs that have been occuring for months up to a year, and what has Trendy done? Absolutely nothing. They seem to have a complete and utter disregard for things that make an online multiplayer tower defense game what it is. I wanted to like this game. But I can't care about a game if the devs can't either.
