Tee-El Dee-ar, Adun:  While this game may not be a proper
, it is quite a good videogame for people who like the genre, and I would call this one a Twin-Stick Hack-and-Slash.  Most of the negativity toward it is because
.  It also has a nearly Dad Joke sense of humor about it, so if you are annoyed by intentionally silly/troll-y humor, steer clear.
Just to be sure you're under no illusions, this game is
an ARPG like Diablo.  It is a twin-stick.  You select a character,  you select a mission, you hack, you slash, you beat the baddie at the end, you move to the next mission.  There are no trips to town--there is no town.  The hub is the map screen where you select missions and your character loadout.  There's no wandering around, because there's nowhere to wander because the missions themselves are very much on-rails. There's also no standing around deciding which items to pick up after you kill a big group, because there's no Diablo-style inventory to manage.  There
items to collect, but these are just progression unlocks which you can pick and choose before the mission.
I've noticed people compare this game to Gauntlet, but lacking experience with that game, I can only say it controls like
with only minor differences.
If you've never played a twin stick, (do try AS:RD, linked above, as it is excellent and free) they are actually designed for a controller with a stick on the left that you move with and a stick on the right which you aim attacks with.  For we keyboardists, you move your character with WASD and determine which direction you aim with the mouse.  I will be referencing the keyboard/mouse controls since that's what I use.
This game has one control oddity in that it determines
with your mouse position, whereas in the other twin sticks I've played (again,
and also
), you dodge in the direction of your
.  This means that in
, you can aim at a target while simultaneously dodging away from it while using a keyboard.  But in Sanctum 3, you first have to move your mouse cursor to a position opposite the opponent you're dodging away from, and then return the cursor to the enemy's direction once you complete the dodge in order to aim at them again.  However, it also means that you have
over which direction you dodge, since with WASD you can only move in the eight cardinal directions.
Each of the game's four classes (six with DLCs) has a basic attack on left click, a "Bash" on the right, two special abilities on number keys 1 and 2 (light and heavy respectively), and using a potion defaulted to mouse wheel click, while selecting a potion was bound to mouse wheel roll.  Your left click is your general purpose Kill-It, your right click bash is for enemies with shield icons over their heads, indicating a strong defense.   Using your Bash on these enemies will temporarily stun them, allowing you to chop/slice/stab/perforate them up with your left click.  There are also traps in the game which are reliably disabled with the "Bash".  The special skills vary between the classes, but all seem to be limited-use-but-refillable group attacks of varying effectiveness.  One mechanic which is unique among my twin sticks is the ability to pick up mid-sized enemies and hurl them at other enemies.  This seems mostly for flourish, since there are other effective ways to kill enemies, but it is amusing and effective enough in its own right.  Edit: After testing this further, I can say throwing is actually QUITE effective, handily bowling over a dozen other combatants with a single throw.
You can modify your character's equipment and skill loadouts between missions.  All the characters have at least three or four options of special attacks to slot into their 1 and 2 keys, and armor and weapons can also be selected to affect appearance/minor stat changes.  There is also an equippable type of....
called a "Battle Spirit".  These, when applied to your weapon, give bonuses.   For example, the first one you get, the "Battlemage", applies a change to chain lightning between enemies when you attack.   He also sometimes says stuff like, "OH BABY!"  That's a good example to see if the game's sense of humor will bother you, actually.  Does it bother you that sometimes your weapon will scream "Oh baby!" at you?
The story is a serious story told in a not-serious-at-all way.   This isn't to say that it is poorly-executed-- the voice acting is above-average for videogames, and it all makes sense.   It's just quite silly in places.
Overall, I am having an unexpectedly fun time in my first-ever
-rated game, and I think if you give it a chance, you might as well!

The world has room to explore, but not so much where you can easily become lost. The game is filled with a neat but creepy early 1900s (city constructed in 1940s) vibe and music that blends so well with this world. I do have problems with motion sickness playing First person shooters but I was able to push through and enjoy the game to a great extent. Without rushing, the game took me approximately 15-20 hours to complete and I'm currently playing through my second time with the PC version.
The regular price of $19.99 is a bit steep for a game that has been out for over half a decade. The game really is fun. I enjoyed the actual gameplay. The combat feels really fluid. It's nice to be able to stop time. This is the closest thing I have ever played to a turn-based first-person shooter, and I think that's downright cool.
But I have a couple of complaints. After the end of each (extremely short) mission, you are treated to a seizure inducing flashing of the words "Super Hot" until you move on to the next mission. The game pulls you forcibly out of the game play after every successful sortie, and it is disorienting (which I am sure it was meant to be, but still), uncomfortable, immersion breaking, and just generally annoying. If I were a pre-teen hopped up on way too much caffeine, this might be okay. But I am an adult and neither using cocaine nor ecstasy, so this is not an enjoyable experience.
My second complaint is that it's difficult to gauge the player hit box (a detriment of first-person perspective), so I find myself regularly being hit by projectiles because I didn't give myself a wide enough berth. I know I could just move further out of the way so I am guarenteed to be safe, but being close to death is half the fun of time stopping shooters.

I found myself with an itch for 3d platforming after playing the new Mario game for awhile (a family member's copy).  So I picked this game up to scratch the itch, and whlie it's not as polished as Odyssey, it's still a heckuva fun game with cute character designs, good level design, and fairly tight control.  I also have to give special props to the voice actors the game company hired for this game   Well done, ladies & gents! The boss fights I'd actually rate above the fights in Odyssey both in presentation and in gameplay.
I have some minor gripes about camera control in certain areas, and certain collectibles that feel like they're in a glitchy area you weren't supposed to be able to get to intstead of something that feels like a secret area more natural to the landscape.  But there's only a handful of such instances.
I have heard some other reviews criticizing the game for its length, but I got about 10-15 hours out of it myself in a single playthrough (and that's with getting the achievements but not exhaustively all the extras).  That seems about right for a game like this to me.  I would love to play more levels, but I think it's generally a plus to leave a game wanting more where it came from.
On the topic of difficulty, I think I should point out getting some of the achievements are more tedious than difficult.  The majority of the game is pretty easy though, even the bossfights.  It's about on par with a lot of nintendo games aimed at being challenging enough to be fun, but not so difficult as to be aggravating or frustating.  It's usually more about figuring out which abilities to use when and where, rather than pulling off tightly timed jumps in sequence.  Which is all to say I think the game is generally well balanced, but could probably use some more challenging achievements (like a different achievement for each boss beaten while wearing the one-hit death badge, and/or achievements for not using hat powers  on bosses.

Short version: Extremely creative game that is a lot of fun to play, but ultimately suffers from a shallow campaign that leaves you with a redundant challenge mode. Price at time of review: $24.99. Actual value: $15.
What I like about Superhot is that it doesn't take itself seriously at all, but still accomplishes a great playing experience. The  developers know their own shortcomings and cleverly use it in the story line of the campaign. It's funny to play a redundant game that pokes fun at it's own redundancy, but I am left thinking that actually adding some more features, weapons, and techniques would have been a slightly more difficult way of dealing with the redundancy with a huge pay off. That pay off, in this case, being able to justify a $30+ price tag for the game.
So after about 90 minutes, complete with some boring cut scenes, you open free mode and challenge mode. This is where my criticism is probably the most prevalent. How about adding achievements that allow you to customize free mode? Perhaps freeze time completely when you're not moving, the ability to crouch, or the ability to choose which weapons are allowed on the map. These are pretty simple things that would extend the life of the game by a few hours by allowing players to be creative.
Ultimately, while I do seemingly have a lot of complaints, I can't bring myself to put this review into the red because the game IS an innovate, fun game. Hopefully a sequel will take advantage of the puzzle solving and creative opportunities presented within this concept. Buy it on sale.

Disappointing. The videos and previews of the game are VERY different from the current state of the game. It is no longer the brutal survival simulator that I saw on youtube and on steam. Monsters are very nonaggresive and doctile preferring to stay near their nests and wander around doing nothing. During night time very few monsters bother coming over to destroy my village. And the fights are definitely not as thrilling as the videos made them out to be. There's just one monster with crazy amounts of HP instead of multiple monsters with smaller amounts of HP. This change made the game very...bland. The tower defense aspect of the game isn't very exciting either. Due to the constant restraints of the "building limit" you have to keep upgrading your homebase in order to build more towers. And after you get "permission" from the ministry of labours your building sites are constantly blocked by tree "stumps". When you mine a resource like a tree or a rock for example they leave behind a little "stump" that blocks any construction on where the resource used to be. Now I think I understand why this was implimented. It was probably implemented to "protect" the player from over harvesting resources so that way they always have a "stump" to go back to for more wood, crystals, food etc. What I find troubling about this philosophy is that it is counter intuitive of the philosophy of the game. What I thought the game was about was SURVIVAL, not the forever sand box. The problem with this is two fold: one there already is a survival and sandbox modes so the over arching "protection" from the devs to prevent overharvesting goes beyond what the modes imply; players are being handheld in survival mode and it feels...boring. The second problem is that there is no "end game" for sandbox right now (neither for survival) so it doesn't matter.
Over all I thought this game was going to be breakneck difficulty like dwarffortress, but instead it was a hand-holding, carebear boredom. I like difficulty and I found none here. I was so bored I left my base to run for a couple of real life hours without me and when I came back it was just fine (except for a few people gone missing).
If you wanted a care-bear experience with mild tower defense you found the game. If you expected dwarffortress with some cool tower defense aspect to it, you won't find it here.

The meat and potatoes of Sunless Sea is reading and exploring the in-game fiction and the accompanying "choose-your-own-adventure" style gameplay.
It's like someone took the nightmare-infested, Victorian-Era dystopia of the webcomic "The Watcher of Yaathagggu", where the very shadows around you influence and warp reality in undesirable ways. Then they described it all through the kind of nebulous, otherworldly prose one might sample in HP Lovecraft's "The Dream-Quest for Unknown Kadath". Finally, they sprinkled the end product with odd chunks of ridiculous fantasy-oriented self-satire, like one would expect to find in Terry Pratchett's "Discworld" series. Strangely, it all holds together remarkably well, unless the existence of talking rodents and empire-building monkeys ruins the otherwise all-encompassing sense of dread and lurking horror for you.
... Oh, and there's a nautical trading simulator in there as well.
10/10

We'd been at zee for a long time, running dark to conserve fuel and avoid the attention of the pirates and great beasts. Despite my best efforts -- spinning tales of comfort for my zailors, brazenly defying Nightmares, even initiating an affair with my engineer -- I'd managed to let my Terror get all the way to 100%. The achievement pops up; "Lose Your Mind". This doesn't bode well, but I'm a mere ship's length away from home port, and docking will reduce terror to 50%; a much more manageable level. Surely I can hold out just a little--
I'm instantly presented with a choice between murdering my entire crew (with 12% chance of success), or attempting to win them over (9%). Failing either one, I was told, would end my game. I did the only thing I could do, and somehow managed to kill everyone aboard, save two. We made harbor and, with a fresh batch of new faces, set out to zee once more.
Time passes.
An adventurer whom we've been running jobs for finally announces that he has all of the supplies he needs to make his final journey and I, having proven my capability, am his first choice of transport. There's just one problem...my trusty ship lacks the capacity to hold his cargo with room for food and fuel. We're going to need a bigger boat.
I buy a bigger boat and hire on twice again as many zailors as I already have. We load up and set sail, but not before I accept just one more smuggling job from my "friend" with the bad eye and the concealed knife. Corsair's Forest? I've been there a dozen times; consider it done.
It's not until we're two days out that I realize my new ship has half the speed of my old one, and my triple-size crew are a hungry bunch. We're running low on supplies before we've even reached our initial destination, but we make the drop and start to head home.
Then the realization strikes. If we dock in London now, before finishing that smuggling job, I'll have to cough up the fee plus a hefty chunk of interest, not to mention lose a valuable connection...but the nearest trading port is in the opposite direction.
It took every scrap of food we had, but we managed to reach Mount Palmerston without resorting to cannibalism...again. We traded with the devils for supplies and loaded up on coke freshly dug from Hell. On our way home we made port at Pigmote isle, where a civilization of guinea pigs threw a banquet in our honor -- their returning saviors, though this time we were the ones in need of saving.
After a harrowing encounter with a manic Jillyfleur brought hull integrity to 1%, and a misbehaving Clay Man took five lives before we subdued him, we were desperate for rest and repair. An ill-fortuned shore leave on Gaidur's Mourn pushed Terror to worrying levels, but we had our package. As we pulled out of the port, a straggling pirate ship fired one last shot across our bow -- but the shell missed by an arm's length and we were homeward bound. Two days later, limping into port with a skeleton crew, I breathed a sigh of relief that I'd narrowly escaped losing my mind for the second time in the space of a week. My sweetheart and child welcome me home. I say nothing of the suicides -- surely they were suicides? -- that only I had been privy to. I pass on an uncanny artifact to my son; someday he, too, will be a zee captain, with enough cares of his own. No need to trouble him with details.
My friend has another job for me, and the Admiralty has need of news from the outlying colonies. I take a loss on a purchase of a smaller ship, name her after the one I'd traded to begin with. Eighth of my house and 211 days at zee, I sail on.

When i first heard of Telltale developing a batman game using their style of story telling i thought to myself "That's a peculiar choice" (Considering their past titles like The Walking Dead, The Wolf Among Us & Game of Thrones). However, so far this has been a refreshing breakaway from those worlds and taking on the Batman Universe is definetly grasping another portion of the audience. Now let's get to why you are here.
I only began playing the first episode after a few small updates were released (like the 2-40mb ones) so improvements could have been significant to non-existent. Regardless on my system which i will list briefly underneath this topic was mostly good. I hear of some codex bug but i have not encountered it and the only real complaints are the sometimes stuttery cutscenes. Audio is well in sync with movements, no crashes or freezes and framerate never dipped below 80 for me (on G-sync). Now my rig is fairly good, not beastly but a good gaming PC so anyone using a decent gaming PC should be fine. I cannot speak for integrated graphics because well.. why would i use it when i have a dedicated graphics card?
+ A bold move after arkham Knight :P
+ Simple yet satisfying detective work
+ Playing as both Batman & Bruce Wayne
+ A Batmobile that transforms into a sports car
+ Morality choices that have a larger affect on your story
- Shift + Q or E QTEs? maybe because i grew up using a console it is a bit harder for me on K/M but thats a bit annoying.
- Slightly too short timer for some of the QTEs. but that might just be me
- The batmobile looks a little boring but the fact it transforms is a nice feature
- The game shortcut you create doesnt work for me (have to open game in library)
- Game launches everytime asking Win7 or Win8+... really? come on.
- No apply option for Resolution until you go back to the main menu then you get the prompt to apply it.
Only episode one is available at this time but i like the way this game is going, hopefully the future episodes are even better. So if you are on the fence about buying this game, well you could wait until it's on sale or maybe get a friend to buy it and overwrite his or her saves :P. However so far i do recommend this game to Telltale fans and batman fans, although what kind of batman you are into may provoke consideration.

Listed as Game of the Year in 2007 by several Gaming sources such as IGN, Game Informer, X-Play.
Owned Bioshock on Xbox360 for years. Once I saw a major steam sale for the Bioshock Trilogy, it was a no brainer! The PC version is just as smooth and I haven't noticed any flaws with video or audio. I play with a Logitech Wireless Gamepad F710 and I have no issues whatsoever.
The game has a great story that keeps you pulled in and interested in exploring the underwater city named "Rapture". I won't spoil the story but you start off with nothing and feel very vulnerable at first in this Survival/Action-Rpg type of game. There are a few weapons to acquire and magic abilities to be earned throughout the length of the game, along with a wide variety of ammo types and upgrades! Ammo can be hard to acquire for awhile (possibly depending on Difficulty, I play on Normal), so you really feel the need to conserve when you can on resources.
The world has room to explore, but not so much where you can easily become lost. The game is filled with a neat but creepy early 1900s (city constructed in 1940s) vibe and music that blends so well with this world. I do have problems with motion sickness playing First person shooters but I was able to push through and enjoy the game to a great extent. Without rushing, the game took me approximately 15-20 hours to complete and I'm currently playing through my second time with the PC version.
The regular price of $19.99 is a bit steep for a game that has been out for over half a decade. It should be more like $5-10 bucks but if you can catch it on sale, it is definitely worth collecting, especially if you haven't played this game before. If you got the time to sit down and play, it won't dissappoint.

The Long Journey Home is a punishing but rewarding experience.
Like a good rouge-like game should be, TLJH offers you freedom of choice - but with that freedom, you can send yourself hurtling straight towards a concrete wall, or teach yourself how to fly.
That is the beauty of the game. It doesn't hold your hand, but it doesn't hold you back either. You are going to fail - a lot, but at the same time that danger makes every success an achievement.
If you're not prepared to sink hours into learning how best to control your ships and conserve fuel then this game is not for you. If you're interested in investing into the game, learning how to deal with the different alien cultures and fighting tooth and nail to succeed then I welcome you the one of the most challenging games this year.
See you on the other end of the universe.

The Enigmatis series is definitely more than basic HOG material, and Shadow of Karkhala actually plays more like an adventure game, with a real story, than a basic HOG.  If it weren't for one problem, I'd recommend it without reservation.  As it is, I have to caution you about the problem and let you judge how much an issue it will be for you.
I'm afraid fellow reviewer Mugros is right.  8 to 12 second black screen load times, often for just 1 or 2 seconds of video.  It's hard to think of a better destroyer of mood, whether it's tension, excitement or fear, when you have to just twiddle your thumbs waiting for the game to continue.  The climatic boss battle is interrupted by about six of these loading delays, including a back-to-back pair where you get one line of dialog with no visuals before the 2nd delay kicks in.  This just drains the thrill right out of it.  He's also right about the frame rate issues in the bonus story.  I also noticed that this particular game is very slow to shut down, taking about 15 seconds.  This delay is consistent when playing online or offline.
My system has 24 cores, 64GB, and comparably fast and large hard drives.  Murgros was using a solid-state drive.  It's hard to see how our systems could be considered under-powered for a 2D adventure game with occasional video overlays!

Rise to Ruins is a pleasant combination of town management and a dash of tower defense that is easy to get into and has satisfying progression throughout. Starting with a small village, barely defending it, and then finishing it off with advanced technology is an enjoyable cycle to play through each game. At the moment, the game is well worth $10. With more content, it could certainly reach up to a $20-$25 value game.
Two SMALL concerns though:
1. Expanding your town across the entire map is difficult, if not impossible. This is probably a mechanic to ensure there's always enemies to fight on the map, but more expansion (maybe half map?) would be more satisfying.
2. The problems your village is facing should probably be a little more pronounced than an openable window in the top of the screen. It is noticably better than to be spammed with "YOUR VILLAGE IS DYING" every 10 seconds, but an occasional icon change or flash would help me before my entire village thirsts to death.
What I'd like to see (don't know what the dev is planning):
1. Simple army management, so the player can occasionally send an excursion against the enemy or keep a standing army at the walls.
2. Unique resources for story mode maps + trading of these resources among your many towns. To give some more feeling of progression.
3. More late game buildings and towers. The specters are almost too difficult, and "more towers" isn't a satisfying option.

Five Nights at Freddy's is a first person, survival horror, point and click game. You work at Freddy Fazbears pizzeria, a place were the main attraction is Freddy Fazbear and his three friends. They are animatronic robots programmed to please the crowds, but have an unpredictable behavior at night. You are the night security guard, unfortunatly, and have to keep an eye on these animatronics while making sure that they don't get into your office and "forcefully stuff you into a Freddy Fazbear suit".
The gameplay is simple, you are stuck in your office and have the ability to control the lights and doors to your office. You can also monitor the building through the cameras scattered around. To spice things up a bit, you have a limited amount of power that gets drained everytime you use the lights, doors and cameras, meaning that you have to leave yourself exposed in order to survive. The game also gets progressively more difficult after each night.
This game has all the ingredients to make you extremly paranoid, due to the lighting, sound effects and creepy animatronics. The game awards you for remaining calm and using your recourses efficiently, and punishes you if you screw up and start to panic. It's also worth mentioning that the game will occasionally attempt to ruin your concentration by, among other things, flash detailed 3D images of perticular animatronics (notably terrifying).
The story is very appealing. Scott Cawthon (the creator of FNAF) left us few clues, notes, messages and easter eggs for us to add up, only to find a creepy story that fits perfectly well into the game's setting.
I really enjoyed playing this game at first during the first nights, it was a unique yet terrifying experience that few games has given me. But during the final nights the game was so difficult, it made me use a boring and repetetive strategy called "rinse and repeat" in order to complete the final night, which took away my freedom of choice to complete the game "my way". I didn't feel like playing the extra nights because it felt like a chore.
This points out the biggest flaw and possibly the only flaw this game has, you need both skill and luck to complete the game. It could be a pro that adds to the experience or a con that ruins it.
Anyway, this is a superb horror game that i would recommend to anyone who is interested in horror games. I can almost guarantee that you will scream like a little girl at least once while playing this game.
10/10 would get stuffed into a Freddy Fazbear suit again.

A Hat In Time is a perfect example of why I enjoy playing video games. You also meet other children who are more worried about killing you with devious traps than they are about helping you. At first you feel scared and alone and when you first get decapitated by a bear trap, get impaled by spikes, get stabbed by a giant spider, or have a spear put through your head you realize than limbo is as unforgiving as it is creepy. With all the things it does right there is one problem.... The game is very short. It took me about 3 hours to fully complete and i thought the game was amazing but i also was a bit dissapointed on the length. When I first heard of this game, I read the description, then decided I had to buy it. I mean, who wouldn't want to buy a game where the premise behind it is 'London has been stolen by bats'?
Since buying it though, I have come to appreciate what a brilliant game this actually is. London now rests on the edge of a vast, underground sea, the unterzee, and you are the Captain of a sailing vessel. What your ultimate goal is, be it gathering wealth, fame, or hunting for your father's lost bones, it is your place to sail the unterzee, exploring weird and exotic places, trading unusual and rare objects, or even carry coffee to the surface.
There are quite a few different factions, all of them clamouring for control over some aspect of the zee, whether it is the anarchists vs the admirality in London, or the Wildweald Court in the Empire of Hands, the brothers at the Chapel of Light, or the sisters at Abbey Point. All have their own agenda, and it is up to you if you assist them, hinder them, or stop them completely.
Add to all of this a dark, yet quirky sense of humour, solid gameplay that is easy to get the hang of, but difficult to master, and an eerie soundtrack, and you have a very fun game that will keep you guessing.

There's little explination for what has occured, and you start out as a little boy wandering in a dark field searching for something, but you don't know what. One thing i didn't expect was the difficulty of this game. I died more times than Kenny from South Park in that game, but i kept on for reasons I don't really know. The puzzles were really hard to solve by the end, and i needed a guide to complete the game. The ending is hardly satisfying though, and i felt like the game was a waste to play because of it, but then i realized it was that strenuous journey to get to the end that made LIMBO a worthwile game. It was beautifully crafted, and I was sort-of proud to be able to complete it. I felt like I was really in a trance, and at the end i just woke up from it.
It's not the best game, and some people won't be patient enough to play it all the way through. But in the end LIMBO was meant for one purpose, to transport the player into a trance, and see if the player could get out of it. It does a decent job of it

Once you get your head around tackle/ assist zones, you'll find Blood Bowl is an extremely strategic and tactical game. It's basically super-violent chess. If you take the time to learn all of the mechanics and little nuances, you'll be rewarded with a great gaming experience. This sophisticated rule-set is counterbalanced beautifully by the incessantly crunching violence of the game's stylisation, which makes it this complex gaming oxymoron, simultaneously intellectual and mindless.
In keeping with the prevailing ethos of early Games Workshop, the game is brutal and unforgiving: your favourite palyers will die and you will be subjected to the unpitying randomness of the dice. Suck it up. Savour it. In terms of the philosophy of games, I find that this kind of game mirrors life most accurately; when you expect your Kroxigor to tackle the living daylights out of an elf, he'll roll double skulls and die. Great, I say. Who wants some patronising game that leads to you to believe in the fallacy of a 'sure thing'? I know I don't.
Anyhoo, 10/10 would be tossed mercilessly hither and thither by the winds of fate again.

So I guess most of the hate comes from fans of the original series which is Sacred and Sacred 2. Although I'll admit that I haven't had much experience playing the other games, so i am taking this game as a stand alone, but as far as I can tell, this isn't really a traditional RPG. It's more like a Gauntlet Legacy kind of game. You choose stages, you run through and kill enemies, get health and energy as you progress to survive and use skills and then eventually you level up.
It's not a bad game on it's own. I really very much enjoy this. I am just getting my girlfriend into gaming and she is playing this game side-by-side with me and it's pretty fantastic. The controls are very smooth, the skills are very useful and simple to understand and the Level Up system works decent for the type of game it is. You get items you can use and those stock can increase as you do certain stages. You can purchase more of those useable items after using them in stages so you'll never really run out. I am playing on the 3 star mode, which is the hardest I can get at the moment and even still the game isn't too hard.
Don't know if that's bad or good but as a stand alone game that really shouldn't be expected to play at all like the previous titles, I have to say that this is a VERY fun game. I was expecting it to be crap since it got so many overwhelming negative reviews but it's a great game and I am having a wonderful time playing it. The story is a little lack and the added humor seems a bit forced at atime but it's not totally a bad thing. Kinda eases up the player through the tough levels.
So, overall, I'd have to rate this game 8/10 for what it is. It's not the best of the best, but I think it's a bit better than the previous Gauntlet title that came out. Just think of it that way. Instead of being a direct sequel to the other games in terms of gameplay, think of it as a different version of the world and the type of battle system you can get through a Gauntlet-esque type atmosphere.
It's fun, good graphics, smooth gameplay, not much else to say. I totally recommend this game as a STAND ALONE to the other 2 titles. :)
EDIT: I did play with an Xbox One Controller, so that is a whole lot smoother than the keyboard controls. I really didn't like the keyboard controls, especially how you aim with the mouse. Very frustrating, so I just used a controller.

What a charm. It's refreshing to play a great 3D platformer other than another Mario game, though it is quite reminiscent of them. The controls are solid and work well with the environment. The graphics are beautiful, with many technical options in the menu. There are also many camera settings for adjusting how far and how much the camera tracks you. Characters are amusing and jokes are great. Attention to detail is spot on; there is so much content packed into the nooks and crannies of the game's various worlds.
The platforming is tight and fair, and there is a lot of it. Cliffs and edges seem to flow organically with the world, yet jumping points from location to location are distanced just right. The player character receives different upgrades that augment platforming or attacking, all of which work well with the environment.
Something I spent a lot of time on is the ability to freeze time and control the camera to take high-resolution pictures, complete with an on-the-fly depth-of-field slider. This is a neat feature that allows for a plethora of beautiful stills of the game to be made.
This game took what was great about 3D platformers before it and added some of its own charm with its unique characters, innovative platforming, and attention to detail. I highly recommend picking this up.

Sometimes a game comes along and defies all expectations. A Hat in Time did that for me. I initially thought nothing of this game as nothing more than another "me too!" kickstarter game designed to exploit fans of dead genres, in this case the 3D platformer. My cynicism was enhanced by the imminent arrival of Super Mario Odyssey, a game that looked to be shinier, bigger and overall better than this little indie game. However, a friend said the right words and I reluctantly found myself clicking the purchase button, ready to play a few hours and leave it by the wayside.
I got 100% in A Hat in Time long before Odyssey even arrived.
A Hat in Time took my cynicism and replaced it with punching mafia and solving murder mysteries on a western train. It only asks one thing of you: to dive into its world like Hat Girl does into her ballpit, without any reservations And what a world it is. The first world alone involves you fighting cookery themed mafa with hilarious accents on a delfino-styled island town of impressive heights. From there it just gets crazier in the best way possible, as each world offers a unique scenario and overall tone. You'll find yourself leading a marching band on city rooftops in one level while collecting evidence for a thrilling and noir-drenched whodunit murder mystery in the next. Did I mention those two levels are in the same world? "Mafia doesn't care about consistency, mafia cares about fun!"- actual quote from the game. All of this is held together by genuinely good writing (unlike my unfortunte example). Every scenario is presented with a wink and smile and even the satire is generally treated with some wit and tact and not just blatant MANDATORY COLLECTIBLES AMIRITE LOL crap. The quirky nature of the game never feels forced, it manages to make all these disparate elements consistent. It even pulls off some genuinely touching moments, including an ending that was both surprising and touching. Think less Yooka Laylee, and more Psychonauts.
Of course, a world can only be as interesting as the people that inhabit it and ohmygod ohmygod you guys I love these people, starting with Hat Girl. Simply put, she's equal parts adorable and badass. She expresses a child-like wonder in her interactions with the world and pluckiness thats also countered by hilarious sarcasm and cynicism (seriously, read her diary entries after completing each level). Yet at the same time she's an intergalactic time traveller who aint afraid to do what should be done to return home. She's the perfect representative of the game: whimsical, quirky and just plain bizarre. The supporting cast equally holds up well and receive the same level of effort and care in how they are characterised, my favorite character being the Devil himself. He steals every scene he is in and you can tell that the voice actor had way too much fun playing this maniacal devil may care figure. It says something that I genuinely came to care for a cast of characters that included: an opportunistic foul mouthed movie director, a terrible mafia cook and the Devil himself.
That's all good and great, but how are the mechanics? How does it play? To answer both, good. First of all, Hat Girl controls really well. Befitting her small stature, she is quick to the chase with a generous movement speed. She also has a sunshine-styled dive which when combined with a generous double jump can get you to a lot of places. She's a bit floaty compared to Mario, but she still gets the job done. In terms of general structure, its simple. Collect 40 timepieces across 4 worlds, in each world you can collect yarn pieces which are used to make the titular hats, pons (basically coins) to buy badges that change gameplay and relics which unlock bonus levels when assembled. The number of things to collect is remarkably restrained and it never feels like you're being buried under tons of useless busywork. Everything has a purpose and feeds into each other.
The mission structure matches the diversity and variety of the games tone and story beats. The first world is your typical sandbox, but everything after that deviates from typical 3D platformer structure. The second world is essentially a collection of linear but incredibly varied props set on movie stages while the Third world, Subcon Forest, starts off small but sections are opened up when you complete certain tasks. It's probably my favorite world in terms of sheer exploration. Whats great about these stages is that they're just as fun to play as they are to read. The murder mystery mission for example. It may sound like a mission that is fun to experience the first time around but a drag on later playthroughs because of its emphasis on answering questions and solving a murder but its actually a really fun stealth mission where you avoid agents and even collect key cards to unlock new parts of the train mgs style. The mechanics work perfectly in tandem with the story beats. There are no "talking section", both gameplay and story go hand in hand with each other. It's pure gaming flow.
There are also the titular hats to take into account. Compared to Odyssey's groundbreaking use of hats to fundamentally change Mario's moveset and interaction with the environment, A Hat in Time falls short. Saying that, they are still remarkably useful with special mentions going to the speedster hat which makes a quick character quick...er. One hat in particular, I wrote off as gimmicky and useless only to be surprised when the game utilised it in one of the best levels of the game (think of the lens of truth from ocarina of time but much more fluid). Switching between them is almost instantenuous and the level design encourages their use. They're also really cute.
There is a lot more I wanted to talk about, like the amazing hubship (corgi simulator needs to be a real game), the boss battles which every other 3D platformer needs to take notes from and the timewarp missions which are out there psychonaut style. But I'm kinda tired so I'll wrap this up. A Hat in Time is a fantastic 3D platformer. It's constantly creative in its writing and design. Sure its a bit too short and easy, the fifth "world" was nothing more than a bossfight. But what's there is good. Is it as good as Super Mario Odyssey? I dunno about that, but what I do know is that this game is cute as heck. And thats enough for me.

LIMBO is a game that will draw you in instantly and refuse to let go. Brought to us by the aptly named Danish company "Playdead", we have a puzzle-platformer that will chill you to the bone. This game is an example of the lines blurring between videogame and artistic expression. The music is soft and haunting, your footsteps light yet almost too loud, the sound of insects fills you up and the ambiance immediately puts you on edge. You play as a young boy whose peculiar character design brings out both a protective instinct and a feeling of unease. Though the game is entirely in monochrome, it is nevertheless breathtakingly beautiful and each location feels strange and unique. Death is a major theme, it is omnipresent and strikes when you least expect it. You should be warned that if you are sensitive to themes revolving around children dying brutally, painfully and for undiscernable reasons then this game might not be right for you. On the other hand, if you are not at all affected by children dying then you might miss some of the meaning behind the game. The story is complex, masterfully told and entirely up to interpretation. LIMBO's puzzles range in difficulty from moderate to hard and many will require some trial-and-error. No challenge ever feels unachievable, making for a good balance between fun and difficulty.
Overall, I would recommend this game for anyone who is interested in a darkly existential experience that won't be forgotten. I would not recommend this game to people who are easily shocked by child violence, though most people should be able to cope with it.

This game combines an amazing imagination with the ability to explore an ocean; it's a masterful achievement in the exploration genre, due in no small part to the combination of danger, intrigue, enigma, and ambiguity that it throws at you from island to island.
The game's mechanics are simple, and yet they function together to create one tense moment after another. It forces you to take risks to see what is just beyond the next wave, whether in the form of terror, food or fuel. Random encounters that force choices at sea, and the ever-watchful eye of the gods of the Zee make for an eventful trip in any direction.
None of the game mechanics is over-developed or under-developed. Combat, exploration, and menu-choices-as-story all come together to complement one another in a game that really forces confrontation with a world moreso than a game. If the story pushes you from isle to isle or if the thought of everything from warring guinea pigs versus rats, to an isle where everyone wears masks and participates in a ritualistic society interests you, this is the game for you.

TL;DR: A great Run & Gun game with amazing graphics and great music, with extreme hard but fair difficulty.
A Must-Buy for every Retro-Gamer.
Cuphead "Don't Deal With The Devil".
After 3 years of waiting for it's release, the wait was worth, as it deliveres the perfect Run & Gun Gameplay I've been wanting soo much to be revived. Hopefuly, we'll have more Run & Gun games in the future that will follow Cuphead's steps.
Let's get the obvious out of the way:
Graphics: Fantastic! If you're a fan of old 1930 cartoons, you'll love the unique art style that this game proudly shows, as everything in this game is made by hand-drawing. Everything is beautiful to look at and the animation is greatly detailed. Definitly it's strongest point.
Gameplay: Simple as it can get. You dodge everything that is thrown to you and shoot down your enemies. Like old fashion, the bosses don't have any health indicator, as it should be, but clues are thrown into the mix, like becoming more aggressive, or changing their forms. There is a variety of weaponry you can choose, and end up being used at least once for a specific boss, and along side weapons, there are charms that can help you with sustaining damage or dodging projectiles or enemies.
Dificulty: Now here's a tricky one. Retro games (Specially Run & Guns) were always easy to learn, hard to master. Cuphead is one of those cases where you'll die alot, but it's never the games fault. Do not pay attention to the people who say the game is too hard or is too unfair. Nothing in the game is unfair. It can and will get hard the more you acomplish, but when you die, you learn from your mistake. You start memorizing the bosses's attack patterns, and the more you study them, the easier it gets. It's not a final exam, but memorizing the attacks always help. It's how most Run & Gun games work.
Audio: The sounds are satisfying to listen to, and the music is amazing. It really captures the old instrumental vibe that every 30's cartoon had. I can guarantee you, it won't go through your head to turn the volume down or to even turn the music off. It is that good to listen to. And never 2 musics are the same, every stage and worlds have their own unique theme.
Replayability: In the end of every level, you'll be graded depending on how good you do. You can always replay the same levels to aim for a higher grade. There is also the Expert Mode, where it changes the bosses attack patterns, by making them faster or stronger. It actually has a 200% Completion, so see if you can beat all the bosses in a higher difficulty, see if you know your Cupheaded ways.
Final Thoughts: It is an amazing game that I recomend for every Retro fan to get. The difficulty is insane, but fair and passable, altho sometimes it might be annoying, but not game-breaking. Haven't run to any game bugs, and it runs at 60 stable FPS. Great graphics, amazing music and tight and responsive controls.
Verdict: 9/10

This game is amazing, one of Telltale's best. They have masterfully captured the source material and nailed that Batman feeling.
This might be the best representaion outside of the comics to date, it's representaion being an equal to - if not even better than  - the Arkham franchise. They perfectly captured both the personalities of both Batman and Bruce Wayne, and his relationships with the other characters.
I have seen complaints about the performance but I played it as soon as it was released and had no issues, it ran at 50 FPS nearly the entire time with only a few small drops near the beginning. And I had no issues with bugs either, just a couple of small audio bugs. Aside from these small things the game runs great.
The combat scenes in the game are badass as f*ck, they perfectly capture Batman and it's clear that Telltale Games did their homework. The fight scenes have been vastly improved from past games and it makes you feel much more involved thanks to the updated QTE system, though if you are strongly against QTEs this might not be the game for you.
Speaking of updated, Telltale have greatly improved their engine since their last release making this easily the best looking Telltale game to date, the textures look amazing and the animation is a bit more refined, though it is still very unnatural looking at some points.
The game's soundtrack is just amazing to listen to, and the theme feels like a Batman theme.
One major thing you may notice throughout this review is the theme of it being very "Batman" and if you are a fan of the Dark Knight you will probably love this. If you're not a fan there's no such guarantee, but if you want to learn more about the character or get into the Batman lore, this may be one of the best ways to do it.
Overall I love this game, it's probably my favourite Telltale game, and I cannot wait to play episodes 2 through 5.

This game is delightfully charming in almost every avenue. Its music is fantastic, its controls are tight, the artistry is a callback that's as gorgeous as it is reverential. Everything is crafted with care. The odd transformative enemies with the not-quite-solid-enough-to-support-a-body bone structure that the old cartoon characters used to have are all present. It's a fantastic treat.
Enough gushing, brass tacks:
If you like platformers, if you like side scrolling shooters, if you like 1930's motif, you'll like this game on that alone, I think $20. That said, this game is difficult as all hell. It is brutally unforgiving, but rewards good play and knowledge (which often comes at the price of dying). Co-op scales this up a lot, so if you're playing with a friend, prepare to suffer. (It is still very fun, just understand going in that it is NOT the same game as single player, but I don't think in a bad way. However, you will die). It's not all doom and gloom as far as difficulty goes, there is a 'simple' mode on each level, so you can more casually enjoy the style.
This game's individual levels are predominantly 'boss rushes', in that each level is mainly comprised of a unique boss that you have to defeat, the only traditional side scroller levels are titled aptly "run and guns" are used to gather money for various upgrades. Combat is straightforward, though nuanced given the aforementioned 'upgrades' you can buy, i.e. new weapons or accessories that alter how you fight. The parry system, which consists of being midair, then 'slapping' the particular target, does offer an interesting option for players, since parrying in a lot of situations is an optional choice that offers decent reward for some risk.
All in all. It's hard, it's delightfully fun. It's not for the faint of heart, but if you want to challenge yourself at a price that I consider a steal, I think that this might be right up your alley.

Since the first trailer for this game, I was on the fence about this game. The setting and tone were great, but all the gameplay segments that I saw seemed kinda meh. Then I played it, and while it did take some getting used to, everything fell perfectly into place. This is a game about preparation, planning, and resource management above all else. It has a pretty wrapper, a unique and memorable cast of aliens to befriend/shoot at, and wonderful music, but beneath all of that, the game itself is all about making choices (FTL style choices, not BioWare) and living with the consequences of them.
Something to keep in mind is that this is not an easy game. It can be punishing, especially in the beginning, and you WILL play the first steps of your journey many times over, but over time the game teaches you to be cautious; don't fly full thrust at everything, don't land on every single planet if you can't affort to take some damage, shoot a certain group of friends on sight if you must, and so on.
I don't think this game is for everyone. It's cartoony and simple appearance belies a sometimes brutal game underneath, but if you're someone who enjoy games like FTL, and are willing to adapt your playstyle to what works best for survival, I think you'll get a lot out of this.

The premise of this game is really good, and I can see a lot of good things that could have come from this. However I feel that it ultimately fell flat.
While it seems interesting and mysterios in the beginning, once you get a bearing on how to do things, the game becomes fairly simple, and ultimately boils down to small, slight interactive stories. That's not nescessarily a bad thing, but when 80% of your time is going from planet to planet, repeating what feel like the same minigames over and over (getting into orbit and landing at point x, y, & z on the planets) it really loses your interest.
I would love to follow one race and really learn about them, screw up and start a huge war between mankind and them (as a random example) however I don't even know if that's possible, as I found the grind to get there to be so boring. Ultimately at the end of my 3 hour game, I just quit. There was little to keep me going.
The "relics" I would find amounted to little to nothing. Some of them would lead me to coordinates of derelict ships, where I would find more relics to lead me to more wrecks. The wrecks all looked the same, they were all pretty boring. Every time I thought I had found something interesting it would just amount to "here's some coordinates" and while at first that was exciting, after the fifth time following them and finding nothing interesting I just lost interest. The most interesting thing that came of that was the "Temple of Pleasure" or something along those lines. I was hoping for some sort of story or quest line from this, but all I ended up doing was paying 20 credits for a little bit of funny dialogue. The person I sent in was even infected, I was at least hoping for a comment about that, but nothing.
In the end I feel that this game ultimately lacks depth, or at the very least it bores you to tears well before you manage to get to it. I feel that a 2-3 hour run should have at least garnered me something a little more interesting than a few interesting one-liners and 5 trips to wrecks that all look the same, and have nothing new to them. This game hardly deserves to be called a roguelike, while some people may get into semantics over the definition, it just doesn't have anywhere near the complexity or depth to hold the name.
Unless you can power through hours of tedious tasks just to hold on to the few threads of semi-interesting dialogue, then don't even bother giving this game a second thought.

Reviewing both main game and DLC as seperate, and short points will be below the line on both if necessary.)
Welcome to Mount Massive where player will experience disturbed, twisted and violent side of humanity.  A place where science, religion, ideology, sanity and instanity blends together to form something that is barely recognizable which you will be experiencing this survival horror nightmare through the eyes (first-person perspective) of Miles Upshur an independent reporter acting on a tip that there is corruption going on at the asylum which needs to be expose but as you go deeper into Mount Massive Asylum you will realize
Consist of your General, Graphics and Controls which from my perspective is well organized to not only make it easy to navigate and use but also allow players to change the setting anytime in terms of both preference (with the exception being able turn off film grain) and playing style using keyboard or controller which both are fluent and highly responsive in terms of the menu.
The game honestly variable and depends solely on the player for example it took me 16 hrs to complete due to wanting to find and read every document in the game and yes dying quite a bit.
Now when it comes to Outlast whether the story is new or old in terms of its premise and setting depends on the amount of entertainment you consume which I will leave this up to the viewer to decide.  But I will say this when it comes to the story in Outlast the game does a solid enough of a job to keep you interested in terms how the story presents itself and amount of detail put into it; for instance scattered throughout the asylum are documents which you have the option to find and read that not only give very well detailed optional background information about the asylum and its inhabitants but also exact time lines to give you an idea what is going on and why?  Another thing to mention is Miles (protagonist) doesn't use voice dialogue instead all of his emotions, thoughts, observations and some of what he hears is written down which the player has the option to read it, however in order for Miles to write key things down the camera has to be up at all times.  Last is the occassional minor cut scenes that introduce's to the main and secondary enemies along with enemies/allies (you see what I mean when playing Outlast)
Now as I mention there are two types of controls for instance the keyboard works great for the most part in terms of gameplay especially when you are able to change key functions (key binding), now I did came across a problem where the Miles will either slow down or stop when trying turn corner while running but was able make it manageable by changing in game settings and mouse settings outside of the game but this is probably due to me using a keyboard mouse (laptop mouse) then your standard mouse while Xbox 360 PC wired controller (already mapped just select A, B, C) is fluent gameplay throughout which I can switch between the two instantly.
Are straight forward and simple which consist of running, hidding blocking/shutting doors when possible (only), smooth set path parkour elements and your only resource available to you is camera with night vision and batteries you find scattered throughout the asylum, now the only small complaint is that the night vision drains too quickly other then that no other problems.
When is comes to achievements (for the completionists) and challenge modes such as normal, hard, nightmare and added insane (Very low battery supply, less batteries to find, enemies kill you even faster and no saves or checkpoints.)
Red Barrels did a great job in Outlast in terms of atmosphere (ambience) for instance builds fear & Tension in multiple ways by using a combination of silent to unsettling environmental sounds and scenery (including patients), well timed music cues, well placed jump scares and hearing the sounds of protagonist disconfort as he gradually loses his sanity combined to form haunting experience that will keep you on edge now I wouldn't say Outlast is the scariest game of all time nor flawless in this aspect which small reason is that certain jump scares could have been more threatening than your occasional "boo!", but the main problem is that as I was going further into Outlast it seemed it was struggling to maintain the fear and/or tension in certain aspects which is due to enemy AI while highly responsive leading into intense and frantic chase sequences either escaping or indirectly leading them to a satisfying demise but down side comes into play is when once you break line of sight purser will go back same path pattern as if you were never there and when there is randomness it's the type you don't want to have an a game while problems are noticeable it doesn't occur throughout the game which is something to take into consideration.
Outlast doesn't have puzzles instead their more like objectives you have to complete in order to progress which consists of finding alternat routes, pressing buttons/switches, find a item, find items to activate switch/button; now base off of my experience these objectives are not complex nor require much thought however I didn't felt like they had to, but if you expecting more then just objects your chances are your going be disappointed.

This is another "game" similar to the likes of the Stanly parable. It is not so much of a game, and more of an experience. An experience, which if you do not do a huge ammount of dawdling and exploration cant last more than 2 hours.
The gameplay consists of walking through hallways, listening to a narrator discuss what you are seeing. The only gameplay clearly visible is the use of a simple puzzle as a mean of storytelling (if anyone had trouble with that puzzle, i am curious to know how you continue to function)
However, the content taht is within the game is difficult to review. Its a bit like undertale, and other heavy story based games, where if I mention something within the game it will ruin the experience. Overall though i would not say that this was an allright experience, but it feels kind of like something i would have found on the likes of gamejolt for freebies rather than a $10 game. Even so it is still worth playing in my opinion, and at the time of writing, it is the holiday sale which reduces the price down to $6, which can be a more justifiable pricetag in my opinion.
Just know that:
1. It is not a game
2. It is entirely possible, on the first playthrough, to beat the game in about an hour and a half.
3. The ideas explored can be done better, and have a very specific person in mind which would give a great emotional response if you happen to be one of those people (social anxiety) otherwise, it may not be a worthwhile experience.
4. For someone to get the most enjoyment you must be soemone who does creative work. Not specifically games, you could be an animator, artist, designer, ect. and still get the same expereience as a game dev.
Overall, i would say for the price of $6 i paid for it, i would give it a 6.5/10, however, I beleive that it should still be played for the experience that it offers.

Starts off well and covers interesting topics, but becomes a bit of a mess by the end. I really enjoyed the use of prisons as a metaphor and the idea of someone's games being a window into their true feelings.
These points are unfortunately undermined, if not outright contradicted, by the conclusion. I'm not convinced that there's a deeper meaning beyond this, other than, "how we interpret things is a reflection of us". I wish the game's message(s) were more coherant.
The levels have interesting concepts and some of them are quite beautiful. Unfortunately the linearity prevents you from ever really caring about them. They're memorable experiences, sure, but you'd miss very little watching a playthrough instead of playing. I don't really like let's plays, but this is one game where I'd recommend finding one.
While I haven't created maps in the Source engine, I don't feel that any of these were particularly complex in nature. They convey a lot of meaning minimalistically and have great atmosphere, but this simplicity also takes away from the game's message. Given what's presented, some of the game's points about the creative process feel unconvincing.
Even if the concept interests you, I'd only recommend buying it if you think it being playable will make a difference. I found that it didn't.

Pros:
+Fun, PMTTYD-esque writing. Delightfully irreverent at times, charged with emotion at others.
+Incredible movement. Platforming is engaging and precise.
+Powerups, while niche in their uses, inject the platforming with even more variety.
+Super memorable characters. I won't go into detail here.
+Well crafted, open levels are fun to race through and explore.
+Each world tells its own self contained story, which is more than enough to keep you engaged.
+Music is fantastic, my head was bobbing along to every tune, and I even found myself listening to it while doing work.
+Queen Vanessa is like if you combined FNAF with the piano from SM64. Nuff said.
~Optimization. While running great under most circumstances, this would benefit from more effective and more drastic LODs, especially on larger worlds. Most levels run great, though I admit I'm pushing the hardware. Most folks shouldn't have an issue at 1080p or 1440p.
(I ran the game at 4K on a setup with a 4790K and a 980ti, ran at 60fps pretty consistantly)
-Overarching plot is somewhat thin, though the individual worlds' stories make up for this.
-Sound design. Some effects are quite a bit louder than the rest of the soundscape, making volume management occasionally annoying. Mustache Girl occasionally sounds like she's right next to the mic compared with everyone else.
-Not gonna lie, some levels look a tad like Gmod. However, I'm speaking strictly about texture work. If some stuff was a little more high resolution or slightly higher levels of detail available, this would be fine.
-Call it a complaint, but I want more! Despite the game being short, it was worth every penny. I'd throw money at my monitor any day for DLC, a full expansion, or (dare I hope) a sequel.
Overall:
Despite my nags, this game is an A+ home run. I'd argue it's on par with any of the greats of 3D platforming; whether that be Spyro, the genesis Sonics, Crash Bandicoot or even Mario 64. Thank you Gears for Breakfast. This game is an absolute gem, and I'd shake every one of your hands for it.

I've been waiting to finish the game so that I can write a review and say this one thing:
THIS GAME IS NOT CUTE SOMETIMES!! IT CAN BE PRETTY CREEPY AND UNNERVING!! TOT
Phew, got that off my chest! For real, I went into this game blind expecting a "cute-as-heck" 3D platformer inspired by the likes of Super Mario Sunshine, and that's *kinda* what I got, except after the first world there's just SO MUCH CREEPY AND UNFRIENDLINESS GOD.
CUTENESS: Okay, Hat Girl's design is very cute, and knowing that, the game rewards you with cosmetics to dress her up. The first world, Mafia town, is the cutest and brightest level of the game, and at first the game's format will remind you of SMS (each level zooms to the area of interest, you explore a large world and return to it to collect the main objects except with different tasks, bright blue water, etc. The Blue time rifts are also clearly inspired by SMS's "Secret of ..." levels.) The characters at first seem silly and friendly, like when you first meet Mustache Girl and the harmless mafia.
DARKNESS: But as you progress to Dead Bird Studio and Subcon Forest, you realize the light colorful cuteness was all just an ACT!! O_O In just the second world, the game throws stealth mechanics at you, dims the lighting, and changes the music to either minor key, ambience, downbeat introspectiveness, or suspense. (As someone who believes in the power of game BGM soundtracks to affect the overall feel of the game, I recommend just listening to most of the tracks online to get a feel for the atmosphere of this game.) Seriously, many of the game's levels are dark and gloomy, including the purple time rift bonus levels, which also throw in an abstract uneasiness. Many of the game's characters turn out to be antagonistic, unfriendly, or straight up rude, and the humor darkens as well. Subcon Forest for example, is darkly foggy and features a talking noose, fire spirits celebrating death, and the selling of your own soul. (Chapter 4 in particular, with Queen Vanessa, is probably the scariest thing I've ever played in a "cute" game). The game's worlds just don't feel human; there's almost no consistency to the reality of each setting, and it's as though there's nothing to rely on but yourself.
So, that's my main actual criticism of the game. I bought A Hat in Time expecting a cute colorful platformer just filled with comfy moments, and the actual game turned out to have fairly little in the way of "comf".
GAMEPLAY-wise though, this game deserves a lot of credit. This very much feels like a game designed with classic 3D platforming in mind, as all the platform placements and mechanics seem to mesh very well together. The dive, wall-run, wall-climb, mid-air mobility, and double jump options all make it feel great to just jump around. The different-powered hats are also each very useful, and there are two very quick options to switch between them without going through a menu, so hats are more fun than annoying to use - the collectible placements also really take advantage of the hat powerups well, as does the entirety of the Alpine Skyline world. The Sprint Hat in particular, especially with the scooter badge, is a great way to add speed and mobility to the game. And knowing the history of A Hat in Time, you have to really hand it to the devs for creating a game with not just smooth mechanics, but HUGE worlds.
POLISH: There are times where the game's camera will follow very closely to you, and there are also certain slippery slopes you can get stuck on, and those moments can get annoying. There's often way too many collectibles than there are uses for, which sucks because this is a collectathon type of game (yarn and pons run out of uses after getting every hat powerup and badge). Otherwise, the game is overall well-polished.
OVERALL the game is a fun 3D collectathon platformer on its gameplay merits, and I enjoyed it, and I would recommend it! However, I can NOT recommend this game if you are looking for a cute, cuddly, comfy sort of experience- the game's aesthetic is just too unnerving, unhuman, unfriendly, and creepy at times for that. (To be fair though, there are elements of cute humor throughout the game, and the game's ending is shows the friendly side of each character.) If you can look past the surprisingly dark and unsettling aesthetic of most of A Hat in Time, I would recommend it just for its gameplay, but I really do wish the game was as light and cute as it seems to be at first.

I absolutely LOVE this game. It's challenging, but every risk has an equal reward, and learning what you can handle is one of the many ways the zee keeps calling you back for another voyage.
The immersion is beautiful, from the haunting melodies to the way the light plays off the islands. The interface is easy to grasp, although reading the tutorials for at least your first couple of characters is a good call. One glitch, the only one I've run across so far, is that if you choose to wait and elaborate on your past later in the game, it will freeze when you type in your player's name, but fortunately you shouldn't have to do that - it's only a story element, so far as I can tell, and indeed the opening of the game is a little harder if you wait.
The highlight of the game of course is the story. The world is deep and rich and full of nonsense that is completely acceptable because of how beautifully the alternate history (very, ~very~ alternate) is presented and explained not by boring exposition but by hints and references, exactly the way the real world is explained and experienced. The system by which stories are worth different things to different people, worth a few Echoes here or another type of story there or some food and peace somewhere else, makes you feel like a chronicler as well as an explored.
Every hour poured into this less-than-forgiving game, and there have been many, has been completely worth it.

is a first-person shooter that pits you (and, optionally, up to 5 others in co-op mode) against hordes of deadly steroid-infused pigs. Some are small, some are big, some are HUGE, some are metal(?), some have apparently misplaced their skin and are entirely skeletal - but there are two things that they all have in common:
1. They pose a severe risk to human life, especially yours.
2. They must be humanely destroyed by a qualified veterinarian to avert a major public health hazard.
The bad news is that they presumably killed all the qualified veterinarians so you'll have to do the job yourself. The good news is that you have a far more appropriate set of tools than the average vet - these include pistols, shotguns, machine guns, grenades and more.
The basic format of the game is a round-based FPS where each round is represented by a new day. A round can consist of anywhere between a few and a few
angry hogs. Each day you're given instructions by the Farmer, who needs your help to stem the tide of porcine peril because, for some inexplicable reason, one of his legs is missing and he's pinned to the wall of his barn with a pitchfork. The Farmer's musings are often hilarious and his voice-acting is great, but each day's task needs little explanation: kill the pigs -
the pigs!
There's only one map (the farm itself) and it's not very big. But there are various tools scattered about the environment to assist you in your task - an electric fence that will quickly turn any nearby pigs into pork scratchings, a meat grinder that (somehow) turns pig carcasses into useful pickups (ammo, grenades, power-ups) and water fountains from which you can replenish your health. Your arsenal of weapons and the tools around the farm are unlocked as the days go by but it won't take long to unlock everything you need for some serious pig-slaughtering mayhem. There are also plenty of secrets and easter eggs to be found all around the game.
Every 10th day you'll encounter a mini-boss and every 20th day you'll encounter a
boss, so large that its final destruction produces an eruption of pig gibs that turns the entire sky red with blood. It's hard to describe just how satisfying this is but perhaps a quick screen-shot will help:
Not quite enough blood with your bacon? Well hold on there partner, we're just getting started:
Still not enough blood for you? Then you should probably seek professional psychiatric help. Moving on, there are also periodic "revenge days" where every weapon is loaded with explosive ammunition; let's just say things get messy.
Originally an XBox Live Arcade title, it has now made the glorious transition to Steam where it has rapidly grown bigger, better and brasher than it ever was on the humble XBox 360. Developer "Big Corporation" is very active in the community, respects community feedback, implements good suggestions in a timely fashion, makes regular updates to the game and is all in all a great guy. Big Corporation genuinely loves the game and is constantly improving it, something I respect and admire in a developer.
It's a simple but satisfying game and notably offers exceptional value for money - $0.99 (or your regional equivalent) at full price and you'll often find it on sale for 10% or even 20% off, so it could be yours from the spoils of a quick rummage down the back of the sofa for loose change. Needless to say, it's hardly going to compete with your triple-A FPS games but rest assured you get a whole lot of game (and a whole lot of fun) for the extremely modest price of admission.
This is my nomination for the 2016 Steam Awards' "Best Use of a Farm Animal" category because what better use can there possibly be than turning it into an excessively bloody mess with an arsenal of lethal weaponry? It's a serious question, feel free to answer in the comments!
So to wrap things up, pros and cons? Honestly, at this point you don't need a list of pros and cons since you should have stopped reading by now and bought it already - did I mention it costs less than a dollar?

LIMBO: Endgame Review
(TLDR - Quick 'n' Dirty Version: Gruesome fun puzzles -  just get it!)
Oh my goodness, this game. LIMBO has been on my radar for a while now, and I've been using this downtime between major releases (that I want) to plug away at my "back-stack"  - I picked up a Special Edition retail copy of LIMBO from EB, which came with a DRM-free PC/Mac DVD, some 3D glasses, cool pictures, a sticker and a Steam key. Not bad for $9.
Now, for the actual game itself. Players control an unnamed boy who enters limbo to rescue his sister - ah yes, that old chestnut. We might let it slide just this once though - the purpose is quickly forgotten as you're engulfed by horrific, made-to-order Death Noir in all its glory. Once you fail at the puzzles enough times to get over watching the boy being pulverised, mangled and dissected, you realise there's a gritty, shrewd humour pervading it all. In fact, the developers described the gameplay style as "trial and death," constructing puzzles so the player would fail first (in the most gory, horrible way of course) before finding the correct solution. There were many times where I triumphed initially through sheer luck and went Yeahhh! - only to find myself walk smack-bang into another trap and laugh at the dark irony.
The game does look beautiful in its own way - high contrast and depth of field help to highlight what the player can interact with. The aesthetic is very film noirish, with a gritty, grainy texture and filtered light to enhance the atmosphere as the player moves through the world in a side-scrolling (mostly) platform-game fashion. The soundtrack is minimalistic and consists mainly of eerie noises and sound effects. I haven't tried the old-style red and blue 3D glasses, but I can see how they'd enhance the experience.
As for the puzzles, many people have complained they were too easy. I found the difficulty comparable to that of Portal; the puzzles were neither too hard nor too easy, progressed logically and I got them all eventually. For what it's worth, I think a good game puzzle should stump you initially, but stick in your head and wake you up at three in the morning with an Oh my God, I'm such an idiot! And then you try it and it works, and you feel so clever for having figured it out. LIMBO had enough of those puzzles in there for me, so I found the challenge to be highly satisfactory.
Other people thought that the length was too short, but for time-poor gamers like me, I think the length was fine (especially for the money I spent). With my work and family commitments, I could only dedicate an hour or two to LIMBO each night, but that was enough to get through a few puzzles in one go. People with acres and acres of time could easily finish the game in one sitting - I believe there's an achievement for doing so with fewer than five deaths - but for the rest of us, the game conveniently autosaves at each chapter, and the chapters are fairly short. It was also handy to be able to tell how far through the game I was by checking which chapters I'd unlocked for reloading.
The only whinge I had was about not being able to customise the key bindings. If you're using a keyboard and mouse, you seem to be stuck with the arrow keys for movement and Ctrl for action, which did not suit me at all as a left hander and a Nintendo kid who only started playing PC games in the WASD era. I had to temporarily abandon my nice new Corsair Vengeance K70 and pick up my Xbox 360 controller, which I found to be much better for this game.
I was horrified at the gruesome imagery at first, but I'm glad I stuck with it and went to LIMBO and back. Get it if you haven't got it.

While Enigmatis 3 gives a nice, cinematic conclusion to the trilogy, its on-the-rails plot, insane moon logic, and tedious hidden object scenes make a huge step backwards compared to the masterpiece that was Mists of Ravenwood.
Trilogies like to shake things up by the third part, and Enigmatis 3: The Shadow of Karkhala is a great example for that. This series, previously known for its great supernatural crime mysteries, suddenly decided to go Tomb Raider with a trip to the Himalayas, completed with every tired archaeological adventure cliché under the sun. Moreover, it is not even a good adventure with its tired plot dumps and railroaded, restrictive, sometimes downright lazy level design and progression.
Speaking of progression, the gameplay is one of the greatest enemies. The hidden object puzzles feel tedious and needlessly drawn-out, but it is mild in comparison to the illogical point ‘n’ click mechanics, which may force brute-force trial-and-error at some parts with their unpredictable solutions.
I won’t dissuade anyone from Enigmatis 3, because, in the end, it is a nice, cinematic conclusion to the saga—but it is the only reason to be invested in this game.
