Cuphead is Contra. Granted, a Contra with only two proper levels per world and a half dozen nasty bosses, but it's Contra.
The 30s/40s cartoon aesthetic is on point without a hint of modern cynicism or faux-retro nonsense. It's a beautiful, charming game in every sense.
It is HARD though. Because you have infinite retries and the level select goes straight to the boss or level, the game takes the liberty to make the bosses tough, elaborate affairs. We're talking Ys levels of boss design. After world 1, you should expect to be clocking anywhere from 10-40 deaths just to get a handle on them. They're all tough, imaginative, and fun. Most of the deaths are pretty fair, though there are some pattern combos that the bosses can do that ring a little BS to me, but because death is such a small penalty, it's hard to get that mad.
Cuphead understands everything it is referencing on a fundamental level, from the classic cartoons to the classic game design, this game really is as good as it looks.

The second game in that trilogy is very celebrated and I played it with hope. I ended up really liking it despite some flaws, so I was eager to complete the story with this third episode. Well, every little flaw from the second one seems to be magnified in the third. In fact, while I usually avoid pro/con lists because I find them to be an easy way out for reviewers, I think it's worth it this time, if only to accurately record how you can go from a memorable game into a mediocre follow-up without seemingly changing anything to the formula.
Pros:
- The graphics are a bit better-- some 3D effects, notably. The music isn't memorable but isn't too bad either.
- Some of the actions are more dynamic. They wanted to give it a more action-oriented feeling, thankfully without the actual action (they know their target audience.)
Cons:
- Yes, that was it... Two pros. Get prepared for a long list of cons, and I didn't even take notes so there's probably more to say.
- The game is probably a tad longer than the second one, but it's a con here because there are less things to see, less things to do, and it's always blizzard-blizzard-blizzard and the occasional "oh, no blizzard... Just give it 5 minutes and the next scene will have blizzard in it." That's a Far Cry 4™ from the second episode's beautiful scenes.
- In fact, you're given a map early in the game, which implies you'll be moving a lot... Yeah, between two screens. Every time you move onto a new area, you get locked out of the previous one. You simply never get to use the map, as it has no point.
- Mini-games are easy as hell. I don't even know why they bothered with the Skip button... I recently played the Robinson Crusoe series of hidden object games and they were much more challenging and enjoyable. And they're always the same kind of puzzle game. Also, if in real life I was an anthropologist/archeologist/generic scientist looking into the legacy of another people, I would definitely steal everything and send it to a museum, seeing that every little device I find is broken and needs to be fixed. Do they have no respect for their own culture?! Or is a political statement? That the White Man is easily fooled by a "sort these items by their color" puzzles? I'm not even sure my 3yo would consider them an obstacle... Or he'd just wreck everything for fun.
- Hidden object scenes are much more annoying (and as often happens, they're repeated multiple times). The only chances where you'll get achievements are at the beginning and in special scenes where you have to find graphical representations of objects (because you're less likely to make a mistake). It doesn't happen a lot. It took me a lot more effort than it was worth. Damn auto-saving!
- I liked the second episode's random 'evil' pictures that showed up in the scenery. In this one, they're integrated and never flicker, so you're just condemned to closely look at every single picture and hope you don't miss anything. I ended up using a community guide to find them all, and of course I'd missed a couple in the beginning.
- While Enigmatis 2 was already a bit like that, the third one really follows the stupidest possible path: find items, use them somewhere, this unlocks another item which you can use somewhere else to unlock something else. The linearity in this game is sickening. There is very little thinking, just tinkering.
- Voice acting is as mediocre as before. But this time one of the characters (Fang's father) sounds like he recorded all of his lines over the phone. Then again, with the lines he was given, I'm not surprised he couldn't bother.
- The story is just a rehash of the second episode, with Tibetan folklore put into the mix. I'm not sure if that's uninspired or just plain insulting to them.
- Enigmatis 2 had a rushed but satisfying ending. Enigmatis 3 has a rushed ending. Satisfying? You don't even get to see the main characters' faces in the last picture. Ah ah. It's just a mess.
- So? Doesn't matter, there's a bonus chapter! We'll get our proper epilogue! Uh... No wait, it's a prequel chapter? Again?? With that character whom we already know was killed by the villain? So... We're going to be living through her last few hours right? Oh, they know how to sell their exciting plots. And here we go, valiantly going into a dead-end story that has no relevance for the main story and frustrates even more those who went through Enigmatis 2 and hoped for a good ending. Nope, you don't get that.
So, guys, you don't get my thumb up this time.

Outlast is a unique Survival/Horror that plops you in the middle of an insane asylum where you collect batterys to survive and run away from scares. Sounds cliche', right? It's not though, and that's what makes Outlast so awseome! You follow Miles Upshur, an investigative reporter who's set to uncover what's inside Mount Massive Asylum. After a rather breif search of a few rooms, our Peter Parker gets jumped by a rather big man, being sent flying towards the first floor. That's it, you're now stuck with all the crazy patients. Armed with a Camcorder and...running, you try to find a way out of the hellhole you've been put into.
As for the Gameplay, most of it is pretty smooth. Upshur controlls great for the most part, with my only complaint being how he jumps. Sometimes you just pathetically hop instead of climb or jump over an obstical. This is an annoyance when trying to run away from you're loony friends. I also found that closing doors is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ most of the time you'll close the door with you on the wrong end. Maybe I needed to slow down for these parts, but I dunno. Besides from running and hiding, you'll also want to explore the hallways and rooms for batterys. See, the lunatics can't see in the dark, but you can-when you have batterys for your camcorder. Once you hit 0, you'll only be able to see what's infront of you.
One final thing before I give my verdict is how the "enemys" work. Some psychopaths will rush at you and attempt to kill you, while others will just watch you. It's this element that keeps you on edge 24/7, you'll never want to let your guard down. This is what makes Outlast so different, this factor, along with great attention to detail, is what makes me say that Outlast should be bought-no doubts.

It's not getting home, it's the attempt that matters.  That's the takeaway I have from many goes at TLJH.
The Long Journey Home is not a game that begs you to love it.  It's a tough, rogue-like journey across the galaxy that expects you to die and retry over and over, each time learning a little bit more about the systems and planets that you can survive and those that will leave you stranded, unable to jump to another system or land on a planet, with your crew slowly suffocating. But each time you will get a little further.
On the way, there's a cast of quirky alien races and crew members, each of whom bring something different to the mission. Some are aggressive, others imperious, others are helpful.  The character and mission writing is wry and amusing like the best UK science fiction, and includes sly references to many sci-fi tropes.  Each time you play, the aliens and locations you encounter will change, and how the missions unfold also depends on which crewmembers you have chosen, so there's a lot of replayability here.
While the gameplay could be simply described as Spacewar x Lander, the systems you visit feature complex gravity wells that mean learning to play well and fly the ship efficiently grant huge rewards.   Landing on many planets will immediately wreck an un-upgraded lander, so it's up to you to learn which combinations are safe as you go, as the mission danger indicator is only somewhat helpful. The galaxy is organised into distinct sectors, and these generally become more dangerous as you get closer to returning home, but even the initial sector includes planets that will ruin a run if you attempt to land there.
The planet and ship design is imaginative, and overall the game has a somewhat cartoony Saturday morning TV look, without going for the overtly 2D comic styling of Galak-Z. Alien characters are more creative than those found in most space strategy games. TJLH has a soundtrack that veers between space opera and folksy, but it's very well done.
Things I would improve are an option to skip landing and docking cutscenes once you have seen a given planet or station type. I find myself pressing 'B' a lot.
And as a space genre nerd, I would also like to have some more spaceflight-y numbers describing planetary conditions and how these compare to lander performance to enable me to decide whether to land, such as gravity vs lander thrust, estimated wind velocity range vs aerodynamics (so I know whether the lander will be blown over every time I try to touchdown), surface temperature vs thermal resistance.  These are currently presented using adjectives such as 'Deadly', 'Strong' and 'Inferno', which I have to estimate vs my lander upgrades based on experience alone. An estimated range, giving how far above safe tolerances the planet might be, would make the planetary landings a little less like guesswork at the beginning.  And of course, this ship module could be damaged during the game, falling back to the current readings until repaired.
As a perfectionist, I'd like to know overall what percentage of the missions/stories I have seen in all of my runs.
Other than that it's a great game, and I look forward to bringing my astronauts home safe one day.

Let's just get it straight out of the way...This is not like the previous Sacred games.  So if you're looking for that kind of experience then you will be very disappointed here.  Because it is such a drastically different game, I won't be judging it compared to the previous games.  That's just an unfair assessment and this game has gotten most of it's hate simply for that reason.  Since this game is a hack 'n slash action RPG, then that's what I will be comparing it to.  So games such as Champions of Norrath or Dungeon Siege 3 since those are ones I've played in the past.
This game is actually pretty decent.  It accomplishes what it's trying to do, which is provide a fun hack 'n slash gameplay.  It's a simple system that anyone can easily jump into and be good at.  You're wiping out big groups of enemies, using spells or combat arts for more wide spread destruction, performing executions on knocked down enemies, evading attacks, and it all happens with just a few buttons.  There's no complicated control scheme of having to hold one button in order to open up alternative attacks or something.  It's just a fast paced, simplified system that allows you to get into the action and accomplish things in a visually pleasing way.
And visually, this game is gorgeous.  The environments are extremely well done.  A lot of detail was put into this world and it's something that you can just stop and admire.  The character design is also good, but maybe a bit lacking.  I suppose it's understandable since the camera view is always pulled away and so you don't get a good look at the characters anyway.  As I mentioned, the combat is visually pleasing.  With different colors happening on the screen that are associated with your weapon swings or the different abilities.  It's a very pretty game.
So if the game is nice to look at and it's a decent hack 'n slash gameplay, then you're probably wondering why a lot of people hate it.  The biggest problem this game has is there's no real depth to it.  Every good action RPG of this sort will always have the ability to progress your character.  They will allow you to level up the character and distribute attribute points, you will collect "loot" or equipment to further improve your character, you will be able to change their appearance, etc.  Sacred 3 has none of that.
Character development is pretty much non-existent.  You do gain experience points and level up but it's never shown if that actually does anything.  There is no stats to say how strong your character might be or anything.  So the only purpose I've seen with leveling up is to meet the level requirements to unlock new skills.  These skills, combat arts, spells, whatever you may want to call them, are one of the very few customization that you can do.  You're only allowed to have two skills equipped and you get to choose which ones you want from a handful of them.  You can also upgrade each skill to make it more powerful.  The same thing applies with weapons you obtain.  You don't find any loot in this game but instead you get an item drop from a level boss.  These weapons can be upgraded in the same way as the skills.  There is also "weapon spirits", which for the most part are kind of useless, and they mostly will annoy you.
Which brings us to the voice acting.  In general, it's not too bad.  They won't be winning any awards for their performance but I've definitely heard a lot worse.  Some characters aren't as good as others and will probably make you laugh at how bad it comes across.  But the worst part about the voice acting is they don't know when to shut up.  Whether you're being told what to do by the guide character, or you're being taunted by the enemy, or just the constant ramblings from your weapon spirit, it gets a bit annoying.  On top of that, somebody thought it was a great idea to include jokes in almost everything that is said.  Some of the humor is good but a lot of it is just kinda meh, and it gets irritating after a bit when almost everything is being said either in a joking manner or they try to slip a joke into the line of dialogue.  Such as the narrator, for example.  The purpose of a narrator is to explain what is happening to progress the story.  But this one is tossing in joke after joke and you just get tired of it and don't want to listen to him anymore.
The lack of depth that I mentioned also applies to the gameplay itself.  There is so much potential that is clearly visible with this game, but, whether by choice or not, they stripped it down to the absolute basic stuff.  The environments are so detailed and there is little pathways or doorways and stuff and it makes you wish you could go explore in that direction.  But there's really no deviating from the main path.  For example, in Champions of Norrath there was caves and dungeons scattered around the map and multiple pathways you could take.  Sacred 3 has a linear path that you follow with the odd side path going into a dead end that has a chest of gold.  It's very bare bones and stripped down to just going along that path and slashing away at enemies.
In conclusion, I do recommend this game but there's some conditions that go with it.  For what it is, it's a fun hack 'n slash game.  It allows you to kill swarms of enemies with a relatively decent combat system.  There's just not much to it and basically what you see in the first 5 minutes of the game is what you'll be doing for the next however many hours.  It's not a game to sit down and pull an all nighter with because you'll probably be bored after an hour or two.  So if you're looking for something simple when you need a break from everything, then this is the game to do that.
As a side note...this really shouldn't have been called Sacred 3.  If they wanted to go down this style of gameplay then it should have been a spin-off game.  A lot of people hate on this game for the sole reason that it's not like the previous two.  Either way, this game has so much potential and it could have been something amazing if they added in more depth to the gameplay mechanics.

Unlike many, I don't play games for the joy of figuring out mechanics and strategies. I don't play for the rush of defeating the boss (although it is a nice feeling), or to waste time, or to get bragging rights.
I play for the stories. And Sunless Sea is a game of stories. Yes, it's about the terror you feel when you're at 5 hull and low on supplies and you don't know if you'll make it back; it's about trying to survive; but mostly it's about the stories. (Like the time I was being chased by a Lifeberg, backed my way into the channels that block the north, and sat there shooting at it happily until it died, frustrated and unable to reach me. But more like the island full of insane postmen, and the one with the spiders, and the one where they only speak in questions. What /is/ the difference between a question and a riddle?)
Ultimately, it's not for everybody. And since I often binge-play it and then don't come back for months, I occasionally forget my current goals, which is frustrating. But this is one of the few games I'm happy to give up cumulative days of my life to.

Disclosure: This review is from the perspective of a long-time Fallen London player.  If you have no knowledge of the Fallen London universe/lore and play-style, you will probably have a somewhat different experience.
Pros:
+ Getting to sail to and visit all the places you've learned about in Fallen London
+ Chance to learn more about Neath/Bazaar/previous cities lore (especially the Khanate! I've always wanted more Khanate content)
+ Totally has that Failbetter game texty atmosphericness
+ AWESOME SOUNDTRACK
+ Snarky item descriptions make me happy inside
+ One of the best-looking indie games I've encountered
Cons:
- Initial learning curve can be steep
- Repeated death of captains can be hard on those who identify strongly with their characters
- Death (& other menaces) feel awfully permanent and unforgiving (especially compared to Fallen London, where they are mild inconveniences at worst)
- Walls of text can be off-putting to those who aren't used to it
- Not sure if lore is accessible to non-FL players
My recommendation?
Try playing Fallen London a bit first (it's free!) to see if you like the setting and narrative style first.

is a 1st person point & click adventure game that contains some  'hidden objects puzzles' and even more other types of puzzles.
Like in the second installment, the hidden objects puzzles usually require a bit more than just clicking on the correct objects: you often need to click on a container to reveal a hidden object or you may need to click on an item to use it on another item in order to produce the hidden object you need. These are small additions to the traditional hidden objects puzzle but it does make them a bit more varied and interesting.
If you don't like hidden objects puzzles, there's an option to replace them with 'pair-matching minigames'. You know, the memory game that requires you to remember what picture is on the bottom side of some cards, in order to eventually click on two identical cards and remove these from the board. The goal is to remove all the cards from the board. Contrary to the second game, there are no Steam Achievements for the pair-matching minigames this time.
only has 11 hidden objects puzzles. That's a lot less than the second installment had, which already had considerably less than the first game in the series.
So this time, you'll be solving a larger variety of puzzles. Of course, there is also the classic exploration and collecting items to use on other items to further the story, like in other point & click adventure games.
The story is a direct continuation of the story from the previous Enigmatis games, so I recommend you do...
...and play them in order. In this third and final chapter, our detective is still chasing the mysterious preacher with the help of Richard Hamilton, a private investigator she met in the first installment.
The story of the third chapter is only great as a conclusion to the story of the trilogy as a whole. But by itself, the story of
isn't that good, really, and it's certainly the weakest of the three games. New players thinking of picking up this third Enigmatis game without playing the prequels shouldn't bother because they will be utterly disappointed. The storyline set up in the previous installments is summarized in
but it isn't explained well, so you'll be more confused than anything else. Also, you won't understand the motivation of the two protagonists and the antagonist at all, so you won't feel involved with the story.
The way to advance in the game, be it through adventuring or through solving puzzles, is always logical so it's never frustratingly hard. Should you find yourself stumped, there's a hint button that you can press. It will point you to the next point where action is required, or allow you to skip a puzzle altogether.
Most of the puzzles in
are fun but a bit easy, which takes away the satisfying feeling of being challenged that the previous two games offered.
It takes about 7 hours to complete the game. After that, there is a bonus chapter you can play through, which will take you less than an hour.
has 5 Steam Trading Cards. You'll get 3 while running the game.
There are 34 Steam Achievements. The practical and technical problems with the achievements from the second installement are gone (see
for more on that), so much like in the first game we're left with achievements that motivate the player to not use the hint button, to not just click around like crazy until something happens, and so on. The 'collections' achievements are back, too, but they are a lot more difficult this time around. They are optional, of course, but they add a bit more challenge to the game for those who want the achievements, which is what I think Steam Achievements are supposed to be like.

Fair enough. Let's get started.
It's a first person survival + exploration simulation, with mild walking simulator and horror elements, in which you're stranded in the middle of the Canadian wilderness, struggling to preserve your life in the bitter environment.
Most of the time you find yourself lost, confused, and unsure of where to go.
Although there are many survival games that could be dubbed similiar to the Long Dark, nothing is truly like it, and most likely, nothing is as good as it either.
One of the main differences is the environment. It's set in an Artic wasteland. Little shelter. Few supplies. Most survival games are either deciduous forest, or zombie based. This fits into neither of those categories.
The weather is brutal, with harsh wind and immense temperature drops at night. You can fall through ice, get attacked by wolves, and fall off cliffs. But if you're smart, you can survive it.
Another thing that I really love about the Long Dark's gameplay is the exploration. Granted, in the most challenging difficulty settings there is little time for exploration, but the beauty of the world is truly captivating, and it's a joy to wander through the treacherous landscape. Ironic, isn't it?
Finally, the last major gameplay element I'll mention is how
this game is. You have to worry about everything. EVERYTHING. Wind. Temperature. Shelter. Hunger. Thirst. Fatigue. Broken bones. Infections. Hostile wildlife. Giant man eating ducks.
Okay the latter poses much less of a threat than the previous ones but I think you understand what I mean.
They have a calorie counter for crying out loud, what else could you want?
The Long Dark may or may not be a huge troll. And I'll explain why.
The developers set you up against very difficult challenges, inside a cruel and unforgiving world, but they make it so beautiful. It's like they show you how beautiful the sword is, before they chop off your head. Irony, you see.
But, really, the world is gorgeous. You're not blown away by the realism of it (like you are by the gameplay, more irony, you see), but it sure is stunning. I have the sceenshots to prove it.
The lighting is phenomenal, the textures are masterfully constructed, and the landscape is truly a work of art.
I also really like the almost hand-drawn feel of the visuals. Feels kind of rustic.
I also should mention, though it's not visual based, the sound design of the game.

The sound mixing is astounding. The way that the sounds of the wind and the distant wolf howls and your foot prints on the snow and the opening of your backpack all blend together so fluidly and dynamically really adds to the experience.

This game is the sole game that restored my hope in the survival game community. After games like Dayz and The Forest both of which have let me down. I started avoiding survival games on Steam. I saw the trailer for this game and just shoved it off as another game which would be abandoned by the devs after 4 weeks and left it. Then when I saw a youtube video of it about 2 weeks after launch I though "this looks pretty fun." So I went and bought it. This is what my first life was like (Keep in mind this was the 2nd or 3rd build of the game so it wasn't on unity 5 yet)
1st day
Alright this is a bit laggy, lets throw this onto low settings. Better
OK so there is a big lake here and I see what looks like an office on one side and cabins on the other. lets start with the cabins. Get loot and food and such. I start walking to the other side of the lake when I see a black blur near the big building. I take my tme getting across the lake as I didn't know you couldnt fall through the ice yet. As I get closer I see my first wolf. This was before you could choose peaceful mode so everything attacked you. I see him start running towards me so I run to my right and hope to get around him. He cuts me off and we get in a fight. After fending off the wolf I make it into the building before he can finish me off. Looks like I'm at 14% health. Maybe theres some medical supplies in here. I find a bandage and use that but there was no anitisthetics. Look in my pack and find that I already had some. I decide to go sleep for what it tells me to and then die from starvation.
10/10 is what I would give this game. After 28 hours, I have never had more fun in a survival game. I came into this thinking it would be buggy and take forever for updates but these devs have done better than some AAA companies in the short time this game has been out. Switching to the Unity 5 engine made a huge difference in performance (for me) and made the game look better and run better all at the same time. New zones came out and added many more hours of gameplay and days of survival. Different modes came out for people who just want to explore rather than fight wolves and they have even made a makeshift bow. Now I havent been able to use it yet but I know that feeling of invincibility of finding a rifle and then the crushing defeat as your round misses seeming to go off into F*cking narnia when the wolf is coming at you fangs bared. The graphics arent the best but that doesnt matter in this case. I have never been so impressed by an indie game before. ON a finishing note LOVE YOU HINTERLAND STUDIOS!!!!

This game gets the thumb mainly because unlike most civ-style games getting established doesn't mean getting comfortable.  Your beautiful and harmonious town can suddenly turn into Dante's sequel when you forget to replace on person who died off of old age in an important job.  This game can and will kick you square in the Jimmy now and then (sometimes seemingly unfairly).  I've never found a sim game that balances on such a razor's edge of food, and materials.
Now it's not all fight and famine (okay there's a lot of famine) you also get to experience the joy of knowing your citizens.  That forty year old lady is shacking up with the eighteen year old next door.  This is her third pregnancy with three different men!  You'll follow the cougar queen, or the man that seems to do everything well.  Through luck or by skill he seems to make every place he works produce better.  Or the lazy, unemployed guy meandering to the grove you told him to harvest last winter.  When people died, I actually felt the impact.
Then there is the trading port (can I really spare all of those tools for a couple of sheep?) that will leave you in a moral dilemma as to what you can and can't spare for items you desperately need.  Then should you accept these immigrants?  You need more workers, but are you making enough food and firewood?  Will they bring disease with them?
Every aspect of this game has a give and take.  You can't take decisions lightly.  It's hard, but extremely rewarding.  Well worth the purchase.  Just make sure to save OFTEN and make sure no one's around to hear you screaming at it.  "There's firewood in the freaking bin!  Why are you still freezing?  Get some firewood!  Oh, wait, my wood cutter died... my bad."

Horror at it's best.
Outlast is a unique Survival/Horror that plops you in the middle of an insane asylum where you collect batterys to survive and run away from scares. Sounds cliche', right? It's not though, and that's what makes Outlast so awseome! You follow Miles Upshur, an investigative reporter who's set to uncover what's inside Mount Massive Asylum. After a rather breif search of a few rooms, our Peter Parker gets jumped by a rather big man, being sent flying towards the first floor. That's it, you're now stuck with all the crazy patients. Armed with a Camcorder and...running, you try to find a way out of the hellhole you've been put into.
As for the Gameplay, most of it is pretty smooth. Upshur controlls great for the most part, with my only complaint being how he jumps. Sometimes you just pathetically hop instead of climb or jump over an obstical. This is an annoyance when trying to run away from you're loony friends. I also found that closing doors is a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥ most of the time you'll close the door with you on the wrong end. Maybe I needed to slow down for these parts, but I dunno. Besides from running and hiding, you'll also want to explore the hallways and rooms for batterys. See, the lunatics can't see in the dark, but you can-when you have batterys for your camcorder. Once you hit 0, you'll only be able to see what's infront of you.
One final thing before I give my verdict is how the "enemys" work. Some psychopaths will rush at you and attempt to kill you, while others will just watch you. It's this element that keeps you on edge 24/7, you'll never want to let your guard down. This is what makes Outlast so different, this factor, along with great attention to detail, is what makes me say that Outlast should be bought-no doubts.

This game is a blast to play. If you like games kinda like No Man's Sky, this will definitely be something fo you.
At the beginning you get to choose four members for your crew, each person with own personality and skills for individual professions and tasks like doctor, technician, repairing ship hull, refilling fuel etc. They can also get injured in fights or ill while exploring space. So management of your crew, ressources, fuel, ship status etc is essential for surviving in the dark deeps of the universe.
You can travel between solarsystems and visit every planet in each system. With your landing capsule you have to consider gravity and thermal conditions of each planet while landing. This makes it very challenging because your capsule behaves differently every time.
After landing safely you can keep flying over the surface in order to find new ressource sources for fuel or even trading purposes.
In space you have to keep in mind that each planet has an own orbit you have to manage your speed in order to stay in the desired orbit, gravity of the sun and other planets has to be considered too. There are many different alien races you can meet in your journey, with merchants, traders, or even hostile ones you have to fight against, they all have their own sort of humor and personality too, some will interact with you, others won't even undestand you untill you have the according translation tool.
While exploring you can reveal so many secrets like hidden stations, abandoned planets, with technologies you can aquire in order to upgrade your ships (mothership, landing capsule) or build new ones.
I personally love games like this, especially the overall graphical style of this game. Each planet looks different in therms of biological and geological conditions.
You can spend hours by just landing on different planet, gathering ressources, and searching for hidden secrets, meeting new races, exploring asteroid belts etc. etc.
This is why i totally recommend this game. Controls are quite a challenge but with a good learning curve. 8/10 from me.

This game is challenging, it took me a while to get used to controlling both the ship and the lander module, but once you figure it out, it is fun dealing with the different environments you encounter. Use of a controller is highly recommended!
The setup is that your jumpdrive malfunctioned and took you way further away from Earth than was planned. Now you'll have to find your way back with limited resources, so you'll have to gather resources to refuel and keep your ship in shape along the way. There's a lot of content with aliens to meet, quests to do, random events, items, upgrades etc.
You jump between systems, within systems you try to steer your ship into orbit of interesting planets and locations and then deploy your lander to explore the planets and gather resources and/or other interesting objects or people.
I like the art style, but I think the UI could have used a bit more polishing. For example, it's hard to tell how much you damage your ship or lander when you bump into things since your focus is on the middle of the screen (where your ship/lander is) and the hull status bar is in the bottom left corner. Like I already said, it took me a bit of time to get used to the controls.
While the game is by no means perfect, I enjoy and recommend it if you aren't easily frustrated by somewhat more challenging games.

Made it through Episode 1 and I have to say I enjoyed the game.
The cell shaded look is pretty neat and fits nicely with the game.
The QTE's aren't that bad although if you are playing with a controller you might not be able to execute your finisher and have to resort to keyboard for that.   But the switchover is seamless.
Crowdplay is a neat idea and is more conducive to a party environment and not for viewer interaction on streams.
The reason being is because the others in crowdplay only get colors and not actual text options so if you are streaming the game on something like twich with it's 30 second delay the participants won't have enough time to wait for the stream to catch up and will only have about four colors to choose from that has no context.
It is pretty neat in that it allows for other people to actually override your decision if enough people vote for a particular one that you didn't vote for.  So if you have a large enough group participating the main player could very well have his decisions made for them by the crowd, whether they agree with it or not.  It sure as heck happened to me at several points on the run.
All told Episode one was a good start and I want to see where this goes.  I want to see what consequences my terrible decisions as batman have as the game progresses.

Looking to purchase this game and you can't decide if it will be worth your money? Or perhaps you are just trying to figure out what this game is about and the main objectives? Let me help you!
ABOUT:
Five Nights at Freddy's is an psychological indie horror game. It's not like Silent Hill or Heavy Rain in the psychological aspect, where every choice you make effects the game in some way. In fact, you don't have a choice but to sit in a room as a nighttime security guard for Freddy Fazbear's Pizza, a restaurant where kids have a grand time! Pizza, songs, and animatronic animals such as Freddy Fazbear, Bonnie the Bunny, Chica the Chicken, and Foxy the Pirate. Kids love them! And once the place closes up, it's up to you to watch over them. But why would you need to watch these animatronics that just stand there all night long. I'll give you a hint: they don't just stand there.
GAMEPLAY:
The gameplay is rather simple! You sit in an office with only a limited power source. Probably for reasons that have to do with a few deaths that occurred there once. Your shift starts at twelve A.M. and ends at six A.M. You must survive for five nights (hence the name, Five Nights at Freddy's). You cannot move anything but your head left and right. Both to your left and your right are doors. For now, they are open, of course. There are two buttons on both sides: one to turn on a light and one to close the door. Of course, both of these things drain power, which you must conserve as much as possible. You also have a screen that shows you what various cameras in the building see. In order to access the camera, you must flick your mouse downwards, which could get annoying sometimes. I have had times where I am in deep danger and I turn my head to the left, but my mouse goes downwards on accident! But that's rather rare. If you look at the camera and go to the stage cam, you'll see the beloved-by-kids animatronics! You're main objective is to keep them out of your office.
REVIEW:
It's a very simple horror game with only mouse controls. That being said, it's very frightening. It's actually terrifying. It has amazing atmosphere and sounds. Sounds are a huge part in the game, so I would recommend using headphones (as much as you probably don't want to with a game like this). The game is extremely easy to hop into. The first night is very easy but gets more difficult with every night that passes. It keeps you on edge. The animatronics have a very creepy design to them. It's also extremely fun. It's worth the money, for sure. I would absolutely recommend Five Nights at Freddy's to any gamer who enjoys a scare (and a really good one at that).
PROS:
Very scary
Atmosphere
Controls
Plot
Animatronic's design and mechanics
Very fun
CONS:
Why do I stick with this job?!
Might be a bit boring a times for some (doubt it)
THANKS:
Thank you for reading my review! I hope it helped to inform you on everything! :)

As the last chapter in the Enigmatis trilogy, this wraps up all the loose ends. That in itself makes this game satisfying as you finally find out what happens to our protagonist and her friends and enemies alike. This installment still manages to twist and turn the story to keep you interested. Some scenes do seem a bit similar to the previous games but not enough to bother too much.
I must say that I actually enjoyed the characters and their interactions. The characters have CHARACTER, they aren't there to just help you along. Especially after three games, I've grown quite fond of some characters. I doubt that the personalities leave you completely disinterested - at least, not all of them.
The snowy backgrounds still bring out a lot of colorful locations. Actually, the colors stand out even more because of it. The scenery of the game isn't as dark as in the previous ones, which may put off some people. I personally liked it, not just because I like colorful backgrounds but because it symbols the end of this journey. As for the animation, I have mixed feelings about it. I liked how the art seemed even more realistic, especially when it came to the humans. They still didn't change their expressions that much to show how they felt.
Gameplay was a bit frustrating. If you play to get all the achievements in one go, you must be extra careful or you might miss something. I had to restart the game many times because I kept forgetting to pick white feathers or morphing objects that I didn't have any access to once I realized my mistake. Luckily, if you miss few feathers at the beginning of the game and you restart it, you can get the achievement quite easily.
In the end, I enjoyed this game and the journey from the first to the last installment. Especially since I managed to get all to achievements after such difficulty and was left satisfied. This series is a great add to the collection of any hidden object gamers, new and old. Whether you buy it on sale or not, it's worth it.

A fairly faint positive recommendation, mostly for the sake of completing the trilogy.
As the game is the 3rd in the series, I have no doubt that readers have reference points about previous ones  so I'll be short with the review.
The game wraps up the story fairly well, even though the ending is quite lacking after the 1st game's eerie atmosphere and the 2nd one's bleakness. The third game lost it's Enigmatis-identity, the gameplay turned into the standard, superlinear, non-backtraceable HOG as most of the games are, while the predecessors had a fixed location and gave more and more access of it's buildings, parts and such. The hidden object scenes are littered with objects that require more than one - often 3+ - actions to do, in one case it was 6! This halts the gameplay, and in the meanwhile I think the animation quality also dropped.
All in all, it's an okay game by Mundi standards, but in my book this is the weakest game from the series - lack of a consistant area and therefore the constant moving forward-forward-forward made the game much less of an investigative one. Would worth to pick up during sales or from a bundle to finish the story, but it could have been so much more.

This game is very much like most MMORPGs: The base game is free and playable, but expansions, some accessories, exotic dragons and mini-game add-ons require gems (the game's purchasable currency)
A lot of reviews complain about the loading times, but in my experience the game loads and runs smoothly. (I have a GTX 650 Ti graphics card and run on Windows 10)
You raise a dragon from baby -> teen -> adult. My hideous zippleback reached adulthood at level 11 after the second day of playing.
You can also have multiple dragons, though extra stable slots will require gems. Gems can be earned by sending emails to friends to join, and after a few days of consecutive log-ins you'll get some prizes and gems as a thanks for your loyalty. Apparently there were campfires where you could sit around and play a very slow game of "gem farming" but it was disabled in later updates.
There are mini games where you can earn gold and experience for you and your dragon: Fishing (requires gold to buy bait, though I think you can get worms from compost)
A matching elements game (think bejeweled with the periodic table)
Dragon racing (your dragon needs to be an adult to participate, but you can borrow NPCs' dragons until that happens - unfortunately, Hookfang is the only free dragon to borrow)
Fireball Frenzy, where you ride your dragon through an assault course and shoot targets to score points
Eel blasting: This is a mini game you can play with your dragon - your dragon fires at eels of a certain colour as they pop out of the water
You can even run a farm, and it's basically a 3D Farmville - you have to wait for HOURS for your crops to grow, but if you want to speed it up it'll cost you a gem or two.
And of course there's quests the NPCs give you, which are basically fetch and retrieve quests.
I don't think it's an awful game, but it suffer from "BUY THIS STUFF" syndrome. So sadly I'm going to have to give it a "No, not unless you like to grind."

Bioshock is a phenomenal and groundbreaking video game with one of the most imaginative gameworlds ever.  The underwater utopia of Rapture is an artistic and fun city to explore.  Bioshock’s innovative narration tells the story of Rapture’s high-class citizens through the accessible audio logs scattered throughout the city.  The voice acting is brilliant and following the tales of these secondary characters spruces up Bioshock’s overall story.  This method of narration is very effective, because it doesn’t interrupt the main focus of Bioshock: the gameplay.  Simply referring to this game as just a first person shooter is doing Bioshock a disservice.  It features revolutionary RPG mechanics and unrivaled level design.  Scrounging around an area for unique ammunition, Eve hypos, and invaluable weapon upgrade stations are rewarding experiences.  Most importantly, participating in Bioshock’s clever level design will prepare you for the chaotic skirmishes with Big Daddies, which are menacing guardians that protect the little Adam factories with their massive drills, rivet guns, and rocket launchers.  There are two forms of currency in Rapture: dollars and Adam.  Dollars are acquired through conventional means, such as searching crates or cracking safes.  However, Adam can only be gathered by the orphaned girls venturing through Rapture in search of “angels”.  Unfortunately, Bioshock is no masterpiece, especially the PC port.  You cannot rebind plasmids or weapons to a particular hotkey, and hacking machines are time consuming and temporarily bring Bioshock’s exciting gameplay to halt.  In addition, the game is also plagued with some mouse sensitivity and audio problems.  However, the sound and mouse issues are fixable.  Bioshock’s unrivaled story and groundbreaking gameplay mechanics deliver a nearly perfect gaming experience.
Gameplay: 19/20 … AWESOME (The hacking mini-game is sluggish and will interrupt any exciting combat against a crazy splicer or a Big Daddy.)
Story: 10/10 … PERFECT (Atlas’s struggle with Andrew Ryan conclude wonderfully and the protagonist’s intermission with Sander Cohen during mid-game is quite possibly my favorite level in a video game.)
Graphics: 5/5 … PERFECT (Some people report that Bioshock suffers from frequent CTD’s.  However, I haven’t experienced one single crash through two entire playthroughs.)
Sound/Music: 4/5 … AWESOME (Turning EAX on is essential.  Otherwise, only a few SFX can play at once and those few sounds that play cut each other off.  This is VERY noticeable during skirmishes with alarms and turrets.  However, people report that turning EAX on causes even more audio problems.  Thankfully, there are fixes for all of these sound problems.)
Controls: 4/5 … AWESOME (The default mouse speed is brutal.  I had to manually change the sensitivity value in the ini file.)
Overall: 93% (42/45) … AWESOME

So many wonderful things happen in this game. Got cursed by a sea god, and found my wife and child dead upon returning to port. Jeez, high stakes here. Chased by a living iceberg, fled to a narrow fjord that the iceberg couldn't enter, and spent days chipping away at it with the deck gun until it finally keeled over. Spent dozens of hours on an epic quest to discover my father's bones, long lost at sea, only to discover he wasn't fully human! Fought an ill-considered battle against some behemoth of the deep, which wrecked my boat and killed most of my crew. The journey back to London was a nail-biting epic - fleeing from other mosters at reduced speed, creeping around in the dark, desperately charting course for a temporary haven to buy more fuel and supplies... when I finally made it it felt like a real accomplishment.
The narratives and atmospherics of this game are just amazing. I am lost to sunless sea...
which is not to say it can't be improved! Some of the story lines seem to peter out early, without a satisfying end to what had been a tantalizing opening. Sea combat can feel a bit routine after a while. And the world could be a bit more dynamic, in terms of things changing in reponse to the player's actions. A better interface for making notes and tracking missions would be good - as it stands now, I have to keep a pad of paper next to me to jot things down, remember what's where, and what I was up to last time I played. And a broader selection of useful boats would be nice, together with maybe a warehouse in town.
But these are all minor concerns. This game is already a masterpiece, and will become more so as more stories are added to the already rich mix of captivating strangeness.

While although I love a good story, and I love a good setting, Bioshock didn't provide that for me. It is probably already well established that the game has boring shooting mechanics, and a poor RPG system at best, but I also felt that although it could be VERY beautiful at some points, the setting is lackluster. Rooms look similar to me, and there is nothing enjoyable about spending most of the game in cramped hallways. The story, the other talked-about part of this game, is also kind of lackluster, not because it relies on you looting the audio books to enjoy it, but because even if you still do that, the story is very much something that feels disjointed, like you are playing a different game. The story that your character goes through is delivered in a less than gripping fashion, and the lore found in the audiobooks feels unconnected to your own story.
I love a good story and good lore in games, and I really enjoy a nice setting, but only if it has a reason to be there (take another game from 2K, Spec Ops: The Line, a game with audio logs that explain your setting beautifully). The game sometimes shows you some beautiful parts of Rapture, but doesn't show you them enough.  It doesn't help that the sound and music are sub-par, and can even take away your immersion into the world, where it should be helping it. This is a game that is worth it on sale if you really want to play it, but if you are looking for a game that deserves the metacritic score that this game got, look elsewhere.

There's only a handful of games I've ever played that I can actually call works of art. The Long Dark is one of those. The team at Hinterland deserves every kudo in the world for putting this beauty together. Here's just a few things I can say with absolute confidence on the game, since this is still in sandbox mode.
Style - Seriously, this style is lovely. There's something about the art of the game, simplistic yet detailed, just enough so that you don't get distracted from what you're doing, but enough to give you something interesting to look at. For some reason, the art for the sky was awfully cool? A lot of use of cool/cold colors definitely lended to the feel of the game in more ways than one.
Atmosphere -  This may be one of the most atmospheric games I've ever played. The landscape, the sounds, the sights, even things like your character's labored breathing. There was something legitmately chilling about the sight of ice-coated trees and the shriek of wind in your ears. I played this mostly in July, and it made me want to bundle up like it was December. You really do get immersed in the game through this.
Story - The hints of what's happened to you are legitimately frightening, and you get a chance to build your own story in sandbox mode. You know the storm took down your plane and knocked out the power, and you know you're alone. Seeing a ghostly aurora at night just adds to the nightmare you're facing in a spectacular way. The progressive desperation you end up in during some playthroughs builds a hidden storyline. In some games, you die very quickly, starving or freezing or getting mauled. In others, its a long haul through survival, and so the story becomes yours. The game just provides the opening line.
Controls/HUD - Very simple, very easy, and stressful in the best way possible. I found myself constantly checking my HUD to see how I was doing, and the point-and-click nature of it was helpful even when I was, well... dying? Nothing complicated, just enough to speed you along. Crafting was simple enough as well.
FEAR - Lord above did I have a a lot of this. I was caught between stressing over things like sprained ankles and what I was going to eat (DOG FOOD? AUGH.) and not monitoring my temperature. Then I have wolves prowling, a bear near the fishing shack I was using, and night coming on. I go to do some exploring for the first time and I end up at Derailment. A sad, lonely chord plays, and then there's wolves on me. I made a very unflattering noise when that happened. It's frightening without being gory or unnecessary, and that's fantastic.
Realism - For the most part, this game nails this right on the head. There's just a few things I scratched my head over (in terms of starving within a day despite being fairly idle, stuff like that) but they were things I could look past with little issue. The carry weight, the need for warm layers of clothing, the means of obtaining food and how much you can lose by opening a container improperly, etc. Absolutely awesome, and as a northerner, these things seemed very close to home. Good on you, Hinterland.
In short, I can't recommend this game enough and I can't wait to see what the finished product looks like. I'm absolutely thrilled with the result we have now.

Crowdplay is a neat idea and is more conducive to a party environment and not for viewer interaction on streams.
The reason being is because the others in crowdplay only get colors and not actual text options so if you are streaming the game on something like twich with it's 30 second delay the participants won't have enough time to wait for the stream to catch up and will only have about four colors to choose from that has no context.
It is pretty neat in that it allows for other people to actually override your decision if enough people vote for a particular one that you didn't vote for.  So if you have a large enough group participating the main player could very well have his decisions made for them by the crowd, whether they agree with it or not. All told Episode one was a good start and I want to see where this goes.  I want to see what consequences my terrible decisions as batman have as the game progresses.

Five Nights at Freddy's, what can I say about this game?  It is very predictable and gets stale very quickly, the scares are not very impressive and the only one that is even slightly decent is the Foxxy jumpscare, watching him running down the hallway is the only thing that could catch someone off guard but it only ever works one from what I've seen, after that one startle people tend to just worry about closing the door in time to not die and don't get scared by it after that.
This game has a simple premise, you're a night shift security guard who is paid to sit in an office and watch cameras overwatching the venue.  On your first night you are told the dark secret that has now screwed you, that the robots are going to be roaming around the venue and will stuff you into an empty Freddy suit if they see you.  There are five nights to the simple game and then two bonus nights with the seventh night being a customizable night.  I only bothered playing up to the fifth night because that's all I feel was necessary.  I understand that the other two nights are more difficult but I had no intention of wasting my time playing the game anymore than I had to.  The five nights only took me 40 or so minutes to finish and I did not fail a single time, zero deaths.  Very easy game especially once you find a pattern to operate yourself by.
This game is known around as a very scary game but I completely disagree, the scares may work on most people but even with most people I can only see the scares working once as they never change and they are very predictable.  I do not like the idea that you are forced to stay in one spot, I prefer being able to move about during horror games and I feel it makes the game much more scarier which is why Amnesia and Outlast are ranked at the top of my horror games.
There's really not that much to say about this game other than it is short and doesnt offer all that much in scares and has zero replay value.  I can not see anyone going through the entire game more than once, the only night I can see people playing multiple times is the seventh and final night.  The only reason I think people will play that night multiple times is because people will change the difficulty settings trying to prepare themselves for the difficulty setting known as 20/20/20/20.
In conclusion I don't think this game is really worth investing all that much time in, however it is only $5 so if you dont have anything else that you could be doing then feel free to get it and at most spend an hour finishing it.  If you're looking for a very good horror game then this game is definitely not what you're looking for and I doubt the sequel will be much better.  A predictable horror game is not what you want.

A worthy end to the Enigmatis trilogy. It has its flaws, but the presentation and gameplay is thoroughly enjoyable and on par with the rest of the series.
If you haven't played the previous two Enigmatis games (Maple Creek and Ravenwood), I highly suggest doing that first, because the story in Karkhala begins a few days after the Ravenwood adventure ends, and some of the details and subtle nods to the earlier games will make a lot more sense.
For achievement hunters, there's no need to plan for the usual "1.5 playthroughs". The pair matching achievements are in-game only.
I won't cover the basics, because it's a direct continuation of the overarching series plot. The main characters are the same and the focus is once again on finding and stopping the Preacher at all costs.
The setting is the most drastic change, taking place in the Himalayas. I gotta say, compared to the haphazard way many HOPAs handle foreign settings (looking at you, Tibetan Quest), the culture is presented pretty well. The devs clearly did their homework, which makes a big difference regarding immersion. It's refreshing to not see stereotypical "runes" as a stand-in for the regional writing/language, or artifacts and artwork that don't match the local flavor. Some things are indeed a bit westernized, but I suppose that's to be expected for the genre. I'd have liked to see more interaction with local people instead of focusing on an American research expedition, but it was well done nonetheless. There was also a bit of tongue-in-cheek humor with the research team all butchering Fang's name, while your character is the only one who pronounces it correctly.
If you're the type to watch cutscenes, the pacing and exposition are pretty good. There were a couple of unexpected (yet decently-spaced) twists to ramp up the drama as well. The ending felt a little rushed (defeat the bad guy, look wistfully into the sunset, roll credits), but there's more substance to it than in similar titles. The bonus chapter is good too, which is a rarity in itself.
I was caught off guard by this game. After the intro cutscene it
throws you into a pseudo-action sequence that gives you no time to think before getting sucked into the story. There are a few other active sequences further into the game, which I found to be a surprisingly nice change of pace. There are no actual fail states of course, but the tiny adrenaline rush they provide is just enough to pull you into a deeper level of immersion.
I didn't run into any bugs or hangups in puzzles, but the latter half of the game was plagued with abnormally long loading screens. I didn't think there was anything to really justify that much lag between scenes and puzzles, and based on other reviews it seems I'm not the only one who noticed them. Thankfully the only spot where it actively messed with a spoken line (for me at least) was more toward the end, so nothing important was missed. But other than adding some extra waiting time, they didn't interfere with gameplay.
The soundwork in this is by far the best in the series. The VOs were excellent as usual. (It sounded like they had a different actor voicing Rick than in the first two games, though I could be wrong about that.)
The music was particularly good, and never subtly repetitive or annoying like certain themes in titles like Nightmares From the Deep. Though the last two stations on the car radio are songs from the previous games, so they're a little on the grating side. The Extras section lets you save the music files, but I really wish they offered the flute title song (or any of the flute songs) as a download, because those were fantastic.
Graphics-wise? Come on, it's an Artifex Mundi game. "Gorgeous" is just a side note. It may not be one of their spam-your-screenshot-key titles, but the artistry still oozes out of the screen.
Not too easy, not too difficult, and tweaked/varied enough to not feel like yet another shameless rehash of the typical puzzles in these games. If you're colorblind you should know that while there's a hell of a lot of reliance on color, there's also a more-than-usual emphasis on pattern/shape and texture, which might make up for it.
The HOGs are good, but I hesitate to vomit praise all over them. There were no ESL errors that I can recall (even in the bonus chapter!), but certain isolated clutter piles seemed a little unpolished or low quality, to the point where I couldn't tell what some of the clutter actually
. That made finding certain types of items (unlabeled bottles or small containers, for instance) needlessly difficult. Plus a handful of items were almost entirely hidden behind other things, so instead of looking for the actual item you'd be hunting for something that looks like a piece of it (edge of a binocular eyepiece, corner of a book, etc). I wouldn't say that detracted from enjoying the HOGs themselves, but it wasn't the same level of 'wow' as the rest of the game. They were more or less forgettable compared to the puzzles.
is a great end to the fantastic Enigmatis trilogy. It can easily be played and enjoyed on its own merit, but I recommend playing the first two games in order to get the most out of the story. If you've already played them, you probably don't even need to be reading this right now.
TL;DR: It's worth your time. Enjoy.

Note: Rise to Ruins is currently in Early Access. The version reviewed was InDev25d.
Rise to Ruins is a village simulator with some god game elements, from indie developer Raymond Doerr. It was previously titled Retro-Pixel Castles.
In Rise to Ruins, you're given a group of settlers with whom you have to found a village and survive for as long as possible. Like most games of this type, there's no real end goal -- or at least none that I'm aware of -- instead you tend to play until your village is wiped out (or nearly so) and then you start again and try to do better next time. The game includes seasonal climate changes and a day/night cycle, both of which present further complications and challenges, but which are great additions to the game.
The game is played from a top-down overhead view, with characters (people and monsters) drawn from a three-quarter perspective to give them a bit more personality. You can adjust the zoom from a functional-but-not-quite-far-enough minimum, allowing you to see a fair bit of the surrounding area, up to a chunky-pixel maximum, where a single villager takes up a fair portion of the screen. At minimum zoom the game looks quite nice, with map tiles being well drawn, and characters looking like colourful ants. At maximum zoom the characters look a bit too blocky for my liking.
There are no real graphics detail settings, though there are particle and shadow settings, and the obligatory windowed/full-screen options. (ProTip: Don't play in full screen; it's very buggy.) It's not a graphics-heavy game by any means, but it chugs along nicely even with a hundred or so villagers all going about their business.
Music has a nice fantasy/mediaeval theme that suits the game well in my opinion. Sound effects are functional, but nothing special.
Rise to Ruins begins with an overhead map of the game's continent, from which you select a region in which you want to settle your first village. These locations differ in available resources and, I think, climate, so choose carefully. (You can found multiple villages in different regions, but you only have a limited pool of villagers, shared between them all.)
After you've chosen a region the game takes you to the region map, from which you'll play the game proper. There's no real tutorial at the moment, but the game gives you some help in the form of pop-up tips. These are a bit lacking, though. For example, I had no food growth and no food, but nothing in any of the tips told me I should build anything until it was too late, and even then I didn't know the best place to build it. An in-game tutorial would really help; the youtube tutorial video notwithstanding. Still, although you should be able to work out the very basics pretty easily, it's a steep learning curve when things go wrong and you don't know why. The Steam Discussions are a useful resource.
Anyway, you choose a section of promising looking land -- water, rocks, trees, and wild food, if you can find it, are all good -- and build a camp. That then lets you build other buildings, too, and before long you're harvesting resources and growing your camp into a little village community.
As is common to many god games, you don't have any direct control over your people; you can assign them to tasks -- builder is the only one available to begin with, but as you build more buildings, more jobs become available -- and that's about it. To harvest resources you select and highlight them on the map, and your people are supposed to harvest as many as they need, and no more.
You very quickly need to build up some basic infrastructure, including housing, food growth, water processing, and some rudimentary defences, the latter being required because you never know when a wandering monster might wander into your village and start attacking your people. Combat seems to be stacked against you, too; you don't have any really good 'troops' of your own, and the tower-defence style of defence doesn't quite seem to work: monsters bash through walls rather than being funnelled to your 'kill zone', and it's sometimes hard to even notice them in the first place, with no ability to automatically focus on important events.
You also have a small collection of god powers, which you can use by spending your collected essence: another resource, but one that's harvested by you rather than your people. I was a little disappointed in these, as I'd been hoping for a bit more range and depth to them, but what's there is useful and well thought out. I guess it would be fair to say they're more like Populous than Populous II.
Rise to Ruins has been in Early Access for about two-and-a-half years, so you'd be forgiven for worrying that it had been abandoned. It definitely hasn't, though: the developer releases regular updates and is active in the Steam Community for the game. As you'd expect from an EA title, though, Rise to Ruins does have some bugs. My first hour with the game consisted of about 15 minutes of playtime, followed by 45 minutes of trying to recover from a crash. The game just wouldn't restart and instead sat there spinning Windows' blue wheel of doom until I killed it. I eventually manually edited the settings and turned off full-screen mode and after that it worked again.
You'll encounter minor issues, too. Even with many idle people I found that building would often stop due to no resources being available, so the automatic resource harvesting seems to need a bit of adjustment. The UI is a bit wonky and controls aren't what I would choose, either, but they're functional, and the developer has stated that he reworks the UI every now and then, so what's here now may not be here forever. There's a big message reminding you to press the middle mouse button to cancel whenever you're in the middle of an action, such as designating resources or using god powers; it's lucky it's there, since middle mouse button to cancel is not intuitive at all.
Pros:
+ Detailed and in-depth simulation; there's a lot to learn
+ Different game modes from casual and explorative (sandbox) to VERY challenging (survival)
+ Solid design with a dedicated developer
+ Nice music, nice graphics at lower zoom levels
Cons:
- No proper tutorial, making for a very steep learning curve
- Some bad bugs, especially in full screen
- Some awkward controls
- Combat isn't that great
I've only just begun to learn some of Rise to Ruin's intricacies, but I can see there's a lot here. It still has plenty of rough edges, but the developer releases frequent updates and is always responding to comments.
If you have the time to invest in it, I expect you'll find Rise to Ruins very rewarding.

Blood Bowl is an amazingly fun and deep tactical and persistent tabletop board game. It's the Warhammer races playing american football against eachother, what's not to love? I've been a huge fan of blood bowl in one form or another (BBCE, FUMBBL, tabletop) since 2010 (over 3000 matches played), but Blood Bowl 2 is the one that really brings it home for me. The excellent modeling and animation work give a much more powerful feel to the game than any other form ever has.
Be advised that Blood Bowl is a
game first and foremost. If you get into the game (and you should!), be sure not to spend too much time in single player mode. The 'campaign' is basically a tutorial, slowly introducing game concepts to you. If you want to get playing quickly, you are probably better off looking for youtube videos (
has a good set of tutorials for the basic rules, and for more advanced gameplay help
)
When you do go to multiplayer (and you should!), it's worth noting that the 'main' non-competitive ladder has a fairly low standard of play. People there will concede matches a LOT. If you do not enjoy this, then you can join the champion ladder. While this is competitive, losing matches there will not result in a reduction of your rank as a coach, you can always start over fresh with a new team. Be advised that anyone who concedes more than 5 matches in a season (which last 6-9 weeks so far) across all his teams gets kicked from the champion ladder, so if you want the right to give up and stop playing a match, then this is not the place for you.
The real heart of blood bowl 2 lies in its scheduled league play. There are dozens of great leagues around, and if you can commit to scheduling and playing a game per week, then leagues are the way to go.
Be advised that when you are new to the game, it is often difficult to tell the difference between someone minimizing risks better, and someone rolling better dice. Blood Bowl is renowned for people cursing at 'Nuffle' (the dice god) for their terrible luck, but with insight and learning, this is truly a skill-based game at heart.
Blood Bowl is an amazingly fun, deep, tactical, persistent game, and Blood Bowl 2 makes it gorgeous too!

Given that the game is free for people to play and you get the whole experience without needing to pay for anything, the game is pretty alright.
That said, once you've invested yourself into the game, there is a lot of glaring issues that quickly stand out.
For the sake of saving time, i'll just list the issues off in short formfactor:
-$300+ worth of DLC.
-Newly released heros are $15 per, at base.
-The new hero designs are odd as they encurage you to stay on your builder, but the end game NEEDS your DPS
character or there is no point in trying.
-Speaking of end game, there is hardly any. I hit it in less than a week, and that's just due to grinding and not knowing the systems. I could've gotten there in 3 days if I wanted to.
-The scaling nature of stats in this game do well in giving the player a sense of progression, but simply take any semblence of skill out of the game. Nightmare 4 is hard as hell at first, but get your toxic shot bow and **boom**, it becomes a joke of a game.
-The tone of the game at the start makes it seem as if the game is taking itself more seriously, but that is quickly turned around by the "bubblegum" art style, which is good and bad in it's own right.
-The story mode is something akin to the original "Titanfall" and I have no idea what is going on. For all I know, a bad guy manages to smash the cyrstals that hold "The Old Ones" back and now you have to kill them, again. This game is clearly not relying on the story to sell, but more on gameplay.
-Balancing is fine from what I can tell. Nearly every hero is great in their own way, but holy crap are some heros downright needed. The archer is a must or a bust for high end gameplay.
-With regards to leveling, it's basically the same thing as end game. Your hero never really changes significantly. You just become bigger and deal more damage late game. There is very few ways you can make a build.
-Most of the complexity comes through managing the four heros you can have at a time, which makes you the builder and dps guy, reducing the need for other players. So unless you make a lobby yourself, you often make all the defences yourself and have someone else just dps the siege engines when they come along. This ends up making this werid multiplayer where people become their own island, but need other DPS people to deal with one ad. It's poor gameplay, at least with regards to teamplay mechanics.
Even though this game has many gameplay and fundemental flaws, it's a decent game to play for 30 minutes and come back to in a month.
Do you want a game you can sink hundreds of hours into to learn all of the deep stratagies? Look somewhere else.
Want a game that feels like it would fit in on a moblie phone that you can occasionally play when you have nothing else to do? This game is perfect then!

An independent platformer developed by a Danish company called Playdead. Limbo has a unique, eerie atmosphere that usually characterises the horror genre. The atmosphere is the result of the dark (black and white) presentation and the lack of music throughout the adventure.
It is one of those trial-and-error games where in order to successfully solve a puzzle in many cases you either need to react quickly or you have only one chance for a perfect execution. If you fail you can start all over from the previous checkpoint and you should also watch how the boy dies (often in quite a gruesome way). To be honest, I can easily imagine that this unique presentation deters some gamers from even trying out the game. Its trailer, in fact, presents the game's one-of-a-kind aesthetics very well.
There is a nice learning curve here and the game has some easter eggs for you to collect - mainly for the purpose of extra achievements, of course. If you love hardcore gaming you can complete Limbo in one sitting with fewer than 5 deaths to earn the hardest achievement of the game.
Limbo has a unique atmosphere. While it is not a long platformer it certainly is a great game. Unfortunately, due to its length and genre I consider 10 EUR a bit too expensive - still, we all know there are regular discounts so until it happens it deserves a place in everybody's wishlist.

Story driven survival game set in frozen willderness after the world as we know it has ended. Doesn't that sound great? Well, yeah, it does. But only on paper. To be honest, I was really dissapointed when I finally got to play the much anticipated story, after all these years of EA. The game teases you with some cool cutscenes and than let's you hanging on the cliff for way too long, and the only thing you can do is to follow the game's instructions and complete the boring missions. Basically what my point is that the actual story is way overridden by some wierd, boring and simple fetch quests.
The survival elements also don't do any good during the story telling, because it prohibits you from fully enjoying the story, by which I mean, I couldn't enjoy the game as it was constantly annoying me with frostbite and  hypothermia.
And I know, the game is supposed to be challenging, but that should be kept apart from the story parrt. At least things like not being able to sleep when fully rested, crafting when exhausted, etc., where suppressed.
The actual story was "meh", nothing special. I feel like they were forced to release the story mode by someone for several reasons:
1) in-game cutscenes were clunky and far from being smooth
3) the main quest felt like side mission.
4) the gameplay just doesn't felt right and the often occuring bugs didn't help this at all.
Final verdict:
If you're here for the sandbox, or "survival mode" as it is called now, than you can buy this game with peace in your mind.
But if you're here for the story part, the "WINTERMUTE", you should either wait for a sale, or just watch it on YouTube. And even though I'm a fan of this game almost from the beginning, it breaks my heart that I have to NOT recommend it.

spoiler alert! if you want to enjoy this game as much as possible, don´t read anything, anywhere.
first, you will die.
this is different to any survival game i have played. and i did see many of them. on the long run you will run out of scrap metal, so you will loose your ability of gaining food, so you will die. but... i would bet a lot of money that you won´t get that far the first few (many..) tries you play it.
unlike other surival games the "dead point" where you have unlimited suplies to survive, is never there in this game. you will constantly have to "fight" to survive.
the first tries you will probalby die cause little mistakes, then you will die cause wolfes kill you or you just freeze to death.
if you like sandbox survival games, this game isn´t even an alpha. i got no bugs, no gamecrashes, and not the feeling of beeing in an incomplete game.
first try was on hardcore mode (as all survival games in the past were kinda easy..), i found a wolf (or he me, depends on the line of sight..) and he killed me, quite early. i thought well, this might be a bit to hard. so i got on normal difficulty. first 2 tries again a wolf got me, but the third one (i just finished..) did last 42 days.
i never had a game where i was happy to find a pair of socks. or later on, i had a party finding one (!) round of ammo for the rifle. one round means (at least) 2 days of survival...
if you have better equipment, and know your way around it gets easier to survive. you know how it goes. you try to evade the wolfes, but your plans for the day are quite often useless. (there is a storm and you can´t see anything, or you had to spend a round of ammo for a wolf, and you should never waste any food, so grap it and go back to camp..)
orientation is fun. playing a game without automap or any help is just great. i am back again playing bard´s tale, dungeon master, or ultima, where you had to make your own maps, or remember waypoints. but even then, in a storm, you will get lost really easy (seeing only about 10m or so..). this is hardcore. and i like it.
crafting means a lot of time, which means a lot of food, which means, it is not easy. :) repairing is the same. there are some things that may cause your realistic sense to go red, but not as many as in other games (e.g. you may eat many kilos of meat a day, or a few boxes of matches have a weight of half a kilo, and few things more.)
all in all this is one of the hardest and best survival games i played. and i recommend it.
