The galvanizing action packed conclusion of the Enigmatis series begins only a few weeks after the last clash with the Reapers, the Raven and the Preacher.  Though this concluding chapter is stand alone due the private investigator's narrative recap of previous events and the retelling of Reaper history, if one has played the first two installments there is an innate impatient enthusiatic eagerness to track the Preacher down and finish this battle of wit, perseverence, and destiny - decisively.  In the end there can be only one - the Preacher, is the last Reaper alive, and ultimately either evil, destruction and mass death will be released back into the world in the form of the demon Asmosdai or the tenacious private investigators will stop it.
Storyline: A few weeks after the events in the American redwood forest tourist park Ravenwood where the Preacher defeated the Raven to become the last Reaper alive, our private investigator is back on his trail.  She knows now that there is only one Reaper left alive, and that the final Reaper's last and only duty is to sacrifice his life to resurrect his master, the demon Asmodai, bringer of destruction and death.  Now teamed up with another private investigator, Rick Hamilton, who for 20+ years has been tracking the Preacher and wants revenge, she begins at Maple Creek where her harrowing destiny began approximately two years before.  She must find where the last Reaper, the Preacher, has gone and stop him at all costs.  She and Rick journey to the highlands of the Himalayas after deducing the Preacher's destination, Karkhala Mountain, to stop his nefarious evil plan of ressurecting the demon Asmodai.  Along the way they encounter a scientistic team investigating an ancient monastery and discover an equally ancient group of Chosen guardians just as dedicated to stopping the rise of the demon Asmodai as they are.  Mystery, adventure, intrigue, betrayal, and murder are all part of this legendary battle between the arch-angel Raphael and the three-headed demon Asmodai.
Gameplay: Smooth combination of point and click, hidden object puzzles (HOPs), mini-games and interactive game play.  Stunning artwork with a vivid pastel pallette, 3D elements (title screen, snow and blowing wind), and a fast travel map. A prequel bonus chapter about Brittany and an extra menu with replayable HOPs, mini-games, cutscene videos, wallpapers, music, etc. 3 sets of extra hidden objects: 21 morphing Tainted spirits (look like evil skeleton ghosts or balls of mist), 15 Feathers and 8 Flowers. As usual with Artifex Mundi there is an alternative matching game if one does not want to play the HOPs.  For achievement hunters: all achievements can be earned in a single playthrough. Yeah!
Return of the evidence board:  This unique and exclusive feature of the Enigmatis series would have been missed had it been eliminated.  Part of the fun of this game (and the series) is finding the evidence and piecing it together much like a real investigator would.  The evidence board, now located in her cellphone, uses the pictures she takes and places them on this internal evidence board and is used for deducing answers to the relative and important questions of the investigation.  For those new to this series the evidence board will be an interesting mini-game puzzle whose clues will piece together the mystery.  For those who have played this series before the evidence board seems a bit weak since most of the mystery is known or can be guessed/ deduced very quickly.  There is a twist or two so do not count it out.
Hidden Object puzzles:  3 different kinds.  Finding a item within a picture, Find assembly pieces, and the majority are very interactive list finds.  The interactive list finds require the player not only to open drawers, jars, cabinets, etc. but in many cases to assembly the find clue such as putting wings on a statue or assemblying something that requires more than one piece.  Adds to the difficulty a little bit but the interaction is fun since the player needs to figure out what needs to be done to create the list find.  It is almost a mini-game Hidden Object puzzle.  Quite fun and unique.
Plus I swear the difficulty level slowly rises throughout the game since the last couple of list finds were tough.  Either that or someone spiked the difficulty level at the end.  Either way the last couple of HOPs are quite the challenge. My head scratcher was when the camera equipment fell all over the floor.  I am sure my difficulty came from the fact I had no clue what half the word finds actually were.  I know now since I had to look them up to figure out what the things were I was looking for.  Not often I run into such a head scratcher, and I am by no means putting that down.  I enjoy a good challenge and learning something new while doing it is always a bonus.
Mini-games and puzzles: Mazes, logical, matching, recipe and a balancing act while crossing a downed tree.  Mostly standard types of puzzles but fun and well intergrated into the story line.
This leads us to what I call interactive game play.  The puzzle mini-games in most cases are so well intergrated in the storyline the mini-game is no longer separated from the point and click elements.  The best example of this is crossing a tree log like a tight rope walker.  It is a mini-game but it is also direct storyline as well.  There are other interactive puzzles like moving a chest about to use as a climbing surface (not a mini-game or even point and click).  The line between actual mini-game and the point and click "puzzles" has been blurred in such a fashion that gameplay has become interactive. Very nice and quite inventive since the player for the most part really does not stop and think "oh this is a puzzle".  It is that smooth.
I think I covered everthing.  Highly recommend even if one has not played this series before.  It is stand alone and everything is explained.  For those who have been following the series this is a MUST OWN game.  The INTERACTIVE boss battle at the end is epic.  Worth full price.

My first ever captain was a philosopher wanting to write a book about the sea under the earth. This game marks its existence as a unique and dark adventure that's somewhere between a bad-budget indie and a professionally-developed masterpiece. The game itself can be pretty dark at times, so if you're waiting for the next Hello Kitty Island Adventure, I would look elsewhere.
Playdead toys with the idea of 'less is more', and benefits off it big time. I was pretty impressed by how nice the game played out. Not a lot of games like this keep me immersed, but LIMBO was a fresh breath into my library.
Fair notice to potential buyers: If you measure the game based off game time, you can get about 4 hours of playing before getting to the end. This doesn't include achievements, which can add in the neighborhood of about an extra hour.
The pictures in the store are essentially screenshots of gameplay; no touch-ups or re-done graphics. I was pretty impressed by that alone; I think a lot of us, at least several years ago, are so used to game producers creating special shots for promotional material, that we can't trust any material to be a representation of the game. Thank you Playdead for keeping everything representational of what you produced.
The game plays off as a puzzle platformer; some times it's more of the journey, sometimes it's more about getting pieces in the right places. Either way, there's a central plot that continues to feel important throughout the game beyond the traditional "Princess was in another castle" alerts.
For replayability, aside from the achievements, there is no real reason to replay this game. It's not a matter of 'they didn't add more because they don't care'; there isn't much they could have added while keeping the spirit of the game the same.
Overall, I highly recommend this game. One of the greatest $5 purchases I've made on Steam.

Currently one of my top three games of all time, Bioshock has set the standard for games. It has a beautiful setting. The AI is very complex. The story is brilliant. The gameplay works perfectly with the setting and story. Everything fits together perfectly. Never at any point did I feel as though the game needed anything nor should it have excluded something. Where to start?
The story. You are the lone survivor of a plane crash in the middle of the Atlantic Ocean. Oh, crap right? No, it gets worse. You take refuge in a lighthouse nearby only to be taken to an underwater city known as Rapture. The city was founded by a man known as Andrew Ryan and you see the entire place has fallen into chaos as you enter it. People have mutated into monsters after injecting themselves with a chemical called "Adam" and your only help is a man on a radio called Atlas. As you explore the city, trying to piece together what happened, you slowly uncover just who you are fighting and how Rapture fell.
The gameplay works perfectly with the story. You scavenge supplies because this is a city in absolute chaos and you have to. You have to shoot people on sight because it’s Rapture. You either shoot first or die first. Each gun functions differently, has different uses, and you can carry all of them. That's right. No stupid two weapon rule here. Early into the game you inject the Adam into yourself and gain superpowers as the game progresses. There's just one minor catch. You get Adam from the Little Sisters. Sounds easy right? Just walk right up and take the stuff from the kid? Candy from a baby. Scroll up. Yes, that guy. The guy on the cover of the game about 9 feet tall and a drill for a hand? Yeah, that's a Big Daddy. Notice how I said "a Big Daddy?" There is one of those for every Little Sister in town and you've got to kill it to get to her. Don’t' worry. It won't attack unless you get too close or shoot it. The people you take on in the beginning of the game are Splicers. They injected massive amounts of Adam into themselves and want the Little Sisters as well. So it is first come first serve. There are about six different Splicers. Some has pieces of pipe, a few have guns, others can climb on walls, and some can shoot fire at you. No problem. You've got a wrench and a bag of chips.
Bioshock is a beautiful game to say the least. It holds up to 2013 graphics no problem. The city is amazing to look at and explore. The character designs are very well done. They don't feel like big dude 1 and 2. You can tell who is who and the Splicers do look like people undergoing physical deformities.
The atmosphere is fantastic. The game goes for the Horror FPS style and does it with grace unlike other games. *cough* Dead Space *cough* Ammo is constantly low and the dark environments giving a slightly disturbing chill. You know how graphics have reached the Uncanny Valley? Bioshock's doesn't but the environments have that "not quite right" feeling about them. Everything is just slightly off. The place looks like somewhere you might want to live if it weren't a complete mess and Splicers were running around. Combining this with excellent lighting, songs such as "How much for that Doggy in the Window" playing from banged up Jukeboxes, and some shadowy figures around the corner, someone is bound to change their pants after playing this game.

I'm at a complete loss of words after playing this game.
I bought this game mainly because I enjoyed playing the Stanley Parable, and I thought that this game would be intriguing as well. Now generally I am not someone who gets emotional over movies and games, but interacting through the mind of this developer gave me the chills. I felt like I could connect with his pain in so many ways, yet somehow, it was relieving being able to see his journey.
I would love to say that I know the answer to this game. The answer to validation, to knowing your work isn't poisoned. But completing this story follows a feeling of emptiness. A feeling that many narratives avoid, because it most often angers the player, or depresses them. But somehow, it just, works with this game.
I can't really explain it. I'd love to say I know how, but I think Davey made the right move sharing Coda's work. Our work defines us, we pour our emotions into it, no matter what that kind of work this. We can't keep this inside us forever, we need to talk to others, and in a sense, we NEED validation.
I rarely right reviews for games, but this game really hit me hard, and whether you're an emotional type of person or not, I would really recommend playing this game. It's soothing in it's own way, and I'd love to hear your take on it as well.

If anything, Cuphead’s the sort of game that demonstrates how important presentation is. There is absolutely nothing bad that I can say about the art direction or how things are animated. The devs shot for something and they executed on it perfectly. This is the sort of work that deserves to be rewarded, and despite what I’m about to write I think that the game is worth buying simply as a big ol’ “♥♥♥♥ you” to all the lazy indie (and non-indie...) games that get released these days.
As a game, Cuphead comes across as more of a demo, or at least a smaller part of a much greater whole. It’s been pretty clear since the beginning of development that the game was going to be a boss rush, which I was initially alright with. Having actually played Cuphead, I’m having second thoughts here. The problem is that by simply throwing you into a boss battle, there’s no buildup. In the (post-Demon) Souls games (yeah, yeah), the stage leading up to a boss is rarely that difficult, but it helps get you into a certain mood. You anticipate what will lie ahead, sometimes picking up clues along the way such as in the game-spanning buildup to the fight with Gwyn. I think that you can apply this sort of thinking to basically any game with well-designed boss encounters: the stage is part of the boss because it gets you thinking about what the boss will be and it can even be used to introduce new mechanics that you’ll need to master to defeat the guy at the end. Playing Cuphead, I could easily imagine the stage that would lead up to each of the bosses since each was so unique; the (6 total) run-and-gun sections actually accomplish this somewhat, but are their own entirely separate and optional thing.
The bosses ARE the game, but they could have been fleshed out more. Each one only lasts a few minutes at most (usually ~1:30), and I feel like that’s a real shame. The current system doesn’t allow you to restore health which probably put a limit on how long fights could be. Hollow Knight, another recent and good indie game, has bosses that take significantly longer to beat, usually 4-5 minutes, which mind you is around 3 times as long as the Cuphead bosses. In that amount of time you’re able to get a much better understanding of how each boss works, and it doesn’t feel like they show up just to die immediately after. What’s worse, each of these minute-thirty boss fights is split up into multiple phases, so each phase is going to last an average of 30 seconds. 30 seconds is not enough time for an idea to fully develop. The Sally Stageplay boss has a phase that really caught me by surprise but before I could even finish processing that surprise the phase was over. In a perfect world where the devs had an infinite amount of time to work on the game, I think that it would have been better to cut down on some of the less-memorable bosses (such as the dragon in World 2) in order to lengthen the stronger ones. The puppet in the genie fight is beautifully animated but only has one attack: why not double, triple, or even quadruple its health and then give it a few more things that it can do? With changes like this, it would also probably necessitate the addition of a way to regain health during a fight, which could possibly be tied to the (currently almost useless) parry system.
I do have some other minor nitpicks – again, parries seem like they were thrown in without much thought outside of a few instances (the springs in the rat fight, the slot machine in the frog fight), every trinket seems useless compared to the smoke dash, and the existence of ultimately meaningless shortcuts on the world map only furthers the feeling that this is a demo of the complete version of Cuphead. Despite these issues, what this game does well it does exceptionally well, and maybe companies like Capcom will take some pointers from Cuphead next time they try farting out a triple-A title that looks like a mobile game.

In a nutshell:
Visuals:              Stunning and smooth.
Audio:                Crisp and delightful.
World:                OMG.
Gameplay:         Simple mechanics that can turn an accountant into an adrenaline junkie.
Learning Curve: Easy to learn, but fighter pilot reflexes are helpful.
Replayability:     Can't. Stop. Playing. So, probably good :)
My thoughts:
I've never had so much fun being completely rubbish at a game. For me, the game is hard but every death is my own fault rather than the game being unfair or glitchy. The repetitive nature of the gameplay works for this title, helped by the stunning, thematic visuals and toe-tappingly, wonderful audio.
The whole early day's of cartoons has been captured beautifully by the developers, all the quirks of the day melded into an addictive, one-more-time, game with fun characters and mechanics. It's a game that I can pick up and play for 10 minutes and walk away satisfied. But it's also a game that I could easily spend hours in front of if I'm not careful.
Cuphead is a game that I shouldn't actually like. I only bought it because of the interesting artwork and music shown in the trailer. I do not normally enjoy boss battles and frantic shooting game play, and repetition can frustrate me. But this has smacked those barriers down and made me cry with joy.
I'm not sure that I'll ever finish the game, more so because I'm not very good at it, but it will be a title that stays installed until my computer enters silicon heaven.
Final recommendation:
If you like fun, I believe that you will find it with Cuphead.

You're stranded. Far from home. Really, really, really far. It's not called "The
Journey Home", after all.
Making it back home will require wits, guts, patience, and one thing above all: sacrifice.
The two main "game" mechanics - the starflight should be easy to grasp for anyone who has spent any time playing KSP. It's easy to master, and some of my favourite moments are gliding through a solar system and listening to the tranquil soundtrack.
The planet landings are where you make or break (mostly break). It will take some time to get used to them (controller recommended), but there's a lot of variety in the environments you land in, so every landing you're on the edge of your seat. (And it's your own damned fault for landing on a "deadly" planet. What did you expect?)
All games basically boil down to the kind of decisions you have to make, and in TLJH those decisions are always meaningful ones.
You will need to manage the increasingly dilapidated state of not only your ship, but also your crew. This is not a game where you grind for resources to upgrade your ship to a battlecruiser. This is a game where you scrape together 2 borates to escape radiation death from a black hole. Why would you even jump to a black hole, you ask? Well, I might have made a "few" enemies along the way.
Because you are not alone in the galaxy. Which is both good and bad news. Who is what will be something you figure out run by run. All I can say is that these are the best aliens since sliced bread. They are all interesting and novel (and believe me, I have read a ton of sci-fi), and nothing is what it seems at first glance. The galaxy itself is a mystery to unravel.
The game masterfully executes its theme. You are always surviving by the skin of your teeth. By you are doing so by your doing, and that feels awesome.
If you enjoy getting pushed to the limit again and again, and you are a fan of good writing, this is the perfect game for you.

(disclaimer: received game for free)
TLJH is a space game that bucks the trend. Never have I played a game which so perfectly captures my understanding of the reality of a human crew space mission. Most games want to give you a tough avatar, so your ship can take a pounding, fly anywhere, refuel for nothing and protect you. TLJH spins that on its head by making your spacecraft a precious and fragile resource.
The early part of the game is punishing. There is no hand-held tutorial or lengthy explanation of survival strategy. Learning all the mistakes which will kill your crew and destroy your ship can be frustrating. The game forces you to consider your first few forays as the training the Daedalus' crew would have undoubtedly undertaken. Even down to simple tasks such as lining up the drill head or staying stable on a planet with high winds have to be learned on the hoof.
But there is a point during The Long Journey Home when you realise that you have been steadily trained with an impressive array of skills and judgement. You feel like an EXPERT. Asteroid fields, which once represented certain calamity, now offer a safe and manageable way to gather resources. You become adept at judging whether a system or planet is worth visiting for its resources, which crew member to send, on which on-board issues to spend your precious and limited resources. Is the Lander drill only collecting Hydrogen at 70%? I might live with that. I'd rather fix the Fuel Efficiency. The Long Journey Home is, in keeping with its name, a marathon rather than a sprint.
Brimming beneath this voyaging simulation is a universe of surprising personality and content. Numerous alien races, with a multitude of named NPCs come your way and offer detailed quests. Ancient and recent ruins litter nearby planets. Brothels, tournaments and obscure games played with stones all randomly colour your journey through the black. 15 hours in I have seen very little content twice.
Lastly, despite essentially being a grown-up Thrust clone, The Long Journey Home is incredibly beautiful. It's the treatment Thrust might get if a major movie studio decided to adapt it. I'm an Elite Dangerous veteran, but TLJH still surprised me with its light-mottled wreckage drifts, vast planetary horizons and forests of tall crystal. The sound is minimalist, but perfectly captures the bleak loneliness of the journey, occasionally interspersed with life-threatening drama.
Perhaps the only sticking point I can see is the price. The simple play style and interface does not seem at first like the sort of game to command $40. The vast alien cultures and depth are hidden away, perhaps unfortunately, behind a text-comms interface. Having played it, I would pay that price. It certainly has the depth to warrant it, but perhaps it will put players off by looking too indie for a full price tag? My advice would be: don't hold back. Don't miss out on one of the years most truly unique and beautiful titles.

Hopefully you really like Lunar Lander like I do though, because a third of your time will be spent playing Lunar Lander as you fly down to planets to gather materials, deliver goods, and having encounters. Planets will have various hazards as you fly in them and they can be really challenging to survive. But later you'll get upgrades that can make it less deadly.
The Visuals are solid, flying through space is just beautiful. There are times when you could take a screenshot and it'd be an amazing desktop background.
The music and sound effects are awesome. The soundtrack is your usual space music, but it is played beautifully. Sound effects give a good ship feel when you're flying around, crashing into things, and shooting at other ships.
The game is quite difficult at first, but that is par for the course with any rogue-like. Learning with each run as you explore space on your adventure to return home.
A nice touch I like is the conversations your crew has as you're flying around. These are affected by how they're doing health wise, who's on the crew, and what events have taken place.
Overall, heck yes I recommend this game. If you've been hungry for a space exploration game that feels like you're actually exploring space, this is the game for you....as long as you like Lunar Lander.

If you'd like to see a more in-depth review instead, please check the video link below:
Otherwise, here's a summarized pros and cons list.
1) Decent resource management with the 3 main resources.
As you continue on a run (which can last upwards of 7 hours), you start thinking on the risks associated on collecting the resources from potentially dangerous planets. These are metals to repair ship hulls, gasses to refuel the ship, and exotic matter to recharge the jump drive. Balancing the uses of the resources, to either repair and refuel ship or to sell for credits used to purchase upgrades and medicine, will be the most compelling gameplay aspect in TLJH.
2) Interesting setup for some aliens.
Travelling through space, you'll meet about 5 alien races per run you take (runs are randomized so you'll meet different races depending on the RNG of procedural generation). They have pretty interesting premises and personas that's meant to keep you from getting bored with core gameplay loop of resource collection.
1) Simplistic resource collection
THe resource collection process itself is really simple. Essentially, it involves a mini-game of trying to land a small craft on a planet's surface to drill a hole to dig for resources. The challenge comes from balancing the use of thrusters for the softest possible landing since harsher ones damage the lander's hull while also injuring its pilot. You'll mostly be holding down the thruster button while orienting the ship to whatever direction you'd like to head towards. Some planets have low gravity which require you to use the back thrusters instead but the execution of the mechanics are the same.
2) Lack of a story and character development
The game has 2 things to push its narrative, the stories of the aliens and your crew members. Aliens are handled much better than crew members. You're given the ability to talk to, insult, praise, question these aliens about all alien races in hopes to learn more about them. If you meet the right aliens of each race, you'll be given a quest that gives you something else to do while developing their individual backstories. Problem is, the frequency of this happening is random for every run and you have no way of finding the aliens with the interesting quest. Leaving it up to luck, these interactions happen far too little to keep you engaged throughout the 8 hours it takes for each journey. As a result, it doesn't save the game from being a chore after awhile.
Things are worse with crew members since you can't even talk to them. The only times they chime in are when they give a sentence or two about their lives during random moments while you're travelling in space. Sometimes they'll be a little witty but for the most part, a lot is left to be desired from these moments. Since so few back and forth takes place between you and these members, and between the members themselves, the execution of this form of "character development" doesn't make them feel very human. Couldn't really care for any of them by the end.
3) Simple combat
Was happy to find there was space combat in the game, not so much when I found out how simplistic it was. Essentially, you have a ship with shields, side cannons, and a boost button. So all altercations boil down to taking laser fire with shields that recharge over time, trying to angle your ship to orient a good shot and boosting your way out of danger whenever you get the change. No secondary fire, no way to rewire power to shields, boost, or cannons. The only things that change are the enemy ships you fight but that just changes the different attack patterns. To it's credit, you can buy cannon upgrades later on that  change the spread and damage of your ship but it's still disappointing to see how repetitive combat gets over time.
4) Overall just really repetitive
Without compelling space combat and far too infrequent meaningful interaction with aliens, alot of your time here will just be on resource management, resource collection and possible space combat, 2 out of 3 of which are too simple to keep you attention. As such, the game just feels repetitive after 2-3 hours or so unless you're REALLY into resource management.
TLJH spends alot of time highlighting its more basic mechanics at the cost of the more interesting ones. The game has alot of content but it distributes it so sparingly in an attempt to warrant multiple playthroughs. As a result, it makes individual runs feel repetitive and boring which does not incentivize players to have a second or third go at returning home. I would only recommend getting this at 20 dollars instead of 40.

I bought this during the sale for $3.74 and still cant quite bring myself to give it a thumbs up.  This game is a very simple, very linear, hack and slash.  You travel along on a terribly confined, predetermined pathway killing mobs.  At the end of each pre-defined pathway, there is a "boss" style mob.  You kill the boss mob and finish that pathway.  You move on the the next "pathway" and do the same thing again-over and over.  That is the game in a nutshell.  The scenery isnt engaging in the least and there arent any "drops"(random or otherwise) of items or equipment to make the game interesting.  All that drops is gold but I havent played long enough to know what the gold is supposed to be used to buy.  I may never play that long.
As far as comparing this game to previous Sacred games;  In many, many cases I have found that a new game in a series is pretty good but doesnt meet the expectations of those who played previous installments so the new installment gets a bad rap.  That is not the case with Sacred 3.  Sacred 3 deserves a bad rap all on its own merits.  Previous Sacred games are very busy games with a ton of things to do, tons of plot and sub-plot to remember story and quest wise, and lots and lots of interesting equipment drops and so on.  In truth, Ive always thought that previous Sacred games are TOO busy lol!  Anyway, Sacred 3 is not busy at all.  Sacred 3 is mindless in fact.  As I said above, you travel down relatively short corridors killing everything that comes at you, kill a boss and then you're done till the next corridor.  That is it.  Also, I think the charector scripts are supposed to be amusing but it comes of only as juvenile and silly.  Like another reviewer said; "Turn off the sound to make the game a little better".   Bottom line is that $3.74 is pretty cheap.  If you've got it to spare then buying this game probably wont be the worst decision that you've ever made.  BUT, should you chose NOT to buy Sacred 3, you wont be missing anything, I assure you.

Please note that I am not a native English speaker, and I apologize for the mistakes in advance. I have successfully ventured back to earth in exploration difficulty in 7 hours and the following review comes from my experience of that run and I am very disappointed.
The Long Journey Home could have totally been an advanced version of Out There (by saying which I am not condemning it a ripoff), considering the resources Daedalic had. Unfortunately, it ended up being an all-around worse version of Out There. I felt sorry for it being one of Daedalic's 10th-anniversary works and a failed attempt to shift to another genre. 10 hours that I could otherwise have spent playing all those better games released in May.
The outstanding aspect of the game -- I use "the" without "one of" for a reason -- is its soundtrack. From the main menu background music full of prospect and hope, to the intense track played when engaged in melee, to that arraying unique themes of each alien race representing their culture accordingly, its music scores are well composed.
Now I am going to complain its horrid control for some time and superficially it's its most glaring issue, but noted that the biggest problem lies underneath: its resource management.
Gravity well is refreshing at first, as I grew up reading tons of sci-fi works I'd love to see gravity slingshot implemented in games and by carefully planning ahead my ship manages to save most of the fuel in traversing one galaxy -- which is intended, since resource management is the core gameplay element. That said, combining with its near-sighted top-down view and the minimap that's not informative at all about the gravity field, you are literally not allowed to plan ahead and all you can do is to keep pressing the thrust button to change your course inefficiently, if not futile. And manual control takes up a fair amount of play time, making the experience a chore from start to finish.
I am not done with the manual control part. When you engage an alien ship or a probe, a space station, an asteroid field or a wrecked ship you are transited into a close-up view where you manipulate your ship in detail. The control is wonky at its best, and often times obnoxious -- and it's almost a deliberate waste of time: you wait for a loading screen (if it's a ship or a probe, add a 10-second cutscene), then you see them. After you finish whatever you intend to do (if you are to dock a station, two more 10-second cutscenes), you press the thrust and boost button for like 10 seconds before you meet with yet another loading screen and you are back.
Melee is horribly done. Both battle party just fly around pew-pewing each other with their Nerf gun the whole time the Nerf gun is also used to mine asteroids. I used plural here, but in fact, in every asteroid field, there is only one that can be mined, by which I mean if you hit other asteroids there's not one single feedback: your Nerf bullet just magically vanishes upon contact. There's no momentum, no explosion no nothing at all, but again they can tear through your hull endurance like a piece of wet toilet paper.
Still, I am not done with the control part just yet. When your ship is orbiting a planet you may send down your lander -- and you are going to regret it. The lander control is pathetic. I believe it's a deliberate decision to make it the way it's so that you are going to waste a huge amount of fuel and lander endurance just to meet up with their "daily resource management quota". And on every planet there's just virtually nothing to do -- you get to see 2 ~ 3 spots to mine, and occasionally a ruin to unearth or an alien outpost, where you trade a bit and have repetitive conversations across all planetary outposts of the same race, which is underwhelming.
Now I am finally done with the control. As mentioned above, the resource management is the core gameplay element and the culprit here. Of course not merely resource management, but the combination of it and the risk & reward of exploration together -- and that's why I mentioned Out There at the beginning, because it best represents a perfect miniature space exploration model: a self-sufficient cycle and risks & rewards of choices complement the cycle making it meaningful. In The Long Journey Home, however, it trivialized the meaning of choice and distracts the player with pitiful manual control, resulting in the control being most of the "risks" part. Daedalic, I think we need to talk about the term "player action": it does not literally mean "action", mate. Besides, the resource management itself does not hold up: the game just felt like it should differentiate itself from Out There so they decided to screw up every aspect Out There has done right by breaking down inventory into items and resources, not allowing you to fix and build things yourself, introducing a universally accepted currency and distract the player by forcing them to control the ship. In a way, it trivializes risks and challenges in player choice but it also adds unnecessary annoyance and tedium.
Other problems are minor comparing to control and resource management, like bad UI, celestial bodies not orbiting (taking control issues into account, it's actually making things a lot easier) and stuff.
What surprises me is that for a company known for high-quality point & click adventure games Daedalic managed to present an underwhelming narrative. Each crewmate has their unique background (which determines how efficiently they can use items), starting item and they engage in conversation when cruising, but that's all you can get from them and this even comprises a fair amount of the narrative, because the dialog is written based on their backgrounds. Side quests are scarce and poorly written with rewards unknown to the player party aforehand (that's some "risks"). You can talk to any alien encounter with a wild array of dialog options that first look amazing before you notice the same race repeats the same thing like a broken record, with very limited meaningful feedback. And yes the alien races are totally sci-fi stereotypes, but I am generally okay with that.
And thus concludes the review. I don't usually write negative reviews because I don't want to look impotent rage and I want people to look at the bright side of a bad game, but this is outright bad -- its design is beyond the question of fixes. Just in case Daedalic would remake the game from scratch, I should declare that this review may be updated following major patches.
I doubt whether
, a veteran writer of Rock Paper Shotgun has received any goodie from Daedalic (
I think he boarded the hype train and got overly excited), or else I cannot fathom how he could write all those amazing stuff about a no-good game like this before he got his hands on it. But I guess people do make mistakes, like I once held high hopes for this game.

** Closed Beta Review (I won a beta-key) **
Those ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s put her in a cage and left. They asked and we delivered. I wanted, but could not decide otherwise. Helpless and alone with only a glimpse of hope my crew had landed in a hostile galaxy full of strange aliens. The Meorcl, who literally get in your head forcing your decisions, are only one of many aliens in The Long Journey Home.
The game is awesome. I had the opportunity to play it in the closed beta and here is what I think:
This game does not focus on a single super awesome mechanic slowly expanding it as you play. It is all about stories. The story of your crew members, of the aliens and yours. It is quite a challenge to keep your♥♥♥♥♥♥together and focus on the one long term goal: Getting home.
Content
At the beginning you choose four crew members out of 10 and every one of them has unique interactions with their colleagues and the artifacts that you can find. The galaxy is generated with a seed you can define at the start and always contains four out of eight major alien races and some smaller alien races. You will find many many quests ranging from small errands to galaxy changing revelations. There is an incredible amount of content. After 50+ hours I had not yet seen all major alien races! Let alone the many quests, alien characters and crew member relations I still have not experienced.
It looks beautiful, has its own style, exceptional writing and an amazing soundtrack.
Oh and there are tons of cool pop-culture/game references to enjoy!
Gameplay
I don't want to describe too much of the gameplay here, because watching a let's play or stream for that is far better.
Basically there are five layers:
The galaxy map (chose your way through the galaxy),
the star system navigation (get to and orbit planets with as little fuel as possible),
the encounters (fight alien ships in space - kinda sid meiers pirates style),
the planets (lunar lander style)
and the conversations/visits (dialog system, which is not based on multiple choice)
All of them work very well with the theme of the game. Space is a dangerous place.
The navigation and landing may seem clunky at first, but they are really not. Once you get the hang of the physics you will soon orbit planets in no time and master most landing missions with minimal damage.
Difficulty
If you expect an easy play-through, because I said it is about stories, you're very wrong. It is really hard to get home to Earth. Your ship is slowly falling apart (nearly every jump damages a ship module) and your crew will suffer injuries. The developers did a great job to prevent instant death. Instead you will slowly get to the point where you can't continue your journey, and it is always because you made too many mistakes along the way.
This may be the core of the game: Fight versus the inevitable. Try again and again to just get one sector, one star system closer to earth with hope to find valuables that bring you even further.
The last sector - without spoiling anything – is special. It is a challenge of its own and personally I don't like it. Even though I understand why it is designed that way, it feels somehow disconnected to the rest of the game. At least if you made it to the last sector and then even make it home, that feeling is far more rewarding than just reaching the last gate.
Conclusion / tl;dr
If you don't enjoy a difficult challenge, can't stand science fiction or only like shooters, then this game is not for you.
Otherwise a nail-biting (and funny) experience awaits you in The Long Journey Home. When you finally manage to get home, you will probably want to try again with a different crew, ship or seed to explore even more and unravel all the hidden mysteries.

The final installment of the
series of hidden object games is here! That’s right, if you haven’t played the first two titles stop what you’re doing and fix that post haste because it will make your enjoyment of
that much better. It’s time to stop the villain, simply known as the Preacher, once and for all before demons can be unleashed unto the world. There is action and adventure around every corner, it’s up to you as the detective to find clues and solve the case by finding a way to defeat the Preacher, but it won’t be easy.
While the previous two games took place in America, this title takes us to the mountains of Asia where the Preacher is on his way to summon his demon master Asmodai. Our main character has teamed up with Detective Hamilton from the first two titles and the pair set off on an outrageous adventure. There are plane crashes, blizzards, dead bodies, magic and more involved, plus a mysterious child named Fang who may be the key to everything. The story is rather straightforward, though does throw in a curveball or two that even I didn’t expect. The writing and pacing create a real sense of urgency as the main character races to stop the Preacher.
If you haven’t played the previous two games, this one does give somewhat of a recap so you won’t be too lost, however, the energy in this game is created from the build up of the previous titles. There aren’t many characters in this game; the focus is on the protagonist, Hamilton and the Preacher. Brittany is a helpful side character as are Fang and Po but I found things most enjoyable when it was just the two detectives and I wish the game focused more on the Preacher. That being said, everything is tied up very well in the end.  I was satisfied but also disappointed that this was truly the end. I would personally love a series of detective games following this main character and Hamilton.
As far as gameplay is concerned, this is your traditional hidden object game. You move around and talk to people, interact with objects and collect useful ones in your inventory much like a point and click title. Some items you can examine closer and you may have to combine them with something else or another type of action. There are plenty of hidden object scenes to keep you busy that offer a varying level of challenge from easy to sometimes frustrating but never unsolvable. The puzzles are also in the same nature though most weren’t too difficult. We see return of the evidence board and deduction mode, except this time it’s on the protagonist's cell phone since we’re so modern now. Throughout the game you collect evidence and piece it together to further the story. My only issue with this is, at this point, there isn’t much to discover. We know what’s going on, we know why and we know what to do. As such, this feature is actually not used as much as in previous games with only a few deductions even available sadly.
The graphics are top notch. This game is crisp and new, filled with great animation and scenery. The character models are well done and their animation is very fluid. The locations are all gorgeous and I appreciated the attention to detail in the beginning when we revisit Maple Creek, it looked just like in the first game, location-wise. The hidden object scenes have great resolution and are easy on the eyes, no need to worry about squinting much. The music is perfect, you can even save the tracks from the game since this is a collector’s edition. Voice acting is well done and well directed. The cast is small but well selected and helps players stay immersed in the game. One issue I noticed were pronunciations of the name Fang. Other characters said it like a wolf’s fang while the main character said it differently and it made it sound more naturally Asian. I’m not sure if this was on purpose or an oversight but it’s not that big of a deal, Fang is mute so she can’t really correct anyone either way.
This trilogy was a great ride but now with
it’s come to an end. If you’re new to hidden object games or new to this series, don’t hesitate. It’s fun, spooky and very exciting. I really enjoyed this title and despite finding some faults here and there I’d say this is a game I’d have no issues replaying. It even has a bonus chapter which tells us more about Fang and Brittany- it’s a little short but a nice addition to the game. There are Steam trading cards as well as achievements to collect if you needed even more reason to purchase this game. It’s time to stop the Preacher!

Another indicator is that you can get much more Yarn Balls than there are hats and there's nothing to trade them for, a very obvious choice would be to just make it so that you can trade Yarn Balls for coins that you can use on the slot machine that gives you cosmetics but the developers chose not to and so you're just stuck with a large amount of Yarn Balls that you can't do anything with because you've already unlocked all of the hats. This game also has a weird ending, it just ends, there's not a whole lot of levels and the story also has no real sense of progression, things just happen, then there's an unexpected bossfight and then it's over. Of course story is pretty much unimportant for a game like this but it still bugged me. It doesn't really have to do something with the games length, Super Mario 64 is also only about 15 hours or so long, but this game just doesn't feel complete or finished when you beat it. I don't regret buying this game and will still recommend it but it just feels like this could've been so much more. Maybe the Devs will add more content later and if so I will certainly change my review but as of now, this is my opinion. If steam had a point system  this would be a 7/10

SUPERHOT IS THE MOST INNOVATIVE SHOOTER I'VE PLAYED IN YEARS!
In all seriousness, SUPERHOT really is a fresh take on shooters, it is great for people who can appreciate a game for it's enjoyable mechanics and gameplay, and don't need a fully fledged story and GPU taxing graphics (although the story/lore is spread throughout the whole game, including secrets, minigames and the likes, and the purposely simplistic look is still quite aesthetically pleasing).
You don't beat the game when you're finished with story mode, it's more of an primer to the arena and challenge modes, the latter of which take the story levels for a spin and introduce new features and limitations, forcing you to change up your playstyle. The Endless aka the arena mode is just killing red guys. As many as possible. With constantly spawning reinforcements.
This game is obviously not for everybody, whether you'll enjoy the experience or not will depend on your expectations and attitude towards it, if you like games like Hotline Miami, and/or are a completionist, SUPERHOT is definitely a good pick for you. And if your satisfaction of hitting insane shots, slicing through dudes with a katana and watching the real time replays of your slow motion killing sprees barely drops after thousands of kills, you'll know you have received the signal.

Here are my taughts after playing trough 90% of the campaign and trying out a bit of multiplayer.
1. If you are a player experienced with the tabletop go buy BB1 Chaos Edition instead of this unless you prefer the better looking graphics. BB1 CE is still way superior to BB2 if you want genuine gameplay.
If you are a player new to Blood Bowl it's an awesome game however I recommend you buy this game on sale since in my opinion it's just not enough bang for your buck.
Pros - Beginner friendly, Better graphics, slightly better AI
Cons - Expensive in comparison to the content that you get. Being beginner friendly comes at the cost of many functions from the original game not being available (see below). Gameplay isn't optimized for PC but rather for console.
As a genunine fan of the tabletop and in general I very much enjoyed BB1 Chaos edition I must say that i am in general dissapointed with BB2. This game still feels like it is in beta 1 year after its release. There is no option but to have your skills forced upon you, there is no passing template from a potential possition etc.
Perhaps one thing that realy bugs me out is how much the adaptation for the console verision shines trough in the PC release, it makes the playing experience feel alot wonkier than BB1 Chaos Edition. Despite BB1 having its fair problems with bugs I still prefer that verision so far. Positives in BB2 are definelty graphics and so far I havent encountered as many bugs as there were in BB1. I'd also like to say that it's probably a lot more beginner friendly than BB1. There AI in singleplayer is also somewhat better.Maybe I just had to high expectations from this game since ive loved the game for more than 15 years. However at its current state I simply cannot recommend the game unless you buy it on sale.

I only played this game several hours ago, but it's stuck with me since then. I can't begin to explain how fantastic an experience this was. I feel that to say too much about the game will severely limit your experience going in, but unlike a lot of games that I have played this year, hell, in my lifetime, none have had quite as serious an affect on me as this one has had.
I know people have criticised the game as being pretentious, but I would urge you to set aside that attitude immediately, and trust the game's creator to deliver a story which both holds a mirror up to content creators and reviewers/critics, even (if not, especially) those with the best of intentions.
It's difficult to quite put into words without explaining it, a lot of the twist at the end heavily contradicts anything that you could put into a review, other than whether or not the game was good or bad. The deliberate ambiguity of certain aspects of the story certainly reinforces this.
What's also important is that it's perhaps the ultimate bridging of narrative and gameplay. Again, without wishing to give away too much, the game goes a long way to show that the 'walking simulator' that many people seem to look down on can still be used in new and interesting ways, to tell stories that no other medium could tell. This narrative is one that is unique to video games.
There is a lot more to this game than everything I have just said (including several moments in the game that hit, emotionally, very close to home), but I do not wish to give away too much, and would recommend that people experience it for themeslves. Please buy this game, it has completely changed the way that I assess my own work, and how I approach the work of people around me.

SPOILER, but in regards to an article from Destructroid:
There's an article from Destructroid where one of the authors praises it as its "best new IPs", but suggests you have the refund window after finishing this game as there are legitimate reasons to return it, to summarize her explanation. The author then goes on about the technicalities of the work possibly being stolen, thus the narrative being non-fiction and therefore the game's assets, etc. was profitted under someone else.
For me and unless the story is true and thus the other party has already agreed to release the assets, objects, levels, etc. for Davey to have it released as a full game, whether the agreement is on paper or from voice, then there should be no problem. In all of reality, this game is just a game. The story in the game is fake. Fake story = fiction. The Destructroid author was misinterpreted. Of course, if one party didn't agree to release a game and the other person ends up profitting over the person's work, this game would not be legit to purchase on Steam.
As for my review of this game, the story will make an eventual 180 when you will eventually expect it. There's something about the story that starts out as silly and gets darker as you get to each level. Then you realize that every level from beginning to end, there's a superficial to deep connection, from how the assets of the boxes and its placements, to the mazes of the stairs and houses, and the dialouge of the game and responder, which developes the narrator's reason for talking to you, the player.
You'll love this game if you are a fan of the Stanley Parable or see a good future in narrative-driven video games.

Cuphead is Contra. Granted, a Contra with only two proper levels per world and a half dozen nasty bosses, but it's Contra.
The 30s/40s cartoon aesthetic is on point without a hint of modern cynicism or faux-retro nonsense. It's a beautiful, charming game in every sense.
It is HARD though. Because you have infinite retries and the level select goes straight to the boss or level, the game takes the liberty to make the bosses tough, elaborate affairs. We're talking Ys levels of boss design. After world 1, you should expect to be clocking anywhere from 10-40 deaths just to get a handle on them. They're all tough, imaginative, and fun. Most of the deaths are pretty fair, though there are some pattern combos that the bosses can do that ring a little BS to me, but because death is such a small penalty, it's hard to get that mad.
Cuphead understands everything it is referencing on a fundamental level, from the classic cartoons to the classic game design, this game really is as good as it looks.

I could recommend this hardware, if it was at a steep discount, to someone looking to build a new PC and using it as a barebones kit (My situation), but I would not recommend it for its intended use.
Straight and to the point: The hardware (for the i7 model) is good, but SteamOS is (as of Nov. 29th 2016) embarrassingly unpolished, to the point that it is an aggravation at nearly every point when trying to use basic Steam functionality. There are some positives to the software, but they're buried under broken basic functionality (Web browsing, chatting, navigating your Steam library... even simply staying connected to the Internet)
This box may be a good deal if you plan to put another OS on it, but there is another version (The Alienware Alpha) which comes with Windows pre-installed, which might be a better choice for that. Reviewing precisely what came out of the box means reviewing the box as-is with SteamOS, and it just doesn't do what it says it does.
Specifics: On the upside, the box boots up quickly, and offers a very simple interface for quickly getting to your games. It works well with controllers. On the downside, you cannot sort your library (You can filter it by category, but you can't, for instance, order it by space on disk or playtime as you can on the regular Steam desktop client), the chat client has broken down on me (last message received not visible, no fix aside from reboot), I've lost Internet connectivity (Unfixable save for a reboot), and the web browser interface is both extremely awkward visually and very buggy (can't scroll using mousewheel or pageup/pagedown, sometimes can't scroll with any means whatsoever on web pages, rendering it useless)
You may notice I haven't reviewed the Debian desktop features (Resolution issues and a few minor interface/control bugs don't stop it from being basically functional), nor did I decide my review based on the available software (Or lack thereof). This is because these are basically known aspects of the device, and I have based my review on how well the device performs what it claims to perform (Allowing you to use steam and play SteamOS games). It has serious issues doing those things, and I think that anyone I recommended it to would find those issues grating and unexpected.
As far as the performance goes, it performs very well on games optimized decently for Linux, and even on some (Such as Attila) that have known Linux performance problems. In short, the hardware (Again, this is an i7 model) is quite up to the task of running games, though not every game that claims to be SteamOS compatible seems to be truly playable (Ark: Survival Evolved has very steep performance issues on Linux, and crashed frequently in my tests).
Compared to Windows or Linux, the machine is significantly less hassle to set up. Configure your controller (If you have one and wish to) and do a minute of fiddling with screen settings (If that), and input your Steam password, and that's it. You only need to put it in once, also - this isn't like a Linux box that constantly demands your password to function, nor is it similar to a Windows machine that needs constant updating and virus protection. Issues aside, it does basically 'just work', and it boots up quickly. Since it's also cheaper than the Windows version, this does give it a nice console-like niche. Compared to a console experience, I'd say it seems less polished, but I don't have a strong base of experience with modern-generation consoles to base that off of.
It is for all of these reasons I say that I could only recommend this hardware for uses beyond its original intention. When competing with a Windows or Ubuntu gaming PC, it has not only game compatibility to contend with (in Windows' case, at least), but actually has a worse interface than the regular Steam desktop client. I intend to change this review if these issues are resolved via patching in the near future.

Some games aren't made by their campaigns. This is one of them.
SUPERHOT is made by its replayability. That explains the relatively short campaign, which actually suggests such replayability.
All in all, it's a good game, and was worth my 2-3 years of wait. Not like I was "OOOOOOOOOOOOMG SUPER HOT SUPER HOT," but I was waiting.
There's still plenty to do after the campaign, with the ENDLESS Mode and the CHALLENGES, composed of several kinds with apparently 25 levels each, which gives you quite a lot of stuff to do.
Gameplay is smooth. Only two detectable bugs, as of now:
1-) Phantom walls, especially around corners of narrow obstacles;
2-) Punching will occasionally result in an instant kill, especially if you face framerate drop at the moment of the punch.
Summary:
+Gameplay is what we expected: plan ahead, dodge, disarm, kill, etc., in the best bullet-time fashion.
+Game is difficult, but fair. Expect occasional yelling.
+Simplistic, almost-monochromatic graphics and absence of musical soundtrack fit the game perfectly.
+After the campaign, gives you a series of challenges and an endless mode to keep the glass skull-cracking going.
+Makes you feel pretty badass.
+Well polished.
+There's the Hotswitch resource that really adds umph.
-Bullet collision can be somewhat disappointing, since a shotgun shell fragment can stop your 5.56mm round. Happens.
-Very tiny bugs.
-Short campaign that surely could use a continuing.
?Low variety of weapons, but what more could we ask for? A crossbow? Shuriken? Oh, if we could actually use the electric drill instead of just throwing it.
?Campaign is story-telling, not decision making.
8.5/10

A great game, the gritty and dilapidated place is an awesomely atmospheric setting and the gameplay, while simplistic, is tense, pulse pounding, and awesome.
The game is set in a Chuck E Cheese style kids restaurant. You play the night guard sat at his control desk for the monitors. Too bad the animatronics are out to get you and your only defense is the monitors, the hallway lights, and the shutter doors. Too bad again that all of that takes power of which there is a finite amount. You've got to make it through the night(s) all with a limited supply of power and a group of terrifying robot animals after you.
It does somewhat rely on jump scares, as your death results in a loud noise, so you can deduct points for that if you want. Personally, I love the game because there are moments where I'm low on power and surrounded on all fronts, I can only spare enough to shut the door for a few seconds at a time to keep them away when they're right at my door step. A single second too late on the button can mean instant death and too long before turning it off means you're at the mercy of these kill-bots down the hall.

Three years after its initially promised release date, this Kickstarted game finally came to fruition. While that sounds like development hell on paper, what did the people at Gears for Breakfast manage to make?
A very nostalgia driven adventure in the most idealist of ways. It takes many ideas present in various Nintendo games of all generations and genres, mixes and matches them, and ends up with the best of it all in one cute as heck 3D platforming adventure. Every world, every level even, is boasting with personality and charm in ways that games like Yooka Laylee failed to deliver. Every character you meet is memorable, the stunts you can pull off with its speedrunning-friendly movement will keep you hooked and wanting more, and the Paper Mario-esque writing should guarantee a damn near constant smile on your face. If you want a game that's just a love letter directly to *fun*, this is it.
Also the game runs pretty great, has an uncapped framerate, and is completely open to modding anything: the very definition of a good ♥♥♥♥ing PC game. The worst thing about it is that there's no Linux port, so here's my +1 in support.

The ride was real.
When I first purchased this game, I played a variety of teams. First, I tried humans, then orcs, and ended with dwarfs. The dwarfs were the only ones I felt comfortable with, since they all had high armor, and the block skill, which is pretty much essential in Blood Bowl. Now when I first played this, I thought the game was repetative, and that it was lacking content. For the first few months it was out, I was right. They restricted the content flow into a steady stream of DLC, and it made me feel cheated.
However, that changed after some time. After owning the game for a while, I stopped playing for a good couple of months. When i came back, I realized I had 2 more choices for teams to play with. I was surprised, to say the least, since I didn't buy these. But as it turns out, they gave this to all players who bought the game previously for free. I was very happy, they started listening to critisism, and while a few issues haven't been fixed in the game (Animations and Models for example) it is still very worth your time.
The gameplay is random. You can surely give your players skills, but once they enter the field, even your most experienced player can be obliterated in the first pitch. This is a mixed bag of goodies, resulting in unrelenting rage from your players constantly getting bad rolls, to sheer joy when you crush the opponent once and for all. It made me think no longer as a strategist (even though it stuck around) and made me think more like a high stakes gambler. "Should I rely on the Troll-Slayers Dauntless skill to activate against that Treant?" I'll often ask myself, and most of the time, I'll decide it with a coin flip if I really cannot decide. But I digress, there is a fair amount of strategy in this, and I appreciate that.
My overall opinion of the game is that it got a rocky start, and seemed a little confused, but now, I can confidently say this a game well worth your time and money if you like random fun and having dwarfs punch orcs in the groin.

The game is very good and could be feasably released as it is. I see many people comparing it to Banished - which is a fair comparison. However, in my opinion, this game has already overtaken Banished with its mechanics. Banished was released and forgotten by its developer, has no end game and no requirement to expand unless you want to go until your village collapses in on itself (though I do like the game very much and you'll probably enjoy it if you enjoy this). This game also has no end game, but it recieves updates, tweaks and there is a rapid difficulty curve with the incoming mobs that forces you to expand.
Something else I've noted in the negative reviews is that NPCs fail to pick up items on the ground - which is not true. They do not pick it up immediately, but they will do so when an NPC of the appropriate job comes along and is empty handed. NPCs also do not "cross the village" to attack mobs on a regular basis. Some wil break off from their job when nearby a mob or fight - potentially to fight or run. In general, there is no major issue with the AI, assuming you have everything needed for it to function. The most notable frustration is that when they are attack in the middle of a task they will drop their item to fight or run. Once they calm, they are confused and it's hit or miss as to whether they'll continue their job or start again. You may want to use your Godly powers to aid them.

I played the Blood Bowl board game a long time ago with my friends, and we had a lot of fun.
Because of that I later bought and played Chaos League from Cyanide and enjoyed it.
The A.I. was really bad but in multiplayer matches the game was a blast.
You could switch between RTS and TBS, and the commentators where funny and a novelty for me.
When BB2 came out, a friend besieged me to get it and play with him.
In the end he gifted me this game when it was on sale.
Before that I mostly bought and played videogames in stores or online on GOG and so I had to reactivate my steam account, which was 5 years dormant (I initally wanted to play Dark Messiah in multiplayer back then).
I downloaded steam and reluctantly had to accept the terrible eula and allow intrusive data collection to be able to play BB2 in multiplayer.
The Blood Bowl Board Game is good. Maybe be the best and most fun system GW ever brought out, and luckily they abandoned it for a time so there is a great GW-independent community which kept the board game alive and some of them played the digital blood bowl 1 and jumped on blood bowl 2 when it came out.
The BB2 videogame however is not that great.
The Sound is good and the commentators, one of the trademarks of cyanide sports games I suppose, are ok(they soon become a little repetitive). Music is pretty much forgetable on the rare occasions it comes into play.
The graphics are, compared to modern standards, mediocre at best. The 3D models in your team have variable heads but for some races not enough to avoid clones in your team. Speaking of clones, it seems the spectators in the stadium all come from the clone-factory on Kamino, ... recently I spotted some ork drummers in the audience, which could mean we arrived at two models? Yeah? Same with the
Animations are a bit clunky and there are a few glitches when models interact.
The game-menus where you manage your teams and play in leagues are just awful and counter-intuitive.
I would think, since the rules pre-existed, the developers only had to adopt those without the need to create a game concept from zero and could focus on the polish.
They failed in most part imo. The programming is worse than in all low-budget indie-games I encountered. The dynamic camera gets stuck very often in animation scenes (if you havn´t turned them off) so the game continues elswhere without you seeing what is happening. The randomization routines feel off the charts, and seem inplausible after (superfical) testing.
There is a single-player campaign, meant perhaps as a tutorial(?), which is grotesquely awful in all aspects: bad tutorial, bad storytelling, no fun.
Another negative aspect of the game: From the time of purchase you get all supsequent released races, but pre-Release they cut the playable races down to eight, to sell the single races later for 6.99€ if you don´t buy the game early (for 45€ without discounts).
The undelying game mecanics are good as is the community for the most part (both no achievements from cyanide).

Pros:
-Love the pixel art style of the game
-Tower defense aspects set it apart a bit from other Dwarf Fortress-likes, combat is an extremely core part of the game and that's not a bad thing at all.
-Totally reasonable price. I got it on sale for $5, but even the default price of $10 is reasonable. I bought this less than a week ago as of this review and I already have over 24 hours put into it. The dev is also extremely active so I'm confident in the game's future.
-Plenty of content already - a lot of resources, items, and buildings to create.
Cons:
-Slow pace. The dev has already expressed he has no plans to include a 2x/3x speed option like in games such as Banished or RimWorld, however he will be including a Haste spell to speed your workers up. From what I can tell, this spell will really only be truly useful in the very first 2 or 3 days, because after that you will want to save your mana to blow up enemy spawns. So I don't think that the Haste spell will really solve much. The dev has stated higher speeds would be unnecessary because of the pace of the game, but I find myself with tons of downtime at every stage of the game. If it is a problem of implementation, I can understand, but I see no reason why an optional 2x or 3x speed button shouldn't be added.
-Difficulty does not continue to scale. Now that I've done a few runs and I have a strategy for early-mid game, I'm completely ironclad and unstoppable by around day 11. More enemies will probably need to be added (remember you can always do resizes/recolors of existing sprites, nobody gets too upset about that as long as it's not rampant) that can add to more of a late game challenge.
-Defense is pretty easy. All you need to do is make a large perimeter for your base and include a single choke point. Because of the enemy AI, they will walk across the entire map just to get to that choke point. I would recommend adding a certain distance threshold for enemies so that if they have to walk a certain distance to get around a wall, they will instead attack the nearest wall. This will force players to maintain multiple points of defense instead of one easily defended chokepoint.
Misc suggestions:
Quarries like in Banished - on rock floor areas, maybe you could add a building that allows villagers to mine a set amount of rock and iron from a 10x10 spot or however large you'd deem it. My reasoning for this is that I often run out of stone toward the end of the second year, and this would add another way of getting some. It's basically like they're hollowing out that part of the ground.
Diagonal roads - just make it so that when roads are connected to another road by only the corner you use a particular diagonal-road sprite. This is for both aesthetic reasons and because diagonal roads are obviously useful given by their automatic creation by the NPCs' pathing.
Alternative food sources - domesticated animals, fish.
Towers that induce status effects (slow, bleed, decrease armor, etc)

Spiders, Nightmares and Confusion
A Review of Limbo
Limbo is a rare gem of a 2D puzzle game. One of those games you can pick up on a lazy, boring Sunday afternoon and get lost in. It has a lightweight story to go with the puzzles, but don't let that put you off if you're not looking to commit to a story in the next game you play. Not paying attention to it won't take anything away from the game, mostly because you'll be wondering how the ♥♥♥♥ to kill that spider.
£6.99 may seem a little pricey for a game which can be completed in a short amount of time if you put your mind to it, but then again it's also a timeless classic of game that you can return to many times and still be surprised by. I don't know if it's the dark, misty landscape of the world, or the inevitable and somewhat distracting gory deaths (don't take the term gory death lightly), but every time I've revisited this game, I always find I've forgotten how to solve the more complex of the puzzles, a valuable characteristic for a game, as it lures you add yet more chunks of your day to the total game play time.
The game's controls are very simple, arrow keys to move around; with the up key allowing you to jump and grab on to chains, or climb up the sides of crates. Crates play quite a vital part in solving puzzles and can be dragged around by holding control when next to them, but be warned, they are just as susceptible to large, spinning blades as your characters limbs are.
Overall a brilliant game. I'm sure if you dug around for long enough you could find a problem with it, or an aspect which you don't like, but they most certainly aren't obvious which is enough reason for me not to go looking for things which would ruin an otherwise fantastic game. If £6.99 sounds like too much for you, give the steam demo a shot and see if you change your mind, and, well, if that doesn't help, maybe pick it up in the steam sales.

I'm a big fan of Fallen London, Failbetter's previous browser-based game - which is still very much alive and you should check it out.
For me it comes down to game mechanics.
Fallen London is a browser game that ekes out it's literary rewards using a scarce resource: "actions". The idea is that most players will use up their actions then go and get on with their lives until more have regenerated. Captivated players will pay for "Nex" to buy a bigger pool of "actions", and also to play certain special storylines. In this context it makes perfect sense to string the experience out, because they want to hit that balance where they provide just enough entertainment to keep casual players engaged, but with enough held back so that rabid players will be prepared to pay for more.
The regenerating "action" mechanic allows Failbetter to "ration" the game.
Now, Sunless sea shares the Fallen London mythology, and also shares the story based gameplay. However, instead of rationing "actions", now your access to the story elements is rationed by "distance". In Fallen London you just click on TRAVEL to move from one area to another. In Sunless Sea you have to move your ship, possibly encountering giant sea creatures or pirate ships, which you then engage in, frankly terrible, combat or ideally avoid.
Whereas Fallen London has downtime where you go and do something else, Sunless Sea has downtime between stories, where you still have to remain engaged with the game. If you enjoy the combat, that's a bonus, but if, like me, you find the combat dull, then you're out of luck because no matter how good the story writing is, getting to it won't be worth it.
I'm not some longtime Fallen London player who is upset about an arcade upstart. I literally only registered for Fallen London because it was going to give me bonus stories in my newly purchased Sunless Sea, which I was really excited to get playing after reading the reviews. A month later I've spent twice what Sunless Sea cost me, in Nex to play Fallen London and I don't regret a penny of it.
Here's the thing, reading the forums it's clear there are fundamentally two kinds of Sunless Sea players who are enjoying the game, with some overlap between them. There are the people who love the mythos and endure the meta game to get at it, and there are those who are maximising the amount of Echoes they earn, and reducing the game to a spreadsheet to get them. I just can't fall into either camp, so I'm calling it a day.
In context, I'm a  longtime Nethack, general roguelike and Dwarf Fortress player - the death mechanics don't bother me, the glacial grind at the start of the game does. I appreciate that Sunless Sea isn't a roguelike or even a roguelite, and they shouldn't advertise it as one, but a little diversity in the start wouldn't hurt.
The user interface also has some issues, and the lack of a minimap is baffling, forcing you to constantly switch back and forth from map to play area - highly disengaging.
