My friends on steam know that I have to completely love a game, or absolutely hate it, to bother with a review. Unfortunately that surprise is ruined by the thumbs up spoiler they put on these reviews. All I can do to make up for that spoiler, is tell you what you will be getting yourself into with this title. Bear in mind, this game is a trilogy and I have only played this installment (What can I say, I love Chaos on Warhammer, and the succubus looks like that girl all of us took home after drinking a case of beer, but you wake up next to the orc, so.....)
What is it?
Age of Fear two is an rpg/war strategy hybrid with some micromanagement (of your forces) and turn based gameplay. There are two complete stories with each installment, and each story is long enough to be its own game. There are multiple paths, quite a few secrets, 100s of units and items just as the description says, and every one of them is useful, as are all of the units. There is no filler here, as everything has a purpose and a time when it can be invaluable to you. Right away the game assumes you have experience in the genre, and as such it gets you going with some challenging battles early on, although it does give you a tutorial on how to play in the first couple of missions. There are countless skills to master, and some of your units can actually evolve into elite classes (Fire Emblem/Shining Force fans will be pleased with this feature, as its very well done, I just wish ALL units had an evolution tree, but hey, a good number of them do, so...) Units carry over from battle to battle, and you can select how they grow, from buying stat upgrades for them, to buying skills and spells, no two units are alike. The game uses a rng dice system, based on D6 so it isnt as frustrating as alot of games which use a rng. By keeping the numbers low, it actually FEELS like pen and paper combat that, lets face it, started the genre and is a system that few developers successfully pull off. But THIS game did, with a gold star! The AI is also VERY capable. In over 40 hrs of playing, I had YET to see the AI do something stupid, instead they will advance on you slowing guard each others flanks, rush in to save a comrade, this developer isnt lying when he claimed his AI was excellent in his description!
Youll move through the story, mission by mission on a world map, with some non combat related surprises along the way as well that can also benefit you. There are optional battles, and battles that progress the story. I am kind of hoping re-doable skirmish battles are added at some point as well, which would REALLY up the replay value for us grinders, but its a solid game nonetheless. Other then your hero units, your units need to be careful of permenant injuries and perma death, which always adds a bit of tension, especially when some units that you get in some situations are NOT replacable, so if that awesome, 6 headed hydra you got for making a certain choice at a certain time dies, your S.O.L. until the next playthrough. But as long as you use care, such special units dont go down with ease. Units are also limited (they dont cost gold, but items do) unless your playing on easy, so use them wisely. How many you can field, depends on Hero upgrades. You can have 30 in your roster, and so far I have been able to put 15 on the field (I'll be honest that I have only reached about the middle of the campaign so I dont know if thats the limit or not). I LOVE that this developer has faith that his fans are not to stupid to handle a large roster like this. Most games cap you out at 6 to 10 units, and that always disapointed me. The best games, like Fire Emblem, or my favorite classic Dark Wizard, give you large rosters, and I must say this game really has the vibe of the later 2 in gameplay. You can even choose to stay on the field when a battle ends, to search out any secrets, so you dont have to risk your units doing it during the fight. Another GREAT feature, to be sure!
The story is tongue in cheek with a serious undertone. There are some great story moments, some moments that made me laugh my♥♥♥♥♥off due to top quality humor, but there are a couple of cringyworthy moments as well. I read the whole story for both campaigns in the mod files, and I would say its a solid B+ for fantasy fans, maybe a tad higher. The anti-hero in the picture, the succubus Bel Kara, kind of grows on you quickly, with her smug "I can do whatever the hell I want" attitude, and her genuinely ♥♥♥♥♥♥ aproach to everything, she is a very well done protagonist for the Chaos path, and I hope to see more of her in other stories. All of the characters from all instalments cross paths at different times as well. Im starting to think there is a larger, connected plot to it all, but im not sure yet. As for the music, its a perfect fit. From the inspired war drums, to classic rpg scores, the music never falls short on setting the right atmosphere for every situation.
There is only a couple of weak points I can see, and they are by no means game killers. One, I already mentioned, is the need for either a new game plus feature, or redoable skirmish battles. We players who are into this genre are usually grinders and completists as well, and if they were to add those, it would litterally double replayability. The other would be the graphics. This series is NOT made out of the same eye candy that the sucubus is. Its a top down, 2D view, and it works for what it is. So if your the type of gamer I am, you will not mind these graphics at all, in fact by the second or third battle, I actually didnt mind AT ALL. But if your looking for modern, ground breaking graphics, this aint it. As for the voice acting, its decent enough (It would have been MUCH better if a female and others spoke the parts in the narrative for the characters, but is otherwise good to acceptable.
Overall
I HIGHLY recommend this title to fans turn based srpg/fantasy hybrids. The developer of this game is constantly upgrading it, and when he does, I was told he upgrades the whole series. Once you see the vast number of units, Items, upgrades, maps, and other surprises I wont spoil here (if you wanna know, buy it!) You will know what I knew a few hours in. That this was a labour of love, and created at a standard I really wish more indy games would thrive for. Ive seen people BEGGING in online forums for a game like this, and at least now, I can respond with "Age of Fear is a Masterpiece well worth a look!"

People weren't kidding, this game is awful. It's basically a hack and slash game without anything that makes that genre good. There's no loot, except small amounts of gold. You use that gold to upgrade the few abilities you get every like 5 levels, which is about every 10 actual stages. Most of the abilities are the same anyways, like when 2 out of 3 abilities i unlocked were just AOE abilities. When you upgrade abilities it just ads a little damage or some other stat. There's no skill trees or character progression. On levels you fight the same 3-4 enemy types throughout the whole game, and all you do is spam attack, or sheld bash then attack. That's it. Levels are fairly long but since you do the exact same thing it gets super boring. There's some aspect with spirits but its never explained and I found no way to use it during the game. Mouse and keyboard are terrible and you're forced you use controller, for a franchise that was originally PC ONLY. Nobody is playing as well, meaning playing this in a group, which would be better slightly is improbable. There's no single player, meaning hilariously you can't even pause the RPG game you're playing. The terrible game design came to a head on one of the side chapters. In combat its really hard to see with the 20 enemies your fighting while you spam attack, if you're getting hurt, and dodging is impossible besides the most obvious attacks. Many enemies that aren't trash mobs have way too much health, but can somehow take 1/3 of yours in 1 hit. You get 2 potions per level, can never upgrade the amount you get, and can't refill them at all during the level. On this level, which was about 20 repetitive minutes, I fought about 5 mini bosses, as well as these terribly designed towers that have too much health and suddenly rain down arrows on you without any warning every 3 seconds and die 1/2 your health. Needless to say I used my potions.
I finally made it to the boss, who is one of the worst designed boss fights ive ever seen. He has 3 attacks, but does them completely randomly, and without any tell or warning. The best part is 1 is completely unfair, and it invovles him sending metal all over the map in a spiral pattern, which if you get hit with any part of it it doesn about 1/3-1/2 your health. So if you are standing next to him you are screwed. The other terrible problem is there is no down time where you can hurt the boss where he doesn't do abilities, nor is there any way to stun him to deal damage. You can't stay away from him to avoid his super attack bc there's no ranged attacking in this game. So this means running in, hitting him a few times, and hoping it's his other 2 attacks. He also has a ridiculously high amount of health, meaning after 5 min of this he was only at half health, and he could do 1/2 my health at any time with 1 hit of his attack. Add this to the fact I have no potions, and theres curiously almost no health in his arena. Finally I died and had to restart the fight from the start. After abou 6-7 times of this I saw it really wasn't my fault and it's jsut another terrible aspect of the game by the devs. Reading online apparently you need to play more and level your character, even though I was the "recommended level" the game listed for the level. Also you cannot change difficulty during the level. I decided I didn't wanna level up more, then play the boring 20 minutes before him on this level just to fight him again, just because the devs don't know how to make a game. So I bought this game over a year ago, played it for a little while and tried to return it in frustration. (I was unable to do so, due to the exceptionally long game times.) So now a year later, the bug to play again has bit me and I've given it a try.
The interface is still shoddy, glitching at times to select a command other then what you wish (IE. Stand-Up instead of Blitz when your player is on the ground). Icons on the screen bug out and repeat across the screen making it a jumbled mess at times. Finally, unless you customize skill use system, the game becomes just a bunch of random dice.
Speaking of dice, lets talk about the RNG of the game. It's utter♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ I have spent, five turns with re-rolls (10 attempts) trying to pick up a ball on a 3+ chance (that's 67% in game terms). I own the board game, this NEVER happens in the board game. Why? Because real dice don't do this. The probability of this happening is so minute that in 25 years of owning the board game I've never seen it happen.
But if Cyanide's RNG is to be believed, it happens every game. But only to players. In a player vs player game this happens often, but vs. an AI... Well the AI never suffers such horrendous dice rolling and always gets what it needs. This is called "Artificial Inflation of Difficulty." Bad programmers do this rather than find a way to increase the AI's ability to play. It's a short cut used since the days of the Nintendo Entertainment System and Atari. It was used back in those days due to the size constraints on program files being what they were. You couldn't program something that complex because you on had a few MegaBytes or so to fill. This game is over a thousand times larger and more complex. Why resort to such shoddy programming?
In the end, if you want to play Blood Bowl, buy the boardgame if you can find it. Or by the original video game, the RNG is still bad but at least you won't feel like you were cheated out of $45-60 for the game plus DLC costs.

When I first bought Banished and started playing I was immediately hooked.  A game that seems so simplistic is actually quite challenging.
While Banished won't win any awards for graphics they are adequate.  The animations of the citizen models and animals are quite good.  I have not seen the game slow down at all, even with a large map full of buildings and crops the game runs well.
The gameplay can be as challenging as you want, feeling brave?  Do a harsh mountain environment with natural disasters.  First game?  Then maybe go easy, turn disasters off and start with a couple houses.  The choice is yours.  The game is easy to jump into and start playing but complex enough that you do have to think and plan ahead.  Like most "City Building" games this one has you managing resources, some renewable and some not.  For the non-renewable resource the game allows a trader to visit your town so that you can buy some supplies.
The replay value of this game cannot be underestimated.  With over 100 hours in this game for far I am still just as hooked as I was after 1 hour.  The replay value is awesome.
Very few crashes, once in awhile a citizen will get "stuck" between buildings and starve.  Other than that I have not ran into any bugs with the game.
Active mod community and steam workshop.  Mods that are out right now are great.
Overall 9/10.  Would recommend to other Steam users.

So after 20 hours and two deaths in this game, I managed to save up enough money to buy a new ship.
I feel that that sentence alone is sufficient as a review, but let's continue.
Sunless Sea is nothing if not a slow boil.
There are a multitude of dangers in the weird, Lovecraftian world that you sail around, but you learn pretty fast that the best way to survive them is to simply turn your ship around and run away from them. Eventually, as you explore the 'Zee', you'll discover that there are certain safe routes between the islands and you can start charting milk runs that will run you through 12+ ports, gathering smatterings of resources here and there until you get home and add another little pile to your fortune.
Each of the ports your ship checks in at  has its own little stories, adventures and chance encounters. The writing in the game, while somewhat overwrought at times, is solid and while there is a constant temptation to just skim things and hit 'continue', I usually didn't do that.
But the problem is that so much of the game is locked behind obscure requirements that are quite literally impossible to figure out without a trip to the game's wiki. I spent an absolutely horrific amount of resources trying to finish my gunner's side mission. The last step is to go to a place called Station III and talk to a guy working there, but Station III is locked and will remain locked until I bring some kind of copper box to them. Where do I get this box? I don't know! And I have no way of finding this out besides Google.
On another occasion, I found a shipwreck that I could explore by bringing special 'Foxfire candles' inside. My next trip to London, I bought some of those and went to the ship and found... nothing (the candles were still used). Confused, I gave up and looked up the wreck on the wiki and found out that it's apparently impossible to find anything inside there until you trigger a quest in another town.
So it's weird, convulted and a fair chunk of it is sailing through empty seas avoiding fights. I'm thus tempted to give this a 'No' recommendation, but I suppose the writing is strong enough to tip it over the edge.
Still, consider this about the most lukewarm recommendation a game could ever receive.

Lots of mixed reviews for this game.
I played the original table top game back in the 90's (2 different versions of it). I'd say it's pretty damn faithful to it in the fact that now matter how well you plan you're going to end up rolling a 1, another 1, a 10 and a 12 and your favourite player is going to die horribly.
The dice rolls aren't off, dice are dice and nuffle hates you.
Sure there's a lot of races missing and there's a lot that could be done regarding customization but that's all fluff that players of the older pc version are used to.
I actually got the first version after getting this one and found it clunky and horrible regardless of the extra features.
At the time of this review I've got about 290 hours in the game, only played 3 races + the campaign/tutorial and not played MP yet. I've more than had my money's worth even with buying all the dlc.
People don't understand that creating a new team requires all new models (for the most part), animations, programming and sound and not something the team working on the game can knock up in an afternoon and give away for free. I'm not a fan of paid for dlc but in this case it does have value and is worth the price. Just because you've been used to playing with 27 (guess) teams on the previous game, table top or fumbblr you have to realise that in a new engine it's not cheap.
All that aside it's not without it's issues. The AI is a bit clunky at times. I've never been fouled by the AI and they've never used the quick snap event. The UI is better after the last update but still a bit icky at times. A few rules are a bit silly (bank stuff and stadiums).
All in all though it's a good faithful adaption of blood bowl albeit with a few changes. If pressed I'd give it 8/10 and hope more people discover it, buy the dlcs and we end up with more teams :)

It is quite something that, while I think it is one of the most original and interesting game releases around, I have to recommend against it.
Sunless Sea, as a story to be unraveled and explored, it is fantastic. It packs a great amount of literary content (and I do mean by "literary" given how many words this has), solid worldbuilding and the constant feeling of "there is much more in the background", thanks to how the lore is revealed to you: snippets, fragments and bits that by themselves may seem quirky, odd or totally alien, but as you go around and learn, a bigger picture starts to form. Exploring the mysteries of the Neath and the Unterzee while avoiding whatever unknown terror of the depths, the dread of hunger, the lack of critical fuel or even the very wrath of strange gods is
, to say the least.
If only this was an interactive fiction, though.
Sunless Sea, however, is a game. While story and ambience are clearly paramount in this, the "game" part is, well, not good enough. Since you need to engage with the game in order to explore the story, it suffers due to bad gameplay: once the novelty is gone, you will be instinctively drawn to keep your beaten old steamer around the familiar routes of Fallen London and try to grind some measure of resources to make sure you can survive your next journeys. Sunless Sea makes very clear, from the beginning, that it wants you to take chances and explore - but when you have lost a few captains and you are generally aware of how things work, you realize how woefully lacking is the earliest part of the game and how much of a slog it is to make a modicum of improvement.
(This doesn't get any better even after that.)
Which brings to the problem. The game's economy is focused on the three critical resources: hunger, fuel and terror. Managing all three may seem like a juggler's act, but a few tries here and there will give you the hang of things. Echoes, the currency proper, is the solution to the balancing act. You can afford a better engine, which makes journeys faster; better weapons, which makes you able to fight whatever the zee throws at you; a better ship, which makes everything more useful. Because of that, players quickly realize that they need cash early on to overcome the slog.
And, of course, you start to grind. Because you are grinding, you are not exploring. Because you are not exploring, the game loses its charm and effect FAST. But you need to cash in order to explore without being an awful drag. Of course, given how things work and the very orientation Failbetter wants for Sunless Sea, they quickly took care of the means to make money that were seen as "gamey" (see "The Sunlight Trade" if you are curious).
Sunless Sea is very original and has a lot of entertaining stuff, packed to the brim with lore of their setting (which comes from Fallen London) and the siren's call of a big, unknown Unterzee beckons and dares you to explore all of it. However, the sluggish, dragging-by-its-feet gameplay, an extremely repetitive early game (again: once the novelty wears off) that quickly becomes plain boring and a lack of alternative means to allow its players to just
means that is not for everyone.

Possibly one of the worst games I've played.
The story tried to be complex or deep but failed. It's cliche with twists I spotted a mile away. I started counting the tropes. The only thing that was remotely interesting was finding out the origin of the protagonist. Otherwise, narration is redundant information through ♥♥♥♥♥♥ radio monologues.
The gameplay is awful. Gunplay is atrocious, poorly-planned, and frustrating. I understand ammo management is an element of the thriller genre, but dealing with it across 8-9 weapons with three ammo types each causes fights to devolve into scrolling through weapons for a bullet to load and fire. This is simply poor game design. The enemies you fight are extremely homogenous. They all jump around, tank bullets, and succumb to the same repetition of plasmids/wrenching. Sometimes they have guns that they mag-dump into a wall you're behind. Of course they're only carrying one bullet when you kill them. They spawn in non-sense locations just to make it seem like you never have a break, which ruins the immersion.
Player customization is also subpar - the abilities you earn through Adam are underpowered and unappealling. I stopped caring about customization when I realized it had no affect on my experience whatsoever. The role-playing game elements failed: there were no roles to be had - no investment in a playstyle - leaving the game an FPS with the usual two or three engagement tactics.
The missions are almost all fetch quests - the most uninspired task you could assign a FPSRPG player. Only you have the willpower to walk all over town picking up junk for rewardless progression. Also prominent are "enemies flooding the room" defense tasks and the occasional escort mission. The landmark missions staked in this mire are best described as "flip this switch / push this buttion to hear more story".
The only thing this game has going for it is it's atmosphere. No, not even it's horrid map design, just the atmosphere of the environment.

As of the writing of this review, the story mode has not been released and this is completely based on the sandbox game play.
If I were to sum up this game in a single word, it would be "unforgiving".  Playing the game in anything but pilgrim mode (Which is designed to give you a free tour of the areas I feel.) you are pretty much consigning yourself to death.  You WILL die.  Just how and how soon are the questions.  How will death come for you?  Will she visit as you search for supplys in the form of a wolf in the woods?  Likely.  Will you be caught out at night and freeze to death because you lost track of time? Will the cold mistress come when you are just meters away from shelter in a freezing blizzard?  How soon will death come?  Will she greet you on your first day?  Or after several months when you decide to take on the charging wolf with a knife in the effort to save your last precious rifle bullet?  But rest assured, she has not forgotten you... for she rests on your every decision and is your sole companion.  For death likes to play a game of touch and go.... she touches you... and you go.
If you like survival games but are into a more realistic plot? Then this is a good game to consiter.  No zombies here. Tired of dealing with griefers?  Welcome home...  here, you are alone.... well, except death... she likes to follow you around and see what you do next... btw, she likes wolves. Want a challenge?  WHEN you die in game, so does your charater's save.  When you are on your back with a wolf in your face, and you are stabbing it with your knife, you are fighting for your charater's life.  If you emerge the victor, it will be short lived if you can't stop your bleeding.  But when you make it through one more day... there is a feeling of satisfaction that you wont get if failure only ment reloading a save file.  This game is about making smart choices, having a plan for when things go horribly wrong, and being equiped/prepaired in an unforgiving wilderness.
The game is based on a geomagnetic event.  Which is when the magnetic poles switch.  The last time this has happened predates recorded history, so the possible effects are unknown.  But there is more than one way to make the lights go out.  Look up the Carrington event (aka Solar storm of 1859) for such an example.

A real survival simulator...
i'm normally not one for the survival/crafting genre, but the long dark has got me hooked. while other survival sandbox games have you romping where you please, collecting what you will at a leisurely pace so you can craft whatever you like, The Long Dark  has you seriously considering nearly every choice you make. should i spend the few resources i have to make a fire that'll only last an hour so i can boil some drinking water or do i craft hunting supplies and risk trekking through a whiteout? granted, its still in early access,only offers sandbox mode and some mechanics are a little unbalanced, but it's still worth the asking price in my opinion. i can't think of any other game where hearing my character say," looks like i made it another day" is actually rewarding to hear. i wouldn't say TLD is an especially challenging experience,but it can seem a little aggravating to an impatient player,especially early on.its one of those games where its as hard as you make it,but once you've got a handle on things,its a fun challenge to go on for as long as you can. There is no tutorial,so i'd advise checking out the button mapping before playing.there's no map,so you'd better take mental pictures and memorize landmarks. there's very few weapons and even fewer forms of ammunition,but most enemies can be avoided or scared off. TLD is expecting you to do the one thing that would actually keep you alive out in the wilderness: Thinking.
it's been along time since i've played a game that actually brings on tension like TLD. if you've played the first resident evil,you'll remember the safe feeling you got whenever you just barely made it to a save room. the same edge can be felt here,but its not because your being chased by zombies and your low on herbs...it's because you just got a fresh rabbit to complete your mittens after so many failed snaring attempts, but on the way back to home base you sprain your ankle and and you've only got one hour of daylight left."its okay,i'll be fine" you say to yourself,"i'm almost home,almost safe" you'll think. the storm is getting stronger,your socks are almost in shreds, and you're out of potable water to immerse you sandpaper tongue,but it'll be all good when you get indoors...and then you hear it...the pack,and they're not far off. getting home alive actually feels like ...winning,for lack of a better word.but the reprieve is soon lost as you realize you'll have to go right back out there if you wanna live long enough to enjoy those rabbit fur mittens you almost died for. these are the kinda experiences you don't find too common in modern games; in-game circumstances founded by your every action will determine whether you live for two days or two hundred.
I can't wait to see where the game goes after further development,because as it stands now,i personally love getting lost in The Long Dark.

The following is copied from my review on
and is for an as yet unreleased early access title
[Disclosure: Game copy supplied by Developer]
The Long Dark is published/developed by Hinterland Games, this is hinterlands very first title. The Long Dark is an exploration focused survivor simulation game, set after a geomagnetic disaster. This means all of humanity’s technological might is removed. It is quite literally you versus nature - flora and fauna.
The Long Dark is set in a Canadian Rocky-esque environment, the story when it’s completed will focus around your character who crash landed his aircraft after the geomagnetic disaster. You will have limited food and clothing and the “goal” is to survive as long as possible. It’s cold, you don’t know where you are or where to go. What you do know is if you don’t find shelter and supplies soon you will die.

As you venture out into the great unknown the stark reality of your situation really hits home, it’s nothing but trees and snow, the isolation is near crippling the only way you’re going to see another human face again or make it back home as if you find a way to survive. First things first you’ve got to survive until tomorrow, the only way that’s going to happen is if you find food, water and shelter. As you scavenge for supplies the rich bounty of nature begins to unfold, you see rabbits and soon some deer, you stop a while to admire the beauty of nature cast against the serene yet deadly Alpine backdrop. Suddenly a fast dark creature appears and attacks the deer that you have been watching, you realise that it’s a wolf, you slowly back away and disappear while it devours its prey. You now have a new challenge you must defend yourself against the predators of the wild. It’s getting dark the wolves are close, the danger of their howling the second only to the howling of the wind. If you can find some shelter and light a fire perhaps that will keep both at bay. You reach an empty cave and light a fire, you can no longer hear the wolves you’re safe for now. As you rest beside the warm glow as you fall asleep you wonder “how long will I survive before I enter The Long Dark”

The sheer scale of survival is accented by the gameplay you have limited resources you must manage to survive. The biggest factor is time you spend time for example collecting wood for a fire, hunting for food or boiling down snow for water. Whilst I found certain aspects of the gameplay difficult those wanting a challenging survival will enjoy this very much. If that’s not quite what you’re into simply set it to “pilgrim” (easy) mode. For the ultimate survival “Bear Grills” experience you can of course select “stalker” (hard/realistic) mode.
Mechanically the game is very robust and solid the Unity engine works really well for these kinds of games. The only issues I found were likely to have been rather subjective, for example forging for 30 minutes to retrieve a single piece of wood using the “forge wood” option. However I will be submitting a few suggestions to the developer. The animal AI reacts extremely well the deer and rabbits will run if they see you, the wolves will correctly track and hunt and the bears are likely to be the equivalent of the behemoths that they are in real life.

Graphically as indicated the game is simply stunning. The whole game feels like a water colour painting with rich beautiful sunsets/sunrises, weather mechanics/physics where you can see both your and animal tracks in the fresh snow which is an excellent addition. The iced environment limits the amount of water seen, however the waterfalls are suitably beautiful. The soundtrack is subtle but impactful and adds to the isolationist atmosphere. The sound assets for items for example tin cans sound exactly as you would expect.

Overall this game whilst difficult was a big surprise I thoroughly enjoyed the time I spent and is another game I am excited to see finished as I mentioned there are a few things I would like changed or tweaked however I am fully aware this is in alpha release, and may of course be subjective. Playing this game you will understand the following phrase “it’s cold, dark and there are wolves after me”
Final score 9/10

In a nutshell:
Visuals:              Stunning and smooth.
Audio:                Crisp and delightful.
World:                OMG.
Gameplay:         Simple mechanics that can turn an accountant into an adrenaline junkie.

My thoughts:
I've never had so much fun being completely rubbish at a game. For me, the game is hard but every death is my own fault rather than the game being unfair or glitchy. The repetitive nature of the gameplay works for this title, helped by the stunning, thematic visuals and toe-tappingly, wonderful audio.
The whole early day's of cartoons has been captured beautifully by the developers, all the quirks of the day melded into an addictive, one-more-time, game with fun characters and mechanics. It's a game that I can pick up and play for 10 minutes and walk away satisfied. But it's also a game that I could easily spend hours in front of if I'm not careful.

Final recommendation:
If you like fun, I believe that you will find it with Cuphead.

Bioshock is my favourite FPS game. I wanted to play it to do a 3rd walkthrough just recently, but for some reason I could not make it run on Windows 7. I know there are some bug fixes, tweaks out there, but eventually, I decided not to bother with them. Initially, I played this back on XP and also on Vista as some of the effects required DX 10.
What makes Bioshock a unique FPS game is its atmosphere. The protagonist finds himself in an underwater city called Rapture after an airplane crash which was meant to be a sanctuary, a safe haven from the atrocities of the world by its creator, but right at the beginning you quickly realise something went awry as almost all the inhabitants of this marvelous city want to kill you. And also each other.
These residents are all obsessed with ADAM, a substance found deep under water. Or more like a substance that was extracted from slugs found in the dark, cold abyss. This substance grants its user superhuman powers, powers that are just like magic: you can set things on fire, you can grab and throw objects at your enemies, you can control machines etc. Clearly, humanity's greed got the better of it, again, as it seems everybody is set out to grab more and more ADAM to seize power. And what are those huge fellows called Bid Daddies who wonder around in thick armor escorting (protecting) little children (girls) who are characterised by two things: they have a huge syringe in their hands and their eyes are glowing.
The game offers you conventional weapons found in any other FPS games but makes it more interesting as you have various types of bullets available at your disposal. And while you hold your weapons in your right hand at the same time you can cast your spells with your left hand. You can also hack things so that you can purchase items at vending machines with discount and in case you hack turrets or sentry bots you can quickly get some allies. In order to use your Plasmids (spells) you are required to get some EVE (similar to mana in many RPGs). It is inevitable  to fight Rapture's monstrous creatures called Big Daddies to get some ADAM with which you can purchase new Plasmids (or the better version of the one you already have).
It's worth checking every room, every corner in Rapture as you can find some hidden treasures. Notable are the audio logs that expand upon the background story and you can get to know the main characters of the city better and also understand what their agenda is. The game has morality choices, too: although you fight Big Daddies the very reason you want to defeat them is to get close to the little girls they protect. You extract ADAM directly from them and you can decide whether or not you want to let them live. This means you can have two endings at the game.
The game has a superb art design and lovely music. Its atmosphere can be creepy, scary at times and exploring Rapture is a fun experience between fierce battles. This is highly recommended to anybody out there who loves the FPS genre; bear in mind, though, that the game has issues with Windows 7 so it's best to look for the solution beforehand.

It only takes about 20 minutes of gameplay to realise this game isnt quite Call of Duty. The game is dark and gloomy,the music is sad. In Call of Duty or Battlefield you feel happy after getting a kill. Your enemy falls to the ground mybe making a grunt or scream. In Red Orchestra/Rising Storm (RO/RS) is different. Let's set up a little scenario. You're playing as a rifleman on the German side. You just ran across the open and now you're tired,you've entered a house to take cover and catch your breath when you hear some footsteps. A quick look at the map confirms there are no allies around,so you step into a corner and zoom in on the entrance nearest to the sound. You crouch down and hear the footsteps get closer. finally,you see the tip of a Mosin-Nagant. You're ready. The Russian fully enters the room and turns towards you. You fire. The bullet hits the Russian in his stomach,the shot is fatal,but he is not dead. He is bleeding out. The injury is too much for him to bandage himself,and all he can see is his screen fading to black. He panics and shoots. You have already clicked a second time to bolt your rifle,you
finish him off,but decide to save the extra round,and perhaps not risk being heard for sure. The Russian fires another round. He is bent forwards,his character clutching his stomach. It's rather quiet and you can hear the Russian calling for his mother before falling onto the ground,a blood pool forms around him. You reload your rifle,crouch down and get ready to exit the door he came through. You slowly peek out,check left and right before making a couple more steps into the open. You think it's all clea- *ping* You've just been shot in the head by an enemy you couldn't see. this isnt CoD or Battlefield,there are no killcams or special views showing your killer. This will happen a lot. Have fun.

The Beginner's Guide starts as a story, narrated by the game creator Davey Wreden himself, about the games created by a fellow developer named Coda: this narrative slowly turns into an heartfelt tale about game development, society, dreams, creativity and what ultimately makes us who we are.
What follows is a walking simulator that, thanks to a strong narrative and surreal level design, will easily capture your attention with its nice visuals while challenging you to reflect on the story you're listening to.
-great art and gorgeous, surreal level design
-extremely nice minimalistic soundtrack
-great narrative backed by an excellent use of symbols and metaphors
-I personally found it quite emotionally engaging, even downright moving at times
-lots of food for thought
-the value of the game is all in its message and narrative, if you don't care about them there's no gameplay to be found and the gorgeous vistas won't simply be enough
-the narrative can sometimes feel a bit too direct or pretentious
-quite short at 1,5 hours
The Beginner's Guide was a truly emotional journey for me, what started as an interesting voyage inside a developer's mind slowly turned into a reflection over the creative process, over how being recognized and connecting with others can help or hinder our identity, over how willingness can at times be a dry spring and a multitude other things.
Levels vary from interesting to awe-inspiring and the muted soundtrack helps create a truly surreal experience, one that helps making you feel as if you're traveling through not only someone's work but also their mind.
The true strength of The Beginner's Guide is not the fact that it feels like a metaphor in motion, nor how well its story describes Wreden's train of thought though, but how said story and thoughts can be sometimes be a mirror in which we see ourselves.
I consider The Beginner's Guide an essential purchase to be honest, but I can also easily see how this is a very divisive game: if you are ok with walking simulators, want a great, surreal narrative and desire food for thought then I urge you to experience it. And if you are in any way an artist and/ or familiar with the creative process I feel you'd absolutely experience this story as it'll surely touch you and make you think about what you do.

I've only played a few turn-based strategy games (though I intend to play a lot more), but Age of Fear felt different from those I have tried – in a good way. The tabletop-style maps are not fundamentally all that different from the grid-based battlefields of Fire Emblem and XCOM, but I personally got a warm fuzzy sensation from painstakingly positioning my troops where I thought they would be most effective – plus, the lack of a clearly-defined grid makes human error a more distinct possibility, as there were times when an enemy was able to charge through a gap in my formation that I'd thought I'd sealed up. The fact that each movement can only be conducted in a straight line also forces the player to plan ahead, lest reinforcements end up trapped behind the allies they are trying to save.
In my experience, most battles will be decided by a massed melee at some point or other, but the various factions have their differences. The Orcs have tough infantry and monsters that suit a no-nonsense play-style, whilst the Demons have a suitably chaotic array of troops, from imps and spiders to berserk barbarians and lightning-spitting cannons; as for the unplayable (in single-player mode, at least) factions, the Humans have skilled archers, swordsmen and knights, and the Undead have a plethora of supernatural units combined with the ability to raise more cannon-fodder from their deceased enemies. In the aftermath, the player is taken to a menu where they can recruit new troops, teach veterans new skills, equip or sell items that have been found or stolen in battle, and purchase other pieces of equipment. The capacity to customise your main heroes is quite extensive, and even your lowlier soldiers can carry a couple of potions, allowing for a wider range of tactical possibilities than I'd originally expected to find.
The visuals are simple but effective; different units are easily recognisable, and although the animations are pretty basic they get the job done. The tabletop-gaming aesthetic serves a useful function, too: in, say, an Orc-versus-Orc battle, your troops will have different coloured bases from your enemies, so you can distinguish between them at a glance. Age of Fear might not be a treat for the eyes, but it's no eyesore either – I'd much rather have functional graphics that work reliably than a glitch-ridden mess, and I'm glad AoF has the former.
The two campaigns each took me around seven hours to complete; the occasional plot-based decision, varying difficulties, hidden secrets and achievements all offer a player excuses for replaying them, if you're that way inclined. Compared to the first game, I found the stories to be a touch weaker – the Orc campaign felt as simple and unfulfilling as, well, I'm sure the average Orc's life is, and the Demon campaign was about as embarrassing as I'd expected it to be from the moment I learned that a succubus would be the main character. Perhaps having a female narrator for her quest might have helped; as it was, the torrents of flirtation and innuendo uttered by the gruff-voiced narrator were a nightmare that almost had me yearning for the oblivion of The Void.
OVERALL
AoF2 is an odd sequel: the core gameplay remains the same, so it's unlikely to win over anyone who disliked the first game, but rather than sticking with their established characters and factions the developers were bold enough to compose two entirely new campaigns. Frankly, in narrative terms I preferred the campaigns in the original, but as far as gameplay goes this was another solid experience. I'd recommend you approach AoF2 as an expansion pack rather than a sequel, albeit an expansion that is as large as the original game: if you found AoF1 pleasant enough and want something similar but not entirely identical, this should scratch that itch nicely.

If you love 3D platformers, then you will find lots of joy with this game.
It got inspired by some of the old-school - most people know them as milestones - platformers, such as ‘Psychonauts’, ‘Super Mario 64’ et cetera.
This game didn’t match my expectations at all - instead it exceeded them so much, that I can frankly state that I haven’t got so much fun in a long time: It is the icing on the cake of a lot games I've been playing over the past couple years.
Everything in this game is seamless to its own ambitions as indie game: The controls are razor-sharp when considering that this game is mostly a platformer; the art style is gorgeous which mixes perfectly with the overall tracklist of themes, as they couldn’t be composed better, and what is more is that most musical themes are adapting on the world, they are so stunningly dynamic.
Both, the artstyle as well as the music are vivid and fitting the world’s theme.
Speaking of world themes: Do you wish to explore a town inhabited by the mafia or will you rather go on a spooky trip through the night, but hold on, you can also be a detective and investigate a murder case… just to name but a few.
About those worlds it can be said that they are gigantic spaces, some linear, some focused heavily on free platforming and exploration.
Whereat those linear levels concentrate more at the narrative of the world, thus providing very interesting dialogues and charming levels, the exploration driven worlds on the other hand makes you feel lost in their spacious areas submerged with content.
Instead of progressing further to the main quest, you can find yourself most of the time trying to climb objects for optional content, as the platforming is so much fun that it distracts you ultimately from your main goal.
And even though those levels might appear bland due to their sheer size, there is yet little to zero lack of consistency, on the contrary every wrinkle of the world is plastered with exhilarating stuff.
Almost nothing of that came along to me as padding to artificially enhance the game’s length.
The games world even encourages you to explore freely at the very first missions, thus I skipped the tutorial to some degree.
Moreover it can be said that these maps are consisting of refreshing game-design, even though it is supposed to bring back that old nostalgic vibes, it yet feels like something completely new: Nothing feels like it has already been done before in the same way, and even if there are elements that are considerably taken as reference by the developers, they yet invented those principles further and absolutely nailed them.
If there is one term I could use to describe the aforementioned, I would simply call it a brisk experience.
However there is one more importance to this game, basically it’s charm: There is so much love put inside of those characters and dialogues that I can’t help but say that it feels alive and not like a conversation between two robotic entities.
Furthermore, those conversations between the characters are really hilarious, but also are some of the jokes inside of the game.
All that being said, I can recommend this game without any major complaints, since the only complaint that I have is that it was not as long as other games, but fortunately the content that it does have is absolutely worth your time: I rather play a short but good game than a long dragged out game.

There are definitely a lot of games out there that have me coming back to them throughout the years: Minecraft, Pokemon, Dungeon Defenders 1 and more. Dungeon Defenders 2 is shaping up to be that type of game.
While many players dislike the addition of Siege Rollers, I honestly do enjoy having them in the game as they add an element of activity that differs from other Tower Defense games. It allows players to access a different niche of the game that prevents AFK-ing, although Onslaught Mode to farm gear for their level before tackling the other portions of the game. The inclusion of Incursions which require active play time and specified map loot have been vast improvements to DD2 since it's original inception. (Oh god, the gear drops were even more horrid back in the initial few months.)
Though their are complaints with skins, few at the moments with minor changes, and microtransactions, which in my opinion is kind of disheartening. It makes sense as the game is now a Free-to-Play game and Trendy Ent needs to make some form of constant cash flow. I can see them being valid concerns for the long run, hopefully they maintain microtransactions strictly to new characters and cosmetics. (Anymore and I'll be seriously concerned.)
The devs themselves have been responsive and active on the forums and the community, as angry as it is now for many reasons (none of them too concise on a single issue from an overall look of complaints), are quite friendly and have been helping both new and veteran players alike farm maps for items, level new characters, and provide feedback. (Always positive from my experience.)
Updates are quite common, almost monthly, and hotfixes come out almost weekly to rectify issues and solve initial problems that come out with builds as the game progresses through its Alpha Stages. The characters, both new and old, are unique in many ways but do not so differently that it becomes a hassle to learn an entirely new character or playstyle.
Definitely a recommendation to play and it'll only get better through time. Also be ready to grind for gear, not as tedious as most people point out and it's a game that you can easily dip some time into, but at the same time, playing an hour or two every so often won't leave you feeling like you haven't progressed. (Try pushing yourself up each level for newer gear.)

Blood Bowl 2 provides you with a real "sport" aspect, something which was a bit lacking on BB1, and very nice animations, cleaner information, and overall a much more polished experience.
The real flaw of BB2 is the lack of Career Mode. However, as I discovered hours later into the game, you can pretty much compensate this by creating your solo team and then entering a World League, in which you can play several seasons and qualify for a World Cup every season. Custom World League itself has been improved and streamlined since launch, and this really compensates  for something that was so lacking.
The next flaw in the game would then be the AI. On that area I can't say it has been fixed. AI can beat you at times (once every 20 matches for instance) but fails on many occasions.
Other people are also asking for the full roster of 21 races.
We have a fair number of races, but the point I see with the DLCs is that Expansions could have been better - because with expansions, you also refine features. Here we received race DLCs - and races are really nice, and these DLCs have also been provided for free to so many people - but we haven't seen so many refinements.
However, I've seen the much asked Stats (player and team stats) come into the game, something we've requested at launch, proving the devs listen to us.

In BB2 you have:
- a single player tutorial campaign with the Reikland Reavers; a welcome things but an easy campaign, and so much less than a career mode.
- a hidden career mode but without the nice career map we hade on BB1
- ability to create your own teams and play them in custom solo matches or multiplayer!
- multiplayer and multiplayer leagues, which are much improved over BB1. This is where BB2 currently shines.
- graphics and rules implementation are cleaner and better
- AI has been improved from Troll status to Black Orc status.
On its own Blood Bowl is a great turn-based strategy game, with a lot of risk management involved.
The computer version is ver comprehensive and plays like a great game, with animations,sporty-feeling made with all passion and heart.
This deserves a thumbs up.
Some people will find rules or dice are hard on them - but game design wise, this game allows the player to manage his risks pretty well, much better than many other boardgames I've come to experience (here I look at Heroes of Normandie, which doesn't allow risk management),.
It is sad AI also cannot handle the big thing, or that Career mode was hidden and less implemented.

Holy what? Over 8 years on Steam and 18+ years playing this type of game, I've never been inspired to write a review until now. I'm a huge fan of turn-based strategy, rpg's, adventure, and fantasy work so this seemed right up my alley. Such a great concept, unique mechanics.. I really liked it in so many regards, but they totally ruined it on a few different fronts.
1. The actual software ran abysmally on my computer. If you played more than 5-6 battles in a row the game would get so laggy that it wouldn't be able to scroll or respond to commands until you waited 30-90 seconds or just restarted. Second, clicking in one place often gave a different result then when you clicked there previously, wtf? Finally and perhaps worst: there are mouse-over tips and explanations, that only activate every 8th-10th time you try and you have to hold your mouse *perfectly* in the right pixel point over the button/tooltip. You no joke spend 10% of your time in this game trying to read this really crucial gameplay info and if you're one pixel off, you lose it.
2. Writing. wow. I feel like they put some "work" into this (which is generally a good thing) but they bombed pretty hard. I've never actually seen something so neck-bearded-fedorah-wearing, cringey, and intent on sending a message of "women are evil and i've been broken up with in an unfair way" that it actually bled into the storyline. It's really kind of shocking. I'm a pretty center of the road dude and this is one of those times where I realized that this is what they mean when they say that there are toxic cultural messages in computer games. Just stop it, it's making everyone uncomfortable. Ask a female friend what's up if you really don't get it.
3. Difficulty levels. This one's a minor faux pas in that grand scheme but it mattered to me. There are 4 difficulty levels. Novice, intermediate, accomplished, impossible (paraphrasing). I started out intermediate (the recommended setting for all skill-levels, apparently) my first run and played through the whole campaign no problems. Second campaign I feel like I've got it down and try the accomplished setting. I've played through and restarted going on 12 times now and still haven't played through. I know some folks desire this, but for me I want to sort of step up in difficulty to learn more, not just run straight into a wall.
4. Attention to detail. There's some really annoying stuff here. Misspelled words, obviously bad grammar (their =/= they're). Either hire a college undergrad to proofread your copy for $50 or spend a little more time on it. Trust me, it's worth it.

It is quite something that, while I think it is one of the most original and interesting game releases around, I have to recommend against it.
Sunless Sea, as a story to be unraveled and explored, it is fantastic. It packs a great amount of literary content (and I do mean by "literary" given how many words this has), solid worldbuilding and the constant feeling of "there is much more in the background", thanks to how the lore is revealed to you: snippets, fragments and bits that by themselves may seem quirky, odd or totally alien, but as you go around and learn, a bigger picture starts to form. Exploring the mysteries of the Neath and the Unterzee while avoiding whatever unknown terror of the depths, the dread of hunger, the lack of critical fuel or even the very wrath of strange gods is
, to say the least.
If only this was an interactive fiction, though.
Sunless Sea, however, is a game. While story and ambience are clearly paramount in this, the "game" part is, well, not good enough. Since you need to engage with the game in order to explore the story, it suffers due to bad gameplay: once the novelty is gone, you will be instinctively drawn to keep your beaten old steamer around the familiar routes of Fallen London and try to grind some measure of resources to make sure you can survive your next journeys. Sunless Sea makes very clear, from the beginning, that it wants you to take chances and explore - but when you have lost a few captains and you are generally aware of how things work, you realize how woefully lacking is the earliest part of the game and how much of a slog it is to make a modicum of improvement.
(This doesn't get any better even after that.)
Which brings to the problem. The game's economy is focused on the three critical resources: hunger, fuel and terror. Managing all three may seem like a juggler's act, but a few tries here and there will give you the hang of things. Echoes, the currency proper, is the solution to the balancing act. You can afford a better engine, which makes journeys faster; better weapons, which makes you able to fight whatever the zee throws at you; a better ship, which makes everything more useful. Because of that, players quickly realize that they need cash early on to overcome the slog.
And, of course, you start to grind. Because you are grinding, you are not exploring. Because you are not exploring, the game loses its charm and effect FAST. But you need to cash in order to explore without being an awful drag. Of course, given how things work and the very orientation Failbetter wants for Sunless Sea, they quickly took care of the means to make money that were seen as "gamey" (see "The Sunlight Trade" if you are curious).
Sunless Sea is very original and has a lot of entertaining stuff, packed to the brim with lore of their setting (which comes from Fallen London) and the siren's call of a big, unknown Unterzee beckons and dares you to explore all of it. However, the sluggish, dragging-by-its-feet gameplay, an extremely repetitive early game (again: once the novelty wears off) that quickly becomes plain boring and a lack of alternative means to allow its players to just
means that is not for everyone.

Do you ever ask yourself, when your brain is suffering again from the passive action gaming feeling of a Call of Duty, what happened to the times when you were excited just by the simple feeling of running from the left to the right of the screen, through wonderfully designed levels with the power to tell you a simple, touching story, which you will never forget? If you did, I welcome you to the dark world of LIMBO.
And the boy went out into a big, dark forest.
Limbo is a side scrolling puzzle game, which was released in summer of 2010 for the Xbox Live Arcade Network and is the first release title by the Danish studio Playdead. Obviously, it has nothing to do with the dance of the same name, but it is linked to catholic theology, which describes limbo as the place before hell, a place where everything is uncertain or, you might say, in limbo.
The game starts with you awakening in a dark forest. You are a little boy and your journey begins. Where the journey is going, and why you are going on it, is entirely unknown to you. This is why everyone experiences Limbo in his or her own special way. The game offers you a frame for the story, everything else is a matter of your imagination.
On your journey you run across a gigantic spider and little kids, who flee at your sight or try to kill you immediately. Except for them, you are alone. There are traps everywhere, which tear you apart. But why is everything so brutal, why is everything so dark? Why do the kids want to stop you? Why? You want to know why, and so you continue walking, but with every inch of uncovered screen more questions begin to emerge.
And so you ask these questions over and over again, while solving the puzzles around you to continue your way, and Playdead proves, in this way, that the best stories are those which evolve in our heads.
But why does the game lure you into its world so quickly? This effect is due to the fact that the game mechanics and its style match each other perfectly. The boy looks like a puppet out of a shadow play, and, although he never speaks and we can just see his gloomy eyes, we can infer his fragility by the way he moves, jumps and climbs upon walls. His little legs and arms swing around like little wooden sticks, so every strike can break them and harm his little body. And it does! The boy is able to push crates and to pull switches, but he cannot swim or use any weapons. If in danger, the only thing he can do is to run, and you can only hope that you are faster than the big spider. In these moments you can feel the panic flowing through your veins and it makes you push the buttons a little bit harder. You empathize with the little, dark character quickly and after a few minutes the same thing happens to you, that happened to my previous sentences. He becomes you. You become the boy. You feel what he feels, and you do not want to get (him) hurt.
The world which surrounds him matches the boy in his monochrome style. The screen consists of several layers, which divide the fore- and the background and gives you the feeling of being lost in a huge forest and later in the game, a city. The edges of the screen blur constantly, evoking the feeling they could easy spread over the whole picture. This oppressive feeling is intensified by the sound, which in fact only consists of the low tapping of the boy’s feet and some animal noises coming from deeper within the forest.
Limbo is not a very long game. Once you figure out how the game works, you play through it in about three to four hours. After the first half of the game, the setting of the forests is exchanged for a dark city. In contrast to the forest with its flowing grass and dark trees, the city looks more static and less alive. Black gears give it a steam punk-like look. In this part, the game loses some of its unique charm.
But nevertheless, the game is worth playing, since it offers you the possibility of feeling and falling for a very simple story. It is a bright star in the dark sky of emotionless shooter orgies, which kill every single feeling you have for their screaming characters after the first hour of non-stop shooting. Limbo does the complete opposite of these polished games. It takes all the colours and the light away. But it reminds you how you can find some beauty and light, even in the darkest of stories.
This is story telling at its most minimalist level, but it proves what story telling is about. But this is for you to find out!

Difficult games fall into two catagories: Those that are challenging, and those that are frustrating.  This game, alas, falls into the later category.
My main issues:
1.  There is no good way to control overheating in summer.  Especially when the 1200hp Zombie is fighting them all in the middle of the day.  They stand and fight and die of heat exhaustion.
2.  The monster difficulty seems to grow exponentially.  On day 3, it's not uncommon for 700 to 800 hp monsters to waltz through my defences.  By day 5, they're close to 1500 hp.  I've never made it past that point, so I can only guess how vastly overpowered they become.
3.  The inability to rotate buildings.  When most buildings are rectangles, it helps to compact your base.
4.  The monsters just break through the walls, rather than going through the killing maze.  It's impossible to concentrate enough fire when they come through whatever wall is inconvenient to them.
5.  What it boils down to is a tower defence game with a focus on the infrastructure behind the towers.  It's not what I was expecting from a village simulator.  I'm not a big fan of tower defence games to begin with, so this was a rather sad realization.
6.  There are no guards or soldiers.  You get golems who can't stand a chance against anything but a slime.  It would be nice to have soldiers who could sortie out and soften up the monsters.
EDIT:
I am changing my review to positive.  The developer is prompt and courteous, and there seems to be a lot of changes in the works.  I kind of forgot the game is in alpha still because of how well it looks and, aside from the frustrations mentioned above, works.
I suppose, deep down, I'm afraid of getting burned by another Towns.  Thankfully, I don't think that's a concern here.  I look forward to the continued development of what portends to be a great time waster.

What can I say? ... It is a fun and engaging game.
I was a little sceptical when I heard of the title, but after seeing a Let's Play session with TotalBiscuit on YouTube, I was convinced to give it a go, and with a price of 19 EUR, it wasn't too much of a gamble.
It is a pretty simple game. Controls are easy and the learning curve is not that steep. I did spend the first few captains just sailing around scraping in enough money to cover fuel and supplies. But eventually I grasped how to make sure that I could earn enough to cover those and find other ways of earning money.
The story in the game is good, and the writing is both fun, quirky and interesting.
On the down side I would say that combat with other ships is too easy at the start, though I have great problems with crabs and bats, but that is probably due to my ineptitude for that kind of combat.
Also a better journal would be nice. It is ok to track missions I am currently on. But I have no way of recording which missions are available in which ports and what I need to get them started. So I have to remember that I need 7 Stygian Ivory and a Hunter's trophy to start a specific mission in Godfall.
So I end up having to do a speadsheet or notebook on the side to keep track of these, otherwise I forget where to go for what missions.
But the payoff in fun is good. My second captain ended up far from shore with no fuel and almost no supplies. What does a good captain do? .. he prays to the God of Salt, who generously hear his prayers and teleports the ship to the wrong side of the map and still no fuel. I even end up at a port with no re-fueling options. Scrounging through my last supplies, I get enough fuel to limp to a port where I can refuel. Sadly I don't have much money, so I buy what I can, and a little supplies and head off towards London far far away.
I actually manage to almost make it before my supplies and fuel run out again. Now what do I do?? .. This time we sacrifice two sailors to the God of Stone, and magically get some fuel ... but the rest of the crew is getting hungry, and before I aarive in London, one more sailor have mysteriously disappeared while the crew's hunger has been reduced.
I thanks my lucky stars when I set foot in London. I made it!! ... sadly the customs officers raid my ship and confiscate a box of unstamped human souls, which I was smuggling for a shady character in London. Same shady dude is then awaiting me on the docks, and he is not happy that I lost the cargo. Now I know how Han Solo felt.... He attacks me and my crew, and since we have been decimated by god sacrifices and dinner, he kills all of us. Dammit. So close.

Black and white. There’s something about a monochrome palette that administers the uneasy feeling of the unknown. It’s the darkness we fear the most and LIMBO uses this aspect to the fullest deepening this feeling into our psyche. The neo-noir, manic-depressive look is LIMBO’s style that feels new and innovative. The game begins, well, as soon as you move the thumbstick. There are no prompts throughout the game, only your inquisitiveness in experimenting with objects and physics can help you solve the puzzles…
…and the puzzles can get quite challenging. Not always from a logical perspective but sometimes from the execution of the solution. Timing the jumps and grabs can be difficult yet rewarding but rarely frustrating. The world is eerie and thick with atmosphere. There are no allies or dialogue or back-stories, just an imperative to keep moving right. To what goal? Who knows?! But everything between you and the goal is trying to kill you in horrific, disturbing ways and the bleak setting never gives way to a colourful conclusion. This is horror that will delve deep into your consciousness and should be played at night, with lights off, home alone and with headphones. And an Xbox 360 controller to improve the accuracy of the platforming.

Pros:
+gorgeous painterly artstyle; I honestly can't believe this is a Unity game
+runs like a dream
+cozy as♥♥♥♥♥♥when things are calm, stressful as hell when things go wrong
+really immersive, like edge of your seat stuff; I even refrain from snacking or getting cozy while playing just because it draws you into the harshness of the Canadian wilds
+very simple and intuitive, basically everything you need to know is right there in a pretty UI with easy controls
+no ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥t: stay warm, find food and water, get shelter, keep moving, watch out for wildlife

>to search a car you actually get in and sit down; its warmer inside, you can search the glovebox, flip the visors, look behind the seats
>pretty reload animations on the rifle
>you can track wounded animals by tiny drops of blood they leave behind

>really well modelled wind that can carry your scent to animals, put out fires, make it hard to light matches, and chill your body
>the color of ice indicates its thickness: watch your step

Overall, one of my favorite games, and makes me really hope more games follow this example.

To call this game immersive just doesn't do it justice. There are so many details that make The Long Dark what it is.
You shiver when you're cold. Your stomach grumbles when you're hungry. You move slower going uphill or against the wind, and breathe hard after a run. You are in the environment, you are part of it.
You have to balance the rewards of exploration against the dangers. Wolves will hunt and kill you. You will get lost and freeze to death in a blizzard. But you need to find the necessary tools for survival: clothing, weapons, medicine.
There's a sense of progression without the usual tropes of XP leveling and unlocking skills. You'll learn more about survival, about the map, about your limitations. You'll settle down in a homestead, find a gun, stock up on food and supplies. You can start to live comfortably. But don't get cocky; make one mistake and you'll die, and all that you've worked for will mean nothing.
This game is poetry.

Just Cause 2 was one of my first purchases on Steam once I returned to the platform after being sick of consoles. I never played the first game and didn't hear very good things about it but the sequel got pretty decent reviews so I decided to check it out.
I was shocked at how huge the world was, the things you could do with the grapple arm, and all the things to destroy. This game at one point held the record for the largest world map in a contemporary open world game but it may have been surpassed at this point (haven't checked). Regardless this is a HUGE game. And while the majority of what you will be blowing up will be the same thing, it just doesn't get old (especially seeing that 100% notification). Of course if you want you can go along with the story missions which aren't particularly interesting or different from other missions. They often feel like longer regular missions with checkpoints and slightly grander feats to achieve. Unfortunately the story itself is not particularly well told. The voice acting is decent to bad as well which can sometimes be distracting.
If you didn't come for the story and are just looking to do crazy stuff and blow♥♥♥♥♥♥up, however, then you have come to the right place. There are tons of collectibles spread out across the huge world map, tons of vehicles to drive (or try to drive, driving in this game isn't great) or fly (flying is slightly better). You could literally play this game for hours and not touch any story content. Taking over bases and villages is always satisfying even if it gets a bit repetitive.
In terms of achievements this game is one of the most grindy I have ever played. You don't have to 100% the island (which would be cruel) but you do have to get to 75% of completion (including races, challenges, activities, takeovers, etc.) which can take a long time. There is also an achievement for driving every vehicle that can be quite time consuming but overall do-able.
Just Cause 2 is a great looking game with some phenomenal game play to go along. It gets borderline repetitive but you'll likely be having so much fun blowing things up that you won't notice.

It only takes about 20 minutes of gameplay to realise this game isnt quite Call of Duty. The game is dark and gloomy,the music is sad. In Call of Duty or Battlefield you feel happy after getting a kill. Your enemy falls to the ground mybe making a grunt or scream. In Red Orchestra/Rising Storm (RO/RS) is different. Let's set up a little scenario. You're playing as a rifleman on the German side. You just ran across the open and now you're tired,you've entered a house to take cover and catch your breath when you hear some footsteps. A quick look at the map confirms there are no allies around,so you step into a corner and zoom in on the entrance nearest to the sound. You crouch down and hear the footsteps get closer. finally,you see the tip of a Mosin-Nagant. You're ready. The Russian fully enters the room and turns towards you. You fire. The bullet hits the Russian in his stomach,the shot is fatal,but he is not dead. He is bleeding out. The injury is too much for him to bandage himself,and all he can see is his screen fading to black. He panics and shoots. You have already clicked a second time to bolt your rifle,you
finish him off,but decide to save the extra round,and perhaps not risk being heard for sure. The Russian fires another round. He is bent forwards,his character clutching his stomach. It's rather quiet and you can hear the Russian calling for his mother before falling onto the ground,a blood pool forms around him. You reload your rifle,crouch down and get ready to exit the door he came through. You slowly peek out,check left and right before making a couple more steps into the open. You think it's all clea- *ping* You've just been shot in the head by an enemy you couldn't see. this isnt CoD or Battlefield,there are no killcams or special views showing your killer. This will happen a lot. Have fun.

This is Telltale, so expect some of their usual perks and flaws.  Good storytelling that provides something familiar, yet different from the established canon, a la their rendition of GoT.  On the other hand, there were a few times were my decisions or intentions weren't reflected by the game or dialogue, an unfortunate downside to a dialogue choice system that often boils down whole lines into a few words. This is one of those games that are all about experience and your own reflections. Gameplay does not really matter. There are no impactfull choices like in "Stanley's Parable", so if you're expecting something like that, you may feel disappointed. Yes, this game is short. Yes, there's not much "to do" once you're playing it. But for me it was an amazing experience. It was something that I can relate to on so many levels that it almost scares me. I related to this game as an creator, as an author, as fan of someone else's work, as a friend, as reviewer and the most importantly, as a human being. I was wondering what people think about me when they read my work. How they try to "catch" the glimpse of an author between the lines. I was wondering how many people around me have that... specific impact on my and on my work. And what kind of impact I had on others. Was it good? What about my own sickness?
I love games. Even more, I love games with the good story, so I've played plenty that I could relate to, but there are only few that actually made me think about my passions, my choices, my creation and helped my see things differently, helped me reevaluate things. This is one of those games and it makes it worth every money.

This game is an absolute delight. If you are either a fan of the classic platformers or a generally new face within the genre such as I then prepare for an adorable romp through the wacky world of A Hat in Time!
TLDR: Design is fun and can be really beautiful at times, Characters are a blast and I really wish I saw more of them, Music is great with more than a few stand out tracks, story leaves me wanting more in both good and not so good ways, challenge is well balanced in my opinion with a few areas that felt delightfully rough, and overall I had a good time. I wish I didn't rush through though.
Movement is a blast and the level design is made in a way that isn't too challenging for the gaming novice but rewards those who try to be creative in the way they get around. In many games such as these I always felt that collectibles were not something that I cared too much about as they merely grant maybe an additional life or just a few points to the score, but the different collectibles in this game (aside from the main story-required macguffins) provide you with additional abilities or traits that can make your traversal through the world easier, allow you to accomplish tasks at a faster pace, or just grant you another layer of defense against various threats.
I do enjoy the art style for the most part. Certain aspects like drawn on mouths and the lack of certain facial features were a bit jarring at first, but the design of the world rarely disappointed! This is coming from a poor individual whose computer cannot handle the full graphical settings of this game, but the lower settings still looked really nice and I was able to mind the occasional frame drops. (Wish I had the ability to enjoy the full experience though...) The final world was not my cup of tea since I am not the biggest fan of backtracking giant areas, but it was an isolated incident that really wasn't mandatory unless you are going for the complete experience. You can honestly finish the game rather quickly as you are able to face the final boss well before you have collected all time pieces, but where is the fun in that?
I won't go into detail about certain events that I cared about the most to avoid too many spoilers, but there were many hits and few misses with a lot of the plot points in this game. I would have loved to see more appearances of a lot of my favorite characters while playing through the game! More story would have been neat in general, but there are future worlds being developed so I can wait a bit to see more! Oh also I like a lot of the tracks in this game. Musical delight indeed!
I apologize for the less than organized review, but I hope I was able to separate it enough to highlight and call into question different aspects of the game. I also really like the workshop feature. I saw a few people importing worlds that allow the excellent movement options to flourish in new environments while others provided even more was to get around in an already amazingly fluid game!
On one last note I miss that cool looking kid from the 2-player announcement from the kickstarter. I heard they were getting rid of that. Kinda makes me sad but it is their decision in the end.
Thank you for your time if you decided to read this silly thing. Hope you enjoy/enjoyed the game!
