I'd like to clarify some of the negative reviews.  This game "isn't that bad".  I won't say it's good, and I'd give it a neutral rating if possible.  It IS NOT WORTH full price.  But it has gone on sale for 3.75, and even been in the $1 tier of a Humble Bundle, and it is a fine/fun game for that price.
This game's negative reviews are primarily given for one reason: Expectations.  It is disliked, even hated, because of what it isn't.
What this game isn't:
- Not a Diablo-clone (action RPG) like Sacred 1 and 2.  It can't really be considered much of an RPG at all.  It only has minor RPG elements.
- Not made for keyboard and mouse.  It's made for a controller.
- Not a high quality AAA title.  It has good graphics.  It has a terrible script.  It has intermediate voice acting.  The game mechanics are unoriginal.
- Not worth $50;  probably not worth $15.
What this game is:
- Overhead beat-em up.
- Minor RPG elements, like leveling up.
- Designed for a controller
- Designed with local co-op in mind. (I've not played it local co-op, so I can't speak to the quality of that experience)
- Worth $3.75.
This game will not be the next big thing in your library, but it could be a fun beat-em up to play with a friend.  A positive review on this game is gonna get some hate, because, like I said, this game is HATED for what it isn't.  It actually offends the fans that this game isn't what one would expect from a sequel to Sacred 1 and 2.
But if this game wasn't called Sacred 3, it wouldn't be getting all this hate.  If it were called Sacred Citadel 2, or some obscure name like Arcania Heart, it would probably have much more positive reviews (except for the unreasonable price-tag).
Meh, it's OK I guess.

This is an enjoyable strategy title which offers good value for those who can forgive a little clunkiness. The game is rough around the edges and thing like the UI and graphics options are areas which could use significant improvements (you can only load games from the main menu for instance) but the core gameplay loop is solid and quite fun if you do not need your hand held. Upgrading your units and heros offers good prgression and makes it painful to lose any veteran unit but not fatal as the game will offer you better units types and even veteran units as the campaign progresses. The campaigns are of a decent length, providing enough oppurtunity to build your party and develop a distinctivve fighting force against a pleasant story backdrop which can be easily ignored if so desired. Personally, I found the writing to be more palatable than some of the bland mush common to today's AAA fare but the voiced story text between missions felt like wasted effort since I much preffered to read it myself which was also considerably faster.
The gameplay really stood out for me and I wish there were more games which offered a similar level of depth. It feels like you can approach most battles with a good variety of approaches but you still have to think and poor choices will result in you losing units and battles. Another aspect I really appreciated was the speed of the game along with the ease of access it offered. The game offers enough complexity for a challanging and varied campaign but it doesn't hide a lot of things and it doesn't overcomplicate things. Likewise, you can get straight to the action and are never forced to watch the same accursed combat animation or cinematic camera pan to an enemy over and over and over again (I'm looking at you XCOM 2). The number of units on both sides also stays just within manageable throughout where you don't end up waiting minutes for the enemy to finish it's turn and niether are you burdened with tedious micro of a myriad fo your own units (in most cases anyway).

A Hat in Time is one of those games with huge levels, that have small missions to obtain an item at the end of the mission before being brought back to the main hub... Personally, I love those as they play the strings of nostalgia in my heart.
Game play: Fun and fast with a good flow feel to it. If you're someone who's like me and likes to dive everywhere you know what I'm talking about. Game is quick to pick up on with controls that aren't too difficult. It can be a bit annoying rotating between hats if you're someone who isn't used to leaving an analog stick tilted until you leave the menu. You grow to get used to it though. The game is somewhat flexible in what you can do and when you can do. If throws in elements from other kind of games like Zelda where you cannot complete a task without finding the item to complete the task. You are not bound to one area and are absolutely encouraged to look through other areas and coming back to finish the one you started... There are some customization options also, with a workshop to come.
Story: The story does make you feel for the antagonist a bit in a very humorous way(?) I mean their reasons are justified, but what they do ends up being a little extra towards the end. Which is fine for plot reasons.
Music: Great. The music is dream like and wonderful. I cannot applaud the music enough.
Faults: Every game has some faults. For me personally it would be some of the mechanics. I'm usually a player with little patience and tend to try to do stuff as quick as possible, and the game is very good at keeping up, until I miss that one swing because the game didn't register that it was a hook-able spot. Camera might also be your nightmare, but we all remember the camera for Mario 64, so if you managed to master that monstrosity growing up, this is cakewalk.
Overall I recommend this game. I really wish to see more for this game, like extra levels, but the way it is now? I enjoyed it. :)

Sacred 3 is a bit of a mixed bag, and innovates the series in an opposite direction, but is a decent time waster when on 75% off.
I had never played a Sacred game before this. So when I saw this game I was impressed by it's art style and the dungeons in it's screenshots. However the game was immediately swarmed by negative reviews and as it stands it is one of the worst games on Steam.
But does it deserve that distinction.
As someone who only now (as of this review) just played Sacred 2, I have to say I had better first impressions of Sacred 3, but that's not to say that the criticism is unfounded.
First of all, the game is level based, instead of open world. The story is about generic evil bad guy overlord called Zane tries to take over Ancaria. And the Seraphim form a team of warriors to fight him off. Pretty boring stuff. The levels while linear as hell are at least nice to look at, and the visual effects as enemies are slaughtered are satisfying. However, the combat is poor. Clicking the left mouse button attacks, right mouse button counters (in a way, it just stuns most opponents when they are about to strike.) Pressing 1 or 2 activates a special ability. Yes, you can only have 2 abilities instead of a full bar. And as abilities go they are pretty generic. You can also dodge roll, but it sucks. Because you roll in the direction of your MOUSE, and not in the direction of your WASD or whatever you use. At least with keyboard and mouse controls. It might be better with a controller.
Customization of characters and equipment, ready for it? Is ♥♥♥♥ing NONEXISTANT. Weapons are gained at certain points in the story, and upgrades are basic up damage, up crit, up range etc. You cannot get new armour or anything, and levelling up just gets you more upgrades. It might actually be better if levelling wasn't in the game at all to be honest, but they had to make this as RPG-y as possible I guess.
The story and dialougue is the most unfunniest bull you will ever hear and read in your life. And this is someone who loves games like Stick RPG 2 and Duke Nukem Forever (DNF's writing anyway, the gameplay can go to hell). I find the writing in Sacred 3 some of the dumbest♥♥♥♥♥♥I've ever had to hear, and it looks like a game script I would write at the age of NINE. Freaks sakes. But I actually enjoy the writing, because we all need some lame humour in our lives every now and then, and Trump jokes are overdone.
And the dlcs are kinda... mediocre. You get basically more missions of the same friggin gameplay, which is actually my biggest complaint about Sacred 3. It is repetitive as hell. Even the side missions are killmobs.gif. Because it repeats. Over. And. Over.
The game, in my opinion, can be best described as an unfunnier Borderlands, with no loot worth playing for, and cringier dialogue.
So why do I recommend it then?
Like I said at the start, I find it a mixed bag. I have stated all negatives so far, but there is one thing that I recommend it for.
When you are bored as hell, or stressed, and just want to play something stupid. Something you don't want to pay much attention too. Just an arena for you to beat up orc and trolls. That's what it's for. It also helps if you are drunk, but hey.
Do get this on a sale though, you don't want to pay full price for something that is basically fun for 5 minutes at a time.

Once I got in to it, this hooked me well enough that I played through until the end of one of two campaigns in it, but there are too many rough edges for me to recommend it overall.
One of the core mechanics here is all your units (not just your heroes) earn XP, and the stat gains they get from that are
given how few HP they start with. They can also
in battle, so I fear losing those upgrades.
In many tactical games, that means figuring out how your units can use the terrain for advantage over the enemy, but here the maps are little more than window dressing. There's no taking the high ground, or staying in cover for a defensive bonus, or even breaking line-of-sight.
Enter summoners. They throw away that "every soldier is precious" idea entirely. Summoned minions de-spawn after a few turns anyway, so there's no hesitation about using them as disposable meat shields. They even feed their combat XP back to their summoner.
But wait, there's more! Summoned units are not
useful for shaping movement on the battlefield, they can also act on the same turn that they're summoned. And one of the types of summoned units has a ranged attack, which is otherwise hard to come by early in the campaign.
The other bit of level design I got stuck on is that there's a battle that is widely regarded as unwinnable unless you have a unit that can stun-lock the teleporting baddie with the one-hit kill strike, and despite the campaign offering that unit to you right before that, it's real easy to end up without them in your party, since you probably were already at your maximum number of party members.
As for the story, there are a few good one-liners, but I didn't care for the voice acting, and I was surprised it ended when it did.
The user interface has a lot of room for improvement. The rendering performance is especially disappointing in the later battles with lots of units on the field.
There are things I liked. The variety of units that you play with, ranging from knights in shining armor to giant half-demon spiders. And the upgrades you get, either through loot or XP, give you something a little different to play with every battle.
There's potential here, and I'll be curious to see what comes from this developer in the future, but players can pass on this one.

Personally I find the Warhammer universe pretty dumb, and sportsball really isn't my thing. Edit: Ok, after 138 hours in game I have to say BB2 is a much deeper and more interesting game than I gave it credit for - a solid 8 out of 10. With the Legendary expansion there's a massive ammount of play available, and improvements to the base game make it a fine entry point into the series. An absolute gem, not to be missed.

Damn I shouldn't have gone out of my cabin so late....night time fell like a rock...a storm has moved in ...I can hear wolves close by .... I'm low on flares never mind ammo....wasn't there a bear here abouts too....where the heck is that cabin?!?
The last time I was this worried about resources and things that go bump in the night I was playing System Shock 2...or STALKER Shadow of
That does seem to have been a while ago right? Well those two oldies, when fresh ( BTW I still play both ever so often) brought some great immersion and challenges to the plate.
In The Long Dark ( TLD ), available on early access on STEAM and XBox, you have just crashed your plane into the winter wonderland of Canada after a mysterious magnetic global disaster. TLD is an immersive game that brings a unique look, great open spaces, unforgiving weather, limited resources plus the wild life that's out to get you.
In the current Sandbox version ( v.244 as of this review ), story mode on it's way by end of 2015, you have one objective...SURVIVE.  Simple right? No...no it isn't... BUT it sure is fun. TLD has three game styles...Pilgrim ( easy ), Voyager and Stalker ( yeap named after that classic ). You can meet an untimely end in each version. There are many ways to live and DIE .... you pick how. Death by freezing....death by starving...death by wolf...death by bear...death by phaser ( okay not that one ) let's just say death has your name and location on the map. Speaking of Maps ...right now Publisher Hinternland says there are nearly 20 square kms to explore in the current areas...Mystery Lake, The Ravine, Coastal Highway and Pleasant Valley. Oh and by the way you need to find the transition points between those.
Once you settle in you can scavenge for goods to live amongst the remains of humanity. You can go back to nature and live off the land. TLD has multiple items to craft to help you prolong your life but don't worry the game does provide a How to manual once you find the appropriate local to craft at. You can play the game any way you want to. There are multiple man made locations to explore as well as the ones nature provides and in some places both worlds meet just to challenge you some more.
TLD is so well put together that you forget you are playing an ALPHA version of the game. As such there are a few bugs to be found but as of v244 the game is very stable and Hinterland is quick to apply hotfixes plus updates to further improve the game. I can't wait for the finished story mode version. Hinterland has more Episodes planned with more challenges and fun.
In the mean time I think I hear a bear coming my way ...time again to discover if I have what it takes to keep on surviving..... in The Long Dark.

At first my computer launched the game using my itegrated graphics card which has no power, hense the 10fps. So i had to change my nividia control pannel settings to launch the game using my high powered nividia processor. The game would then launch to a white screen. SO i had to go to my game settings change the compatibility settings to disable autmatic dpi scaling. Once I did all that the game ran beautifully and I absolutely loved the first episode, the art style, voice acting, just everything. Firstly, let me say that I clearly understand why many people have a mixed opinion on this game at late. Yes, this game has been in development since 2013; since I started university. Yes, it is taking way too long to finish and people are losing patients with the long wait to a highly anticipated game, especially since the flatout license has been passed on to a developer that had dragged the Flatout name through the mud. In fact, I'm getting frustrated over the long wait for this game.
Because from what there is at the moment, this game is fantastically fun and has huge potential, with a mix of Flatout & Destruction Derby. The visuals are beautiful and gorgeous to look at with huge amounts of detail, from paint scratches and shattering glass to the environment of the tracks and even the garage you are placed in at the start. The sound effects are blissful and wonders to the ears without being overpowering; everything from the crunching of cars into each other and other world objects are addictive to hear. The racing is fun with the mixture of destructable scenary from the Flatout games and rally style racing. Alongside everything else, the modding community is awesome to see, providing everything from racetracks from Destruction Derby 1 and 2, extra cars and other features!
If I were to add any flaws to this game, there is honestly only two; the framerate when the screen is cluttered with many cars and effects going on in one place. And finally, and the most obvious among the many negative opinions among gamers; the game is taking to long to finish off fully and the updates to the game are usually far between each other.
Other than that, the game is fantastic and has huge potential, and in fact it is one of my favourite recently made games! To everyone else, I completely understand you frustration over this game's overly long production cycle. But bear in mind that Bugbear is a small indie game producer now compared to its days when it produced the Flatout games. But hopefully, now that they have a permenant backer, the game could be close to completion. And with the amount of work they put into this game and the potential this game has, I'm looking forward to the final outcome! :)

So here's a recipe for Chocolate Chip Cookies.
Ingredients
1/2 cup (1 stick) unsalted butter
3/4 cup packed dark brown sugar
3/4 cup sugar
2 large eggs
1 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
1 (12-ounce) bag semisweet chocolate chips, or chunks
2 1/4 cups all-purpose flour
3/4 teaspoon baking soda
1 teaspoon fine salt
Directions
Evenly position 2 racks in the middle of the oven and preheat to 375 degrees F. (on convection setting if you have it.) Line 2 baking sheets with parchment paper or silicone sheets. (If you only have 1 baking sheet, let it cool completely between batches.)
Put the butter in a microwave safe bowl, cover and microwave on medium power until melted. (Alternatively melt in a small saucepan.) Cool slightly. Whisk the sugars, eggs, butter and vanilla in a large bowl until smooth.
Whisk the flour, baking soda and salt in another bowl. Stir the dry ingredients into the wet ingredients with a wooden spoon; take care not to over mix. Stir in the chocolate chips or chunks.
Scoop heaping tablespoons of the dough onto the prepared pans. Wet hands slightly and roll the dough into balls. Space the cookies about 2-inches apart on the pans. Bake, until golden, but still soft in the center, 12 to 16 minutes, depending on how chewy or crunchy you like your cookies. Transfer hot cookies with a spatula to a rack to cool. Serve.
Store cookies in a tightly sealed container for up to 5 days.
For a Rocky Road Bar:
Lightly butter a 9 by 13-inch baking pan. Make the batter as per cookie recipe and fold in 1 cup chopped walnuts along with the chocolate chips. Spread batter in prepared pan. Bake until the edges are light brown and the batter sets, about 45 minutes. Cool slightly and cover surface with 4 cups marshmallows and 1 cup chocolate chips. Broil at least 8 inches from the heat until marshmallows turn golden brown, about 2 minutes. (Keep an eye on the marshmallows, and turn the pan frequently--they go from golden to char in a wink.) Cool, cut and serve.

It also reminds us that games aren't always about shooting zombies, racing fast cars or scoring a bunch of points. It's about telling a story, giving the player something meaningful. It's those games that leave people mesmerized and walking away with a memerable experience.
The Beginners Guide is a game I strongly recommend people play.

The past months have been particularly good for platformers it seems. Sonic Mania (DRM issue aside, I had a good time playing it), Cuphead, now this.
Now, this is from the perspective of someone who did not back this game on Kickstarter but backed Yooka-Laylee. Recent years have reintroduced my love of the sorts of platformers as seen on the fifth/sixth generation consoles, especially in the vein of Banjo-Kazooie or Psychonauts. Seeing a group of professionals who worked on Banjo-Kazooie form a new studio to pitch a game had me happily chip in around $12. Putting all drama aside, when I finally received my copy I've put in at least eight hours, and while I contend that reviews were a bit harsh to it, and that there are some positive things going for it (Grant Kirkhope's score being a pretty big one), there were some gameplay gripes I had and I didn't find it that memorable. Not a fan of its voice grunts either, especially when compared to Banjo-Kazooie.
So why did I bring this up? Well, when I received this game as a gift and played it, I found quite a few things about it that just blows it out of the water. There may be some things that needed polish, and it shows, but the characters are charming and well-acted, the worlds they inhabit grip me, with the sorts of themes that I would see in platformers of the sixth-generation era (especially Psychonauts or the Gamecube titles). I also find myself digging the music, as it does remind me of quite a few games that I have known. Also bearing in mind that this game was made lovingly by fans with a background in modding iirc, while Y-L was made by industry professionals, and the former is $10 cheaper at release. With all this, I just don't have the incentive of going back to playing Yooka-Laylee, while I can see myself playing this more.
This is just a really charming game that I certainly wouldn't mind 100%ing on more than one playthrough. If you haven't checked it out, please do.

Most reviewers do not seem to understand what they have bought, so let me give it a try.
BB2 is a board-game adaptation of the popular GW tabletop/board game of the same name.
While the older Chaos edition has a lot more variety in terms of available teams, BB2 improves on the frankly horrible UI, Sound and Animation quality. While one can argue that the older designs are more charming and characterful, the new models are look pretty good, especially for a board game adaptation.
The gameplay remains faithful to the board game, while tweaking the rules and resolving some balancing issues inherent to the game. It's debatable whether the developers have succeeded, however it has generally gotten better since the release.
The Multiplayer has become more accessible, but as always it is basically unavoidable to get involved with the community and to organize your own league to play online in any serious way. The organization of said leagues and the games has been greatly improved.
Real time mode was removed, it was after all a silly addition in the first place.
Player customization has unfortunately been somewhat reduced.
The teams are pretty balanced, much more than they are in the board game, but imbalance is not a bug its a feature. Beating a strong team (like the Lizardmen) with a comparatively weaker (or less blunt) team is one of the great sources of rewarding gameplay.
Both ballplaying teams and bashing teams can win. Ballplayers are at an advantage however and bashers must play with some brain if they want to have a chance. This is not a game of brute mouse skill or reflexes, but rather of strategy and planning. You should not expect that just because you play chaos or orks that you can play like a drunk potato on Ritalin. Surprisingly the fast and fragile teams are a lot easier, which is balanced by their inability to dominate and submit the enemy.
For new players the campaign, frustrating hours of crushing defeats or heavy reading online are the three unavoidable options. The game is arguably much more complex and punishing then the genera average and even knowing that the learning curve is unexpectedly steep.
So after saying all that what is the fazit?
A resounding recommendation.
Even though frustrating at times, the fun to be had exceeds most multiplayer experiences I have had in years. The authentic and refreshing hard to learn, harder to master approach drew me in just like the first official videogame adaptation did. If you have a heart for this kind of game, check out the Crendorian Invitational videos on YouTube. Wait for a sale and buy the game. Unfortunately you have probably lost the opportunity to get 4 of the new teams for free, but still, 15 to 25 bucks for the base game is a pretty good deal.

Video Review:
What is it?
Sunless Sea is a rouge-like adventure game where you play as a steamship captain of the Underzee. Your victory condition is determined by what you choose at the beginning of the game, which could be a lust for wealth, knowledge, or to find your past (although you could happen upon other ways to win as you play).
Gamplay consists of choices that you have to make throughout the game. It could range from choosing whether to listen to or attack a bandit to choosing a side in the rodent wars (not joking). Beyond that, you must ensure that your vessel is properly stocked and you need to plot a course. The outcome of these choices is often determined by one of the five stats that your captain has.
It is also worth noting that Sunless Sea is not an action filled rouge like. The action is mostly played out in the text that the game provides that player. You will also fight on the open Zee, but that is a small portion of the game overall.
Pros:
-This game has an amazing sense of humor. It comes straight from Wells, Shelly, and even a bit of Crusoe while mixing in Lovecraftian horror.
-The choices are numerous. You can go anywhere in the Underzee form the beginning of the game, and from that you have a plethora of things that you could do.
-The choices are impactful. Deciding to go one way can open a whole new path for you, but it will also cut off another. You'll always feel like your decisions in the game matter.
-The narratives are interesting. I love the stories that have been put into this game. They are mysterious and captivating, and that is a must have for such a narative driven game.
-The atmosphere is palpable. The game sucks you into the dread and mystery of the Underzee. From the wordy style to the beautiful art, the game keeps you on edge.
Cons
-There is a lot of reading. Personally I don't see this as a big downside, but if you don't enjoy reading (or want to see lots of neat explosions) this might not be the game for you.
-When you die, you have to do it all over again. This is a particular problem for Sunless Sea. The only thing that actually changes between deaths are the locations of the islands. You will have to play through the same story every time you die.
Overall, I consider this to be a great game that is well worth it's price tag. I'll be playing a lot of it in the days to come.

You start out in this game as a dude who wakes up in a forest, unaware of who you are, why you're there or even your objective. It does quickly become apparent after around 10-20 minutes into the game that it's a very dangerous place and certain people don't want you there, it then becomes apparent that your primary goal is to survive and escape this dark and ominous world you find yourself in.
Going through this game I'm suspecting that around 95% of you will experience every possible way to die in Limbo at least once, but that doesn't take away any fun or create annoyance, it's actually all part of the experience and actually adds enjoyment to the game to see the many inventive ways this cruel world can kill you. As you make your way through you'll have to solve varying puzzles to progress and also avoid horrific death traps which will kill you in an instant. The game is very shrewd and does become more challenging throughout, I had a few head scratches throughout the game, but if you just stop and think for a minute... the answer to continue your journey becomes pretty obvious. The gameplay is very simple, merely needing your directional keys and 'ctrl' in order to grab things and move, it's simplicity adds to the brilliance. I'm genuinely amazed how such a simple game has had such a lasting effect on me, it's certainly one of those games you will never be able to forget.
The scenery and atmosphere of this game is what makes Limbo what it is. The animation is fluid and It's film noire and morbid ambience make for a sensational world in which you can immerse yourself in and get very emotionally invested with your character. The aura of the game is eerie and very, very ominous. You know something wanting to kill you is never more than five seconds away and that thought can keep you suspenseful and on the edge of your seat. Whether it's a world trap, animal or even a young creepy, ravenous murderer; this game will ensure you cannot rest for one second in the world of Limbo, which makes for a fantastic game.
This game is definitely one that everybody needs to experience at least once, the game should take you around 4-5 hours to complete and you'll definitely want to run through it a few more times to get another taste of the amazing atmosphere that Limbo creates. Not only is this one of the best 2D sidescrollers you'll ever experience, it's one of the best games you'll ever encounter when put up against all other genres. A remarkable and enjoying experience.
Pros:
- A Beautiful and atmospheric world.
- Amazing sound effects and music throughout the game.
- Great storyline.
- Shrewd and engaging puzzles.
As I cannot even fathom a fault in Limbo, it's got to be a definite 10/10.

I can and cannot reccomend this game. I both love it, and hate it. It's full of a rich story, which, when augmented with the free browser game "Fallen London" thats made by the same team, is even deeper, but the gameplay itself has some issues.
Firstly, as others have aptly noted, the combat system is more or less just plain meh. Its frustratingly difficult in the beginning and later on is just rote method of blasting enemies. Secondly, while it can be fun to roam around and discover things for yourself, the game can become tedious with all the running around trying to figure out what particular item you need when. Thirdly, it drags. Not just when it comes to item acquisition, the game just gets boring. I put 30 hours into it, more or less loving it, and then finally, after I dabbled in the sunlight trade ( look on the guides for more info on THAT ), I just got BORED. The game had mostly lost its charm. It seemed as if it was either too hard to get money through regular methods, or too easy with the sunlight trade ( I do believe they've nerfed the sunlight trade in the latest update, but I haven't look into it- so don't go by that assessment entirely ).
The point is that its a slow game with a really rich story. You'll find yourself slogging across the Unterzee questioning your sanity for even playing the game anymore, but still enjoying the immersion. And also, when you DO discover that item you've been needing for hours, its absolutely wonderful!
Lastly, the game is a roguelike, you can turn on manual saving, but the default setting is rogue. You die and lose a ton of your gains.
Bottom line: I'm on the fence. If you can get it on sale then go ahead for sure, full price.... idk. I'm not saying not to, but I can't guarantee you'll like it.

Sunless Sea is a game from the developers of Fallen London so i went in expecting to need knowlege from that to enjoy this but the opposite is true, i played both and know squat. The world of the unterzee is as vast as it is confusing, you won't find all of it's secrets in one run in fact you'll be surprised to find out anything before your first captain is with the drownies at the bottom of the unterzee or in the belly of a zee beast but that's ok, this game is made to be enjoyed through several deaths.
Lets start out simple, the graphics are great for what this is. You're playing a 2D overhead exploring game, don't expect crytech graphics with frostbite action but expect beautiful terrifying buildings, lost islands that will invade your dreams or give you nightmares. Simple beauty is what i'm trying to say here, in my library of tripple A games with "real life graphics" this is one of the most beautiful because the images stick, when you see Irem or the Sea of Statues you don't easily forget them, they're all as different as can be yet all as haunting as the game implies.
Combat is simple in Sunless Sea and expet to get into a fight often, you keep the enemy in sight of your guns and let them charge while staying out of their range and try to sink them and take their cargo or flesh depending on what you killed. There are skills that help with combat by making you hit harder or make you harder to see but that's not something i'll go over th game does it well enough on it's own. One important thing i need to stress is not to get cocky, from the very start you can run into enemies that will sink you faster than the titanic, learn what is where and when to run.
Now my favorite part of Sunless Sea is the story, you need to find it. You are free to make whatever destiny you want, run between ports grabbing things for people or taking reports for the admiralty, sink ships or monsters and become the most powerful thing on the unterzee. There are several ways to win the game but none of them come easy, explore and make your own destiny in the unterzee or find the fastest way to retire you'll have fun either way and uncover things that might make you change course.
One thing i want to note about the game is that when your captain's run is over, win lose or draw, you can make a new one that can get special boosts depending on your last captain's choices. For example if you made a will your next character will start off with more choices over your items, if you made some heirlooms you'll get more money for your next captain, you can even find things in the game Fallen London for your next captain.
Sunless Sea is a great game, it's as long as you want to make it but terrifying all the way to the end, not in a horror game type of way though don't expect any jumpscares unless you happen to stumble upon the eye. At the time i'm writing this Sunless Sea has only been on full release for a short time and there are some things it needs like more stories to fill in spots and some more items to strive for but overall i give it a 9/10, great game just in need of polish.

To note, I've been a fan of Failbetter games for around five years now since I started with Fallen London (if you haven't played it, it's also great - possibly the best browser game out there, which got me through a lot of long shift-work nights years ago) back when it was still called Echo Bazaar. I participated in the Kickstarter for Sunless Sea and anxiously awaited its arrival.
That being said, this is probably the best game that's come out of Kickstarter thus far. There's something in this for just about everyone, whether you're into immersive gameplay -- there are over 250,000 words of writing in this -- or if you're into combat and mechanics. Beyond all of that, however, the world of Sunless Sea and Fallen London in general is leagues better than many triple-A games in terms of quality, depth, and the ability to pull you into it. By the third or fourth hour of playing Sunless Sea, you'll be cursing the Glorious Servants of the Dawn Machine and sigh in relief at the sight of Low Barnet and Ravenna's Rock as London pulls up over the horizon. You'll hedge your bets against whether you should betray your country to your enemies for a chance to trade at their port or if you'll try to curry favor to get a trading license in another, more expensive fashion - despite the fact that both paths have their cost.
Foremost, Sunless Sea is a game about isolation and terror, and surviving that to continue your journey. When you begin, the game has no mercy for you whatsoever. You start off in a tiny steamship with a small crew and a friend from your childhood (based on the background you pick) as one of your officers. The Unterzee is a vast, unforgiving landscape filled with strange monsters, vicious pirates, and enemies of London and Her Eternal Majesty, the Traitor Empress. You may run out of fuel, or you may run out of supplies and possibly be forced into cannibalism. Fear of the wide ocean might cause your crew to mutiny against you as you descend into madness.
As you continue on, making your way around the Unterzee and plying your trade as either a privateer, a servant of the admiralty, or just as a general explorer, you'll open up new areas in the map holding different locations with new and strange storylines, as well as possible new ambitions for your character. If you've selected your ultimate goal at the end of it all to find wealth and retire in a mansion with your spouse and children, this may change drastically if you suddenly find an intriguing method of traveling beyond the known boundaries of the Unterzee, or maybe even find an island where you can set up your own private kingdom, allied or not with London.
Your characters will die when you begin, and they will die frequently. On the chance that you manage to work your way through your ambitions and win, you will open up new venues and opportunities for future captains that follow in your character's footsteps when you start a new game. For instance, in one game session, I found an island that I colonized, declared independence and allied myself with London. From here on out, all of my future captains in my legacy share a benefit to their stats due to the choices I made previously.
That's the second most important aspect of Sunless Sea: choice. The choices you make in the game will absolutely affect the game world. Do you support the rebels in a strange foreign land, or the leaders? You only get to choose once, and your choice will forever be cemented during that play-through. Do you align yourself with London or the Far Khanate? Are you smuggling illicit drugs into port or are you playing the smugglers and reporting it to the admiralty? Choices sometimes burn bridges and sometimes open up entirely new avenues on which you can travel.
For the players that are more into role playing aspects, there are elements of romance and intrigue. If you find a sweetheart in London, what do you do when that officer you had a tryst with comes calling to request another fling? Infidelity can mean you lose your sweetheart, your children, and the comfort you took from your family. You may acquire inklings of the Great Game played among the powerful and elite and begin to build a network of spies in various ports throughout the Unterzee. You can anger the gods of the zee and suffer their curses; make the god Salt angry and you could return to London and find your spouse dead and your child gone.
Having had Sunless Sea since its early release on Steam, the game has grown in major, major ways. Combat is very challenging, where you maneuver around your enemy and attempt to find a firing solution while your enemy does the same. The game itself is not strictly built for the grind mechanics that a lot of roguelikes are. While there are some occasions where you can make a decent amount of money trading things, you might find that it's a finite opportunity, like selling sunlight to the servants of the Pirate King or trading Sphinxstone to a mysterious builder in London. Even still, when those opportunities run dry, another story opens up, along with other choices that will color the rest of the game. These were not options at all until within the last few months, and Failbetter Games is constantly adding new things to the game. Also -- if you're a Fallen London player, you can link your Sunless Sea game to your Fallen London account.
I cannot recommend this game enough. If you enjoy roguelike games, and if you like games wherein survival and story is at the forefront, or if you just want to rock out with some cannons and blow your enemies to hell, then this is the game for you. With beautiful hand-drawn artwork and a real sense of forboding that seeps into you without even noticing it, you'll get so much out of this game that it's more than worth the price.

Limbo is not a bad game, but neither is it particularly good.  It has its strong points certainly.  Foremost is the art style.  It's dark, atmospheric and moody.  Of course, this is the main selling point.  Some of the puzzles as well are well done.  However, the bad can easily overshadow the good.  Many of the puzzles are overly simple, while many of the others are dependent on the player simply making guesses about what will happen then proceeding through trial and error.  Most damning however, is the fact that some of the puzzles can't even be properly be called that, and are instead simply exercises in jumping where an error of even a tenth of a second kills the player.  This is a cheap trick to work into a puzzle game and it destroys the intellectual aspect in favor of button mashing, especially considering that many play with a keyboard, not a controller.  Overall, a disappointing execution of a promising game.

The Beginners Guide is a game I strongly recommend people play.

This is the first Steam refund I have ever asked for. I believed this game would fit up to the extents that were advertised by its creator; The Stanley Parable was a trippy game. And while it had no clear end, it was funny in its performance. It was special, unique; something never done before.
This? This game was a movie disguised as a "game". And it's not a movie that even has an ending, either.
If you are someone that loves to be left looking for answers, deeper, or artistic meaning, I could not recommend this game more. However, I just bought this game maybe for a fun time, or an ending that would blow my mind. Something creative! Instead, I got a movie cut short by an "author" trying harder than a baby to walk to be dramatic. There was no ending, no clear purpose; The Beginner's Guide was a short experience that left you emotional; but not crying, simply confused and almost angry with a creator that seemingly could not be bothered to actually try and communicate their purpose.
EDIT: I have just done some snooping around; The Beginner's Guide has nothing to do with its title, Coda is not real, and this game was created simply as a therapy session, or maybe a "cry for help" from its creator. Davey fell into a depression after The Stanley Parable was released, as he felt his work had lost its meaning. This game is meant to explain that, but of course he does not mention this and simply leaves this abstract, depressed thought behind for us to fall for and him to cash in on. Nice going, Davey.

FIrst off - I am writing this review using my childs account because the hardware registers itself to the first person who logs into it.  You apparently can't do a review otherwise.  I will reply to it with my main account if you have questions you can send them there.
I purchased the i5 Model for my kids bedroom.  They keep fighing over their gaming rig (I have my own that's off limits, they use an older one I built a while back).   My requirements were simple:  It had to play a good portion of their steam library, it had to be compact and it had to not get in it's own way.   The Alienware Steam machine seemed like a good fit.   I thought of the Alpha - but I figured without a good place for a keyboard and mouse I wanted something where it was not going to be needed.
I ordered the unit on the 4th of November, it arrived on the 10th.   My first task after unboxing was to get it setup and start loading games and testing.
Some games they love are not available - Anything Lego (including Lego Worlds), Blockland, Beam.NG - not available.   But some of their mainstays were:  Stanley Parable, Portal 1&2, Limbo.  I decided to buy a few new games during the steam machine launch sale.  I added ARK, Shadows of Mordor (for me), the Trine Collection and Dirt Showdown.   I have two accounts for the boys, one that will only be one this machine, and one on the their PC rig.  This way they don't kick each other off - but I needed some games to make the Steam Machine enticing.  They wouldn't have wanted to learn the controller otherwise.  I'll get to that soon.
The controller needed a firmware update to work properly (it was jittery before the update).   The boot process and update process is very streamlined.  There two types of updates:  OS and Client.  They are performed seamlessly.   Booting, connecting to the wireless network and adding accounts was very easy.   The controller isn't quite as intuitive as it could be in the UI - but I did get used to it.
I started testing games.  Portal 2 loaded quick - but surprisingly was at a real low resolution.  I pumped it up and it played really well.  Getting used to the controller was a task.  I think we take gamepads for granted - they've been in their current state for so long we forget that they actually had a learning curve.  Well, the Steam Controller has a steeper curve.  I would compare it to learning how to type and use a mouse for the first time.   While I know what everything does as far as how to use an analog stick, use a touchpad, use the buttons - the muscle memory just isn't there.
I tried Trine next.  One thing became really apparent - some games need a little babysitting to get working and Trine 3 was one of those.  It came up with a config page right on start that was really awkward to use.  Software Developers need to do better.   Including Valve.   No game should start lower than 720p on even the lowest iteration of Steam Machine.   Better hardware detection is needed.   Anyways, this title I did fool with some controller mappings.   I didn't get too deep into gameplay, but it worked, albeit the controls would need some practice.
I finally tried Dirt Showdown.   It played wonderfully.   The graphics were good from the get-go.  The Controller was well mapped by default.  It felt strangely natural to use the steam controller for racing.  I decided to add motion control for steering - and that worked really great.  I'm surprised not much is mentioned about motion control in most of the mainstream reviews.
My next task was a non steam game... Minecraft.   A must for my kids.   I am no newbie to Linux, having worked with it since Slackware was a new distribution.  However I haven't used it too much recently - so had to dig a little to figure out how to install Java.  Once I got that squared away, I wrote a very simple .sh script to launch minecraft, then asked the community how to get it in to the Steam Library and got a quick response.   It played awesome after a short config session with the controller.   It almost plays like the Xbox One version now.  That's a huge plus..
Now, I know there are benchmarks circulating that aren't shedding SteamOS in a good light right now...  But to be honest, as far as playing PC games in a console format, I really didn't need benchmarks - the Alienware Steam Machine runs them as good or better than our Xbox One.   To think that there is a large amount of room for improvement as Valve and the developers close the gap with the graphics is a bonus to me.   I'm not trying to make this thing scream FPS, I'm just trying to let the kids have some fun playing their games.
Next was the kid test.   My 6 year old was in awe.  I don't know how he knew, but he said "is that a steam machine?".   I must have mentioned it before.  In any case, he was initially frustrated with the controller for games he's already played with an Xbox 360 controller.   But for the games he hadn't (especially ARK) he was willing to spend the time and learn.  He picked it up rather quick - and while not perfectly proficient, he's now going back to the games he knows and playing.  I've had to help with some of the mappings - but I don't feel the need to setup an xbox controller quite yet.
Now - let me get into some pet peeves:
I wish you could turn the machine on from the controller.  You can't.
It's not entirely stable.  I've had games crash.  I've had the system reboot.  But it's been minimal, and seems to be game specific.

The system comes with Games not Available to play on SteamOS.  Really?   C'mon Alienware.   Also a bummer that Rocket League isn't yet available.
The web browser needs work - and a lot of it trivial stuff like auto complete in the keyboard overlay, one button shortcut to the URL box.
The controller should be customization for the UI.  It's not - or maybe I'm missing something?
No groups or discussions in the UI... huh?  why?  Steam Community is it's strength, why the disconnect there?
The GPU is not upgradable.  Yeah, I know they compromised because of size/cooling/performance... but thbbbbt....
----------------------
Those are my major gripes.   Most of this is easily fixable.
I am going to recommend the steam machine.  But on the prefix that people buying the system know that there is a bit of a curve with the controller and that not everything is 100%.  Even the available game in the library are hit and miss.  Some developers seem to have taken the time to really think out the steam controller (Shadows of Mordor), others it seems an afterthought (Trine).
I am still learning - and so are my kids.  But I feel this will only get better as time goes by.  I'm not giving up my PC rig for one of these, but as a second system I say go for it!

My kids are still going strong with the Steam Machine.   I found one Lego game that works - Lego Minifigures Online.   I'm having trouble getting it to log my child in automatically - but once in it plays great.

At the time of writing this, Sacred 3 has a 'Mostly Negative' rating on Steam. I honestly can't think of a game I've played recently that is 'mostly negative' other than this game, and that includes quite a few garbage titles acquired through greenlight bundles and the like. 'Mostly negative' is an extremely low rating for Steam, frankly, it puts the game in the same kind of expression as one would describe taking a shortcut through an alleyway to discover a dumpster fire.
Or I guess in this case, someone wrote 3 on the dumpster fire. Anyway: Sacred 3's two biggest problems are likely that it was launched at an AAA price-tag and that it is marked a sequel to Sacred 2, instead of a sequel to Sacred Citadel, the latter being a side-scrolling beat 'em up but from what I've read far closer to Sacred 3 than Sacred 2 was. The game is now $15 and I was kind of astounded to see it in the dollar tier of a recent humble bundle, so I picked it up.
Anyway goods and bads:
+Beautiful, AAA level graphic quality for a game of this genre. Tons of scenic variety, lots of beautiful details. I really can't overstate how nice the graphical and aesthetic work is here.
+Fun, frantic, high energy combat with some RPG trappings... Reminds me a lot of small dungeon WoW, but more frantic. Contary to other reviews, you can and do change up your skills, weapons and some other minor stuff, but it's not anywhere near a RPG really.
+Lots of fun boss fights
+Excellent, abundant voice acting. Your character, your weapon "spirit", your telepath and usually the boss of the dungeon all talk. Gives the game a lot of personality that changes up as you play.
+Good score
-Incredibly lacking in enemy variety for game length. Mind-bogglingly so. They put together more models and skins than actual enemy types. The enemies you do fight have personality, but you fight the same guys over and over.
-Combat gets repetitive due to lack of enemy variety, game can be a bit grindy
-Some visual elements don't translate well, and often enemies winding up a tell can't be seen, or they're allowed to attack from offscreen, or there's just too much stuff constantly flooding in to move properly. Game is missing that last bit of polish and gets real janky at times.
-Game has SOME RPG trappings, but not nearly enough and a lot of it doesn't make sense. There is only one kind of random drop in the entire game, everything else is scripted and often nonsensically. The talent trees are simplified, and you only have 2 skills with four other inputs at a time - attack, dodge or block, light art, heavy art, bash and execute - and the two you can change aren't staggered well so you don't end up switching a lot. Most of the weapon spirits aren't well balanced, so again, you tend to get stuck with certain set ups for long stretchs of the game.
-Your telepath who feeds you instructions is usually charming, and the voice actress does good work with what she is given, but in some cases they didn't record enough dialogue or re-use/repeat dialogue way too quickly. It can get really annoying at times. Again - that last bit of polish.
-Story and humor have tone all over the place. Some of the jokes are just awful. While most of the voice acting is excellent, the "big bad" is poorly written and just sounds way too hammy. The game is about 25% more shlock than it needs to be.
Anyway, is Sacred 3 great? Well, it has great graphical assets, which I assume the original pricetag was informed by. The rest of the game is ... Okay? Good in parts, but usually just above average, kinda terribly unpolished in patchs. It's certainly not the 'mostly negative' hobo in a dumpster fire it sounds like. I can totally understand people who paid $50 being upset at it, but for the current asking price or out of a bundle, I think it's pretty okay. It
have been a much better game, and titled Sacred Citadel 2, and it's a real shame I doubt anyone will ever do anything ever again with the excellent art assets.

I will list the positives first then move on to the negatives.
The graphics are great, the animations excellent. Unlike in Blood Bowl: Chaos edition, the animations actually add to the drama rather than distract from it due to their clunkiness in CE.
Even in the 8 race basic edition, there is quite a bit of variation in the races, so players of different styles can experience very different play styles.
Private leagues and competitive leagues enforce rules that make it less likely, that people concede games mid-game, so there is a lot of possibilities to play proper matches in good humour. The developers are also continuing the development of these features, and are also adding new teams as DLC.
However, there are quite a few problems as well. First of all, in the official casual ladder people concede constantly, since there are no negative rewards for doing so (I myself recently conceded a match after I lost half my team to injuries in the first half. In my defence, it was the first match with that team and there was no way I was going to keep it. But still, it was a douchey move, my opponent certainly wanted to finish the match.).
There have been several bugs, like the infamous reimbursement of money used in the inducements stage before a match.
There are only 8 teams in the basic game, and the dlc are about 7e a piece, which, if you get them all, adds up to a quite an expensive package. The dlc are also coming by at a rather slow pace, since the game is already a year old, and there have been only 5 new teams so far. This adds up to only about half of what CE had.
The most serious problem with the game is, that there are no "fun" teams available at the moment. The teams are all more or less competitive, and there are no teams that are designed to be fun and not serious. For example goblins, halflings and vampires aren't great, but when one gets bored of being hacked to death by chaos, dwarves or the undead (necrotic or not), it would be fun to unwind and lose with a team that is not even supposed to win all the matches.
All in all, it is a mixed bag and I recommend it to anyone who finds the setting interesting, but you need to be prepared to study the game and watch some tutorials on youtube. It is great fun when you get into it though, just very frustrating kind of fun!
In my opinion is a good game.

I love this game because it requires the player to figure out where and what the problems to be solved are. It is a beautiful discovery game, it always leaves you wanting more, and its secrets are elusive.
This game also makes me terribly sad because it suffers from serious design problems that prevent the game from being played in the intended manner.
There isn't varying content in the early game to justify the permadeath aspect. What could be a different experience each time, with a randomized pick of 3 possible storylines for each island and no way to predict which of the innumerable sets the game will generate each time, is instead the exact same scenario repeated every. single. time. you. restart. after. death.
London could have had characters which depend on which of the other storylines the dice have yielded, but instead they are all the same every time.
The world is too empty for its concept, with an artist who is more productive than its writer. Its writing, which by all accounts should be its bread and butter, is sparse. There's a lot of it, but it's sparse. There isn't enough of it for the size of the game, and the game is too greedy with its prose, saving it only for the deepest mysteries and not giving much of its treasures to new players in the early game.
Furthermore, the pay offs at the end of most stories don't give answers and invite new questions, but rather unsatisfyingly dance around any sort of conclusions.
In addition, the game robs itself of its most interesting possibilities. There are no stories interrupting and changing the tides of battle. There are no Ahab battle epics. There isn't any player piracy potential due to an embarrasingly persistent balance problem -- still there as of summer 2016 -- preventing the player from capturing ships. There are no letters of marque to introduce political intrigue on the high seas.
The developer has in the past remarked that more content doesn't solve design problems. But this is a permadeath game, and varying unpredictable circumstances is the only way to pull it off. He is wrong in this case. There are whole beautifully drawn islands that remain nearly completely empty and completely predictable the whole game. There are promised story lines that were severely pared down or simply never completed, and unpromised story lines obviously omitted and sadly attested to by the beautiful art that lies awaiting them. The world is so interesting, but this game is like reading the first chapter of a fantasy epic and never getting to experience the rest of the story.
The developer has also remarked that due to the number of art pieces vs the number of words in the game, it proves that a picture is worth 300 some odd words. The finished game would prove the adage: a picture's worth a thousand words.
I still recommend the game. I hope the developer decides to fill out what is there rather than solely expanding the scope.

Limbo is not a bad game, but neither is it particularly good.  It has its strong points certainly.  Foremost is the art style.  It's dark, atmospheric and moody.  Of course, this is the main selling point.  Some of the puzzles as well are well done.  However, the bad can easily overshadow the good.  Many of the puzzles are overly simple, while many of the others are dependent on the player simply making guesses about what will happen then proceeding through trial and error.  Most damning however, is the fact that some of the puzzles can't even be properly be called that, and are instead simply exercises in jumping where an error of even a tenth of a second kills the player.  This is a cheap trick to work into a puzzle game and it destroys the intellectual aspect in favor of button mashing, especially considering that many play with a keyboard, not a controller.  Overall, a disappointing execution of a promising game.

Sunless Sea is a story-driven game about exploration and taking risks, but what truly sets it apart is its phenomenal writing and unique setting. As the story goes, London has been taken underground by bats, and it now sits on the coast of the Sunless Sea - a large, underground body of water, covered in darkness and chock-full of nasty beasties. Your job is simple. Make a living here, or perish. As you sail across the sea, you will discover ports and settlements, all of them full of unique stories and events. These all set the theme for the game: a strange mix of humour and horror, bizarreness in every sense of the word, but without breaking the suspension of disbelief. You have to experience it to believe it.

The previous issues I had with this game's Kickstarter exclusive content have been fixed by the devs. The overwhelming majroity of the exclusive content has been added, for free, to the base game, and what remains exclusive is so tiny and petty that I cannot, in good faith, justify giving the game a negative review any longer.
Because, at the end of the day, this is an amazing game. It's not for everyone. If you're looking for a complex trading sim or deep and engaging tactical combat or infinite replayability or super detailed character progression, you're gana be very disapointed.
But what this game does well, specifically story and atmosphere, it does better than almost any other game I can think of. AND there's an actual game behind all of that story! Sure, the game behind the story is a little rough around the edges, a bit unfair at times, and not the deepest or most engaging game, but it's something to do between lulls in the story and elevates this from a simple "choose-your-own-adventure-novel" or something like that into an actual game that just so happens to have one of the most interesting and well written stories in gaming.
So if you don't mind reading (there's no voice acting and every single thing you do generates a small mountain of text), and you want to experience a world that is both unique and awesome (in the classical sense), with a very light side of trading sim/naval combat this is the game for you.
If, on the other hand, you want detailed nautical combat or a complex trading sim, I'd advise you to look elsewhere.

After 26 hours of play, I've decided to write a review. There are many good reviews already, so I'll try to make it short. Sunless Sea is mostly an exploration game and interactive fiction, with some rogue-like elements, including permadeath with the possibility of passing things to your next character, and semi-procedurally generated environnements. The universe is mysterious, intriguing like Lovecraftian universes should be; you get stories there and there, and you have to put the pieces together. The 2d graphics are gorgeous in my opinion, the art style is great, and the shaders are beautiful. And the writing is great.
The game feels a lot like interactive fiction. There are two main aspects to the gameplay. There's sailing the
, where you explore the vast
, fight enemies, using your keyboard to move and attack, while keeping an eye on your fuel, supplies, and Terror level. And then there's the reading : when stopping at a port, the game feels more like an interactive fiction. There are many interactions, with different conditions, choices, and sometimes a random element. The two aspects of the game complement each other. There are also random events when you're at sea, text can pop up while you're
, with choices to make most of the time. If you've played Fallen London (the game), you may be familiar with the storylets system used in the game. If not, you may want to check some gameplay videos, just to see if it's your cup of tea.
Sunless Sea is primarly a game of
. You'll have to make
of choices. And not only in the "interactive fiction parts", but also while explorating. If you go that far, will you manage to get back to Fallen London (the main city)? Will you be able to buy enough fuel and supplies if you buy that thing? Can you afford to take a detour to go to this place?
The game can be hard when you start. My first captain died after a few hours, with no heir, and no legacy anyway. My second captain survived 20hrs+, and he's still alive (although it's probably because I can be very cautious). I don't find the game that hard. It's just
grindy. Discovering new places feels great, but you won't always discover places, and sometimes you may not have enough fuel/supplies/money (to buy those) to go further into unknown territory. Making money will seem hard at first, but once you understand how the game works, what each places need, and where you can get what you need, making money and progressing the game will be easier. If you're cautious like me, you may survive for way longer than you thought, and even secure things for your next captain!
Keep in mind that exploration and reading+interacting are the main focuses of the game. The combat system is not great, you have no way to dodge an attack, and most of the time staying close behind an enemy will grant you a boring and relatively easy victory -- because enemies can't fire backward. So that's one flaw, but not
important, because once again that's not the focus of the game.
I'm a little worried about the replay value on the long run, because my second captain is still alive after 20hrs+ and I've discovered a good portion of the map. But with a different ambitions, different choices (and the choices that come after), different focuse (combat, or exploration, etc.), I think I could go with a third captain when my second one dies.
Sunless Sea is a great game, and you should buy it! It's a great mix of exploration, a little survival, and interactive fiction, with lots of stories to read, and choices to make. The universe is intriguing. The lore almost secret. And the writing is good. The game may not be perfect -- I'm looking at you, combat system --, but it's still great!
One advice for future
: when leaving port to sail the
, stop at as many ports as you can, even the ones you've already visited, because reporting back when returning to the main city will earn you some money and fuel.

There are some real standout characters both from physical design and voice acting standpoints.  Who doesn't remember Sander Cohen after they play this game once!
The graphics still hold up today (just finished a playthrough 1/9/2014) with both the characters and backgrounds having great detail and art. Of course, the game has the iconic big daddy fights that are a lot of fun and a real challenge on hard difficulty.

So dark and brooding, yet also whimsical and quirky, is this game known as Limbo.
Or is it rather a mystical piece of art?
Thrust into this monochrome world, there is not much, it seems, that could happen. Those two white dots blink as you walk, then sprint, through the seemingly desolate landscape. Suddenly, you encounter a simple bear trap. You walk into it, you get snapped by the trap, and you die. Yet moments later, you resurrect, ready to once again attempt to cross the path of the bear trap.
As simple as that sounds, it presents nothing of the challenge that lays ahead. Gradually, more and more traps face you. Tumbling platforms, giant boulders, machine guns and sawblades join the array of deadly machines pitted against the tiny boy. Pitted against you.
Yet all you can do is proceed past them, slowly but surely. You work your way through this haunting and surreal maze, frustration ever building, until finally... You break past the last barrier in your way and you find the answer, the reason, for which you suffered that punishment. For enduring so much.
Limbo is an extraordinary work that has sent many a chill down my spine. From the unique atmosphere of the black & white world, to the eerie but beautiful ambient soundtrack, to the breathtaking yet simplistic story behind it all, Limbo is an absolutely stunning experience that is not to be missed.

Sunless Sea is first and foremost about its writing. It's what you come here for. Everything from the short snippets of the daily life aboard your Zee-steamer that show up in your logbook, to the stories you find on the Unterzee's numerous islands, is insanely well written. This a world with depth (pun intended), novelty and beautifully realised characters and locales. The gameplay itself, at least outside of combat, moves at a steady and relaxed pace, but the undercurrent of tension is always present. At any time, you have five resources to manage: Your hull (ship's health), fuel, supplies, crew and terror. Lose too many crewmen, or see everyone on your ship go mad with terror, and it's usually the end of your journey. But the game encourages you to take risk. Playing it safe staying in home waters, where the towns are sane and the worst you'll find can be taken out with three cannon shots, will soon leave you starved for the resources you need to survive at sea. No, the game demands you venture forth, into darkness and danger, into tension, risk and reward. When you inevitably die, it's not the end, though. Depending on your preparations, you're able to pass variable amounts of your skills and resources on to your successor, and then the game starts again, a new captain setting out from Fallen London, onto the deep, dark sea.
Everything about this game is thought through, and if you don't mind reading and playing a slower-paced game, you'll find a bounty of brilliant words and spine chilling tension in Sunless Sea.

The Long Dark is one of the best survival games I've played. The setting of the game is quite beautiful and interesting. The maps are also intimidating enough that a new player will feel like the maps are large and hostile while a more experienced player will be at home in them. The game can be very peaceful and relaxing half of the time and very intense the other half.
The game doesn't rely on zombies or cheap "survival game" tropes to make the game enjoyable. Instead, the game has a gritty and "real" survival style that sets it apart from other games of the genre. This is one thing that makes TLD worth it over other survival games. The art style and design is also a unique atribute of this game that makes it quite memorable.
The biggest downside of the game is the story mode, after many years of the devs saying it was coming it finally arrived over-hyped. The story is boring. While many people who like TLD might enjoy a more slow paced game, the story is sluggish without taking its time. The beginning of the game is sort of a tutorial which is good for new players but completely halts the "action" for around 30 mins. This also goes against one of my favorite things about TLD, which was the way you kind of have to figure things out with no tutorial. The tutorial takes away some of the discovery aspects of the game for me and I wish the beginning of the story was different. The update that was released with the story also changed things like the UI and menu and made both MUCH less aesthetically pleasing as well as gameplay changed that hinder the game in so many ways. I feel like since the story came out, the game has taken a huge turn for the worse. Before the story update the game was 9.5/10 for me and felt perfectly balanced and beautiful. But now, the game just doesn't have the same feel that it did before. This is really sad to me because it was one of my favorite games on steam.
In short, don't play the story or try and find an older patch to play somehow.

Ep1 review–
The game runs fine on my potato! Thank the elder noodle deities.
That said, Telltale's Bats is a little disappointing for a starter episode. I like the fact that most of the time, you're actually not wearing the cowl, but it's going to be on the strengths of the next episodes that this series can eventually be recommended. This is just such a stock Telltale experience for now, and the "detective work" bit is a travesty. They even lifted bits of the boring CGI forensics minigame thing from the Arkham games. Come now, dream up something novel! And I don't mean "what if Joker was real-ly grimdark?"
I'm not into the, uh, thing where someone instantaneously figures out Batman's identity. That's silly, and also nicked from *cough* somewhere else.
Harvey Dent I can't get a grip on. His personality probably isn't lifted off previous Bats work, which delights me.
Productionwise, the ep1 visuals are overall pretty good and at least thought out, although the art's in probably the least personal style I've seen in a Bats product. These guys would probably make The Joker look like John Cusack. The voice work is decent, but the soundtrack is just a dreary Hans Zimmer imitation. It seems Batman has exactly one soundtrack these days, and it's some military drums to a bunch of arpeggiated string orchestras. Guh. Shut up.
I suppose I'll edit this review later when the season has had its run, but right now I don't think people who aren't mega Bats fans benefit from shelling out the full price. So can I greenthumb something if I think it's not that hot on full price? Eh, I guess I can. Don't buy full price, but thumbs up tentatively. Don't let me down.

These are some Pros/Cons I found in my 12 hours of playing (had to start over about 3 times until I got the hang of it), 1 full in game year was my final play through (Didn't die, just stopped playing)
Pros:
* The game is quite balanced, if you play it like a tower defense game
* No limit to the number of walls, so you could build a maze if you want to
* Weather mechanics that do things rather than just for visuals
* Villagers aren't completely ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥
* You can help the villagers build things by dropping resources on buildings yourself
* If a villager sees a floating rock they get confused
* You can amass a golem army
Cons:
* Stone Slingers couldn't shoot over walls that other ranged weapons could (bullet, bow, fire)
* The game lags quite a bit after playing the same map for awhile
* The game lags with alot of things on screen at once (Could probably hide things off screen to save on resources)
* Enemies like to "wander" into the village with a path from across the map, instead of only when they are "wandering into the village"
* Walls prevent you from building on the other side once closed off
* Villagers only repair things inside your "circle of influence" leading to walls being destroyed that lie outside it
* Stone walls can be damaged by fire and can be caught on fire, yet skeletons can't be caught on fire
* When a villager sees an enemy, they sometimes run like babies
* Skeletons are too spooky
* Spectre's have insane amounts of health
* Villagers can starve too easily if you don't build at least 5 farms at the start
* Having to stockpile food for summer doesn't seem right
* Villagers can "overheat" in the winter, while it's snowing
* When the "Problem Report" states that one of your villagers is on fire, there is no easy way to find them and save them
* Villagers can catch fire while in water
* There is no Smite ability that you can use

I feel it's only right to fully justify my utter distaste for this "game" as so many of you are so fond of it. Here's everything that I found to be make this game utter crap. I've tried to like this game, I really have. I keep playing it even though I know I hate it just to try and give it more of a chance but every time it disappoints me all over again. And it really is disappointing as it has everything that should make a  good game.
This will also be the very first game ever that I shall be deleting from my Steam Library. That's how bad it is. I horde all of my games but this one, this one is by far one of the worst games I have ever played.
1:Guns. My how this game like to give you the ultimate arsenal and then make it a complete pain to use. To get a new gun you have to sit through two cutscenes and buy one thing at a time. Then on top of that if you want more ammo you have to do it all over again as the enemy only carry a variety of about 4 weapons. So you should probably just get used to their guns as that's what you'll be using for the entirety of the game as those cutscenes get rather boring.
2: Travelling. On the rare occasion I got into a vehicle it seemed like the game was trying it's hardest to throw me out of it. If you hit the smallest rock in the road the the car spins out of control and rolls for a good 18 miles. Sure this looks awesome but it's not very helpful when you're trying to get somewhere. So the majority of my time was spent with the parachute and grappling hook which really is not the fastest way to get around. So you have this big, open, vast world to traverse your way across which you shall not be doing as you'll be using the extraction to get places.
3: The wolrd. Sure, this game has a big beautiful world for you to cause havok in (havok used VERY loosely) but it's so damn empty you can't really do much in it. If trees were destructable great, at least then you'd have something to break but as you can't drive off road this is a losing fight either way.
There's loads of tress, loads of sand and loads of snow. That's what you'll be seeing.
4:Destruction. Pahahaha!. Spend your time causing "chaos". That's a bigger lie than No Mans Sky. You can blow up small red barrels (like in every game ever) and big red barrels. Sure there's a few small things inbetween like statues and antennas but after driving for half an hour to get to them it just doesn't fill the hole.
5:Missions. Now you have several different missions in this. And by that I mean you have different places to get missions. Mission variety is veeeeeeeeery limited. Whenever you do a faction mission don't expect to be drawn in, they last a whole whopping 10 seconds. Literally "go here, break this, listen to someone". The breaking isn't even fun. I've had more fun and been more amazed by destruction in Red Faction 1. The agency missions are a bit longer but still doesn't leave a lasting impression of any kind other then "I paid for this".
Oh I nearly forgot, there are more missions available here. Lots and lots of races. How better to cause chaos and convinve big nasty people you're on their side then to run around town and race. The amount of races in this game is ridiculous. It's like they put all their focus into that and left everything else for the crunch period.
6:Collectathon 9000. My god, the collectables. So, so many. And if you're hoping to upgrade the equipment and vehicles you'll never use you're gonna need to get them. Especially the armour upgrades as you die faster than a childs hopes and dreams as they watch their parents drive away from the orphanage leaving them behind.
The good stuff? It's pretty. I suppose. Unfortunately that is not enough to keep me engaged in the game. Just skip the first two and go straight onto the 3rd. They sort out pretty much every issue this one has. You're not missing anything, you're saving yourself from this torturous experience.
