It's a fun game but right up front: it's extremely shallow and not difficult at all. Despite what so many people would have you believe, the "challenge" of Banished lies almost entirely in the atrociously stupid, counterintuitive AI and how to build to compensate for it. That's pretty much it. Other than that, it's just a repetitive citybuilder with no progression. Everything the game has to offer which, in it's vanilla state is very little, is unlocked right from the start and restricted only by the amount of resources and people you have available to build and staff it.
If you're wondering why I recommend the game it's because what it was designed to do it does extremely well - build nice looking towns that start as a group of destitute exiles and can end in a thriving city with many thousands of people. With the right mods it can be a beautiful thriving city, limited only by your imagination, and you really do need to mod it. Vanilla Banished contains almost nothing. All those beautiful houses and cities you see in the screenshots? Those are mods, almost always Colonial Charter and/or New Medieval Towns.
That's all this game is good for. It is NOT a deep simulator of any kind and a child can make this thing work by simply following a few basic rules. And don't be put off by the AI. The idea is to build the town in a way that the stupid AI can accomplish the things it needs to accomplish to survive, and you can do this easily. After that, you'll really only notice it if you look for it. If the stupid AI bothers you that badly you're looking for a different game, which is fine. Banished isn't for everybody and there's a common misconception, often promoted by the game's biggest fans, that Banished is some amazing piece of simulation software for smart people. Well, it isn't. It's just a screenpainter that any 10 year old can excel at once they've learned the basics.

I might be a bit late to the party here, but I posted this to the subreddit for this game a while ago and forgot to add it here as a review as well, so here we go.
I watched the beginning of NerdCubed's video on this game, telling me to go play it without knowing anything about it, and since I had some time to spare I thought "why not?" Dan hasn't steered me wrong before.
And he still hasn't.
I hesitate to call this a "game" as it is most certainly a piece of art delivered in the medium of a game, but I'm not here to argue about what is and what isn't a game.
I feel like this "game" is aimed at the kind of people who are willing to play a game for the experience, rather than the gameplay, which I fall pretty well into, as I'm generally not very good at a lot of competitive games, and prefer to look at things artistically rather than competitively, or objectively. This is probably why none of my friends enjoyed Life is Strange, and why they all prefered to play League of Legends. The kind of person who will like this game is most certainly the kind of person who listens to music without doing anything else, I mean just sits down and listens and sees where the music will take you, and that is really what you're doing with this game: just letting go and seeing where it takes you. I really hate reading comments from people who look at this game objectively, as they're clearly not who this game was made for. If you spent your time in this game complaining to yourself about the lack of gameplay or graphics, then there's no point carrying on, as this game was not made for you.
Another thing that bugs me is people asking question like "what do the 3 dots mean" or "is Coda really real?" and my response to both of them, is that it's up to you. After The Beatles released "I am the Walrus" critics and fans continued to ask them what it means. It doesn't mean anything, or rather it means whatever you want it to mean. If you need the meaning of a song or a game to be spelled out to you then the impact isn't going to be as large. This is the EXACT same reason why jazz and classical are stereo typically "the highest/most pretensions form of music" and pop is just♥♥♥♥♥♥ It's because pop doesn't have anything left to infer. Jazz and classical set a mood, and tell a story that is up to you to create from what you hear. It's not "told" to you, but it's there, and it's different for every person.
It's okay if you don't like this game, or if you don't like jazz music, there's nothing necessarily wrong with League of Legends or pop music, it's just that I personally prefer the former because I like spending the time to find what something means to me (and also that I'm♥♥♥♥♥♥at League).

In short, Dungeon Defenders II would have been a good game, had DD1 not existed.
The game is quite close to a neutral level to me, however I still can't recommend it much. That said, if there was an indifferrent option, I would select tht instead. Dungeon Defenders 2 is a decent game in its own right, although certain controls can be more complicated and somewhat difficult to remember. For some gamers, myself included, controller support is a must-have, however DD2 lacks this and uses a keyboard and mouse only. Unlike DD1, it's a generally more complicated game, in that the maps are slightly more complicated and use more paths to make things harder. That said, the game is generally easier if you've played DD1 or DDE.
As a rating, I give DD2 a 4/10, because it isn't a bad game, but it dismisses some redeeming factors and negates their usage, such as the forementioned controller. The game is still early access, and as such, I would call it one to watch, and with any such improvement, my review may change to recommendation.

- The unique gameplay aspect of it: The times moves only if YOU move.
- VERY addictive.
- Beautiful to look at it, especially if you see slowly the fragments of an enemy fly away from you.
- Many different kind of situations you need to overcome which make you more think more strategically before you act.
- Fast reload function which make you feel more aggressive and excited to continue playing a level without feeling you wasted time.
- Tons of Extra Missions which can play differently the game [for example in some missions you use only a Katana, in other you play the game with a specific time limit, etc] and an Endless mode to play
FOREVER!!!
- Cool little aesthetic stuffs you can see/watch/play which help to built the unique atmosphere of the game.
- It have some VERY interesting secrets. Cool.
- Many updates in the future as told by the Developers. SUPER!!!! HOT!!!!
[Cons:]
- The idea behind the story of the game is ok I guess, but I hoped for something more unique. The story get a little more interesting if you find the secrets I told above.
- The Story mode of the game is very short. I believe you can literally finish it in one sit.
- For the people who looking a variety of things you can see and do in the game, will get disappointed. You just kill the same red dudes the whole time with some exceptions.
- I was hoping for more complicate behavior for the enemies. A good idea would be the enemies could throw the weapons at you as well, or even cut your bullets if they are holding a Katana. I hope for a future update or mode like this.
- Only three type of guns: Pistol, Shotgun and Rifle.
- The Katana is cool, but is slide only horizontally [I hope I am wrong of course].
- The aesthetic stuffs are worth only to see them only once. They don't offer a lot sadly.
- The Extra Missions are the same levels you played in Story Mode.
[Conclusion:]
For the players who love FPS in general and want something unique to play, plus the fact is very addictive and fast like Hotline Miami and Devil Daggers, I highly recommend it.

It's turn 16 and we're down by one. I sit here caged in by the biggest and nastiest Ork-folk you ever did lay eyes on.
We square up against the Dwarves and make ready for the final push. First I see Big Terry go down in a firestorm of fists and beard hair, quickly followed by Thalin the Arsechewer. Crabcake the Vile, the ever lovable Troll is knocked away from his position of protection by a squad of several Dwarves. Time stands still as the Dwarves lock their beady little eyes onto me, their hunger for the ball in my hands is almost palpable. The squad that toppled Crabcake come at me swinging once....twice...three times. I dance away form them all, my wiry little Goblin frame aiding me but for how long who can tell?
I see the Dwarves array themselves in a defensive formation, enough to make even the biggest of Black Orks soil themselves in fear. To score the final touchdown to tie the game I will need to duck and weave into several centimetres of angry, bearded, Dwarves.
I say a quick and possibly final prayer to Nuffle and I begin. Fists fly through the air but I dodge them, fluid as water. Victory is within my grasp now, I hear the sound of dice rolling in my mind as I take the final step across the line and score the touchdown. My team roars their approval and the announcers in their stand cry praise for my unexpected victory.
For a single moment Ol' Rat-face the Goblin stands tallest amongst the Stonard Firearses.

This game should really cost $30. The value in graphics, boss design, and sound of the game is worth more than $20. I will say though, a few bosses felt unsatisfying in defeating them, as they were notably weaker than the other bosses in the same zone (and I believe the concept was to have each zone have bosses of the same difficulty). However, I would say about 90% of the boss fights were both enjoyable and, when you did manage to defeat them, incredibly satisfying.
For people curious about game time, I completed the whole game on normal in 10 hours. After defeating everything on normal difficulty, you then have access to expert difficulty which enables you to earn an "S Rank" on any boss. I would say getting S Rank on every boss is going to take me another 30 hours or so, but honestly some boss fights are so enjoyable, both visually and mechanically, that I could see myself playing this game for an hour here or there after completing all there is to the game.
Overall, Cuphead is a game that, for this price, is well worth anybody buying, even if you don't particularly enjoy the genre.

Beware: This game isn't for most people. I bought it upon a recommendation from a friend (don't worry, we're still friends) while simultaneously trying out the related browser based game "Fallen London". The gameplay looked kinda neat and relaxed, which was what I wanted at the time, and I liked the look of the graphics.
While I can't complain about the graphics, it's the gameplay that turns me off. While you are captaining a ship, this navigation aspect of the game is secondary to the text based gameplay which the game mainly consist of. There's tons of reading, and if you're the kind of guy that's used to quickly skim through texts while playing you shouldn't buy this game. I mean it, only buy this game if you got book worm tendencies (nothing negative about it) and this wonky kind of steampunk universe is appealing to you.
Sure, there's some fighting sea monsters going on, but that part is so simplified that it's just something you need to get over with. You need to manage your fuel/supply economy while navigating the sea but that's about it and it's just not very fun. Simply put, the game lacks complexity apart from the text based stories.
My recommendation is to try out fallen London first (it's free, google it), and if you like that type of game then you might wanna try out sunless sea. If you're like me however, and abadon your fallen london account after two days, then this game is a waste of your money.

Holy heck, this game is the PC 3D platformer I've been waiting for, and right now I'm going to say that I really *really* love this game to hecking death and beyonf. It deserves every amount of praise it gets and if you're a fan of 3D platformers or are looking for a first platformer to get into, this is the game to get. Why do I think this way? Glad you asked, I have many reasons!
1. The controls feel SO good, and there is so many options to do things with the amount of control you have over the cute Hat Kid, honestly she feels on par with Mario from Super Mario Sunshine, if not better.
2. This game has a LOT of charm, every chapter oozes with delight and creativity, and it makes me so happy. Also, Hat Kid is so adorable, her voice actor did a pretty good job making the cute kid be cute.
3. Speaking of voice acting, 95% of this game is voice acted and it ranges from great to amazing. It makes every character have personality, and I don't think the game would be the same without voice acting.
4. The game looks beautiful, even with it's take on a cartoon-like artstyle, it just looks so pretty and I want some of the level intro cards as my wallpaper.
5. The soundtrack, oh my god, this game's soundtrack is equally as amazing as the game's looks itself, goregous tunes, catchy tunes, and it all just blends together with the current situation, I need to buy the OST to just listen to. (Which is more then 5 hours long, dear lord this game is so good)
6. The one thing that really got me excited for the game was the MOD SUPPORT, and from what I've been seeing from the Beta, almost anything is possible. Yes, as of this review the workshop/mod tools are in beta, but they are shaping up to be really good!
I might be missing some points here, but there are more if I missed any!
If there is one thing I don't like, but this is a minor problem, is the game length. I'm not going to spoil how many of the main collectables there are, but the length of this game will make you want more. But there is more on the way with 2 free DLC chapters in the future, AS WELL as a New Game+ mode along the way. But right now, if you want more content, the Workshop beta is the place to get that content, quite a lot of it is already on there!
This is my personal GOTY, I've been waiting so long for this game and it is way better then I hoped it would, and I'll surely be a part of this game's modding community, making content for this excellent game. I wholeheartly recommend it.

A beautiful game where you must survive in the Canadian Wilderness fighting the elements, and wildlife to survive. I could go on writing a huge review or I could just sum it up in 2 words. Absolutely amazing.

+ Setting is superb. As strange and comically-sinister as it is, it's really easy to buy into it.
+ Writing is absolutely fantastic and is the heart and soul of the game.
+ Art is evocative, goes hand-in-hand with the prose style to create the game's unique atmosphere of wonder, whimsy, and dread.
+ As of the time of this review, new content is being added regularly (new stories), and an expansion is on the way.
= While the writing is good, once you've read through certain quest texts, you will probably simply click on your usual option and skip over the text on subsequent playthroughs.
= It's a reader's game. If you prefer less text in your games, you might want to give this one a miss.
= You will find items, meet people, and have no idea how they will be relevant. Where do you sell what item? Personally, the trial-and-error nature of it all is an enjoyable part of the experience but it could easily annoy other players.
- Early game is extremely, painfully repetitive. Since dying is so easy in this game, you have to restart and play the same quests in the same areas many many times.
- The combat is functional but not at all enjoyable. Most of the time, it's just a nuisance. I find myself simply relying on avoiding it because I can't be bothered.

Somehow, the developers did more with two colors that most do with thousands. The game is short, but memorable. The puzzles are deadly, but enjoyable. And you will wish that every game had put as mush love into the simple jump as this game did. 9/10

Your running is limited to a stamina meter, the kick back on guns feel just right, and the way your character seems to go into a panic where they lose their great aim when under heavy MG fire or artillery, it all feels just right. When I go into a match and put on some headphones, I feel so immersed into the environment with the amount of realistic sounding bits. If I could play this all day every day, I would.

I've never really thought much of this game. I bought it to give it a second chance. Let's take a look how good it was.
Visually the game is good. The environment looks fine, but models are rather strange. Sounds are average, but the game has some nice songs playing from jukeboxes, radios etc. which fits the setting.
Gameplay is quite awkward. Even though it has some good features (hacking, plasmids), the action itself doesn't work that great. Enemies run around like idiots, which makes them difficult to hit. You never have enough ammo, but you can buy that from vending machines. Weapons can also be upgraded, though effectivity of these upgrades is sometimes questionable. Sometimes the game tends to be frustrating, but mostly it's alright. But then comes one part where you keep losing your maximum health. It happens quite often, like every five minutes. Developers probably thought it was a good idea to punish you for exploring instead of rushing towards the goal to stop this health loss. They were wrong. Thankfully, you can explore what you missed later after you find a solution for this situation, and even your health gets back to normal.
And the last thing to rate - the story. Hard to say anything about it since you hardly experience it directly. In order to get information about Rapture's past events, you must collect tape recorders and they slowly, like pieces of puzzle, let you see the whole picture. It's an interesting way to tell the story. The story itself seems above average.
Even though it didn't get to the list of my most favourite titles, the game as a whole isn't bad. Rapture has a very original atmosphere and the architecture along with music makes the place feel alive. This game's weakest point is the gameplay, but it still is quite fun. Let's just hope the developers learned from some of their mistakes and polished the other two Bioshock games more.

This is such a fun racing game. I've thoroughly enjoyed every moment. And there is still so much potential here. The physics are great, the vehicle models look fantastic, and the handling lines are excellent. The tracks are fun and challenging, plus they're frequently improving existing tracks and adding new ones. Of course, none of those things I just mentioned are absolutely perfect, but I think that there's plenty great stuff here to build off of now, and the main focus should be to create in-game goals, challenges, and an end objective. Currently the game consists of racing just to race. You earn money and experience, but there's really no point to those things in the game's current state.
Understanding that this game is CURRENTLY IN DEVELOPMENT, I would still absolutely recommend it to any fan of the racing genre. If you're turned off by the idea of spending $40 on an incomplete game, drop it in your wishlist and wait for a sale.
Yes, this game has been in development for over 3 years, but no, that does not mean it is a bad game. Most of the negative reviews here are from impatient turds with no understanding of the time and effort it takes to produce a game, especially with a small team.

Returned to the game two weeks ago and now finished all the content...
So here some of my thoughts and feedback! It's great feedback!
PROS:
Good map diversity... I like how every map has to be farmed to get every drop type... not just 1 efficient map back in 2015. Keep releasing more maps.
Incursions mechanics are fun. Altar of athame and the fire demon lord incursions are my favorite. More maps should have these unique mechanics. I don't like power surge though... that one is annoying to play.
I like how everything in the game can be acquired for free from medals. However i think the rate of medal income is too low. increase medal income by 100% or 200% and it'll be good.
Heroes actually do dps now and make a significant difference.
The new outdoor tavern is really nice looking.
Unique item modifiers... like that monk weapon that makes mobs explode on death in serenity aura. Keep adding these items in... they make for great interesting builds.
Pets actually matter now, especially for dps heroes. My legendary kitty pet's ability chunks for a million damage (great for taking down siege rollers). Keep making pets more interesting.
CONS:
Higher lvl characters in low lvl games... When new players ask for help in game lobby high lvl players usually join. They summon towers and just 1 hit everything. That just ruins the fun! High lvl players should not be allowed in low lvl games... or there should be a sync system.
Defenses are EXTREMELY imbalanced... Why is poison dart tower twice as powerful as cannonball tower and the apprentice's counterpart or any other ranged tower? This makes no sense... 90% of people I play with use poison dart tower... The other builds like trap+frost or mystic or lavamancer or dryad all need way higher gear ipwr compared to the posion dart build to be viable. The only other tower that's even close to poison dart tower is the twin skeleton tower.
Bosses are way too weak. They are terrible. Not even bosses anymore... I remember when ogre and giant book boss were powerful. Theyre now more like regular mobs except with 20X hp. They just go splat like everything else.
Siege roller is way too powerful compared to all the other bosses. Did the siege roller steal all the other bosses power? Every other boss should be at least as powerful as this boss... this is the only actual BOSS in the game...  The only other boss that still has balls is Betsy (Harbinger is also too easy).
Endgame mobs are too weak in general. They just walk into the firing line of a poison dart tower + serenity aura and they go splat. No focus required.
Flying mobs are still too weak. Put up an anti air tower (poison dart tower AS USUAL) and they go splat.
what happened to the emphasis on combos...? I remember the geyser trap + electric aura created an awesome combo... just like oil + fire. Why were all these combos nerfed?
Some of the new hero defenses arent very creative. Its just the same trap archetypes with minor deviations... like the dryad's tree. It's just a serenity + blockade. Harpies are just another ranged tower like canonball. Slime is very similar to traps. Or ev2... buff beam is just a better boost aura and proton beam is just a better electric aura with a slow. New heroes should be more unique, not just be better versions of the free heroes. Gunwitch is great though!
Uber spheres... No one uses them anymore... I haven't seen a single lightning strikes or flamethrower or cannonball. Ive only seen one guy use elemental traps.
Premium heroes buy spheres with medals and not gold... the 4 free heroes can buy spheres with gold... why do I have to spend medals for my premium hero spheres?
Inventory management is still VERY clunkly (i read devlog 93... looking forward to the changes)
CRASHES and BUGS still not fixed from 2015... Not that many but occasionally i'll crash or something will bug out like mobs getting stuck in unreachable places.
OVERAL:
Great and fun game but has many flaws...

Banished is one of those games you can spend hours living a comfortable village life, until in a few short moments everything goes horribly wrong. That simple concept is what makes this game great.
Banished is essentially a real time city builder game, where there is no real end goal, apart from loosely aiming for the in-game achievements. Set more or less in a medieval era, you must run your town, providing food, shelter, education, and a generally good quality of life to the citizens of your town. The core of the game is around balancing of resources, and making sure all essentials are kept in check. No food and citizens starve. No shelter and they freeze to death come winter. No healthcare and a plague could wipe out the populace. Now trust me when I tell you that when your resources become imbalanced and a shortage of something occurs, civilisation can fall very, very fast. This created tension, and when you are trying to push your town to the limits, avoiding this certain death can make the game so addictive, because in the back of your mind you know this game will be unforgiving if you make a mistake. The graphics are also tidy for a fairly simple game.
The brutality of this came can also be a downside however, as if you have spent a lot of time building a town for something to go wrong and it more or less dies out, rebuilding or starting from scratch could seem too much work for some players, so they might just give up there. Also there is limited replayablity here. Granted if you play this game to its potential it should get you 40+ hours (thats how long my main playthrough lasted, max pop ~980), but there's not too much incentive to play on after hitting the 900 population achievement, apart from going for a few of the more challenge like achievements.
Summary:
Pros:
-Simple concept
-Addictive gameplay
-Tidy graphics
-Unforgiving gameplay creates tension
Cons:
-Unforgiving gameplay could be frustrating
-Somewhat limited replayability.
Final Verdict:
8.5/10
A very good game for a few dozen hours fun. Highly recommended.

In 2013 the internet was graced with a small prototype FPS called SUPERHOT and it quickly took the web by storm. Many people played through the prototype and found it to be a totally original take on the first person shooter genre, thus wanting more.
Fast forward to today, February 26th 2016, the day that we get the full version of SUPERHOT. In short it’s a much longer and expanded version of the prototype that has also been given a story. In many ways this helps the game succeed but it does also hurt the game in small ways.
I’m going to do my best to avoid actually covering the contents of the story, because truthfully the story is great. The story is pretty damn incredible and is told through an interesting way. SUPERHOT’s main menu actually acts as an operating system, with you the user. In between levels you’ll instant message with your virtual friends about SUPERHOT. It’s an interesting technique which makes the game, a game within a game. It becomes clear pretty quickly that the game is that much better when played in VR but it’s not bad at all when played on your computer. The story spans about 2 to 2 and half hours. This length isn’t bad, I’d argue it’s actually the perfect length for this type of game, however SUPERHOT has launched at $25, which is rather pricey for a game of this length.
Once you complete SUPERHOT’s story you are able to play through Endless mode as well as challenges but whether those two help justify the game’s price tag is really up to you. Challenges essentially place you in a level but will require you to complete the level in specific ways, for example you are only able to use a katana, etc. It’s a good addition to the game though it’s not something I will personally play too frequently. Additionally, endless mode allows you to choose a level and play through until you die, as enemies will never stop spawning. Again, it’s a fine addition though not particularly my cup of tea. In my opinion the reason to play SUPERHOT is it’s story and the game play, but the real question you should ask yourself when considering it are whether the amount of time you’ll put into the game is worth your $25.
Enough about the game’s modes though because what makes SUPERHOT shine is the game play. It’s incredibly rare that a game launches and brings out a new take on a classic genre, but SUPERHOT is absolutely the game that does this. It puts the FPS genre on its head and it’s incredibly well done. SUPERHOT is not the best looking game ever. It certainly has its own style and it isn’t by any means bad looking, but it is somewhat bland. The world is mostly white and gray with all enemies standing out in a bright red color. The game is a first person shooter however the catch is that the world only moves when you do. This creates a really interesting sense of game play where you can literally run through clouds of bullets and catch the enemies’ guns midair while also giving yourself time to think about how to proceed. Though SUPERHOT is 100% a shooter it’s also very much a puzzle game and you’ll find yourself repeating the same level over and over trying different methods until you find success on the other side. There are a few different weapons from guns like the handgun, shotgun and assault rifle as well as the melee weapons which consist of the katana and your fists. Each level presents something new and the game never ceases to be fun.
Additionally upon completion of a level you will watch a re-run of your successful play through without the slow pauses you’ll make completing the level. It’s a cool idea because though it may take you a minute or two to play through the level, you can watch what it would then look like in 30 seconds, almost like it would look in a movie. SUPERHOT also allows you to edit or cut down your video and upload it to a website the developers set up called
. This is actually one of my favorite features of the game because it encourages players to get the coolest run they can, and then instantly allows them to share it around the world.
SUPERHOT didn’t run without issues however. I kept getting hard frame rate drops seemingly out of nowhere. It’s a strange thing too because I was actually playing the game prior to its official release with no problems, but since the launch day update I’ve had plenty of frame rate issues. I have to assume this will be patched and fixed up real quick but it is another thing to take note of for now.
SUPERHOT is a really fantastic game, and it’s the kind of game that truly re-defines a gaming genre. It’s a game that everyone should play at some point in time. At its current price, however, you really need to determine how much money your enjoyment is worth. At 2-2.5 hours for the story that’s rather pricey in the current gaming age we live in, especially for games on Steam. Now that isn’t to say the game isn’t worth it. It’s an incredible game that packs a lot of fun into a short time. Additionally the current release is available only on Steam (Windows, OSX and Steambox) but it will be coming to consoles soon with the Xbox One first sometime in March 2016.
Overall I think you should definitely play SUPERHOT. It’s fun and original and well worth your time. The only thing you need to decide is when to buy it.

A Hat in Time is a game I'd been anticipating ever since the kickstarter first appeared in ...2013? Wow, that was a long time ago... In any case, the game's a fantastic 3d platformer, brought up to a modern standard -- with a few quirks.
The control is fantastic. Hat Kid has some of the most fluid control in a 3d platformer ever. The diving and dive-cancel mechanic is tons of fun to pull off, as well as the ground flip you can do to get more speed. They're also very broken, and can be used to skip over a majority of the fun grapple-based platforming segments.
The scenarios and characters you meet along the way are really fun and memorable. The gameplay never gets stale -- there's always something new to do. All this is accompanied by an great, upbeat soundtrack, with lots of variety and charm.
Some complaints:
The badge system is kind of obnoxious. By the end of the game, you only have 3 badge slots you can assign badges to. One of these will usually always be taken up by your grapple. If you want to use your camera, you have to equip it first. This is a minor complaint.
Inconsistency in quality. You can kind of tell what parts of the game were modeled and designed first. Some parts of this game, such as models, effects, and environments have an inconsistant look to them. Some animations look absolutely amazing, while some quite literally weren't changed from the beta build of the game. Some characters clip through other objects during their animations. Some dialoug doesn't have voice acting. These inconsistancies got to the point where it was incredibly jarring whenever I noticed them.
Of course, all of these problems are cosmetic, and don't ruin the game, persay... They just take you out of the experience for a moment.
But good game anyway. Buy this game. Just do it if you want a fun ol' romp. What have you got to lose? They're working on the free dlc, so there's even more cool stuff on the way!

One of my favorite games of all time is Ambrosia Software's EV: Nova.  For those unfamiliar it's an old 2D space exploration/combat sim with a text-based storyline.  I've been looking for a game that can bring the same sort of atmosphere, play style, and story-telling for years.
So I was pleasantly surprised when I stumbled upon Sunless Sea.  The game has a difficult learning curve, you'll often find yourself in compromising positions early in the game as you try to scrape together enough fuel and supplies to maintain your voyage.  You'll have moments that tickle your ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ as you sail around massive Zee-Beasts that could, at any moment, annihilate your ship and crew, while you silently pray you don't see those telltale red exclamations.  This for me is easily the best part of the game.  In the early stages where you still have so much to explore and you risk everything trying to cobble together a little money and means.
However, that's pretty much where the comparison ends.  Sunless Sea is still essentially unfinished and my biggest issue is that once you figure out how to make money easily the game starts to fall off pretty quickly.  Many of the questlines are more tedious than they are challenging.  There aren't any missions where you have to fight off a multitude of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥off Zee-Beasts or break through a blockade of enemy frigates.  Basically, once you hit mid-game you just swing around giant throbbing zee♥♥♥♥♥♥and laugh as you pare monstrous zee-beasts and enemy dreadnoughts down to size.  The game kind of stagnates in difficulty after you make some decent progress.
My other qualm is that many of the storylines and characters don't really develop to a satisfying conclusion.  You can improve some of your officers traits by compiling various oddities and ferrying them around to distant ports, but by the end you feel less like you've achieved anything and more like you've just completed a burdensome chore.  Again this could be easily corrected by the addition of difficult combat scenarios or interesting plot devices, such as having to permanently sacrifice one crew officer to advance the abilities of another.  Right now your crew officers don't interact with each other whatsoever, which is a little disappointing considering the drama and intrigue that could be possible.  So at the moment Sunless Sea is really lacking a certain level of polish.  Very unfortunate considering the brilliant work that FailBetter games has done in developing the atmosphere and playability of the game.
My suggestions to the developers would be as follows:
-First of all, thank you.  You have worked hard to create a visually mesmorizing game with limitless potential that is fun and beautiful.  Now get back to work and finish the masterpiece that you have started.  You've carved out half of the Statue of David, but without that perfectly chiseled marble ballsack, your audience will be left wanting.
-Really get creative with some of the plot elements and don't be afraid to create ambiguous choices.  Not every scenario should have a win/lose outcome.  Players enjoy having to doubt their choices and seeing their decisions come back to bite them in the♥♥♥♥♥later on.
-Ramp up the difficulty!!!  I don't want to feel like I'm the King of the Zee just because I have a Corvette class cruiser and a forward turret.  Create some smarter enemy AI, like beasts that will submerge and then rush your ship to attack, instead of just kind of aimlessly drifting around.  Or enemy ships that shround themselves in mist so you can't find a firing solution.  Or something that fires nets to impede your ship's mobility.  As it is, combat versus the single enemies provided is simply laughably easy and needs to be improved.
-Create a diverse system of enemies.  Maybe you need a dreadnought with powerful slow-firing weapons to take down that Nomad, but what if a swarm of Jillyfluer surround your ship?  Suddenly you're swarmed and you need a faster firing turret.  This applies to weapons as well, I think most weapons in the game have the same firing speed (warm-up time) and they all have the same range dependent upon the weapon type.  Fix this.  Create some diversity in the arsenal and you create diversity in the game,
-On that note, the lump of Blue Scintillack is an utterly overpowered item and is far too easily attainable!  I think I stumbled onto it within an hour of playing my first captain and it just completely shifts the difficulty in the game and allows for the player to take advantage of combat mechanics too easily.  Sinking 300hp frigates in my 75hp starter ship without upgrades isn't fun it's stupid.  Either get rid of it or make it far more difficult to attain because it provides far more firepower than even the best weapon in the game for absolutely zero cost or effort to the player.

Overall, I really love this game.  I wouldn't have even bothered posting a review if I didn't have confidence in the developers to improve the game into the incredible classic it has the potential to be. They have captured lightning in a bottle here and that this game can appeal to a wide variety of fans from casual gamers to hardened adventurers.  The chilling atmosphere of the game, arguably the most important and elusive element to create, has been rendered masterfully in Sunless Sea.  I would just call for some real reworks of the content and difficulty.  With those improvements made, I could see myself playing Sunless Sea for hundreds of hours and enjoying every minute.  7.5/10 would recommend.

A gaming masterpiece.
This is a love letter to video games.
In A Hat In Time, the player assumes control of Hat Kid, a (mostly) silent character, on a spaceship, eager to get home. An unexpected snag hits, and off to journey to 3D platforming worlds you go!
The story setup is brief but it works. A Hat In Time succeeds because although it advertises itself as cute-as-heck, it’s also fun-as-heck, peck-as-heck, and while there is a time and a place, this is the place. And this place draws you in, because while it’s not the biggest (it’s the first game released by Gears For Breakfast), nor the baddest (a Kickstarter project 4+ years in the making, with a modest budget and a modestly-sized development team), it does exude quality across the board regardless, in many aspects, taking many forms. A Hat In Time’s positives include:
+ FUN FACTOR/FUN. Lots and lots of fun! This game GETS IT. From the moment you wake on your spaceship and are placed to inspect your immediate surroundings, this game invites you. At first it is but a whisper. You go over to the dresser, chuckle, a tiny glimpse of the clever writing that awaits you, you then turn your head, and… there is a pool of pillows in your bedroom! Well then, dive in!
And that’s what it’s all about.
Diving in.
A Hat In Time wants you to interact. To explore. To dive in, to soak in its unique blend of personality and charm. Here’s your ticket, all aboard, passenger! You’re invited to this vibrant, crazy train! Nostalgic and trailblazing, A Hat In Time pays respect to the old and the new. The little things. The big things. This world is alive, full of details, both large and small, some random, some not, from Roomba rides, to scooter horns, to pattycake with the man in blue, to random posters plastered in various worlds, to talking owls, to curious crows, to picture taking, to jokes, to jokes WITHIN jokes, to clever responses, to humorous interactions, to easter eggs, to random jumps on floating cookies, to scary ledges, to tightrope mechanics, to engrossing music, to the vibrant surroundings and atmosphere, the list goes on. Which all amounts to --
Fun. A BIG bundle of fun! The game doesn’t have to tell you to HAVE fun, because the world IS fun. The worlds are a playground for Hat Kid, she herself a world of her own, able to convey, through facial expressions and body animations alike, a wide range of emotions such as joy, sadness, or her unmistakenly unwavering child-like innocence, sarcasm, and hope. Hat Kid’s adorable idle animations, her 'running-in-place’ animation, environmentally specific animations (keep a lookout during cold/mysterious/scary areas), cute voicelines (Her “Bye” to the Badge Seller awww <3), her “Fireballs,” her “Boo-yahs,” and so on and so forth, as well as her dedicated buttons to ‘blow kiss/smooch’ and ‘raspberry’, all come together to make her a ball of recklessly positive inspiration, ready to take on any adventure that comes her way.
+ CONTROLS. This is tight, responsive platforming paradise. Controls are crisp, enabling Hat Kid to move well to your desire. Her moveset includes running, a standard jump, a double jump, a long jump, a parkour-inspired wall jump, a dive, an air dive, a dive cancel, an air dive cancel, umbrella swipes, air homing attacks, etc. not to mention equippable hats and badges that add various skills and abilities to her arsenal. It seems like a basic layout, and it may appear so on the surface, but her runs, jumps, dives, and cancels provide a level of precision and a gateway for advanced play that allows for mid-air error adjustment, correction, and control, allowing her to maneuver platforms with relative ease.
Her toolbox further rewards skillful players who are able to chain these abilities together to make use of speedruns, which are an embraced option in the game. A Hat In Time even goes as far as to include a speedrun timer in the options, for those willing to take on the challenge of going fast, fast, fast!
And because Hat Kid controls quite well, particularly resourceful players will be able to discover shortcuts and different ways to finish a stage. This is a mark of a good control scheme, as well as well-planned, well thought-out, and well-executed level design.
+ GENRE-BREAKING ELEMENTS. In a manor of speaking, this game surprises as it transcends its predominant 3D platformer roots and manages to mix genres such as stealth, mystery, and horror into one. I will be brief here because these sections are best experienced by the player itself, but will say that these sections make sense for each specific adventure, and are appropriate for each specific setting. It executes this wonderfully and it comes through beautifully. It does not feel tacked on, or existing just because it can, but is rather interesting and highlight some of the best and most memorable parts of the game.
+ SOUNDTRACK. Clocking in at over 5 hours, A Hat In Time’s soundtrack, almost all of which are composed by Pascal Michael Stiefel, along with a few other notable names (Grant Kirkhope + artists with remixed renditions of specific tracks), is genuinely one of the best parts of A Hat In Time AND (IMO) one of THE MAIN reasons to get the game. One of the most important elements for game immersion, A Hat In Time’s soundtrack is excellent, with memorable, catchy, and ambitious sections, spanning across different genres to create a defining mark and a long-lasting impression. Mindful players will recognize nostalgic sections/references amongst specific tunes (but it’s not a prerequisite, as the soundtrack, as a whole, is fantastic enough to listen to as a standalone, without the coat of nostalgia to cast judgment).
Simply put, this soundtrack is one to hold in high regard, in and outside of the game. I do (and will) play stages JUST to hear certain tracks, they’re that good, and such a joy to listen to! The variety here is astounding, likely offering something to suit the tastes of everyone.
+ OPEN-ENDED DESIGN. The game supports Steam Workshop, which means that it encourages mods/mod support (currently in beta). Options exist for new dyes/costumes, new hats, new abilities, unique levels, recreations of stages from beloved games, added difficulties, and so on and so forth. Intriguing possibilities abound, and we’re just at the tip of the iceberg.
+ HUMOR. A good chunk of the game’s personality and charm can be attributed to the humor and strong writing, clearly inspired by beloved games of old. Most of the humor here is appropriate for kids, although some border on the twisted and the macabre.
Whether it’s Hat Kid’s mannerisms, her interactions with objects/characters, the characters themselves, or a specific activity within a specific stage, A Hat In Time puts a nostalgic, yet distinct style to accompany and enhance these specific worlds, never artificial, and as wacky as the wacky worlds that they are set within. It just… fits. It’s ok to smile, and to laugh along :).
As far as negatives go, world 5’s main antagonist needs more screen time, more backstory, more motivation to emphasize why this character set out to become the very character this is in the final act. More fleshing out in this aspect is needed; as is, it ended up being too abrupt.
---FINAL THOUGHTS---
The game, per Kickstarter achieved stretch goals, will have worlds 6 and 7 arriving as free DLCs, and will have co-op modes available in the near future. There is much to look forward to!
Get this game and transport yourself to an amazing, memorable journey. Support a development team that put obvious love and care into their work! The charm, the precision, the detail – this is a fine example of gaming bliss. One that should endure – in time.
My wish is that Hat Kid becomes recognizable enough to the point that she becomes a classic, iconic, beloved video game character.
A Hat In Time cherishes the past, shapes the present, and has a promising future.
Play it. Be charmed by it. Enjoy it.

This game is everything you hope it will be when you watch the previews - immersive, engrossing, beautiful, and brutal. There are moments when you just stop in awe at what you are seeing! Best of all, this is survival done right. You don't get to "base up" and live safely after a few play-throughs of learning. Sure you get better, learn the tips, live longer, but you still fight to survive every day, sometimes every hour in this game.
Yes I had a few hard deaths, some brutal moments where I wondered if I would ever last more than a few days, but the reward when you figure it out is that much better. And even when you die, the game has a hold on you. I remember fading out one time looking up at the most amazing night sky ever. I couldn't wait to start again.
In terms of style, you need minimal hand-eye coordination. This is a game of constant decision making. EVERY decision has tradeoffs: run or walk, rest more or head out now, fight or flee, take a risk or wait out a storm, take the easy path or go up that ridge to see what's on the other side?
I'm hooked. I find myself thinking about this game at work. Wondering what I should do to eke out another day or two. I got this game on sale, but it would be easily worth it at major label prices. And it's still just Alpha. Amazing.

Changing my review after a lot of updates, as I promised I would. The dev was nice enough to inform me of incoming updates with problems I had, and the changes are substantial. Defense is still very much a tower defense game, but with a colony survival aspect behind it. If you don't have the proper setup, you will get rolled over by the enemies very quickly.
Eventually it seems that the only way to survive is to pull all your leveled-up people (a system that is not explained at all) and go to another area. Realistically you COULD build up until you've conquered an entire map before moving on, but that would take so long it's not really worth it. The game badly, badly needs speed controls.
The dev, who is amazingly connected with his community, has said in the future he plans to add "haste" or "slow" spells, but that doesn't solve the overall problem. Sometimes you don't want to wait around. Sometimes you're okay with the enemy building as fast as you are. Haste and Slow spells will help, yes, but will not solve the problem that eventually the game just gets too grindy.
All in all I do recommend this game. Much like Orcs Must Die gave us a third-person tower defense game, this game gives us a colony simulator defense game, and I love that. It's very fun, very challenging, and aside from the few gameplay problems (which the dev will absolutely fix eventually) a gem of a game.

The sole developer, Raymond Doerr, is offering up a first class Early Access experience. He seems to be astoundingly active, quickly answering messages on twitter, Steam and the dedicated official game site, which is itself well maintained with an artful attention to detail.
Updates come thick and fast, with a casual little suggestion of mine turning up in a patch a day later. Very gratifying! You can really see how determined he is to make this something great, accounting for every piece of feedback. So I'm fully reassured that, even though it's almost two year's since the successful Kickstarter, Retro-Pixel Castles will eventually reach a proper, full release, however long is need to make it a really great gaming experience.
As of the current version, inDev22e, I'd say that the game alone is only just about worth it's price tag. There are a couple of nights worth of obsessive play in there, building out your village and defense setup, provided you have a modicum of patience to get into it. After failing initially, I personally watched the handily linked 'tutorial' video, to get the gist of a few basics. The in-game tips were very helpful too. But having figured out how to survive the initial onslaught, the excitement does trail off... The transition to starting a new village map is currently a little rough and without any campaign mechanism in place yet there's no particular motivation to go through the motions more than a couple times.
However, it looks like the game's meta is due to change with the upcoming monthly major update and there are a lot of promising additions lined up. Really looking forwards to the future of this project. :-)
Bear in mind that while this game is the same genre as Rimworld, it's pretty distinct from it - it's more like supervising a colony of ants, with no capacity or need to micromanage each little person. I feel the villager AI works pretty well, but it's best not to worry too much about the fine detail, just plan out your build strategy and keep an eye on those monsters. Also, there's a significant (and hopefully growing) tower defense aspect to the play, with it being possible to build little mazes for enemies to path through while getting shot. Quite a novel marriage of two of my favorite, most addictive game genres!
Also be warned that the game can run a little choppily under certain circumstances, but is getting better optimized with each update and refinements are also due that should help avoid overly demanding conditions. Likewise I experienced a couple of crashes initially, but the frequent auto-save meant I never lost any progress and I've been unable to replicate the problem after recent updates. Continuous improvement.

Retro-Pixel Castles: The Godlike Village Simulator is developed by Raymond Doerr and published by SixtyGig Games. While still in Early Access, it shows promise and it is by no means a small feat, given the fact that this title is the dev team’s first Steam project.

Even though there’s not one playthrough similar to another, Retro-Pixel Castles does offer the necessary tools and assets needed for both the survival as well as thriving of the miniaturized society being simulated in our case. If there’s one good thing that comes out of such random scenarios, is that boredom has a hard time setting in provided you are familiar with the god game formula. It’s definitely harder than economic simulators/city builders that are more abundent on Steam. You have to constantly keep an eye on your villagers and protect them from natural hazards and foes, while also having a clear expansion pattern as the resources on the maps do encourage some planning ahead. The game’s tutorial felt a bit thin on content and tips, but there’s still room for improvement. While it may seem rather difficult for beginners, once you know how to prioritize your building projects and manage the initial small population, things become much easier.

The audio-visual department is the one that might require some more tinkering from the developer’s side. Music and soud effects seem quite repetitive while the fonts have a slight resolution problem. Zooming in or out would be nice touches as the pixelated graphics don’t bother me at all. In such a game which features enough gameplay complexity as it is, the eye candy can be safely overlooked.
EDIT: Trading Cards have been added to this game.

+ Steam Trading Cards
+ Randomly generated assets
+ Freedom of choice with an open-ended storyline
- No Achievements
- Still in Early Access
- Sounds are repetitive
It is truly unfortunate that we have such a limited selection of god games on the Steam Store, but we must make do with what can be found already as well as the newly released ones. Retro-Pixel Castles is just such a title, both promising and with a charm of its own. More than enough to stand out and not be considered just a shout-out to an often neglected genre.

TL:DR - Do I recommend this game? Yes.*
*However, be advised, this port only runs smoothly if you have a decent build. In my case, I am overkilled (5960X with 3-way SLI 980 TI). I cannot speak for all PC users here, but I think an SLI build  and a good 6 core processor is needed for the poor optimisation.
Story:
In Telltale fashion, the game is solid, and the story gets you hooked into the dilemma of Bruce trying to live up to his family legacy, which is currently being questioned due to Gotham's seedy underbelly. The usual caveat from Tell Tale games is, apart from major game choices, most minor ones do not change the overall outcome and climatic end to every episodic release. As such, depending on your viewpoint, you will either feel accomplished, or left wanting more closure.
Gameplay:
The QTE segments are a bit more fluid than other games released by the publisher, but if you are using a gamepad, the game has a tendency to sometimes not register your cue presses on time, or is a bit time squeeze happy with the split second decisions, not giving you the chance to take a breather to analyse the button presses required.
Everything else, is standard fare in the point click adventure, you point, click, and find information relevant to the tasks required. I have to say I quite liked the streamlined detective segments provided by the game as it tries to show people why Batman is the world's greatest detective in the DC superhero lore.
Graphics and Sound:
Nice and lush quality as expected from the company. The atmosphere, the look, and the sound emanate Batman, and you can even customise what colour Batman's tech looks like (I stuck to Black and Blue). However, as many users report, that apart from programme crashes, having a moderate or less than stellar build causes framerate hiccups and drops. Hopefully patching and optimisation will fix this.

Harder than it looks! Cities go from 'thriving' to 'dying' in the span of two years, from population boom to population drop, from resource-rich to resource-starved. Build too fast, and you outstrip your resources in a matter of months. Build too slow, and your population can't keep up with age. And that's not counting the potential of a random tornado tearing apart a perfectly-built city, or your people ravaged by disease or badly-placed crop-killing blights. A fragile balancing act that is unforgiving and vicious even on the easier settings.... and yet a game that has eaten up 500 hours of my time and counting.
In short, while I love this game and can't suggest it highly enough for those who love that fragile balancing act of building your world, it is not a game for the easily frustrated. Challenging, enjoyable, and easily one of my favorite resource management games as of yet, but absolutely unforgiving on *so* many levels!

TL;DR at the bottom!
Do not be fooled by the small ammount of hours i've spent in-game (i have alot of games on alot of platforms!). I have been following this game since its development was announced. I'm a huge fan of survival and sandbox games, but i think the choices in that category we have right now are quite limited.
Banished is not like the others. It has a bit of a learning curve and it can be challenging at times, but if you get into it (and you will!), you must be prepared to have your life sucked in like you've gotten cursed by a succubi! (My point is, it's addictive!)
You chose your starting conditions, climate and environment to start your settlement in and your only end goal is to survive as long as you can! For starters i recommend the anything but the easy start so you can place your buildings wherever you want, this way you can have your settlement how you like.
I guess it's a bit of a survival city builder. It's quite harder than your typical city builder though. Think the Anno series, but quite harder and on a smaller (yet more detailed!) scale! You have to carefully manage your ressources, production and population, as losing control of any of them for more than a few in-game season stage can be devastating, especially for beginners! Don't worry if your village starve to death, freeze to death or suddenly all die of old age (due to a bad management of population control), and beware of the Death marches! Losing a few settlement at first is part of the game, since this is how you learn your errors and how to correct them.
It's like when you first ride a bike ; You will fall on your face a few times but you this will only better your mastery of the two-wheeled machine!
Don't feel bad if this happens, everyone's been there, just carry on and start a new settlement. When you finally get a stable settlement with a nice population that's surviving quite well, you'll be proud of yourself and will feel a sense of acomplishment (which is quite uncommon in games nowadays!) that you deserve!
Once you think you've got a good grip on the game's mechanic, feel free to try some mods that really makes the game bigger and better, like the Colonial Charter series. It's really fun and it keeps the game fresh!
(Blackliquid, the CC mod development team, releases updates quite often so you've always got some new cool stuff to try out!)
Verdict and TL;DR
Overall, this is a challenging yet rewarding gem of a game. It's well worth your money and you'll spend enough time playing to know this! Sometimes you may get frustrated or tired of some of the sh*t that can happen, but most often that not it's the player's fault, and you will always notice that and come back to this amazing game sooner rather than later!
Have a good one, and watch out for them sneaky winters!

OUTLAST (MAIN GAME)

-A whole lot of other stuff
CONS:
-The big guy is such a stalker

OUTLAST: WHISTLEBLOWER
PROS:
-Equally as terrifying as the main game
-Lots and lots of blood and guts, sometimes exploding in your face (I've seen worse).
-Interesting antagonists, especially a man by the name of Eddie Gluskin.
-The DLC added a few extra hours to the game, bringing my total playtime to almost 14 hours. Not bad, but part of that 14 hours was sneaking around in the dark without any batteries trying to figure out where the hell to go.
CONS:
-The Walrider, obviously. Thank goodness it had a less prominent role.
-That's about it, actually.

When playing an open world or sandbox game for the first time, do you ever pick a blank point clear across the map and walk there simply because it exists? Sunless Sea is a game designed around that playstyle, and for anyone that loves exploring for the sake of exploration, I can recommend it unconditionally and without a shred of doubt. If discovery strange and exciting regions alone isn't enough for you, read on.
Pros:
- Exploration. The game is fantastically written, but more importantly, its written with a degree of whimsy that only strengthens the desire to uncover all of the game's islands. There really is no predicting what you'll discover, but every port is interesting and most tie into a wide variety of quests and activities. Sunless Sea's exploration is similar in concept to Wind Waker, but unlike that game, only one island is uninhabited.
- Music. There are, sadly, only around 10 tracks, but they all fit the atmosphere perfectly and are worth listening to even out of context.
- Great art. The game isn't technically stunning, but the artistic vision both in world design and character/location portraits is fantastic.
- Deeply interconnected. Items, decisions, and attributes tie into each other in surprising ways. You're very rarely harshly punished for not having a specific item without warning, so there's a lot to figure out without the risk of unfair deaths.
- Decent roleplaying elements. You're never given exact control over what your character says, but the gist of every decision is under your control, and many decisions have significant, permanent consequences. Roguelites rarely have this level of characterization.
Cons:
- Combat. Ships can be dealt with by staying behind them. Every beast but one can be dealt with by constantly ramming them so they can't get their own charge off. It's also painfully slow in addition to being easy before you acquire a forward gun.
- Easy. I beat the game with my 5th character. The first 4 all died  as a result of taking unecessary risks that I knew perfectly well were unecessary. If you're careful constantly, you simply aren't going to die in Sunless Sea. That's good in the sense that you might stand to lose a lot of progress, but it renders the descendant mechanics largely pointless.
- Sometimes makes you click a lot. There's no option to sell things in bulk or to repeat the same event as many times as possible. Since there are times in the game when you're going to want to do the same thing 30 times in a row, it's very annoying that each time takes two different button clicks.
- Performance. The snow and dust effects cause serious framerate lag, and I had rare issues with crashes and freezes.
Notes:
- The comparison to Wind Waker also applies in that a lot of your time is going to be sailing back and forth with little to do in the immediate term. If it bored you then, it probably will here as well.
- The game continues to be updated with new content and stories. Some of it is minor, but there's already been a major new win condition and associated quest added.
Overall, Sunless Sea is a unique and highly enjoyable exploration roguelite that's easily worth the $20 asking price.

Outlast is a first person horror game which was released in mid 2013 on the PC while also being released afterwards on consoles. It is own by approximately a million users on Steam too.  The game is also built on the unreal engine.
The game is based around a story rich campaign told in first person narrative style set in a psychiatric hospital which has been overrun by murderous paitents.  Your character, Miles Upshur, has no means of combat, other than shoving enemies out of your way. You are forced to use the technique which most would do when faced with the types of enemies in this game, running for your life and hiding like a little girl under a bed.  You also carry a notebook and a camcorder, which is used to document the events inside the hospital. The camera is used as your mechanism of seeing in the dark, but obviously in good horror genre style it has a limited supply of power - so you also have to explore the hospital for batteries to keep it turned on.
Outlast is built on the Unreal engine; so the graphics are top notch; they really capture the scene and will have you cringing in horror at some of the sights you will see. The lighting is absolutely perfect, along with the rain effects when outside.
You can go as deep as you want with the story; you can either follow the plot by just wandering around the halls and purely just going off the scripted events that happen or you can delve very deeply into the story by finding all kinds of documents scattered around in drawers and cupboards.
This is easily the scariest game I have ever played. On top of the stunning visuals that are almost life like, the game has the best audio you will ever find in a horror game; footsteps, background screaming, musical tempo changes. They are all amazing and you won't find a game which captures it more perfectly than Outlast.
Outlast is hard; the first "level" chucks you straight in at the deep end as you have to scramble around a beefed up guy to turn the power generator on; this is the first of many challenges you will face in the game. You have to really stick at it at times to try work the best method of progressing around some events. You will be very lucky to complete the game without running into any problems.
The whole game took me seven hours to complete; this was my first playthrough and there sadly isn't any other reason other than collecting all of the documents to play through it again. The story is linear and you will end up with the same ending each time.
Regardless of the lack of replay ability, Outlast is easily one of the best games to come out in recent years and horror fans will absolutely love it. If you aren't into jump scares this may not be for you, as there are plenty and you will probably find yourself alt F4ing out many times.

I'm about four hours in to the game and I love it to bits. As Ars Technica called it, "blue collar sci-fi" is definitely shaping up to be one of my favourite aesthetics, which is absolutely nailed in this game. Interesting enemy types keep you on your toes and look different. Even the ship silouhettes of ships evoke the gorgeous designs of the Alien series (mainly 1 and 2. Less sleek lines, more hard angles).
As someone who has used Linux before, using the ingame LUI to navigate was far less intimidating than I imagined it would be. The fact that every command has a man page made it so much easier than having to pause, look up a YouTube video, then go back. The immersion was almost entirely complete. Make it VR compatible and you could probably get some pretty good PTSD from this game.
While the LUI is very nice, it would be great for commands to have short versions (navigate/ nav, transport/ transpo or trans, generator/ gen for example). While there is an auto-fill, I haven't been mentally quick enough to just mash the space bar when it happens. I don't know if a lot of people are, but maybe I'm the problem there. Other than that, the syntax of the commands is very simple and easy to understand (more often than not: order, unit, destination/target).
UPDATE: Just discovered the Alias command. This is a great function and fixes all the above problems. Turns out reading the manual matters.
I've loved having the schematic and camera views. I spend a lot of my time in schematic view and often use camera for when corridors are too tight or the drones have problems with pathfinding, such as when a tight corridor has debris forming a chicane. Schematic view complements the LUI and allows you to designate multiple tasks quicker. Camera view is great for trying to cut the pie on a door with a turret or quietly scout ahead with a stealth drone. One view wouldn't work without the other.
I share some concerns with other people about the story not really being defined. I know the reason behind this as the devs discussed it in the forums, but the lack of emphasis on the story meant that I don't think I'd ever looked at the theories or objectives until last night. I'm sure this will be dealt with.
The wear and tear system is about as cruel as cruel gets, but not entirely unfair. You can get a long way off the back of a module before it breaks and failure probability takes a long time to shoot up to around 25%. The only problem I have with modules is that in a reset, you should at least spawn with interface. Most of the game is locked off until you get it.
This game has something that is so unique that I've never been able to pin down before, like when I first bought Payday 1. This bold, enjoyable, edge of your seat, high stakes gameplay with its own feel and own universe to jump head first in to. It gets you learning to work with what you got, to think and work under stress very quickly. You have to plan every single move on a derelict and be flexible for when the plan comes apart under fire.
I bought TypeRacer: BDSM Expansion on special for about $9.99, an absolute bargain for what you get.

Fun game if you enjoy the base building type of games.  (I do so I loved this game.)
For the most part, the gameplay and buildings are fairly straightforward.  There's definitely a learning curve to this game, though.  You will most likely have to start over at least a couple times. However, once you figure out your strategy and build a solid defence, the only struggle may be to have enough food during the winter.
As it's not finished yet, the game is still lacking, but I got 15 hours of good gameplay out of this game in it's current state. (Owned it for about a week as I write this).  I got it on sale for about $5 which is already well worth the price even without the fact that it will be updated.  My personal check for games is that it's, at least, satisfactory if it provides enough fun game play for one hour for every dollar it cost.  (So 3 hours/dollar so far is pretty good.)
Quick tips if you want them:
-Focus on a good defense ASAP. There's always room for improvement. Like dont even worry about having all the necessary housing.  You start in spring so the villagers can go a few nights outside.  Just build a good wall and defense towers (and ammo supply) ,  And use natural barriers to your adventure (forests and mountains.)
-Don't spready yourself thin, too fast.  You start off with only so many people.  If you start building and employing all the different manufacturing and refining buildings, Your people will be spread thin among all them and it'll take forever to get more important things dones.
-Edges to waters aren't as defensive as you think.  If you build a wall ending perpendicular to a body of water, monsters can still swim around the edge (Depending on what the quickest path is.)
-Destroy spawners asap.  Use the Fireball power on any spawners that pop up (red squares on minimap).  You don't need to destroy them completely.  If you hit them, they'll slowly burn until they're destroyed (unless it starts to rain.)

enjoy this chicken stir fry recpie
- Serves 4
- 10 mins to prepare and 10 mins to cook
- 325 calories / serving
- Healthy
INGREDIENTS:
- 1 orange, zested and juiced
- 2tbsp soy sauce
- 2tbsp sesame oil
- 250g (8oz) tender stem broccoli
- 5cm (2in) piece root ginger
- 1tbsp sunflower oil
- 1 garlic clove, finely sliced
- 1 red pepper, deseeded and thinly sliced
- 150g Straight To Wok Noodles
- 400g (13oz) chicken fillet, cut into thin slices
METHOD
Step 1 - Mix together the orange zest and juice, soy sauce and sesame oil and set aside.
Step 2 - Blanch the broccoli in boiling water for 2 minutes, then drain well and set aside.
Step 3 - Finely shred the ginger. Then heat a large frying pan or wok, add the sunflower oil, heat it until sizzling, and fry the ginger till it's crisp.
Step 4 - When it's done, remove with a slotted spoon. Add the chicken and garlic, and stir-fry until just browned. Remove the meat using a slotted spoon and set aside.
Step 5 - Add the red pepper and broccoli and stir-fry for around 2-3 minutes until it's just tender. Add the soy sauce mixture, bring it to the boil then return the chicken to the pan

This was my favourite game of last year, and it is criminally underrated. Don't let the unimpressive graphics fool you, this is a superbly crafted and engaging game that had me playing way too late into the night, bloodshot eyes glued to the screen. In the far future, humans seems to have vanished, and you (a lone space-farer) must board various derelict ships and explore their remnants to find out what happened. You do this via drones that you send onto ships and program (via commands that you type into a very basic interface) to explore, open doors, and sometimes fight (or more frequently, run away from) monsters. It has rogue-like elements, so if you fail (get stranded in space with no drones - which will happen a lot) you have to start again from scratch, but the research progress you've made remains. You can commandeer derelict ships and upgrade them, and you can also upgrade your drones. I can't really describe how fun and addictive this game is - just try it for yourself.

The Long Dark is one of the best survival games I've played. The setting of the game is quite beautiful and interesting. The maps are also intimidating enough that a new player will feel like the maps are large and hostile while a more experienced player will be at home in them. The game can be very peaceful and relaxing half of the time and very intense the other half.
The game doesn't rely on zombies or cheap "survival game" tropes to make the game enjoyable. Instead, the game has a gritty and "real" survival style that sets it apart from other games of the genre. This is one thing that makes TLD worth it over other survival games. The art style and design is also a unique atribute of this game that makes it quite memorable.
The biggest downside of the game is the story mode, after many years of the devs saying it was coming it finally arrived over-hyped. The story is boring. While many people who like TLD might enjoy a more slow paced game, the story is sluggish without taking its time. The beginning of the game is sort of a tutorial which is good for new players but completely halts the "action" for around 30 mins. This also goes against one of my favorite things about TLD, which was the way you kind of have to figure things out with no tutorial. The tutorial takes away some of the discovery aspects of the game for me and I wish the beginning of the story was different. The update that was released with the story also changed things like the UI and menu and made both MUCH less aesthetically pleasing as well as gameplay changed that hinder the game in so many ways. I feel like since the story came out, the game has taken a huge turn for the worse. Before the story update the game was 9.5/10 for me and felt perfectly balanced and beautiful. But now, the game just doesn't have the same feel that it did before. This is really sad to me because it was one of my favorite games on steam.
In short, don't play the story or try and find an older patch to play somehow.

So I picked up RPC a couple of days ago, having kept an eye on it several years back on TIGSource, and I have to say that this game is one of the best I've played in a long long time. Combining my two favourite genres, TD and RTS with a pinch of Roller Coaster Tycoon, I have so far had an absolute blast.
The game starts you on an island world map with the choice of your settling point - You can even go in and look at the maps first before setting up. Once you do that, you've got to balance the livelihoods of your population whilst being besieged by armies of monsters. You begin by gathering the basics - Food and Wood, but over time becoming accustomed with a diverse collection of structures and materials. Production lines form, your civilisation grows, squeezing in between valleys and digging into the safety of bedrock, rather than risking expanding outwards. In turn, beyond your bastions, holes open in the ground in increasing number as more enemies spill onto the map, slowly colouring the minimap red.
The gameplay remains perfectly in flow with a fluctuating day/night cycle and on top of which 4 seasons that constantly mix up gameplay with various weather and effects on your settlement. You really have to stock up for winter (And the first year I massively over prepared, but better safe than sorry!) HINT - MAKE AS MANY FARMS AS YOU CAN - 28 farmers was a sustainable number for me (Whilst enriching wild food collections at the same time!).
Most tower defences suffer from the same issue over time that they become tedious as you perfect your strategy. The twist that has hooked me for RPC is you have the option to send units to "limbo", essentially a menu screen where you can dish out your settlers to a variety of different lands on the map. I spent an hour just surveying the various maps and looking for potential choke points, weighing up the different collections of resources in each area, hesitant to send my villagers to certain doom after such a firm foothold on my first settlement.
To add to this, I found myself grappling with the dilemmas of logging regulation (Do I flatten the forest to supplement my bow towers with arrows, but deal with the long grow back time and pathways destroying the treeline opened up) and I found myself picking single people to inhabit my future settlement to avoid breaking up my many many married couples (170 villagers so far!)
Another fantastic mechanic is the line of sight for defences - Punishing players who box themselves in by preventing them from expanding beyond their walls. There were many times where I'd tear down a couple of the inner walls to frantically assemble some lines of trenches further forwards whilst fighting off hordes of monsters then patch my defences back up before nightfall. It puts a lot more risk in expansion and forces you to avoid greediness.
The game has such depth that I've sunk over half a day into the Retro Pixel Castles over the weekend.
It's just such a good game! I can't put it any simpler than that, haven't felt so transfixed about a strategy game since I discovered Age of Empires 2.
Admittedly, the lack of a built in tutorial is something that could do with addressing, but obviously with Early Access I'm sure it's something that'll come about in time. The video that was linked in the game did provide me with enough information to get started with, so thank you for providing that. Having said this, discovering the functions of the game over time has been quite satisfying in itself - I'm still unlocking the mysteries of essence!
It's a bit of a far fetched request (Especially with the number of units and stuff going on at once, but I would adore a co-op mode for this.
Either way, amazing work, and I look forward to any approaching updates for the project.
