A dark and eerie adventure into an underground sea. The stories you will uncover are Lovecraftian in the nature and slightly unsettling. Sunless Sea is all about exploring and dying and exploring again.
- One of the most original stories that I have ever seen in a video game. Mostly text-based, but this adds to the spookiness, as you're left with your own imagination to picture the things you've seen in the Neath.
- Map randomization at the start of every new Character ensures interesting replay value.
- Beautiful Indie-style graphics that mezmorize
- A Challenge. It is difficult, but the more you die, the more you progress.
- Amazing soundtrack that adds to the tension and feeling of naval exploration.
- Interesting and highly original characters.
- Fairly challenging combat system
-
allows for an easier play, allowing the player to save manually. When you first start a new game, "Merciful Mode" will be turned off.
- The ship you use in the beginning drags along a bit. Until your first upgrades, it is very slow and therefore makes the game seem slow.
- Your character might die often when you first start. This discourges some, but it's a rogue-like.
- The Dawn Machine.
- Sunless Sea is an incredible experience. If you enjoy reading, especially Lovecraft, Poe, Barker, or anything in the horror-suspence genre, you will love this game. The obsurdity, terror, and tension you will feel is pretty incredible. You will also be forced to make dozens of decisions which will affect your character and their story. Definately a game on my top 10 list.

Nurgle, and Necro are on the way too.There is also the occasional bug, crashing here and there, but nothing has ever affected me personally aside from hilarious camera angles.
Over all it's a solid game. If you're at all interested in the turn based strategy (with some rng), warhammer, or football you may very well enjoy this game.

Absolutely brilliant platformer! 8.5-9/10 very easily recommended if you like 3d platformers even slightly!
I grew up in the N64 'Golden Era' of 3d platformers and this game exudes with the charm and personality of those games while adding some good voice acting to improve. It follows the Nintendo ethos of having multiple, swift movement options but improves it by adding badges to change some techniques slightly and add visual flair. The game looks fantastic and runs pretty consistently with a cute cel-shaded art style and bright vibrant colours. There aren't a billion things to collect, I've 100%'d the game in 10hrs but that's a good thing, each of the levels are so unique and well designed with their own themes both visually and gameplay-wise. But above all, it has the polish, attention to minute details, memorable world designs and fluid controls that Yooka Laylee was somewhat lacking.
The X-Factor for this game comes in all of the worlds being like Super Mario 64, small and each Time Piece is objective based making it easy to keep track and maintain progress - EXCEPT for one world which uses the free roam style of Banjo Kazooie to great effect and is a nice change of pace. It didn't choose one style or the other exclusively, it gave a taste of both these brilliant formulae for platforming worlds and it works damn well.
Pros:
- Great art style and solid visual presentation
- Soundtrack is appropriate and very catchy in some places (favourite are Time Rift and Band Song #1)
- Not too many collectibles, so no DK64 burnout just some good fun exploring and snapping
- Controls are tight, smooth and very responsive (Hat Kid is the female Mario)
- Story is ridiculously light-hearted and very tongue-in-cheek (excl. a sad mini-story #Vanessa)
- Each of the 5 worlds are unique and not at all boring or similar to one another
- Camera is brilliant for a 3d platformer about 95% of the time
Cons:
- I'm really scraping the barrel, but there was some slowdown during intense changes in scenery such as Lava episode in Mafia Town
- Camera is a bit funny sometimes, but DON'T let that deter you please. It's simply something that all 3d platformers must bear, the camera will sometimes get stuck in tough spots but it never lead to me dying or losing progress in a platforming challenge
- No DLC yet (seriously Gears for Breakfast, we need dat dlc rite nouw ;) )

I got so mad at this game. I got so flipping mad at this game. I was yelling at my boyfriend at four in the morning and if the controller I was using wasn’t my roommate’s I probably would have thrown it. This game made me SO MAD.
It was pretty good, though.
You have to enjoy physics puzzles; there are puzzles that involve momentum (some of the most frustrating for me), gravity reversal/rotation, and one solitary puzzle that involves stealth. The graphics are minimal but done very beautifully in their style. I really appreciated the sound and music, which was very atmospheric and set the mood perfectly.
The game does a good job initially of introducing the player to the mechanics in an organic and intuitive way. There is no “PRESS A TO JUMP!” tutorial, which would be horrifically jarring in the setting. You have to press buttons to find out what they do (not a difficult task, as you only have directions, menu, jump, and “use” buttons) and the game presents you immediately with basic puzzles for you to solve, simple ones that allow you to learn the mechanics of a game. I’m a huge fan of this approach - I hate tutorials - and it plays well here.
However, as the game moves on and puzzles get more complex, it can become tougher to discern what, exactly, the game wants you to do to get past a certain obstacle. It would have been nice to have some visual cues to indicate to the player that a particular puzzle utilized stealth (only one puzzle in the whole game, which had both me and my boyfriend scratching our heads about how to be ‘stealthy’) and something to indicate that momentum was a factor in puzzles would have been nice. Another problem I had was that very rarely an interact-able item would look like a background item, which really frustrated me on one level toward the end (I believe my exact words were “This is bull****, this game is bull****, this is the most bull**** crap I have ever played.” I am so very eloquent).
Maybe I am just bad at picking up on gameplay cues; the argument could certainly be made that all those frustrations can fall squarely on my shoulders. And honestly, despite my frustrations, the game was pretty enjoyable. I was really mad about the super-precise timing on a few puzzles, but when I did eventually get it, I felt pretty awesome. And once I figured out how to stealth my way through that one puzzle, I was pretty pleased with myself.
There aren’t too many puzzles in Limbo - I didn’t count, but maybe twentyish? - and the game can be finished in probably four or five hours of dedicated play, likely less if you solve the puzzles faster than I did. Don’t expect too much from the “story” - there’s less of a story and more of an atmosphere, which is fun because you can sort of infer your own story - and don’t expect an explicit resolution, but Limbo is a pretty fun game if you enjoy a 2d physics puzzler, and the atmosphere is pleasantly creepy. On the whole, I’d recommend it. But maybe not if you get mad at games and break stuff, like I do.
(And don’t feel TOO bad for my boyfriend. He gets his.)

You slowly awaken to the sound of wind whistling through branches and snow gently kissing your face, opening your eyes to a stark gray sky. Covered in almost 8 inches of powder snow. You wipe the newly landed snow off your face then get up briskly, shaking the layer of snow off yourself like a large dog, You take a moment to look around this unfamiliar frozen land to orient yourself. Towering trees and majestic mountains as far as the eye can see, with no signs of life in any direction.
You open your camping backpack and check to see whats inside. Finding nothing except a plane ticket to Jasper, Canada, a bedroll and a cell phone which doesn't turn on. "Of course my iPhone is dead when i need it" you say with a smirk on your face. Surprising yourself that you still have a sense of humor in a moment like this. But that humor quickly dissolved when you realize you are alone, in a place that looks like something out of a national geographic documentary.
Your instincts  kick in, "The Sun rises in the east, sets in the west. lets head east." It must have been 10 minutes before the snow storm cleared away enough to see a building not too far in the distance. It was a large metal structure covered in icicles. Trekking through the snow to the entrance door you start to feel your denim jeans get soaked, and boots becoming very heavy. This find couldn't have come at a better time, you grab the frosted door handle and turn it.
You step inside the building and begin to close the door, only for the gale force wind to take hold of the door and slam it closed. The windchill is instantly gone. "Is anyone there?" you ask before taking another step into the lobby, your voice echos throughout the building. You notice opposite of you a room with a frosted glass window, a gentle ray of sunlight shines on the floor. You enter the room and begin to scavenge whatever you can. An hour passes and you find a good amount of canned soda, and energy bars, thinking to yourself "Almost sounds like what i lived off with during college."
It takes another hour to scavenge the place finding a box of matches, beef jerky and a brochure with the writing "Jasper Hydro Dam" on it. you make your way to a large heavy door in the buildings engine room. You use most of your strength to turn the large wheel clockwise to open the door, only to see a man sitting on the floor face down. It Startles you to the point where you fall back, screaming "HOLY $%*&" landing on your butt. With the mysterious man frozen in place, you slowly approach and check his pulse. His skin was as cold as the ice and hard to the touch, this man must have been here a while. Next to him lay a hunting knife,  a bottle of painkillers, and note saying "I wish i could've seen you on your wedding day, I'm Sorry - Love Dad". The quiet room suddenly became even more silent as you grab the items and exhaled deeply in grief. You pick up your backpack and head back toward the entry door. As you walked into the lobby the window that had a ray of light no longer was shining,
this would be your first night alone.
It was then you decided to use one of the empty metal barrels to start a camp fire for the night. A spark dances off the match as you strike it, gently placing it on the newspaper youve managed to find in the structure. You knew this fire wouldn't last long if you didn't have some wood to keep the fire going. You foraged for the next two hours gathering reclaimed wood from the feet of chairs to shelves. ending up with a good pile of wood that would last you the night. You place the logs down on the crackling fire. I curl up inside my cotton bedroll on the floor which rested next to the radiating heat. You fall asleep minutes after laying down.
The smell of charred wood lingers in the cold air as you wake up. Looking across the room, you notice the light in the window returns. You gather your belongings and head toward the entry door once more. You grip the handle and turn it, opening the large heavy metal door to a much more calm beautiful morning. You take a big breath of fresh air and let it fill your lungs with a refreshing coolness.
You take a step outside, and another. Just as you take another step a deep loud growl pierces your ears, quickly looking in the direction, A large black wolf leaps into the air and lands on top of you digging its dagger like claws into your flesh and, its large teeth into your neck. tearing you apart. You try punching and screaming like a madman to fend it off but just don't have the strength.
Just as everything begins to fade to black and all hope is lost, You quickly open your eyes to find yourself sitting in an airplane, next to a frosted window with the view of the aircrafts right wing, You touch your neck in relief and rest your head back.
Suddenly the plane starts to have turbulance, a loud repeating beep, and a distant computerized voice saying "Engine Malfunction...GPS Malfunction......Raise Altitude Immediately." emmits from the cockpit. A flight attendant stumbles out of the cockpit, "LADIES AND GENTLEMEN PLEASE FASTEN YOUR SEAT BELTS, THIS AIRCRAFT IS GOING DOWN. PLEASE REMAIN CALM!"

I rate RPC 722/1000. This game strikes a great balance between city-builder in the Banished-eque style (workers moving resources to construction sites) with an ever-more-challenging flood of zombies that your towers must dispatch. It is much more goal-centric than banished as you have to grow your village fast enough to build and maintain sufficient numbers of towers to defeat the growing horde of enemies. The road system is particularly good because the quality (speed) of the roads has a dramatic affect on worker productivity.
The pixel-graphics were actually TOO pixely for me and it was often difficult to tell what the villagers were doing. More interactivity that let the user know what was happening in their world (statistics, graphs, better colored overlays) would have helped. The game needs to scale the difficulty up more from day 21 onwards. Once I passed 21, I could make it to 60 mostly afk.  Finally, the game desperately needs a speed setting (hence the afking) to allow the simulation to run and the difficutly to increase.

Original Post:
The Long Dark is a phenomenal survival game based on guts, determination and luck.  I've spent many hours backpacking across the brutal Canadian rockies in search of shelter or food.  The game is not graphically advanced and the gameplay is not as crisp as many FPS games out there, but there is a magic to this game that keeps drawing me back into it.  The inherent risk/reward of wondering which path to take through the woods is nailbiting fun every time.  The most recent update has added a variety of challenges to players both new and experienced.  Rather than hiking from one location to the next, I am forced to make a base camp and defend it for several days to cure animal hides and heal from wounds.  This small shift in how resources were gathered made me change my playstyle all together.
While the game is pre-release at the moment, the Hinterland team makes regular updates and puts work into their product.  I'm looking forward to the full release and the addition of the story mode to this game.  I've already gotten hours of enjoyment from this game making my purchase worthwhile.  If you're tired of running from zombies give this game a try and see if you can survive . . . the long dark.

As an EA game goes, this one is probably the best case scenario. The dev, Ray, is very active with his burgeoning community, and very active in creating updates, be that new content or bug fixes or optimizations. Activity is great, but it seems like he has a giant whiteboard filled with circles and arrows and charts and scribbles--I'm imagining a mad scientist--and he's following that haphazard genius plan to create his dream game, for surely that's what RPC is for him. Even so, he actively listens to his community to tweak mechanics, stats, and so forth, or even introduce entirely new ideas.
I can't get enough of this game, simply because I want it to be fully completed with all the depth and craziness it will surely have in the end.
Even now, hours of play under my belt, when I think I know what I'm about, I start a new map and suddenly can't seem to quell the hordes of zombies and skeletons. Because it's EA, RPC can run out of content, but that drop has steadily become smaller and smaller in the few months I've been watching and playing this game. The game, nonetheless, possesses a level of challenge that can still be surprising, even in its very unfinished state.

If you're looking for a solo survival game and are an adventurous type of person, this is just the game for you. Overall, the game so far is fairly basic and easy to use once you know you know you're way around the maps. The objective is purely to survive as many days as possible and your only enemies are nature itself, the wildlife, and surviving the cold. Your most important needs are to get food, water, and shelter, and hopefully a weapon to fend off the wolves and bears.
The Beginning:
The start of the game can be a bit confusing, as you are currently plopped into a random location in one of the maps. You're biggest need will be to find shelter right away, as the cold will get to you fairly quickly, then of course food and water.
The Core:
As you progress of the first few days, it will be important to gather lots of supplies. The easiest resources to get are wood and water, with food being a tad bit tougher. Getting as many tools and such are important as well to your survival. The game allows improvised crafting at the work tables in certain buildings and also allows you to patch up your clothes for enhanced buffs and protection against the wind and cold. You also have the ability to tear apart your clothes to harvest resources necessary to patch up your other clothes you already have on. You can craft anything from clothes, fishing equipment, and hunting iteming that help you survive throughout the storm.
Endgame:
There really isn't any way to "win" the game. The best description of end game is really just seeing how long you can survive. Once you have all the tools, plenty of medicine, food, water, shelter, good clothes, and a hunting rifle, you're pretty much set to face anything. Depending on how well you know the maps, these things can be gathered at varied speeds.
OVERALL:
This is a game for the outdoorsy people who just like to try to survive and explore areas. There's no real progression for the game right now, and not sure if it might be added in later with the "story mode." If you're looking to have a game that's very sandboxy, then this is it. If you're looking for progression, you probably won't enjoy it as much. Personally, I enjoy it and have a good time playing it.

TL;DR: Recommended for people who want to scratch a quick, fairly realistic tactical RTS itch. Easy to learn and pick up.
Although it is a very bare-bones game, with no campaign, dynamic or otherwise, custom battles, tutorial (aside from a slightly hidden help-me that can only be accessed in-game during a mission) or even an options menu (it would be nice to have volume control, if nothing else), Firefight is still a very satisfying tactical RTS.
Control infantry, tanks and artillery on a large map, inching forward before making contact. Fix the enemy with suppressive fire and attack from the flank. Watch your men get butchered on an open field because you ignored step one and two. Even though it's a slow and methodical game, it can be very stressful and fun clearing out treelines and industrial areas, leapfrogging infantry sections from one building to the next while other squads and tanks cover them. Though there are no campaigns, the - in my opinion - sufficient selection of maps and missions make for fun 30-60 minute challenges each for those who don't want to make huge time and emotional investments.
Apart from the limited features, which understandably could be a turn-off for many people, the only gameplay complaints I have are tanks' pathfinding, often moving far away from where they were ordered without obvious explanation, and the inability to make them target an area I know an enemy to be coming from. When tanks are your only anti-tank weapon, it can be really annoying to be forced to toss a coin and hope you shoot first.
Finally, I don't recommend games based on features that may be added, but this game is effectively a rewrite of an older game by the same name and developer. This gives me reason to believe that this game may be expanded with more features like campaigns and other fronts.

Overall

I have learned.
I have heard the song the sisters sing. I have heard where it leads. I have seen the end of a tale too long.
I have learned.
I have sailed to the Isle of Cats. I have discovered Red Honey, and the horrific truth that lurks behind its sweet taste.

I have learned.

I have found the thing that lurks, deep, underneath the surface. I have seen a nightmare made flesh, and then woken it.
I have fled the advance of snow and ice. I have prayed it would stop following me and find another. I have been taken by the mountain that moves.
I have learned.
Many have died to know what I know. Many more will die to unlearn it.
I am in love.
I will see you swimming. I will see you floating.
I am in love. And I am hungry.

An absolutely wonderful simulation game that takes the concept of managing a community all the way back to the dark ages. Keep a vigilant eye on your resources and what your citizens are doing, or you'll find them dying of cold and starvation. Once you've mastered the learning curve (which I can almost guarantee will happen only once you've done some out-of-game research), you can begin the fun of slowly expanding your humble hamlet as you stop fighting to survive and instead look to trading with foreign merchants for livestock and plants your town lacks.

Age of Fear 2: The Chaos Lord is a nice little turn based-strategy game. Set in a fantasy realm (Who would have guessed given the title), it is a rather classical experience of recruiting/evolving your units on a seperate screen and sending them into fight after fight. Think of the Tactics Ogre series or FF Tactics. Between the fights there are usually two pages of story which sometimes features minor decisions.
While the story is absolutely allright, it is far from being innovative. The decisions usually mean that you have to choose between "picking an optional fight for reward" or "moving on". Still, it adds some fluff to the campaign.
The main feature of the game is the connection of tactic combat and evolving your units. Here the game holds up well, allowing different tactics to succeed, although those that do not put your units at risk (summons!) tend to be a lot easier than the more direct approaches.
The game is based on Java, which led to some stuttering on my PC in big fights, but I never encountered any bugs. While the backgrounds are quite boring, most of the units are nicely designed and the effects of spells are absolutely adequate.
So, all in all, I can absolutely recommend this game.  In a sale für 2,50€ it is definitely worth every cent.
I consider the regular price to be a bit too high, as the two campaigns are a bit short. But then again, some AAA-titles offer less and charge 50€, so it is up to you. Besides, you support a very active team of indie developers with your money. The designer is very close to the community, answering every thread and asking for opinions all day long. There are also regulary updates, often twice per week which add new ideas.

Incredibly immersive and fantastically absurd, this is a wonderfully written and diverse piece of interactive literature.
Your life can range from a heroic explorer of the world who serves London and civilization while writing romantic novels about your adventures in your free time.
Or you can be a swashbuckling wealthmonger who who enslaves guinea pigs for fun and manically cackles over the piles of money stained with the blood of whoever.
OR you can become a holy vessel of the divine forces that be and drive a bloody crusade through the world, while making sure to get back to Volcano Island in time to have tea and a lovely chat with Grandma Satan.
Overall goals vary wildly.  The game gives you a selection of vague criteria to end it but the best idea is to set your own personal goals.  Build your own character and instead of min maxing, think to yourself "Would my character sell a crewmate and dear friend to cannibals just to churn out a profit?  Absolutely!"
Overall it's an enriching and captivating experience for those who like to read and forge their own story.

I thought this game was quite nice, and an interesting perspective into a supposedly troubled person's mind, although the ideas and frustrations expressed are something that I think are universally relatable, which is part of what makes this game so poignant and powerful. I hope, if the story told by the narrator in this game is real, that he gets back in contact with Coda and they can become friends and Coda starts making games again. I think they're really interesting. And if the story is true, then the narrator's goal was met. People played the game. I personally enjoyed it, and I believe that several others have too. I particularly liked that the first "level" was a Counter-Strike map because I'm really into that game. Maybe even if Coda doesn't want to tell a story anymore, he can make maps for multiplayer games. It's something I'd like to learn how to do. Maybe we can all learn from him.

This is the kind of game that after playing it for a few hours, you realize that your motivations and experiences paint a picture of so many classic elements of fiction (indeed, non-fiction) without stating so in boldface type.
"That old sailor... he drinks to forget the terrors." You'll do this.
"They say he made a deal with... unseemly forces." You can.
"Legends say that in their greatest time of need, captains plead to old gods and make unspeakable sacrifice..." I did. It was a mess.
The mechanics of the game that produce these outcomes are sublte and anxiety ridden at the same time.
Even something that can be seen as a flaw in design might be one of the greatest features: the game has a somewhat randomly generated map, but some elements are in fixed locations and others are always in generally the same area. As a captain on the Zee, you may have read or heard of locations but some non-trivial groping in the dark is required to find them. This may sound simple, but here's the biggest thing: setting sail without a good set of objectives is a death sentence. It may not be a sudden death, but you'll end up in a bad way if you think you can just sally forth with some coal and a couple of boxes of SPAM.

Do you remeber Stronghold?
Mix it up with the feeling of Lemmings when you watch the villagers work (you can't give them orders), the feeling of Settler 1-4 when you watch the villagers carry ressources to houses and construct them (yes they are not magically all over the island but have to get hauled), and Tower Defense games (all kinds of monsters come and try to invade your small settlement, defended by guard towers and the bare fists of the souls you want to protect), and you have this gem here.
The game is as of now (31.07.2016, indev 20) allready fun to play and has no buggy edges and balancing breakers you normally find after the first 4 hours of playing an alpha or early access game. And you will feel, that the developer knows whats fun. There are this and those little features that really show some love to game design. Ofcourse it only costs 10 € atm, so dont expect big unit and building lists or a really long motivation curve of 40 hours.
I strongly recommend it, because I really love Tower Defense and Economy Simulation games. That is one of the games you can allready play in alpha and still call it some nice time.
Btw. I got stomped at the 6th day of summer on an easy start map, and you are expected to survive the winter when there is no food and the zombies are tripple the forces.

Also, this has happened to me a few times, after following the blood trail (in clear daylight weather) for a few minutes, it just disappears, I don't know if this is a glitch or actual gameplay, I like the concept of the trail disappearing, but would be great if this were confirmed.
Apart from preferring death to be less punishing by allowing me to load back to my last save before dying, makes sense, right? I enjoy every other aspect of the gameplay and the graphics and even though the game is incomplete and only the sandbox version is available to play, without any lag or loading time, might I add, the game is an absolute bargain at $19.99 on early access. I would fully recommend this game to any and everyone who enjoys this genre.

First run: I misunderstood how the temperature/cold mechanic works and froze to death in my sleep.
Second run: I amassed a lot of materials, and then stupidly drank unpotable water twice. Then I ventured out to get more wood for the fire and died from a combination of dysentery and freezing in a snowstorm.
Third run: I played it smart, slept in an actual building instead of outdoors, and almost made it a full 24 hours! Then I was unceremoniously mauled to death by a wolf.
Such are the ways of The Long Dark. This game is pretty unforgiving but I still find it to be a fun and worthwhile experience.  There's definitely a learning curve and a lot of mechanics go into keeping yourself alive, but after you figure each one out it gets easier to do the basic stuff. The hard part is actually finding materials to make stuff with, and also learning where it is and isn't okay to sleep (like in a snowstorm....) Even then, some runs just end because of plain bad luck. But I think that's part of what will draw people back to this game: the unpredictability of it.
On the technical side, it controls very well and I have yet to see any bugs. I'm pretty fond of the graphics and color palettes in the game- it's nice to see a sandbox survival game that isnt HYPER REALISTIC RAAARGH graphics for once. Reminds me of Eidolon a little bit. The only problem is I could see surviving getting a little boring after a while, so here's hoping they implement a story soon.

A very well designed platform puzzler. It's got a really creepy vibe, and some very disturbing imagery. The atmosphere is incredibly well done and really draws you into the world. When you're running through the forests, you lose the sense that you're playing a game, and feel like you're watching a little boy going on an adventure.
You'll die often in your first playthrough, and possibly enjoy watching the many ways your little shadowy avatar can die.
Oftentimes, you'll feel like the little boy is really playing in very dangerous situations, and one wrong move will get him killed.
The puzzles all make logical sense, and are pretty easy to figure out and execute. There were only a few more "challenging" puzzles for me.
It's a short amount of content, clocking at roughly 3 hours if you solve the puzzles quickly, or much longer if you're not really good at solving puzzles. But for the quality of the content, those are 3 hours well spent.
Whether you like solving puzzles, enjoying well designed games, or creepy imagery, this game should not be missed.

Unfortunately, the combat number generator is broken. I can't tell you how many 90% attacks I missed, though I can tell you that I missed enough to stop playing the game. Any percentage over 50% seems to actually have a hit percentage 20% lower than advertised. I started calculating my hit percentages by reducing anything over 50% by 20% to find what % I actually might hit.
I get it, someone statistically might really miss the first ten 90% chances to hit. But I feel I played enough to get a real feel for the RNG and it is not right. The concept of 1HP/hit with stronger attacks simply translating to greater hit percentages is not my first choice of hit solutions, but I am willing to work with it for the chance to experience upgraded units and build my strategic force as long as I feel the RNG is fair. I feel like I have a handicap, however, every time I initiate an atttack over 50%. (playing as Orcs, btw)
I have to step away from the game for now, but I intend to try the game again in a few weeks or a month or two. I hope my "luck" or the RNG changes and I can enjoy this game. Until then, I cannot recommend this game.

Your units can only move in straight lines, so attempting to get more than one guy on the same target is a chore.  Your units permanently die, which is kind of neat, but you don't have any method of healing them, so its really up to the random number generator instead of any sort of tactical play that determines if you preserve your guys.  The maps have random areas where you simply can't walk, for no apparent reason, that is very difficult to notice, so your flanking maneuvers are further frustrated by magical impassive terrain.
Also, the writing is bad and plot flimsy.  The graphics are about twenty years out of date, which I knew going into the game, but still disappointing.  The background noise often sounds like someone chewing for some reason, which is kind of gross to listen to on a 10 second repeat loop.

In my last run, I sailed off of the West, North, and East edges of the map. Wound up with a useless hoard of memories sealed in stone, trying to find a port to drop it off at. Limped back to London and ran out of fuel, wounded myself in a vain attempt to gain the intercession of an old zee-god.
Got a nice shiny diamond instead.
So I opened my box full of sunshine and perished in glowing cheery happiness.
10/10 would sink beneath the waves again.
To put a more objective spin on it--this is great for its atmosphere and the surreal world that you get to explore. From there, it's a matter of playstyle (and how completionist you want to be). Will you ever fully explore the game? Probably not, unless you're willing to put 100+ hours into it. If you're not okay with that, then this game may not be for you. I'm not even sure that I'll complete all of the victory conditions.
But, for me, this game isn't about finishing anything in particular, it's about striking out into the dark, discovering new things, and coming to a fuller appreciation of the weird world. Can it get repetitive? Possibly. I mean, yes, the stories reset when you die. Though if you finish up a storyline on a previous captain, there's nothing that says your next captain has to explore the same island--just gather up a port report and move on. Your new captain has bigger things to do.
It's a game where you'll keep building larger and larger circles of gameplay, applying your lessons from failure to your future runs, knowing what places you can skip and how far you can afford to cast out beyond London. You'll learn to plan routes so that you can pick up Port Reports on the way out and back, to provide fuel and supplies for future runs. You'll work out the most efficient ways to achieve early objectives, only to be stymied by later ones. You'll stumble into great menaces, and be prepared for them the next time.
And if the notion of paying terrible prices in order to achieve things like sailing off of every edge of the map intrigues you, this is your kind of game.

I have been a long-time lover of city-builders, and I was very excited to play Banished, but upon playing it... I found it very lacking.
My biggest problems are with the mechanics, which are the most important ones in a game like this. The whole premise is that you need to build a suitable village for a group of people who were ( assumably)  banished. You start out with some basic food, tools and clothes, and then you are on your own.
The initial set-up is challenging. I had to do a lot of juggling with the jobs that my villagers occupied, because some jobs would stall or pause in certain seasons or without enough resources. This is not necessarily bad, but with the mechanics of Banished, this becomes a down-right nightmare.
Say I have need of food, and I assign one of my miners to become a fisherman instead. Randomly, one of the miners will be chosen to fish - no matter the location of his house. So this man will spend far too much time walking to his destination to work, and he is only effective when he works at the location I assigned him.
The food crisis is over, and I assign one of my fishermen to be a miner... And it is not the same man i had as a miner previously.
In the end, this means that nobody lives near their jobs, and that their effectivity is greatly reduced. With perfect play, this can all be prevented, but that brings me to the next point;
When you have everything settled...... there is nothing to do.
There is no king you need to keep happy, there are no politics of any kind. Buildings always have a direct function, and so they never take more than half a day to build, unless you do not have the materials. When everything was going well I found myself bored, but as soon as something got out of hand, there was almost no way to effectively turn it back around without massive losses.
There are tons of small aggravating things in this game;
- If you build too many houses, the people will stop marrying and making babies, because  each person occupying a house.
- If you stop building houses, you will get the problem that people will ALSO stop making babies, because there is no more room in their house for a child.
- Mines and quarries are so ineffective that they are downright useless, and the few stone/iron resources given on the map run out quickly
-There is little to no character to the townspeople, and there is not even a line of text for them to show unhappiness with. They only have stars to show their happiness, which can be fixed by a church or a bar.
-Some buildings need to be in remote locations, but the people that work at them do not live in these buildings, forcing them to walk a far way and waste valuable working time.
I had very high hopes for this game, but compared to the citybuilders I was used to by the time I got this game, it was a big disappointment.
On a more positive note; the music and visuals are very enjoyable.  When played casually on the easy difficulty, I found it a very good game to relax with, and it was satisfying to see the farmers harvest their crop.
I do not recommend it for people that were looking for a citybuilder like Ceasar 3 or Children of the NIle, but if you want to have a relaxing time building a small village with bland villagers, this game is good.

This game is not really a roguelike. It's also not an FTL clone (though I have never played FTL...enough time was wasted on Youtube for me to know). It's an open-world RPG dressed up as these things because they're "cool" with the kind of people who read RPS and Eurogamer, whereas Skyrims and Dragon Ages are not as "cool," even if grudgingly acknowledged as fun.
So, why is it an open-world RPG? It's open world because once Captain N is extruded from the character regeneration device (there's permadeath, but with inheritance), you are free to sail to the farthest reaches of the zee (the sea is what surfacers sail), with no pretense of a plot. Or, rather, no pretense of a MAIN plot. You know, the pile of overwrought, hyperheroic narrative garbage that nobody who plays Elder Scrolls games normally bothers with. There is seemingly a trillion and a half of minor plots, however, which, while not entwined, work together to bring a sense of immersion and wonder I haven't experienced since Morrowind's wall map landed in the hands of my impressionable teenage self.
This open world is, indeed, very similar to Morrowind, but thankfully with much better writing (this is the only game where writing intended to be funny made me chortle slightly). There are major and minor powers suspended in a precarious power balance - you a representative of Fallen London, but there are many others, much stranger, and not all human. It's deliberately weird, almost like a pleasant nightmare. The weirdness is coherent and viscous. There is a sense of wonder and genuine exploration. Surprisingly, despite its cartoonish 2D, the game can make you feel genuine dread, because the friendlier the port is, the more likely it is to be inhabited by eldritch horrors. And then there are giant crabs (a source of knowledge and smoked meats). If you liked Morrowind, you will love this setting, built from elements of fantasy, mythology and steampunk.
That it is an RPG is rather obvious. You have stats (determined during character creation), traits (determined mostly through choices), items (ship, equipment, supplies and "curiosities") and even a party (your officers). The stats, together with luck, determine outcomes of stories (which are often unlocked, and bestow, traits). The stats are improved by experience ("secrets" in game jargon), which directly correlates with your effort at exploration, both on sea and on land. The party is there to enhance your stats, but they also come with their own stories, and romance possibilities because that's now a traditional element of RPGs, thanks to Bioware.
The boat...movement gameplay outside of stories is solid. This is not a boat simulator or a strategy game. It's a narrative-driven RPG. So, no, you won't be manually computing your targeting solution, because you're not playing Silent Hunter. It's also not the most exciting arcade game in the world. It does its job and possibility of combat against some zea monster maintains the necessary tension at zee. This is also not a trading game, though profitable trade routes exist, if you insist on grinding your way to riches. It's a game of exploration and adventure, heavily driven by walls of text. If you don't like walls of text, this game won't change your mind. Nevertheless, the resource management bits are a strong point, because lack of supply and crew morale (which the game, appropriately, measures on an inverse scale as "terror") often influence your decisions on land.
Of course, the only other part of gameplay are "choose your own adventure"-style port stories. Surprisingly, these elevate an otherwise basic game to glory. First, wrap your head around this revelation - all cRPGs (except, maybe, Crusader Kings 2, because wargame-y parts intervene) are basically "choose your own adventure"-style stories. They may be rendered in photorealistic 3D, but the "choice" almost often comes down to selecting A or B, with predetermined outcomes. And this is in games like Dragon Age or Mass Effect, which the press worships like a Golden Calf because they're not literally just Call of Duty with more intelligent cutscenes. Thankfully, the Sunless Sea is down from the mountain (or up from the cave?) to cast down the false gods. The same choices may yield different outcomes depending on your situation, stats, and luck. Sometimes, the same "quest" is not the same - there's a "fetch quest" at the beginning which appears to have different follow-ups every time. Quest lines are dynamic, evolving while you're at sea and outcomes of these quests influence gameplay.
In sum, it's a fantastic narrative-focused RPG with a rich, weird world, solid, if basic, gameplay mechanics and profound, clever writing. Buy it, play it, read it, die in it, then repeat.

I personally enjoy this game, but I don't recommend it. I place out cons of this game first.
1) Bugs, many bugs and developer ignore it / take a long time to fix it
So there's a recent meta (defense combo), but we found out the defense is buggy, which makes it overpowered. I've started this game about 3 months ago, yet to be fixed by now (21 - dec - 2016)
2) 1 hit on the core and lost
This won't happen on easy difficulties (Normal, hard, nightmare 1). This often happens on Nightmare 4 games, those monsters deal extremely high damage and your core just have about 2k health. They deal up to 20k damage, even able to kill you in 1 hit.
3) Grinding system, sucks.
You may ask "what do you mean by it sucks?", well, we grind our weapon from different maps that offers us the same weapon (legendary) with different stats, yes, thats it, different stats. But for example I just want (Hero dmg) and (Elemental dmg), sometimes you might replay the game up to 10 times, even up to 30 just for the stats.
4) Unfair leveling (IPWR level)
For those who yet to play the game, IPWR means Item power. So when you just started, your average IPWR is around 30 - 150. But you can instantly jump into any public no IPWR requirements, grind loot from there and instantly jump from 200 - 600. This is a huge disavantage for those who started the game a long time ago and grind slowly from Nightmare 1 to Nightmare 4 difficulty.
5) Spheres are in a complete mess
Once again for those who yet to play the game, spheres is a token (or whatever you call them) that gives you a stats, for example +40 hero damage, +10% experience loot, etc. There's some of them which cost a lot (Indeed alot, because you need to spent 2 weeks or even 1 month to get it), and they're useless, pretty much. Because if the current meta defense doesn't require it, you won't find any help with the sphere if you are not someone that like to research.
I've spent around nearly 200 hours, and i've gotten bored and lost interest to the game, this game is base on the angle you play it, if you don't like it, just deal with it, because no one is going to change the meta UNLESS the developer does.

As a fan of the first two games in the series, I had high expectations for the third installment when it came out.
After the first few minutes of gameplay, I knew that the game wouldn't meet my expectations in any way. Deep Silver and Keen Games left out everything that made Sacred great. Instead of a huge open world with ridiculous amounts of sidequests and places to discover like in the first two games, Sacred 3 features a set of missions that have to be completed. The missions themselves are extremely linear, with only one route from beginning to end.
Instead of an inventory and a huge pool of items, weapons and armor, there's... nothing. However the characters do have a few different weapons to choose from, with no weapon being necessarily better than the other, just different. The only loot you'll find is gold, which you can use to buy new skills.
This is a shell of a game that features very little interaction other than killing stuff. No quests, no NPCs to talk to, nothing... just a few switches to press here and there. There is a bit of dialogue during the game. However that dialogue consists almost entirely of horrible attempts at humour and bad jokes... and I mean really bad, like kindergarten level bad.
Although this game bears the "Sacred" title, it doesn't resemble Sacred in any way or form. I wouldn't have a problem with this game if they released it as some sort of spin-off or something. I mean it would still be a bad game, but with the "3" in the title, it drags the entire series through the mud.
To me it seems like Deep Silver witnessed Blizzard's success with their overly simplified Diablo III and ordered Keen Games to do the same with Sacred 3 in order to make a hit game. That plan failed, although the game is fun a short while... but like Diablo III, it gets boring really quickly.

Instead of a semi-open world it has been changed into a series of select a location, fight through the enemy lines, rinse and repeat. If you're looking for a solo survival game and are an adventurous type of person, this is just the game for you. Overall, the game so far is fairly basic and easy to use once you know you know you're way around the maps. The objective is purely to survive as many days as possible and your only enemies are nature itself, the wildlife, and surviving the cold. Your most important needs are to get food, water, and shelter, and hopefully a weapon to fend off the wolves and bears.
The Beginning:
The start of the game can be a bit confusing, as you are currently plopped into a random location in one of the maps. You're biggest need will be to find shelter right away, as the cold will get to you fairly quickly, then of course food and water.
The Core:
As you progress of the first few days, it will be important to gather lots of supplies. The easiest resources to get are wood and water, with food being a tad bit tougher. Getting as many tools and such are important as well to your survival. The game allows improvised crafting at the work tables in certain buildings and also allows you to patch up your clothes for enhanced buffs and protection against the wind and cold. You also have the ability to tear apart your clothes to harvest resources necessary to patch up your other clothes you already have on. You can craft anything from clothes, fishing equipment, and hunting iteming that help you survive throughout the storm.
Endgame:
There really isn't any way to "win" the game. The best description of end game is really just seeing how long you can survive. Once you have all the tools, plenty of medicine, food, water, shelter, good clothes, and a hunting rifle, you're pretty much set to face anything. Depending on how well you know the maps, these things can be gathered at varied speeds.
OVERALL:
This is a game for the outdoorsy people who just like to try to survive and explore areas. There's no real progression for the game right now, and not sure if it might be added in later with the "story mode." If you're looking to have a game that's very sandboxy, then this is it. If you're looking for progression, you probably won't enjoy it as much. Personally, I enjoy it and have a good time playing it.

I like RPC, I really do. At the moment there's not much to it, however. If you like building villages, micro-managing resources and villager needs, RPC has a few good things going for it, but there's also a lot holding it back, including the word "castle".
It's tough; really tough actually, and if you screw up, you pretty much have to make a new profile to try again, you can't just pick a different area on the map. This is a minor annoyance given that you can easily screw yourself over, especially while just learning the game.
I like that there's enemies to defend your castle against, but they -easily- overwhelm most defenses, and at the moment, the only way to defend is tower-defense-like mazes you have to build, where half of the towers are pretty much useless. I found the fire towers to draw way too much power to be useful and the rock towers near useless since they have to be out in the open,(can't be behind walls) right where enemies can easily swarm it, making the point of it, to roll a rock down a line of enemies, useless. Real castles didn't work this way, they had gates, moats, walls you could sit on and shoot down, etc. I really wish there was more "castle" in this game. There really isn't, it's more akin to Retro-Pixel Villages.
It's a fun little game, I like the aesthetic, and I like most of the resource managment and crafting system, but I'm gonna wait and come back to it later when/if/hopefully they add more "castle" elements like walls with gates and such, I'm tired of making mazes and getting overwhelmed, and when more later-game content comes in. Very nice so far though! I will revisit and re-review it in the future.

Bioshock is a game like no other. The game is a first person shooter (FPS) that draws you in with a amazing story which is unlike any other first person shooter you have ever played. The creators of this game included such detail in the story that it literally makes you feel like a part of the game. In many ways Bioshock is an experience more than a FPS. Without giving the story away I can say this, the game centers around a character which finds in a mysterious underwater city. The city which was meant to be a paradise turned into something much worse, people turned on each other and with the use of genetic engineering have all become deadly and cunning enemies. You yourself will have to modify your genetic structure to have a chance at finding your way out of the city and back to the rest of the world. At every turn these enemies lurk, and at any moment you may find yourself surrounded by them. There are several great components to the game including power ups for your weapons, different types of ammunition, crafting, machine "hacking" and many more which all make this game stand above all other first person shooters I have ever played. This game does not have a multiplayer but it does have full controller support.  I wholly recommend this game to anyone whether they be new to the first person shooter genre or not. Truly this is a great game. In the past I have said that games are good but would be better if the cost of the game was worth the experience, with this game however ever bit of money you pay for this game will be worth your time. I hope you do play this game, I was hesitant at first, and now after playing the game I don't know why.

Let's put it this way: SUPERHOT is a first person shooter with a 'bullet time' mechanic in its very core. The only reason that this game is acutally playable is because of the slow motion, or else literally no one can beat it unless you have a crazy reaction speed.
In terms of gameplay, it is not exactly fast-paced, but that is the best feature of the game. The game gives you time to strategize in beating the level as the difficulty rises as you advances. Though it gives you time to think of strategies, it is unforgiving in terms of failure as it is an instant death if any of the enemies touches you. One point in mind is that the hitbox can be pretty confusing as sometimes misses that seem impossible will occur.
The price of the game really depends on how much you would like to invest in the game as the campaign is really short. I beat the game in around two hours with multiple failure on later levels, which is really short for a game with this price level. BUT in my opinion, this game is designed for it endless modes and challenges rather than the main story. So if you are into having challenges and endless modes in your game, SUPERHOT is the game for you.
In conclusion, this is a 'love it or hate it' kind of a game. This game also open up a possibility of another opportunity for people to design levels and mods if the devs would allow it, I really hope that this game do support mods in the near or distant future.
P.S It’s the most innovative shooter I’ve played in years.

You go into the lighthouse and go into a submarine like object called a bathysphere. It brings you down into an underwater city called rapture. You go into the city only knowing it is dangerous scary (this game is not really a horror game) and along the way you are given information by a guy named Atlas. These start off basic like fire ice telekinesis but through the game you can get powers that will shoot bees from your hand or create a decoy to attract enemies. Another amazing thing about this game is the enemy you have
Main enemy splicers - People who have been driven crazy by Adam and eve and are addicts
Splicer variants - There are lots of different types of splicers (ex spider splicers can climb on walls)
Little sisters - Kind of an enemy little sisters you can harvest or save them. When you harvest little sisters you get more Adam but kill them in the process. If you save them you get less Adam but depending on how man little sisters you harvest and save it will change the ending.
Big daddies - Giant creatures in suits that protect the little sisters. You must kill them to get to them.
Overall everything about this game is great. Try the demo. This game is amazing and definitely worth the asking price. I would pay up to $60 at launch and $35 at the time of this review (5/11/14)

Great survival game that requires you to strategize how to approach derelict spacecrafts with your small crew of drones to explore and scavenge.  The game gives you an array of tools to outfit your drones to fill certain tasks, such as: powering sections of the spacecraft, sensors to detect enemies in adjacent rooms, towing/gather tools to bring scavenged supplies back to your ship, and so on.  You are constantly on the verge of running out of gas and supplies, which really pushes you to take risks, hoping that the risks will reward you with what you need.  At the same time, many of the ships have aged to the point of being volatile to enter, so time in a lot of instances can be of the essence.  The immersion is also great, as it only allows you to use your keyboard to type simple commands to order your drones about and open/shut doors.  The interface has a great aesthetic to it and really makes you feel like you are in a tiny command center in charge of an away team on a spacecraft.

The world of Sunless Sea is an intriguing one. It's a slightly whimsical twist on an ocean-themed Lovecraftian-esque horror.
The problem with this is that absent incredible graphics, it takes very high quality writing (and a lot of it) to pull off a world such as this.
The writing that is present in Sunless Sea? Is good. Not stellar, but pretty good. They manage to squeeze a lot of subtle themes and a 'feeling' of the place in to a few short sentences.
So what's my objection? Why do I say I don't recommend buying the game?
What is written is good, but there isn't enough of it and it doesn't always work perfectly. As an example (mild spoiler for an early game location), there's a mansion/house on an island with three sisters inside. If you do a thing or two in the wrong order upon discovering this house, the game mentions that you are aquainted with the sisters, but 'things have changed'... despite not having known what things were previously, giving no context for what has 'changed'. Even if you do things in the 'correct' order,
. The writing associated with the sisters, the mansion, their stories? It's
identical to how it was when you first met them.
Then, suddenly one day, everything changes (long, long after the game suggested things were changed). Without warning. So 'things have changed' for eight identical interactions, and then suddenly once everything seems routine, things are different. It turns out that your character (or the game interface?) psychically intuits 'changes' in the world without those changes being evident in the writing presented.
Similarly there's another 'quest chain' that seems merely capitalist in nature. 'Take this stuff over here and we'll pay you'. Every time you do it, it's exactly and perfectly identical, meaning that if you're here for the story or writing, it doesn't seem like there's any story or writing to be had at that location. The game interface, however, suggests the quest has further stages to it, without that implication being present in the writing.
If the location in question is positioned out of the way (the map is semi-random), you then have no reason to visit the location frequently, other than to grind out money MMO-style. Then, suddenly one day without explanation, the quest changes. No reason for it changing, no explanation for why the government (the government is involved) has ceased doing things the way they always have, just... things are suddenly different. When you follow that particular quest to its end? The end is abrupt, without explanation, and seemingly pointless ("here's some money, go away").
If things are changing, if events are progressing, you'd expect the writing to reflect that. The writing does not, leaving a lingering feeling of narrative whiplash behind as the abrupt and inexplicable changes in the world happen seemingly at the roll of random dice, while the game's design expects you to realize that progression is occuring within this narrative arc based on UI tooltips rather than engaging and varied writing.
Combat-related upgrades, short of a few early-game purchases, are entirely out of reach for any but the most experienced players, and most players can not obtain the experience necessary to become rich enough to purchase those items without winning combat reliably. A near-Catch-22. (The answer to this is avoid combat entirely, or exploit the AI. More on that later.)
The writing is sparsely available. Almost all of it is relegated to far-flung ports of call, so experiencing more story or more writing (the 'strong' point of the game, and likely the reason you bought it) requires mind-numbingly boring journeys across a nearly-empty 'zee'. Vast amounts of the game involve sitting motionless at your computer, staring at your ship as it moves in a straight line from one port to the next. You occasionally might want to fiddle with the lights or might need to steer to avoid a rock or monster, but generally you'll spend easily more than half of your game staring at a boat, rather than reading.
This sparcity of writing wouldn't be a problem if each port-visit brought new content, a new thing to read, something worth the time you spent 'zailing', but more often than not you'll only see the same content the last time you visited. That several-minute voyage you just made? Well, it ended in a visit to a place you've already seen, with writing you've already seen. Congrats! It's like you're re-reading the same chapter of a book over and over again. Fun, right?
As mentioned previously, combat upgrades are not readily available even to a character that has played for a significant time. There are a
small number of upgrades you can purchase without replacing your boat, and replacing your boat itself is prohibitively expensive. At the time of this review, I've played two captains (the first lived four hours of in-game time, the second 15-16). I never even came
close to being able to afford a new ship hull, limiting both my upgrade options (hulls have an unlisted, unexplained maximum speed regardless of engine power, and the starter ship can only outfit one category of weapons out of three categories).
This wouldn't be a problem if combat was something you had to actively seek out, but frequently you have to actively avoid combat encounters, and you'll end up needing to do that (or exploit the very bad AI) in 80% of the areas you'll be visiting.
Yes, you read that right. I ended up exploring very nearly all of the available map with my second captain, and short of areas very close to Fallen London, I'd always have to avoid combat. Nearly everything outclassed me. As an example, the starter ship has 75HP. Enemies you may come across while still exploring and learning the map could have 600 or even 1000HP.
In my most recent case, my fairly successful second captain, which had managed to survive and explore for 15+ hours,
From my perspective? It was a combat encounter that only occurred because this hulking behemoth (that I couldn't really see) of an enemy just happened to brush against the top edge of my visible screen. Before I even realized I was being shot at, I was under half-health. A second or two later, I was dead, and 15+ hours of exploration and work was gone.
The game was asking me to explore and 'zail' in to areas where doing something that isn't even obviously a 'mistake' could end up with you dead before you even realize you're in danger.
Worse yet, many of the quests in the game
(without explaining that combat is where to get the required items). You'd think that a game that prides itself on its writing would have something in writing explaining that 'fishing' in the game is done with your guns. If you want to read the narrative, the whole point of buying the game? You have to engage in near-suicidal acts (combat in the starter ship)that are made only survivable by exploiting the very weak AI. Survival in combat is a matter of rushing the enemy and kissing your boat to it. The AI gets confused, spazzes out, and tries to move away from you. So long as you hug the enemy, it can't fight back. This is true for all animals, and also true for the other ships in the game so long as you hug those ships' backsides.
My most 'successful' outings were the ones where I risked running out of fuel before reaching a place where fuel was affordable or even sold. I'd expand more, but apparently there's a character limit. I'll work on paring down this review to squeeze more in later.

For the first seven or eight hours, Duskers feels like it could be one of the best rogue-lites out there. The way the game creates its tense, claustrophobic atmosphere is a great showcase for what good writing and some well-placed sound effects can achieve despite minimal graphics and only rudimentary gameplay. The controls fit the theme to the point that you really do feel like a drone operator, carefully managing his precious metal-minions through potentially alien infested wrecks and salvaging everything that is not nailed to the floor (literally).
After putting in some extra hours, however, the atmosphere starts to slip and with it the enjoyment you get out of Duskers. Moving through the derelict spaceships becomes a routine task and you start to recognize most of the sounds; the atmosphere just deflates at this point. If your game is thriving on the fear of the unknown, you have to give the player enough stuff to not know about to be engaged in the long-term - Alien: Isolation suffered from a similar problem. Still, Duskers is a solid game, but I can not help but feel it is a missed opportunity: With more content, more variety in enemies and events, maybe even some friendly encounters, the game could have been up there with rogue-lite classics like FTL or Spelunky.
Nonetheless, Duskers is a decent execution of a good concept; it just lacks the content to really keep you hooked after about 12 hours. The game is a solid buy during a sale, especially for fans of scifi horror in the vein of Alien or The Thing.

Where do I start with a game like Sunless Sea... In truth I am rather torn...
The combat system is weak. Simplistic to the point of tediousness. Many times I found myself thinking "Ugh... more pirates... sigh... why bother"
The "Sunless Sea" tends to feel a lot more like a Sunless pond. Its disipointing lack of size kills the mood pretty fast. Worse yet is the fact that there is little to do when you reach a new Island. In a game like Sunless Sea every location should inspire a feeling of awe and wonder. I should be delighted to find a new island! Waiting to be explored for all it's treasures and mystery... or... its horrors lurking in the dark.
Exploration into the Dark and Mysterious should be a priority in a game about one's adventures in a sunken city. I would lov to see new events occure on Islands frequently. That would make every visit a bit more memorable and maybe add replay value. This unfortunitly isnt the case with the current build.
If there is one thing they did correctly, Its the atmosphere. For how small the map is, it's dreary colors and rather soothing music paint an facinating picture. I want to learn more about the world of Fallen Londen and all the islands within its deadly waters. I want to know what life is like in this world. See the pale faced people and hear the echo of horrors deep in the endless darkness.
PROs:
Beautiful and Mysterious world. So delicious it almost makes the game worth buying on it's own.
CONs:
Boring combat ruins the pace of the game. More content would do Sunless Sea well.
In the end... I think I can recommend this game... BUT wait for it to go on sale. There isn't enough to the game for it to be worth full price. Its an experiance unlike any other game I have played up to this point and YOU should experiance it too!

As of writing this review it is during the steam game awards and let me tell you I wish you were able to pick 2 options because this game definitely hands-down should win the "Best use of a farm animal" award and definitely the "I thought this game was cool before it won an award" award.
Now onto the review.
This game first came out for Xbox 360 probably a year or two back if im right and I had a great time with it all the way to the end. Now I'm here to tell you this PC version though and let me tell you there is so much that's different here that it feels like a new game entirely.
Blood and Bacon is a game where you play as one of 6 characters, you go to a farm to find a farmer in a barn stuck to the wall with a pitchfork in his gut and missing leg, every new day you get to in the game the farmer will tell you some tips on how to survive and over time you will either learn to love him or hate him, and every day you come to kill all the pigs each day and then you talk to the farmer at the end of the day to start the next one.
Now I'm sure your wondering, "why is this game so Overwhelmingly Positive if it is such a simple and small game?" Well if you have seen the trailer before looking at this review I will tell you that it is definitely the blood bath you see in it. With now up to 4 player coop where even more pigs spawn in depending on the number of players in your game you can find one hell of a time. And trust me, some days you will literally see nothing but "Blood and Bacon" at the end of some days.
This game has lots of unlocks and a TON of secrets or fun things to do around the farm. Some you will find on your own or learn from the farmer. Meanwhile the farmer has lots of fun and interesting quotes to say depending on finding secrets on the farm, shooting the farmer, or from simply flashing your flashlight in his face.
And customizable camera angles is one of the 'bigger' features this game has. With three different camera angle options on top of customizing them yourself and moving the cameras allows you to make the game first or third-person or whatever you see fit.
The bosses are fun and definitely challenging to learn and do for your first time and I am sure you may think 'wtf' on day 10, then 'what the hell' on day 20 leading all the way to the final day where you will definitely need some help because these bosses are of a Dark Souls quality here. Which comes onto the second topic here...
Multiplayer is definitely a fun blast to play and with the new 6-player horde map you can unlock even more secrets and one of the now 9 characters they have in this game now. Not only that but this game also has....keyword here.....free hats for your characters if you find keys which requires you to look around for secrets and such. But there are also other secrets leading to the farmer to say some 'clever' farm jokes and even sing a song.
When you play this game you will DEFINITELY see pig parts flying around and definitely some blood flying all over the farm. And yes, you do fight hundreds of pigs at a time some days and revenge days are where this game really shines.
Trust me, this game is worth it for it's 0.99 price and at the time of this review 0.79 price. Definitely worth the dollar price and why would you ignore this game during it's sale? I have bought this game many times and I never regret a single time I purchased this game. And by the time your done you will see pigs in a new light and definitely have a hunger for BLOOD & BACON.

A hidden gem for any TBS fan.
Two campaigns of ca. 15 battles each interspaced with some of the most amusing storyline (very much tongue in check, in a refreshing manner) will definitely return your moneys worth.
In the beginning your troops will die and any single one you manage to rescue into the next stage is cherished. The longer they live, the better they become. Towards the end they are nigh unstoppable, but that is when you can increase the difficulty to even the odds (I did).
I might start a second playthrough, now that I'm aware of what I can expect and select my troops accordingly.  I selected at least one of every type to find out what upgrades are available on the first round (spiders and bats for example are very situational and need careful consideration, it might be better to include an allpurpose unit like a mage or succubus instead etc.)
What I like is that the two campaigns favour a different playstyle....As orcs you have a very solid melee wall and try to snipe the opposing frontline with hypnotize to turn their own troops against them....As succubus you flood the enemy with summons and snipe with fireballs, not caring if it hits your own summons.
Loved both ways:)
Oh and a small tip, hidden stashes are automatically detected, as soon as one of your troops can reach the spot...so to find anything (not every map has secrets), walk a fast runner all around the map before leaving the battle(use of t-key was very helpful here).

I have been a long-time lover of city-builders, and I was very excited to play Banished, but upon playing it... I found it very lacking.
My biggest problems are with the mechanics, which are the most important ones in a game like this. The whole premise is that you need to build a suitable village for a group of people who were ( assumably)  banished. You start out with some basic food, tools and clothes, and then you are on your own.
The initial set-up is challenging. I had to do a lot of juggling with the jobs that my villagers occupied, because some jobs would stall or pause in certain seasons or without enough resources. This is not necessarily bad, but with the mechanics of Banished, this becomes a down-right nightmare.
Say I have need of food, and I assign one of my miners to become a fisherman instead. Randomly, one of the miners will be chosen to fish - no matter the location of his house. So this man will spend far too much time walking to his destination to work, and he is only effective when he works at the location I assigned him.
The food crisis is over, and I assign one of my fishermen to be a miner... And it is not the same man i had as a miner previously.
In the end, this means that nobody lives near their jobs, and that their effectivity is greatly reduced. With perfect play, this can all be prevented, but that brings me to the next point;
When you have everything settled...... there is nothing to do.
There is no king you need to keep happy, there are no politics of any kind. Buildings always have a direct function, and so they never take more than half a day to build, unless you do not have the materials. When everything was going well I found myself bored, but as soon as something got out of hand, there was almost no way to effectively turn it back around without massive losses.
There are tons of small aggravating things in this game;
- If you build too many houses, the people will stop marrying and making babies, because  each person occupying a house.
- If you stop building houses, you will get the problem that people will ALSO stop making babies, because there is no more room in their house for a child.
- Mines and quarries are so ineffective that they are downright useless, and the few stone/iron resources given on the map run out quickly
-There is little to no character to the townspeople, and there is not even a line of text for them to show unhappiness with. They only have stars to show their happiness, which can be fixed by a church or a bar.
-Some buildings need to be in remote locations, but the people that work at them do not live in these buildings, forcing them to walk a far way and waste valuable working time.
I had very high hopes for this game, but compared to the citybuilders I was used to by the time I got this game, it was a big disappointment.
On a more positive note; the music and visuals are very enjoyable.  When played casually on the easy difficulty, I found it a very good game to relax with, and it was satisfying to see the farmers harvest their crop.
I do not recommend it for people that were looking for a citybuilder like Ceasar 3 or Children of the NIle, but if you want to have a relaxing time building a small village with bland villagers, this game is good.

Updated review (as of 01/28/17)
Let me start by stating that I have never played the original Dungeon Defenders game.  So for me, Dungeon Defenders II (DDII for short) was my first experience with this franchise.  I have no knowledge of how DDI played and I will not be comparing DDI with DDII in this review.
For me, DDII did something other Tower Defense games have never done.  They combined awesome tower builds with the ability to have a 3D environment that you (the character) can also run around and interact with.  This means that, in DDII, if you are not optimizing your towers as well as your hero damage and contributing both equally, you are not really playing the game the way it was meant to be played.
The game also has its fair share of issues, like any other game, and it’s also worth mentioning that it is still in early access so anything I mention is subject to change.  When I started playing this game in mid-November of 2016, quite a bit had already been changed in DDII from the inception (or initial launch of the title).  For example, the campaign got a huge revamp right before I started and now it is designed to take you from lv1 to lv50 and get you started in Nightmare I difficulty out of the gate.  This was not the case originally.  The reason I mention this is, there is a massive update coming which will change and address quite a few issues most players have with the game, how you gear, progression within the difficulty tiers, inventory management, game balance and so much more.  It’s important to understand, in my opinion, that the game is still early access and will continue to get better over time.
All that said, I have really enjoyed my time with this game thus far and it is free to download so you can try it risk free.  I am so excited for the new changes coming in February 2017 (or later depending on TrendyENT) and I can highly recommend this game to anyone that likes the idea of a tower defense game that is much more action oriented.  Since I haven’t really mentioned it, your character gears and levels up and it is very similar to diablo style games, loot based systems, where you are going to be grinding for better gear/drops so you can not only enhance your towers' defense power but also your hero power.
Now that the dark souls series is finished, I needed a new game to make me want to heave a controller through my monitor.  Now I have it, thanks Studio MDHR 10/10

A nice little game with really nice developers. They are active in the steam forums and answer questions and listen to your recommandations and critics. Now you have even the chance to give them input, what you would like to see in Age of Fear 3.
About the game itself:
The fights are challenging and sometimes quite hard if you play on Experienced- or Master-Difficulty. Even experienced turn-based players should try and easiest mode first, because some of the mechanics need some experience to really understand them or at least very good reading of the tutorial informations given. Keeping your units alive is probably the most important about this game, to evolve them in the way you wish them to be. Also you should keep an eye on wich units get the exp, to speed up leveling of specific units.
Yes, the story is textwalled, but I enjoyed to read those and I liked how the storyline evolved, at least the one I played through so far. There are even slight possibilities to chose wich arc of story line you wish to follow. If they even could change the ending, I can't tell so far, but I don't think so. But they offer you different battles and items and perhaps even special units.
If you play, you should be aware, some of those fights you have to lose. So if an opponent looks far stronger than you, don't get frustrated and give up. Your loss has to be then probably and offers perhaps some new units, you couldn't get your hands on otherwise.
And yes, the graphics aren't the best of the best, but they aren't the important stuff. The combat is important and the AI is well programmed and lets you suffer, if you don't plan your actions well. So if you like a challenging old school game support these indies.
P. S.: And no, you don't really play only evil ones. Yes, you can play an orcish story line (wich I can't argue about much so far) and a demon story line, but the demon is far from pure evil but selfish and manipulative for sure. ;)
