Faces of Illusion is a forgettable hidden object game. It does its job as it should, but never thrives for more than acceptable quality.
Faces of Illusion: The Twin Phantoms is what you may call comfortably average. It uses all the basic modern hidden object game elements to bring a decent experience, but does not even attempt to stand out in any way.
It is a shame, as it has a few shining moments. For example, the pacing is great: we start our story by witnessing a kidnapping, only to follow the hot lead through a theatre, a mansion, and even the Notre Dame. It never really sits down, but the dry dialogues and clumsy voice acting hurt its quality quite a bit.
The same goes for gameplay. The hidden object scenes are entertaining, thanks to their good variety (although some item placements are a bit evil), but the puzzles are the same tired ones we saw a million times already, with a difficulty that is shameful even in a casual game.
If you can enjoy mixed bags that surpass the requirements for a fun enough HOG, Faces of Illusion will not be a bad pick, but do not expect any lasting impressions.

Listen: the water slaps against the ship. Look: the lights of home fade into the darkness.
The darkness encloses you in infinite possibilities. Some slumber beneath the water. Some, more worryingly, wake. But the ship sails on.
Sunless Sea isn't quite about exploration, nor is it entirely about combat. It seems to be about a certain mood--something wistful, melancholy, and beautiful all at once. There are wonders out here, yes, but the warmth of home is far away. It's one of the most atmospheric games I've ever played, and can in the space of a few hours be horrifying, beautiful, heartbreaking, and surprisingly funny.
It's also immensely difficult. You will die. A lot. And though you can carry over certain things between characters with a Legacies (you get at least one, and can earn more), it's still possible to LOSE a legacy. But these deaths give the game a lot more weight. You find yourself connecting with your characters and your randomized world more, and you can pick different choices in a second--or third--or fourth--playthrough.
While the game is a lot more balanced in favor of the player than it was a few months ago (thank God), be aware that it'll still probably be tweaked a bit more over the course of 2015.
TL;DR: get the thing. Also, stock up on food and fuel. Being alone at sea in a ship that can't move, with a crew that can't eat...well, goodness. You would be in quite the pickle, wouldn't you? Or perhaps you'd just be pickled...

This game is absolutely enthralling. I want to get back to it every second I have free time, even though I have already lost...how many was it...5 villages in only 8 hours? I seem to not be the best deity for these people...
This game captivates you with its unique design and the music in the background only further emphasizes this--I feel as if I were transported back in time to when these villagers lived.
Perhaps one of the best parts of this game is that it give you a very brief intro, and then throws you into the game with only the most basic knowledge--trial and error is essential to this. Not only do you consider how to manage/assign your villagers, but you also have to consider building priorities, landscape, potential areas of threat from monsters, and of course, managing your resources.
In considering any downsides, the one thing I might have an issue with is that often times when I want to hover my mouse over a fight between my servants (ha) and the monsters, all I am able to see is a health bar of one person, especially if multiple entities are in the same square. All I really want is to make sure my people's health bars are still doing well. Maybe add some sort of way to view the villagers’' health bars outside of hovering the mouse over them?
All in all, great game, and I will continue to try to prevent the total and inevitable destruction of my people!

I play mostly BB:CE, so i'm looking mostly at differences between the two versions. The new button layout, once you get used to it, is superior and actually makes sense now. Be careful switching between both versions; misclicks happen. I love the new stadium options, allowing you to customize your team's pitch. It reminds me of the special play cards in the TT game. I'm not as in love with the new graphics as the general opinion seems to be; there's a lot to like but not everything. The stadiums are pretty, but the new larger overlay is what you see most of the time, and that's the same for all pitches. The fans all have the same face. The uniforms look more similar to eachother, and as has been pointed out many times, do not change as a player advances. However, there are some real highlights. The new CW helmets are fantastic. The troll-slayer has a great, eager look to him when he moves. The troll's jaw is excellent. There are tons of these tiny nifty details. The GUI is better too, with clear and obvious choices on rerolls, apoth, bribe, and such. The on screen information during play is a weakness, as the skills are now icons and some of the team info is obscured. I like the new version and I hope they address some of the issues, which would seem to be easy fixes in most cases.

Wow. You shouldn't need anyone else to say what's great about this game at this point because I'm sure between the youtube videos and the hailstorm of positive reviews this game already should look like a solid purchase but let me just say that within this game beats the heart of a true platformer. I never would have imagined such a small company could strive so boldly to earn a place among the Mario franchise titles and come so close to reaching it. The controls are fantastic, the levels all play wildly different from the others, and the characters are so memorable I already get the feeling of dusting off an old cartridge every time I launch this game. It's like couch gaming with an old friend.
It does need some work still. Mod support is not nearly as robust as I'd like (bugs will happen often), it is fairly easy to glitch the game out in certain places, and overall the game is possible to 100% in a fairly short amount of time. However, nothing has left me wanting. You can play the zones in (almost) any order and they have this nice flow that ends each world just before it starts to feel old. There's endearing characters at every turn, and while overall the game is very easy it has some nice challenges too. I can forgive the game for being short, because every minute is well made.
Overall, anyone who loves platformers will love this. In a world of serious, competitive, shooters and MOBA's, A Hat in Time is there to remind you that games should make you feel happy. They should entertain and captivate us.

This game is simply amazing.
Blends the frantic pace of a bullet hell game with the quiet contemplation of a puzzle game. The game is expertly executed and rewarding in it's simplicity. Some levels are exceedingly hard, but even after trying them over and over again the level of frustration at failing is minimal, you are excited to restart and do it again. Also, the end of each level features a playthrough with no time dialation of your entire run, which makes all of your matrix moves look even more awesome. Replays are also available to watch from the main menu.
The story is very eerie, it reminded me a lot of the tone you felt doing the "Subject 17" content from Assassins Creed 2. However, as a down side, the story is more suggested at rather than fully explained, and so when the game ended there was a moment of confusion, as you never really figured out what was going on, which was a bit frustrating.
The only other downside is the length. I have 3.1 hours on file, some of that I was AFK, and have completely beaten the story. There are challenge modes within the same levels and an endless mode available, but for $25 (at release) that seems like a less than expected value.
All in all, the game is very intereresting and delivers some really excellent gameplay. If you are not price sensitive, buy it now. If you aren't as flush with cash, wait until the game goes on a good sale. Either way, this is a game that is worth playing.

Let me just start this off by saying I want to recommend this, I really do. I love the developer and I loved The Stanley Parable but I just can't rightfully recommend this game.
Let me just start off by pointing out the price, as it is slightly pivotal. It's $10 ($6 if you're getting this during the winter sale. as I did) for about an hour and a half to two hours of gameplay. And while I understand that The Stanley Parable did this as well, it did this in a way that even once you've completed some of the stories there is still more dialogue and more to explore and more to be done, and it is genuinely fun.
In this "game" (I am not using quotes to undermine it, merely because it is more an interactive story) you follow a linear path through the past games of a creator, told by a narrorator who just so happens to be Davey, the creator of both of these games.
SPOILERS AHEAD:
Towards the end of the story it becomes more and more clear that he was searching for meaning where meaning was not, and that this game did not delve into the troubles of the fictional character "Coda", but instead into the mind of the developer himself and his struggles with self worth.
And while this game is good for what it is, it has a very select audience. In my personal opinion, I would have most likely given a more positive review for this "game" had it been only a few dollars, but this much money demands a game, or at least some replay value, that just isn't there.
In all honesty, if you want to play this "game", save your money and go watch a full playthrough on YouTube, you get the same effect and get to see everything this game has to offer without spending the money on it.

After playing this game for 7 hours, I feel I'm ready to give this a real review. I want to love it, so, so much, but I just can't. There are so many problems with this game that it makes it unbearable. If they were fixed it would at least make a fan of the HTTYD series such as myself at least deal with the minor issues, but sadly, it's not like that.
I'm going to list some problems as I think of them so please bear with me:
· No Volume bar, it's only on or off.
· Even when both sound options are off some sounds still play, ex. leveling up, your dragon's breathing, etc.
· Random crashes, a lot.
· Quest arrow will just not work sometimes.
· When doing collection quests the NPCs sometimes won't give you the items needed, making you have to re-log.
· Some quests you finish, just to find the same quest available again making the whole quest progression system very confusing.
· Friend list is broken, like, really broken.
· It costs gems (real world currency) to delete a character, wtf.
· I had to delete my old character because the quest he was on updated making the NPC I had to talk to not appear thus making the quest progress impossible.
· Quests are really boring, to be honest. There's no variety.
· Membership gives you some unfair benefits such as 20% discount on ALL items in the store, access to some special fishing thing in your farm, gold bonuses.
· Anything good in the store costs gems such as the compost, improved fishing rods, good saddles, and lots of other items that are basically needed to get ahead in the game.
· Membership costs a♥♥♥♥♥ton for what you get, $10 a month, Jesus.
· When you go to the credits section of the game you can jump off the cliff and forever fall through the world. This really surprised me and you would think that they would have fixed it by now. It's not.
So now some good aspects of the game:
· Fishing is kinda fun
· Toothless is in the game AKA the best dragon ever
· The UDT system is kinda neat but affected heavily by hackers
That's about it.
Now, if you still want to go ahead and give the game a shot, go ahead. I hope you have a lot of fun. For the others still looking for a good kids game, I heavily recommend Wizard101 or Pirate101. Thos games are without a doubt the best kid friendly game I have ever played.
In the end, I feel this game is incomplete and not worthy of your money, or your time. It's something that you would casually play just to have a little fun and not take it seriously or play it hours on end every day. I really hope the developers solve some of these bugs and create a better game, but it's been out for 2 years, I don't see them redeeming themselves anytime soon.

A quick perusal of the screenshots, some reviews, and perhaps a video or two may still leave you wondering just exactly what Sunless Sea is.  Though I have barely scratched the surface of it as its pace is deliberate, what you are looking at is essentially an interactive choose-your-own-adventure.  Wait, don't go!  This isn't a bad thing at all and you may wish to stick around to see why.
First off, if you are familiar with the browser game,
, then you will feel right at home; otherwise, if you're on the fence, I would recommend you go sign up and play a little bit of it to get a good idea of what Sunless Sea has in store for you (and it's worth it because it's free).  Essentially, Sunless Sea shares a lot with the mechanics of Fallen London - that is to say that you will spend most of your time going to places and doing interesting things - but the main difference is that you now have a little ship and must sail the darkness of the unterzee.
The short of it is that at some point in time, London fell underground, among a few other cities, and is now surrounded by a vast subterranean saltwater abyss known as the unterzee, home of zee-monsters, tomb-colonists, and a whole other slew of Lovecraftian nightmares.  Unlike
, which mostly keeps your feet planted on the ground,
puts you in the role of a Zee Captain (one of many - this is a roguelike, after all), charged with exploring the darkness and discovering all of its secrets.  Well, small correction there - you can actually select your current captain's ambition, which doesn't necessarily mean "explore everything".
Throughout the game, you will make your way from place to place, discovering ports, creatures, horrors, and whatever else, all told through wonderfully-crafted prose.  The basic nature of it is that in each location, you will be able to start 'stories' or 'storylets' that play out like a choose-your-own-adventure, but not all are self-contained.  Often, by completing certain story sections, you will gain 'traits' that can describe anything from basic supplies to fragments of information.  You'll need these to earn money and other traits that will help you along with other stories you discover, but precious fuel and food is always short in supply and pricey to boot.  You need these, of course, to manage your ship which is your main means of transportation and also your only avatar, but fear not - it has cannons!
Marking this game away from
proper is the exploration component in which you actively sail and manage your ship and crew, fighting off dangers and discovering new places and things.  While the browser game has the benefit of always-updated and changing content, there is more than enough buried in
to keep you occupied until the next expansion pack.  That being said, the game moves at a deliberate and relaxed pace, but make no mistake that this is a simple walk in the park - tension exists in the form of hostile things, and the further away you sail from London, the more dangerous it gets.
As such, there is a bit of a grind element to the game, but it is a rogue-like, after all, in the sense that if your captain dies, he or she isn't coming back.  However, there is the saving grace that should you survive long enough to author a will, you can pass a lot off (including the map you've explored) to the next captain.  But, of course, you still have to grind that new guy up just like you did the last one, so repetitiveness will inevitably sink in without someone constantly writing new stuff behind the scenes.
That being said, if you really enjoy discovery and have an active imagination, then this game will delight you, especially if you have any inclination towards Lovecraftian-style writing.  The world of
and indeed
is not a rose-tinted one; it is grim, foreboding, yet darkly humorous and whimsical at the same time.
You won't hear a single word spoken in this one - it's all text driven, accompanied by haunting tunes and the constant hum of your ship engines chugging away at the black below, but if you let yourself sink into this world, you'll come to love it just like its parent game.

Please, make the game fun! Focus on track design. Then career. Leave modifications for the last part. First game ever.
I'm outside. The snow storm is wreaking havoc. It's freezing, but happily I spot near me a large building. Lucky me. I enter the dam. It's dark. It's gloomy. I can hear many, too many, unknown noises in the distance, barely audible, which adds a shiver along my spine. It seems safe nevertheless. I walk slowly into the main room instead of going back outside in the cold ; I'd rather keep myself warm, like a fly desperately attracted by light. It's even gloomer here. Nothing happened... I feel safe now. I enter the room with the command panels. I scavange for food and supplys. After all, I know how to survive. Probably. I will need those things sooner than later anyway. I stop when I find a flare. I smile widely. I will be able to keep wolves at bay. I hear something. Footsteps. Not mine. I turn vividly my head ; I think I saw something, thought followed immediatly by a growl nearby. Adrenaline rushs through my veins, the heart is rapidly pulsating. I drop the flare.
I see IT now. Large. Black. Running toward me. I scream and try to get out of here. I collide with one of the tables on my way out. The wolf jumps then on me, is jaw wide open. I feel bitten repeatedly. I bleed. I kick. I punch. I bite. Whatever ! Everything is a blur. I start to loose consciouness. I die.
It's been all in all around five minutes of playtime. I cannot describe you how much I was immersed in the game and how much loud I screamed when I saw Fluffy, the iconic wolf.
A tensed game time.
I love The Long Dark ever since.

Dungeon Defenders 2 is one of the few sequels that, in my opinion, is better than part one. I like the way the makers stuck the idea of a tower defense rpg, improved a lot of things, but at the same time brought back some old dungeons and nostalgia. I like the fact that this is a great multiplayer game since the best way to win is using the symbiosis of multiple classes and builds. That doesn't mean you can't play it on your own, if you grind enough and you are lucky to have the currently overpowered character you can easily play it on your own. But it's only the beginning and although slowly the game and characters are getting balanced regularly. Well, what I didn't like is the insane speed in which new classes were released at some point. There are two ways to get them, by playing a lot and collecting rewards or by buying them. For someone who is not planning to play this game on a daily or weekly basis the pace of changes might not be enjoyable. Some times I would have wished for more new working maps than characters, but since most of them are out now I'm hoping for more content in the future. And since I've been playing from the start I lived through my share of bugs and glitches, but I expexted that from the beta. Good things take some time, just like getting used to this hybrid will.
I really like the graphics and the animation with love for little details. I appreciate that it is not a pay-to-win game and that most things available are cosmetic and can be unlocked by playing. I like that there are multiple ways to play a map, incursion, difficulties... And also maps on which you have to do more than be afk like the bling king. By now they have improved the lobby making by far, but at the same time used people's egos against the community since its harder to join a high-end game with bad equipment. If you ever need a little boost, let me know, I think the community needs this in order to live and prosper. Which brings me to my number 1 rule for beginners: fill your deck, make as many characters as possible, symbiosis is the key. You can always make more, but you need builders for the tower defense and also damage heroes for the rpg part.
Overall a great game that takes some getting used to for most rpg players but guarentees a lot of fun :)

This game has its moments but lacks in some aspects. The core idea (space-recycling) and art design (graphics, sound) are spot on but i believe that avoidable technical problems paired with some questionable game design decision limit the overall experience.
First of all there seems to be no long term motivational game mechanic. Maybe i did not reach the "mid game" phase but as far as i can tell there is no such motivational element. After the novelity of the setting, control and the basic game mechanics are discovered (all of which are good) the game is pretty much grinding through one spaceship/space station/special location after another. This would not be a problem if it would not start to feel like work too quickly while not offering enough in return for the player.
Secondly i dislike the "reset" mechanic. Why is the player not allowed to choose his initial ship/drone configuration? The common workaround among players seems to be to roll the dice until you draw a configuration that is to your liking. I'm sorry but in my opinion this is just bad game design. If the player can do something by grinding he will most likely do it. Don't force the player to waste his time with the "reset" mechanic. To me this looks like an overzealous attempt to earn the rouge like badge.
Lastly - The input:
* Swallowed key presses! Oh boy. The game seems to swallow key presses whenever it feels like it. This is especially helpful when you are frantically trying to control your drones in a derelict spaceship that is slowly breaking apart. I am not sure if this is a bug or intended behavior. Nevertheless it is annoying as hell.
* Non-existent support for non english keyboard layouts!!! This issue is so cliché (american developers not testing with non-us keyboard layouts) that i refused to believe this game suffers from it until i did a google search that confirmed that this game is in fact not playable with a german keyboard layout on Ubuntu 16.04. Nice bonus: the input configuration dialog that allows the player to remap the keys crashes when you try to bind to certain keys (umlaut keys). I kid you not! I can't wrap my head around how you can develop a game like Duskers which has keyboard only input and mess up the keyboard input part. I mean come on. It's 2017. Write localizable software. Please?
Edit: Workaround for Ubuntu 16.04 that actually helps: change your keyboard layout in the system settings.

is a fantastic experience where your imagination fills in the blanks – a sci-fi horror survival game with a unique premise and full of surprising moments and unique player stories to be told.
One sign of a great game is when players can recount interesting stories about it, unique to their playthroughs. In
, every mission has this potential. The content of derelict ships and stations are randomized – so you don’t know what’s coming next. Your small fleet of drones are in various states of repair and equipped differently. Things can, and do, break down in the middle of missions.
Part of the fun of the game is having to plan carefully, but be able to deal with a full-on meltdown when something unexpected happens and it all falls apart. Small problems or mistakes can quickly escalate to life-threatening situations in a matter of minutes. Keeping your head is important but you feel genuine panic when things go wrong in a heartbeat, your drones facing total annihilation. This game is tough, but rewarding. Get out of a scrape unscathed and you can give yourself a deserved pat on the back.
uses a deliberately crappy 80’s interface (inspired by the original Alien movie), which you interact solely with the keyboard. Drones are controlled directly or through typed commands, which only adds to the atmosphere. It’s immersive, feeling like it really is just you on your computer on the mothership, placing you right in the hot-seat. However, don’t let the typing or the basic visuals put you off, and if you don’t survive long on your first attempt, don’t worry. This is a survival, rogue-like game. Each attempt you learn more, logs and missions uncovering the backstory are also preserved between runs, allowing you to make progress each game.

The tagline "no zombies, just the cold and whatever mother nature can muster" sums up The Long Dark pretty well. If this would be for you, llike me, your first foray into exploration and survival genre games then be prepared for something of a learning curve. But, it's well worth it, the maps, even though the game is still pre-alpha, are really encouraging. The world is far bigger than you'd think and although it might be smaller than the open-worlds of titans "Fallout", "Skyrim" or even "Red Dead Redemption" it is still a massive challenge to get from one area to another. A classic example of this is also a great example of why The Long Dark is worth getting; its a classic case of the rather clichéd expression of "how you get to the detination being the worthier part of the journey". I found myself dropped off at one of the random spawn points of the map on one of the road sections of the area not under several feet of snow, I scavenged in nearby fishermen's shacks for some food and warmer clothing (finding little of either) and proceeded up the road as it wound along the edge of the map's massive frozen lake. Chancing a couple of ice fishing huts for more supplies I was stuck out on the lake as a snowstorm closed in; pretty soon it was a complete whiteout and I had to try to ride it out in the ice-fishing shack, with nothing but a pot belly stove and a can of peaches for company. Even with the stove exposure nearly killed me; with my characters heartbeat pounding in my headphones, he expressed that he'd given up hope of living much longer. But then, a miracle! The storm broke just long enough for me to see a small island with a weatherbeaten shack atop it that I scurried to as quickly as I could, on the verge of death, inside finding enough supplies for a few more days.
Back this sort of experience up with a very original look, in terms of art style (which should look crappy by modern standards but somehow doesn't) and a wealth of ways and means of both surviving and dying horribly and you've got a really good survival game which should be excellent once the full version is released.
It's the different experience you can have each time that makes this game so playable, one time you can survive for a week and the next you'll be eaten by wolves on the first day; it's left completely up to you the player to do better each time you play, all  the while hoping that mother nature has a bit of pity in her that day.

First horror game I played.
I saw it at the store and noticed many people commeting this game scares. But I thought: "I will not get scared in a game."
I took a quick look at a video showing some gameplay of the game. And I thought: "definitely I will not get scared in it."
With so many good comments, and being the game at sale, I decided to buy it and try it out.
Turned out that the game creeped me out...
There is much gore but it did not add on the scare factor to me... guess I'm already used to it enough on other games. If you just look at a video of someone else playing it doesn't look much intimidating.. you probably will just pay attention to the gore or some visual details as being the scare source. But when you are there, controlling the player and immersed in the game, you will find out that the true scare source is completely other... what matters is that it has a very tense atmosphere, composed with great sounds and lighting effects and adding to it the defenseless sensation that you live in the game, really makes it terrorfying. If you think sound may not be a big deal in this type of game, I assure you the sounds of this game generate a great emotional effect... I recommend playing it with a headphone on good volume.
Also very good was that the atmosphere does not give out hint about what is coming. For example, I've played other games that by the music that is playing you know there is some enemy near or not. But this game sometimes makes a suspense sound when there is nothing coming and sometimes everything seems peaceful and then something happens. So you are always (except when you are repeating a part because you died) on your toes, without knowing what will come.
In my opinion the first part of the game is more scarier, since you know less what to expect, you are more surprised by what happens and becomes more desesperated trying to stay alive. Later when you understand some patterns they become a little more predictable, and cause of that are less scarier. But anyways, there were very tense moments to the end.
I completed the game in about 7-8 hours in hard dificulty. If you play in normal you will probably end faster since you should die less. Due to its short duration, I would wait for a sale to get it. I recommend playing this game without watching spoilers.

I was in Pleasant Valley, the newest addition to the game from the devs (thank you very much). I decided to go out exploring a bit more, as I had already explored roughly half of the area already. I was in quite a dire need of food, and to my luck, I saw a black bear in the distance. Rifle loaded, I shot and killed it, then proceeded to harvest some of its meat. However, the wind had picked up, to the point where starting a fire was near impossible. But instead of falling back to my original campsite, I decided to press on, regardless of the wind. I eventually came upon a small broken down house with enough shelter from the wind, and cooked some of the bear meat that I had. I then continued. The wind died down, and I was following along a frozen river, just exploring. But then, the sky began to darken. I realized my mistake of letting time slip away. I then began to frantically look for a place to stay. All the while growing more fatigued and encumbered by the weight of my backpack. I then had no choice but to chop up about four blocks of softwood enough  for four hours of burning fire, and rest. I rested for two, so I could wake up and tend to my hunger and thirst. However, I woke up to another blizzard, and my fire had been blown out. At this point, it was about 10 at night, I was uncomfortably fatigued, and I was freezing fast. With nothing but my lantern to guide me, I made on in the windy, dark night, Stars began to cloud my vision as I grew more tired, as the 2 hour rest was not very effective. I was frantic, wondering if this was how it would end. But, out of the forest, I found a shelter that was still intact. I entered, ate a few scraps of my bear meat, drank a bit of water, rolled out my bedroll, and took a 6 hour rest. And by God, I slept like a baby.

A lot of people are having issues with this game in terms of running it. I haven't experienced it myself, but do keep that in mind before you purchase it - I'm sure these issues with be fixed soon, but it's pretty unacceptable to have them in at launch.
Those issues aside, and from a purely creative standpoint - this is another strong showing from Telltale games. The scripting is clever and well wrtitten, the scenes are directed beautifully and in such a manner that puts most mainstream film releases to shame. Telltale's trademark art stryle fits the tone very well - the muted colours and harsh black lines help paint a sinister picture of Gotham and it's inhabitants. The black lines also do wonders for Bruce Wayne's jawline, which looks square enough to sharpen a sword on.
The setting is familiar, and seems to blend together influences from several different version of the Batman world. The underslung trams and perfect skyscrapers look futuristic, modern, fresh - and when compared with the boarded up, thug infested underbelly of Gotham's less fortunate neighbourhoods - you can't help but see both sides of Bruce Wayne's double-life reflected in Gotham's two very different looks.
The pacing of the story is excellent, as scenes move from dark alleys where thugs threaten to gut you for your wallet, into even darker parties for the elite, where every guest wears their smile like a mask. In favour of the thug, at least he wouldn't pretend to be your friend before sticking you with a blade.
The story also moves in an interesting direction, and not the one you may expect. I've only been exposed to the most mainstream Batman culture, that of movies and the occasional TV show and so comic book fans may have seen this before, but the plot here makes Bruce and Batman question everything their life has been built on - pretty powerfull stuff, considering Batman's unshakeable resolve, based upon his past, is his most effective weapon. What happens when that starts to fall away?
On the less good side, I've come across two issues in my first hour or so of playing which makes me think, along with the massive issues others are experiencing from a technical side, that this game almost skipped the QA phase alltogether.
I tried to access the Codex on the Bat Computer before I was prompted, which mean't I couldn't get out of it and had to reload the save before I could continue. There was also a scene where you are interrogating a thug, and I was careful not to physically harm him despite the numerous chances the game gave me - in the next scene, Alfred proceeded to tell me how much of a monster I really am, because I beat the man to within an inch of his life.
Is the game worth it?
Sadly, this game seems to have been rushed out - I came across two issues in the first hour that are pretty massive holes, and while they don't ruin the game, they're things that should have been picked up instantly by any QA tester worth their salt.
However, we play Telltale games for the story, the art, the pacing, the directing and the tone. This game has all of that, as you would expect. I would recommend picking it up, as it's better written and directed than most films released today.
Also, there is no sign of Superman.

Longer review:
The Beginner's Guide had promise. It wants to make the audience feel like it's bringing them into someone's life to learn about it, but it ends up becoming a ham-fisted, emotionless narrative with no clear theme. Is it about depression, anxiety, accepting oneself? Or is it about guilt, greed, or failure? The writing flip-flops in this regard toward the end, rendering any psychological analysis moot.
Arguably, a realistic depiction of depression and anxiety is not prevalent in this game, and anyone who searches for meaning in it cannot distinguish fact from fiction. Alongside that, the game loses credibility almost instantaneously once it presents the "creation timeframe." Not only are the assets relatively new, and clearly not of common, often grotesque graphical resources available in 2008-2011, but the creation times between "levels" are nonsensical. The creators want you to believe that in 3 years, with months between each game, the maker of the levels--"Coda"-- improves not a single visual or audio asset. Already, suspension of disbelief is on edge, as this is presented as a "true story" being given to the audience unabated.
But barring the thematics, the actual writing is atrocious, right alongside the narration. How many times do I need to stand still and wait for this clearly made-up character to finish talking? Mumbling the words "Um...", "really", "just", and "So...I guess" over and over again? It's MEANT to sound like an average friend conversing with you, but comes off as extremely unnatural, as people don't force themselves to stutter about their personal philosophies.
Again, the thematics are ham-fisted at you. Instead of letting the audience put their own meaning into things, the narrator forces his interpretation of them on you. "To me, this represents...", "I can't see any meaning in...", "You'll see later on the meaning of..."
"Where does this game shine, if it still gets a 6/10?" The layouts of the levels are great. The detail placed into them is fascinating, and each gameplay element is short and sweet. Yet again, the writing hampers enjoyment. You will frequently be derailed from wandering these environments, or forced to stay in one area for minutes at a time, due to the narrator's omnipotent desire to push you along or keep you in one place.
A much better way to give a game like this is to present it WITHOUT DIALOGUE. To experience the game by oneself, to interpret meaning into it from one's own head, is what the game tries to do, and would shine at, if the narrator didn't shove his own ideas into the plot on such a frequent basis that the sense of exploration and discovery, putting the pieces together on one's own, is lost.
Games like Journey and Shadow of the Colossus work on the same principle: minimal dialogue, with full interpretation resting solely on the player. Without plot devices, the player can enjoy the gameplay much more--it will be a surprise to find out about the creator, and the person who sent these games out, rather than the narrator constantly foreshadowing the ending for you with every other sentence. Many games online work like this, too, and often are available for free.
If someone wants actual strange gameplay, they should check out LSD Dream Simulator, an abstract dream exploration game (3D), Yume Nikki, another strange exploration game (2D), or 50 Short Games by Thecatamites, 50 truly out-there, dream-like games, by a real person, who had no limits or ulterior motive--the complete opposite of "Coda". There are scores of better games out there, that handle depression and anxiety more accurately, or with more exciting, unrestricted discoveries to make in regards to plot or gameplay. While The Stanley Parable mod was excellent, and the remake was alright, this is not the narrative game it was meant to be.

FEBURARY UPDATE IMPROVEMENTS: So just played the recent Feb update and I am happy to say THAT THEY FIXED THE HANDLING!! The handling is much better now and I can play the game with a challenge again! A lot of the tracks have also improved visually and the new multi route track is very fun! This bumps it up from mixed to a positive review, I'll leave the old one down below for those who haven't read it as some of the information still applies.
Old review:
THIS IS A MIXED REVIEW, STEAM PLEASE MAKE THAT AN OPTION.
Well as you can probably see, this game has been under fire a lot recently.
The bizarre thing is that was back when I thought the game was better. I'll split this in to pros and cons for an easier read as to why.
Pros:
The tracks are fun and well designed. Some tracks aren't finished and the AI is slower on these tracks but several of the tracks feel very finished and far along.
The complaints of no updates are misinforming for the most part. Whilst yes updates have been slow, the content has improved ten fold since release and they are lots of tracks to choose from and a decent amount of cars compared to initial release.
The racing is fun with a great mix of destruction and racing.
Mods add to the experience with cool paint jobs, new tracks and even new AI and damage systems which are better for the hardcore race fans.
AI manages to be challenging without having to cheat. Although they could do with adding difficulties to the game as the AI seems to take one or two laps to work out how good you are.
A 24 car field to race with, very fun and chaotic.
The old handling system was fun to race with and gave the AI a fair chance against good drivers. The player and the AI felt like they were on a level playing field.
Cons:
The recent December update ruined the handling system making cars too easy to handle and the AI feel way too easy, even without the assists.
Again not all tracks are finished meaning the AI can be super easy on some tracks and challenging on others.
Derbies feel a bit too unforgiving. The more aggressive you are the more you get punished, meaning you have to skirt around the arena waiting for everyone else to get wrecked.
Updates are slow though this is meant to be stopping in February with a promise of faster fleshed out updates.
The Racefest and real 2 life mods vastly improve the game. Without them the damage system feels too forgiving and AI pack is less fun to race through.
Playing with friends seems impossible, no clear ways to set up servers and a poor multiplayer system meant me and my friends had to give up playing with each other unless we played with randoms on their servers. Something we did not want to do.
Upgrade system seems to be fairly basic and can be a pain in the♥♥♥♥♥if you don't play the game a lot. Would rather it be removed altogether or made less bothersome to manage.
Overall this game is great fun with the right mods and the old handling system, I loved how challenging it was as I am tired of AI being way too easy to beat if you are good. Unfortunately the new update has ruined the game for me as it makes the cars way too easy to drive even without assists. Bugbear need to add difficulty levels to the AI and find a good balance between simulation and arcade because right now the AI drive like they are struggling with the car whilst you can powerslide round every corner and don't have to worry about spinning out at all.
TLDR: Great game but handling needs reworking in order to keep the AI and single player experience fun and challenging.

My thoughts on Banished...
This game has been produced by a single person, so first off congratulations on such a tough task!
Banished is a city/town building game which combines survival elements found in many recent games. It has a vast array of building types, jobs for citizens and can be extremely engrossing.
Graphically this game looks wonderful, small details here and there offer the world a lot more depth. Colours looks fantastic as seasons come and go, caking the landscape in snow or lush green hills.
The tutorial lays everything out for a newcomer to the series, though making sure you complete every single one provided is key to success.
Lastly this game includes mod support and some mods that the community has cooked up are really interesting but NOT required to enjoy this game since the vanilla version is extremely well done.
Props to the developer and i look forward to future DLCs for games you release.

Bioshock is an experience that will not leave me for years to come. From the very first few moments of the plane crash, to the first time you encounter a big daddy, to the confrontation with Ryan, and the completion of Cohen's masterpiece, Bioshock is simply amazing.
First, visually it is stunning, even two years on. The art design, more than the technical graphics is absolutely astounding. That and the water looks incredibly real, and the feeling that everything is leaking is wonderfully atmospheric. The way the plasmids destroy your hand is fascinating, and seeing the decay in a once mighty utopia is something that words could never fully describe.
The audio also greatly contributes to the game, with the audio diaries standing out in particular. Listening to them in order gives the player a wonderful and frightening picture of how Rapture tore itself apart. The side stories that the audio diaries give you a glimpse into create memorable and emotionally interesting characters that the player never actually meets. In fact, some of the most memorable characters in the game are already long dead by the time the player arrives. It is the reconstruction of their actions that is so fascinating.
The Music, both composed for Bioshock (the score) and the period music that plays throughout Rapture is incredible. The pieces that you hear on jukeboxes and radios are classics that add to the atmosphere of Rapture as a time capsule greatly.
The gameplay, from a shooter perspective is fun and varied, with many different types of enemies, and a good variety of weapons with upgrades and different types of ammo for each. In addition, you have plasmids and gene tonics, and various upgrades for them which really enhance the gameplay level. You can invent new ammo and tonics, buy supplies, and hack about any machine in the game, including turrets and bots to help you. There are so many ways to play that game that it can even be a little overwhelming at times, and it does tend to make the game a little too easy.
Even so, Bioshock is an incredible experience, and even just for the story and exploring the environment, it is a must buy, and one of the most memorable games I've played in a while.

I've played this for quite a few hours now, although I've also watched my girlfriend play the game for around double that time. I really like the basic mechanics of the game, but it could do with a bit of tweaking here and there.
I like the variety in the clothing. However, I think a little more variety is required in a few other items, like: Different hatchets/axes, possible a rifle with a scope, a machete, maybe a few more different items of clothing.
In the pacifist mode (& all modes) there need to be more dangers from the environment... Things like bear traps that have been left behind, or poisonous plants. At the moment most of the medicine is pointless in pacifist game mode. I think so far I can recall using painkillers a couple of times to resolve broken ankles. Some more threats from the environment would help make it useful again.
In the medium game mode, the wolf encounters need rebalancing a little to make it more realistic. It would be better if the wolf didn't attack you every time, or if you had more ways to persuade it not to attack you... like throwing meat on the ground to try & placate it. In both the medium & hard game mode, more variety in animal threats would also be good. You could add human NPC survivors as a source of threat, (& potential source of supplies).
A co-op mode would be awesome. I guess that would require significant rebalancing to maintain the difficulty though.
I guess my last criticism is that there needs to be some way of being able to keep going. From whay I understand of the game, eventually I will die because I simply can't repair my tools anymore. This could be corrected by adding a few infinite sources of some materials. You could possibly make sewing kits from cured gut and bones, maybe a car could provide an infinite source of fuel, & the garage by the coast could contain an infinite source of scrap metal. Maybe infinite spawning of some items in random places would keep the game playable for longer.

When I first heard about this game, the concept bothered me.  A game using only the keyboard, no mouse.  What was the screen for?  How could this
be boring?  What would you even try to accomplish?
Then, after purchasing it, I realized why all of these strange features were the beauty of this game.
Having only a console window and keyboard at your disposal, your gameplay success relies on your wit, reflexes, typing speed, and strategy.  You don't need to clock a high WPM to enjoy this game, but it might help.
Such restricting control gives a unique elements of risk and stress to the game; you control everything, yet often feel nearly powerless...  Limited vision of drones, foolish drone AI running into boxes, and the terrifying unknown all work against you as you attempt to find life in this empty space... life that isn't out to take yours, that it.
If you like typing, tactical, strategy, survival, or exploration/adventure games, this is a unique gem.  If you can't play a game without the use of your mouse, I actually still recommend; it's refreshing (and terrifying).

Duskers has an astonishingly eerie atmosphere and engaging gameplay, full of uncertainty and apprehension. You never know what exactly might happen and if you will make it out alive, but you can be almost certain that SOMETHING WILL go wrong. And you WILL have to improvise. Quickly.
Duskers is designed so that if you're lucky in a mission, you never actually SEE the monsters lurking in the ship (but you KNOW they are there) which is exceptionally creepy. The way Duskers does this all so remarkably well is why it is one of the most thrilling games I've played in a long time.
The only problem is that there aren't enough monsters in the game-- there should be atleast 10 more, because once you've seen all the monsters and know what they do, they're not as mysterious and scary anymore. A lack of an obvious ending or clear objective took away a lot from the experience for me as well (which I should clarify was, apparently, a deliberate choice and not just laziness. But in my opinion, the game could have benefited from an ending objective.)

I remember buying this game while it was on sale since it was an early access game, but after sinking about 22 hours I regret not being able to pay the full price so that I can support the dev. That being said there are various pros and cons with RPC
- Graphics: This is a more personally pro for me, but I love the graphics on this game. The retro style is easy on the eyes and it's not hard to differentiate various things. That being said, if you expect crazy graphics from this game, this ain't the game for you
- Controls: The controls are very easy to learn and get used to. Granted, I would like more hotkeys for various buildings/spells but I'm sure that they'll be implemented later on. Nonetheless, the controls are easy to learn and master
- UI: The information that you need are so easily presented/accessible that you can see whatever you want either immediately or with a few clicks
- AI: Except for a few hicks, the AI is pretty solid. Your workers will prioritize the buildings without fail and your guards will defend as best as they can. There really hasn't been a point where I've raged because of silly AI
- Long Term Playability: The only real problem that I have with RPC is the lack of content in the late game. Once you're able to get to the late game harvesting buildings, there's really nothing else to do. However, I see this as a short term problem as this game is early access and from what I can gather from the dev's plans, this issue may be resolved
- Difficulty: Similar to the problem above, once you get to the late game there really isn't anything that can threaten you. Is it impossible to fail, no. In fact, if there is a huge wave of monsters, you can and will fail through either poor management of spells or poor AI. However, as stated before this is mostly short term as this is early access and could be fixed through variety or increase in difficulty
: RPC is a great game, its retro style graphics and simplistic menus can lead towards hours of enjoyable gameplay. However, the lack of late game buildings/progression as well as the lack of difficulty past the initial phase of gameplay does bring the game down a lot. There has been quite some times where I would be bored since there was no new goal for me to reach or no new threat for me to fear. However, if these issues were to be fixed, this game would be extremely enjoyable and challenging.

This is a Telltale game by the numbers.
If you have played any of their modern releases, you know what to expect by now.
The production values for this seem to be a cut above the rest and it looks
nice enough, although the engine is really showing it's age at this point.
*
.
The overall quality seems to straddle the middle somewhere between Tales From The Borderlands and the Michonne "mini-series". It has better visuals and design than Michonne, but far less actual content or polish than an episode of Tales From The Borderlands.
As a first episode, this might feel a little slow to some since a good portion of it's (
) running time is spent setting up this new take on the Batman-verse.
Personally, I didn't mind, as I enjoyed being presented with Telltale's new versions of established and familiar characters.
Some of these who vary quite radically from how we're used to seeing them.
As usual with these games, you make a number of choices throughout, but none
of them feel particularly substantial. Perhaps even less so than in most previous Telltale titles.
The QTEs make a prominent return (
) as well as some smaller "minigames" of a sort where you get to reconstruct a crime scene or fly a suveilance drone to plan out your next move.
There's no real variance to either of those either though, and I'm actually unsure if you can even fail the QTEs this time around, as all it seems to effect is a gauge that fills up in the lower left corner - but there seemed to be no real downside to messing up a few of them here and there.
It's not the best version of a Telltale game we've seen so far, but, all in all, I'd say it's worth it for people who really enjoy Telltale games and Batman fans who are interested in seeing their new take on the universe. For others, maybe not so much.
I don't think the story is strong enough to appeal to people with little-to-no interest in the source material.

It has 33 levels in the main story mode, and each level is a sort of set piece stunt event, so some might happen in only one or two rooms. You can play through those levels in loads of different ways and the challenge modes add variety and new graphical tweaks to the mix.  If you want an FPS that does things a bit differently then go for it.

I'd advise against jumping in on this game right now. I ran into several bugs - performance is a little sketchy, sound sometimes comes in and out, and I ran into a blocker within the first 20 minutes of the game that completely blocked my progress. I had to restart from the last scene to progress - no idea how that wasn't caught during testing.
The game itself does a poor job of acknowledging your choices (at least in Episode 1). A few examples: In one scene, I explicitly went out of my way to avoid harming a thug, instead relying on intimidation. In the next scene, Alfred was chewing me out for "beating him half to death". I endeavored to be completely open and honest with the press, and stay on the level, but the press still suggested that I had ties to crime while playing a clip of me refusing to shake a mobsters hand. It's very obvious the writers wanted the story to go a particular way, and when you acted against that, then they just force it anyways. Coming from other games like the walking dead, this game doesn't even make an attempt to really make your choices visible.
The action scenes themselves are full of pointless QTEs, and on the mouse/keyboard setup they're very awkward. Hitting shift + q or shift + e is very unusual and it takes a lot of getting used to. The game would be better without the QTE however. It would be simple enough to leave it as a game about dialogue choices and some minor targeted clicking for batarangs etc.
The first episode is very short, I finished it in around 2 hours. That said, I don't feel like it was fully wasted time or money. The art is beautiful, and the dialogue is entertaining even if it's all railroaded.
Hopefully things improve in future episodes, and they get some patches out to help people with their technical issues.

TL;DR if I had to pick one early-access survival game to recommend above Rust, DayZ, H1Z1, THIS game The Long Dark would absolutely be it, hands down.
Wow...I've bought a few survival games but this one...words cannot fully express how much I have loved playing this game so far! And they can't express how big a rage quit I did dying 10.5 days into the most extreme difficulty just as I found my first ever rifle.
First up: it's Early Access, so I'll put as the first real point that I have not encountered ANY bugs so far in 10 or so hours of playing, massive +1 from me.
The art style is new to me, and I really like it even though I normally look for realistic graphics- I think you get so drawn into sheer survival in this that you no longer really notice the graphics after a while anyway.
The map seems huge to me- especially when you break it down into chunks when travelling as the weather + food/water supplies you have on you limit you to stopping regularly anyway. So the fact that only one of the three freeroam/survival maps has been released, and the story mode map hasn't been revealed yet, seems very promising indeed.
Loot drops are more than enough to keep you going for just under a week ingame on the hardest difficulty as of right now, and after that there are multiple hunting opportunities including fishing, deer, rabbits, wolves, and bears, all of which can be eaten (raw or cooked!) and eventually worn as clothing with enough time spent crafting (ok you can't wear the fish but that's just realistic). There also various plants which can be used in crafting, and some which can be eaten or even made into hot tea for those freezing post-apocalyptic Canadian nights.
Lastly the little touches, like blood trails which don't despawn too quickly so you can follow your prey as it bleeds out, and footsteps which act the same so you can trace your way back to where you came from (assuming a blizzard doesn't intervene), really impressed me as I enjoy attention to detail like that in a game. And the fact that it's single player, so I'm not constantly being insta-killed by other players, yet it's still challenging enough with wolves/bears often in the way of where I want to be, gets a thumbs up too.

What do you get when you purchase Blood Bowl 2? Quite simply, a great muliplayer experience if, and only if, you are a good sport and not a rage quitter. Rather than a basic review, I will point out the differences between this version, and the previous installments.
First, there are less races. More are coming, but really, this is a minor problem. You won't see the Halflings, Vampires, Ogres with snotlings, or Goblins. These 4 teams in particular are mostly uncompetitive anyways. More teams are being added and there are enough to keep you busy from the start.
No single player experience worth mentioning exists. It really didn't exist in the previous version, either. Why? The AI was terrible beyond reason. You could easily win nearly 100% of your games once you knew the holes in the AI. If you check the message boards, players complained endlessly about the AI being stupid. Having a worthless single player campaign in Blood Bowl 2 follows the same trend as its predecessors.
This game is all about multiplayer. Having an easy cakewalk in the previous games will not teach you what this game is about. You have to understand that winning consistantly is difficult. Bad things can happen on every turn. You will only understand the unforgiving nature of this game by playing against real life people. The dice don't care about you. Rolling back to back failures happen just as astounding lucky plays do. The game is played by assuming you will fail the next roll.
Rage quitting isn't smart this time around. Be warned you will not gain star points for disconnecting, and your opponents will love you for it, because they will receive free points. Take your beatings when they are handed to you, and try again. At some point, your opponent will suffer from having horrible luck.
I suppose its worth mention the UI isn't the greatest. The previous versions has the same problem. No loss there, either.
Verdict? If you want to experience Blood Bowl like it should be, get this version. Keep in mind the original game was a board game that required another person, obviously. Wishing for a deep single player campaign is irrelevant. Playing Chess or Checkers against an AI is just as pointless. You learn more playing against actual people.
If you are weak, and would have your self esteem injured because you can't win every game you play, Don't play this game. If you can handle a few good beat downs, I'll see you on the pitch.

If you love naval exploration games like Sid Meier's Pirates! and have a fondness for dread-inducing, Lovecraft-inspired horror, do not ignore this game.
The visuals are simple but effective, providing a fantastic sense of atmosphere with relatively rudimentary 2D graphics. The music is fantastically haunting, when it's there - you'll often be left to wander the seas in eerie silence. The writing and storytelling are dense, complex, and sophisticated.
The scares in this game come not from monsters jumping out of the dark to eat you (though the dark waters hold plenty of unspeakable horrors to fear) but from the tension created from the storytelling, and the knife-edge balancing act of maintaining your fuel, food, and sanity. This isn't a game that will startle you, but it will create a sense of mounting dread as the story's horrors slowly build, and an unwavering tension as you struggle to manage your supplies and crew.
With its simple mechanics and text-based interactions, Sunless Sea isn't made for the adrenaline-pumping Call of Duty crowd. But if you want a game that feels like settling down for the evening with a nice (or not-so-nice) bit of classical horror literature, you owe it to yourself to explore the Sunless Sea.
You'll want to keep a light on.

Longer review:
The Beginner's Guide had promise. It wants to make the audience feel like it's bringing them into someone's life to learn about it, but it ends up becoming a ham-fisted, emotionless narrative with no clear theme. Is it about depression, anxiety, accepting oneself? Or is it about guilt, greed, or failure? The writing flip-flops in this regard toward the end, rendering any psychological analysis moot.
Arguably, a realistic depiction of depression and anxiety is not prevalent in this game, and anyone who searches for meaning in it cannot distinguish fact from fiction. Alongside that, the game loses credibility almost instantaneously once it presents the "creation timeframe." Not only are the assets relatively new, and clearly not of common, often grotesque graphical resources available in 2008-2011, but the creation times between "levels" are nonsensical. The creators want you to believe that in 3 years, with months between each game, the maker of the levels--"Coda"-- improves not a single visual or audio asset. Already, suspension of disbelief is on edge, as this is presented as a "true story" being given to the audience unabated.
But barring the thematics, the actual writing is atrocious, right alongside the narration. How many times do I need to stand still and wait for this clearly made-up character to finish talking? Mumbling the words "Um...", "really", "just", and "So...I guess" over and over again? It's MEANT to sound like an average friend conversing with you, but comes off as extremely unnatural, as people don't force themselves to stutter about their personal philosophies.
Again, the thematics are ham-fisted at you. Instead of letting the audience put their own meaning into things, the narrator forces his interpretation of them on you. "To me, this represents...", "I can't see any meaning in...", "You'll see later on the meaning of..."
"Where does this game shine, if it still gets a 6/10?" The layouts of the levels are great. The detail placed into them is fascinating, and each gameplay element is short and sweet. Yet again, the writing hampers enjoyment. You will frequently be derailed from wandering these environments, or forced to stay in one area for minutes at a time, due to the narrator's omnipotent desire to push you along or keep you in one place.
A much better way to give a game like this is to present it WITHOUT DIALOGUE. To experience the game by oneself, to interpret meaning into it from one's own head, is what the game tries to do, and would shine at, if the narrator didn't shove his own ideas into the plot on such a frequent basis that the sense of exploration and discovery, putting the pieces together on one's own, is lost.
Games like Journey and Shadow of the Colossus work on the same principle: minimal dialogue, with full interpretation resting solely on the player. Without plot devices, the player can enjoy the gameplay much more--it will be a surprise to find out about the creator, and the person who sent these games out, rather than the narrator constantly foreshadowing the ending for you with every other sentence. Many games online work like this, too, and often are available for free.
If someone wants actual strange gameplay, they should check out LSD Dream Simulator, an abstract dream exploration game (3D), Yume Nikki, another strange exploration game (2D), or 50 Short Games by Thecatamites, 50 truly out-there, dream-like games, by a real person, who had no limits or ulterior motive--the complete opposite of "Coda". There are scores of better games out there, that handle depression and anxiety more accurately, or with more exciting, unrestricted discoveries to make in regards to plot or gameplay. While The Stanley Parable mod was excellent, and the remake was alright, this is not the narrative game it was meant to be.

I enjoyed this game (NO NO WAIT, don't downvote me yet!) for what it was. It's dumb, hokey, cheesy, and mindless, but sometimes that's what you want. It doesn't take itself seriously AT ALL, and you have to be in for the ride or you'll hate the entire experience.
In fact, the game I would most equate Sacred 3 to is the recently-redone Gauntlet. It's formulaic as all get out, linear as it can possibly be, button-mash-tastic, full of dumb humor, and complete with so-streamlined-I'm-embarassed-to-call-them RPG elements. And yet, it's fun.
There's an overworld with scattered, self-contained short levels, there's a few classes to pick from, leveling up is handled automatically a la Diablo 3, there's no loot drops (but your gear levels up and gains new abilities), and then there's the dialog. Ohhh boy, the dialog. Sacred 3 apparently takes itself as a joke, with corny, hammy, 4th-wall-breaking, innuendo and pop-culture reference filled, joke-a-riffic dialog. Did I mention yet that you really need to go with the flow to enjoy this game? I was enjoying it, but I uttered more than a few "ugghhhh"s during my time.
This is a great pick-up-and-play game, easily digested in small chunks. From the overworld, there's a series of story missions and little side mission things that you can pick from, and after 20 minutes at most of bashing and smashing, you're back at the level select screen and on to the next one. The side missions are the shortest of the bunch, lasting only 5 minutes at times, but they're rather essential as they help you level up (the recommended level on the story missions will quickly outrank you if you skip all side missions), and they give you additional potion slots of various types (health, energy, defense+, etc.).
The story missions are quite a bit longer. They almost always include a pre-rendered cartoony cutscene with voice-actors hamming it up, they almost always include some sort of turn-this-wheel-6-times-while-enemies-spawn mechanic, they almost always include some sort of dodge-the-falling-stuff section, and they almost always include a big huge boss fight.
I found the bosses to be quite fun. The combat itself is a blast in general, but the bosses up the ante. They almost always spawn other enemies around them, they usually have some sort of environmental hazard around them, and they're not too difficult as long as you can read their patterns. Don't expect to be frantically gritting your teeth while you're on the razor's edge of life or death, but you have to be somewhat coherent to surive.
Speaking a little more on the combat, in the first few levels, you're just mashing attack over and over, but the combat evolves. Dodging becomes crucial, there are shielded enemies you have to bash, you can leap in the air and slam down on stunned enemies to insta-kill them, and there are spell attacks you have to interrupt before they can be pulled off. It's great. You'll be flipping around the arena, bashing a shield enemy and beating on him a bit before leaping to smash a faraway enemy in order to get out of harm's way. There are combat skills and such that get recharged with dropped energy, but they're nothing really special. Big slashes, aerial attacks, some chain lightning, shouting to stun enemies, etc. They can get you out of a pinch, but they're not enough stronger than regular attacks to be THAT useful. They recharge quickly, though, so don't feel like you need to save them for clutch moments.
The only real weakpoint I experienced with combat is the QTE "restraining" mechanic. Essentially, if you've really been wailing on the boss or mini-boss, there's a little QTE section where you can mash a button for about 10 seconds to "restrain" them and do small bits of trickle damage the whole time. It's kind of pointless, since you could do just as much damage by just continuing to wail on them, and even though for the most part the enemies stop attacking you (in single player. Multiplayer they keep going), if your objective is to defend a crystal from some grenade-lobbing goblins, they'll keep attacking THAT while you're locked in the QTE. Luckily, you're never required to do the restraining, so I just opted to skip them most of the time. No big deal.
All in all, the gameplay is fun, but rather basic. Slog along a linear path listening to cheesy, jokey dialog, slaughter some easy enemies and minibosses, turn a wheel 6 times, dodge some falling debris, and then kill a big boss. Do a couple short little side missions, and then rinse-repeat. In fact, repetition is a bit the name of the game here, almost as if it was intentionally designed to be that way. This game will take around 10 hours to beat if you don't grind or backtrack, but it's repetitive enough that you DEFINITELY don't want to do it in one or even two sittings. I've put 12 hours in, and that's over the course of maybe 4 different sessions. I can't recommend forcing yourself through much more than that at a time. You'll know when the game is starting to wear on you, and listen to that little voice in your head. Quit while you don't hate it, and come back later for more.
The graphics here are a lot better than I was expecting. The geometry isn't Crysis-levels of complex or anything like that, but the texture work is phenomenal, the areas are all colorful and bright, and clearly a lot of work was put into designing unique "biomes" to progress through in the campaign. There's a bit of repetition, but nothing wearying. It's INCREDIBLY well-optimized, too. You could max this out at 1080P with a 4-year-old midrange card and still get 60ish fps.
Sound and music are nothing worth remembering, and some of the little spirits you can bring along (they each have certain passive effects) have annoying dialog lines, but the worst offender here is the "help" text. When you're beating the crap out of enemies and not doing, for example, the leap-smash, expect to hear your spirit chime in with "helpful" advice every 5 seconds about how you should be leap-smashing. "Looking for peace? SMASH the enemy... with a hug!" Yeah, okay, I saw... "looking for peace? SMASH the enemy... with a hug!" Yeah, I SEE IT! "looking for peace?" AAGGGGGHHHHH! Luckily, you can turn that crap off in the options, which I did with vociferousness, and you should too. The mechanics of the game are not tricky in the slightest, so why they thought an overzealous "help" mechanic was needed is beyond me.
Overall, if you (and a friend) are looking for mindless, slaughtering fun, and you're capable of taking everything for the joke that it is, you should have fun here. I know I did. If, however, you're a big fan of Sacred and were excited to see a 3rd one come out, RUN AWAY, there is nothing for you here.
The big test is to watch a video on Youtube. Any 5 minute chunk of gameplay will be indicative of the whole game, and if that doesn't turn you off, check it out! It's worth the $6 I spent, in my opinion. Oh, also, USE A CONTROLLER.

The biggest problem with this game is the intense amount of waiting to join a game, or leav a game when it completes. Not to mention that in order to replay a mission EVERYONE needs to hit Replay, otherwise you spend like 2 minutes waiting to get back into a lobby and then another 2 minutes trying to get into another game instead of just replaying the level immediately.  I don't know why it's set up this way, looks like an artifact of just doing the bare minimum to get network functionality running so the game is in a playable state.
The UI is also pretty buggy, The developers themselves said it's in for a major revamp as they're very not happy with how it's turned out.
However, when the game works, and you get into a group that knows what they're doing, it's pretty fun. While people have gotten the science down to where you can basically just afk to win, sometimes there are a few OH CRAP moments and you need to hustle to win.  Incursions are a little more interesting since you usually have to actually do something in order to win. There are a few maps with invincible enemies that just go straight for your crystal, for example, an there are level gimmicks to destroy them that you can't do with just towers or your characters. There's others where you have to deliver objects to certain locations, boss fights, and one where towers only last for 35 seconds but can be built instantly.
And if you just prefer the regular defense style, Onslaught version of it gets harder and harder until you finally fail.
The premium currency can only be used to purchase cosmetics, bags, characters, and character slots.  However, the triggering PDT/SA/FT combo can be done with just the starting four characters, Huntress / Monk / Wizard respectively, and the Squire has got some really good walls to complement the build if you need it.
Other characters are nice to have but the tower combo with the basic 4 is so OP you won't need them and can buy them at your leisure with the in game currency.  The premium currency cannot be spent on anything else, so if you want to have good stuff in game, you'll have to actually play it. There is no way around it.

I am going to start with as of last update. They assured everyone that the game will be finished, maybe not at the predetermined date but we waited this long I am okay with it as long as it keeps getting better over time.
TLDR, its fun, and a splash between simulation and arcade, but it clashes in certain places. Content is a little thin right now but the game is moving forward slowly but steadily. A very solid 3.5/5 as it sits in its demo state. Tech demo bonus is a blast.
Now lets start with Pros. The game looks good. Cars have a nice destruction to them, the tracks are more realistic right now and they feel like real courses. (though the few mod tracks I have played with jumps and more arcade style play is more my personal speed) The interface of the games menus are set up like a Warthunder style, pick crew, check parts, chose paint and stuff like that all confined to neatly set drop downs. There is multiplayer, and it works pretty well for what I have played and it feels a lot better to drive with a bit more unpredicatbility since the AI just stick to the middle of the tracks and take turns very safely. The sound effects so far are good. Cars are loud and crashes have appropriate noises and smashes to acompany the shatter of lights, windows, and the car in general. The music as of right now is... forgettable? Its serves its purpose but it isn't anything that is gonna change your life.
Now some cons. It still feels like a demo. Which at the time it is. Tracks are pretty, but certain assets are not set in stone and unfinished still. The cars all look very nice but there is only a handful to chose from (and one lawnmower, which is funny and welcome) There isn't a single player really, and there isn't anything to progress too right now. So you just race for the sake of racing which can do it for some people, but the controls are a mix between a simulation and an arcade and it feels off sometimes. And I can't imagine most people who like simulations taking it seriously as it is, and I can't see arcade style races enjoying the bit of simulation that you feel saps a lot of the wacky stuff you could otherwise do. But if you like both it serves it purpose as an inbetween. And for a game about cars, especially lately, I feel it a bit odd to have so few customisation options.
To finish with some personal thoughts. I absolutely adored the flatout games. They changed my whole way of thinking when it came to racing games. As a kid I hadn't played anything like it. Where there wasn't wacky missle powers but you could still destroy another racers car. It was so rewarding to take a turn just right, ruining the storefront you drifted through to get your turbo meter up, and then hit the boost at just the right time to scream around the corner. The ability to play so aggresively and be rewarded, or play it safe and cool and be just as well off. The maps were tight, interesting, and fun to play again and again. The main single player wasn't much of a story but the feeling of progression came from upgrading and getting newer faster cars. Going throught the multiple teirs and different styles of racing. I would highly recommend it to anyone.
I feel like this game is... trying very hard to appeal to both the simulation drivers like gran turismo and forza, while trying to keep its more arcady and fun feel and it clashes more than blends. They have a wonderful destruction engine and it seems to be used hardly at all in most races because the tracks are very realistic, with only the figure 8 right now feeling like the "for fun" map. I could just be hung up with it since i love it so much, but flatout seemed to really hit all the right spots of welcoming new people with controls that were forgiving enough to let them play correctly and eventually you could really press the controls and your skills to the limit, all while staying above a 50mph speed on sharp turns because you could always pocket a bit of boost.
I would love to see this game lean a bit more toward jumps, and obstacles, and things that really show off what attracted me in the first place which was the wonderful sight of car being crunched by stuff in the tech demo. But the way it is crashing is so punishing because there is no way to reaccelerate, and one medium crash could set you out of first place instantly which seems to go so hard against all the work they put into the flying car parts and paint rubbing. But that doesn't mean completely lose the realism, I do like what is here. The tracks feel real, which is a neat experience in its own right. And i would love to see both some sick♥♥♥♥♥jumps in some maps and some tight turns and competetive driving in others.
I would like to see the turbo boost come into this game. Just something that makes this game stand out from many other racing games where crashing is the end of a race. When you have car programmed to lose bumpers, don't punish people for seing that lovely piece of programming.
Bugbear keep up the good work. Value good content over consistent releases.  I am excited to see where this game goes.
