An experience at a level that most games try to reach, but seldom do.
This game has it all. A gripping story line, amazing audio, and graphics. For being released in 2007, the graphics are on par with newer titles. With 20 hours of game play you will not be disappointed. Rapture is skillfully designed, and is truly a work of art. The dark environments are easy to get immersed in, and fit nicely in the horror genre. The game is based in the 1960s, and with the music and visuals you are reminded of that, but the game has a very futuristic feel.
There are plenty of weapons, as well as plasmids to use. Different weapons and plasmids work
best at defeating certain enemies.  But this game is not your standard shooter. With the ability
to save up "Adam" to boost your skills, weapons and plasmids like a rpg, just not as complex.
There's also crafting involved with items you collect throughout the game, again not to the depth of a true rpg.
You have freedom to explore the confines of Rapture, and I suggest that you do. Be sure to pick up all the audio recordings to follow the story, as most of the story line plays out through these recordings. You will also find needed information in the recordings. You can replay all the recordings by using the "M" if you miss something or simply cannot hear what they are saying do to background noise.
The biggest downfall of this game, the originality, the dark and macabre world setting maybe too obscure for the average gamer to appreciate.
If you enjoy horror/survival games, then this is a definite must have, as well as a nice addition to any gamers collection.

Slimes are also a fine enemy, but I find that late game they're all I run into - and it ruins the overall feel of the game. The lack of a true endgame is a downer to me, but it's not a big deal to others - so I'd say it's subjective.

Let me begin by saying THIS IS NOT, I SAY AGAIN
A RUN AND GUN ACTION GAME!!!!!!
Red Orchestra 2 is a Tactical first person shooter that is, in my opinion, one of the prime examples of it's kind. Can the skills you acquire playing say call of duty or halo or other such "run and gun" games roll over into this game? to a point, sure. But this game is less about being the 1-man badass that gets the awesome kill-to-death ratio and more about being able to work with and communicate effectively with a team. This is not to say communication skills don't HELP in said games, however while they do help there, they are almost essential here.
Red Orchestra 2 (and Rising Storm, the Pacific theatre attachment to this game) place players in the boots of an average grunt, which depending on the map may make you a Japanese, Russian, American, or German soldier. Every weapon behaves differently, from the smallest handgun to the largest anti-tank rifle (Or Tank itself if you're playing such a map). Players may begin the game by playing through a campaign which essentially acts as a tutorial for the Multiplayer section of this game. You start a match by first picking which side you fight for then which class, Unlike COD or MOH there are no "Custom" classes. However I personally think this further drives home the fact that not EVERYONE needs to be a sniper, or a machinegunner or an assault trooper (although I will explain why those last 2 choices are honestly an awful idea in a moment).
Let me be brutally honest with you, the reader, for a moment. The last time I truly, honestly played a shooter that I truly enjoyed online was Medal of Honor: Allied Assault...a game that came out 12 years ago. Have I played other First Person Shooter games since then? of course! I've tried several of the Halo games, and the first "Modern Warfare" game was very close to being a game I enjoyed but something about it just pushed me away from action games.
Red Orchestra (Both 1 and 2) brought me back to FPS games. This was a game that focused less on players throwing out as much lead as possible over a teeny-tiny little map and instead gave players maps that genuinely felt like battlefields. Here was a game that cut away having players fighting at ranges so close you could practicaly spit on each other and instead, focused on battlefields that encourage mid to long range combat.
Dont be afraid however! maybe you aren't the world's greatest marksman, maybe you didn't like playing as a sniper or despise campers, there are just as many maps that are inspired by the room-to-room urban combat that was so prevalent in Stalingrad and throughout Russia. On top of this every player has essentially a "Morale" feature, the more shots that hit dangerously close to you, the harder it will be to see or aim, which gives a purpose to machinegunners.
However, despite all the praise I've given it, for the 'Run and gun' players out there, I'm not going to say this is the "End all, be all" game for you. Do I encourage you to at least give it a try? I would be ashamed if I didn't say you should, however i'm also going to be blunt and admit this MAY not be the game for everyone. Best of luck to you if you buy this, and I look forward to seeing you on the battlefield!

I've played this for quite a few hours now, although I've also watched my girlfriend play the game for around double that time. I really like the basic mechanics of the game, but it could do with a bit of tweaking here and there.
I like the variety in the clothing. However, I think a little more variety is required in a few other items, like: Different hatchets/axes, possible a rifle with a scope, a machete, maybe a few more different items of clothing.
In the pacifist mode (& all modes) there need to be more dangers from the environment... Things like bear traps that have been left behind, or poisonous plants. At the moment most of the medicine is pointless in pacifist game mode. I think so far I can recall using painkillers a couple of times to resolve broken ankles. Some more threats from the environment would help make it useful again.
In the medium game mode, the wolf encounters need rebalancing a little to make it more realistic. It would be better if the wolf didn't attack you every time, or if you had more ways to persuade it not to attack you... like throwing meat on the ground to try & placate it. In both the medium & hard game mode, more variety in animal threats would also be good. You could add human NPC survivors as a source of threat, (& potential source of supplies).
A co-op mode would be awesome. I guess that would require significant rebalancing to maintain the difficulty though.
I guess my last criticism is that there needs to be some way of being able to keep going. From whay I understand of the game, eventually I will die because I simply can't repair my tools anymore. This could be corrected by adding a few infinite sources of some materials. You could possibly make sewing kits from cured gut and bones, maybe a car could provide an infinite source of fuel, & the garage by the coast could contain an infinite source of scrap metal. Maybe infinite spawning of some items in random places would keep the game playable for longer.

SuperHot tries to advertise itself as a John Woo simulator, where time slows down through your gun battles and allows you to plot out your actions play-by-play. But the entire game is designed as a twitch shooter, and without sensory cues of where enemies are like footsteps and voices due to the entire game being drowned out by a "wind tunnel" effect apparently caused by the slow motion, and the entire color pallet being black, white, and red you're constantly being snuck up on by people and getting killed with a single shot that grazes your shoulder. And of course, despite every other "twitch shooter" in existence, the game requires you to (for some reason) lead every single one of your shots and determine where your enemy is moving. This would be all well and good if you had a sniper rifle a few hundred yards away, but this is handguns and assault rifles with enemies no more than thirty to fifty feet away.
So it's a twitch shooter that requires you to precisely aim shots and know where your enemies are while you're lacking one of your basic human senses. And to top it all off, the plot is only about an hour and a half long, so congratulations, if you purchased SuperHot you spent $20 for a two-hour long frustrationfest with clunky gameplay and a useless "gimmick" that tries to sell itself as innovative. And the plot, which I will not spoil (just watch a Lets Play or walkthrough) is INCREDIBLY pretentious, to Matrix levels, throwing out random bits of plot that just shove the message of the game right in your face, a message we've seen a million times since computers became a mainstream appliance, and the game acts like it's so smart. And the ending literally tells you to tell your friends the game is "the most innovative shooter you've ever played." No, I'm serious, it tells you, to your face after the ending, to try to sell the game to your friends by saying it's innovative and awesome. Don't buy this game, put the $20 towards something with ACTUAL innovation and gameplay that wasn't designed by someone trying to be artsy and "deep."

TL;DR if I had to pick one early-access survival game to recommend above Rust, DayZ, H1Z1, THIS game The Long Dark would absolutely be it, hands down.
Wow...I've bought a few survival games but this one...words cannot fully express how much I have loved playing this game so far! And they can't express how big a rage quit I did dying 10.5 days into the most extreme difficulty just as I found my first ever rifle.
First up: it's Early Access, so I'll put as the first real point that I have not encountered ANY bugs so far in 10 or so hours of playing, massive +1 from me.
The art style is new to me, and I really like it even though I normally look for realistic graphics- I think you get so drawn into sheer survival in this that you no longer really notice the graphics after a while anyway.
The map seems huge to me- especially when you break it down into chunks when travelling as the weather + food/water supplies you have on you limit you to stopping regularly anyway. So the fact that only one of the three freeroam/survival maps has been released, and the story mode map hasn't been revealed yet, seems very promising indeed.
Loot drops are more than enough to keep you going for just under a week ingame on the hardest difficulty as of right now, and after that there are multiple hunting opportunities including fishing, deer, rabbits, wolves, and bears, all of which can be eaten (raw or cooked!) and eventually worn as clothing with enough time spent crafting (ok you can't wear the fish but that's just realistic). There also various plants which can be used in crafting, and some which can be eaten or even made into hot tea for those freezing post-apocalyptic Canadian nights.
Lastly the little touches, like blood trails which don't despawn too quickly so you can follow your prey as it bleeds out, and footsteps which act the same so you can trace your way back to where you came from (assuming a blizzard doesn't intervene), really impressed me as I enjoy attention to detail like that in a game. And the fact that it's single player, so I'm not constantly being insta-killed by other players, yet it's still challenging enough with wolves/bears often in the way of where I want to be, gets a thumbs up too.

Sunless Sea is one of those rare games that is heavy in story and atmosphere, so much so that it can drag you into its world and leave you demanding to know more.
This is not an easy game to master. The general rule to start off with is...prepare to die.......a lot. There is still a lot the game is yet to implement in terms of story, gameplay, and balance. However, once more options become available, this game will really soar.
In terms of world creation, this a wondorous world, that of a New London submerged into an underground world after a hypothetical disaster. You are a Zee Captain, able to chose from a variety of backgrounds from a Street Urchin to a Philosopher, each giving bonuses and a starting crew member to chose from. Or you can chose no background, and remain a figure of mystery across the zees.
Recruit crew, make echoes (The currency of the Zee), upgrade your ships, kill monsters and pirates, become a merchant/smuggler, the choices are many. And if things go badly, you could leave yourself stranded at sea, the victim of cannibalism amongst the crew, or a vicious mutiny to depose your leadership.
The sound in this game is exceptional, and creates great atmosphere to the surroundings of the underground Zee, often you'll be caught in the music and forget about what you're doing for a brief second, before being brought back to awareness by a swarm of bats.
The map is random, which makes for fascinating exploration, and rewards are offered for exploration as well, which is a great incentive to get out there and check out the wide and open Zee.
All in all, this is an excellent game for those who love games heavy on story and background, who love well-developed worlds that become apparent piece by piece, and don't mind exploration.
While a few elements need addressing, such as the difficulty in making money (Which forces the player into a lot of grinding) and a few more story/quest elements to give more options, this game is a little gem that is worth playing and has the potential to get even better once it expands.
The world of the Zee is fascinating, and you'll be left wanting to know more. No matter how many captains die in the attempt to explore it.

What first struck me as a unique FPS turned out to be a visually striking puzzle game. Time only progresses when you move, and the point is for you to eliminate all your foes in a select area, or die trying. You will see the trajectory of bullets coming at you, and you will relish the dance you will perform as you dodge them. The campaign is rather brief, but in a game like Superhot, you are buying into the mechanic and the eventual endless and challenge modes. Simple, addictive, and mind-blowing in its originality.

I cannot say enough of how GOOD this game is! It is slow (especially to start) and you need patience, but once you get into the game and let yourself into its world... I feel almost like I'm a little kid again playing a game where there was no internet or strategy guides to be had at the click of a mouse.  If anyone has ever played the old DOS game Solar Winds, THIS is it's spiritual successor.
The Lovecraftian environment is just plain fun. The mechanics of the game have been tweaked perfectly so its not too difficult, but not too easy either.  Resource management, trading, exploration, naval combat, consequenced decision making (yes, your choices REALLY matter in the game), and EXCELLENT writing all make for one of the best games I have played in a long time.
The sense of discovery and wonder at what is going on is truly wonderful, and oh the amount of content! Definitely too much for one play through.  The randomized maps may rub some people the wrong way but it really adds to the replay value and sense of discovery.
The music fits every location perfectly and the sound effects are of high quality. The graphics (for what they are) are very pleasing and the landscapes you come across are beautiful.
I have been playing for almost 16 hours and I feel like I am just grazing the surface of this game. Truly WORTH THE MONEY and I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a delightful, and fun pass time.

Expansion is a case of doing the same the thing again and again, pushing the boundaries of your little town outwards and never really going back to tinker with your town. Having said that, if you enjoy this genre you should definitely pick this up.  If it's on sale, all the better.

This is not exactly a bad game, and for a pro, I'd say it's quite catchy and interesting at very first. The idea of a slow-paced building sim + resources management looks great at first glance, but it wears out very quickly as the mechanichs and the whole concept of "challenging" becomes a boring rinse repeat;
First, I've bought this game because unlike "Sim City" alikes, you deal with just a handful of people, where everybody perform a task for the good of the "whole". The concept sounds interesting, and again, challenging, but the execution didnt paid off, and why? The factor that makes this game "difficult" (it's not really challenging, its just meant to be hard) is because pretty much everyone MUST be working at something, the balance is way too strict, so if a few babies are born, food wont be enough anymore, people starve later. Same If some farmer die of old age, or even a random rock crush a random miner (yes, just like that...) or some forager or wood cutter gets killed by an animal, it unleashes a chain of bad events that cannot be countered within a resonable timeframe, everything is just too slow! months and seasons pass by and people just walk and roam slow regardless of their impending doom, there's no way to make them work harder aside from just removing some people from one profession to another. even so they will follow all the protocols wich makes it cost an entire season just for a ingot to get to the blacksmith, and while that does not work efficitently, other areas will lack... suddenly people start dropping dead left and right because the lack of food, or firewood, or because they did not had tools in time, and without them, workers never fills the quota wich leads to the lack of every possible thing. Rinse and repeat, a bunch of people die and you get to start again with a few survivors...
After realizing how the mechanics of this game works, it gets boring after a few hours of fast fowards just to try to get a a few houses built or a bridge, wich by the way, will kill you! laborers will take logs to the construction sites as soon as they find one by the storage. No lumber, no firewood... and you know where it goes with this...  More often,  you find yourself expecting that a baby or two will be born or for someone to finally grow up so you can finally assign him to work at the mine because realocating anyone else for that matter would cause the total system colapse... and when they grow up, someone dies... someone gets crushed... this back and forth gaming is frustrating to say at least, theres basically no margins for Plan B or surplus.
Once again, just because the balance is always leaning towards the bad side of events, it doesn't makes the game challenging and furthermore fun, instead, just punishing after a couple of hours.

Well, I spent about an hour writing a review and then Steam seems to have eaten it, so here's the Tl;Dr.
Mystic needs some love, her stats are a jumbled mess, doesn't mean she's bad, just awkward to play.
Matchmaking needs a lot or work, expect a lot of loading time, it's Early Access so I give it a pass, same with the handful of bugs I've found.
This game desperately needs proper character unlocks, and offline play. The current system of doing daily missions for character unlocks via defender medals feels awful and gives a false draw to keep playing in the hopes that the new characters are different enough to make the game feel like a different game once you have enough hours to start getting bored.
Playing with friends is a lot of fun, and the overall artistic design, including visual, audio, and level design aspects are very cohesive and well done. Be warned though, matchmaking does some crazy stuff to your groups.
Most characters have a variety of builds and fun playstyles, as I said before, the Mystic needs some cohesiveness to her stat scaling, but everybody else seems alright, still waiting for the Barbarian and Jester, but Jester is very unlikely, the flashbacks of behind lines Ogre spawns tell me it probably won't happen.
Abyss Lord (The summoner from the first game basically) can actually do more than try to play chess in a tower defense and pretend to be an actual hero with a high damage and attack rate pet. He gets proper spells and attacks now, and can temporarily upgrade towers into better versions/give them abilities.
I recommend the game because it is free and honestly a lot of fun if you can get past the typical beta style problems of poor optimization and shoddy matchmaking.

The fact that there are no zombies, maurading raiders and other players involved makes this a unique game to play.  Each and every day is a struggle for survival until you can build up food and wood at a secure location.  With limited resources, you are forced to risk the dangers of exploration to survive as items do become depleted with use.  I highly recommend this game to people with brains who are not brainwashed into simplistic first-person-shooters and RPG games with bad dialogue and storyline.  NO story is needed here, at least not and indepth one.  I certainly hope Hinterland adds in better defenses against wolves, a prybar and hatchet are currently ineffective against them.  The difficulty modes goes from simple to tough-as-heck to "HOLY #%$@!!!"  I personally dislike difficulty levels, either you win or you don't.  I believe some add ons are necessary such as a compass, a map (or one you can make on your own), chainsaw or better axe, and rope as each time you fall five feet, an ankle goes out.  Flares should last a bit longer.
All in all, I enjoy this game, 28 days of survival up to this writing but it is in easy mode.  I tried moderate mode and got eaten by wolves on the second day!  The game assumes nothing so you have to think about what you want to do and figure out how.  Meaning, USE YOUR BRAIN BECAUSE YOU CAN'T JUST SHOOT THINGS UP!  This game requires patience as in real life survival and quite a bit of thought into everything you do.  Examples such as, Do I go out for all 14 hours of daylight or be conservative?  What direction shall I explore and for how far?  Do I spend three days to build up wood and food?  Where is the best place to deploy a small game snare?  The game allows free thinking and range of movement.  Think of it as Skyrim but with no dragons, people, magic or...ANYTHING!  Easy right?  Not at all, make is even more challenging.  I love it.

Being a fan of Dungeon Keeper and resource-gathering and structure-building games like Startopia, let's just say I really wanted to love this game. I don't even like it.
There's just not much game here. All buildings seem to be lackluster and blatantly 2-tier right up front. Little is hidden. Want wood? Lumber jack or advanced lumberjack. Want stone? mason or advanced Mason. The buildings are rather bland and show little innovation or setting/theme.
Basically you set your people to work by painting resource gathering areas on trees, stone, etc. Then you construct buildings to process these resources so you can make a defense tower or two and some magic makers.
You have a set of spells, once again all presented up front with little in the way of unlocking or earning their acquisition. Fireball for killing. Healing aura for ... healing. You can guess the rest. You've seen them in just about every other god-game.
My point is, re-hashing all the tired old god-game concepts from the 90's to now in a cute little pixel style doesn't show much originality and doesn't necessarily make the game fun. Grinding through several hours of this in attempt to enjoy it I finally realized, this simply is not a fun game yet.
I hope, sincerely, to update this review later upon release, praising it for it's clever spell set, tiered growth and scaling, intense combat mechanics creative buildings, hearty and lore-filled setting and my attachment to the characters I'm leading. Right now it just has none of these features.

Excerpts from my video review:
"I have to say the detective scene and the scene where Batman looks for the most effective way to work through the guards denotes a severe lack of meaningful interactivity and choice that is still unfortunately a typical hallmark of Telltale Games. It’s not that they’re BAD it’s just that they’re empty. Showing no real ability for YOU the player to deduce what’s happening or decide on how to go about taking out the guards, it’s all simply a dressed up version of connect the dots which is a shame. I WANTED the opportunity to use my own brain to try and figure things out. To use MY deductive reasoning to figure out what’s actually a clue and what is superfluous information, but you’re just not given that opportunity here and that is a real shame."
"there have been numerous reports and player reviews on the Steam page stating that a lot of people’s gameplay suffered from stuttering, 10 frames per second or less, and some people even reported having issues adjusting the graphics settings. Now, I experienced none of these issues outside of that one with the codex which I did see at least one other person leave a review on Steam stating they had the same issue so it is repeatable. However, Telltale did put a disclaimer on the store page stating “If you are experiencing performance issues, you may need to update the graphics card drivers to the latest available. If you are using a laptop, please use your dedicated graphics and not intel integrated graphics.”
All in all, however, this is a very standard Telltale Games offering, which is the first of 5 installments of what is shaping up to be a fantastic Batman visual novel. Phenomenally well written, superbly voice acted, and in keeping with the Batman Lore, this game is a must-own for lovers of the Batman Story."

Absolutely fantastic. The Long Dark is the first survival game I've played where the aspect of fearing for your life and desperately trying to survive lasts longer than a couple of hours. Death lurks behind every corner even into the late game, and the constant push to live longer the next time keeps the game addicting.
One really important aspect of it is resource management, which I've found lacking in basically every other survival game. In The Long Dark, not only do you have to worry about fending off wildlife, finding food and water, and staying out of the cold, but you also need to plan ahead with your very finite resources. The environment is not infinite in this game, there is only so much to be found in the ruins of civilization.

I cannot say enough of how GOOD this game is! It is slow (especially to start) and you need patience, but once you get into the game and let yourself into its world... I feel almost like I'm a little kid again playing a game where there was no internet or strategy guides to be had at the click of a mouse.  If anyone has ever played the old DOS game Solar Winds, THIS is it's spiritual successor.
The Lovecraftian environment is just plain fun. The mechanics of the game have been tweaked perfectly so its not too difficult, but not too easy either.  Resource management, trading, exploration, naval combat, consequenced decision making (yes, your choices REALLY matter in the game), and EXCELLENT writing all make for one of the best games I have played in a long time.
The sense of discovery and wonder at what is going on is truly wonderful, and oh the amount of content! Definitely too much for one play through.  The randomized maps may rub some people the wrong way but it really adds to the replay value and sense of discovery.
The music fits every location perfectly and the sound effects are of high quality. The graphics (for what they are) are very pleasing and the landscapes you come across are beautiful.
I have been playing for almost 16 hours and I feel like I am just grazing the surface of this game. Truly WORTH THE MONEY and I highly recommend this to anyone looking for a delightful, and fun pass time.

One of the worst name i've seen so far but Retro-Pixel Castles is an excellent game. To put it short it's a survival city builder with tower defense components.

Patch comes out pretty often adding   substantial content & features (please don't trust me and check the changelog by yourself as you should always do with early access titles). If you're not into too much reading they have an interesting Dashboard "Map" in game where you can actually follow very precisely what will come out sooner or later.
Back to the game. Retro-Pixel Castles current state is pretty good. Everything is working so far (pathfinding, building, villagers levelling) for you to try it and the gameplay gives a nice feeling of pressured Banished which i was really expecting. Indeed, you'll have to develop a village strong enough to resist against roaming monsters.

I'm not typically one to write a review for games, but I felt the need to write one (Albeit breif) for The Long Dark.
This game feels different from your average survival based game, and it doesn't pull any punches. This game can challenge you to plot your moves beforehand, and even then, you're always taking chances. You can easily freeze to death, get hunted down by wolves (and apparently bears, though I've yet to come across any), die of any number of medical issues (sickness from eating food raw, to injuries from falling, to bleeding out.), and of course from starvation.
Also, as a point of reference: You're going to die. Probably a lot... It will take time before you get the hang of it and learn all the locations, what might be lurking around the corner and what you can find and where. Don't get discouraged. Death is inevitable, but each play will give you better foresight and knowledge for the next one.
Although this game is in Early Access, it's well worth the money at this point in my opinion. Should the Devs keep their promises (As far as I know, they have thus far), it will be a survival game in a league of it's own.

I'm not usually one for reviews, but I feel that this game is one of the few that needs a review, since it is just so darn good.
Sunless Sea has been described as an FTL but with ships rogue-like. While I understand why they drew those conclusions, I don't feel they are entirely accurate as to what exactly the game is. First things first, this game starts off very, very slow. But, that is the intention, as it eases you into the game, and lets you delve into the game's greatest strength: it's story-telling and atmosphere. There is a lot of text in this game, and I do mean A LOT. If you don't like reading walls of text, this game is not for you.
You will die, quite frequently to begin with I'm sure, as you learn the correct routes and trades that you can do to get some early game profit. For me though, even repeating the same few things at the beginning of a new legacy does not bore me, as there are so many chance encounters than no two playthroughs feel quite the same.
Sunless Sea, to me, is a fantastic game, especially if you are into atmospheric storytelling and slower paced gameplay.
EDIT: Spelling is hard.
I completely forgot to mention that although you will die quite frequently, you can choose what you want to carry onto the next heir, and also unlock things as you play the game that give more passive bonuses to the next heir. All the more reason to explore and not fear the Unterzee!

I understand the message, or the larger artistic and personal points that The Beginner's Guide is trying to make.  The problem is that I can see the seams in the production.  I don't believe that the narrative Davey tells us in the voice over is true.
I firmly believe that this game is just an attempt to prod players into asking themselves certain kinds of questions, especially about self-worth.  And for what it's worth, it has succeeded at this goal magnificently going by many of the rave reviews and recommendations it has received.
But players who are not prone to navel gazing, who are self-actualized people, are just going to find the game boring and self serving for the creator.  Their most charitable response would be, "There are problems in life, learn to deal with them and grow up."

I wanted to like this game. It's a isometric action-fighting game of the type I really like. However, it's very linear, without the open world questing and the diversity of loot and skills that were in the previous games in this series. That can be ok since the various missions are fun, and the graphics/animations decent. I would have enoyed it enough to finish the game if it weren't for the ridiculous difficutly spikes you encounter when you reach the bosses at the end of each mission. Many of the bosses can kill you in just a few hits, and they frequently stun/trap you so you can't move. You have very little diversity in skills or attacks, so all you can do, regardless of the boss type, is brute force attach them while trying not to get hit. Not creative or fun. Given the poor dodge mechanic (see below), how hard bosses hit, and the lack of diversity of skills you have, the boss fights are immensely frustrating. When you die, you go back to the previous checkpoint. If you quit for a bit, you have start the entire mission over again. So the only way I could pass some of the bosses was to replay missions until I leveled up enough to survive them. Very frustrating.
So, whereas I can play Grim Dawn, or Path of Exiles, or Torchlight, or any of the similar games all night and enjoy every minute, I find that I can play Sacred 3 for a short bit before I am so angry at a boss fight that I want to uninstall and curse the game's designers. I keep hoping it will get better, but it doesn't.
There are some pros of the game:
- Generally fun combat.
- Decent graphics and animations.
- Multiplayer works fine, though there aren't many people to play with.
Cons:
- No open world gameplay, or RPG elements, or any of the standard features of a Diabloesque game.
- Linear missions, and entirely linear maps.
- Horrendous difficulty spike when you get to the final bosses for each mission.
- Bad dodge system. The doge system is essential for the boss battles, but you always dodge in the direction you are attacking, not the direction you are moving. The movement is with WASD, but the dodge direction is controlled by the mouse direction, same as your attach. So, as an archer, if you are shooting at a creature/boss and it charges you,  when you dodge you just roll right into whatever you are shooting at, no matter which way you are moving. You have to stop attacking and move the mouse away from your target before the dodge, which is too slow and defeats the purpose of the rapid dodge mechanic. Stupid.
Mixed:
- The story and voice acting. They designers went for over-the-top humor. Sometimes it's funny, but mostly it's lame,
I bought this game for very little, so I got my money's worth. If you get it for a couple bucks, you'll probably wnjoy it enough for a bit, until you get frustrated and quit.

Ahh to recommend this game or not..... I really want to.... I really wanted to like this game.... but still can't recommend it and here's why.
Firstly I'd like to point out that I know this isn't truly a sequel to Sacred 2 and that my opinion on the game isn't influenced by this, I wanted to give an unbiased opinion on this game as a stand alone.
So as you may be aware it's a linear action RPG.... and by linear every single map is virtually a straight line with no chance of going off and exploring the areas. The map zones are nice and the graphics are good enough; but you always feel really limited over what you can do. Aside from the fighting you get to run along a corridor and avoid falling debris..... on every major map zone - not always debris, maybe lightning, but basically the same thing and it gets repetitive quickly. Same goes for turning a wheel 6 times to move a bridge, open a door etc - happens too often and it becomes doing the same thing again and again.
The controls feel weird at first but after a few zones you get used to them although even at the end you'll miss attacks or dodge in the wrong direction after you've lost the cursor on screen in amongst the action.
The different characters are varied enough with some options to change and upgrade attacks and weapons which is done by coins collected during missions. The lack of loot in game felt odd but wasn't as bad as I thought (and I love looting in games usually) so don't let this put you off.
As for the dialogue..... well..... they try and be funny.... main word being try. Sometimes they get it right and it can make you laugh, but a lot of the time it'll make you groan at how silly it is.
Oh and you get a spirit which is meant to help you out and talks as you fight........ by the end I'd been called babycakes at least 100 times - and that was annoying the first time!
To give you an idea on how long the game it, I've completed the main quest without skipping a zone in just under 9 hours - there is an option to play online with others but I'd never seen more than 4 people online at once.
So like I said I wanted to like this game, I am a big RPG fan especially action-RPGs and didn't want the fact it was not Sacred 2 to change that, but on it's own it's just not a good enough game. Fans of the genre should wait for a sale - I picked it up for £3 so am happy with that with what I got - it's not worth the £15 it's currently priced it.

BioShock is one of the most revolutionary FPS of all time. Combining firearms with melee weapons and the power of "Plasmids," are what really make BioShock shine in areas where other generic shooters do not. It has RPG elements, allowing you to literally evolve yourself throughout the game. While the combat is slightly dated, and a bit stiff, it still feels satisfying when you blast an enemy with a stream of eletricity and beat their brains in with a wrench. The story is fantastic, and is nothing like I have ever experienced before. The game starts with Jack--the protagonist--on a plane. After some inner monologue, the plane mysteriously crashes near a lighthouse and you are forced to swim towards it. Once inside, you take a ride on a bathosphere, where you enter the underwater city of Rapture, a city where the artist would not fear the censor. Where the scientist would not be bound by petty morality. Where the great would not be constrained by the small. That's about all I can say without spoiling any major plot points. BioShock is also extremely immersive, and the fact that it's set in the year 1960 only helps it, with its creepy classical music, strange aesthetic, awesome architectural designs, and even the designs of enemies. In conclusion, BioShock is my favorite FPS and my favorite game series in general. The game may be $19.99, (usually $4.99 during sales) but it is definitely worth the asking price. With all of that said, buy this game, would you kindly?

Now THIS is the kind of roguelite game I've been looking for.
The idea is that London has sank a mile below the surface (it was stolen by bats[yes, as in the little winged hellbeasts]), where there is a sea under the Earth. Since this setting is in the late 1800s, it's steamboats and artillery shells as far as the eye can see. It's a little like FTL, in that you manage your hull integrity, food and fuel as you explore a partially procedurally-generated world. The first half of the map or so, where all the starting areas are, is pretty much the same every trip, but everything changes at the far reaches.
You can upgrade your ship, swap out commanders (things like engineers, cooks, etc) and get into combat. The combat is the only thing about this game I don't like, in that it's repetitive and worse, melee enemies (things like giant crabs, sharks and giant eels) hit you with attacks that are completely unavoidable unless you are directly up in their grill the whole time. I wish there were a few more options at my disposal in combat. The game also doesn't always tell you what can and can't be upgraded on your starter ship, so beware if you're just jumping in.
I also would complain about how much echo it costs to do anything compared to how little you get. Yeah, going to the other end of the map wand scouting out there will get you a cool 2-3k  echo, but it takes forever to get out there, and you'll probably burn through that much money in supplies, terror alieviation and fuel alone. I mean, even scouting the island with the sisters makes you 5 echo and costs about 50 in supplies/fuel to get to. The economy in this game needs to be fine-tuned, I think. I get it's a roguelite, but I've had to start over simply because I don't have enough money to do anything anymore. So that can get a bit frustrating.
The real draw here is the story, as strange as that sounds for a roguelite. There's the overarching story, but the bulk of it concerns your crew and your personal quest. Each port you go to has a new and interesting tale (though if you don't like reading, it may be a bit of a stumbling block) that is sometimes expanded on by further interaction with its inhabitants. Some of these are funny (like rat-people fighting gerbils for control of a jewel) some of them are unsettling (a land of basically mummies that can't die) and some are horrfying yet hilarious (I watched a sacrifice that was immediately followed by pies at the local  pub), and some are just horrifying (I'll never forget watching my crewmen eat each other). It's a very strange mix of eldritch (you probably notice Lovecraft getting name-dropped a lot in these reviews. There's a reason for that), funny and whimsical that I find really intriguing. I also like how when you scout each port, there's a little bit said back at Fallen London, to add more characterization to how it views the other under-earth entities. All told, there is a surprising amount of depth to this world, and it makes you want to keep on exploring to find out more (and get more supplies, so your crew don't eat each other).
Then there's what you yourself can do. Will you start a tryst with a crewmember? A spy on shore? Perhaps you'll finally see what your First Officer's banging on about with these strangely friendly three sisters hanging out at a mansion all by themselves. Will you accept the bruiser's offer for supplies in exchange for future favors rendered or ignore him since you know what that does later on in the game? It's very much a 'make your own story' game, and it does it pretty well.
Of course, at sixteen hours, I realized there was a bit of a problem: I'd already done most everything, and though most events came with different results, good or bad, I'd seen most of those too. I also found myself wishing on occasion for more options or closure. A good example would be the Scarred Sister, whose story I won't spoil (it's probably the saddest one in the game), but you never really get any closure there. Never any idea what happened and why, or any chance to make things right. Same with the Wistful Devilless, who just kinda dissapears after the visit to your place, never to be heard from again if you don't have high enough rep with her. The makers of the game are putting out more content if you sign up on their website. I had no problem doing it, but I know some might. On top of that, It's too early to tell how often and dense these updates will be.
If you're a lover of story-driven games, I'd highly recommend this. If you're looking for gameplay, you might want to try something else (Darkest Dungeon, perhaps, if you don't mind a game based entirely on dice rolls).

TL;DR if I had to pick one early-access survival game to recommend above Rust, DayZ, H1Z1, THIS game The Long Dark would absolutely be it, hands down.
Wow...I've bought a few survival games but this one...words cannot fully express how much I have loved playing this game so far! And they can't express how big a rage quit I did dying 10.5 days into the most extreme difficulty just as I found my first ever rifle.
First up: it's Early Access, so I'll put as the first real point that I have not encountered ANY bugs so far in 10 or so hours of playing, massive +1 from me.
The art style is new to me, and I really like it even though I normally look for realistic graphics- I think you get so drawn into sheer survival in this that you no longer really notice the graphics after a while anyway.
The map seems huge to me- especially when you break it down into chunks when travelling as the weather + food/water supplies you have on you limit you to stopping regularly anyway. So the fact that only one of the three freeroam/survival maps has been released, and the story mode map hasn't been revealed yet, seems very promising indeed.
Loot drops are more than enough to keep you going for just under a week ingame on the hardest difficulty as of right now, and after that there are multiple hunting opportunities including fishing, deer, rabbits, wolves, and bears, all of which can be eaten (raw or cooked!) and eventually worn as clothing with enough time spent crafting (ok you can't wear the fish but that's just realistic). There also various plants which can be used in crafting, and some which can be eaten or even made into hot tea for those freezing post-apocalyptic Canadian nights.
Lastly the little touches, like blood trails which don't despawn too quickly so you can follow your prey as it bleeds out, and footsteps which act the same so you can trace your way back to where you came from (assuming a blizzard doesn't intervene), really impressed me as I enjoy attention to detail like that in a game. And the fact that it's single player, so I'm not constantly being insta-killed by other players, yet it's still challenging enough with wolves/bears often in the way of where I want to be, gets a thumbs up too.

Is Duskers a fun game? Yes. Would I recommend it? No, because of one simple reason:
A lack of content with no mod support.
Duskers is a little like No Man's Sky in the sense that the first few hours are filled with fun and wonder, but everything afterwards becomes a disappointment because the game turns out to be far more shallow than it initially seemed. As a player, I yearned to explore more of the randomly generated galaxy in Duskers because I wanted to see what other horrors, mods, and derelict types I would encounter in the empty universe - but in the end, it turned out that there was really very little else to see besides what you find in the first couple of hours.
Here's a quick rundown of where the content was most lacking:
--Enemy types: there's only 4 different enemies. FOUR. They also behave pretty much identically with the exception of the last one.  This was definitely the biggest interest-killer for me.
--Derelict types end up mattering very little. Government A? Salvage C? Military B? It really doesn't change the layout in a particularly noticeable fashion, with the only differences being 1-2 extra ship defense turrets or something like that.
I really, really wanted to give Duskers a thumbs up - I loved the aesthetic, I loved the atmosphere, and I loved the unique command line interface - but unfortunately, after a few hours, I came to realize that there's really just not enough actual content here, and that's heartbreaking for fans of this niche genre like myself.

If you are looking for a legitimate sequel to Sacred or Sacred 2, do not play Sacred 3.  The vast majority of the reviews for this game are simply based on disapointed fans that were expecting a true Sacred experience. If you can see past this, read on.
If you are looking for a decent, linear hack and slash ARPG with some above average combat mechanics, its worth picking up on sale (under $20). There is not much character variety, but the actual enemy encounters and bosses are fairly well executed. The environments are nicely laid out with overall good art and have some unique mechanics to keep it interesting. I suggest playing on the hardest difficulty from the start to keep it challenging. Once you beat the game it unlocks a brutal difficutly called Deity for the hardcore. There is no loot in the game in the sense of dropped or collected gear or items. Instead they decided to unlock new abilities and weapons through leveling up. Its an interesting change of pace and makes the combat feel more like god of war than Diablo. Which can be a good thing if your looking for something more than a button masher. You will need to have good timing and strategy with your blocks, dodges and stuns to be successful in the harder stages. Play with a controller for the best experience.
The dialogue is probably the worst in gaming history. If you want to constatly cringe and see just how bad it can get, prepare yourself for an interesting ride. You can easily turn off voice and you wont notice the text since it does not affect the game at all.
The game can be finished in about 10 hrs and other than trying to max out character abilities or playing on higher difficulties, there is little replay value. The Orc playable character DLC is worth picking up for a couple bucks. Hes strong and has some fun, skill based abilities.
If you are an action RPG fan that is fine with more linear console style gameplay, its worth playing.

Banished is medieval theme city-builder where you control small population that must build their houses, fields and everything necessary to survive and prosper. It's probably one of most comfy city-builders available on Steam. It's made by just one guy, which is phenomenon looking at how well it looks. It's easy to start, difficult to master, as even smallest mistake may cause your villagers to die. And it will happen - you will restart your towns many time due to starvation, lack of firewood, tools or natural disasters. It may sounds repulsive, but early-game is most pleasurable part of the game.
Why I cannot recommend this game? Mods are big part and community added a lot of new features and improvements to the game, that are vital, as core game has many defects. But if you install any mod, even smallest grapical change or GUI improvement, it will block your achievements. That's right, installing mods cause you will never unlock any achievement for this game. And they give a sense of direction, because all of them are difficult to unlock and forces user to build from the beginning toward them. What's worse there's no information about that in Steam Workshop or when installing mods in-game.
If you can overlook this horrible dev mistake which for me should fail certification for Steam, it's nice title to get for 5€, spend a bit of time in it and move forward.

I love this game. With only 22hrs on record i can say it was well worth every penny.
-Id have many more hours if it werent for me favoring fps games.
Lets review the Pros and Cons
Pros:
-Very few bugs. (Like all games there are a few that are hard to run into, but still exist)
-Town's Folk AI is amazing. Unlike most other games like this that ive played, the ai on this game dont end up idling and dying off after a few hours of gameplay.
-Versitility. By this, i mean there are many different ways to play the game. You can be resource hungry (and hoard loads of stone, iron, wood etc) You can be population crazy (and create tons of homes along with an abundance of food) or you can be exploration / settlment crazy (and expand across the map as fast as you can)
-Difficult. As this may be a con to some, i think the difficulty of this game adds to the gameplay. Ive made towns and thought all was going great, until winter came and 1/2 of my town froze to death, then due to the lack of farmers, 1/2 of the remaining population starved to death, only to be left with a handfull of school children which were slowely picked off by the cold.
-System requirements. As i run with a pretty 'top of the line' pc, i know several friends that play this game with old school computers with no problems and without having to adjust quality settings.
Cons:
-Trading. Sometimes when the trade merchant is supposed to come around on his boat he doesnt. Making waiting on him tedious. Though realistic, it adds a little bit of frustration when expecting shipments.
-Travel. All your citizens walk everywhere they go. therefore if they find the need to travel across the entire map for something stupid, they will most likely freeze to death or starve to death. Though this is fairly uncommon, it is irritating.
-Tutorials. The tutorial is EXTREMELY important in this game. But it doesnt cover everything, making you run to youtube for the rest. It takes some time to learn the game because of this and the tutorial is slow and boring. Not so much of a con, just a personal complaint from every time i go back to play this game.
Overall: i'd give this game a 9/10 because of its excellent development, smooth ai, and lack of bugs.

Specific land motivation - instead of just motivating the land in a general circle, maybe motivate certain resources. Differentiating between friendlies and enemy health - maybe its just me, because i'm slightly colorblind, but I have a hard time telling the difference between the health bars when theres one of those massive heaps of blood and fire. This is not a game about exploration, as it claims, and it certainly doesn't reward you for doing so (high fuel/supply cost for wandering, no indication of where you should wander, major ports that award you nothing unless you have a reason to be there, powerful enemies that will simply ruin you). It seriously takes 1/3 of a barrel of fuel just to exit the inner harbour of the starting port.
It's also definitely not a game about trading, because I swear, half the ports I went to didn't even have shops. Never mind shops that actually had things worth buying or selling.
Naval battles are a frustrating joke, so if the game is about that, it's a really irritating game.
I don't think it's a game about questing, because most of the quests I got wouldn't even tell me where I was supposed to go. "Here, smuggle this contraband for me." "Where?" "Over there. Watch out for port inspections while you have it." "Okay, how do I get there?" "..."
So what is this game about? This is a game about dying.
That's it. Go out, die, repeat. Eventually, you will be able to pass on something interesting after you die, like a weapon, or money. Once you're really good at dying, you'll be able to own a house. I mean, not you. You probably won't own a house, or if you do, you won't use it much. Your descendents will own a house, which they will (maybe) improve for whoever is in their will.
Actually, once you really figure out how to die, you can start the game with many of these hurdles already surpassed. For example, at the minor cost of only four starting captains, I began the game with a house, an ironclad will, 950 echoes (money, or roughly 9 times the normal starting amount), and the 2nd best gun available at the starting port.
The best part is that none of these captains ever left the port. I was literally able to accelerate my game by DYING IN THE STARTING PORT. If I wanted, I could have sent my captains off to die in some random corner of the sea (I mean, "go exploring"), at which point I would have had a massive advantage in knowing roughly where the various landmarks are, and what enemies lurk nearby.
I'll probably keep playing it, which is to say I am going to keep killing my captains in the starting port, just to see how much stuff I can start the game with. Although maybe I already am playing the game. I hoenstly don't know.
The dialogue system is interesting, but the UI is a little messy. Interactions often have unexpected results. "Would you like some tea?" "Yes, I would." "Oh dear, the house is burning down. Unfortunate." "..."
The atmosphere is phenomenal. Would make a truly fantastic game about trading and exploring.
Definitely don't recommend, unless you've got a fetish for genealogy.

Duskers is fun in an alt-game style using console commands to control your fleet of salvage drones through puzzles.  There is a real-time aspect that is paced just enough to allow you time to enter panicked commands and flee / react accordingly.  This cadence for difficulty balancing works well with this hybrid mouse/console action game.  It's permadeath, but you maintain your research (discoveries and quests) across lives.  There's drone management and ship management with upgrades and seizures to keep things interesting.  You never have enough fuel so exploration is at a premium.
However, for me the game ground to a halt when the organic, viral enemies were introduce mid-game.  These mobs replicatre rapidly in-room withouth showing up on motion scanners, and their silent growth can make holding a generator active with a drone impossible, as well as block off access routes and become impassible.  It was just too much of a wrench thrown into the game which sucked the fun out of it as well as derails your own cautious grind towards greater power.  After a few attempts, I found that at this stage the game required so much micro-management (and cursing) that the earlier, fun think-and-react style play disintegrated.  I eventually put the game away as it just wasn't enjoyable anymore; despite its potential and promise.  And if a game just goes back into the abyss of your Steam library, then what good is it?  That's why I don't recommend it.

Right off the bat, to give you a good idea of what the game is about, lets talk about pros, cons, and what you'll be doing during the game.
The Game
You make a small Background for your character, a "Zailor" in the wide and sinister underground vault known as the "unterzee". You hometown is Fallen London, the only safe-ish port to which you will periodically return to manage your posessions, trade, rest and recover your mental sanity.
The game itself consists in going around on your boat, with your officials and crew, facing the countless dangers of the pitch black unterzee, establishing relationships, managing fuel and food, trading, fighting monsters and doing quests (often very creepy stuff), all trying not to get mad and start murdering (or eating) people.
PROS

-Lengthy and detailed writing with lots of plots and mysteries

The short of it: an innovative game with great puzzle-solving features, but with one major issue that brings it down a bit.
The long of it: Duskers is a game right up my alley - a sci-fi horror environment where you're a lone human on a starship forced to loot derelict starships to survive in an universe that has seemingly gone dead... though not entirely, as the derelicts have "occupants" of sorts. The drones you use become your companions and your lifeline, and the game's rogue-like nature means that you never know what to expect, forcing you to problem-solve and change strategies on the fly. Honestly, I really enjoyed the core gameplay, even through the frustrating moments when luck conspires against you and your hard work comes crashing down. Even though the game uses a typing interface for most of the drones' commands, it's done pretty well and with plenty of helpful information.
But there's a serious con, at least for me, and yes there's ***SPOILERS*** here.
The game states that your objectives are to survive, uncover the mystery of humanity's downfall, and see if there are survivors out there. It actually LIES about the last two objectives. You have a bunch of text logs that get uncovered as you explore various ships in various ways, expousing theories on what happened. But I began to get suspicious about where things were going after "solving" one theory that went nowhere, so I went a-Interneting. Turns out, there's no true answers, no final confrontations, no hidden sanctuary. The game really is only a "survive until you can't" kind of game, and that is a MAJOR letdown to me. The best rogue-like games I've played, like FTL or The Binding of Issac, had end-games, conclusions. You felt like all your failures, all your frustrations, were heading to something. Here, there's just endless ruin. I intially played through the frustrations because I thought the game had something at the end to offer. If it had been advertised as just a survival game, if it hadn't pretended to be more than that, I might not be as disappointed. I stopped playing as soon as I found out the truth, and that definitely knocks that game down a few pegs. ***END SPOILERS***
Verdict: I'm still recommending it despite my disappointment, because I did enjoy the hours I spent playing. The gameplay is novel and addicting, and pretty polished at this stage. But I will say that A) if you buy it, know that it's a game of endless survival and nothing else, and B) you might want to wait for a sale.

Apart from QTE action scenes, you will search areas of interest as Bruce and of course as the world's greatest detective. You will uncover rumors and a conspiracy that I've never seen in Batman's universe. While the Arkham games are known to give you some choice and tactics, this game gives you a unique twist to that (as you can tell it's clearly a unique game).
Telltale's uniquely drawn cell shaded graphics never get old to see. Is it the best graphics? Yes and no. The art style is exactly how it should be and it isn't going for realism.
The sounds of combat, music and voice acting are all top notch.  It immerses you in right away and keeps you hooked until the end of the episode.
While the first episode was fantastic there are some problems. Both AMD and Nvidia GPU's either ruin the FPS or it makes it unplayable in fullscreen. Even while tinkering trying to figure out how high I could get the resolution, I gave up and just left it on the default options that it originall booted up on. UNTIL THEY PATCH THE GAME DO NOT MESS WITH YOUR OPTIONS. DEAL WITH THE WINDOWED MODE FOR NOW.  While this is definitely a rough start for the game, it isn't as bad as the PC launch of Arkham Knight (which is definitely worth the buy now if you're interested) but it's annoying that a much simpler game didn't launch smoothly. Regardless, Telltale is doing Batman......justice. *ba dum tss* I wholeheartedly recommend this for fans or anyone who has any interest in Batman. If you liked the first episode and want more Telltale action, I recommend getting The Wolf Among Us. It's complete and is just as unique and interesting.

You know what, it takes time. Much like what this game is about (This is going to be a really indepth review for those actually considering purchasing this game, so hold on)
At it's core, SUPERHOT wants you to believe it's a real game, not a short indie game. To be fair, it is essentially an indie game but there's so much more to it.
What would you do if you had an innovative game mechanic and a great physics engine? You would create a game like SUPERHOT. The game, if you take aside all it's other mechanics, is basically an innovate shooter where time only moves when you move. It's straightforward and could make a great, CHEAP game (Unfortunately this game is a bit below compared to its price), but the devs made it much more. Here's how:
- THE DIFFICULTY: Holy crap is this game hard! You will be frustrated within your first 30 minutes into this game! I almost refunded the game because of Level 5, but Googled a tutorial instead.
- STORY: The story, is honestly one of the best I've seen in previous years. Without spoiling much, it had an innocent non-complex, arcady tone to it, but it becomes much more of a conspiracy as the game goes on... (Although do note that the story itself is only around 2 hours, but it unlocks some great modes once completed)
- MECHANICS: It does get old eventually, but I love the innovative playstyle!
Overall, if you're willing to spend a couple extra bucks, it's a great buy.

First things first.  The game is NOT "Overwhelmingly Negative".  It's actually quite damn good.  The reason people have given it such a horrible rating is simply due to the fact that it doesn't follow in Sacred 1 & 2's roots.  Yes, that's a bummer, but the game is a damned good hack'n slash.  Including all the DLC it took me 13 hours to beat it and was level 26.  I did not do any grinding and I did not do any MP or Co-op, but might venture back in and try it out.
They should had named this something else besides Sacred 3.   Perhaps something along the lines of Sacred: Ancaria Adventures.  Then it wouldn't had gotten such a bad rep.  The graphics were beautiful and there's a continued voiced story line which was great to have.  The voices were comical and not to be taken seriously, but acceptable and enjoyable.  Lots of power ups and a few weapons to choose from.  Once you get your weapons that's all you get and then you just upgrade them.  I didn't have a problem with it.  There is NO loot system.  All you have is gold from drops or chests and use this gold to upgrade your weapons/armor and buy items (potions).
This game does take place in the Sacred world and if you're willing to play a hack'n slash beat'em up with this lore you're in for a treat.  Keen games did a fantastic job.  Great game and worth a play through!  8/10

Blood Bowl 1 has been one of my favourite games to play with a friend. It's only flaw was the lack of multiplay in season mode. So I've been waiting anxiously for BB2. Now that I've played it for about 60 hours, I have a mixed feeling with it.
The game is basically Blood Bowl 1 with updated graphics and multiplay. That isn't a bad thing. BB1 already had everything in place. First complaint comes from single player campaign, as you can play it only with human team. After playing through the campaign, I started coaching my own team online. And there was the games' major problem. I had bought the game and both DLC teams, so I knew the team options are going to be limited. In fact, it almost crippled the whole game. I really miss the Norse or Amazon teams, as those were my favourite in BB1. Also, knowing that I have to pay even more in future to get more teams pisses me off.
If you liked BB1 as a game, youre gonna like BB2 also. So ask yourself which is more important to you:
1) Lots of different teams to choose from, but multiplaying only as hotseat
or
2) Improved graphics and possibility to play online, but (very) limited selection, of different races/teams
If you chose option 1, I suggest you continue playing BB1 and wait BB2 discount offer . If you chose option 2 and don't mind paying extra for more teams, go ahead and buy this game.
*If you are an experienced Blood Bowl player, you may want to add me.. ;)

This game makes me want to tear my hair out. I want to reccommend it, because of how addictive it is, but maybe that's the problem. I know that nothing in this game makes any sense, but I keep coming back for more. This game is a drug.
You see, the difficulty in this game is very high for a city building sim. You might kill off dozens of settlements before you even learn the ropes. Then, just when you think you have a stable settlement, half your population will die of starvation because they wouldn't help each other bring in the crops at the end of the year. Or because a few settlers are hoarding all of the food. Or some other bizarre reason that makes no sense. Or, you might not even get that far because your settlers refuse to have babies unless they have their own house.
You play as a communist dictator, telling your settlers what jobs they will spend their lives performing, how much they are allowed to produce, where they are allowed to live, and so on. It's all very challenging, but I often feel like I'm just fighting with bad AI. Overall, I think it's a good game, even if it's a bit rough around the edges.

Definitely not going to recommend this to anyone. If you want it for the sake of collecting the whole series, as was my own reason for getting it, go ahead. Just make sure you don't set any high expectations for this game, and most of all don't compare it to anything you know of the previous Sacred games.
The in-game graphics certainly look better this time around than they did in Sacred 2, but the gameplay is not nearly as nice - from a fixed camera view, which can impede certain moves in battle, to doing the map one mission at a time. It's true that Sacred 2 was almost tedious in how large its open world map was, but comparatively I'd much rather go back to doing whatever missions I feel like doing at the time and be done with it.
The upside of this is that Sacred 3 is definitely more competitive in nature now than its predecesor was. You need to reach checkpoints in the game versus saving whenever you want to and dying and respawning at a checkpoint will cost you some of your gold gathered in the mission.
Overall, I really think it wasn't nearly worth the wait for the game to have been released and they could simply have ended the series with Ice and Blood. If you want to play a Sacred game, play Sacred 2: Fallen Angel.

Faults:
- weak, if any considerable narrative
- monothonous
- gamebreaking bugs
- grossly overpriced [20€], worth 10€
Apart from that,
is a minimalist in design and narrative, immersive core science-fiction, difficult and unique rougelike tactical play with a puzzlegame heart. The user interface is somewhat complicated with a DOS-style console to enter commands, definitely requiring precision, but fun if you know how to handle it. Fortunately, it is graspable.
What you do in
is you loot derelict spaceships in a mysteriously devastated, extinct post-apocalyptic world. The narrative regards solving the question of what has led to this state, with the protagonist just awoken from a cryosleep. Since the derelicts hold danger, next to lore and precious scrap, drones are used to penetrate them.
All in all, a good release with exceptional potential, delivered simplified, sometimes recklessly. 7/10 wHATs grade. Could be so much more only with adding to the narrative, but the entire production neither seems particularly rushed nor lacking anything special. It is just slightly missed, as if a blurry image, but still recommendable to fans of science-fiction themes and those demanding tactical challenges.

At first I thought this game was kind of a space horror experience. I was relieved when I understood that that while it can be frightening, the scope of the game goes way beyond that.  The game does create an atmosphere of isolation. That can sometimes feel unnerving and when you encounter an enemy it can be terrifying, but it also means you develop weirdly strong sense of attachment to your simple-minded drone workers. And when you accidentally forget to close that door and you lose your drones it is quite heartbreaking. I guess it's kind of a real-time puzzle (is that even a genre?) game, with a heavy adventure influence. The way the player experiences the storyline is novel. The sense of being eternally out-gunned makes the game a challenge. The controls are also pretty novel. You end up typing most commands and your drones are sometimes unable to execute them for various reasons and while you're tinkering trying to fix the problem, the ship you're on begins falling apart or enemies begin trying to break out of their confines. Everything feels hectic. You'll die and if you can possibly realize that the frustration is a part of the fun you will love this game. But there's a logic to almost everything. And as you get more confident with the mechanics of dispatching enemies/avoiding dangers, Duskers feels, just for a moment, far easier than you first realized. Luckily there's plenty of surprises (and heartbreak!) awaiting you on your next ship.
I also like how the game works on minimum system requirements. Pickup Duskers if you like atmospheric, difficult, exploration games with a lot of depth that reveals itself for the dedicated gamer.

For the non-spoilerly in regards to the Destructoid article, the reviewer can♥♥♥♥♥♥off. Just because you're not sure whether or not the story is fiction is not a reason to suggest refunding this game. People aren't aware of the genre "Realistic Fiction" these days. The story is what makes this game very phenomenal and it was worth every penny.
Now for the spoilers:
When I first heard of the game, I thought the game just had a pretentious story. Narrator meets Coda, who happens to make video games for fun. Coda shares his games with Narrator and the Narrator, enjoying the games but assumed something was wrong with Coda because the games were so bizarre, began sharing Coda's game with other people. The game (as told by the Narrator) take on a repetitive yet deeper meaning.
The narrator thought that the messages were by Coda, for Coda; but the messages were by Coda to the Narrator. The narrator felt accomplished sharing Coda's games with others but Narrator felt empty when Coda stopped contacting him and stopped making games.
The narrator thought the games represented Coda's social anxiety and Coda choosing to isolate himself from people. That wasn't the case.
At the end of the game, Coda admitted that making games for himself was fun until Narrator felt like he was doing Coda a favor. Coda didn't want anything to do with the Narrator anymore.
tl;dr Narrator thought Coda was the bad guy but it was him, Narrator!
The game in this story has a lot of meanings that are left up to the player to perceive. My take on this game is that the story is something I would make the mistake of reading on Yahoo; games aren't always made for everyone to enjoy; behind every video game is a human/are a group of humans with feelings and expectations for themselves.
Play it for yourself; I doubt you will regret it.

text:
It's like  Rogue Legacy meets FTL meets some measure of Lovecraft meets 1800's London and Steampunk all at once. The backgrounds and soundtrack have lent this game a whole eerie yet grasping curious feel. You'll start off in Lost London with little to nothing to your name and venture out, no idea where you're going or what you're doing. And the then the game twists your arm...slowly.
From watching a mansion burn to eating nothing but salted bat wings and watching glowing crabs pass beneath your hull whilst out of fuel in the middle of nowhere and your crew eating each other as a shark approaches your silent guns...my word.
I am absolutely in love with this game simply for the logbook and text and some of the information tidbits and how easily this game crafts an absolutely alien world in a matter of seconds as you explore unknown territory and your map lights up and you discover yourself and your ship all alone in a foreign area, low on food and fuel and begging the gods to help you.
Do yourself a favor...DO NOT READ THE WIKI for this game. It will ruin the magic for you here. Go out there, play, start your engines, run out of fuel, eat your dead and pray to fickle gods to have mercy upon your souls. Just hope you have enough crew left to pilot your ship once your plea for fuel has been granted...
And as your ship sinks, your crew flounders around you and the fish begin to devour you in the murky depths of an emotionless ocean...carry on your legacy.

I spawned next to the railroad tracks in my third world (I died the 2 previous times) and thought, "Hey, this is a different spawn, cool!" As I was anaware of my new surroundings, I went up a suspicious looking hill and discovered a logging camp. I scowered about, whilst freezing, and found a lovely little furnace with a dead man adjacent to it. I stuff the furnace with all my wood (*chuckles*) and thought,"hey, I might survive." I soon realised that I was dehydrated, so I left the camp in search for another cabin. Now I am freezing and dehydrated. As I walk along a frozen riverbed, I see a large bridge-like structure. I am in a great rush to get in due to dehyration and coldness of the Northern Canada air. I walk in and the immense joy was that of finding out that your parents made you bacon for breakfast, in other words, it was joyous. I found bullets, clothes, food, water, tools, and even a gun! after I go into the pits of the dam, I walk back and open the door to the main room. All seems fine and dany until I heard the gargantuan bark of a wolf. I turn around to clarify that the wolf was outside of the broken window that I noticed previously, but my discovery will haunt my kaki-colored shorts forever. A massive wolf comes running as fast as me running to the bathroom after eating Indian food. I couldn't react fast enough to shoot it. The beast throws me to the ground and I proceed to smash it's face in with my trusty axe. In about two seconds after the wolf jumps me, the screen with black and said, "You have survived for 1 Day and 11 Hours." I just stare at my screen slackjawed and think, "I need to write a review on this game."
Final verdict: 9.9/10
