Bioshock is an atmospheric game that creates a dark beautiful world. The overall story might not satisfy some, but as you continue to play the game you fall in love with Rapture and why it was created. The underwater city is not chained by morality and as a result you will encounter disturbing imagery that captivates you at the same time. It is a great shooter that has RPG elements, which increases the variety of gameplay options and allows you to experiment. The choice you make in regards to the storyline also provides another reason to play the game again. Even if the ending is lackluster, the tension and awe you feel throughout the game is extraordinary. Bioshock delivers an enjoyable and immersive experience that should not be forgotten or missed by any avid gamer.

Preface-
The Warhammer/40k franchise has always been a well-known staple of tabletop gaming. I am more of a D20 player, myself, but I've always admired Warhammer and its sheer level of depth despite the mechanical simplicity. I love Games Workshop if for no other reason that they have a VAST library of video games within the Warhammer franchise. It's difficult to find players for tabletop matches, let alone be willing to teach/learn all of the mechanics and nuances of the variety of games. PC gaming, especially, opens the doors for AI battles and relative ease of access to real opponents. Bloodbowl, and other Warhammer games have given me a workaround to play against enthusiasts and novices alike without having to memorize too many new rules.
That said, if you're a Turn-based strategy player, you're already well aware of the potential heartbreak of RNG. And Bloodbowl 2 is no exception. There are moments where it's baffling how an opponent can dodge so effectively, even if the odds of failure are only 1/6. Times where clutch plays are thwarted by that dumbass rolling double 1's and dropping the ball.
The rules are very simple, and compared to the first Bloodbowl game, much more accessible and novice-friendly. The UI improvements are substantial and the graphics and audio are fun, and fitting. The announcers are great, and when they grow stale, the option to turn off the audio (or down) is available.
Despite simplicity, the depth of strategy is excellent. I truly didn't think, while playing the tutorial, that it could reach the level of complexity to keep me stumped during a turn. But risk/reward in this game feels very tangible, and the violent, dark-humor atmosphere is simply perfect.
I hope there will be future DLC or expansions that add additional customization options, however. They are pretty lackluster. And, to avoid aforementioned repetitive audio, record additional announcer voiceovers. Perhaps even a variety of announcers.
TL:DR:
Fun. Great audio. (Needs a decent sountrack). Strategy layer and UI exceptional.

Pros:
1. Incredibly deep gameplay/strategy, after 600 hours I still feel like a noob, every team can be developed differently according to how you like to play, and more than half the teams haven't been released yet so still plenty of variety to come.
2. The game looks great and the UI is mostly excellent with some occasionally annoying exceptions which the developer has been regularly but slowly fixing.
3. The community. This is the best thing by far, Bloodbowl isn't a game with a huge player base but it seems like once you start playing you don't stop, a huge amount of strategy guides available, all the streams I've seen have a very welcoming chat and once you feel like you've got a grasp of the basics there are a lot of private leagues with some really good and friendly players.
Cons:
1. Steep learning curve with a not great match making system can lead to some impossible games when you're just starting out, the tutorial will teach you the basics, but very slowly, I'd recommend watching some streamers and asking questions in chat over playing the tutorial, and when you search for a game stopping and starting the search every ten seconds or so will help to avoid the more ridiculously impossible match ups.
2. Time. Games can take over an hour to play, there's no speed mode so if you don't have that kind of time then this isn't the game for you.
3. Salt. Everything in this game is decided on the roll of a dice, there will absolutely be times when you know you're playing someone who isn't close to being as good as you but he'll wreck you because he'll get every dice roll his way. The better you are the better you will be able to allow for the variance but sometimes you're going to be left disgusted.
4. No competitive rankings. There's nothing currently like the ladder in hearthstone to judge yourself by, the main match making league is perpetual so really you have to join private leagues to find proper competition. Cyanide have put up prizes for a world cup competition but reallistaically only the very best players have a chance of qualifying for that, definitely my biggest problem with the game currently.
Edit: I now have over 1100 hours on this game and still addicted to it, to update the pro's there has now been a year of DLC teams being added, with two more imminent, all done to the same high standard as the base game teams, and all definitely beatable by the teams you start with, so don't feel like you need to pay to win here.
With the cons, the match making has been improved somewhat, with everyone going into a pool with a max 5 minute waiting time, which generally has improved the fairness of the games. There is now also a Champion ladder where experienced players can challenge each other to get the best record with the race of their choice, the winners all going into play-offs to find the overall champion. This new mode has really improved the match making experience, allowing you to find a real challenge even if you don't have the time/interest in signing up for private leagues.

Dredd vs Death is an early 2000s budget game by Rebellion. Back in the bronze age, 'budget game' was code for 'less quantity,' and had very little to do with the actual quality. Games that didn't satisfy the minimum level of competence and quality were relegated to the bargain bin, which wasn't something any developer with aspirations of a career ever wanted to be associated with. For a look at a typical bargain bin title, the marine sharpshooter series will bring you up to speed on just how super horrible those were.
Being a contemporary of the halo generation, Dredd vs Death is mechanically rather modern, to a point (two guns, dedicated punch and grenade buttons, partially regenerating health), while being built around oldschool - almost vintage - themes and ideas. For instance, the game assumes that when it tells you to arrest people, that you'll arrest people, rather than shoot them. If you shoot them, you get a game over. Whoa, man, what is this!? A fail state in a videogame!
Jokes aside, it's a curious blend of two styles of gameplay. You are, as the title might have hinted at, judge Dredd. You are judge, jury, and executioner, and it's your job to uphold law and order in a world where there is none. Missions range from preventing vandalism to cracking down on supernatural dudes made of fire who feel the need to turn incredibly fat people into zombies. Dredd, being a firm believer in LAW, has zero tolerance for zombie XXXXXL fatties, and is not impressed by the little wheels they have to hold up their incredible girth.
Fighting skeletons in the sewers also doesn't impress Dredd. Justice for all, but justice comes at a price, and that price is freedom. Armed with this most profound knowledge, you will arrest, shoot, and lay the verbal smackdown on everybody, no matter who they are, regardless of where you are, or the odds stacked against you. Dredd's quips make Duke Nukem look like a serious, sensible, and sophisticated character, which is only fitting, because Duke was inspired by characters like Dredd.
Unlike Duke, Dredd actually has to follow certain rules, and has basic objectives that must be completed. Unless they shoot first, Dredd is required to challenge suspects, so they have at least a microsecond to consider surrender. Shooting a perp who's surrendered is a crime. In case it wasn't obvious, not doing enough LAW will damage Dredd's ego met- LAW meter. Full depletion of your LAW meter results in a non-standard game over. Finishing levels with high LAW unlocks stuff, golden eye 64 style. It's in your best interest to sentence suspects to hundreds, if not thousands, of years of imprisonment for a wide range of crimes. Illegal possession of goldfish, being too fat in public, smoking outside designated smoking areas, holding liberal views, and simply being in a position where you could have potentially obstructed justice are common crimes.
This game doesn't mess around. Like masterchief, Dredd can only carry two weapons. Unlike masterchief (or perhaps very much like masterchief) Dredd will always carry his starting pistol. The lawgiver has 6 different firing modes, a scope, great handling, and other than limited ammunition, very few downsides. Essentially, it's a Megaman buster. Your secondary weapon more often than not ends up being something you bring along to perform a specific function, or fill a particular need. Judge weapons have extra features and gubbinz, while civvie weapons are basic 'press mouse 1 to kill people'-deals. In each mission, you are allowed 3 stun grenades, which can potentially force a crowd of perps to surrender instantly. You're also allowed full, infinite use of the FIST OF DREDD, the application of which is enough to crush the strongest enemy under the weight of the LAW. Dredd's melee attack feaures into his arsenal like Duke's mighty boot, rather than the gimmicky melee attacks you see in more modern games, and enemies are placed, designed, and spawned with the assumption that you'll use it.
So you have a pistol with multiple firing modes, a secondary weapon, your fist, very limited stun grenades, the ability to verbally challenge perps with one-liners, and an arrest button. Half your lifebar is of the regenerating type, and the other half isn't. You can carry a maximum of 3 HP restoration items, which are used automatically when your lifebar reaches 0, and that's it.
It's an incredibly honest, shameless, pointed game, that sticks very close to the source material, and Dredd as always provides tongue in cheek social commentary that's as relevant as ever - possibly even more relevant now, since social justice became some kind of movement. A decade and then some after its release, Dredd vs Death not only serves as a link to the ancient past, but also highlights how far the videogame industry has fallen. The budget game of yesterday is far more competent, entertaining, and bold than the trendy hipster titles of today.
It's short by oldtimey standards (6-8 hours), but not really by modern ones, and features things like unlockables, zombie mode that don't cost money, arcade missions, coop play, splitscreen multiplayer, bot matches, reasons to play well, great voice acting, a no-nonsense plot, razor sharp commentary that never gets old, and is unburdened by censorship, DLC, political agendas, handholding, sprint buttons, cover systems, and most importantly of all, and this cannot be overstated...

So, before we start. I've been looking forward to this game since 2015 and its kickstarter. I didn't back the kickstarter because I was a peniless student without a job at the time, but I was still looking forward to it.
Flash forward to two years later. I brought the game only yesterday as I was in a busy period, but let me tell you... The long wait for this game was well worth it.
A hat in time is one of those "Good old 3D-platformers remade". But unlike Yooka-Laylee, it's actually good! The movement feels good, the camera acts how it should (i.e, you can always see you character), and let's be real, it's pretty much perfect.
I have a few complaints, but I'll save that for the end.
From the first time I loaded up the game, all I could think was "this looks awesome". Everything is consist. Everything looks like it's meant to be. The crazy spaceship that you're in... you don't quesiton it because it fits. The first island, "Mafia Island" feels natural somehow. There's no need for suspension of disbelief becuase it all feels natural to the game.
You can practically fly around the game with the amount of movement you're given, and yet the platforming is still a challenge as it should be... (Sometimes because of the controls and camera, but we'll get to it).
The characters all look awesome. You can tell that a lot of love went into how everything looks. Especially Hat Girl (Cause I don't know her name haha). It's kinda awesome. Even the small amounts of dialogue she speaks just sounds amazing. It's perfectly done. Then there's the NPCs. They were amazingly done to. I love the Marfia from as far as I've gone. I love talking to the random characters around and just hearing their random voice lines. Oh yeah, all the dialogue is voiced to!!!
The music of the game... I decided to buy the deluxe edition from the start, but holy cow. I did not realise just how amazing it was going to be. I love the music. I even spent a good 10 minutes in front of the TV in the ship listening to the dog bark remix of the song hahaha...
Anyway, this game is amazing. But let's mention the downsides.
The camera doesn't have any elevation control and doesn't give you any options to pan it in order to make sure you stick the jumps (At least by default). This makes platforming a bit annoying at times.
Hat girl feels a bit slipery at times, making platforming a bit hard... She loves to run up walls a lot and screw up some of the more dangerous sections.
I want to like Mustache Girl because her voice is amazing.
Before you get the magnet badge, collectables really love going underwater and being unreachable.
Well, that's what I think about "A Hat in Time".
It's amazing. Totally get it.

Duskers is a n example of what hacking games should be... and it's not even really a hacking game.
In Duskers, you give commands to remote drones via a console as they helpfully explore derelict ships to replenish your ever-dwindling supplies. As you type commands for them to execute, you must navigate them past decompressing sections of ships, hostile alien creatures, and radiation. Careful planning and a little luck are your tools as you strip the abandoned ships as bare as you can before moving to the next one.
Now, the obvious relation to a hacking game is that you give your drones all their commands by typing them into a command console, but this isn't what I'm referring to. The thing that makes Duskers such a good blend of tactics and strategy is that it brings a finite set of rules and challenges to the table that can mix to form a wide variety of scenarios. You quickly find that gathering intel before moving forward is a great help, and that there are multiple approaches to almost any situation. Every move is risky, but you reduce that risk by stopping and looking, listening, and scanning, first.
For example, your motion detectors pick up movement in a room next to your drones. After you watch it for a while, you think you know what kind of threat it is. You can open the airlock and flush it into space, but that may damage the structural integrity of the ship you're scavenging. There's a door on the far side of the room; perhaps you can open that and the alien will wander away from the room you want to enter. There's also a turret in the room, waiting for you to find a control console somewhere else to activate it.
This game makes you take methodical approaches to different situations, letting you come up with strategies you've worked out after gathering as much information as you can. Perhaps your plans will turn out sound, and perhaps not. Either way, you gain experience not only in the game's mechanics, but also in critical thinking and situational awareness.
If you like strategy, tactics, or feel that other hacking games you've played are too "on rails", pick this game up. You'll be glad you did.

"General Tiberatum ventured forth into the Sunless Sea, with his crew and officers on board, and the mechanical safety of a very large deck gun. He was sure to beat the legacy of his predecessor, and find Gaider's Mount in his very first adventure."
Not only a beautifully done world; fleshed out with interesting characters and overall world design. Sunless Sea is a pleasure of the mind. Every text flows with beautiful descriptions and often witty writing. There is no such pleasure than to spend long minutes just reading the text upon text about the Sunless Sea.
However, if you're not much of the reading type. There is not much else going for this game. Though I feel that the overall design and gameplay elements are functional, that alone is not enough to sell the game. As an avid reader, I love just pouring over the text and building my lore about this world. Not just that, but I take pleasure in fleshing out my own characters with their own "play style" and making stories of the sunless sea on my own.
There are moments of pure tension, running from one corner of the map to another with the fuel ticking down. Also moments of subtle humor as you encounter engineer rats looking to make a few money. All of which are cohesively tied together with beautiful writing on the developer's part.
But if you don't like reading too much, don't get this game.

It's interesting in a weird way. There's more shock value than horror value here. Steep learning curve, imo, because you won't always have what you need to determine the behavior of some enemies and sometimes they kinda just come out of nowhere, and I don't like the idea of consulting a guide for how to combat something unless it's broken.
It turns out that probability is real. Your stuff starts out white and deteriorates with use. Use raises the failure rate, or the chance something permanently dies. You're good at white, you're taking a risk with yellow, and you're a thrill seeker when it turns orange. At any time beyond 0% could something just turn red and be junk.
The whole "I'm a lone pilot in space" deal kinda washes away when you lose the first time, because how it picks back up is that you still have ALL the logs you gathered from your previous playthrough, so it's like "wait, how did this new pilot get those? Why is there a new pilot? So there are survivors?" and it just kinda snowballs from there and ruins the atmosphere. Misleading information I don't really appreciate, but I still find the game to be fun in that it's a survival game from a command console-type control.
I think the execution of the game could benefit from a few upgrades here and there, but it's fine as it is as well.
The way the game works is that you start out in some random ship and system and drones, and you're just trying to survive as long as possible. There's no food or anything complex like that to manage, you just keep going until you lose the means to do so (like losing all your drones).
I forgot to add that there's no music whatsoever. That's not a bad thing, though. It helps to focus, honestly. If anything, it's more about ambience here than it is for the music. And you might hear a buzzing noise come from the computer when viewing certain parts like the drone view. The game is causing that buzzing, not the computer in general. Your computer is generating the buzz, though, which, I've found, happens in the drone view.
There are objectives that give a sense that you're progressing, but I've read that the main goal is to survive as long as possible. Unlike other games I've played, these "communication archives" are actually nice to read, even with the corruption that purposely obscures certain things.
There are daily and weekly challenges where you compete against other players to get a high score in clearing out a ship or system, respectively. These are separate from the main playthrough.

I've just heard a rumour on the docks that my competitor, Zepher, and his crew have been lost at zee.  'Tis too a common occurence for us zailors, but how else are we to survive down here in the dark.

We have several assignments from the Admiral to gather inteligence...I always wonder if he knows the dangers we face out here sat behind that old wooden desk of his.

I swore to my crew that I would invest our next earning directly back into the ship and it's maintenance.  Giving them some small comforts is all I can offer in this bleak world.
Before we set off, I have one more piece of cargo to hand into the Antiquities office.  It's a strange looking thing, and my limited vocabulary is unable to describe what it might be...what I want it to be is plenty of Echo!
As I walk back to the dock, a strange bald man with small round sunglasses and a bowler hat approaches me.  His demenour seems one of intent and secrecy. I step back as you can never be too sure as to strangers intentions in this place.  He introduces himself as a middle man for a wealthy benefactor that wishes to provide me with fuel and supplies.  "What's the catch?" I ask.  He tells me that there is no catch bar occassionaly me having to transport good from London to a destination from time to time.
I internally struggle with this choice, do I accept and continue building my legacy, or do I reject and die the next time I'm out on the zee....These are the choices I'm having to make every day now and it's wearing on me.
As I get back to my boat I see my crew waiting for my return and news of our next journey.  I begin to explain when several large boxes begin being loaded onto the boat.  "Where did these come from?" the crew query, as I look down to the dock and see the bald man tipping his hat to me.
"Set sail!" I command....Hoping we can reach the bald man's destination and come back safely......

Sunless Sea is a game of exploration, of strategy, of forethought--but more than anything, it's a game of
. The world of Sunless Sea (and Fallen London) is of Victorian London stolen and twisted by dark supernatural powers, resulting in its inhabitants getting on with life as best they can. Each port, is interaction is described with fascinating and absorbing snippets of writing.
Playing the game involves sailing your steamship out into the darkness, avoiding (or destroying...or being destroyed by) pirates and monsters, eventually steaming into various ports. Everywhere you go you find curious interactions, quests to undertake and hints of rare items to obtain. And, once you die (as sometimes happens in these games), you have the opportunity to pass on one or two bits you've collected to an heir for your next game.
If you want to explore a highly original, fascinating dark fantasy world described through excellent writing, this is the game for you.

I admit, I am one of the people who gets lured in far too quickly to early access survival titles. But The Long Dark is one of the few games in this genre that does it right, or at least is on the right track. There are no zombies in this game, no mutants, no carnivorous dinosaurs, instead you face against the environment alone. Which may not seem as difficult but as you quickly learn; the cold is the harsher than any zombie.
The atmosphere in this game is incredible. While there are wolves and bears in the wilderness who wouldn't hesitate to chase you down and swiftly end the game, the weather is what leaves me in a constant state of fear. It can change in a heartbeat and ruin you no matter how well you planned the days adventure.
At the moment there isn't that much depth, but there is planned story mode which is said to be a huge factor.

This game is more fun than I expected. Definitely involves a lot of text so if you're not into reading much, don't play it. But the text is quite well done, the graphics are very nice 2D hand painted stuff, and it's a lot of fun exploring random places. Combat so far isn't confusing, and is interesting. If you enjoy exploring and worrying about the risk/reward tradeoffs of going to far or potentially screwing yourself over for the chance of something bad♥♥♥♥♥ you'll dig it. If you don't like reading a lot and want a lot of action immediately, this probably isn't for you.
I only have a few criticisms. There's a few text issues where it'll say things like "you receive x <something>" where it forgets to tell me how many X I have received (like 1x, 2x, etc). Also, the quest journal could be a bit more helpful but none if it detracts from the game.

Dev Review:
The dev is very active on his forums.  He is always looking from new crashes to take care of (the stable release is pretty stable now. 5/15/16).  He is an indie dev making a good little game.  He is indeed the developer who listens to you.  Take a look at the discussion board and you will see he has responses on the majority of threads.
As far as game development goes, there have been significant and continual changes in the last year.  Every aspect of the game has matured.  More god powers.  Monster spawns are different.  Monsters will break down walls if they can't find a way in.  There are many more tower types than before.  there are now seasons.  There is a "full map", which lets you take stuff from one village to help with or start another if you survive long enough to prosper. ;)
Game Review:
Very fun little game.  The best way I can describe it is a God/tower defense village sim.  The game is similar to Banished in some aspects, but with the outside threat of the Undead.  It shares some aspects of Majesty as well.  It is a race against time to try and stay safe while the zombies and skeletons spawn (the monster spawning is going through some big changes in the current cycles so I left this a bit vague).
You don't have direct control of your guys which can lead to some hilarious situations; where someone runs from a zombie away from defense towers and deeper into trouble, or circles around a barricade to try and get that lump of stone that was dropped on the wrong side of the wall, etc.  A "grab" God power has been added so you can take care of some of these problems... if you are there to see it.
If you like Banished and tower defense games, or just want some good liero-style blood, this game is worth picking up, especially if it's on sale.  *Read what the dev has to say about the early access game before you purchase.*
Oh, and if you are looking for a god game this is so much better than Godus it's not even funny.
edit: Updating review to current build - 1 year since purchase and I'm still enjoying the game.  At the games current price and my current hours.. I've paid 12 cents per hour of enjoyment. =)

I'll do my best to keep this review updated as the game progresses. (2/1/2015 - Current Ver: Indev12c, Indev13 roadmap announced)
I'm recommending this, but I have a few caveats before I get to my review. If you're expecting a game that is 100% or even 80% realized as of (2/1/2015) then you probably haven't had much experience with Early Access and you probably shouldn't buy this game YET. Or if the feedback-and-support thing doesn't appeal to you, the $15 pricetag might seem a bit steep. Even then, if you're afraid of vaporware (I know I am), read the store page thoroughly as Ray (the dev) has done his best to put your fears to rest. Still mistrusting? I'm here for ya, or go to the website (or any of the links provided on the store page) and form your own opinion
(main website link on store page seems to be broken). I know it's some extra effort than you would normally spend, but Ray is very active on his official forums and he will certainly answer any questions regarding his vision and the current state of development before you make a decision on purchasing.
That said, I feel with the risk of vaporware and rushed products, opinion on the dev in an Early Access review is just as important as the game itself and I'll address that with my opinion first. If you don't care, scroll down and read the game portion. I'll remove this once the game goes Full-Access.
(scroll down for game review)
This man has earned my respect among a slew of Indie "Developers" (Opportunists) that started with Minecraft (Jeb had made a lot of promises like our Alpha/Beta contributions entitling us to free Xbox copies before it was so popular -- didn't happen) and continues to this day with practically every Early Access game on Steam. So much so I've learned to type the simple little word "dev" with a bit of spite in my mental voice. Ray is not that man. While this is an opinion, and one I cannot garuntee in the future, I very strongly feel this way. Just talk to him, you'll see.
Little things like his naming of his updates Indev12-13 versus 0.12.02 (this is no race to the magic 1.0! it's just a progress report) to his efforts to ask/require your input and support when so many people are so rightfully afraid to give it through an otherwise legitimate manner set him apart.
When I was younger, Independently-Developed games were practically non-existent. To be a Beta Tester, you had to send in a resume to a big name company and you had to be hired, it was a job, before your voice ever mattered in the gaming world. I have a job so that's not an option, but through Ray and his SixtyGig Games (and with $15) my voice is heard. That is what Early Access, Independently-Developed games, and Raymond Doerr is all about.
(had to be cut short for the actual game review, the lengthy praise is warranted though, I f-ing hate vaporware and the only way around it are honest reviews)
(Pro/Con lists are not my style, hope you like to read)
On the Steam Store Page, the game is marked as having several noticable influences, but in its current version, I mainly  agree with three of them, and I'll try to break them down.
This is the most obvious influence in my opinion (and also the closest game to ever touch upon what I want in a DF-like game), You have practically zero control over your villagers. You can place buildings to be constructed when your villagers get to it (although in a generally predictable manner), set resource harvesting tasks, and assign free (random) villagers to work at certain buildings. That's about it for control right now, and where most of the DF influence stops. P.S. "Losing is Fun!" theme is well-intact in Retro-Pixel Castles.
You start the game on whatever map you choose with nothing but a bunch of villagers and are free to choose where you place your Village Center (required before you can build anything else and serves as radial zone for where you can place other buildings at first, so choose wisely!), unless someone (or you!) has made a map where the Village Center was already placed (you only get one, this ain't no 4x). Also, when you build your first farm, you have to collect wild food (carrots only, so far) before they can start growing them in the farm (this is a one-time deal, a working farm can populate a new one). While it is ultimately a village sim and has buildings, food/energy requirements, I'd end the tracable influences to Banished there.
This is a big one, as it encompasses the actual challenge of the game. I spend most of my time on Peaceful, because I'm a casual grow-and-love city builder type gamer, but this is one of the rare few games where I'll switch off peaceful and play the regular game because A) Peaceful at this stage is -super- low on content and extremely easy being locked on Day 1 difficulty (you really only need/will ever use 2-4 of the available building types) B) Instead of devoting my city to raising a military, in Tower Defense style, your buildings do most of the work for you (your villagers will fight mobs, dumbly, and you will lose a lot of them, but that's the point! "Losing is Fun!"). Also, currently, you get to have one save, per mode, per map, per profile (you really only need one profile, unless you have a family or RL friends -scoff-) so I can come back to my peaceful cities when I want. So far (more buildings planned in the next update, expect this to change), the only offensive building is a Fire Tower (you can also build walls for defense/mob funneling) which will TD-style automatically fire at mobs close enough. All living things die in a burst of pixelated blood and green "essence" which serves as mana/power for your Fire Tower (and an Essence Collector, which is essentially a battery for the Fire Tower). Every day that you survive, the rate that mobs appear increases, and so the difficulty.
Most of the game and its mechanics are covered above.
At this point, you either love pixel-art or hate it. If you love it, this game does it very well. There's even an option to smooth out some of the pixel animation like essence flowing to an Essence Collector/Fire Tower(which looks gorgeous and well-fantasy-themed even for pixels), but I like pixels so I haven't even bothered. I'll edit this next time I go into the game and look (which may not be til the next update).
Music is a nice, calming fantasy-like tune that fits well into the pixel-art world. I've never had to turn it down or off after several hours, but that's really all I have to say about it, as I tend to not notice game music anyways. Sounds come mainly from birth/death of villagers and are just a quick happy or sad tune that fits with the music-style.
Saved in whatever, and however many, folders you'd like. Ray is currently not very focused on (or very impressive at - sorry man) making maps for the game himself, which brings me to a special point.
This is, as far as it stands now, an Early-Access-Only feature. I've seen those threads pop up, and I've seen maps get added, and updated. Be a real contributor to the game!
Maps are 1-z level (no digging down DF fans, these are humans!) but give a vague impression of depth as dense resources appear "taller" than their regular counterparts and is a nice touch to the aesthetic without complicated mechanics needed.
Currently, Ray is experimenting with map size in an effort to reduce code/program efficiency, so if you get in now, there might be changes.

I really enjoyed Gunstar Heroes and Contra Hard Corps so I knew I would like this. The controls are tight and while the difficulty is fairly high (Closer to Hard Corps than Gunstar) I always felt my deaths were fair. The art of course is beautiful and shows a ton of attention to detail, and the music and sound help make you feel like you're playing a 1930's cartoon. It's all very worth the low asking price.
A couple of nitpicks: The run and gun sections feel a little tacked on (because apparently they were) but the boss fights really need to be seen and played to be believed and more than make up for the more generic sections. That being said, once the game ramps up in difficulty even the run and gun sections are more enjoyable especially when they have minibosses of their own. Some of the super specials feel like they do a little too much damage (to the point where you can just skip a boss section almost entirely if you want) but it's not a huge deal.
I really liked how balanced the powerup items are. They have meaningful drawbacks either through giving you an assigned disadvantage or through making it easy to do one thing but harder to do another. For example, the dash that gives you brief invulnerability also makes you invisible. So while you can use your dash to avoid certain attacks, you lose the ability to change directions in midair while also being completely sure where you're going to end up at the end of the dash. So you can dodge something nasty but also find yourself emerging in the middle of the boss if you're not careful.
Overall, it's been a great experience. I wish more games rewarded the skill you develop while playing it like this one.

It's unfortunate that reviews can't get more granular than thumbs-up and thumbs-down, because people read them as "good game" and "bad game" with no in-between. This thumbs-down is a simple "not recommended."
To anyone actually trying to decide whether or not to buy this, ask yourself these questions:
1. Do you really, really like Judge Dredd?
2. Do you already have a ton of more popular games?
3. Is the price a non-issue?
Yes to any of those, go for it.
Fact is, the $8 you're considering spending on this is the same $8 you could be spending on something else, regardless of this game's context in history. FFS, Deus Ex is $1 cheaper, and I doubt anyone will disagree that it's a better title, despite being 3 years older. Same story with the old Thief, Hitman, and Tomb Raider games. Even games as recent and well-regarded as Dishonored, Hotline Miami, Portal, and New Vegas are only $2 more than Dredd.
With that in mind, is Dredd vs Death a bad game? No. Do I recommend spending scarce time and money on it in the present, over other games at a similar price point? Not unless you really love Dredd and nostalgic gameplay. I do, so I bought it, beat it, left a review for a summer badge, then forgot about it.

I love Judge Dredd and have been reading for ages, so I'm biased towards the Dredd universe.
Visually, this is pretty fun; shows its age really badly, and the animation is shoddy, but it has a very marked visual style. It feels like the character models are based off Mike McMahon's blocky renditions of characters, but that is only conjecture. Rebellion's other 2000AD title, Rogue Trooper, has a similar low-poly style, but I'm a sucker for low-poly character and prop models.
It also has a spot-on representation of Mega-City One. The Stallone Dredd film - for all its flaws - shares this in common with Dredd vs. Death: It got the Big Meg right. Karl Urban's Dredd doesn't come close, although it admittedly went for that realism thing.
Graphics aside, this game is objectively quite bad on a few levels:
1. The controls are dire. Both moving and jumping in Dredd vs. Death are horrendous, and have stopped me playing the game on more than one occasion. You can get through it - as I did - but the controls are too tacky and cumbersome to facilitate really enjoyable playing.
2. The actual combat and gunplay is out and out bad. The guns - even the bloody Lawgiver! - give such boring, weightless audiovisual response that you feel like you're shooting airsoft guns. You do have a cool, dedicated "apprehend perp" button as well as a couple of ways to disarm and rout your foes - making them kneel and surrender to be cuffed - but it works on so few enemies that it just doesn't contribute to the gameplay all that much.
3. Judge Death and Psi-Judge Anderson. In a crushingly oppressive, cyber-dystopian future-hell where a bio-engineered future-cop doles out justice unfalteringly because it is all he knows, the most asked-for characters appear to be a magic judge and then a magic evil judge ghost who has evil ghost pals, and they fight, because the evil ghost pals want to kill everybody. I'm fine with Cursed Earth mutations, but I find these characters to be mind-numbingly boring.
4. The levels. The game world is so sparsely populated - I can understand that given hardware or engine limitations at the time of the game's development - but this should have made Rebellion take stock of what they could actually portray believably and reeled back the environment scale a bit. MC-1 is meant to be an overpopulated hive of unemployed, disgusting future-citizens, but you wouldn't know it if you played Dredd vs. Death.
5. The environments. Unecessarily huge, visually boring, empty. No real exploration to be had or secrets to be discovered.
6. Enemies. Shoot them and they die (Shocker.) Very little variation; the grenadier soldiers can often one-shot you if you get on the wrong end of a pistol in the previous fight and don't have any medkits. You are usually armed to the teeth and won't find much challenge from the average perp - you'll be fighting against the controls more than anything.
To summarise, nice stocking-filler that I bought for the universe alone; it sadly did not deliver gameplay-wise. Rebellion did much better with Rogue Trooper, another 2000AD-universe game that was sadly overshadowed by Gears of War. Dredd vs. Death is only for the pure-hearted Dredd fan. If you want an introduction to the Dredd universe, shut your computer off and go buy some comic books, nerd.

Duskers is a tactical rogue-like science fiction where you awaken from some form of suspended animation into a universe that has suffered from a mass-extinction, leaving you as the last known person alive. You're tasked with compiling data regarding the causes of the event by exploring and scavenging information from abandoned, derelict vessels and space outposts.
Equipped with three remotely-operated drones, you board the vessels in search of fuels to sustain your travels, avoiding the automated defence systems of the derelicts, alien lifeforms, radiation as well as the constant threat of malfunction from either your drones or the derelict itself, potentially rendering your drone's subsystems non-functional, or pipes and airlocks bursting, releasing lethal doses of radiation into the vessel.
I myself would highly recommend playing in this very unforgiving environment as Misfit's Attic have got the atmosphere absolutely spot-on. Just a warning, there are potential jump-scares if you're not careful with what doors you open.
Such a good game!

Having been burnt on early access before, I held off on this till release. Saw the 10/10 reviews on release day and couldn't hold back. I've pretty much done nothing but play since then. If you're not big on narrative, perhaps this won't be for you, otherwise I recommend to everyone unreservedly. The atmosphere is amazing, the writing, the whole feel of the game. It's difficult and challenging but without biting your hand off for making a wrong move. The decision to tie the central game mechanics more to exploration and slowly uncovering stories rather than straight-up trade is brilliant, as that's what we're here for rather than a number-crunching minigame.
My favourite part is that currently I'm constantly feeling like I've just scratched the surface, and that there are so many things that I'm on the verge of discovering; and they're currently adding even more stories/missions on top of that! A near perfect mix of risk and reward wrapped in a package of superb writing and aesthetics, I could not be happier with this game. Any fan of rogue-lites, oldschool RPG's, steampunk, Lovecraft, or anyone who's seen this and thought it looked intriguing; buy it, you won't be disappointed.

Outlast is a game that will make you afraid of the dark. Not only is it terrifying thanks to an utterly disturbing atmosphere, finely-crafted jumpscares (yes, it can be done) and a forboding musical score, it's also relentless and will never let you rest. Need a breather? Too bad, cos the psychopath behind you wants to wear your head like a hat, and he ain't gonna take no for an answer. You reckon you've been in a situation game-wise that made you feel completely helpless? Unless you've played Outlast, you don't know squat, pal.
Now some reckon that Outlast is a tad overrated, usually pointing out the flawed story and questioning why the protagonist doesn't simply leave the asylum. But honestly, in an era where every other horror game has either fallen victim to trends, turned themselves into an action-adventure game (looking at you, Resident Evil), or given up the ghost completely, this phenomenal game is a welcome return to decent, principled horror. Red Barrels (the development team) understands tension, atmosphere, and knows how to leave you beaten,  bloody, bruised, and begging for more.
It's a staggeringly beautiful, lovingly crafted and deliciously creepy game that has well earned the praise it has received. Any self-respecting horror fan will have this gem nestled among the rest of their collection.

RuneScape is a fantasy massively multiplayer online role-playing game (MMORPG) released in January 2001 by Andrew and Paul Gower, and developed and published by Jagex Games Studio. It is a graphical browser game implemented on the client-side in Java or HTML5, and incorporates 3D rendering. The game has had over 200 million accounts created and is recognised by the Guinness World Records as the world's largest free MMORPG and the most-updated game.
RuneScape takes place in the world of Gielinor, a medieval fantasy realm divided into different kingdoms, regions, and cities. Players can travel throughout Gielinor via a number of methods including on foot, magical spells, or charter ships.Each region offers different types of monsters, resources, and quests to challenge players. The game's fictional universe has also been explored through a tie-in video game on another of its maker's websites, FunOrb, Armies of Gielinor,and the novels Betrayal at Falador,Return to Canifis, and Legacy of Blood.
Players are represented in the game with customisable avatars. RuneScape does not follow a linear storyline; rather, players set their own goals and objectives. Players can choose to fight non-player character (NPC) monsters, complete quests, or increase their experience in the available skills. Players interact with each other through trading, chatting, or by participating in mini-games and activities, some of which are competitive or combative in nature, while others require cooperative or collaborative play.
The first public version of RuneScape was released on 4 January 2001 in beta form, and in December 2001, Jagex was formed to manage the game. As the game's popularity grew, the game engine was rewritten, and its beta was opened to paying players on 1 December 2003 under the name "RuneScape 2", and officially released on 29 March 2004.The third iteration of the game, "RuneScape 3", was released on 22 July 2013.

Count your batteries, be careful not to run out because darkness is your worst enemy.
If you've watched walkthroughs or any other video of Outlast, you're likely to think that you know how to beat it and you won't get jump scares. I watched many and let me tell you, I thought I had it all figured out and boy was I wrong! The experience is not the same, you WILL jump on your seat, spill your drink or in some cases, adopt a fetal position and cowardly sit in the corner of your room after a bad encounter.
The game is brutal. You don't want to play. You put it aside and then you're drawn right back to it. The main reason, I think, is the personal reward you get from pushing further.
Don't be afraid of dying, be afraid of running out of batteries because you never know when you'll get another one!

Hopefully, there will be additional seasons... There's a lot of potential here.
Whereas the Arkham series is a story about the action of being Batman, this is a story more about the choices.
Part of that is obvious... Telltale games are very much 'choose your own adventure' style, but there was even some choices in combat that was like 'How far do you take this?'.... kept you thinking.
Speaking of combat, I'm sure a potential buyer with no telltale experience will want to know that it is handled through a series of quicktime events. Failing to press every single button does not spell disaster. Some presses are critical, others are more 'shorten the fight'. Some interesting fight sequences + cinematic camera shots kept it interesting.
I played Telltale's 'A Wolf Among us' and 'Back to the Future', and they each let you save the game multiple times... this let you go through and try different things and see different outcomes. This game does not have that. You have 1 save. You can overwrite it from episode to episode. I suppose this does encourage the idea that your choices matter, but this was the one thing I found annoying since I plan to go down the different paths.
A new thing; or at least something I was not aware of, is something called 'crowd play'. I haven't tried it, so take this with a grain of salt, but it seems like there's an app that your friends can download to vote on choices in-game.... kind of a 'twitch plays pokemon', telltale style. Seems interesting, I just need to find some people who'd be interested.

The bosses are a ton of fun.  Great mechanics.  The different level types are a smooth and nice surprise.  The overall concept of the game is very fun.
So, just a few things that might be a problem for some people.  I feel that the controls are good.  Movement is smooth and it didn't take me any getting use to.  However, the shooting can be a bit difficult at times.  Not often, however, you don't have a true full 360 range.  It is the strict 8 direction range.  So you will find yourself not quite being able to hit targets and have to move your character a little bit.  This can be a little weird at first because most games will allow for a full 360 range.
It's not a huge deal, but it definitely is a more old school mechanic.  Just keep that in mind when fighting things that are rushing at you or firing at things that bosses are firing at you.  You may have to make adjustments in where you are standing instead of just quickly using your attack and taking the object out.
Hmmm, as for now that is actually the only little complaint that I have that I could see bothering others.
The music is great.  I was expecting it to simply just fit the atmospher, but nope, it is catchy as hell and very well done.
Point is, this game is surprisngly a lot better than I thought it would be.  I really wasn't expecting to enjoy it.  Too bad there isn't online co-op, but the local co-op is fun.  The game is perfectly fine doing solo as well.
I recommended picking this game up because it is actually quite the gem.  While making a nod at old school games, I feel that it still offers smoother controls and better mechanics so it isn't as annoying as old school games XD

Updated review to be based on Indev 13 unstable 4. Unfortunately I must still leave the review as it is, while the patch has gone a ways towards balancing the game but has also taken a step back in many aspects it still needs more work.
I know this is a EA game and I really hope things improve down the road, but at the current point I can not recommend this game as even a game.
AI Is glitched, you still have to micromanage how much wood you set to harvest and how much stone you set to harvest as attempting to build multiple buildings leads to all the buildings tending to have all their stone or all their wood delivered, instead of balancing the delivery,the bigger issue is that if your building multiple buildings it will attempt to deliver the last piece of stone but get distracted by a zombie and drop the stone, after that the builder will then go and start working on the other building leaving the building uncompleted for a fair while, sometimes even until the other building is finished.
Death Trap is still there and even worse since the removal of essence generation from the towers and collectors, now you can't even build effective defences, to even get defences in place you have to build all 3 havesting camps, collect and build the upgraded resources and then finally can build defences, but those are useless without collectors, you build those and you have to continually stock them with crystals, all that takes time away from building the essentials like food and housing.  Towers can't even seem to fire over walls which is major source of annoyance... You either limit your towers ability to fire or you have no way of containing your viliagers who will wander out of town for no reason and just idle in "zombie land"
Indev 13 Stable 4 must be substantially bugged, change notes state that spawns have been substantially reduced yet somehow I got a hoard of 14 !! zombies raiding my tower... on DAY 2! not even end of day but end of dawn.
Villagers are smarter but still not there, as above they will walk away from the town or the farthest building into the middle of no where and just idle there... until they see a zombie and then they will rush to it, and then rush to the next and the next and the next... until they die.  Yes they will run away but that only lasts a couple steps and then they will see a zombie and run and attack, it's a game of ping pong now with the run, attack, run, attack action... the game really needs a way to contain the villagers, either walls with gates or a "no go" zone that you can mark villagers to not cross.
Defence buildings are useless, zombies heal faster then the buildings can regenerate, spawn faster then the buildings can regenerate and it appears the more you build, the more zombies you bring.
Once you mark a building to be built you can't pause it (Being worked on but the button doesn't work still), you can't lower it in the queue and you can't cancel it, you can only dismantle it, instant if nothing was delivered to the building, but if the building had even 1 item delivered to it a builder has to go to the building to dismantle it...
Looking forward to the next patch but the game is still too unbalanced to be enjoyable

The good news: you came out of cryogenic suspension in good health.
The bad news: you're critically low on supplies.
The good news: there are plenty of other vessels within range.
The bad news: they're all derelict.
The good news: you have a fleet of salvage drones you can send into the derelicts to gather supplies.
The bad news: your drones aren't the only things moving around those derelicts. And the other moving things are hostile. And the half-broken infrastructure on those derelicts is prone to fail explosively. And parts of your drones and your ship break too. And your only interaction with the outside world is with the drones. And your only interaction with the drones is through a clunky command-line interface. And you may be the last human alive anywhere. And if your drones die, you're next.
So on the balance, it's mostly bad news.

For a simple concept of a 3D platflormer with the touch of different ability elements, this game was a instant hit for me from the moment I started up Chapter 1. From the vibrant level designs of each world to the detail and care put into each character came an amazing experiance I wasn't really expecting at first glance when I first purchased this game. This game would probably be one of the only platformers that I've loved playing in a long time, which shines with everything I hope for in any type of game.
Sure, there's a few downsides to the main game : Camera angles being trickey and annoying in some platforming stages in certain areas (especially in Chapter 3 and some Time Rifts), character models showing slight errors when displayed in certain cutscenes with clipping and even though I don't mind this at all, some people would say it'd be too short of a game.
But with this, the true potential of AHIT shines through and knocks those worries out. The game starts out fun and enjoyable and stays that way until the very moment you exit out. Each stage of every chapter has a ton of replay value with how much space there is to explore with the wide variety of obstacles to parkour through and with the touch of collectables that unlock ability hats, customizable material for Hat Girl to currency that help with buying pins which you can mix and match to your own style and advantage in different areas.
The main selling point of this game, in my opinion, would be the soundtrack, how it creates this amazing atmosphere throughout the story and the variety and personality put to each individual character you come to face throughout that make each area have more charm and give more reason to venture forth to see what they and the enviroment have in store for you to overcome.
I really do recommend this game to anyone no matter personal taste, you'll love it start to finish. It was worth all 4 years of waiting from the developers, and if you wanted to play even more of the game after collecting all 40 hourglasses, there's the big amount of fan made material avaliable on the Steam Workshop to go through.

The survival experience seems disjointed and non-authentic for multiple reasons I'll outline below.
When you enter any building (no matter how small, like a small shack) the game has to load it, thus disconnectinng you in a sense from what was on the outside. For instance, if you are being chased by a wolf, run to a shack and click on the door. There no fighting to make sure the wolf doesn't get inside. It literally can't. The door doesn't actually open and close. The game just loads a new area and you're there in it. The environment needs to be continuous in a game like this.
The crafting and loot system itself seems very... "staged". For instance, the same items are found at the same locations. Workbenches always contain a string. The trappers homestead always contains a small game trap. When you die and have to go back to those locations, immersion is lost because you KNOW items can be found at certain locations.
The map is not randomized, which means that if you die enough times, eventually you will just know where everything is. Not very realistic for a downed plane survivor. Randomized maps would be better, forcing you to rely on survival techniques, gaining high ground to look for houses and loot zones, etc...
I bought this game because I am fascinated by extremely cold environments and I wanted to support the developer.
However, I can't recommend this game yet because the environment, loot system and crafting system seem "distant", "staged" and inauthentic. I'm under the impression due to the "Overwhelmingly Positive" reviews that other individuals are looking at different aspects of the game than I am and ascribing more value to those features. Yes, it's a beautiful game. Yes, you can die at any moment from hunger, thirst, infection, exhaustion. However, due to the things I mentioned, immersion is destroyed - and with a game like this, if you don't have immersion, you have nothing.

When I first played Banished, I greatly underestimated the numbers involved. Its not like a traditional simbuilder where you just keep an eye on income, but you have to keep an eye on literally everything your villagers do. It has a decent learning curve though and it is a very good example of "trial by error". It takes a few attempts to get a good village going, but you shouldn't let that stop you from trying again and again. It's very rewarding to notice you keep doing better and better at the game.
One final important piece to notice though is that this game will start to lag the larger your town becomes. Some people with bad computers will notice a slowdown after 500 inhabitants, I noticed a huge lag/slowdown at 1000 inhabitants. I recommend just playing on a medium map.
Dont expect a thrilling story or objectives and goals. This game only has two goals: expand and survive. It's a great game "to pass time".

Remember that show Survivorman?
It's like that, but a game, and you're him. Incredibly tense, but I can't stop trying to [play the game and] live.
Oh yeah, and unlike Survivorman, I can't even make it a week... (okay, it's getting better, as long as the dire wolves stay away).
The game's in Early Access, so there's a few things that bug me but understandably so:
-No jump/clamber. I died on one of my first because I got stuck alongside a long drop, thinking I could climb a waist-high rock back up, only to discover I couldn't.
-My best playthrough I was dying of dehydration. Except there are *tons* of places with stoves and cups, and can't even use the scenery cups to collect and melt snow...
EDIT: It also turns out that I was just being an idiot and melting snow is a lot easier than it seemed. It's... somewhat counterintuitive but at the same time fairly simple.
-BUT on my best playthrough, I died getting attacked by a wolf. Because I wasn't sure how the defending mechanic worked. I only saw the defend prompt once I was getting attacked, and it was my first time, so...
So for a game in Early Access, I feel that it's good for what it is right now. A tutorial or quick in-game guides would be nice to see in the future.

There are no spoilers in this review.
To begin,
-This game is a completely different genre from it's predecessors.
-The mechanics are more suited for handheld console play (think PSP/ 3DS/ mobile app). I would even go so far to say that this PC port felt more like an afterthought.
Game complexity: I am not against grinding as a game mechanic, because there can be good grinding games where you're constantly on your toes, and then there's bad ones. Sacred 3 falls under the latter - I fell asleep while clearing mobs because there's virtually no challenge - press button, monster dies. HP/Mana management? Choosing the right equipment for the right fights? Fret not, you are released from that burden in this game. </s>
Replayability: The only reason to try out other characters is to see their skills. You can get the same experience from watching a YouTube video of the characters, then you're back to facing the same levels all over again.
I wrote this review having owned a PSP myself, and played hack-and-slash games such as Dynasty Warriors, DMC3, God of War, Ryse, and many others. Avoid this game at all costs - even if it was free, your time could be spent on other games instead.

I really enjoyed Gunstar Heroes and Contra Hard Corps so I knew I would like this. The controls are tight and while the difficulty is fairly high (Closer to Hard Corps than Gunstar) I always felt my deaths were fair. The art of course is beautiful and shows a ton of attention to detail, and the music and sound help make you feel like you're playing a 1930's cartoon. It's all very worth the low asking price.
A couple of nitpicks: The run and gun sections feel a little tacked on (because apparently they were) but the boss fights really need to be seen and played to be believed and more than make up for the more generic sections. That being said, once the game ramps up in difficulty even the run and gun sections are more enjoyable especially when they have minibosses of their own. Some of the super specials feel like they do a little too much damage (to the point where you can just skip a boss section almost entirely if you want) but it's not a huge deal.
I really liked how balanced the powerup items are. They have meaningful drawbacks either through giving you an assigned disadvantage or through making it easy to do one thing but harder to do another. For example, the dash that gives you brief invulnerability also makes you invisible. So while you can use your dash to avoid certain attacks, you lose the ability to change directions in midair while also being completely sure where you're going to end up at the end of the dash. So you can dodge something nasty but also find yourself emerging in the middle of the boss if you're not careful.
Overall, it's been a great experience. I wish more games rewarded the skill you develop while playing it like this one.

I played it a while and i have to say it shows promise.
What i missed from similar games like Banished was a challenge from monsters or enemies. Like other tribes trying to kill my people or simply wild animals. Banished couldnt fulfill this wish but Retro Pixel Castles does. Although till now it is limited to Slimes and Zombies (more to come).
Obviously it is Early Access and not finished, it is in many ways very barebone, has at the moment no saving function (end 2014) and misses many other things in terms of controls, layout and look.
But it also is very playable i have to say. There is something you can get out and giving you some fun. Maps are available from the developer (although they are a bit ugly) or you get a community created map (looking much better).
Steamworkshop is missing till now, which makes these a bit "harder" to obtain, but they are there.
The game goes a similar direction Banished goes. You start with a bunch of people, you create a Towncenter, harvest ressources and build other buildings to support your people or get defenses against Monsters up.
You cant control your people directly, which often is a bit painful because you also cant give other commands like a rallye point or make a priority to a building, so you cant influence till now which building they start to build or where they shall group up to fight and defend their town. Also a more direct control over single townsmen/women would be a good addition to decide who is going to be a builder and who will be a farmer (or maybe a guard later on?).
But even while there are things missing and flaws at the moment, it is very fun to play. Different maps give a good feeling of what the Dev can come up with and besides that spice the experience up. Playing on one map is very different than on the next one. Even playing several times on the same map is a variety in experience because the starting points are randomized.
Currently in:

-a mapeditor to create your own maps (is kinda easy, just the dev is doing some very ugly ones)
-different profile without any use at the moment
-a settings option menu
-2 types of monsters (zombie and slime)
-1 type of food
-2 types of usable ressources (stone and wood)
-3 types of non usable ressources at the moment (3 different crystaltypes)
-a kinda good soundtrack (sounds very pixely)
-a very sweet pixel look, zoomable camera (although a bit clunky in performance then)

LIMBO is one of the most atmospheric games I've ever played, though it has a very dark and quiet atmosphere at that. There are a few action setpieces strewn throughout the experience, but most of the time playing is spent wandering the environment and solving puzzles within a fuzzy, dark setting. The control scheme is your basic platformer setup with the addition of a grabbing ability, but the way the player interacts with the environment is very remeniscent of point-and-click adventure games. The puzzles are never too challenging, although some of them had me stuck scratching my head for a good while. Unfortunately, many of these challenges felt terribly unrewarding and often left me with a sour taste in my mouth. The dull mood that pervades the whole game doesn't exactly compliment this, either. It seems to me that the developer intended for the player to feel uncomfortable and creeped out while playing LIMBO, and I certainly was. The downside to this is that there's rarely any variation from this mood, and it begins to stagnate after a while. If this game were any longer, I'm not sure if I'd have finished it.
LIMBO was certainly an interesting experience, but it's not one that I'd be revisiting any time soon. The game as a whole succeeded in keeping me invested enough to reach the end, but it lacked the charm to constitute a second playthrough.
I would recommend LIMBO if you're looking for a short, artsy game to distract your mind for a few hours, but don't expect to get much mileage out of it. If you're looking for something action-packed or you don't think you'd be able to stand staring at a dull black-and-white screen for very long, I'd stay away from this one.

Dredd vs Death is fun and even charming, but it's honestly pretty bad.
The gameplay is...not great.
Essentially, you have your lawgiver (with its many firing modes) and the ability to yell commands at citizens. See someone scrawling? You can run them down, force them to surrender and put them in the cubes for life.
Dredd v Death’s gameplay is that it’s arcade based. You’re always being scored based how many enemies you kill, how many years you sentenced, and how long it took you to complete the mission. In order to get the best score, you cannot kill perps, you have to shoot the weapon out of their hands (or kill their leader unit) then go and individually arrest and sentence each one of them. This contributes to the tone of a Judge Dredd game, but it really ruins the pacing since you have to stop to give a dozen life sentences before moving onto the next dungeon.
The other problem is the mass amount of escorting. There are only 11 levels and 4 of them have escort missions. When you realize that civilians are killed in 1-2 punches, you’ll understand why this is an issue.
Additionally, the difficulty curve here is incredibly steep.  Vampires, the most common undead enemy, take 5 armor piercing bullets to kill on Normal difficulty. They take 7-8 on hard. This is an issue because the lawgiver uses the same ammo bar for every kind of bullet.  More powerful bullets use more ammo. Additionally, more powerful ammo types have a lower rate of fire. What all this means is that on normal difficulty, you’ll quickly run out of bullets toward the end of the game. If you’re playing on hard…Grudd help you.
Although the lawgiver has been lovingly recreated, there aren't a lot of opportunities to make use of it. You'll use standard and armor piercing 90% of the time. Ricohet is basically useless. You're often penalized for using hot shot. It can take 5-10 "high explosive" shots to kill a single enemy. I couldn't even find a single time to use the heat seeking ammo mode. Levels should have been designed to make use of these ammo modes. Instead, the levels are incredibly simplistic offices and hallways. The graphics are pretty bad (even for the time) and the city feels vacant, empty, and lifeless.
The story… is also not great.
Here it is: Dredd’s on patrol. Vampires show up. Vampires are taken to prison. Vampires break out of prison. Dark Judges break out of Prison. Dredd has to go capture them.
There are 11 levels in Dredd v Death. The Dark Judges don’t break out of prison until the end of the lengthy level 2.  Not only that, but one of the levels is just a boss fight, nothing more.
So what is good?
The humor. The humor is this game’s saving grace. You can arrest any citizen for insane trumped up charges such as littering or owning a gold fish. Almost every level includes a silly announcer to match the environment.

A beautifully detailed, I liked the fluid gameplay and the special effects. Levels are designed like arenas, defeat all enemies and you can move on. There is no inventory and constant looting. Eventually, there was an update where we were told they wanted to overhaul the engine to provide better graphics, simulations and multi-threading. The Dev's asked for our patience while they worked on this and assured us it would be worth it. Then over six months went by with no word about anything from any one, no updates, no respones. It seemed clear the game was dead and I stated as much in a review back then.
The Devs then came out and gave one update several months later and all declared the game was just slow to progress, and there was much rejoicing among the hopeful. The next update or two basically broke the game. After that, updates were few and far between and contained what could be termed as empty changes (the last one six changes, one of which was fans added to the stadium..really) or bad ones.
I don't think Bugbear intentionally did a money grab. In all likelihood the main devs, or some of them moved on (be it through other job offers, frustration with management, lost direction, etc). This game now is given updates, but it will likely never be finished.
TL;DR Basically the game's been shelved until Bugbear knows what to do with it, like what happens with many R&D games. The only problem is.. EA is
R&D. Should refunds be given? Maybe, but this is the risk with Early Access. Let the buyer beware, and let the buyer be careful with EA in the future. This game currently has 22% positive rating for good reason, very good indeed.

Great concept and idea. The game is set up very atmospherically, starting with the controls and the graphics. I needed a short time to get used to the controls (not difficult, just different, not intuative), but the the way the controls work, really add to the whole atmosphere of the game.
In itself, the game is many times replayable. Even after 7 hours, everytime I open a door, I fear what is behind it. So I tend to proceed with caution.  The gameplay doesn't tend to change, but neither does it of any AAA title. CoD/BF/CS -> you just shoot your gun, the gameplay never changes. Here, you slowly getting pieces of a puzzle, that will uncover, what the heck is going on in the universe, and why are you all alone. While this happens, the game gets more and more difficult. Your stuff break, so you will have to salvage more parts. You will have to swap vehicle, as your spaceship is starting to get used up. You will have to make careful decision, on what you spend your slavaged parts, and whether you really HAVE TO use an upgrade and risk it to break, or you can survive without it, and you don't have to repair it useing up the few parts you salvaged.
I can only recommend this game. Don't expect a shooter à la "Alien Swarm". This is a tactical/strategy game involving little to no shooting.

Duskers is a game about exploration, with a similar 'gather scrap to survive' theme to FTL, set in a post-apocalyptic decaying universe. The game's uniqueness lies in the way you interact with the derelict vessels you scavenge from - rather than set foot on them yourself, you control a number of drones remotely via keyboard commands, viewing the ships via a top-down schematic. The drones' different abilities are provided by modules that break down over time, meaning you have to react inventively to an ever-changing situation. Obviously, the ships aren't totally deserted, and avoiding the various unpleasant inhabitants means treading a fine line between fear and greed - you'll run out of resources if you play it too safe, but greed will get you killed very quickly.
Duskers is a superbly atmospheric game with a randomly-generated 'campaign' as well as daily and weekly challenges. Although the game will throw surprises at you, it never feels unfair - if things go wrong, it's probably your fault, either through carelessness or greed. If you relish the tension of
and you fancy a roguelike that's a bit different, Duskers is definitely recommended.

If you can look past that, want a Hack'n'Slash, not an ARPG, and are ok with WASD (or better yet with using a controller), it is a solid game. I have never felt OBLIGATED to write a review until today.
After 7 hours in (finished my first World 2 boss), I can say this game is easily one of my favorites.
The early 1900's cartoon aesthetic works so well. Everything is beautifully animated, extremely charming, and fun to look at.
The matching 1900's style music obviously fits very well with the game's art, it's also really catchy and fun to listen to over and over.
The game has really tight controls. Shooting and dashing are very satisfying to do, especially when you pull off some cool dodge maneuver during bosses.
The gameplay is mixed up by these auto-scrollish airplane bosses. I usually hate these types of
levels/fights in games but the way the bosses are designed it adds a good mix of gameplay variety and I'm actually looking forward to more of them.
Albeit I've only played about 3 of them, the platforming levels in this game so far are fantastic. A great mix of shooting enemies and precision platforming make for some very satisfying gameplay.
Bosses are very nicely varied in terms of design and gameplay. Even though you kill them all the same, they all feel unique to play because of how their attacks force you to play completely different each time.
The difficulty of the game is extremely well balanced. I would get to a new boss, get my♥♥♥♥♥BEAT, then in about 10 minutes learn the patterns and pull off the fight. Every death I've had never felt like it was the games fault but my own. Going for an A+ (and eventually S) on levels adds a ton of replay value (hence most of my time being spent in World 1).
I cannot stress enough how amazing this game has been. If you like platformers or shoot-em-ups, PLEASE buy this game. Everything about it is so well done and it's extremely fun and addicting.

If you’ve never encountered this series, Blood Bowl would be best described as fantasy American football. But not the version in which you pick your dream team out of the best players of today, but instead a league made up of the various races from the Warhammer universe. Originally a miniatures board game, Blood Bowl had a few digital iterations and today we have before us the latest one with a ‘2’ added to it’s title. At it’s core, this is a faithful adaptation of the board game. Two teams numbering 11 players fight over ball possession during 16 rounds (8 in each half-time) in an attempt to score by crossing the opponent’s touchdown line with the ball. Unlike the real sport that inspired the game, this nets your team only one point and there are no kicks afterwards. And probably the most important difference – fights are not only allowed, but are encouraged.
While the six-sided dice and random elements might be integral to the game, you’ll still have plenty of ways to skew the odds in your favor and avoid turnovers that force you give up your turn (by dropping the ball or having your player tackled). The basic systems might seem complicated at the start and the game’s manual can only be read on the website. So, to get you started, there’s a campaign in which you lead a human team, Reikland Reavers, through a hilarious story of trials and tribulations of this once-great team and through which you’ll get to learn how the game works. Each match introduces one new mechanic, from basic passing to stadium upgrades. While the campaign is great, it’s tutorial part crawls fairly slowly because in Blood Bowl 2 the matches can sometimes take 20-30 minutes.
Compared to the previous game, Blood Bowl not only looks fantastic, but there are no obvious problems or bugs. The atmosphere during the matches is ecstatic, partly due to the kooky commentating duo of Bob and Jim (an ogre and a vampire) who comment for CabalVision in a typical TV style, but mostly for the excellent art style and high detail of models on the field. It’s absolutely tremendous when your successful moves get replayed in slow motion close-up, while the audience’s cheers drown out the commentators. Blood Bowl 2 is a game that is hard not to recommend, especially if the idea of rugby… erm – American football featuring orcs, dwarves, elves and other Warhammer races sounds like a great pass-time to you, and you don’t mind getting used to a somewhat complex tactical system.
