This game is the bees-knees, the cat-meow, the chickens-ankles!!! Using exclusively the keyboard as a controller, I've never played any game like it. The immersion is flawless to me; I dont feel like I'm playing a game, it feels exactly like I'm operating these drones to do my bidding so I can continue adventuing through space searching for the best ship, the best mods, and the truth behind the plot. The monsters aboard any infested derelict ship force me to play tactically, and thus involves a great deal of strategy (except when you get unlucky RNG). There are only a few different kinds of monsters I've found, but each type uniquely synergizes with one another, so pairing any two types of monsters on one level drastically changes and/or narrows the types of tactics you can execute and enforce. The variety in upgrades, or mods, offer a playstyle unique/exclusive for each individual mod. The scarcity of mods avaiable forces you to adapt with what you have, and evolved based on what you find. I love the RNG because if mixes things up with such subtleness that you'll never play the same level twice, but every level is familiar. The only complaint I have about this game is one specific mob, the swarm, and through that, the broken difficulty curve. The only way to deal with this mob is to avoid confrontation entirely and blowing it out an airlock or interfacing a ships defences against it. These buggers will shred you to pieces the moment they notice a drone, even if it's stealthed. With any other mob, you can generally kite them to where you want them to go with stealth: the swarm is the exception because they're fast, and no matter your greatest effort you'll be hard pressed to escape a room and close the door behind you, leaving certain doom safely behind. You'll be able to hear them somewhat in an adjacent room (all mobs have a unique sound que when moving about a room), and this is the only warning you'll ever have before opening a door or validating their pressence with a motion tracker or sensor. Should you brave a confrontation, your only hope of besting them is to gun them down with a turret, forcing you to activate the turret itsself twice. This leads me to inform the reader about my first playthrough- I first began easily enough, and as I advanced the difficulty increased rather naturally. After my first wipe and reset, I noticed the difficulty never reset, so I started with less to work with through the ever scaling difficulty. It got to a point where when I reset again, I literally crossed my fingers that I'd begin with a stealth module or a turret, and if I got neither I would quite literally wipe if I ever had to face these swarms, which at this point in difficulty was every other level (ship/base/etc), and these two modules are perhaps the best, if only way to deal with the swarms manually. I learned on my own that I could reset all local data, and when starting again I found I was back to the beginning, and I was able to keep pace once again with the difficulty scale, making for a far more fair experience. Basically what I'm saying is, the only problem I find in the game is that if you ever reset, you'll have to play even safer, and have to rely on RNG to get the things you NEED to continue venturing and having successful missions. Let me express this feeling through RPG terms. Lets say you start level 1, grind to 20, and die to a boss. If this RPG played in difficulty the same way, you'd start again, level 20, with the same gear as at level 1, and have to face the same boss in the same level 20 area with worse gear than you had before. Should you miraculously attain this feat, you're still 20 levels behind for the rest of the game unless you pick up an item that gives you those missing 20 levels worth of stats. Does this make sense? If so, is it fair that I feel frustrated that unless I have a perfect game, I'm doomed to get shafted by swarms when I have to reset? This can easily be fixed by just setting a base difficulty for the first system after reset, then every level after that system can start gaining difficulty, instead of confiscating all defences then dropping you in the projects. (Essentially like a training ground to allow you to gear up before taking on the universe, instead of jacking your clothes and deporting you to Greenland.) This complaint itsself is probly the only argument I have to say this game is mean, because it's a miniscule issue and the only issue at hand, therefore no one (in my opinion) has any right to call this game bad. Despite this game playing slower than any game I've ever played, it's tense! I found myself holding my breath on a few occassions, knowing the decision I was to make next left everything I'd achieved on the line to try and find success in exploring this one pivitol room. Does this room have baddies? Motion scans are inconclusive. Can I redirect any potential baddies to another room? Impossible, I'd need remote power. Time to hope and pray its not a swarm, because if it is, not just my gatherer is dead, so is my generator drone and there's likely zero chance I'll be able to tow either of them, let alone grab their modules. If this face-check shows me anything other than success, Im down a generator, gather, and at least one other superior module, which takes away the biggest advantage I have on any given level. Even though the graphics are probly considered sub-standard, I feel like this left my imagination to fill in whatever blanks existed, and this is probly what I love most about this game, and why it can get so tense. I almost poo'd myself by mistaking harmless scrap for one of those mobs that jumps on your face and rips out your spine Predator style. Audio ques have made my heart sink faster than seeing a cop in the rear view. I think League of Legends would kick me to the dog house if it ever found out the relationship I'm growing with Duskers, and I think it's worth it, because to me Duskers is certainly one of the best games I've played since the SNES went out of style. Let that sink in for a second. After hearing about this game in a video on youtube, I threw my money at Steam to give it to me, and to be honest this game is the only reason I use Steam. Duskers is one of those truly original games that are also engaging and fun. The command line is a brilliant interface in that it is a unique gameplay mechanic that works very well to heighten the tension and suspense.
The game is not without its downsides, though. After a while, it does start to feel repetitive. the randomized ship layouts help negate this in part, because sometimes it is quite a puzzle to figure out how to navigate around the various enemies while using the fewest of your scarce resources. Because modifications only take wear when first activated after boarding, the decision to use a particular drone's ability has to be weighed against the cost of the wear on the mod, and the likelihood that it will break. These decisions help to keep the game interesting. Also, the story elements do a lot to keep things fresh. Having a goal in the form of pursuing a story's theory helps a lot.
The story itself has its own problems, though. Read on at your own risk!
Lastly, the game does have a few bugs. Ocassionally, upgrades will disappear or become unequipped. Also, I've experienced some intermittent graphical issues. Fortunately, none of these have been particularly game breaking and, in each case, restarting the game seems to fix things (including the missing upgrades). However, I have read that there is a serious bug that effects Mac users, and can leave the game unplayable.
Ultimately, I would readily recommend this game to anyone who watches the trailer and thinks it looks interesting. It really is. I would not even hesitate to buy the game at full price: I did, and I don't regret it!

Honestly, this is one of the coolest games I've played in a long time.
The whole goal is to move from system to system, salvaging and leeching off as many derelict ships as you can (hint: every single ship is derelict). It's a bit hard to tell from the trailer, but the entire game's actually closer to a hacking style game than anything. While you can pilot drones around manually, you can also type in commands to navigate drones from one room to another, and every single action you do (from gathering stuff to opening doors to interfacing with terminals) has to be typed out. The typing "controls" are actually very simple and straightforward, and they seem to function quite well without any major issues (except some pathfinder issues, but it's not that big of a deal).
This is the perfect game if you're looking to be the last known survivor, in space, without actually ever doing anything yourself

So for the game itself, it's really well done for a first episode. It already makes me wanna play the second episode right now. The graphics are TellTales graphics, if you've played one then you know what it will look like. There are far more QTE's than I expected, but I haven't played Tales from the Borderlands or Minecraft Story Mode so I'm sure it's not the first. That said, the gameplay is basically any other TellTale game, so if you've played one, you've played them all Gameplay wise.
The story, well I don't wanna spoil it, but do not expect it to be like the Arkham Games. This game has choices that do matter for the story.
I would heavily recommend buying this game, but since so many other people seem to be having issues, it would probably be a safe bet to wait for a Patch, however, I will still recommend this game.

Sunless Sea is a game steeped in atmosphere and tension. You are one of a legacy of captains doomed with wanderlust to sail the underground sea, er... zee, in an effort to find your father's bones, or too become rich, or to amass a collection of artifacts. These goals get you started, but the real meat of the game comes with the writing and scenarios you encounter at each and every port.  The underground sea is home to a collection of civilizations carved out of the bones of previous civilizations, where you may encounter talking rats at war with regal guinea pigs, or the tomb colonists of Vederbight who have died but not stopped walking or talking.
The game itself is beautiful and well paced. The tension comes in the cat and mouse way that combat takes form. If you can keep the enemy (ship, crab, thing, etc...) in your sights, and you can keep them illuminated, then you can take aim and fire.  If you turn your lights off, you can effectively avoid an enemy, but at the cost of rising terror.
Terror.  The terror mechanic is interesting. The farther from home waters you go, the farther from the shore you are, you gain terror.  Too much terror and your crew may rebel, or worse.  This introduces a risk/reward factor that keeps you safe if you stay in lighted areas or near the shore, but this will almost always cost you in fuel and supplies.  There is an elegant balance to the resources you have that finds you making hard decisions.  Do I pare down my crew to use fewer supplies on long journeys, allowing me to add more fuel and cargo?
The quasi-randomized map adds to the intrigue.  I say "quasi randomized" because certain landmarks and ports will always be in the same relative areas, but not in the same locations when one captain dies and another takes to the sea (unless you bequeath them your zee-chart, that is).
With it's spectacular writing, beautiful design and elegant mechanics, this is an early contender for my game of the year.
Now, hopefully the soundtrack goes on sale soon.

SO on to the game. Firstly it is an extension of a world and mythology crafted in a browser game called Fallen London. So if any of the lore or the craziness of a London being smuggled a mile beneath the earth intrigues? Play it too.
In Sunless Sea, you are the Captain of a ship in a Lovecraftian unter-Zee, a sunless sea beneath the earth. Through the course of the game you end up meeting the nearly dead, stygian creatures, cannibals (possibly becoming unaccountably peckish yourself), pirates and madness.
As you balance it all, trying to eke out a living, you may eventuall die and pass on to heirs fractions of your wealth and prestige giving everything a rogue-like feel.
Throw in eccentric crew members you recruit, sea monsters to engage in and illicit cargo to trade?
As to the game play itself? You are exploring, as the map randomizes (unless you carry over a Zee chart from a previous career) to master things.
Combat is real time and a balance of trying to evade while keeping your enemy in your sights, leading to graceful figure 8's or not so frantic retreats as a giant living iceberg tries to ram you.
And it all works, from the delicious writing to the wicked sense of humor permeating it all!

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding lemon bars recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

I'd agree with most of the other reviews.  The more interesting aspects of the earlier levels, arresting perps for criminal offences in particular, are abandoned early on leaving 75% of the game as wandering round dark corridors killing legions of undead.  Dredd's Lawgiver is accurately reproduced from the comic strip although there's no role here for the Lawmaster bike.  Equally this is 95% "shoot 'em up".  There's no crime investigation, gathering clues, interrogating witnesses.  There's only the odd puzzle to break up the sort of non stop gun play last seen in "Desperado".  Also being Judge Dredd other than restocking ammo for or replacing your secondary weapon there's no role here for looting and upgrades.

This game is the most unique I have ever played. I bought it in Early Access back in July and find myself still coming back to it and spending HOURS wandering the dark Unterzee... Every trip I make, every route I try, it never feels as though I am simply following a predetermined plotline, but rather constructing my own adventure as I see fit (There are endgame Ambitions, if you wish, but you don't HAVE to follow them). And more than that, I am never simply going to 'zee to sell goods or kill monsters in a monotonous grind. New threads of storyline are constantly streaming over the decks of my ship, setting me out into the world to discover the impossible colors of the Neath, establish a secret spy network in a rival nation's ports, negotiate an exchange between the factions of Hell itself. No voyage is ever boring.
Beyond the stories (of which there are so, SO many), the artwork and atmosphere of Sunless Sea are simply incredible. The first time you cruise past some of the more elaborately detailed islands (I'm looking at you, Frostfound and Kingeater's Castle) you may very well cry. Well, maybe not cry, but you should be impressed. The first time you accidentally zail over that enormous Eye (yes, the one in the trailer), you may very well do something undignified, especially if you happen to be playing in the dark with the music turned up while wearing headphones (not that I did that, of course, but DAMN that was surprising...)
To summarize: This game is hard. HARD. When first starting out, the most basic elements of managing Fuel, Supplies, and Terror will be nearly more than you can handle. But, after you've accidentally drowned, starved, or mutinied a few good Captains to death, these will become easier. Then the challenge becomes leaving the comforting shores of London and zailing East into the great unknown, where large monsters and angry pirates will try very hard to kill you some more. But that's where the fun lies; in exploring the wide, dark Unterzee and discovering the stories therein. You will make hard choices. You will learn strange things. You will discover magnificent locations. If you enjoy dark humor, strange lore, and immersive RPG exploration, this is a game for you.
Lose your mind. Eat your crew. Love this game.

Full disclosure, I backed this game through the original Kickstater and have been immensely impressed with what I received as an end product.
Superhot is a refreshing shot in the arm to First-Person Shooters the likes of which we haven't seen in a while. The central conceit to the game is that time only moves when you do, and that once a weapon has been drained of ammo, you have to toss it away and grab another to defend yourself with. Through these simple mechanics, the game tosses you into a multitude of situations and challenges that all mix it up in increasingly interesting ways. The game almost feels more like a puzzle game than a shooter, with each situation requiring careful planning, quick thinking, and sometimes, pure trial and error. It can be tough, but the game excels at making you feel like a badass when you succeed.
The game's story mode is quite short but is surprisingly compelling, and I won't spoil any of it here as it's worth experiencing cold. However, beating it unlocks the real meat of the game: the challenge and endless modes, which add all sorts of new and interesting ways to play through the game's levels. I'd also be remiss if I didn't mention the game's simplistic but gorgeous art style, though I did find it surprising that such a simplistic game requires a better-than-average computer to run smoothly.
While some are already decrying the game for its price given the brevity of its content, personally I'd weight my response to this game more on the quality of the experience than the quantity, and to that end, Superhot shines. You've truly never played anything like this before, and it's worth experiencing at any price.

This is not the Sacred we've waited for! It has absolutely nothing to do with previous games: no open world, no good story, no RPG elements. Only boring linear slasher, splitted for pretty small areas (ending with bosses).

Duskers is outstanding!
The post-interstellar-apocalypse atmosphere and storyline is very enticing, and the way they blend falling-apart technology between aesthetics and gameplay is very convincing without being frustrating.  The occasional glitch (or recurring crash on macs -- search "rainbow glitch" on the forums for workarounds) can even seem like a natural occurance.
Most importantly, the gameplay is very well balanced, giving the intensity of real challenges and permanent results .  Efficiency and cleverness can get you into a situation where ships seem easy, your fleet and inventory grows, and the storyline rolls along.  Yet a lack of caution or a careless mistake can leave your team of drones decimated and all but destroy your hope to succeed against difficult enemies.  The resulting difficulty keeps things fresh.
In healthy rogue-lite fashion, if you do get defeated, you "Reset" your ship, starting again with less challenging opposition and less equipment, but continuing the story line where you left off.   The result is a challenging and long-lived game, without overwhelmingly frustrating scenarios.

I have tried forcing the game to different resolutions via various means, but to no avail.
After spending some time looking through other reviews and looking for a solution online, I decided to check the Telltale website to see if their support team had any info on the issues.  Lo and behold: Batman - The Telltale Series is literally the only non-legacy game they have listed that DOES NOT HAVE A PC SUPPORT SECTION.  This game was so poorly supported from the outset, that they do ot even have a support section on their own website for the PC platform.  XBox and Playstation? Certainly.
TL:DR
Telltale has released a ludicrously broken game and are not even ready to provide support for it.  Very, very bad look for a company I previously expected great things from.

Before we delve into too many details, I have to say that 2D games have never appealed to me as much as this one has. When I first looked at some of the gameplay, it looked quite bland, as in drained of color and seemed very boring. But I decided to give this game a chance and It did not disappoint.
Duskers is a control-based game that gives you real-time control over all the events occurring on your screen. Although you may only be looking at a monitored-simulation, it truly gives a feel of one being present at the scene as this is happening.
To the objective of the game: As the pilot of a small ship, you are tasked with the job of exploring and unveiling the truth behind what has happened to the other humans aboard ships that are merely drifting in space. Boarding these ships, you may find subtle clues or messages (datalogs) that may shed light to the disappearances or what might have happened. Utilizing drones and a variaty of gadgets they come equipped with (all customizable), you pilot these units aboard frigates, freighters, and numerous other ships alike in order to accumulate necessary resources to keep your own ship from failing while at the same time, uncovering the mystery behind the disapperances of the crew members of these ships.
But here's the catch: You aren't alone.
There are... these... things that are on board those ghost ships with you. And as far as I know, all of them are entirely hostile. They will attack your drones on sight and destroy them. The trick behind figuring out how to navigate around them either stealthily or to eliminate them will be up to the player to discover.
Very well devoloped. I liked this game so far.

Telltale at it again.
Oh boy what do you want me to tell you?
Look. I gotta admit I'm kind of a Batman Fanboy hence me pre-ordering it. I know, I know. We've all sworn an oath to never pre-order anything after <insert game that seriously disappointed you here> but ... come on people do I have to say it?
IT'S BATMAN!
Alright, alright let's cut to the chase.
I was prepared for some garbage I'm not gonna lie. I thought that it might be somewhat enjoyable if you know a tad 'bout Batman and Co.
Let's just say ... I was seriously surprised. It was way more and way better than I ever expected.
Don't get me wrong I know that Telltale knows what they're doing but Dude/Dudette let me tell you ...
It's dark. It's grim. It's Batman.
You're given so much choices ... Choices that Batman and Bruce Wayne have in the comics/series/movies and so on.
If you know Batman than you know that he's always on razors edge and trying to balance between doing everything by the book and ... how Batman would handle it.
So what's this game about?
Right now there's only Episode 1: Realm of Shadows available.
To give you a minor insight what it's about, can't say too much else I'd spoil the story and Telltale games are all about the story, it's about Harvey Dent campaigning for Mayor with the help of Bruce Wayne. Falcone, an allegedly Mob Boss, makes his entrance as well and all of a sudden the legacy of Thomas and Martha Wayne starts to crumble and things take not just one but two or three turns for the worse.
But wait there's more!
You're favorite cat burglar and Cobblepot make an entrance as well.
After a few minutes you can already feel how tense the whole situation and game is and will be in the upcoming episodes.
Things are about to get really interesting.
Now let's talk about all those negative reviews.
All I have to say to those is this:
The game works flawlessly. I've personally not encountered one single problem or bug besides the codex thing (unable to get out of the screen) but that's it.
It looks, feels and plays like you'd expect it from a Batman Telltale game.
What I liked the most are probably the combat segments. I can't remember the last time where I actually pressed so many buttons while playing a Telltale game.
Overall it's a really, really, really good first episode and after playing it you're just drooling all over it in hopes that someone serves you the rest of the episodes on a silver plate.
Even non Batman fans can and certainly will enjoy this episode/game.
Kudos Telltale. You really managed to positively surprise me with this one.
I'll be updating this review with every episode.

Do not purchase the game thinking it plays something like mutant league football.  Also understand that while there are open leagues for matchmaking, Blood Bowl is not balanced for perpetual leagues with many players.  The structure of open online makes it very easy to make "overpowered" teams.  If you do play, your time will be better spent in player-organized leagues where you can learn the game and build up rivalries.

As much as I'd like to love this game (because I love the movies), I just can't. The game falls very short in my opinion for two main reasons. The first is that at times the controls can be frustratingly cumbersome, especially during flight. Sometimes it takes a while to register a turn or boost, but maybe this is just due to timing.
The second is that you're bombarded with advertisements for membership, additional perks and boosts, which I'm really not interested in and probably do little to actually enhance the game itself. I don't mind a bit of advertising; these, however, are in your face, particularly on the loading screens, which I like to contain USEFUL in-game information, such as hints or history.
There's nothing wrong with micro-purchasing in a game. It's down to how well it's presented that counts and, unfortunately, it seems that a lot of the items or areas are unlockable only if you pay, thereby limiting the actual amount of freedom you do get to explore. While you can explore freely to an extent, it's pretty linear in that you must follow the path set out for you and play through before you can really move onto the next.
One good thing about the game is that you can choose between solo and multiplayer, but after awhile it becomes samey and I quickly lost interest. Sad because it has the potential to be a great game.

Sometimes it takes small developer companies - or just one person as in this case - to revive a whole genre. Banished may be related to games like settlers or the anno trilogy, judged by the setting, yet it developes it's own attraction. Unlike these games, the main task in Banished is to survive through the years, starting just with a small population of about 10 people. With every decision comes a new challenge: you build more homes and grow more families? Better care for food and firewood for them to survive. As the population and "your land" becomes bigger the game becomes more complex and you can't allow for many failures. For example, if you need more stone and assign more workers to quarries and withdraw these from you woodcutters or foresters, the next winter will hit hard for sure. Also you cant allow for too less farmers on your fields, because the harvest won't be as rich and the rest of the food on the fields will rot and die out in the winter.
For me this is a clear must buy, if you like games like "The Settlers", "Anno" series or "Civilization". Yet it's no game to turn off your brain; a big population wants to be constantly managed and entertained.

Sunless Sea is a roguelike exploration game that does not hold your hand too much. After the initial tutorial, you are expected to add to what you have been taught and be ready for even more as the game goes on. With an incredible aesthetic that includes a wonderful soundtrack, a fantastically grim art style, and plenty of character in the story, fans of Lovecraft and dark humor may find it compelling. The gameplay has deeper complexities, but on the surface functions simply enough to be understood at a glance. Hotkeys are available and controls are configurable, though the range of actual keys needed is simple enough and will not leave casual players swamped in things to remember. Experienced explorers are rewarded with a map that never stays the same unless you pass your chart down to a successor upon either death or retirement. Retiring offers unique benefits to the next character in which they start with elevated stats, extra money, or extra equipment, potentially a combination of the options if you followed a certain storyline to completion. Making money is not too easy, though with how the economy in the game works, the early gameplay can be tedious, as travel time eats up more time than time spent in ports. However, as you begin to comprehend the mechanics and amass wealth, upgrades don’t make the game very easy, but instead make it possible to survive and go further in the game itself.
Ultimately, I recommend the game if for nothing than the story and music alone. The gameplay is solid, if a bit slow paced, and as you grow the understand the mechanics behind the game itself, it opens up further and further for you to enjoy. It has a learning curve that can be brutal on the impatient but given enough time and patience, the game can immerse you in a world of intrigue and curiosity. As this is the sister game to Fallen London, I recommend checking out Fallen London for those curious about the stories in London that don’t make it into Sunless Sea. For those that also enjoy Fallen London, Sunless Sea is a natural extension of the game. Both games unlock content for one another after a certain point and enables interactions between your Sunless Sea and Fallen London character.
If you're looking for a great steam punk game with some cool action this is the game for you.

Sunless Sea is the most delightful game I’ve played in years. It is full of dark, beautiful, sometimes funny, sometimes disturbing prose. Sailing on the zee, the underground sea where the game takes place, is a dark, beautiful, lonely, and sometimes dangerous experience.
The tone of this game reminds me a bit of the Welcome to Night Vale podcast. The game consists of a library of small stories. Some are filled with terror, some with humor, and many are a mixture of the two.
The stories advance when you are in various ports. It can be a bit hard to keep track of where you’re at in various storylines and it’s not always clear what will happen if you select an action. However, the former seems appropriate for a game base around exploring various storylines instead of one single overarching story. The latter is probably appropriate for a game where terror lurks around every corner.
Expect to die, probably in a terrible way. Your next game will probably go better. There’s more to do than any one zee captain can manage, and a new life will let you explore a different path. Do you want to be a monster hunter? A spy? A smuggler? There are a few different paths you can take.
If you are looking for a game based around trading resources, or where the focus is on strategic zee warfare, or where you don’t have to read a lot, this game probably isn’t for you. This is a game about storytelling and exploration and it is lovely.

Red Orchestra 2 / Rising Storm is a must for anyone who enjoys a WWII FPS that rewards team work. The game has superb map design and makes good use of its realistic damage and ballistics models. The plot and concept of Bioshock are excellent, and for the most part it is very well implemented.
One of the core aspects of the gameplay is being able to choose how and when to upgrade yourself and your abilities/weapons. That idea isn't new in itself, but unlike many other games, the choice isn't an illusion. There are actually many viable ways to fight, depending on your own style and preferences. What makes it particularly interesting is that obtaining the resources to upgrade often involves significant moral choices, and doing the 'right' thing can cost you.
The graphics and level design are good, with many nice touches. Navigation is a little difficult though, and despite often being free to go wherever you want, the environment doesn't always feel very satisfying to explore. The objectives tend to get a little frustrating sometimes too, but that's not uncommon for an FPS.
I won't say much about the actual story, as I don't want to spoil any surprises. It's very interesting and original though, with some fascinating twists, politics, and relationships which unfold in between all the action. The atmosphere is very well conveyed as well, giving a very interesting balance of vibes in different situations.
The ending possibilities are a little disappointing though. There is only one way to get the 'good' ending, and every other path leads to the standard ending. For a game which places so much emphasis on the moral choices on the way through, I would have hoped for some more possibilities.
The great stuff definitely outweighs the bad though, so I can heartily recommend Bioshock to anybody who likes an FPS with a good story.

This game is odd. There are horror games which feel entirely claustrophobic. There are horror games with a direct sense of panic. There are management games with no sense of thrill or adventure. And then there is this game.
Duskers, if you didn't figure out already, is a marriage of Horror and management game elements with a slight hint of extra typing. You're in space, you don't know what's happened and you piece the story together as you go from communications found logged on the ships you board. The story is surprisingly well written for such a gameplay focused experience, and does help to give you a sense of isolation in the rather large map you're spawned into.
The gameplay is the big part here, as there are many different individual pieces that make up the whole experience. Misreading the command log to see if the sensor in r5 became untriggered gives you this sense of sudden realisation mixed with terror. In comparison to another favourite horror game of mine, Alien Isolation, the panic in that game lies in making a break for an exit and crouch walking right into the Alien even after you checked the motion tracker. This is what is so very different about this game. You feel a horrible sense of responsibility (don't we all) over the poor drones you send into harms way, which makes it ever more unfortunate when you try to flush out a leaper and mistakenly leave the door to your generator drone open and simultaneously lose 3 drones because you locked two away behind a door you were sure you could open once the leaper was flushed out. Or when the door next to your only safe room starts being attacked and you have to rush to get all the drones back onto the ship. Surprisingly, the command typing takes nothing from the experience. As someone who takes a lot of time typing, the command system is surprisingly good as I find myself just pressing enter in a blind panic once I finish typing a door close command. There are also so many joys in this game, such as the feeling of commandeering a new ship with 3 upgrade slots or gathering the maximum amount of fuel from a station.
However, a few flaws lie in the gameplay, it's not just full of the outstanding elements of this great game. Once you've collected 10-20 scrap in a single mission, you will realise that it cannot repair the schematic view once you have repaired vital modules, leaving you with a chance of being blind. 20 scrap cannot give you the insurance of all of your drones' health back once you've fixed a couple of ship modules. Whilst this can be seen as a vital element, and I would agree, everything decays at an incredibly fast rate which can make module breaks feel a little bit cheap. This is avoidable somewhat by fiddling around with the options menu, which means it's only a minor flaw.
One other flaw I have with the game is that once you find a way to deal with the leapers, goo, drones and swarms, you tend to become unstoppable in your pillaging of ships for scrap. Another similar flaw is that the enemy types start to get a bit boring after you've been through a few galaxies. Both of these issues could be fixed with more enemy types. For example, an enemy that doesn't move or show up on sensors/motion, and only attacks drones that have their back to it but destroys any drone with less than 200 health points in one hit then becomes inactive for a set amount of time. That's just one example off the top of my head.
Overall, this game is brilliantly done. The atmosphere is surprisingly present despite the retro-digital aesthetic that I enjoy so much. The gameplay whilst a little dull after you've gotten everything is challenging and requires concentrated effort. The fear this game produces is unrivaled purely because it's a different kind of fear. I got this full price, no sale, and feel I got much more than my money's worth. Try it out.

Disclaimer: I did not have any of the issues many people are complaining about at the moment, this is purely based on the story/gameplay itself, not the technical issues that many are currently experiencing.
After just finishing episode one I have to admit this was exactly the type of experience I expected (due to knowing Telltale's format) but also the type of experience I was hoping for. It truly left great first impression to this five episode story. The episode itself lasted me roughly 1 hour and 40 minutes and at not one point was I bored or lacking interest in anyway, every  character that I encountered felt genuine and diverse each unique as their own, all with different views.  I think the tone was set spectularly, and the Bruce's goals were clear throughout. I love the switching inbetween Bruce and Batman (even though we knew it had to happen) I just feel Bruce provides a form of calm before the storm, due to him mainly being the person talking, and then when playing as Batman having impactful fights that really felt like they had some weight behind the punches that were thrown. The fights were structed as fast-paced quick times events, although I pressed a few wrong buttons I do not believe I was punished for it, which leaves me wondering if it was possible for me to fail at these fast QTE's.
Every now and then the animations were slightly lacking in my opinion and also some lip syncing was off but nothing that isn't more than a slight hiccup.
Choice felt a bit lacking story progression wise, but every line of dialogue I could choose I felt would have a different reaction which made choosing said dialogue a lot more intense and interesting to decide. And on that note I believe the voice acting was done well, refering back to what I said about characters being unique, each had their own varied accents/voices that made them standout and was overall well done.
If the series keeps this up I truly think that this maybe one of Telltale's best aslong as they ramp up the story a bit and get some more of our favorite villians within this game.

At this point I think it is pretty obvious that this game is not Sacred nor is it a true follow on to the Sacred series and is just a pathetic little money grab on the part of Deep Silver and Keen Games.
That being said because it carries the name of the Sacred name it is hard to review it as another game....very few “new” games start off with [name of a franchise] 3.
With that in mind, it almost seems like the developers made calculated and deliberate decisions to make the game as cheap, nasty and bad as possible. So bad in fact that it all borders on being malicious.  I can only assume that the developers had a meeting at some point to look at what Sacred 1 and 2 was and then made the decision to take everything that was not so good in 1 and 2 and make it even worse. Of course there where some good things in 1 and 2 as well they had a look and these and decided that the best thing would be to do exactly the opposite.  This is sure to win the hearts of the Sacred fans....oh wait. I guess they rather went out to win the hearts of some new fans.....why then call the game Sacred 3, why not something else, why go through the tedium of some small references to the previous games and it world when you could have done your own thing. Oh but it slipped my mind, this in not intended to be a good game the intention of this was to cost the developers as little as possible so they could put out a piece of software shaped faeces that they could sell for a quick buck.
Speaking of the quick buck, as it it a pretty substantial buck, what does this actually buy you? You get a bunch ruler like linear levels, sewn together in a way that makes zero sense, half decent graphics, voice acting that would have been better if they were done by a ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ gorilla with a railroad spike through its head. The only thing that seems half fair considering the price it the download size of the game....it.....is...huge. This is probably the only thing that the developers Keen games achieved, I wouldn't have though that it would be possible for such a large download to translate to so little content, but they managed it. Just so the noteworthiness of this is not missed, games the size of single a CD translated to hundreds of hours of playtime, where they managed to get 4 DVD's worth of game to only last 10 hours, nice.... Speaking about the size, at the end of the credits it actually gives credit to some or other compression algorithm.....everyone should be well warned never use this as it is clearly beyond useless.
It also struck me from the credit that there were probably 10 times more QA's involved with the game than anything else. They, as along with everyone else, were clearly not doing their jobs.
In conclusion what you get with Sacred 3 is a shameless, pathetic money-grab turd dressed up in a Sacred frock. Done by a bunch of useless developers that should probably look for a different line of work. Hopefully the curse of Sacred will find them as well. (Curse of sacred: every development studio that has worked on a Sacred game has gone bust)

I want to like this game. The concept and interface are both brilliant. The core gameplay is compelling and tense, but I cannot recommend this game because of how punitive it is.
In Duskers there is no such thing as a small risk: whenever you enter a potentially risky room you could find no hostiles, a hostile you can quickly close the door on and back out, or swarmers: hostiles that will destroy your drone within 3 seconds and then hover over the body making it unrecoverable.
To minimally build back from such a distaster requires a drone husk (you find these maybe every 5 ships), and 10 scrap (fully exploring your average ship nets you ~5 scrap), but all of your scrap goes to maintenance because your stuff is breaking at a rate roughly equal to how much scrap you get from fully exploring a ship.
This game isn't a battle of attrition, its a death lottery. No matter high how you are flying at any moment you are one dice roll away from losing your capacity either gain resources or to explore carefully, cosigning you to a slow withering dealth with no capacity for recovery.

I'd have to recommend this game mainly because it's free. Yes, there are microtransactions in the game that are a little steep on their prices but you don't have to spend money on this game to get the most out of it. You can play the game and earn in game currency to buy what the microtransactions are selling, the only thing you can't buy with ingame currency is more bag space, but when you really thing about it, you really don't need a lot of space to store stuff, even for someone like me with 16 level 50's.
I'll admit the game needs a lot of balancing on gear and characters though. Because if you have a good monk with all the aura boosts, a lavamancer with a lot of tower health, and a huntress with toxic shock and tower damager, you can basically solo any map. On top of that, they made it unbelievably easy to get higher Ipwr gear with their campaign update. Because in the past you would have to actually play and grind levels to get to level 50 and then grind even more to get your ipwr up to move to the next dificulty. While now, you play through the campaign and you're already level 50 by the end with 240ish ipwr gear (805 is max) and all you have to do is join an incursion ran by a guy like me who keeps the ipwr level at 0 for people to join and BOOM you're 700 ipwr already. Which is nice, but you still can't actually do anything on your own until you get the proper gear with the right stats, which still takes a lot of grinding specific levels to do.
All in all though, this game has clearly given me many hours of entertainment and I keep coming back to it when I get bored with other games. It's also just a really interesting twist on a way to doing a tower defence styled game and I personally love it.
Hope you all will be willing to give this game a chance as well.

Sunless Sea is a roguelike exploration game that does not hold your hand too much. After the initial tutorial, you are expected to add to what you have been taught and be ready for even more as the game goes on. With an incredible aesthetic that includes a wonderful soundtrack, a fantastically grim art style, and plenty of character in the story, fans of Lovecraft and dark humor may find it compelling. The gameplay has deeper complexities, but on the surface functions simply enough to be understood at a glance. Hotkeys are available and controls are configurable, though the range of actual keys needed is simple enough and will not leave casual players swamped in things to remember. Experienced explorers are rewarded with a map that never stays the same unless you pass your chart down to a successor upon either death or retirement. Retiring offers unique benefits to the next character in which they start with elevated stats, extra money, or extra equipment, potentially a combination of the options if you followed a certain storyline to completion. Making money is not too easy, though with how the economy in the game works, the early gameplay can be tedious, as travel time eats up more time than time spent in ports. However, as you begin to comprehend the mechanics and amass wealth, upgrades don’t make the game very easy, but instead make it possible to survive and go further in the game itself.
Ultimately, I recommend the game if for nothing than the story and music alone. The gameplay is solid, if a bit slow paced, and as you grow the understand the mechanics behind the game itself, it opens up further and further for you to enjoy. It has a learning curve that can be brutal on the impatient but given enough time and patience, the game can immerse you in a world of intrigue and curiosity. As this is the sister game to Fallen London, I recommend checking out Fallen London for those curious about the stories in London that don’t make it into Sunless Sea. For those that also enjoy Fallen London, Sunless Sea is a natural extension of the game. Both games unlock content for one another after a certain point and enables interactions between your Sunless Sea and Fallen London character.

Sunless Sea is the most delightful game I’ve played in years. It is full of dark, beautiful, sometimes funny, sometimes disturbing prose. Sailing on the zee, the underground sea where the game takes place, is a dark, beautiful, lonely, and sometimes dangerous experience.
The tone of this game reminds me a bit of the Welcome to Night Vale podcast. The game consists of a library of small stories. Some are filled with terror, some with humor, and many are a mixture of the two.
The stories advance when you are in various ports. It can be a bit hard to keep track of where you’re at in various storylines and it’s not always clear what will happen if you select an action. However, the former seems appropriate for a game base around exploring various storylines instead of one single overarching story. The latter is probably appropriate for a game where terror lurks around every corner.
Expect to die, probably in a terrible way. Your next game will probably go better. There’s more to do than any one zee captain can manage, and a new life will let you explore a different path. Do you want to be a monster hunter? A spy? A smuggler? There are a few different paths you can take.
If you are looking for a game based around trading resources, or where the focus is on strategic zee warfare, or where you don’t have to read a lot, this game probably isn’t for you. This is a game about storytelling and exploration and it is lovely.

Outlast is one of the very few horror games I've ever played, and damn, can it scare the ♥♥♥♥ out of me sometimes. Outlast is an original plot based around a reporter who goes into an insane asylum. Once you're in, you can't get out. Your only source (other than overhead lights) of light is your camcorder- which uses batteries for night vision. The catch is that your have a battery meter that runs out fairly quick. Outlast really makes you feel alone in such a way that you are scared for your life when any of those... things chases you. Even though they're people, you're scared ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ from them because they not only track you down, but they won't hesitate to kill you. Their AI is VERY keen and if you play on a higher difficulty, you're sure to be found if you're hiding. Outlast is such a great game, apart from the horror, it's actually really fun to play. Unlike other horror games, jumpscares are at a minimum. You're not going to turn around and magically get jumpscared- no, these jumpscares are often pretty obvious but still scare the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of you (i.e. In the early part of the game, there is one of those things in a wheelchair and it's just creepily twitching. The first time you pass next to it, it doesn't do anything, but the next time you pass it, it comes out of it's chair and tries to strangle you).
For a scary game, this does its job SO well. The atmosphere is so creepy and makes you feel empty and like you're trying for your life to just stay alive. Enemies make you almost scream in fear when they start chasing or notice you, and when they pick you out of a locker or where you were hiding, your heart just drops and you have to scramble away from them just to find a hiding spot. The game was so very well made and it was obvious that the developers knew how a scary game should work.
If you're up for a good scare and a VERY WELL made game, definitely check this one out. It's on sale CONSTANTLY, so you can pick it up very cheaply. 10/10

Judge Dredd vs Death is a first person shooter that gives me a huge nostalgic buzz when playing, this game was originally on the Sony Playstation 2 and I used to play this when I was a kid and had a blast!
The PC version of this game really does show how dated this game actually is however with the poor graphical quality (Not even that good for the time it was made) it still looks passable and the unique Dredd dystopian aesthetic with the character assets and environments is somewhat pleasing still.
I did encounter a few problems with this port; the resolutions are really funky and do not scale well with any display and gives weird resolutions like 2047 x 1894 which was odd, you also get the occasional flickering but I guess this is expected to come with a dated game. You do get AA options and AF options to increase the fidelty to polish away the jaggys.
Is the game fun? YES, if you enjoy dumb shooters with quirky mechanics and hilarious at times early day ragdoll physics this game is for you, the npc's give off hilarious dialogue as you arrest them for stupid things such as 'Possession of a goldfish without a license'. There is also co op mode (Not sure about online functionality however split screen works.), and an arcade mode (Not sure about online functionality also) as well as a challenge mode which allows you to unlock cool cheat codes for the main story. As of the time of this review this game is on sale for £1.24 and I think it's pretty fun for an old solid fps with 3-4 hours (Not counting other modes) of classic gameplay. Just don't go into this expecting a triple A masterpiece, it's far from it.
Edit: Split Screen apparently is non existant. Arcade mode is the challenge mode, and I think 'Battle' is the arcade mode with bots or multiplayer.

A very challenging, but enthralling game. There is a lot of depth to the stories, and plenty of choices to be made. Many will lead to bad, but amusing results. An example from my most recent death:
I wandered too far away from friendly ports, and ran out of fuel and supplies. Bobbing in the dark my crew grew hungry, ate the vermin on board, and then turned to cannibalism. Finally an angry glowing bob wandered nearby, and I tried to hunt it in the slim chance I could get supplies from its corpse. However, once it was badly wounded it just floated a good distance away, taunting me. Finally, with half my crew having been turned into supper, I abandoned ship for the lifeboats.
Before this would be the end for my captain, but miraculously I survive and make it to port! I lost all my crew and cargo, but I still have my officers, and a small ship with just enough supplies to make it back to Fallen London. Hoping to turn my fortune around I set off, and soon I reach the relative safety of home waters. Just a little bit more until I'm safe, but a giant crab emerges from the shadows and starts to approach.
My tiny little ship is about as sturdy as tinfoil, and so as the crab charges I put the engines at full speed to just dodge out of the way. The game has warned me that this might cause my engine to explode, but I've been fortunate thus far and so I figure it's a safe bet. Murphy loves moments like this...
My engines explode, but I manage to put out the flames quickly and only lose one crew member. That one crew member being my captain. So another unfortunate soul never returns home, and is quickly replaced by my next captain.

This game is an absolute masterpiece.
First and foremost of course, the art and design. On this point, the game is flawless. Never before have I seen such an exquisite execution of artistic aesthetic: the animation is lush, detailed, wacky, fun, bouncy and exactly what you'd expect; the music is bubbly and jive-worthy; the sound effects are spot on, and the overall sound design is mastered in a way that makes the game even more immersive (for example, the sounds overpowering the music and making it quieter, which is exactly how the sounds of media from the 30's would sound). One of the lead developers said that their goal when making this game was to "make a game that
like it was made in the 1930's". I feel like they have perfectly achieved that goal.
But none of this would matter if the game wasn't fun, and it certainly is. There are enough weapon and item customisation to stop it from getting boring, every boss has unique mechanics, and because of the excruciating difficulty you are forced to learn them by rote. I can see how that might put some off, but personally I love the challenge and I'm more than happy to play each boss hundreds of times if it means I get to stretch the game out for longer. It's not a long game: I've played just under 5 hours and I'm already ~30% of the way through. But I can scarce blame the developers for that, because of the unbelievably huge amount of work that went into this game.
And that's something that is clear everywhere you look in this game. In every frame of animation, in every note of the soundtrack, you can just tell this game was made with love and care and dedication, something somewhat rare in the videogames industry these days. These people poured 3 years of their lives into this game, and it shows in depth and breadth and height.
Cuphead is an exhibition of artistic mastery and unflinching joy. For £15 (or your regional equivalent), that's far more than worth it

What can I say about this game. Well for starters, this is a game where the entire thing looks like its from an old DOS operating system. The style of this game is what drew me to it, because I love retro style games, and this is one of the first that looks like its from an early dos computer, where there is no advanced graphical content (well not much graphical content at least). Your job is to sit in front of a computer, controlling drones with dos command prompt style commands to move the drones, use upgrades, interface with computers, etc, to find salvage, more drones, and most of all, fuel. I also did an hour long live stream of Duskers that you can see the VoD of here:
Duskers is what you get when you combine the methodical, brutal progression of FTL with the nuances and unit management of a top-down tactics game with basically, a DOS UI. And it's AWESOME!
You don't know who you are or what's happened in the universe you're in, you just know that you have control over various drones with different capabilities and you must move from derelict ship to derelict ship, salvaging what you can, avoiding or cleverly overcoming the unknown but deadly adversaries you'll find and trying to make your way forward and find out just what happened.
Duskers doesn't hold your hand but also conveys a lot of knowledge to you organically over time. What can be called the tutorial passes super quick and you'll continue to learn bits about managing your drones in each new level. Everything is done with the keyboard and largely on a command line, which has a limited command set and an intuitive autocomplete function that makes it easy to learn and a very efficient way of directing your units. You drones can be damaged or destroyed but can be repairs, as can other broken down drones you'll find along the way. Each has a set of equipment that bestows different abilities and you'll need to mix and match to get the most out of every salvage operation.
Like FTL, this is a rogue-like. You can limp along as far as you can get but when you're dead, you're dead and the only thing you carry forward to your next playthrough is your increased knowledge. The similarities and inspirations of FTL in Duskers are obvious but it's also a very different experience and stands out well in its own right.

As if XCOM, FTL, and DOS BOX had an orgie and the result was this exact situation.
PROS
Amazing original design - The basic game play loop is clear spaceships and scrounge for resources by using your drones all the while evading and destroying enemies, expand the capabilities of and maintain your crumbling space ship with your limited (and I mean LIMITED) resources, make strategic decisions about where to go next based on objectives and fuel and solve the mystery of what happened to your universe by uncovering various data logs and completing special objectives. If you haven’t tried it I would HILGHLY RECOMMEND this game if you are into indi rouge likes. At least check out an LP of it, if you don’t think its worth the asking price.
PROS
Tense game play - You will have to use all of your senses and concentration to not die. Isolate threats, blow enemies out of air locks, stealth or shoot your way through randomly generated space craft to grab fuel and scrap. Perma death is a very real where just one little mistake can lead to complete disaster.
Cool Meta Game – Upgrade repair and maintain your ship, its equipment and your precious drones between missions. This area of the game is really cool, and the decisions you make here will determine your chance for success in the tactical view. Explore the universe and try to unravel the mystery of why you’re the only one left in it. Your♥♥♥♥♥♥is going to break, a lot, so be careful in what you repair and when. There is a ton of depth in the strategic screen; it really reminds me of xcom. Prepare carefully and you will have success. That is until you leave a door open and inadvertently let aliens destroy your drones because you weren’t’ paying attention!
Slick controls- You have the ability to script bot behavior using dos like commands or control them directly with arrow keys. Instead of clicking buttons to activate abilities you have to type something like : Navigate 1 R2; gather all 1. It really helps with the immersion and feeling generally that you are alone on this spaceship sitting at your console using your robots to scour for resources. The way you control them is both intuitive and super cool!  When you try to use your mouse the game gives you an unsatisfying beep, and nothing happens. This game is nearly completely keyboard controlled, and it really is very cool and different!
Critical thinking skills required - Each level is basically a logic puzzle as you clear enemies and space ships. You have to take calculated risks and use your drones ever changing abilities to clear rooms. The game really forces you to pay attention to every detail on every move in both the tactical and strategic screens. Each move has both risk and reward. A successful run requires you to calculate both accurately.
CONS
There is only one real con to the game, and that is that the objectives to actually beat the game are not very well laid out. If your going in blind and you don’t read the wiki it is tough to figure out how to go about solving the games plot. You will get data logs telling you to do certain tasks. Like go to a specific type of craft and scan all the rooms. There isn't a real good way to track what needs to be done. This con doesn't detract from the fun of the game, as you are mainly trying to figure out how to just survive, let alone completing the objectives. It would be nice if this was fleshed out a little more.
SAVING
I don't know if this is just me but I noticed that I was unable to save from the tactical view.  You can’t really save state, but if you exit the game it will save your current progress. However if you save in the tactical view it will not save and boot you back out to the ship screen. This could be fixed in later updates hopefully. Just save AFTER a mission, and you will be ok!

First of all: this game in terms of gameplay, it has absolutely nothing to do with the first two Sacred. NOTHING.
This important premise goes done, because it can help you a lot to not judge the game negatively from the begin, without any reason particularly founded.
I wanted to give it a chance, after having read the users assaults in the forums, a hatred which, however, was almost always motivated only by the fact that "this isn't Sacred".
Said that, I like the game. From begin I have found friends to play co-op, and also in single objectives to achieve allow you to play for many hours.
In co-op is great fun, the locations of the missions are very varied and graphically detailed, a nice isometric game that sometimes offers beautiful panoramic views.
The interactivity with the map is quite varied, you can break any small object, even if it has no utility except for the energy or health orbs.
Each weapon has its own power and skill tree to upgrade, although the RPG elements are few.
The replay value is very good, after the "normal" level there are two levels of high difficulty, and the map of the world starts from the beginning, even if you can go in all the main missions.
Sacred 3 can give you many hours of carefree fun.
The online system works well, and play in co-op (especially 4) is really fun, and it is this that matters.
If you can disinterest that has nothing to do with the previous chapters, and you can catalog it in a completely different genre, then you can definitely like Sacred 3.
However, if you expect a game similar to Sacred 1 or 2, I do not recommend it, because you will be disappointed.

A quick list of pros for those that don't want to read too much:
Fantastic and appropriate music.
Amazing horror atmosphere.
Very challenging.
Replayability.
Great risk vs reward system.
Many storylines and twists.
Excellent moral choice system.
Very tense gameplay.
A breakdown of what the game is: Story and the Zee
The story: The meat of the game lies here. To win, you need to advance within the story, a text-heavy adventure where you have five stats (iron, veils, mirrors, pages, and hearts) that dictate your chance of success during story events. There is a main objective based on your choices during character creation, but there is a HUGE story progression. And I mean HUGE. Certain events will trigger future events which will close off certain story branches and open others while different characters, cargo, skill levels, etc will open up or close off story branches. There's lots of room for replay here as long as you don't decide to google answers for optimized playthrough.
The story itself reminds me much of Lovecraftian horror. I've encountered quite a few events that read just like Lovecraft fiction, building up suspense followed by something quite strange (usually something monstrous). Like a proper horror (and especially so in Lovecraft), you're often left without a full explanation, allowing your brain to struggle to fill in gaps.
There's a lot of moral choice here, too. Due to how hard it can be for an inexperienced player to make profit, these choices oft-times fall in the category of sacrificing something valuable for money, while at the same time, ensuring you feel a bit of remorse for certain questionable choices. The game does an excellent job of ensuring that even the most amoral players will still feel the sting of immoral choices and yet deliver proper incentive for taking the moral high ground.
The Zee: The Unterzee (or the undersea), to be precise. Sailing dark waters has never been more terrifying. Your money and your hold space make certain that you are afraid to wander too far from home. And the game mechanics make certain you need to wander too far from home to succeed. There's a constant feeling of anxiety and dread. Do I have enough fuel? Do I have enough supplies? If I take on this cargo, will I have enough fuel and supplies to make it home? Is my crew so terrified that I need to worry about mutiny?
Your major aspects when out to zee are your fuel, supplies, and terror. Running with your lights on helps reduce the increase of terror, but eats up fuel. You can go full power to sail faster should your terror be running high or supplies running low, but there's a chance you might damage your ship or lose crew members. Many random events happen out at zee to influence these factors. And as your terror rises, these events often become more menacing. Supplies keep your crew fed, but are also useful for trading in many places.
I've spent many trips barely limping back to London intact and the experience has been amazing. Unlike many games that use proper risk vs reward systems, Sunless Sea ups the ante. Not only do you have to take risks, but you must learn how to plan those risks. This, of course, means you will die quite a bit during the learning phase, but you will get a few captains that you really learn a lot with. Then they die.
There's also the matter of the map. Technically, it's procedurally generated. The western shore is always the same, ensuring you have at least the base ability to get a foothold started in the game. Many places are generated in certain relative areas, as well. Other than that, the placement of the locations throughout the sea is randomized, which will keep the fog of war interesting in future playthroughs as well as ensuring you won't be able to memorize the map for the best possible routes.
Finally, there's combat. Combat involves your ship and a rather small collection of mobs - either sea monsters (giant angler crabs, giant morays, bat swarms, etc) or enemy ships (usually various pirate ships). The combat isn't really exciting, but it does throw a hazard into the game which you can sometimes use to your advantage. Mainly, it serves as an extra tension-driver that you will want to avoid - especially early on. With resources often stretched thin, I found myself making some hard decisions about whether to engage an enemy or avoid an enemy. In any case, it works well with the game design.
I highly recommend this game if you don't mind text heavy games. There's enough non-text exploration and adventuring involved to make the large amount of text interesting. In fact, I often find that after a harrowing sojourn, I welcome plenty of text to read while I collect myself.

Coming back to this game after some time I realise what a class act is really going on here. For me at least, the critical approach a gamer has to take to this game is to make sure they "get" the game play mechanics. In many ways its a stealth game in disguise. The little red "heat" bar, is the "spotted" bar from games like Far Cry (in fact THIS is the game that Far Cry 3 and 4 should have been). Once the player realises that they have to use Guerilla tactics: hit hard and fast and then dissappear until you are at least back in the orange part of the bar; everything else follows through. In fact many of the foibles of the control mechanics have been tuned for this kind of game play. It was not until I got the mechanics that Rico would suddenly automatically dive underwater (another place to hide). The controls seems to be THAT finely tuned. Another thing here seems to be rarely mentioned. The technical innovations that make the open world engine possible. For starters how fast is the loading time of this engine ?!? In other game I'm having to spend a long time looking at a loading bar, but FC2 ... seconds ... how ? Other games promise "open world" gaming. Far cry 1 got it. Far Cry 2 did in their own unique way (but quite different from JC2). FC3 and 4 have an "island" and then mountainous terrain but compared to this, the technical innovations look almost ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥. Compare the vegetation and distance views to FC2 and 3 and they are a mess of bad distance LOD models, pasted on backgrounds (the islands in the distance in FC3) and other GLARING visual bugs and bugs in design. But JC2 is a *REAL* tour de force of this kind of thing. Looking at the islands and travelling around in a jet, for example, is truly breathtaking. Well recommended if the player can take the time to get into the game play mechanics.

You can also drive vehicles with mounted weapons. The Razorback being my favourite with an autoloaded battlecannon and twin machine guns. A few types of helicopters and figther jets are availible. Sadly, the military will not send other jets to hunt you down if you steal one. :(
I had much fun but also raged a lot in the game. I recommend it based on solid gameplay with a few poor controlls here and there. Much fun. ^_^

Play this game only if you hate fun.
This game has a handful of mechanics that really detract from the fun. First, your character dies when he touches water. What is this, 1998? This would not be so annoying, except for the fact that it piggy-backs off of another problem with this game: not solving puzzles correctly results in you dying, and therefore reloading a checkpoint. Tons of these puzzles involve water or some stupid insta-kill mechanic. However, neither of these two mechanics would annoy me nearly as much if it weren't for a third mechanic: it is almost impossible to solve a puzzle without failing it first. So, there are annoying insta-kill mechanics to puzzles that you are set up to fail. This makes the game artificially hard. None of the puzzles are difficult, except for the fact that you get stuck dying at one part over and over just to realize to had to backtrack (yes, another annoying mechanic) a few screens and pick up some object you thought was part of the background to solve a puzzle.
What this game does have going for it are a unique art style and mood. However, after a few minutes of the "soundtrack" (read: ambient synthesizer nonsense), you feel like you OD'd on benzo's and are unsure if the blurriness of the game is the art style or your brain dissolving in your skull.
This game is apparently a great example of minimalist narrative, but I can't get past the gimmicks and archaic game mechanics to care.

I have been wanting to give my take on this game for a while. I suggest playing the game before you read this, or any reviews for that matter.
I, like many others, went into this 'game' with Davey the narrator walking me through, introducing me to a man named Coda's art. By the title, I assumed this was going to teach me how to begin making games. It started out really confusing, and almost boring, as Coda's first set of games were just him goofing around with the development, not making finished products on purpose. Ok, i've seen many unfinished games before so nothing special. Davey starts giving his interpretation on these games, how raw they seemed, and in my personal opinion, I wasn't following the hype he was putting out. It sort of reminded me of those English classes that questioned any and every part of a story, as if every word spewed is some shakespearean masterpiece that we just don't understand yet. When Davey expressed his worry with Coda's prison games, it put Coda in a light that made him seemed troubled, and made me feel sorry for him. Of course, hearing it from a supposedly 'reliable' narrator with no reason to lie, would give me no other word to believe, as the viewer is under the impression that these two people know each other quite well by now. At this point, i'm subconsciously applauding Davey for his unsolicited concern with a friend. Between the door puzzle, lamposts, and seemingly eerie atmosphere, I started coming up with my own idea of who Coda was through his games, similar to what Davey did.
Here's where it gets sketchy for me: Davey shows us an infinitely looping cleaning game by Coda. He says "This is the first game he actually called me up to show me." At the beginning of the game, when Davey is telling us how he and Coda met and became 'friends'. He admits he was being a little pushy and over zealous with getting to know this guy. This is implying that every game shown to Davey was solicited, giving no reason for them to have to be playable or coherent in any way, if he was never planning on releasing them. It leads me to believe that Davey is being a little over dramatic with his diagnosis of Coda. It makes me wonder if they are actually friends, or is Davey just some guy that Coda met and asks him to see his games?
Things get a little more intense as his games get more personal and self destructive. Even though by the end of the game we are exposed to the fact that Davey has some problems of his own (his constant need to be the hero of someone else to compensate for his own shortcomings), we can't ignore that some of Coda's games did touch some topics that made you question his emotional health.
Whether this game was a true story, or elaborately staged, it was phenomenal and thought provoking. I'd recommend to anyone that doesn't mind interactive stories with not much physical involvement on your part.

The game I feel will take everything from you, perhaps even your sanity. While leaving you captivated by its visuals with one of the sorest butts you may of ever experienced.

You left a door carelessly open. A "thing" sneaks in, mauls your generator drone, rushes into your docking shuttle, and wrecks your tow drone. A warning rings out that an asteroid is about to collide with the derelict. You need to get rid of the thing, salvage what you can from your generator drone, and escape the ship. You enter a series of commands: maneuvering your drone to a strategic spot; dropping an explosive trap; retreating; and opening a series of doors to lure the thing to the bomb. Seconds tick by. Your motion sensor detects the thing next to the trap, and you blow it up. You frantically type commands to head back to the docking shuttle when alarms ring out: the asteroid has hit the derelict, right next to where your last surviving drone is, and it gets sucked into the vacuum of space. You, the drone operator, alone on his ship, hundreds of kilometers away from the disaster, wails in despair. You order the shuttle back to your ship. Maybe you can salvage components from the destroyed drone in it. Maybe you can jury rig the other, broken drone that has been sitting in your cargo hold for weeks, and try to find another drone on another derelict to give you a chance at survival. You have a remote power upgrade on your ship; this can substitute to your lost generator drone. There is still hope. Everyone else in the galaxy is dead, but there is still hope. You repeat the words to yourself, aloud, unable to believe them. In space, no one can hear you weep.

I also love the visuals. From the images it looks 2D, and I admit the gameplay is just 2D but the visuals are actually 3D with an overhead view. As you move around the perspective changes slightly, and you can see its actually 3d models and enviornments. And here, noise and post-affects are used as part of the gameplay visuals. They aren't just cosmetic like in all other titles. As the game emulates you viewing your environment through a sort of radar system.
As a programmer I'm not scared away by the command line. And in fact I enjoy it in this game. You can control the robots yourself. But having that option to line up commands for them, lets you do more than one thing at once. Which is a real boon in a game like this.
I highly suggest the Duskers. But I have to admit, there is a good chance you won't get very far in each playthrough. So I stress buying it turn a sale. Half the retail price, won't have you cursing bricks when you keep dying. The retail price will.

This is surely one of the strangest "games" that I've ever played and it's hard to label it with a score or anything. If I had to describe it, it could summarized as a chronicling of a real life, ruined friendship between two video game developers. The game is played running through one developer's various interactive levels made in 2009 to 2011, but narrated by the other developer in 2015 as he used to...uhh...experience them?
I have to say this is really emotional. Like weirdly personal stuff. A deeply intimate tour of depression, antisocial tendencies, self-loathing for one man, and the feelings of abandonment and horrible guilt for the other. I guess I'm recommend it lol but it probably isn't for everyone. Purely from a value standpoint, it's not bad asking for $10 for about 90 minutes of "gameplay" that you would otherwise never encounter in a video game, ever. Very unique. It's definitely asks the player to remain open minded about the medium itself and to explore an otherwise aimless game for the opportunity to dive deeply into two person's behaviors and thoughts for the sake of experiencing something.
