I've been playing Blood Bowl for years and have done almost everything there is to do. I've become an admin of a popular league and have spent hours trying different ways to build teams. This is my view of Blood Bowl 2 from a veteran of the game.
Blood Bowl 2 is Cyanide's recreation of the original Blood Bowl games under a new engine. The graphics and UI are great and this new adaption makes it much easier for new players to get into the game. The tutorial does an alright job of explaining the game and mechanics, even if it could be improved and may be a little too slow.
People complain about the lack of variation in cheerleaders and crowd but really how much do you care about that? They complain because it's not in the game and when it is they won't give it a second thought. The thing that matters most about Blood Bowl is the gameplay. After a shaky start with some skills not being optional or not being in the game Cyanide has done a good job with listening to the community and fixing the problems (hard to believe I know). Some people have noticed some bugs but I personally have had no problems.
While there is a notable lack of a good single player as the campaign is largely a long tutorial, Blood Bowl was meant for multiplayer anyways. In NAF (COL) there is a wide variety of skill levels and tv so it's very good for practice, however the best way to play BB is in a league setting and that's where most of my experience will come from. Find a good group of people and have some set match times and you will have a blast with this game.
The biggest downside of BB2 right now is the lower number of teams and I hope Cyanide picks up the pace with releasing them but that doesn't detract from the overall gameplay too much.
If you don't care about the graphics or ui and just want a wide variety of teams, then by all means go play BB1. However if you want a more pleasing experience then buy BB2 as it has an insane amount of potential once more teams are released and giving your support will only make it better.

If I went by the reviews I'd not have gotten this game nor wasted any time playing it.  I got it on a Steam sale and it is worth full price.
Sure there are flaws, acknowledged.    One of the levels stopped giving me hints and I got stuck.  Exiting the game and reloading (not reinstalling) it brought back that levels hints so I could proceed. BTW that particular map was a little different that it required some thought to figure out how to defeat the judge.
But the game is FUN, not frustrating and I kept going even after sometimes dying a lot.
THIS not the average shooter where the whole world is a free fire zone;  where any sighted  sprite or actor, is likely hostile, and you shoot it.
In DREDD, indiscriminate killing  has bad consequences.  There are citizens that may appear suddenly in your face and , after years of computerized  "shooter training;" instinct is full-auto to THEIR face.  OOPs, reload save.  Even while blasting identified bad guys, one has to be careful of citizens, allied judges or the surrendered nearby.
--some actors are your allied judges.
--some actors are criminal scum but can be disarmed / arrested (for me more satisfying than head splats)
--the arrested /surrendered criminal scum are helpless and you have the moral obligation to avoid having them killed by errant gunfire; most likely coming from your own barrels.
--some actors are citizens and you do not want to see them harmed, and in many cases you are trying to rescue them.
--you can ambush criminal scum to gain a tactical advantage, but it counts against you.
--you can challenge criminal scum and lose tactical advantage, though some will surrender; giving you the opportunity for that oh so satisfying arrest lingo ie "YOU JUST EARNED YOURSELF xxxxx Time IN THE CUBES."
And there is a level where you VISIT these cubes.   Jump off a catwalk on a container then into the iso cube, if curious.  A bunk, a toilet and print across the wall, CRIME DOES NOT PAY.
Unlike Fallout 3, your pockets are not deep.  You can only have two weapons which requires some decisions.   Firefights may use up your ammo of your preferred Judge Gun; and that's another thing, setting  criminal scum on fire with the incendiary round is inadvisable.  You overreaching cop, you. There are plenty of vampires and zombies to try it out on.   Your Judge Gun has all kinds of ammo types which replace gun variety in other games.  There is even some kind of grenade (I have yet to use).
Some levels you can go through Judge Gun ammo quick and there are other found weapons to try.  Once ammo is used up, these found weapons can get you through the level. Depending, although, on how things go, you may be trading them out for different found guns.  The grenade launcher may not be the best choice as blowback bites.   To save ammo, some adversaries can be tackled in melee mode with little risk.  Yes, health can run quite low and it may  require several save reloads to get through a level.
The voice acting is hilarious, reminding me of Duke Nukem 3d, arresting a perp yields "tough cop" howlers such as  "throwing away the key," or "there's an iso cube with your name on it." or "you're taking the big ride;"  to name a few.  Tone quite close to the 2012  movie Dredd. Let's just forget about that Stallone attempt.  I think even Stallone wants to forget.
The bizarre fashion world of Judge Dredd  can take some getting used to. For example, there are  numerous fatties with bellywheels to help prop their enormous bulk.   Apparently though, they are not an aberration as one might expect to see in a singularly unique character;  but a conscious citizen  lifestyle.  Wikipedia explained them  as "Bored citizens who have turned to gluttony as a means to pass the time."
Views  from rooftops and other outside areas can be breathtaking. Mega City One looms in the background, an architectural metropolis.  The skyline is packed with elaborate skyscrapers and futuristic aircraft ply the skies.  For a few minutes at least, I would take in that scenery marveling at its artistic skill.  I like to take a look around at the aesthetics of the environment and not just blow through the level.  There is a nightclub that had some interesting decor, for example.
I'm playing this on an IMAC 27"  WIn8.1, bootcamp with an old USB Logitech gamepad not updated past WinXP  but it works fine on 8.1.  Like all other games,  I just have to re-import the profile after computer reboots and insure the profile is set to persistent (no there is no option to install the gamepad outside the program fldr).
I'm sorry this game was not more popular, it has a lot of good things in it I'd like to see in other games; you do not have to kill the entire world to win.

Please turn the wheel 6 times to continue reading this review....
If you are a fan of the Sacred series, just avoid this game entirely as it will likely lead to depression.  While the name of the game is Sacred 3, it really is just a basic hack and slash game similar to the Sacred Citadel title except priced at $50.  If you were hoping for an open world full of quests, loot, and character customization look elsewhere as this has none of that.
Should you be able to disregard the name and what Sacred 3 really should have been, you might find some enjoyment here.  However, it is not likely to justify price tag.  I will briefly cover some of the pros/cons of the game.  For reference, I have finished the campaign entirely with the DLC character and have seen all the game really has to offer.
Soundtrack - Though it is not amazing and lacks something as epic as Blind Guardian's concert from Sacred 2, the music is fine and has, at times, a dark mood that should fit the game.
Stage Art - Some of the stages look good and there is some variety in their look.
No Loot - With the exception of weapon spirits, gold, and health/power orbs, you will find no loot.  Weapons and armor are dropped and upgraded on a set schedule as you finish particular stages.  Sadly, weapon spirits are often not particularly useful with the exception of a few.  I honestly can deal with no open world but no loot is a low blow.
Repetitive Gameplay/No Open World - You just enter stages from an overworld map.  Here is what virtually all main stages look like.  Enter -> Fight Group -> Open Gate -> Fight Group -> Dodge Traps/Projectiles -> Fight Group -> Find Key (on enemy or in chest nearby) or turn switch (always 6 times) -> Boss.  Smaller stages will have just 2-3 small groups of enemies or 5 waves in an arena style.  You will probably find yourself fighting the enemies like so Regular Attack -> Bash (when icon appears above enemy) -> Combat Art -> Repeat Until Dead.  If you want to test out the A button on your XBox controller, this will do the trick though.
Little Customization - You can select 2-3 combat arts for each of the two slots.  You can upgrade these using gold at set intervals.  Often you have no choice on what upgrade you get.  In other cases, you have two options.  In my experience, the combat arts I got later in the game were not powerful enough to bother with.  I used the same initial ones throughout the game.  The same applies to the weapons.  The later ones were not powerful enough and thus were not used.  After trying a few other characters, the feel is similar with one direct combat art and another that does AoE damage.  If you are looking to create wonderful builds then look elsewhere.
Length/Replayability - Even when spending some time repeating levels, I beat the campaign in about 8 hours.  If you played straight through on normal difficulty, I would imagine it could be done in 5 or 6 hours.  The DLC appears to add about an hour to the game.  While you can continue to play the game after the final boss, the incentive is just to level up which, as stated, seems fairly pointless as you do not get much to really make your character better.
Technical Glitches - Often I have had the game change resolutions or exit full screen mode for no reason.  I have had it crash several times.  It also has caused a popup saying I lack the memory to continue playing.  I am running the game on a laptop with 8GB of RAM and a 2GB graphics card.  I can run games like Skyrim on max settings and this should not be any more difficult to run.  So it is clearly not optimized and has bugs which may never be fixed.
Dialogue - Honestly, I believe they tried to hard to be funny.  However, some lines and interactions might amuse you.  Overall, it seems forced but it might depend on your sense of humor.
In summary, avoid this game like the plague if you want something like Sacred.  You might consider Torchlight 1/2 or Grim Dawn instead.  You could also wait for Unbended (by the original designers of the Sacred series).  Even Diablo 3 is a much better option given it actually has loot.  If you want a mindless button masher, I'd still wait for a price drop as much cheaper titles (such as Castle Crashers) provide just as much in terms of replayability and honestly Deep Silver/Keen Games does not deserve support for what was clearly a quick money grab using the Sacred name.

If you think that video was a cheap way to get you to jump in your seat, this game will literally start throwing corpses at your screen soon enough. BOOO
The first enemy you try to avoid looks like your average homeless guy. For some reason you must avoid him at all costs, or else risk beaten to death with a stick. That's it. You dont get the chance to fight back, draw his attention or try to apply any strategy other than cowering in the shadows while knee deep in water (which, by the way, woudn't it make a lot of sound when you try to move?)
This is one of the major things to bum me out about this game, you basically play as a victim. I understand the disclaimer that in this game you are not a fighter, but would it not have been better to offer any alternatives to sneaking? (like knocking out enemies, performing certain actions to distract them, having something like a cool gimmic, etc)
After about an hour in, I've decided to stop playing. You know what? My life is way too short to hide from digital druggies, murderers, mutants etc. That first enemy you try to avoid? I would have tried to bash his head in, even if he attacked me in real life. And I'm a 5' something guy!
It's a real shame because the atmosphere along with the soundtrack seems something like out of those hooror movies I used to enjoy with some pop corn. If you look at each scene, you will find an incredible amount of detail but unfortunately it doesn't make up for the gameplay. It feels like the creators never really put themselvs into the main character's place.
Tl;dr
Play amnesia or something else instead; If I would have to choose between the game and a refund, I'd choose the refund. It doesnt keep me interested enough to actually progress through the story (and I will probably never will).

Sunless Sea is a game a rougelike exploration/trading game set in a steampunkish/Lovecraftian underground ocean. It brings solid exploration and trading mechanics familiar to the genre, as well as a pretty innovative combat system.
What sets this game apart, though, is its story, atmosphere, and setting. By turns tantalizingly curious, deeply melancholy, bizarrely hilarious, and hauntingly lonely, it encompasses an entire underground world with its own history and life. You can pay homage to the gods of the sea, or spit in their eye and weather the consequences. You can settle disputes between warring factions of an aristocracy of gueinea pigs and a technocracy of rats. You can trade honey that transports you to dreams, discover what lurks on the far side of the mirror, and, of course, explore the reaches of an endless, sunless sea.
The writing is a cut above anything else I have encountered. Delivered in medium length 'storylets,' the text doesn't simply tell a story, it brings to life a warped reflection of Victorian exploration. Failbetter has managed to escape the trap of a wall of text that feels like a chore to read without the slightest hint of dumbing it down for the sake of expediency. The language is rich, deep, and expansive, and delivered in such a way that I'm always left wanting just another story in the next port. And the writing is so good that I am always tempted to make rash decision just to find out what horrible end Failbetter has devised for my captain.
Oh, and the music is awesome. It sets the mood perfectly. I'm not much of music guy, but I really like what they've done here.
I cannot recommend this game enough. For anyone interested in exploring a new, twistedly vibrant world devised by some truly brilliant minds, pick this up, turn the lights down, and let yourself be carried away to the world of the Sunless Sea.

When it comes to big time franchises, few can hold a candle to Madden. Likened to a religion and a holiday by its faithful fans, the latest installment of the football franchise is one of the most eagerly awaited titles every year. However, with the rise in attention being paid to the 360, PS3 and Wii versions of the series, which are continually being touted as the future of football, this year's version of Madden on the GameCube was a radical departure. This year, Madden NFL 08 features a much larger emphasis on casual football fans than the hardcore player. While it doesn't completely abandon its roots entirely, it doesn't significantly build on them either, which makes this year's title somewhat disappointing for gamers on older generation systems.
Now, Madden has been known for placing a major focus upon either offense or defense with each release, typically capturing some element or aspect of the cover athlete's game. This year is a slight departure from that formula; while there is a major emphasis on defensive adjustments this year, the largest addition that's been made to this year's game is the inclusion of the read and react system. An evolution from the playmaker feature of the past, the read and react system evaluates the skills and abilities of every player on a team and assigns specific traits and icons to them based on their known performance. Mobile quarterbacks might be designated as Scramblers, while defenders that are known for jacking up players with crushing tackles are known as Heavy Hitters. As a result, players can hit a button during a down to see if the play you selected will result in any mismatches in an offensive or defensive scheme that you can exploit, or if you need to quickly shift to compensate and counter your opponent's plans.
Weapons are a good idea, but weakly implemented.
As a result, you'll find a potential chess match breaking out between yourself and an opponent (or the computer at higher difficulty levels) at the line of scrimmage, as you find yourself pulling out audibles, line shifts and other adjustments to tailor that down to develop the way you want it to go. However, there are two big issues that wind up almost invalidating the usefulness of the read and react system. The first is weapons are much more ambiguous on the GameCube than the Wii version of the game. For instance, if I see a Power Back lined up in the backfield, I want to make sure that my Heavy Hitter linebacker is assigned to negate his yardage and stuff him at the line. While figuring out these kinds of match-ups is relatively easy to do, it's particularly impossible to know what you should do against a starred weapon. The catchall icon for a character that has "skills and attributes to fit into more than just one Weapon category," according to the game, these players are the best in the NFL.
However, it becomes rather ridiculous to expect that you'll find another star player that will completely negate the abilities of that player, or even affect him in the way that other matchups play out. For instance, Peyton Manning is listed as a Star "Franchise Quarterback," with that classification's description mentioning that these kinds of QBs are always under pressure to perform. What do I need to do, have a safety hold a sign in the backfield distracting him about how much he choked until last year to hamper his accuracy or throwing strength? (Obviously, I'm kidding, but you realize how much this read and adjust system is complicated by such vagueness.)

Just Cause 2 is honestly a fantastic game. You are put in the shoes of agent Rico Rodriguez as he is sent to the South East Asian archipelago of Panau to hunt down his old mentor and do whatever it takes to remove dictator Pandak Panay. A Just Cause indeed. If the other reviews on this page are any indication then it is obvious this game is good enough to define its genre. In fact, if you still haven't got it there is literally no better time than now. Since Just Cause 3 has come out recently, you may question why get this game instead? Although Just Cause 3 is a natural progression from Just Cause 2 and has better visuals and gameplay, this game is still brilliant in it's own right.
Gameplay:
This game's gameplay is innovative, exciting and somehow doesn't get old. It can only really be described as a mashup of Michael Bay, James Bond and a monster truck rally. The goal of the game is to destroy chaos objects and cause chaos in Panau, and the game gives you the tools to do this. The game's patented grapple hook is Rico's signature weapon and can be used to 'creatively' kill the countless grunts of the Panauan military as well as tearing down various governmental assets. Rico also has access to a variety of weapons which can all be acquired via the Black Market and can be upgraded to cause even more mayhem. There are well over 300 settlements in Panau to 'liberate' of Panay's military assets and each is filled to the brim with weapon parts and vehicle parts to upgrade your black market items. Despite there being so much to do, the tools given to Rico, including over 100 seperate vehicles, don't make this momentous task boring. And even after all that, there are still races which can be completed in various vehicles and skydives which can be of varying difficulty.
Despite this gameplay can eventually get repetitive (you find that after 150 hours and getting 99.4% completion) because the things you blow up don't come back, unlike petrol stations in Just Cause 3. Speaking of which there is a glitch in the game which prevents you from getting 100%, so don't waste your time trying to get that without a relevant mod. The AI in this game can be variable, sometimes being very good and sometimes involving an enemy pilot flying into the side of the Berawan Besar mountains.
Overall the gameplay in this game is 9 out of 10
Open World
The world of Panau is vast, with 400 square kilometers to explore, Panau is vibrant. The world is varied as well with mountains, jungles, deserts and the sweeping metropolis of Panau City. Honestly the open world in itself is enough to sell this game providing Rico plenty of room to cause mayhem. The world also features many distinct landmarks such as Panau Falls Casino, Three Kings Hotel, Panau International Airport and the infamous Mile High Club. This ultimately creates the best open world in the Just Cause series and possibly one of the best in gaming ever. The game even provides fast travel to make travelling around the vast world that bit more convenient. The destructiblity of this world is pretty astounding when you consider the amount of possible versions of Panau there could be.
The only cons are that some civilian settlements and military bases can seem a bit copy-pasteish at times and large amounts of Panau actually is covered in jungle which you can't really do much in, these things I've found aren't actually an issue in Just Cause 3.
Overall another 9 out of 10
Performance
Just Cause 2 should have no issue running on any modern gaming computer, or even just a normal computer. It is well optimised with few frame drops (on a worthy computer) and the graphics are highly customisable to allow performance tweaks. Yes, lag is possible, particularly on more casual computers but load times are normally quick, unlike its successor.
Overall an 8 out of 10
Graphics
While not meeting the standard of Just Cause 3, the graphics in this game are superb, with vast draw distances and pretty graphics. Generally blurred textures aren't super common (mostly found on rockfaces) and the water looks fantastic. This game lends itself to fantastic views across Panau and I don't have much to criticise about the game's graphics.
The only con I can think of is that the trees in Panau can look a bit papery, perhaps because the tree leaves are actually 2D sprites that change direction to face you (Just Cause 3 has this same issue)
Overall a 7.5 out of 10
OST and sounds
While the OST in this game is nothing special, as there is actually a distinct lack of music in Just Cause 2, the sounds are actually pretty solid. Explosions are satisfying and gun shots echo through the jungles with reverberation. Music is mostly heard during races and when Rico has heat, but although fits the mood very well, isn't anything memorable
Overall a 3 out of 10 for music, but that increases to 6 when sounds are considered
Story
Your typical Just Cause story. Dictator rules island nation with iron fist and has plans of world domination. 'Department of Infrastructure Improvement' Rico Rodriguez comes along, causes chaos, dictator shoots nuke but plan backfires. The story isn't bad, but it isn't good either. Just Cause 3 does have a better story, but again if you're looking for story, avoid this genre altogether. Characters are mostly forgettable with only Tom Sheldon really being super memorable, but the story and faction missions are good. This game knows how to not take itself seriously, so in reality the story doesn't really matter, just don't be disappointed. Cutscenes do have action, but they sometimes have a habit (particularly on slower computers) of having the sound and video go out of sync, leading to painful cutscenes that just don't work.
Overall story gets a 5 out of 10.
Multiplayer
This game itself has no multiplayer aspects, but there is an offical multiplayer mod which is free after buying the game, which is honestly fantastic, and I wish they'd make a multiplayer mod for JC3. Personally I recommend the NerdCubed Fan Server as it is the most popular server found on JC2MM. Speaking of other mods, this game has a great modding community which leads to an even more chaotic game.
Overall this game is fantastic, and I consider it a must buy for anyone who enjoys a bit of chaos, particularly as it is only £10. Yo uwon't be disappointed.
Overall this game is 8.5 out of 10.

I am disappointed in Sunless Sea, in particular after reading the very positive reviews on Steam regarding the game, and even trying Fallen London out based on the suggestions. As I enjoyed Fallen London I had really high expectations.
Unfortunately I just do not think there is an actual game here. There is a lot of great and really funny content and while I enjoyed the stories and the dialogue which I did manage to encounter the majority of the content is locked behind what is actually very poor gameplay.  All the game actually entails is sailing, really, really slowly between ports with the occasional equally boring "sea-combat" thrown in.
At the moment the gameplay feels like it was added an afterthought to "gate" the access to the actual content, the same way Fallen London has a number of actions which regenerate over time. Or it becomes fun a lot later.
I am trying to come up with some constructive advice on how to make this actually fun and the only thing I can come up with is making this more of a horror game, and less rogue-like.
* increasing the difficulty of the fights to make the sea-monsters or pirates scarier to encounter

After using a drone with stealth to investigate a room with uncertain motion results, I found something that saw right through the cloak. Naturally, said drone ate the dust. Then I hear a loud beep and look at the input console, "Drone 1 is being sucked out into space." Well there goes my only gather module and stealth module. Then if that wasn't good enough, the door that was separating 2 other drones from vacuum gives in. Out those two go. So in one boarding exercise, I've lost 3 drones, not secured any more scrap or fuel (of which I'm scarily low on at this point) and lost all my good upgrades.
This game can provide a shock without having to resort to jump scares, and it's horror comes from something other than fear of having jump into your face, it's horror of the unknown, of what you'll find through that door, of whether that next outpost will be the one where the product of all your work will be lost. This game is an absolute masterpiece.
First and foremost of course, the art and design. On this point, the game is flawless. Never before have I seen such an exquisite execution of artistic aesthetic: the animation is lush, detailed, wacky, fun, bouncy and exactly what you'd expect; the music is bubbly and jive-worthy; the sound effects are spot on, and the overall sound design is mastered in a way that makes the game even more immersive (for example, the sounds overpowering the music and making it quieter, which is exactly how the sounds of media from the 30's would sound). One of the lead developers said that their goal when making this game was to "make a game that
like it was made in the 1930's". I feel like they have perfectly achieved that goal.
But none of this would matter if the game wasn't fun, and it certainly is. There are enough weapon and item customisation to stop it from getting boring, every boss has unique mechanics, and because of the excruciating difficulty you are forced to learn them by rote. I can see how that might put some off, but personally I love the challenge and I'm more than happy to play each boss hundreds of times if it means I get to stretch the game out for longer. It's not a long game: I've played just under 5 hours and I'm already ~30% of the way through. But I can scarce blame the developers for that, because of the unbelievably huge amount of work that went into this game.
And that's something that is clear everywhere you look in this game. In every frame of animation, in every note of the soundtrack, you can just tell this game was made with love and care and dedication, something somewhat rare in the videogames industry these days. These people poured 3 years of their lives into this game, and it shows in depth and breadth and height.
Cuphead is an exhibition of artistic mastery and unflinching joy. For £15 (or your regional equivalent), that's far more than worth it

This is the newest installment of the Games Workshop old and almost cult status board game Blood Bowl and if YOU want a TL;DR version I would say: If you like Blood Bowl this is the DEFINITIVE EDITION for digital media. To learn more, keep reading.
The game have a much more robust single player experience in an campaign compared to the competitions of earlier installments. In Chaos Edition you slowly got into better and better leagues and slowly built your team up until you conquered the best of the best. In this installment you can create league play for singleplayer and play that for sure but the main fun for me was the story campaign. It tossed in gimmicks and things that is not part of the normal game and just made it FUN while teaching you the basics of the game so you know what you face online. It was corny, fun and interesting and took a while to get through before you got to the end of it all and I enjoyed it for what it was.
Online is vivid, alive and thriving with a lot of teams spinning in the official endless league and is a good place to try a few teams, crash, burn and climb till you learn the ropes. You can watch cKnoor’s videos and tutorials, read on BBTactics and slowly just try things out here. The best place to play is probably in the private leagues. Joining a league like the Reddit one, Gman etc is where the fun is and the community, gaming and slow build up is part of the fun. It has less and almost NONE of the issues the endless league have and if nuffle is willing some of these leagues will adapt a way to play that make it fun for new and old players alike down the line.
There are changes to the core gameplay in how some things interact, how some skills work, rebalancing costs on a few chars among other things. If you can look past that issue as well as the fact that there is not the boardgame or the board games many races this is THE version to play online. With the way the developers listen to feedback, change things to that feedback and give away free races for owners so far I would say that joining in on the fun is well worth the money invested.
That said, If you are a player that can not STAND RNG making some games flat out unwinnable at times then well… you will only find rage and salt on this pitch. But hey, You get that luck later as it balance out… if nuffle is willing. It is also not a game that is easy to pick up and just play, it's brutal, hard and unforgiving so I STRONGLY advise that you look up how the game is played before you go too deep into online.

Judge Dredd: Dredd vs Death is like one of those B movies that's really bad and ugly, but intelligent and funny enough that it becomes a real masterpiece and great fun. It was also released back in the era of games like Postal and Carmageddon in a time when being unique was prized, and being crude and over the top wasn't a bad thing, so long as the gameplay was fun.
* Great humour and satire, really tasteless and crude but smart, and funny
* Fast pace, there's always action, or something funny happening
The majority of this games problems come from it's total lack of budget and polishing, presumably due to rushing to meet deadlines. While the problems somewhat add to the appeal, and help make the price great value, they keep this from being a great FPS.
* Probably too short. The price makes up for this, but it can still leave you hanging
* Dated graphics and a lack of settings (FOV, etc) can cause problems
For just £5.59/7.99€/$7.99 this is a very fair buy, albeit for a short playtime of just 4-5 hours. A great multiplayer and tons of characters also lend towards the good replay value. If this is on sale, pick it up. If it isn't, it's probably worth sticking on the wishlist if you have a sense of humour.

Now that I've finally gotten around to finishing the main quest of this game, I feel I have enough information to write a review. It is a phenomenal game.
While the story is nothing to write home about and the controls can feel a bit wonky at times, the gratification that comes from grappling a jeep to the road and causing it to flip into the air or decimating harbors and army bases with a minigun are simply unmatched among games I've played.
This game's main "gimmick" is your grappling hook that spits in the face of physics and basic logic. This 1 inch cord has enough power to hold a car to a helicopter without breaking and defies the concept of momentum, letting you jump off a skyscraper and grapple onto the road below without being harmed. The game also features a respectable arsenal of upgradable weapons and vehicles to terrorize the island nation of Panau with.
There are few negatives that I can come up with for this game, but there are some minor issues:
When you fall from a tall place, you transition into "falling mode" and controls shift accordingly. The distance it takes to transition seems inconsistent and can result in cheap damage.
The DLC seems a bit overdone. I'm not a huge fan of DLC in the first place, and I bought the full version that includes the DLC, but I didn't feel like it added much to the game.
The game is actually incomplete. The developers accidentally left out a few of the collectables, making it impossible to 100% the game ingame, you can still get all the Steam achievements though. I'm honestly puzzled as to why the devs haven't fixed this issue, since it should be a really easy fix.
Lastly, and this may not be a bad thing for some people, Panau is big. Too big. Allow me to elaborate, I have played this game for 131 hours and I'm only about 75% of the way done. The conquering of towns and military bases is a blast at first and retains its enjoyability well, but I don't see myself 100%ing the game any time soon.
Despite these complaints, I've gotten 131 hours of solid enjoyment out of this title and will definitely be playing it more. If this game looks like fun to you and you won't be too bothered by its problems, then this is easily worth its asking price.

Just Cause 2 is an amazing, open-world sandbox-esque game with breathtaking visuals and massive explosions to boot. This game takes a lot of what makes a game like Grand Theft Auto good, adds a grappling hook, and puts in much more destruction into the world. If for some reason you're getting this game instead of Just Cause 3, then you're still going to have an awesome time.
Please note that I have played this game for quite a long time before I owned it on Steam so my hours do not match up with my actual game time.
You are Rico Rodriguez, your typical badass gun with a gun (and a grappling hook). Set after the events of the first game, you're essentially trying to overthrow this evil dictator and confront your old mentor. I'll state right off the bat, that the first game sucks, and the story in the first and second games sucks as well. Where the GTA series has had a pretty good storyline, Just Cause didn't get that bit right yet. You are likely not going to be very interested in the story if at all, and it's fairly tedious to do the missions for reasons I'll explain later on. On the off chance you do like the story, there are some interesting missions and places you have to go, which are honestly pretty fun. But just know, the story isn't the selling point of this game.
What you will most likely play Just Cause 2 for, is the insanely explosive combat, and the highly immersive, open world that it provides. From the open seas, to densely populated towns. From the cold mountain peaks, to the warm valleys below; this game has it all. I've played countless times just simply free-roaming and admiring the beauty of every environment. But what's a beautiful environment without some kick♥♥♥♥♥explosions am I right?
Just Cause 2 features a variety of weapons and vehicles at your disposal. Simply order a drop from your handy black market supplier, or raid a base and steal all their weapons and grab your favourite car from anyone you see. The choice is yours. Combine all this with your multi-use grappling hook, and you can quickly imagine all the possibilities in game. Don't like a soldier looking at you funny? Hook him to your car and take him for a ride. Need a lift? Hook your car to an airplane before it takes off. Two guys, one gun? Hook them together and let the magic happen itself. :^)
My only concern with the weapon/vehicle system was that it felt a bit difficult to acquire the exact weapon/vehicle you wanted. The drop system was very expensive and income was very slow. For a sandbox style game, it felt very anti-sandbox to have those limits in the game.
. But don't let that deter you, there is a lot of raw fun to be had in this game, and you'll spend hours in it just trying out everything your mind can imagine.
Most people play the multiplayer mode, which is a free DLC to obtain on Steam. If you thought single-player was fun, you're definitely going to love multiplayer. It's everything in single-player multiplied by the number of players in the game.
For a game released in 2010, Just Cause 2 is
. The graphics hold up extremely well and even surpass a lot of games that are out right now. It's very well optimized and will run on almost anything that isn't over 2 years old at this point. Explosions are stunning, while skydiving gives you the sense of speed that it should as you plummet into the earth/sea at super high speeds, only to pull your parachute at the last second and admire the spot where you would have died instead.
Music is okay, sound effects are pretty great, voice-overs suck. Much of the audio isn't really the selling point of Just Cause 2. I feel like there could have been more here, but at least the sound-effects carry it most of the time. You'll be entertained quite a bit, but you may notice that there is definite room for improvement.
Just Cause 2 is one of the best games of its time, and is still insanely fun even now. Its graphics hold up extremely well and has one of the largest game maps in existence. Whenever you tire of playing alone, the free multiplayer dlc will add countless hours of fun once again, and will lead to some of the best moments in gaming. Despite a few sub-par aspects of the game (story, voice-acting, etc), this is a game you will have endless hours of fun in, and you'll barely remember anything negative about the game.
If you like a really good open-world game with super-fun gameplay, look no further than Just Cause 2.
9/10 - Must buy.

Wow, this game really blew my expectations out of the water. Coming into this, I expected it to be a somewhat enjoyable platformer, but the $30 dollar price tag for an Indie game kinda had me suspicious. After "100%-ing" the game (collecting all the time pieces and relics), I can fully say that this game was MORE than worth the price tag. The music is beautifully composed (my favorites being from the boss fights), the characters are extremely lovable and memorable, each act and each chapter are all unique (and god forbid, ACTUALLY fun), and it's blooming with creativity. I loved going along with the Conductor's batshit insane movies, I loved the legitamately creepy atmosphere of Queen Vanessa's Manor, I loved zipping around Alpine Skyline, each second of this game was magnificent and enjoyable at the same time. And though it isn't perfect at times (I was kinda disappointed about the ending), you can definetly tell all the hard work and love that the creators over at Gears for Breakfast put into this masterpiece. Yooka-Laylee tried to rejuvenate the feeling of old platformer collect-a-thons by retreading old ground, while A Hat in Time captured that essense by creating something entirely new and refreshing.
And though I know A Hat in Time won't be winning any big-time awards soons (being released incredibly near games like Mario Odyssey and Cuphead), it is one of the best Indie platformers, and one of the best Indie games I have ever played.

The "story" was very emotional for me.  Enough questions are left unanswered to allow the player to come to his/her own conclusion, which can be tough to do but pays off well here.
The controls are simple and balanced.  The game doesn't find its natch by sending volleys of flashy attacks and hordes of repetitive enemies at you like some plat-formers. You do what you can to survive, but you are clearly not in control of your surroundings, and you feel as though your character truly doesn't belong in this place.
The game also does not use an "awesome sound track!" to sell itself.  The game is quiet and eery -- dive into Limbo and see what feelings arise.

There are no words to describe this masterpiece. Is it fun: Yes, especially when you play multiplayer.
This is one of those works of art where it's fun as hell to play with a friend or two, but you will always be asking yourself: What the ♥♥♥♥ even is this game?

Let me sum this game up...
The first two or three hours made me insane, had to restart a couple of times due to "unforeseen consequences" as radiation leaking pipes blocking the way, monster bees crawling through vents appearing in rooms you thought they were safe, ships making strange noises and suddenly breaking apart room by room, failing air vents or simply because i had no motion scanner and was rushing into a room without preparation and caution getting my drones slaughtered one by one resulting in facing the inevitable.
But now I reached a point where I explored a dozen ships, some of them quite huge (30+ doors) and still learning tons of things. And it is awesome!
You really get used to the basic commands (especially when you are already in the IT business) and learn to combine them quite fast, though i kinda miss the "shortened" commands as when programming switches for example... "sh run" is short for "show running configuration" and works as the long one... and in this game where time is of the essence (in my job too though ;-) ), it can be kinda frustrating typing "nav" for "navigation", pressing space to complete the command, following a number for the selected drone(s) and a destination; although the latter is really shortened effectively.
This command/GUI of the game also is completely(!) seperated from mouse control, so do not even try to use it - it simply does not work. For me it's kinda fun, reminding me of the good old days, where the keyboard does the job.
Though I could imagine some will frustrate facing immediate death and not being able to start a "LoL-like mouse button♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥quot; to rescue all the drones.
In short: This game has a HUGE learning curve. Or you die. Simple as that.
Also noticable: The basic tutorial teaches basic stuff, necessary stuff you must know while sleeping. It is neither the only stuff you have to know, nor is everything explained in the more detailed "help" register.
It is all basic. There are many drone addons you will find that are not explained, enemies are completely out of the loop regarding explanation (what are they, what can they do, what should you definitely not do when facing them).
Nevertheless, you have choices of course. You can set quite a lot of parameters defining the difficulty (e.g. you can have an easier (not "easy") starting point or directly a punch in your face, basically).
And then there is this tense atmosphere... Although your life is not in direct danger (you have your drones), you kinda evolve into feeling like in "Alien: Isolation" all the time - at the latest when you realize that a closed door between your drones and a known infestated room is in no way an assurance for their safety.
I would say a 9/10. Worth a buy, though I still have a little keyed up feeling regarding the price tag... It's worth 15€ - don't get me wrong.
But looking at its non-Steam-Summersale price tag of 20€ for complete 2D graphics (though they are great and fit here!), whereas other great 3D games sell for less or the same, it made me thing twice before buying it.
Still: It IS on sale now, so get it :P

Duskers is a fascinating twist on the roguelike genre. In Duskers, you explore spaceships instead of dungeons, and you do so by remotely controlling robotic drones.
Pros (as of version 1.03):
• Fascinating concept
• Simplistic graphics
• Gentle introduction to simplistic non-turingcomplete programming
• There is no reaction time involved, just your ability to plan without typos
• The noisy camera view, and the fact that catastrophic failure is nearly always one typo away, definitely helps set the scary tone
• Reasonable installation size for a modern game (around 250 MB)
• High compatibility: Works on Linux, Mac OSX and Windows, and hardware requirements are not high (requires shader support though, so older GMAs are out of question)
• Keeps you busy for dozens of hours, although I fear it might get a bit repetitive
• Game is still being maintained and updated, so new content and bugfixes are to be expected
Cons (as of version 1.03):
• If you get bad framerate, the game will randomly ignore your typed keys, making it for a frustrating game experience
• Game price seems unreasonably high (right now 17€ with discounts)
• Plot fails to engage the player early on
• No Steam trading cards
• No music
TL/DR: Pricey scary roguelike IN SPACE. Explore shipwrecks, control robots by typing commands. Works on any computer that can run Steam.

It's a real shame because the atmosphere along with the soundtrack seems something like out of those hooror movies I used to enjoy with some pop corn. If you look at each scene, you will find an incredible amount of detail but unfortunately it doesn't make up for the gameplay. It feels like the creators never really put themselvs into the main character's place.

Do you love to hate yourself for buying video games? Then Blood Bowl may just be for you.
Blood Bowl is a game that was originally produced by Games Workshop in the 80's and uses a six-sided die for just about everything that is available in the game. This method for accomplishing tasks, such as throwing blocks, passing, catching, etc. has been transferred to the digital version of Blood Bowl and is fairly straight-forward about the chances you have of completing said action.
While that might not sound too bad for anybody who has never played a dice game before, those who have can tell you that you must be prepared to roll poorly in every game you play. There are games that I have personally played where it feels like a 3+ on a six sided die feels impossible after you've failed to pick the ball up four times in a row with a free reroll... Such is the way the dice-games go. There are times where your team will be one Go-For-It away from a touchdown, and you'll roll a 1, get an armor break, roll max on his injury then die, then you will expend your apothecary for the match in order to re-roll his injory roll because he's a level 3 runner and he's worth keeping. Then you'll roll another double 6 on his injury roll and he'll die anyway.
Does the game sound fun yet? Probably not.
Funny? Probably.
The game has cool and interesting mechanics to it, and all races and players can get skills when they level up, improving their value so that they contribute more to the team. As the members of your team level up, you will figure out how they work well together, and you will learn how to make niches for certain teams that will carry your team to victory. Unfortunately this is a double-edge sword, as this can sometimes create a dependence on certain players, and if they're down or injured it becomes more difficult to function without them. This becomes especially hard for you, the gamer, when you go up against a team that is meant to kill things. When you're sitting in your chair at the beginning of turn 4 of the first half and you're looking at a screen with two players dead, two permenantly injured, and two KO'd you'll be wondering why you bought this game-- I know I did.
If there is anything that this game teaches and teaches well, it is Risk Management. In anything that you do with this game, you should balance the importance of the action with the risk that it will fail, and then prioritize your actions so that you can get as much done in a turn as possible.
It probably sounds like hate this game-- That is not true. I've had a lot of fun with this game, though I've come to a conclusion based on my own experience that it's more fun to play with people you can chat with... Which will not be too terrribly often, apparently. Out of five games, I find that maybe one of those people are willing to chat about anything, really.
I recommend this game with the thought that if you do purchase this game, get it on sale, as you will undoubtedly feel at some points that it is not worth full price. Along with that, you should play with the idea that literally anybody on your team can die at the drop of the hat. Additionally, you should also try to play this game with people that you know, who you can talk to, that you're okay with yelling at/getting yelled at... because it will happen. My god, it will happen.

Dredd vs Death is a short, dystopian fps where you go through the levels helping the citizens of mega city one until inevitablly you are sent somewhere else to help people and fight punks, cultists and undead until you eventually learn that 4 boss characters have escaped from prison and then you help the people where the boss characters went and beat the bosses, until you beat the final one, Death.
The fps gameplay is mostly standard, you get to have 2 weapons maximum and you have to keep the pistol that all judges use. The judge pistol has several ammunition options such as explosive. flammble. and ricocheting options, but I found that they werent particularly useful or even detrimental; lighting people on fire didnt seem to do much damage and if they run towards you then you risk being burned. The high explosive mode doesn't have a huge radius for hitting enemies and most of the time its not worth the time required to change ammo from the normal ammunition. Additionally, on some levels you don’t get much of a refill on the judge pistol and usually have to rely on using an alternate weapon and these alternate pistol modes use your limited ammo faster. There is also some unneeded fluff such as  a reputation system where reputation increases when you arrest people and help citizens not get killed and decreases when you attack friendly targets and people who have already surrendered to be arrested; but this only matters for ratings unless you have the lowest reputation by killing friendlies, then the game will cause a mission failure. At some times there were bugs such as me sniping off some enemies that were set to be killed by a script and that caused a mission failure. Something that can get annoying at times is that its not clear where your next objective is, but the gameplay is fairly passable fps gameplay once you get past the bugs.
The music in the game wasn't particularly memorable to me, but the dystopian setting and various advertisements for dubious fictional future products added to the atmosphere of the game. Given the short length and dated graphics in this game, I wouldn’t go out of my way to pick this up, but it was in a bundle and I got my copy from trading so I figured why not. Unless you really love the Dredd universe no matter the implementation, there are better games for your money.

BioShock is a first-person shooter with role-playing game customization and stealth elements, and is similar to System Shock 2. The player takes the role of Jack, who aims to fight his way through Rapture using weapons and plasmids (genetic alterations) in order to complete objectives. At times, the player may opt to use stealth tactics to avoid detection by security cameras and automated turrets. While exploring Rapture, the player collects money which can be used at various vending machines to gain ammunition, health, and additional equipment. The player also comes across spare parts that can be used at "U-Invent" machines to create new weapons or usable items. Cameras, turrets, safes, door locks, and vending machines can all be hacked to the player's advantage, providing benefits such as attacking the player's foes, revealing their contents to the player, allowing entry to locked areas, or allowing the player to purchase items at a discount. Hacking requires the player to complete a mini-game similar to Pipe Mania in a limited amount of time. The player is given a "research camera" early in the game, allowing Jack to take photographs of enemies to help analyze them, with better quality photographs providing more beneficial analysis. After performing enough analysis of an enemy, the player is granted increased damage, gene tonics, and other bonuses when facing that type of enemy in future battles. Glass-walled "Vita-Chambers" can also be found throughout the game, which the player does not use directly. Instead, should Jack die, his body is reconstituted at the nearest one, retaining all of his possessions, but only a portion of his full health. In a patch for the game, the player has the option to disable the use of these Vita-Chambers, such that if Jack dies, the player will need to restart from a saved game.
The player can collect and assign a number of plasmids and gene tonics which grant Jack the ability to unleash special attacks or confer passive benefits such as improved health or hacking skills. "Active" plasmids—those that are triggered by the player such as most offensive plasmids— require serum (known as EVE) to be used in a manner similar to magic points; EVE can be replenished via syringes. These plasmids also alter the player's appearance to reflect "sacrificing one's humanity". "Tonics" are passive plasmids and require no EVE to gain their benefit; the player can only equip a limited number of plasmids and tonics at any time. Tonics offer a variety of passive benefits. These include an increase in Jack's strength, more efficient use of EVE, resistance to damage or facilitation of hacking machines. The game encourages creative combinations of plasmids, weapons, and the use of the environment.
Plasmids can be collected at certain specific points around the city throughout the storyline, but can also purchased by the player at "Gatherer's Gardens" using the ADAM mutagen from Little Sisters. In order to collect the ADAM, the player must first defeat the "Big Daddy"—genetically enhanced humans grafted to an armored diving suit—that accompanies and guards each Little Sister. After this, the player is faced with a moral dilemma: either to kill the Little Sister to harvest a great deal of ADAM, or to save the Little Sister and gain a smaller amount (though for every three Sisters spared, a gift of a large amount of ADAM is given to the player).

I've seen a lot of funny reviews for this game, but in breaking with that style (which happens to be the style of some of the less serious parts of the game) I wish to express unobfuscated delight in most everything about Sunless Sea.
Sunless Sea is a very different game than most. The gameplay consists of two distinct phases - sailing and being at port. When sailing (apart from random events) the game is a top-down exploration game. You move from port to port expending fuel and supplies, exploring and facing sea monsters. In port the game is entirely text based - with decisions being made through multiple dialogue choices. This may seem a strange design decision, but the writing is very well done and the text paints a vibrant setting of the world that might otherwise be lost.
- Brilliant writing (evokes everything from terror to humor expertly)
- Unique and well-developed world
- Sense of constant dread in the form of resource attrition and threats of the zee
- Replayability from multiple options and outcomes of quests
- A stat system with both a % chance to complete challenges, and ship combat performance based on your stats
- Real consequences to actions - your decisions (or lack thereof) may come back to please/haunt you later
- A friendly development team that delivers on promises and releases content regularly
- Unlike most sailing games, standard trading of goods from city to city is not very profitable (at this point in development)
- Fairly linear progression of ship upgrades - Engine 1 is flat out better than engine 2 (once again, this may change later in development)
- A very long grind to get the best ship (after 40 hours of play and 4 captains I have yet to make half the money I need for the best ship, let alone the best guns, engines, etc.)
This game is well worth 20 dollars and is in no way a risk to purchase in early access, as the developers are delivering on content consistently and in a very calculated manner. I have had a great deal of fun with this game and am not anywhere near done playing it. However, if you are still on the fence about purchasing the game I would strongly advise you to check out Fallen London. It is a browser-based game by the same developers, with the same writing style and challenge style that you will see in Sunless Sea. It is entirely free, and is a great way to see if you will like the way the port portion of Sunless Sea will play.
Good luck, and happy zailing!

I've sunk way too many hours into this game (and way too many ships). I bought it a month or so ago when it had much less content and was much easier and I couldn't put it down. I would prattle on to my friends about Compulsion (the ridiculous engine that eats fuel and makes you speed across the zee), the rejected marriage proposal I made to the Deviless (she thought I was joking! I gave her my soul, even!), the Pull of Nuncio, the Principles or Coral, the best way to get Searing Enigmas, the mysteries of Station III, the riddle of Visage, the frustration of dealing with the Khanate...
I would stay up late reading excerpts of the amazing prose to my boyfriend and both of us were absolutely rapt with attention and immersion into the world of Fallen London. Watching the stories connect with each other and the gating system of content (Something Awaits You means you must spend some time at zee before unlocking more stories or events) keeping me on the edge of my seat...
This game has consumed my life and my attention. I love the concept and mechanics offered by using information as inventory items. I love opening the game to see the "New Stories Available!" button lit up and being excited for more of the amazing artwork and prose being available.
In the past while, the game has been being balanced as it prepares for release. It's made the game MUCH harder. Things I took for granted in the past: "I can take out this 210-point-hull with torpedos and crazy weapons with my 75-hull one-gun starter ship, no problem!" or "a risky challenge? ah, whatever, it's just crew/hull/terror/supplies/fuel!" or "my engines only explode SOME of the time..." or "psch, curses? whaaaatever" are now HOLY CRAP BAD. Needless to say, I've restarted the game a few times lately as the reality of the harshness of the zee has dawned on me.
Basically, if you have an appreciation for story, this game is (name an addictive substance). If you're like me, you'll lose yourself in it and you'll love every minute of it and you'll chortle whenever someone talks about wells and you'll wake up in the morning, look at the sun, and have a voice in the back of your head saying "REJECT THE DAWN MACHINE."
If you're like me, you'll love it so much you'll want to create a d20 campaign based on the universe, you'll want to get a tattoo of a letter of the Correspondance (Don't do this. Seriously. Bad things will happen.). You'll have dreams about the Sundered Sea (the wicket calls), of finally completing the Neathbow or of what lies north. You'll spend time explaining the impossible colours of the Neath as you use words like gant and viric in daily conversation. You'll talk about Maybe's Daughter or the Brisk Campaigner or the Haunted Doctor or even Phoebe and speak of the conversations you've had with each of them over dinner, because you know what brought them to zee and you want to help them even if it means losing them in the process.
So, yes, highly recommended. Lose yourself in this game. The world is amazing. I've never been so proud to have spent so much time with a game.

EDIT:
Well, it's been a few years and the game and expansion have been out for a while. I still find myself coming back, there's something slow and contemplative about this game that you just don't find elsewhere.
The game has had a few balance passes. Outright broken stuff has been removed (boo, I made a lot of Echoes farming sunlight!) but more variety has been added to the starting game and Zubmariner did a really great job fleshing out the mid and late game with way more stuff to do and explore.
Do I still recommend it? Yes! Wholeheartedly!
Do I have a pro tip? Yes. TURN PERMADEATH OFF. The greatest flaw of the game is they want you to treat it like a roguelike, but that means reading the same story over and over and over. Gets boring after a while.
Just turn off hardcore mode, save and load to your hearts content and allow yourself to breath in the atmosphere of the UnderZea.

Short and sweet, but I like that about this game.  Limbo takes platforming into a dark, depressing and desperate world and does not lighten up one bit.
The "story" was very emotional for me.  Enough questions are left unanswered to allow the player to come to his/her own conclusion, which can be tough to do but pays off well here.
The controls are simple and balanced.  The game doesn't find its natch by sending volleys of flashy attacks and hordes of repetitive enemies at you like some plat-formers.  Instead, each encounter feels like a dream.  You do what you can to survive, but you are clearly not in control of your surroundings, and you feel as though your character truly doesn't belong in this place.
The game also does not use an "awesome sound track!" to sell itself.  The game is quiet and eery -- dive into Limbo and see what feelings arise.
Best bought on sale.

You know those guys who are super artsy and everything they do has to be cutting-edge and nobody else understands what they're doing? That's Limbo. It's artistic, yes. Limbo has a unique graphical approach that sets it apart. The story is non-existent, though it seems like it's trying to tell one. It feels like this game is trying to say something, but you can't understand it, so it ends up being open to interpretation.
My main problem is the gameplay itself. The gamplay itself ended up not being a lot of fun. The character moves fairly sluggishly, and it becomes unclear how to clear certain puzzles. The final puzzle threw me for a loop until I realized that there was a switch, not a sign up there. I suppose that's a function of the graphics style. Some puzzles end up being more frustrating than fun. There are redeeming qualities. Some of the puzzles are somewhat interesting, and certain parts of the game have an interesting feel to them. The game also has a certain atmosphere that makes sense in its context.
Limbo is an artsy game that's trying to say something, but without a coherent point. The gameplay is not fun enough to redeem it either, and I have a hard time recommending a game if I'm not having fun while playing it. I was left at the end looking at the screen asking "what?"

I purchased the game because I loved the franchise since I was young. I have grown up and the game still retains all it's value. Proving itself to be great to all ages, holding it's great status since I was a child to almost an adult.
This game is very charming and has a lot of lovable characteristics such as the calming music, sound affects and the design. The game art is very nice and pleasing to look at but is also very interesting, I love the way everything is drawn here it's very unique.
The gameplay feautures a lot of puzzle solving but not in the frustrating way but rather an intrigueing way. It's not the average 'Puzzle game' but rather, the island has it's own mysteries and you solve them yourself with the puzzles using the logical thoughts. All whilst keeping your villagers alive and healthy and trying to gain more tech points, that purchase you technological advancements.
I love every aspect about this game but sometimes, no matter how intelligent you are, you will have to search google. Sometimes you can be correct, however you have the wrong amont of villagers to solve the puzzle.
There are multiple menu options to select audio enhancements, speed of the game and whether you would like to pause it when you are away.
To other players; You can cheat by changing the time on your laptop, it's very simple. Be careful with this as you could starve your villagers. Use the cheat intelligently.
If the colour glitch happens when you exit the game, it's a very simple fix. Select menu, select fullscreen. Select to exit fullscreen and then enter and you'll fix the colour. Very easy.
To pause, click the spacebar. Extremely simple.
It may be a little difficult to get into at the begining because the format is so unique to this game but it is something you will get into after at least five minutes and you will fall in love. It should be more kwown, I'd love for them to continue with the franchise. I think that could be more possible if more people discovered it. I was fortunate to have grown up with it as a child. I love it. I highly recommend this game. ♡

LOAD OF S.H.I.T! THIS IS NOT SACRED GAME ANY MORE.
...I'm really disappointed in this game.
A few months ago, I pre-ordered X Rebirth on steam, and received a console-recycled, bug-ridden, unplayble mess. I promised myself that I would never buy a game again without waiting for reviews.
But I was fooled again, blinded by the pre-order bonuses of Sacred 3, and the fond memories I had of S1 & S2.
S3 is pretty, but that's it. The controls are clearly made for a console. On PC, you move your character with WASD, and you have only 4 attacks/skills (2 on mouse, keys 1 and 2). You evade with space, but have no control on it's direction. Lot's of destructible elements, but you'll often have to strike 3 times before one of your swings actually hit what's right in front of you. All of that make for clumsy control of your character on PC.
Don't expect much of character personnalisation, either. There is no cosmetic or gender choices to make, and only 8 skills per class.
There's also a ever-present comedic routine, fun for the first 10 minutes, but it gets old very fast.
But the one thing I can't forgive, is that there's no loot. Sacred 3 is a Hack&Slash without loot.
